title: Slack is a property of the hand-off, not the flight
description:
Building a cascade-containment agent where the graph decides and the model only talks.

The thing that kept bothering me

When a flight is delayed, the obvious mental model is that the flight has a problem. Weather at the airport, a technical issue, a late passenger.

But that's mostly not where delay comes from. Eurocontrol's CODA Digest measured that 44.6% of European delay minutes in Q2 2023 were knock-on — reactionary delay, not primary. In the US, the DOT's Air Travel Consumer Report for September 2025 lists late-arriving aircraft as the single largest cause.

Knock-on delay isn't a new problem happening. It's an old problem arriving.

The reason is structural: an airline flies the same aircraft on four to six legs a day, and the same crew across a subset of those legs. Flight two is waiting on flight one. The dependency is real, it's physical, and it's a graph.

What made this click for me was the Indian regulator's language after IndiGo's December 2025 collapse — 2,507 cancellations, 1,852 delays, more than three lakh passengers stranded over three days, a ₹22.2 crore penalty. The PIB's finding was that the rosters had "maximised crew utilisation", cutting roster buffers and increasing reliance on dead-heading, tail swaps and minimal recovery time.

Maximised utilisation means minimised slack. The schedule was efficient right up until it wasn't.

The modelling decision that made everything else easy

My first instinct was to put a slack property on each flight. That's wrong, and seeing why is the whole project.

Slack doesn't belong to a flight. It belongs to the gap between two flights:

slack_min = scheduled_ground_time − minimum_legal_turnaround

A flight isn't fragile. A hand-off is fragile. So the model has two edge types doing all the work:

Edge Meaning Properties
NEXT_LEG same aircraft, immediately following leg min_turn, sched_ground, slack_min
CREW_NEXT same crew, immediately following leg min_rest, sched_ground, slack_min

Once slack lives on the edge, cascade propagation becomes something you can write down in one query. Delay spills from flight a to flight b exactly when it exceeds the buffer between them:

MATCH (a:Flight)-[e:NEXT_LEG|CREW_NEXT]->(b:Flight)
WHERE a.status = 'SCHEDULED' AND b.status = 'SCHEDULED'
  AND (a.delay_min - e.slack_min) > b.delay_min
WITH b, max(a.delay_min - e.slack_min) AS new_delay
SET b.delay_min = new_delay,
    b.proj_dep  = b.sched_dep + new_delay,
    b.proj_arr  = b.sched_arr + new_delay
RETURN count(b) AS changed

Run it until it returns changed = 0. That's Bellman-Ford relaxation to a fixpoint — in the database, not in application code.

The max() is doing something subtle and necessary. A flight has two inbound dependencies: its aircraft and its crew. It takes the worse of them, because it waits for both. One aggregation, and that rule is expressed exactly once.

Why "why is this flight late?" is the real feature

Here's the query I'd show a judge if I only had one:

MATCH p = (root:Flight {id: $root_id})-[:NEXT_LEG|CREW_NEXT*1..8]->(target:Flight {id: $target_id})
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.id]                AS chain,
       [r IN relationships(p) | type(r)]     AS hop_types,
       [r IN relationships(p) | r.slack_min] AS slack_at_each_hop,
       length(p)                             AS hops
ORDER BY hops ASC
LIMIT 1

It answers "why is this flight late?" with a path: 6E101 was fogbound → handed its aircraft to 6E117 across a turn with 5 minutes of slack → whose crew carried it to 6E131 across 8 minutes of slack.

No model wrote that sentence. It's a traversal. If the explanation is wrong, the graph is wrong, and I can go look at the graph.

This is the part I think is genuinely underrated about graph databases in agent systems. Everyone reaches for them as a retrieval layer — fetch some context, stuff it in a prompt. But a traversal result is an explanation, structurally. You get provenance for free because the answer is literally the path you walked.

Proof by zero rows

The agent can propose actions: cancel a pair of flights, swap in a spare aircraft, swap in reserve crew. Before any of them can be committed, four invariants must hold. Each is a query that must return nothing:

  • INV-1 — no crew's duty window exceeds its limit
  • INV-2 — no turnaround is shorter than the minimum
  • INV-3 — tail continuity: an aircraft's arrival airport equals its next departure airport
  • INV-4 — every flight has a terminal status

I want to dwell on INV-3, because my first design didn't have it.

Cancelling a delayed flight is the obvious containment move. It's also, often, catastrophically wrong — because cancelling a single mid-rotation leg leaves the aircraft in the wrong city for the rest of the day. The aircraft can't teleport. So cancellations have to be done in out-and-back pairs, or paired with an explicit ferry.

I only found this by writing the invariant down and watching plans fail it. That's the argument for expressing safety as absence-of-a-pattern rather than as application logic: absence of a matching path is the proof of safety, and a query that returns zero rows is much harder to fool yourself about than an if statement you forgot to write.

Forking the world before touching it

Every plan is evaluated on a GRAPH.COPY fork:

fork → apply the plan → re-propagate the cascade → check 4 invariants → score → DELETE fork

FalkorDB's GRAPH.COPY clones nodes, relationships, properties, indexes and constraints, while the source stays readable and writable. The fork is deleted in a finally block — always, including when the work inside throws, which is its own test.

One bug worth confessing: relaxation is monotone. It only ever raises a delay. So my first version of the evaluation loop forked, applied a cancellation, re-ran relaxation — and every plan scored identically. Of course it did: cancelling a flight can't reduce a delay that has already propagated downstream. The fork has to reset to the published schedule and re-propagate from the disruption after the actions are applied. Obvious in hindsight; invisible until the scores came back suspiciously flat.

The constraint that shaped the architecture

I gave myself one rule, borrowed from the hackathon's own:

The graph decides. The model talks. A human confirms.

Concretely, in the MCP server, there are nine tools. Eight are read-only. The ninth is commit_plan, and it takes only a decision_id — never a plan body.

That signature is the whole safety argument. The model cannot invent an action, because there is no parameter through which an action could arrive. It can only point at something the graph already verified and recorded. The worst a confused model can do is point at the wrong decision, and even that is caught:

Every Decision is stamped with the graph revision it was verified against. If the live graph has moved since, commit refuses. A plan proven safe against one state of the world is not proven safe against another.

The test I'd keep if I could only keep one 

tests/graph-off.test.ts

It points the product at a dead database and asserts that every path fails. No cache, no default, no degraded mode, no in-memory fallback. It also greps the source for forbidden datastore imports.

If the product still works with the graph removed, the graph was decoration. This test is how I know it isn't.

It's also what let me add MongoDB for user accounts without weakening the claim. Accounts are the app shell; flights, edges, cascades, plans, decisions and receipts are the product. Dropping the Mongo database changes no number the product reports — and packages/graph is forbidden from importing mongoose, enforced by a linter rather than by my good intentions.

What I'd tell myself at the start

Write the oracle first. Before I had a database connection, I wrote a plain-TypeScript checker that validated the generated schedule against the same four invariants the Cypher enforces. It caught three real bugs immediately: a negative crew-rest slack (I'd tightened hand-offs to min_turn when min_rest is the longer requirement), a rotation overrunning the 23:00 day boundary, and over-eager crew chunking. An independent implementation of the same rule is worth more than another test of the same implementation.

Put every query in one file. All the Cypher lives in queries.ts — none inline in a route, a script or a test. It makes the "here are the queries this depends on" section of the README a copy-paste, and it makes the queries reviewable as a set.

Name your relationships. FalkorDB only existence-checks unnamed relationships. MATCH (a)-[e:NEXT_LEG]->(b) where you actually use e behaves correctly; drop the alias and your counts can quietly go wrong.

What this is and isn't

It's a decision-support prototype on synthetic data. Every flight, tail, crew member and passenger count is generated; only airport codes and coordinates are real.

It is explicitly not a replacement for operations solvers. Lufthansa's OPSD is a mature deployed system; INFORMS reported controllers accepted 26% of its suggestions, and around twenty developers spent four years mostly on data preparation. That 26% is a published figure. Why it's 26% is my hypothesis, not a finding — but it's the hypothesis the project is built around: an operations controller is personally accountable for the decision, and a recommendation you can't interrogate is a recommendation you have to take on faith.

So the position isn't "better plans". It's: see the whole chain, explain every suggestion as a path, and test it against hard constraints before anyone acts.

The containment selection is a scored heuristic with declared weights, not a proof of optimality. The invariants only cover what's modelled — bad input data can still produce a plan that passes verification. And duty_limit_min = 780 is a placeholder parameter, not a regulatory figure; reading the actual DGCA FDTL CAR is still on the list.

title: SpacetimeDB vs. Convex vs. Supabase: The Results from My Machine
description:
I recently came across SpacetimeDB, which promises impressive performance according to its docs, and I wanted to see how it would compare in practice.

So I built a small messaging benchmark for SpacetimeDB, Convex, and Supabase and ran all three locally on my Apple M1 Mac with 8 GB of RAM. I tested five workloads, from sending a single 1 KB message to sending 1,000 messages of the same size.

Here’s what I found.

The numbers

All three databases ran locally, without the usual network trip to a remotely hosted database.

Messages Size per message Total payload SpacetimeDB Convex Supabase
1 1 KB 1 KB 18 ms 21 ms 176 ms
10 32 KB 320 KB 69 ms 178 ms 271 ms
50 1 KB 50 KB 31 ms 609 ms 322 ms
100 8 KB 800 KB 132 ms 1,511 ms 1,014 ms
1,000 1 KB ~1 MB 523 ms 13,204 ms 5,717 ms

The biggest gap appears in the last row.

For 1,000 messages, SpacetimeDB took 523 ms, Convex took 13.2 seconds, and Supabase took 5.7 seconds.

That's about 25 times longer for Convex and 11 times longer for Supabase compared with SpacetimeDB in this particular test.

Why such a difference? To understand that, it's worth looking at how these databases work.

How the three databases work

The biggest differences are in how each system processes writes, accesses data, and delivers updates to connected clients.

SpacetimeDB

SpacetimeDB combines a database with server-side application logic. Its tables are kept in memory while the server runs, with data persisted to disk.

Clients can subscribe to queries and receive updates as the underlying data changes. This makes it possible to build applications where the server and connected clients stay in sync without having to build the entire update pipeline yourself.

Keeping data in memory can reduce the work needed to access it. Combined with its application model, this can help explain SpacetimeDB's strong performance in these tests.

Convex

Convex combines a database with server-side functions and reactive queries. Writes run through mutations, and clients can subscribe to queries that update when relevant data changes.

This model makes it convenient to build reactive applications. But the work involved in processing mutations and delivering updates can add up, particularly when many individual writes are involved.

Supabase

Supabase is a backend platform built around PostgreSQL. It provides SQL queries, transactions, bulk inserts, and real-time capabilities alongside the database.

PostgreSQL handles the data operations, while Supabase provides the surrounding APIs and services. How writes are grouped, how queries are executed, and whether additional features are involved can all affect performance.

These systems offer different approaches to building applications with live data. The database engine matters, but so do the operations being performed and how updates reach the client.

The workload matters

The ranking between Convex and Supabase changes depending on what we're doing.

With 10 messages of 32 KB each, Convex takes 178 ms, while Supabase takes 271 ms.

With 50 messages of just 1 KB each, Supabase takes 322 ms, while Convex takes 609 ms.

SpacetimeDB remains fastest in both cases, but Convex and Supabase trade places.

This is a good reminder that performance isn't one fixed number. Message size, the number of writes, how operations are grouped, and the work involved in delivering updates can all influence the result.

A database that performs well for one workload might not have the same advantage for another.

How much can we conclude?

A benchmark is only useful when we understand what it measures.

I ran each workload multiple times on the same machine, with all three databases running locally. This removes the usual remote database network trip, but the results still reflect this particular environment and the operations being measured.

The three systems also have different architectures and application models. This isn't a comparison of database engines in isolation; it's a comparison of how they handle these messaging workloads using their respective approaches.

That doesn't make the results less useful. It just defines what they tell us.

In this setup, SpacetimeDB was consistently fastest across all five workloads. In the largest test, it was about 25 times faster than Convex and about 11 times faster than Supabase.

Those are the measured results, not a guarantee that every application will see the same speedup.

So, which database would I choose?

It depends on the application.

  • SpacetimeDB is worth exploring if you're building an application that needs fast data access and live updates, especially when you want the database and server-side application logic to work together.
  • Convex offers a reactive application model that can make building synchronized, interactive experiences straightforward.
  • Supabase is an appealing choice when you want PostgreSQL, SQL, and a broad set of backend services in one platform.

Performance is one part of the decision. Developer experience, ecosystem, deployment, scaling, data requirements, and the complexity of your application matter too.

But if we're looking strictly at the five messaging workloads in this benchmark, SpacetimeDB wins. No ties, no exceptions.

Try it yourself

I've put the benchmark in my GitHub repository so you can inspect the code and run the tests yourself. If you try it on a different machine, or with different workloads, I'd be interested to see how the results compare.

Because the most useful benchmark isn't just the one that produces an impressive number, but the one that helps us understand what happens when we build a real application.

And in this case, SpacetimeDB definitely got my attention.

title: Muse Spark 1.2 is now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Muse Spark 1.2 from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. It is a coding-focused update to the previous Muse Spark model. While keeping its general capabilities, 1.2 ships with improvements in code generation, complex debugging, codebase understanding, and end-to-end developer workflows.

The model is built for long-horizon work like generating whole repositories, building out large projects end to end, and sustaining iterative loops where it writes, compiles, profiles, and improves code over many rounds.

To use Muse Spark 1.2, set model to meta/muse-spark-1.2 in the AI SDK:

To use Muse Spark in a coding agent, run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Pi, then select meta/muse-spark-1.2 inside the agent.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

title: Share Vercel Container Registry repositories across teams
description:
Vercel Container Registry now lets you share a repository with other Vercel teams to grant read access to its images.

Sharing is read-only and covers the whole repository. Recipients can pull and use every image, but cannot push, delete, or re-share. You can also share a repository with your own team. Each repository can be shared with up to 100 teams.

Share from the project dashboard under Images → repository → Settings → Repository Sharing, or with the Vercel CLI:

# Share a repository with a team vercel vcr permissions my-repository add other-team # List teams with access vercel vcr permissions my-repository ls # Revoke a team's access vercel vcr permissions my-repository rm other-team # Remove all shared access vercel vcr permissions my-repository clear

Shared images can be used in Vercel Sandbox, accepting a team-scoped image reference in Sandbox.create() :

import { Sandbox } from '@vercel/sandbox'; const sandbox = await Sandbox.create({ image: 'other-team/their-project/shared-repository:latest', });

Repository sharing is available on all plans. Update the Vercel CLI to v58.3.0 or later with npm i -g vercel@latest to get started and see the Vercel Container Registry documentation to learn more.

title: TIL: What the User Count Option Really Affects in GBase Database
description:
During a typical installation of GBase Database (GBase 8s), the installer asks you to select an expected user count:

1 - 1–100
2 - 101–500
3 - 501–1000
4 - 1000+

It's tempting to accept the default 1–100 and move on. For a quick test, that may be perfectly reasonable. But this option is worth understanding before you initialize an instance for a larger workload.

What Does the User Count Option Affect?

The expected user count helps the installer choose initial instance configuration parameters appropriate for the anticipated workload.

Depending on the installation script and configuration template, these settings may include resource limits related to concurrent connections and other instance resources.

In other words, you're giving the installer a rough indication of how many users the database is expected to serve. It is a sizing input, not a guarantee that the instance will support exactly that number of concurrent connections.

Important: The selected range should not be treated as a direct connection limit. Actual connection capacity depends on the resulting configuration, available system resources, workload, and other relevant limits.

Which User Count Should You Choose?

A simple rule of thumb can help:

  • Feature validation: The default 1–100 range is generally a reasonable starting point.
  • Development and functional testing: Choose a range that reflects the expected test environment.
  • Concurrency testing: Select a range based on the planned workload, then verify the resulting connection and resource settings.
  • Larger deployments: Review the generated configuration and size the instance according to actual workload requirements rather than relying on the installer choice alone.

For example, if you're only validating SQL syntax or checking whether an application can connect, a small user-count range may be sufficient.

If you're preparing a concurrency test with hundreds of simulated users, accepting the default without checking the resulting configuration could leave the instance poorly suited to the test.

Don't Stop at the Installation Wizard

After the typical installation finishes, inspect the generated instance configuration to understand which values were selected.

Check the relevant resource and connection parameters, and confirm that they match your testing or deployment requirements. The exact parameters to review depend on the configuration produced by your GBase Database installation.

For production environments, also consider memory, CPU, storage performance, connection behavior, and workload characteristics. The user-count selection is only one part of database sizing.

Final Takeaway

The user-count option in the GBase Database (GBase 8s) typical installer is more than a cosmetic question. It helps guide the initial instance configuration based on the expected scale of use.

For quick feature validation, the default may be enough. For concurrency testing or larger deployments, choose the range deliberately and verify the resulting settings.

A useful installation habit: don't just ask what value the wizard wants. Ask what configuration that choice will produce.

Have you ever discovered that an installation default affected your database testing or deployment? Share your experience in the comments.

title: A Forem API test: publish, edit, unpublish (2026-10-18)
description:
This is a short test note about the Forem API v1. It was drafted with AI assistance and checked by a person before it was published.

What this post checks

An article can be created as a draft, edited, published and set back to draft through the API with the author's own key.

A minimal request 

curl -X POST https://dev.to/api/articles \
  -H "api-key: $DEV_API_KEY" \
  -H "accept: application/vnd.forem.api-v1+json" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"article":{"title":"Hello","body_markdown":"Hello","published":false}}'

The post is set back to draft after the test.

This paragraph was added by an edit made through the API.

title: ColdCraft Studio: Personalized Cold Emails, Written Locally for $0
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle*

What I Built

Everyone has received the cold email that opens with "I hope this email finds you well." It goes straight to the trash.
ColdCraft Studio fixes that. Give it a company's website URL and a short description of what you offer, and it writes a cold email that actually references what the company does. No template, no 15 minutes of research per lead, and no cloud AI bill.

Here is what happens when you click Generate:

It scrapes the company's site for taglines, current initiatives, and mission statements.
A local open-weight AI model reads that content.
It drafts a short email built around specific details from the page.
Everything runs on your own laptop.

Who is this for?

Freelancers and indie consultants pitching web development, design, content, or technical services to businesses and colleges, without spending 20 minutes researching every lead.
Sales reps and lead-gen agencies who need hundreds of tailored emails a week without paying $50 a month in token bills.
The Real Problem
Cold email only works when it feels personal, but right now there are two bad options:

What happens

Cloud AI looks like the answer, but running 1,000 detailed web pages through GPT-4o costs roughly $30 to $50 a month. You are also uploading private pitches and prospect lists to someone else's servers.
ColdCraft does the research and drafting in under 5 seconds per lead at $0.00 marginal cost.

Key features

Realistic email client preview. The output does not look like a chatbot. It renders inside a simulated desktop email window, with a proper salutation, body paragraphs, and sign-off.
One-click dispatch. One button opens your default mail app (Outlook, Apple Mail, and others) with the recipient, subject, and body already filled in, using a mailto: link.
CSV export. Save leads, subject lines, and personalized bodies to a spreadsheet for your pipeline.
Code

DeependraGurjar / coldcraft-studio

A local-first, zero-cost B2B cold outreach engine powered by Ollama and open-weight models.

ColdCraft Studio

A local-first B2B cold outreach tool. It reads a prospect's website, finds a relevant talking point, and drafts a personalized cold email using open-weight models running on your own machine through Ollama. No API keys, no per-email cost, and no data leaves your computer.

Table of Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Features
  3. How It Works
  4. Requirements
  5. Installation
  6. Usage
  7. Why Local Inference
  8. Contributing
  9. License

Overview

Effective cold outreach is slow and expensive to do well:

  • Mass templates read as robotic, often land in spam, and convert poorly.
  • Manual prospect research takes 10 to 15 minutes per lead.
  • Cloud AI APIs speed up drafting but add per-request costs and send your pitch and lead data to third-party servers.

ColdCraft Studio automates the research and drafting steps locally. Give it a prospect URL and a short description of your offer, and it produces a ready-to-review email, typically within a few seconds on modern hardware…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

The stack is small and local-first. After the page is scraped, everything runs offline.

URL → Scraper → Studio → Local AI → Email

Prospect URL: You paste in the company's website.
BeautifulSoup scraper: Strips menus, footers, cookie banners, and scripts, keeping only headings and paragraphs.
Streamlit studio: You add your offer, goal, and tone.
Ollama + qwen2.5:3b: Generates the email as strict JSON.
Output: Email preview, mailto: link, and CSV export.

Local AI engine. I used qwen2.5:3b through Ollama, with an option to switch to llama3.2:1b on lighter machines. Qwen 2.5 is the star of the project. Even at 3 billion parameters, its instruction following and JSON formatting are rock solid.

Smart web scraping. The scraper is written in Python with BeautifulSoup. It removes navigation bars, footers, cookie banners, and scripts, and keeps only the high-signal headings and paragraphs. That gives the model something worth writing about.

Deterministic output. I forced Ollama's format="json" and paired it with a strict prompt framework:

Icebreaker, then Concrete Problem, then Value Prop, then Soft CTA

This stops the model from hallucinating or producing one long, unreadable block of text. Every email follows the same proven shape.

Frontend. The interface is built with Streamlit and custom CSS, so it feels like a focused desktop studio instead of a standard AI demo.

Why Open Innovation Matters

This project is a good example of why open-weight models matter for indie developers and micro-businesses.

Unit economics that work. Say you charge a freelancer $15 a month for an outreach tool. If cloud API bills cost you $12 a month per active user, your margin is gone. With qwen2.5:3b running locally, the marginal server cost is $0.00.

Real privacy. Pitches often involve unreleased projects, internal proposals, and private contact lists. With an open model, none of that leaves the user's hard drive.

No moving targets. No rate limits, no surprise pricing changes, and no provider deprecating the model your prompts depend on.

My First User

I showed an early build to a friend who freelances as a web developer. They regularly pitch website modernization to local educational departments and businesses.

They entered their service pitch, plugged in a regional college's website, and generated an email. Their reaction:

"Usually AI writes stuff like 'I hope this email finds you in high spirits.' This actually noticed the recent curriculum update on their homepage and connected it to my web services. It reads like an email I spent 10 minutes writing myself."

They also told me what they want next: a batch upload feature, where they drop in a list of 50 links at night and wake up to 50 drafts.

That is now at the top of my roadmap.

Try It Yourself

bash
ollama pull qwen2.5:3b
git clone https://github.com/DeependraGurjar/coldcraft-studio.git
cd coldcraft-studio
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m streamlit run app.py

Feedback, issues, and pull requests are welcome. If you have ideas for making local outreach tools better, I would love to hear them in the comments.

title: Codex Swapped Its Default Model and Retired GPT-5.5 in 15 Days. Did Your Evals Notice?
description:
• Book: Observability for LLM Applications
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On September 29, a pull request merged into Codex gave GPT-6.1 Sol "the highest catalog priority" (#49318). That line made it the model the bundled catalog hands a Codex session when you don't ask for one.

Nine days later, Codex CLI 0.162.0 changed where a fresh terminal thread gets its default model from. Six days after that, GPT-5.5 left Codex for everyone signed in with ChatGPT.

Three changes in 15 days, and none of them showed up in your repo's diff. If your agent runs on whatever the default is, the thing your evals measure may have moved while your code stood still.

My take: a model you didn't choose is a dependency you didn't pin. Pin it per task, and write it down next to every result.

What changed between September 29 and October 14

Here is the sequence, from OpenAI's own release notes and docs:

Date Change Who it hits
Sep 29 Codex CLI 0.159.1: GPT-6.1 Sol becomes the default in the bundled catalog CLI users who never set a model
Oct 7 0.161.0 lists it again: default in the bundled and Amazon Bedrock catalogs The same, plus Bedrock users
Oct 8 0.162.0: new TUI threads respect the server's model defaults TUI users who launch without a model override
Oct 14 GPT-5.5 retires from Codex for ChatGPT sign-ins, at noon PDT (19:00 UTC) Anyone who picked gpt-5.5 and signs in with ChatGPT

The October 8 change is the quiet one. The release note says Codex will "respect server model and reasoning-summary defaults for new TUI threads while retaining explicit launch overrides." The pull request behind it (#50013) puts it more plainly: "Fresh TUI threads should use the app server's model settings unless the launch explicitly overrides them." The server here is the Codex app server the TUI talks to, a local daemon or a remote one (#50913). The same release stopped appending "(default)" to entries in the TUI model picker (#51235).

The October 14 change hits the opposite group: people who did pin a model. OpenAI's models page says the retirement covers ChatGPT sign-ins only and API-key sessions are not affected. It points Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users to GPT-6.1 Sol, and Free and Go users to GPT-6 Luna in the desktop app, both "when available."

To be fair to OpenAI, none of this was hidden. Every change is in a release note or the changelog, the retirement came with an exact time and a named replacement, and 0.162.0 also moved the model and reasoning effort near the top of task details (#50727). GPT-6.1 Sol may well be the better model for you. OpenAI says it nearly matches GPT-6 Astra at about a fifth of Astra's token price (Unite.AI, The Batch), though those are OpenAI's own numbers. An upgrade still moves your numbers, and your evals should say so.

Who picked the default? A catalog file

Look at what "default" meant in #49318. Nobody on your team chose GPT-6.1 Sol. It got the highest priority in a catalog file that ships inside the CLI, so it won.

Codex isn't unusual here. Claude Code's model docs say the aliases opus, sonnet and haiku "point to the recommended version for your provider and update over time." Same doc: "To pin to a specific version, use the full model name, for example claude-opus-5-5." So claude --model opus is a moving target by design, and claude --model claude-opus-5-5 is a pin.

Moving targets are fine for a chat. You want the newest model when you ask a question at 11pm. They are a problem for anything you measure, compare or promise to a teammate.


A default model can change between two eval runs without a single line of your repo changing.

Your evals measure the model, so they need its name

An agent eval can be a formal suite. More often it is a sentence in a team chat: "Codex is worse at migrations than Claude Code." "That AGENTS.md rewrite made the agent better." "This task took 40 minutes last week and 12 this week."

Each of those is a claim about a model. If the model was a default, you don't know which one it was. Did your prompt get better, or did the catalog move? Did Codex get worse at migrations, or did a fresh thread pick up a different server default than the one you tested last month?

The model is not the only hidden variable either. Reasoning effort changes results, and #50013 treats it like the model: if the launch doesn't set it, a fresh TUI thread takes the server's default. The account matters too: the GPT-5.5 retirement hit ChatGPT sign-ins and left API-key sessions alone, so the same gpt-5.5 setting meant two different things depending on how you logged in.

So the minimum record for any agent result is four fields: the model, the effort, the account type and the commit it ran against. Without them, a before-and-after comparison is two numbers with no explanation attached.

Pin it per task, then write it down

For daily work in Codex, a profile is the cleanest pin. Per the advanced config docs, a profile is a file in ~/.codex/ with top-level keys:

# ~/.codex/pinned.config.toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "medium"

Start it with codex --profile pinned. PR #50013 keeps explicit profile launches on the resolved configuration, so the profile's model holds even for fresh TUI threads.

For anything you compare, put the pin and the record in the same script. codex exec takes -m for the model (models page), and -c sets any config key (the config docs say a value that isn't valid TOML is treated as a string):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run-task.sh "<task>" : one pinned run, one logged row
set -u
task="$1"
model="gpt-6.1-sol"
effort="medium"
account="chatgpt"   # or "apikey": how this run signs in

codex exec -m "$model" \
  --sandbox workspace-write \
  -c model_reasoning_effort="$effort" \
  "$task" > last-run.log
agent=$?
npm test > test.log 2>&1
tests=$?

printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
  "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
  "$model" "$effort" "$account" "$agent" "$tests" >> runs.tsv

By default codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox (non-interactive mode docs), so --sandbox workspace-write is what lets the agent edit the checkout before the tests run. The agent column keeps Codex's own exit status, so a failed agent step shows up in the row instead of hiding behind a test result on untouched code.

Swap npm test for your own check, and set account to match how the machine signs in. Every row in runs.tsv now carries all four fields: which model, effort and account produced which test result on which commit.

Pinning has a cost, and October 14 showed it. Anyone pinned to gpt-5.5 with a ChatGPT sign-in had to edit their config. OpenAI's list of what to update covers "workspace defaults, saved model settings, managed configurations, custom agents, scheduled tasks, and scripts that still select gpt-5.5" (changelog).

That is the good kind of break. You change one line in a diff, rerun your tasks, and compare the new rows against the old ones.

Where Hermes IDE fits

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent's own CLI in a real terminal, Codex and Claude Code included, each task on its own branch and worktree.

The part that matters here: when you start a task with ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux), you pick the agent, model, effort and account for that task, and you can save combinations you use often as presets (README). Several accounts per agent are supported, so the sign-in a task runs under is something you choose when you start it.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: agent, project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, the model and effort chips, and a preview of the command Hermes will run.

After launch, every session shows its own spend: the cost the agent reports, or an estimate from its transcript marked as estimated, with token totals. Since 2.3.4, a Claude Code or Codex session keeps showing its own model and cost even when the conversation mentions another company's model. The bar above each session puts Model in the same place for every agent.


Codex and Claude Code side by side in Hermes 2.3.4, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with status, context use, cost and branch per session in the sidebar.

What it doesn't do: Hermes doesn't write your runs.tsv, and it can't stop a vendor from retiring a model you picked. It makes the choice explicit per task and keeps it visible per session. The record is still yours. Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic or any other agent vendor.

So, which model ran your last eval?

Open the last result you shared with your team, a benchmark, a "this agent is better at X" message, a before-and-after on a prompt change. Can you name the model and effort that produced it?

If not, you were testing a catalog entry. Tell me in the comments whether you pin your agent's model, or whether you'd rather ride the default and take the upgrades as they come.

If this was useful

Writing the model next to every result is the smallest piece of LLM observability. Observability for LLM Applications covers the rest of it: tracing each call, running evals that catch quality regressions when a model changes, and tracking cost per feature in production. If you run several agents, Hermes IDE is free and lets you set the model per task (GitHub).

title: A Dashboard That Updates Itself — No Data Analyst Required
description:
You already know which numbers matter in your business. The problem is that getting them means digging — exporting from the CRM, re-sorting a spreadsheet, asking someone who's busy. So you check the numbers you care about once a quarter, in a panic, right before a decision.

On October 8, Anthropic shipped a beta feature that changes the digging part: Claude Dashboards. You connect a data source, ask a question in plain English, and Claude writes the queries, picks the charts, and builds a dashboard that refreshes as your data changes. It's in beta on paid plans, and the supported connections are the enterprise-grade ones — BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Redshift, ClickHouse, and Salesforce.

Most of the coverage is aimed at data teams and enterprise BI users. Here's the version for a business with no analyst on staff.

The feature that matters most is the smallest one

Every chart in a Claude dashboard shows the query behind it, along with the last refresh time.

That sounds like a technical detail. It's actually the trust mechanism, and it's the reason this is usable by someone who can't read SQL.

Dashboards usually fail for a boring reason: the owner can't tell whether the number on the screen means what they think it means. "Deals this quarter" — does that mean closed-won? Everything in the pipeline? Does it include the two renewals that got logged funny? When you can't answer that, you don't trust the chart, and when you don't trust the chart, you go back to the spreadsheet.

With the query visible, you get two practical options:

  • Sanity-check it yourself. Read the plain-English question the query represents. If Claude counted "deals" as every open opportunity when you meant closed-won, you'll usually see it in the query's shape and refine the ask.
  • Hand it to someone technical for five minutes. A contractor, your IT person, a niece who codes — anyone fluent can scan one query and tell you whether the number is honest. That's a five-minute review, not a BI project.

A dashboard you can verify is a dashboard you'll actually open. That's the whole game.

What to connect first

For most small businesses the answer is simple: your CRM — Salesforce is the one supported connection that isn't a data warehouse. Connect it before anything else.

Here's the honest boundary, though: if your business data lives in QuickBooks, a handful of spreadsheets, and your email, and you don't run a warehouse, this feature isn't for you yet. There's no connector for your stack. Don't buy a Snowflake plan to get a dashboard — that's building a chimney because you liked the smoke. Revisit when either your tools grow native support or your data naturally lands somewhere connectable.

What to actually ask

The gap between "I have a dashboard" and "I use the dashboard" is almost always the questions. Have these ready.

Weekly — movement questions:

  • "Which deals moved stages this week, and which ones have been sitting more than 14 days?"
  • "Show new leads created by source, this week versus last week."
  • "Which accounts haven't been contacted in 30 days?"

These catch problems while they're still cheap — the stalled deal, the lead source that quietly died.

Monthly — pattern questions:

  • "Which lead sources produced closed-won deals this quarter versus last quarter?"
  • "What's our average time from first contact to close, by month, for the last six months?"
  • "Which customers closed 12 months ago and haven't renewed?"

These are the ones nobody asks because assembling the answer takes a day. With a live dashboard, asking takes a minute and the answer stays fresh.

Start with two or three questions, not twenty. The failure mode of self-serve BI is a wall of charts nobody looks at. Three numbers you check every Monday beat thirty you scroll past.

When you've outgrown it

This is a beta feature that regenerates answers from questions. It is not a system of record for your metrics. Move to real BI — or a deliberately built spreadsheet with fixed definitions — when any of these become true:

  • More than two or three people need the same numbers every day. At that point definitions need to be fixed and shared, not re-derived per question.
  • You need permissions. Salespeople shouldn't see each other's pipelines. If access control matters, you've left consumer-tool territory.
  • People start arguing about whose dashboard is right. That's a definitions problem, and it needs one owned source, not a fresh query per conversation.

Until then, a dashboard you can audit by clicking the chart is more than most small businesses have ever had.

One bonus, mostly for the quarterly report

Alongside Dashboards, Anthropic shipped Claude Motion (beta for Team and Enterprise plans): it builds editable animations you can export as MP4. The pragmatic use is the quarterly update — a 30-second animated explanation of where the numbers moved, made from the same data, without touching a video editor or a design tool. If you send stakeholders a quarterly recap nobody reads, a short animation of the same facts is worth testing once.

The Monday habit

Connect the CRM, build the three weekly questions, and put ten minutes on your calendar every Monday to open the dashboard. That's the entire adoption plan. The tool writes the queries; you still have to form the habit — the numbers don't help anyone who doesn't look at them.

If the owner side of this — which numbers to watch, what to check weekly, what triggers action — is the part you keep deferring, it's written down in The AI Agent Owner's Playbook: the permission ladder that matches tasks to trust levels, the first-month inspection habit, and the escalation contract format that tells an agent exactly when to come back to you. $49 CAD, instant download.

title: How to Choose Colors for a Website: A Practical Guide
description:
Choosing colors for a website can be harder than it looks. A color palette needs to feel consistent, keep text readable, and support the purpose of the design.

Here is a simple process you can use for your next project.

  1. Start with a Primary Color

Choose one color that represents the overall mood of your website.

For example:

Blue can feel dependable and professional.

Green can suggest growth or nature.

Orange can create a sense of energy.

Purple can give a design a creative feel.

These are common associations, not fixed rules. The right choice depends on your audience and context.

  1. Build a Small Color Palette

You do not need dozens of colors. Start with a few practical roles:

Primary: The main brand or interface color.

Secondary: A supporting color for variety.

Background: A color that keeps the layout comfortable to read.

Text: A color with strong contrast against the background.

Accent: A color for important actions or selected elements.

A limited palette is usually easier to apply consistently across buttons, cards, headings, and backgrounds.

  1. Check Contrast and Readability

A color combination may look attractive but still make text difficult to read.

Check the contrast between text and its background, especially for small text and buttons. WCAG guidance generally recommends a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

Do not rely on color alone to communicate information. Use labels, icons, or other visual cues when necessary.

  1. Test Colors Together

View your colors in context rather than judging each swatch separately. Try them on a sample button, a heading, and a card.

You can use a color palette tool to explore combinations, compare shades, and refine your choices before applying them to a full design.

For a quick starting point, explore Clicktoolset and its color tools.

  1. Keep the Palette Consistent

Once you settle on a palette, reuse the same colors for the same purposes. For example, keep primary buttons consistent and reserve accent colors for elements that deserve attention.

Documenting your colors as HEX values also makes it easier to reuse them in CSS:

:root {
  --color-primary: #2563EB;
  --color-secondary: #14B8A6;
  --color-background: #F8FAFC;
  --color-text: #1E293B;
  --color-accent: #F59E0B;
}

These values are only an example. Test your actual combinations for contrast and suitability before using them in a project.

Final Thoughts

A useful website palette does not have to be complicated. Start with a primary color, add a few supporting roles, check readability, and test the result in a real layout.

A small, consistent palette is often easier to maintain than a collection of unrelated colors.

title: Why parsing real estate contracts with LLMs is ten times harder than tutorials claim
description:
When we started building the data pipeline for NovAsia (a property catalog and market tool for Southeast Asia), the plan looked embarrassingly simple on paper:

Grab property PDFs and developer contracts (SPAs).

Run them through a modern vision LLM.

Dump structured JSON into PostgreSQL.

Call it a day.

Two weeks in, the pipeline was completely broken. Here is why standard tutorial advice fell apart in production, and what we had to change to get reliable data out of scanned documents.

The stuff tutorials don't warn you about
Most LLM document parsing demos use crisp, born-digital PDFs with clean typography. In emerging markets like Cambodia and Thailand, reality looks very different:

Phone scans: Half the documents are multi-generation scans or photos taken with a phone camera under uneven lighting.

Dual-language layout: Khmer or Thai text mixed with English, often in adjacent table columns where line baselines don't match.

Physical stamps: Red rubber stamps, signatures, and notary seals placed directly over critical numbers (payment milestone dates, sinking fund fees, transfer taxes).

The 40-page prompt trap: If you shove a 35-page PDF into a long-context model and ask for "all fees and payment dates", it will extract 80% correctly and quietly hallucinate the rest with total confidence.

Three practical changes that fixed it
Instead of trying to find one magic model that does everything, we broke the pipeline down into smaller, boring steps:

  1. Aggressive image cleanup before text extraction

Before any model sees the page, we run basic OpenCV passes: deskewing, binarization, and contrast normalization. Removing phone-scan shadows did more for extraction accuracy than upgrading to a larger model tier.

  1. Section-level chunking with rigid schema validation

We stopped asking the model to parse whole documents at once. We chunk by specific section (e.g., "Schedule of Payments", "Maintenance Obligations") and enforce strict Pydantic schemas. If a field fails validation or falls outside expected bounds, the pipeline flags it for manual check rather than guessing.

  1. Treating tables and narrative text as separate problems

Vision models are great at answering qualitative questions ("under what conditions is the deposit refundable?"), but notoriously sloppy with columns in financial tables. We split table extraction into dedicated passes with explicit row-by-row checks.

The takeaway
If you're building with LLMs on messy, physical-world paperwork, raw context window size won't save you. Most of the reliability comes from image hygiene and strict schema boundaries.

Happy to trade notes if anyone else here is wrestling with noisy scans and table extraction.

title: My webhook catcher's 24-hour expiry taught me that 'ephemeral' is a promise you have to keep with your own memory
description:
I built a webhook catcher for integration testing: give it any POST, it hands you back a single-use HTTPS URL that stores up to 100 events for 24 hours, then deletes everything. Sounds simple. The operational lesson came from what happened after expiry.

The catcher is in-memory by design. No database, no disk, no persistence layer. When the 24-hour timer fires, the events are gone. When the process restarts, they're gone. That's the deal I made with myself: ephemeral means ephemeral.

But agents kept asking why their debug hooks "vanished." A test at 9am, a re-run at 5pm — same URL, empty response. The URL was still alive (the route existed), but the data had been reaped. From the caller's side it looked like a bug. From my side it was the feature working exactly as specified.

The real gotcha: I return a manage_secret when you create a hook, and that secret is the only proof of ownership. But I never persisted a tombstone. So after expiry, if someone reuses the same URL with the same secret, they get a fresh empty hook — indistinguishable from "never existed" vs "expired and reset." That's a security smell. An attacker who guesses a URL could probe for liveness without triggering anything.

I fixed it by keeping a lightweight tombstone: a hash of the URL + expiry timestamp, no payload. Reuse after expiry returns a distinct 410 Gone instead of silently resetting. Cost: a few KB of memory. Lesson: "delete everything" and "prove you deleted it" are different requirements, and the second one is what agents actually need when they're debugging at 2am.

title: How to Get Google Trends Data in Python Without 429 Errors (a pytrends Alternative for 2026)
description:
If you've ever written pytrends.build_payload(...) and seen TooManyRequestsError: The request failed: Google returned a response with code 429, you're not alone. pytrends was archived, Google's official Trends API is still invite-only alpha, and Trends now rate-limits automated traffic aggressively. This tutorial shows a dependable way to pull interest over time, interest by region and related queries for hundreds of keywords from Python, and explains why the usual fixes stop working.

Why pytrends gets 429s

The Google Trends front end calls a handful of internal endpoints:

  1. /trends/api/explore returns a list of "widgets", each with a short-lived token.
  2. /trends/api/widgetdata/multiline returns the timeline.
  3. /trends/api/widgetdata/comparedgeo returns regions.
  4. /trends/api/widgetdata/relatedsearches returns related queries and topics.

Every response starts with an anti-JSON-hijacking prefix ()]}'), and every call needs a valid NID cookie. When you send many requests from one IP, Google returns 429 or redirects you to /sorry/. The common advice of time.sleep(60) plus retries=3 works for ten keywords. It doesn't work for a thousand, and it doesn't work from cloud IPs at all, because those are often blocked from the very first request.

What actually works is:

  • a fresh session (cookie plus new tokens) after each block,
  • rotating egress IPs,
  • per-widget retries, so one failed section doesn't throw away the whole query,
  • honest status reporting, so you know which rows are complete.

You can build that yourself, or use a hosted Actor that already does it.

Option A: a hosted API (about 5 minutes)

Reliable Google Trends API on Apify handles the warmup, proxy rotation, retries and residential fallback. It charges $0.002 per successful query, and failed queries are free. In our 34-query gate runs on Apify, it returned 34 of 34 results in every proxy mode we tested.

Install the client:

pip install apify-client pandas

Run a comparison:

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/reliable-google-trends").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": [
        "chatgpt, claude, gemini",     # one query comparing 3 terms
        "air fryer",                   # a second query
    ],
    "geo": "US",
    "timeframe": "today 12-m",
    "interestOverTime": True,
    "interestByRegion": True,
    "relatedQueries": True,
})

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
for r in rows:
    print(r["keywords"], r["status"], r["errors"])

Turn the timeline into a DataFrame 

def timeline_df(row):
    recs = [{"date": p["time"], **p["values"]} for p in row["interest_over_time"]]
    return pd.DataFrame(recs).set_index("date")

df = timeline_df(rows[0])
print(df.tail())
df.plot(title="ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini, US, 12 months")

Rising queries (breakouts) 

for kw, rq in rows[1]["related_queries"].items():
    for q in rq["rising"][:10]:
        print(kw, "->", q["query"], q["formatted_value"])

Bulk keyword lists

Each searchTerms entry is its own query, so you can pass 500 entries in one run. To set different options for each query, use customQueries:

run_input = {"customQueries": [
    {"keywords": "bitcoin, ethereum", "geo": "GB", "timeframe": "today 5-y", "property": "news"},
    {"keywords": "lofi music", "property": "youtube"},
]}

Every run also writes a RUN_SUMMARY record to the key-value store with the success rate and block counts:

summary = client.key_value_store(run["defaultKeyValueStoreId"]).get_record("RUN_SUMMARY")["value"]
print(summary)

Option B: roll your own (what you need to handle)

If you'd rather run it yourself, here's the minimum:

import httpx, json, time, random

def warm(client):
    # A headers-only request is enough to obtain an NID cookie
    with client.stream("GET", "https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?geo=US") as r:
        pass

def explore(client, kw, geo="US", tf="today 12-m"):
    req = {"comparisonItem": [{"keyword": kw, "geo": geo, "time": tf}],
           "category": 0, "property": ""}
    r = client.get("https://trends.google.com/trends/api/explore",
                   params={"hl": "en-US", "tz": 0, "req": json.dumps(req)})
    if r.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("blocked")
    return json.loads(r.text[r.text.index("{"):])["widgets"]

From here you still need to: call each widget endpoint with its token; rotate the session and the IP whenever you get a 429 or /sorry/; back off with jitter; and treat related topics as optional (Google often withholds them from sessions it labels USER_TYPE_SCRAPER). In practice the proxy bill and the maintenance cost far more than the code.

Gotchas that apply either way

  • Values are relative (0–100), not search volume. Only compare keywords that were in the same query.
  • More than 5 keywords? Use a shared anchor term in every batch (for example "weather") and rescale each batch against it.
  • Timeframe strings follow the Trends URL format: now 7-d, today 3-m, today 5-y, all, 2024-01-01 2024-06-30.
  • Last data point is often is_partial: true. Drop it before you fit a forecast.

Schedule it

In the Apify console, open the Actor, save your input as a Task, and add a Schedule (for example, daily at 06:00). Then use a webhook or the n8n/Make/Zapier Apify app to push new rows into Google Sheets or your warehouse.

Wrap-up

pytrends taught a generation of analysts to love Trends data, but the 429 wall is real. If you need a few queries a week, a careful DIY script with backoff can be enough. If you need hundreds of keywords on a schedule, without babysitting proxies, try Reliable Google Trends API. It's pay-per-result, and failed queries are free.

title: TIL: How to Find the Default Port of a GBase Database Instance
description:
After installing GBase Database (GBase 8s) using the typical installation option, you may notice that the instance is ready to use, but you're not sure which port it listens on.

In this setup, the port may be assigned automatically. For the instance discussed here, the default port is 30490. But rather than relying on memory, you can verify the actual configuration in two ways.

Method 1: Check the Instance Script and /etc/services

First, find the instance name in the generated instance script:

grep GBASEDBTSERVER /opt/GBASE/gbase/ol_gbasedbt1210.ksh

Then look up the corresponding service entry:

grep ol_gbasedbt1210 /etc/services

If the service is registered there, the output should show its configured port and protocol. The exact entry depends on your installation.

Note: /etc/services maps service names to port numbers and protocols. It does not, by itself, prove that the database is running or listening on that port.

Method 2: Check the sqlhosts File

The instance-specific sqlhosts file is another useful place to check connection settings:

cat /opt/GBASE/gbase/etc/sqlhosts.ol_gbasedbt1210

A typical entry might look like this:

ol_gbasedbt1210  onsoctcp  hostname  30490

The fields identify the server name, connection protocol, host, and port. In this example, onsoctcp indicates a TCP/IP connection, and 30490 is the configured port.

Replace hostname with the actual host value shown in your configuration.

For connection troubleshooting, make sure the client uses the correct server name and that the host and port match the instance's actual configuration.

Which Method Should You Use?

Both methods are useful, but the sqlhosts file is a good starting point when you're investigating client connection settings. The instance script and /etc/services provide additional context about the configured server name and service mapping.

If a connection still fails, verify that the instance is running and confirm that the expected port is listening. A configured port alone does not guarantee a successful connection.

Final Takeaway

With GBase Database (GBase 8s), installation scripts may configure values automatically, but you can still inspect them afterward.

Once you've confirmed the instance name and port, document both in your environment notes. This small habit makes connection setup, application configuration, and future troubleshooting much easier.

Have you ever spent time troubleshooting a GBase Database connection only to discover that you were using the wrong port?

title: Use ACP-compatible harnesses with the AI SDK harness layer
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports any Agent Client Protocol (ACP)-compatible harness with HarnessAgent through the new @ai-sdk/harness-acp package.

Previously, every harness adapter wrapped one specific runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Deep Agents, OpenCode). @ai-sdk/harness-acp wraps the protocol instead. It is a meta adapter: rather than adapting a single harness, it lets you build an adapter for any harness that ships an ACP-compatible package.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

Then pass it to HarnessAgent like any other harness:

ACP is an abstraction over coding harnesses, but the AI SDK harness layer stays deliberately decoupled from it. Not every harness supports ACP, and for some, ACP limits or changes how well they expose their internal behaviors, so a direct adapter can produce a tighter integration.

For Claude Code and Codex, prefer the direct @ai-sdk/harness-claude-code and @ai-sdk/harness-codex adapters over an ACP-based implementation; reach for @ai-sdk/harness-acp when a harness has no direct adapter but ships an ACP-compatible package.

Read the ACP harness documentation to get started.
