title: Why I Want My AI Coding Assistant to Ask Before It Acts
description:
Most AI coding tools are built around one promise: speed. Type a prompt, get code, move on.

But after a while I noticed the speed was costing me something. The AI would edit files I didn't expect, delete things I still needed, or run a command I hadn't read. I'd spend the next hour undoing work I never approved.

The problem with "just do it" AI

When an AI agent has full permission to write, delete, and execute, every action is a small act of trust you didn't explicitly give. For a throwaway script that's fine. For a real codebase it's not.

The failure mode isn't dramatic. It's quiet:

  • A helper function gets "cleaned up" and something subtle breaks
  • A config file gets rewritten with slightly different values
  • A dependency gets bumped and nothing works the next morning

What I actually want

I want an assistant that treats my codebase like it belongs to someone else. That means:

  1. Ask before writing. Show me the change, let me approve it.
  2. Show diffs, not summaries. "I updated the auth logic" tells me nothing. A diff tells me everything.
  3. Checkpoint every step. If step 4 was wrong, I want to rewind to step 3 — not start over.
  4. Ask before running commands. A shell command is the most powerful thing an agent can do. It should be the most gated.

The trade-off is worth it

Yes, this is slower per action. But it's dramatically faster per outcome, because I'm not spending my afternoon fixing things I never agreed to.

If you're on Windows and want an AI editor that works this way, that's the idea behind Arcwright — it's free to start. But the principle applies to whatever tool you use: the AI should earn your trust one approved change at a time.

title: Building an Autonomous AI Software Enterprise on FALKORDB: Why Flat Vector Stores Fail and Graphs win
description:
By The GraphCorp Team — Built for WeMakeDevs Graph Hacks (Track 01)

Over the past two years, the AI world has been obsessed with a single design pattern: Vector Databases + Prompt Chaining.

Whether building autonomous coders, research assistants, or multi-agent swarms, the architectural recipe was almost universally the same: dump past conversations and code chunks into embeddings, compute cosine similarities, and inject the top-$k$ nearest neighbors into an LLM context window.

For single-agent chatbots, that worked well enough. For multi-agent software engineering enterprises, it is an unmitigated disaster.

When multiple autonomous agents (CEOs, CTOs, PMs, Developers, QA, and DevOps engineers) attempt to coordinate a production codebase, vector retrieval fails immediately. Vectors have no concept of dependency order, transitive blocking, structural call graphs, or governance custody.

In this article, we share how we built GraphCorp—an autonomous AI software company that uses FalkorDB as its living operating system. We will show why flat vector stores and relational databases fail at agentic orchestration, and how native graph data structures deliver sub-millisecond coordination, zero hallucination, and genuine software delivery.

1. The Multi-Agent State Crisis: Why Vectors and SQL Fail

Consider what an engineering team actually does during a software release:

  1. A Product Manager breaks a strategic initiative into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks. Task $D$ cannot start until Task $B$ and $C$ are complete, while Task $B$ is blocked by Task $A$.
  2. A Developer creates a feature branch, modifies a cryptographic helper file, and creates a Pull Request.
  3. A QA Engineer must determine the exact blast radius of that change: which classes, CLI endpoints, and storage engines depend on that helper, and which test suites must be executed before sign-off?
  4. A DevOps Engineer verifies approvals and executes an atomic merge commit to main, which immediately unblocks downstream dependent tasks.

Now, attempt to model this with today's standard AI stacks:

The Vector Failure: Semantic Proximity is Not Topological Truth

Suppose a developer modifies crypto.py. You ask a vector database for relevant code using semantic search:

# Semantic search misses structural reality
results = vector_db.similarity_search("functions that depend on crypto.py")

The vector store returns documents containing words like "cryptography", "encryption", or "security". It completely misses the fact that cli.py line 42 calls storage.py which calls VaultCipher.decrypt().

Vector search cannot traverse directed call graphs. As a result, agents hallucinate assumptions, skip required integration tests, and merge broken code into production.

The Relational Failure: Recursive CTE Join Hell

Attempting to manage a multi-agent task DAG in relational SQL encounters the Recursive Join Bottleneck:

-- Resolving transitive dependencies in SQL requires heavy recursive CTEs
WITH RECURSIVE task_tree AS (
    SELECT task_id, blocked_by_id FROM task_dependencies WHERE task_id = 'TASK-05'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT td.task_id, td.blocked_by_id
    FROM task_dependencies td
    JOIN task_tree tt ON td.task_id = tt.blocked_by_id
)
SELECT * FROM task_tree ...

In an active multi-agent system where dozens of tasks are updating concurrently, recursive table scans cause table locks, quadratic latency spikes ($O(N^2)$), and transaction deadlocks.

2. Enter FalkorDB: The Graph Operating System

To solve this, we turned to FalkorDB—the high-performance, low-latency graph database designed for connected data.

In GraphCorp, FalkorDB is not merely a database; it is the corporate nervous system. It maintains a unified heterogeneous graph spanning four core operational planes:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   GRAPHCORP UNIFIED ENTERPRISE GRAPH                   │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Organisational Plane  : (Agent {role}) -[:REPORTS_TO]-> (Agent)    │
│ 2. Task & Project Plane  : (Task) -[:BLOCKED_BY]-> (Task)              │
│ 3. Code Knowledge Plane  : (Component) -[:CALLS]-> (Component)         │
│ 4. Git & Audit Plane     : (Agent) -[:COMMITS_CODE]-> (GitCommit)      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Because all four planes exist in the same graph, agents execute multi-hop Cypher queries that cross organizational and technical boundaries in under a millisecond.

(CEO:Agent) ──[:MAKES_DECISION]──► (Decision)
                                       │
                                   [:JUSTIFIES]
                                       ▼
                                  (TASK-02:Task)
                                       │
                                  [:RESOLVED_BY]
                                       ▼
                                (PR-TASK-02:PR) ──[:COMMITS_CODE]──► (c:GitCommit)

3. The Three Production Cypher Queries Powering GraphCorp

Let's look at the actual Cypher queries GraphCorp agents run in production:

Query 1: Topological Task Dispatch (Zero-Polling Orchestration)

Developer agents never "poll" or guess what to build next. They query FalkorDB for tasks that are currently TODO and have zero active or incomplete blockers:

MATCH (t:Task)
WHERE t.status = 'TODO'
  AND NOT (t)-[:BLOCKED_BY]->(:Task {status: 'TODO'})
  AND NOT (t)-[:BLOCKED_BY]->(:Task {status: 'IN_PROGRESS'})
RETURN t.id AS task_id, 
       t.title AS title, 
       t.assigned_to AS role, 
       t.priority AS priority
ORDER BY t.priority ASC
LIMIT 1
  • Execution Latency in FalkorDB: 0.02 ms
  • Result: Pure, non-blocking asynchronous dispatch. As soon as a prerequisite task transitions to DONE, downstream tasks immediately become visible to developers with zero coordination overhead.

Query 2: Multi-Hop AST Blast-Radius Analysis

When developer CLIDev-2 submits a Pull Request modifying crypto.py, the QA Agent does not just run a generic test. It inspects the graph to see who calls this file up to 3 hops away, and which unit tests cover those components:

MATCH (target:Component {name: 'crypto.py'})
OPTIONAL MATCH path = (caller:Component)-[:CALLS*1..3]->(target)
OPTIONAL MATCH (caller)<-[:TESTS]-(test:Test)
RETURN target.name AS modified,
       collect(DISTINCT caller.name) AS impacted_callers,
       collect(DISTINCT test.name) AS required_test_suites,
       length(path) AS traversal_depth
  • Execution Latency in FalkorDB: 0.08 ms
  • Result: QA discovers that cli.py and storage.py both depend on crypto.py, and mandates that test_crypto.py, test_storage.py, and test_cli.py must all pass before the PR can be approved.

Query 3: CEO-to-Commit Decision Provenance

In enterprise compliance, you must be able to prove why a line of code was introduced. GraphCorp enables complete retrospective audits:

MATCH (ceo:Agent {role: 'CEO'})-[:MAKES_DECISION]->(dec:Decision)
MATCH (dec)-[:JUSTIFIES]->(task:Task)
MATCH (task)<-[:ASSIGNED_TO]-(dev:Agent)
MATCH (task)-[:RESOLVED_BY]->(pr:PullRequest)
MATCH (pr)-[:MERGED_BY]->(devops:Agent)
MATCH (pr)-[:COMMITS_CODE]->(c:GitCommit)
RETURN ceo.name AS visionary,
       dec.title AS strategic_decision,
       task.id AS task_id,
       dev.name AS author,
       pr.id AS pull_request,
       devops.name AS merger,
       c.sha AS commit_sha

Every single commit in the Git repository has an unbroken, cryptographically verifiable graph path back to the CEO's original mandate.

4. Zero Demoware: Real MCP Tools, Real Git, Real Pytest

A major problem with AI hackathon entries is "demoware"—agents printing markdown snippets into terminal stdout without actually executing anything.

GraphCorp is built with strict adherence to Rule #3: Genuine Execution:

  • Real File I/O: Agents use Model Context Protocol (MCP) file tools to write source code directly to workspace/dev-vault.
  • Real Git Commits & Merges: Developers create genuine Git branches (feat/crypto-engine, feat/cli-interface), commit with verified author signatures, and DevOps executes authentic non-fast-forward merge commits (git merge --no-ff).
  • Real Pytest Runs: The QA agent launches subprocess test runners via bash MCP tools. If a test fails, the PR is rejected, feedback is persisted to the FalkorDB graph, and the developer agent is re-invoked to fix the defect. 
$ git -C workspace/dev-vault log --graph --oneline
*   f8a93f4 (HEAD -> main) chore(merge): merge feat/cli-interface (PR-TASK-04) for TASK-04
|\  
| * e169230 (feat/cli-interface) feat(task-04): Implement dev-vault Click CLI Commands
* |   86562c7 chore(merge): merge feat/storage-io (PR-TASK-03) for TASK-03
|\ \  
| * | 4ff6e9d (feat/storage-io) feat(task-03): Implement Encrypted File Storage Persistence

5. The Output: dev-vault CLI

In our golden test run, GraphCorp was given this high-level prompt:

"Build dev-vault: an enterprise developer secret store CLI with AES-256 GCM authenticated encryption and Argon2id."

In 6.76 seconds, GraphCorp's autonomous team:

  1. Formulated strategy and parsed architecture specifications.
  2. Built a 6-node dependency DAG in FalkorDB.
  3. Created an isolated workspace with pyproject configuration.
  4. Implemented NIST SP 800-38D compliant VaultCipher using cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM with 96-bit random nonces and Argon2id key derivation.
  5. Implemented atomic file storage persistence with tmpfile swapping and os.fsync.
  6. Built a complete Click CLI interface (init, set, get, list).
  7. Authored an 8-test unit and security suite covering tamper resistance, distinct nonces, and invalid passphrases.
  8. Executed 6 PR reviews, 6 QA audits, and 6 DevOps merges.

The resulting CLI is 100% operational:

$ python workspace/dev-vault/src/cli.py init --passphrase "MyPass#2026" --path /tmp/vault.enc
Initialized empty encrypted vault at /tmp/vault.enc

$ python workspace/dev-vault/src/cli.py set PROD_KEY "sk-live-9999" --passphrase "MyPass#2026" --path /tmp/vault.enc
Secret 'PROD_KEY' encrypted and saved.

$ python workspace/dev-vault/src/cli.py get PROD_KEY --passphrase "MyPass#2026" --path /tmp/vault.enc
sk-live-9999

6. Benchmarking GraphCorp vs. Traditional Approaches

Dimension Vector DB + Prompt Chaining Relational SQL + ORM GraphCorp on FalkorDB
Dependency Resolution Semantic guessing (High failure rate) 45 ms (Recursive CTE) 0.02 ms (Direct graph match)
AST Blast-Radius Query Impossible (Cosine similarity only) 180 ms (Multi-table join) 0.08 ms (Transitive path traversal)
Context Fidelity Suffers severe context drift Rigid schema, high friction 100% Deterministic Grounding
Coordination Model Synchronous chat buffers Polling loops / Locks Event-Driven Graph Unblocking
End-to-End Cycle Time 10+ minutes (manual fixes) Unstable in multi-agent race conditions 6.76 seconds

Conclusion: The Graph-Native Future of Agentic AI

The future of autonomous software engineering is not about building bigger prompt windows or stuffing more chunks into vector databases.

Complex software requires topology. It requires knowing who blocks whom, who calls whom, who approved what, and why.

By grounding autonomous agents in a high-performance graph database like FalkorDB, we can replace fuzzy hallucinations with structural mathematical guarantees. GraphCorp proves that when agents act on connected data, an entire software enterprise can operate autonomously, safely, and at the speed of thought.

Resources & Source Code

  • GitHub Repository: GraphCorp on GitHub
  • FalkorDB Official: https://falkordb.com
  • Live Mission Control UI: Built with FastAPI + Cytoscape.js

Built with passion for WeMakeDevs Graph Hacks (Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data).

title: Design in the material you ship
description:
Designers should understand code the way an architect understands stone: what it can do, not how to cut it. AI now does the cutting.

Early in The Fountainhead, Howard Roark is expelled from architecture school for refusing to design in borrowed styles. The Dean calls him in to explain himself, and Roark gives him a rule instead: “What can be done with one substance must never be done with another. No two materials are alike. No two sites on earth are alike. No two buildings have the same purpose. The purpose, the site, the material determine the shape.”

You don’t have to admire Roark to take the point. He is the architect in the book who spends his time on building sites, among the electricians and steelworkers, learning what the material will and won’t do. His classmates learn to draw facades.

Digital designers have a material too. It is code. For most of the last fifteen years, we have designed in pictures of it. The warning is older than that. John Allsopp asked the web to stop imitating print in 2000, Frank Chimero wrote about working with the web’s grain in 2015, and Jeremy Keith gave its materials a chapter of their own in Resilient Web Design.

The drawing is not the building

A design file is a drawing. It shows one state, at one width, in one language, with the data the designer typed in. The product is every other state.

The name is longer than the box. A short English label can double in length once it is translated. The photo fails to load. The list is empty. The request takes four seconds, or fails. Someone tabs through with a keyboard. The phone is 320 pixels wide. None of those is an edge case to the person it happens to, and none of them exists in the file until someone draws it by hand, which in practice means rarely.

When the file is the source of truth, each of those gaps gets decided by whoever writes the code, after the design is called done, and usually without a conversation. The file and the product drift apart, and the file keeps being presented in reviews as if it were the product.

What changed when the code became the source

When I built 131 variations of one button to study hover feedback, I built them in code. The surprise was what happened to the specification. In a design file, a jelly button is an adjective: tactile. In code, it is a handful of numbers. The pointer starts to count 36 pixels from the edge, the material has a stiffness, and it settles back in under a second. An engineer can build a number. Nobody can build an adjective.

I now work the same way on a product team. The prototype in code is what gets reviewed. The design file still exists, because people like to leave comments on a canvas, but it is regenerated from the code after each pass, never the other way round. Its job is to be a mirror.

Roark’s rule applies almost word for word. A responsive layout, a loading state and a focus ring belong to the browser. Drawing them in a canvas tool is doing with one substance what belongs to another.

You no longer have to write it

This is where the old version of the argument went wrong. For a decade, “designers should code” meant designers should learn to write HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Many tried, many quit, and they were right to resent it. It asked them to become a second, slower engineer. Brad Frost later drew a more useful line, between the front of the front end, which sits close to design, and the application logic behind it.

That argument is over, because AI writes the code. I describe the screen, its states and its numbers, and the model writes it. I correct it by looking at the result and saying what is wrong, the way an architect corrects a site, not by laying the bricks again myself.

Reading code is going the same way. It still helps, and I read diffs most days. But AI review tools read them too, and they are improving quickly. In one benchmark this year, the best reviewer caught 84 of 122 real bugs taken from production codebases such as Sentry and Grafana. The vendor that won ran the test, and two thirds is not all of them. So the claim is not that the machine has replaced the reviewer. It is that the designer no longer needs to be the reviewer.

Engineers reading this will object, and they have a point. In Stack Overflow’s 2025 developer survey, 66 percent named AI answers that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration, and 46 percent said they distrust its accuracy. Someone accountable for the system still has to read what goes into it. That person is the engineer who owns it. The designer has a different job.

Understanding is the part you can’t delegate

What Roark took from the building site was not the skill of riveting. It was knowing what steel will do, so that his drawings only asked for things the material could give.

That is the part AI can’t hold for you. It will write whatever you describe, including things the medium handles badly, and it will review the code against the code, not against what the person on the other end needed. Judging that takes someone who knows the material.

You judge the output by running it, not by reading it. Open it at 320 pixels. Paste the longest real name you can find. Set the network to slow. Put the mouse away and use the keyboard. None of those tests needs a line of syntax.

What to learn instead of syntax

  • How layout flows: what wraps, what stretches, what refuses to shrink.
  • Which states exist: empty, loading, partial, failed, offline.
  • The shape of the data, including what a field holds when it holds nothing.
  • What costs a trip to the server and what is free on the device.
  • What a screen reader actually announces on your screen.
  • How to run the product on your own machine, without help.
  • How to ask the AI to explain a change in plain words.

None of these requires writing code. All of them require spending time with it.

The material determines the shape

Roark’s rule ends where this argument does: the purpose, the site and the material determine the shape. Our material hasn’t changed. It is still code, and it still decides what a screen can be. What changed is that we no longer have to hold the chisel to learn what it can cut.

Design in the material you ship was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: How We Built a Self-Healing Multi-Agent Company Brain on FalkorDB (and Why Vector RAG Failed Us)
description:
How We Built a Self-Healing Multi-Agent Company Brain on FalkorDB (and Why Vector RAG Failed Us)

By Jeeva N (@jeeva5655) — Built for the Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents Hackathon

🚨 The Illusion of "Context" in Modern AI Agents

In early 2026, building an enterprise AI agent follows a predictable recipe: chunk your company’s Notion docs, Slack exports, and Jira tickets, compute embeddings with text-embedding-3-small, dump them into a vector database (Pinecone, Chroma, or Qdrant), and pass top-$k$ cosine matches to an LLM.

It looks like magic on simple Q&A demos. But deploy that agent into an active engineering incident, and it disintegrates.

Consider this actual incident scenario from our production benchmark:

The Alarm: PaymentGateway experiences an 18.4% HTTP 500 error cascade on /v2/checkout. Revenue loss is estimated at $12,000/minute.
The Task: Find the root cause, identify the engineer who introduced it, check who is on call, and trigger an automated circuit-breaker quarantine.

When we fed this incident alert into a standard Chunk-Based Vector RAG agent, here is what it returned:

  1. Chunk #81 (Score: 0.81): "...PaymentGateway checkout API throws 500 error on timeout..."
  2. Chunk #42 (Score: 0.77): "...Payment gateway retry backoff policy should be configured with exponential jitter..."
  3. Chunk #19 (Score: 0.72): "...General error handling guidelines for Go microservices..."

The agent completely hallucinated. It blamed the PaymentGateway codebase and advised tweaking client retry settings.

Why? Because PaymentGateway code hadn’t changed in weeks! The real culprit was upstream:

  • PaymentGateway had an undeclared gRPC dependency on AuthService.
  • 1.5 hours before the outage, PR #482 was merged into AuthService by Sarah Chen, containing commit c3b8f19 which enforced strict cryptographic claim validation and aggressive cache eviction.
  • Under peak load, AuthService latency jumped from 45ms to 2400ms, causing PaymentGateway downstream connection pools to exhaust and throw 500s.

A vector database cannot traverse relationships across services, pull requests, commits, and on-call rotations. It sees words, not connections.

To solve this, we built FalkorNexus: an autonomous multi-agent enterprise operations command powered by FalkorDB.

🏛️ The FalkorNexus Architecture

FalkorNexus is built around a single premise: an agent's context must be a graph, not a bag of text chunks.

graph TD
    User([Incident Commander / Operator]) --> WebUI[FalkorNexus Cyber Command Dashboard]
    WebUI --> API[FastAPI High-Concurrency Backend]

    subgraph "Track 02: Multi-Agent Orchestration & State Machine"
        API --> Orchestrator[Agent Orchestrator]
        Orchestrator --> Triage[1. TriageAgent]
        Triage --> Invest[2. InvestigatorAgent]
        Invest --> Action[3. ActionAgent]
        Action --> Memory[4. MemoryAgent]

        Triage -. Shared State .-> Invest
        Invest -. Shared State .-> Action
        Action -. Shared State .-> Memory
    end

    subgraph "Track 01: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tools"
        MCPServer[FalkorDB Native MCP Server]
        Invest <--> MCPServer
        MCPServer --> Tool1["CALL algo.pageRank('Service', 'DEPENDS_ON')"]
        MCPServer --> Tool2["shortestPath((a)-[*..6]-(b))"]
        MCPServer --> Tool3["CALL algo.betweenness()"]
        MCPServer --> Tool4["Multi-Hop Root Cause Cypher"]
    end

    subgraph "Track 03: Company Brain & Memory Layer"
        FalkorDB[(FalkorDB Graph Engine)]
        FalkorDB --> Multigraph1[Tenant: Enterprise Company Brain]
        FalkorDB --> Multigraph2[Tenant: Agent Shared Memory & SOPs]
        FalkorDB --> Multigraph3[Tenant: User Episodic Sessions]
    end

    Tool1 <--> FalkorDB
    Tool2 <--> FalkorDB
    Tool3 <--> FalkorDB
    Tool4 <--> FalkorDB
    Memory <--> FalkorDB

⚡ Why FalkorDB? (Three Capabilities Competitors Missed)

1. Zero-Leakage Multigraph Topology on a Single Instance

Enterprise systems have strict data boundaries. You cannot co-mingle shared company architecture with an agent's private execution memory or a user's private session thread.

Instead of hacking tenant isolation via node properties (WHERE n.tenant_id = '...'), FalkorNexus utilizes FalkorDB’s native Multigraph Architecture:

from falkordb import FalkorDB

db = FalkorDB(host="localhost", port=6379)

# Isolated Company Brain Graph
brain_graph = db.select_graph(f"tenant_{tenant_id}_brain")

# Isolated Multi-Agent Memory & Shared Handoff Graph
memory_graph = db.select_graph(f"tenant_{tenant_id}_memory")

# Isolated User Episodic Thread Graph
user_graph = db.select_graph(f"user_{user_id}_session")

Each graph has its own isolated adjacency matrices, node indices, and transaction locks on the same FalkorDB daemon without spinning up separate containers.

2. GraphBLAS Sparse-Matrix Math via Native Cypher

When an incident is costing $12,000/minute, an agent cannot wait 8 seconds for a Python library to deserialize 50,000 nodes and run graph traversals in user-space.

FalkorDB executes graph algorithms directly in C/Rust using GraphBLAS sparse linear algebra. We exposed these algorithms directly as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools:

Native PageRank for Systemic Hub Criticality: 

CALL algo.pageRank('Service', 'DEPENDS_ON')
YIELD node, score
RETURN node.name AS service, node.tier AS tier, score
ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5

Latency: **0.9 ms* for 50+ nodes on an active cluster.*

5-Hop Root Cause Traversal in One Query: 

MATCH path = (inc:Incident {id: $incident_id})-[:AFFECTS]->(s:Service)
             -[:DEPENDS_ON*1..4]->(upstream:Service)
             <-[:MODIFIES]-(pr:PullRequest)<-[:AUTHORED]-(eng:Person)
WHERE pr.merged_at > $window_start
RETURN [n IN nodes(path) | coalesce(n.name, n.id, n.title)] AS reasoning_chain,
       upstream.name AS root_service,
       pr.id AS suspect_pr,
       eng.name AS oncall_expert,
       length(path) AS hops
ORDER BY pr.merged_at DESC LIMIT 1

3. The "Two-Run Learning Loop": Self-Healing Graph Memory

Most hackathon agent projects have "memory" that is nothing more than chat logs stored in Postgres.

In FalkorNexus, memory mutates the graph topology itself. We call this the Two-Run Learning Loop:

  1. Run 1 (Cold Start):

    • The alert arrives: PaymentGateway 500 error cascade.
    • The agent takes 5 hops across services, PRs, commits, and on-call schedules, taking 14.2 seconds to diagnose AuthService and commit c3b8f19.
    • At the conclusion of the incident, MemoryAgent consolidates the episode and mutates the graph: 
     MATCH (src:Service {id: 'service_payment_gw'}), (tgt:Service {id: 'service_auth'})
 CREATE (src)-[:HISTORICAL_CASCADE {
     confidence: 0.94,
     last_incident: 'inc_804',
     learned_at: timestamp()
 }]->(tgt)

  2. Run 2 (Memory Accelerated):

    • A subsequent alert hits PaymentGateway.
    • TriageAgent inspects the semantic graph, detects the :HISTORICAL_CASCADE shortcut edge, skips the 5-hop exploration, and resolves directly in 1 hop and 1.8 seconds.
    • Result: 80% hop reduction and 87% latency reduction, proved live in the dashboard!

4. Proactive Pre-Merge Risk Gate & Counterfactual Prevention (Track 01)

Instead of waiting for outages to occur, FalkorNexus features an MCP Pre-Merge Risk Gate (falkordb_premerge_risk_gate). It traverses upstream dependencies, detects missing circuit breakers (circuit_breaker: False), combines PageRank + Betweenness Centrality, and blocks high-risk PRs before production deployment. Clicking ⚡ Auto-Heal Edge injects the missing circuit breaker live into the graph.

5. Live GraphRAG Unstructured Text-to-Graph Extraction (Track 03)

Incident reports, Slack alerts, and postmortems shouldn't sit in static text silos. FalkorNexus includes a 1-click GraphRAG Text Extractor that parses raw unstructured postmortems into typed nodes (Incident, Service, PullRequest, Person) and writes directed relationship edges (AFFECTS, MODIFIES, AUTHORED) directly into FalkorDB with live write-through.

6. Bus-Factor & Knowledge Silo Simulator (Track 03)

FalkorNexus continuously audits organizational resilience. It calculates which critical microservices have a dangerous Bus Factor = 1 and simulates emergency failover routing when key architects like Sarah Chen are unreachable, rerouting incident triage to backup engineers via Team ownership edges.

🎯 Verification & Benchmark Results

We evaluated FalkorNexus against a standard ChromaDB vector baseline on 10 realistic enterprise incident scenarios:

Metric Naive Vector RAG (Chroma) FalkorNexus (FalkorDB GraphBLAS) Improvement
Root Cause Accuracy 18% (Hallucinated local code) 100% (Exact causal dependency) +82% Accuracy
Multi-Hop Traversal Speed 8,420 ms 1.2 ms 7,000x Faster
Cold-Start Triage Time 19.8 s 14.2 s 28% Faster
Run 2 Memory Accelerated 19.4 s (No learning) 1.8 s (Shortcut traversal) 87% Speedup
Concurrency Throughput ~45 ops/sec 848.4 ops/sec 18.8x Higher Throughput
Multigraph Tenant Isolation Leaky (Property-filter hacks) 100% Zero-Leakage Native Multigraphs Mathematical Isolation
Explainable Citations Unlinked text snippets 100% Clickable Graph Nodes Complete Provenance

🛠️ How to Run It in 60 Seconds

We shipped a zero-friction docker-compose.yml that launches FalkorDB 6.0 alongside the FastAPI app and auto-seeds the enterprise knowledge graph:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/jeeva5655/falkor-nexus.git
cd falkor-nexus

# Launch FalkorDB + Web Dashboard with Docker Compose
docker-compose up --build

Or run locally in Python:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python run.py

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 to access the dashboard!

🌟 Conclusion

Agents are only as good as the context they reason over. Vector databases gave agents fuzzy memory; FalkorDB gives them a brain.

By representing services, people, code changes, decisions, and procedural playbooks as connected graph nodes, FalkorNexus transforms AI from a guessing machine into a deterministic, self-healing enterprise operations commander.

  • Live Demo Video: Included in repository root
  • Hackathon Track Submissions: Built for Track 1 (Connected Data), Track 2 (Memory & Coordination), and Track 3 (Company Brain)

title: How a failed SaaS pricing calculator, A Gemini quota meltdown, and FalkorDB led us to build Banana.
description:
Peel Back the Chaos: Smarter AI Coding with Banana

Disclaimer: I genuinely wanted to ask GPT to write this entire blog, slam my laptop shut, and enjoy some uninterrupted sleep. But staring at graph queries and an exhausted Gemini quota right in the middle of testing, I figured the internet deserved to know what happened. Also, the best blog post wins Apple AirPods 5. I'm not above risking my dignity for noise cancellation. 🎧

Why We Built Banana

Banana started as a B2B SaaS pricing calculator. Don't ask me about the name. it's just random. After hours of wrestling with Streamlit and discount sliders, I asked myself:

Would I ever voluntarily use this product?

The answer was no.

Meanwhile, AI coding agents were making the same mistakes over and over: forgetting architectural decisions, breaking dependency boundaries, and consuming huge amounts of context just to understand a codebase.

So I nuked the UI and pivoted.

git rm -rf ui/ components/ deal_calculator.py
git commit -m "pivot: delete pricing sliders, embrace the void"

Meet Banana: a graph-powered memory and context engine for coding agents. It helps tools like Claude Code and Cursor retrieve code relationships, remember architectural decisions, and check explicit rules through MCP.

The FalkorDB Skepticism: "Wait, Is This Just Redis with a Mustache?"

When I first seen FalkorDB, I’ll be completely honest: I thought it was some cheap knockoff of Redis and Neo4j.

"Oh great, another database. Is this just RedisGraph repackaged with a shiny logo, or Neo4j that demands 4GB of RAM just to clear its throat?"

I expected a clunky wrapper over key-value pairs that would fall apart the moment we asked for multi-hop AST dependency traversals.

Then, I actually sat down and dug into the documentation.

It turns out FalkorDB isn't a knockoff. Under the hood, it’s powered by GraphBLAS—which means it represents nodes and relationships as sparse linear algebra matrices implemented in optimized C.

When you ask Cypher for a 3-hop dependency traversal, it's not doing slow, recursive pointer-chasing in memory like traditional graph engines. It's executing sparse matrix multiplication.

Our measured queries on FalkorDB Cloud:

  • 3-Hop Multi-Edge Traversal: 17.4 ms
  • Architectural Decision Recall: 1.37 ms
  • AST Boundary Check: 0.28 ms

It was answering queries faster than Python could even serialize the response JSON. That was the moment I realized: this isn't marketing fluff—it's solving a genuine systems engineering problem for low-latency agent loops.

When Gemini Left the Chat (The Quota Meltdown)

Our Gemini API quota ran out right in the middle of testing.

Instead of feeding the model dozens of source files for every question, we'd already indexed our codebase into FalkorDB:

  • 39 files
  • 42 classes
  • 84 functions
  • 275 import and call relationships

That changed everything. Banana could query the graph directly to retrieve dependencies, inspect code structure, and recall stored decisions without spending LLM tokens on those operations.

The graph became our memory—and our fallback when the model wasn't available.

How FalkorDB & Edmonds-Karp Actually Solve Context Bloat

Here is the step-by-step flow of how FalkorDB turns codebase chaos into deterministic context:

Step 1: Indexing Structure, Not Just Text

Instead of dumping raw strings into a vector database and hoping for the best, FalkorDB indexes our repository as an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) graph (:File, :Class, :Function, connected by IMPORTS and CALLS). Cypher queries traverse these relationships as sparse matrix multiplications.

Step 2: The Liquid & The Pipes (Edmonds-Karp Max-Flow)

"Edmonds-Karp is a famous computer science algorithm that calculates the maximum amount of liquid you can push through a network of pipes before hitting a bottleneck."

In Banana, our "liquid" is code tokens, and our "pipes" are dependency relationships:

  1. The Source: The specific file or function you're editing.
  2. The Pipe Network: Every class, helper, and imported module connected to it, where each pipe's capacity is weighted by PageRank and architectural relevance.
  3. The Bottleneck (Sink): Your strict LLM context budget (e.g., 950 or 2,000 tokens).

Edmonds-Karp runs breadth-first search (BFS) to find augmenting paths through the dependency graph, pumping the maximum volume of critical architectural context through the pipes until the budget bottleneck is reached.

Result? You get complete, unbroken interfaces and immediate dependencies without overflowing your token limit or slicing code mid-function.

The goal: give the agent what it needs, not everything you have.

Ephemeral Graphs: A Scratchpad That Won't Trash Production

When an agent wants to reason through speculative changes—like testing a hypothetical refactor, simulating a breaking dependency, or asking "what if I change this interface?"—you never want it writing directly to your persistent codebase graph.

Because FalkorDB is built on in-memory GraphBLAS linear algebra, creating and tearing down graphs takes milliseconds, not minutes.

Banana takes full advantage of this with Ephemeral Scratchpad Graphs:

  • Whenever an agent enters speculative simulation mode, Banana spins up an isolated micro-graph (banana_scratch_<session_id>) in under 5 milliseconds.
  • The agent simulates AST diffs, tests scenario policies, and checks cyclic dependencies in complete isolation.
  • Once the simulation concludes, the scratchpad is dropped with a single command.

Zero disk clutter, zero persistent memory corruption, and zero risk of hallucinated agent thoughts polluting your source of truth.

Guardrails Without an LLM Call

Suppose an agent tries to import a low-level database driver directly into a UI component.

If that dependency violates an explicit architectural rule, Banana can check the relevant graph relationships and flag the violation without asking an LLM to review it.

We also built deterministic checks for patterns such as hardcoded credentials and unsafe code primitives.

Our measured latency for the tested AST security and boundary check was 0.28 ms.

Not every security problem can be caught with a simple rule, but explicit constraints shouldn't need an LLM call every time.

The Architecture

Banana connects coding agents to an MCP server that exposes tools for code indexing, context assembly, guardrails, and persistent memory.

Behind the scenes, FalkorDB manages three graph layers:

  • banana_knowledge — code structure, dependencies, and architectural decisions.
  • banana_demand — architectural rules, invariants, and constraints.
  • banana_scratch_* — ephemeral micro-graphs for isolated reasoning and policy simulations.

We deployed the service on AWS Lambda, backed by FalkorDB Cloud.

What We Learned

  1. Code is a graph, not just text. Imports, calls, and class relationships matter when retrieving context.
  2. Not every problem needs an LLM. Deterministic checks can enforce explicit rules faster and more predictably.
  3. Memory matters only when it's retrieved. Saving decisions is useful; bringing them back at the right time is what makes them valuable.
  4. Ephemeral graphs unlock safe agent speculation. Giving agents an instant, disposable graph sandbox prevents real-world codebase pollution.

The Final Summoning 🍌

Whenever the coding agent encounters another architectural disaster, circular import, or hallucinated token overflow...

The wheel has spun. The graph adapts. The code survives. Now give me my like. 🎧

Built with: FalkorDB, AWS Lambda, Python, and an alarming quantity of water.

GitHub: https://github.com/Viswesh934/Banana

Live endpoint: https://ssrr3wg2ibyqkh6gph4ehlthay0ovdzp.lambda-url.ap-south-1.on.aws/

Demo: https://youtu.be/OXrqt5gLIxQ

title: Pin flights, a real find hotkey, and colored More tiles
description:
Small changes you feel before you name them

Most of the work in a messenger is invisible: delivery state, encryption, reconnects, the thing that happens when the network drops halfway through a photo. Every now and then a batch of much smaller changes lands, and the app simply feels different. This is one of those batches.

Three things changed in GwinG this week. Pinning a chat or a message now has a short flight instead of a snap. The browser-standard find chord works on every search surface. And the three navigation tiles on the More tab picked up an accent color from the active theme.

None of them adds a feature you can point at in a changelog title. All of them remove a tiny moment of doubt.

A pin should move, not teleport

When you pin a chat, the list reorders immediately. That is the correct data behaviour, but it used to be a hard cut: the row you were looking at vanished from one place and appeared in another, and your eye had to find it again.

The new pin flight keeps the row legible. Before the model reorders the list, the UI snapshots the selected row's rectangle. One frame later — after the reordered list has laid out — a ghost tile flies from the old rectangle to the row's new position in 320 ms. The real row is hidden at its destination while the ghost is in the air, so there is never a double image. The ghost's avatar hero is disabled so it cannot collide with the real row's hero.

The details are where the edge cases live:

  • The destination may be off-screen. If the pinned section scrolled out of view, the ghost lands at the list edge — top for a pin, bottom for an unpin — and fades out. The pin still applies.
  • A second pin may arrive mid-flight. The old ghost is cancelled before a new one starts.
  • The optimistic model update may not reach the expected state. In that case the flight is skipped; the list simply reorders as before.
  • The same chat can be mounted in several kept-alive tab pages. The row keys are namespaced per tab, so the flight finds the exact mounted row rather than a lookalike in another tab.

Pinned messages get the same treatment in the other direction. The message bubble measures a compact source rectangle, and the pinned bar is measured one frame after it mounts. A ghost — pin icon plus the same preview text — flies from the bubble to the bar in 340 ms and fades over its last fifth, revealing the real bar underneath. A missing source rectangle or a squeezed bar (the keyboard can do that) skips the flight; the pin still applies. Unpinning deliberately does not animate.

The whole thing is behind a new Settings → Motion → Pin animation toggle. It is on by default and follows the same rule as the other motion work: it only plays at the Full motion level. Reduced or Off means the old instant reorder, which is still perfectly usable.

The entrance bug hiding in the same pass

While adding the flights we fixed a bug that had been making list entrances look wrong. The staggered entrance used a SlideTransition with an offset of 18. SlideTransition treats that number as a fraction of the child's size, not a pixel count. Rows were starting roughly eighteen times their own height below their final position. The fix was to use a Transform.translate in logical pixels, so the rows now move 18 px.

The second half of the fix was about replays. Rows are disposed when they scroll far out of view, so a keyed entrance could replay when they came back. Each row now animates only on its first build for the lifetime of the Friends view. Rows revealed by keyboard navigation still skip the entrance on purpose.

The find chord should mean find

main+F is the browser-standard find chord. On GwinG it is Alt+F by default, or Ctrl+F if you choose the alternative in Settings → Shortcuts. Until now it only worked in some places, which made it feel unreliable: a shortcut that works sometimes is worse than no shortcut, because you stop trusting it.

It now focuses the search field on every search surface:

Surface What happens
Friends chats list Opens the in-place search box and focuses it. Pressing F again re-focuses the field and selects the current query. Escape still closes the box.
In-chat message search Opens the search panel and focuses its field. While the panel is open, its own handler owns F so the query can be re-focused and selected.
Search tab Alias of the existing focus chord, and F additionally selects the current query.
Contacts Focuses the friend filter above the list.
Create Group → Members Focuses the friend picker; inert on the other steps.
Group info → Add members Re-focuses the friend picker in the add-members sheet.

Two implementation details made the difference. On the chats list, the F check runs before the "the search field already has focus" early return, so the chord also works while you are typing. In the chat page, the search panel registers its own keyboard handler while it is mounted, because the chat page's shortcut scope is inactive when the panel is on top.

No new localization keys were needed. The help rows reuse the existing strings for "Search chats", "Search in chat", and "Focus the search box", so the cheat sheet stays consistent without translating the same idea twice.

Color as a signpost

The More tab has three navigation tiles: Settings, My Space, and Switch account. They were all the same default icon color. Now Settings uses the secondary color, My Space uses tertiary, and Switch account uses primary.

The palette is resolved once from the active theme, so the tiles follow light/dark mode and the user's accent preset. There is no behaviour change, no new copy, and no server sync. It is a small piece of wayfinding: three destinations, three visual anchors, one less moment of reading the labels.

FAQ

Does pinning still work if motion is disabled?

Yes. The data change is independent of the animation. With motion off, the row or message simply moves to its new place without the ghost flight.

Does Alt+F work while I am typing in the search box?

Yes. On the chats list the chord is checked before the focus check, and it selects the current query so you can replace it immediately.

Do the More tile colors change with the theme?

Yes. They are resolved from the active theme palette, so they follow the light/dark mode and accent preset rather than being fixed colors.

Why this batch matters

A language-exchange app is a place where people already have to work a little: find the right person, switch languages, read a translation, check a pronunciation. The interface should not add its own small uncertainties on top of that.

A pin that flies is not a feature. A find chord that works everywhere is not a feature. A colored tile is not a feature. But together they make the app feel like it is paying attention — and that is the point of polish work.

If you want the implementation-level companion to this piece, the shared media gallery and photo albums write-ups cover the same "small detail, real feel" territory.

Get GwinG — a language-exchange messenger with live translation.

  • Android: Google Play
  • Windows: .zip or installer
  • Linux: .deb or portable tarball

title: Drizzle vs Prisma in 2026: Benchmarks, Drizzle 1.0, Prisma 8 and Which to Choose
description:
I benchmarked Drizzle 0.45, the Drizzle 1.0 RC, Prisma 7 and the Prisma 8 RC against the same PostgreSQL 17 database. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Drizzle vs Prisma comes down to how you want to write data access in TypeScript. Drizzle is a thin, SQL-shaped query builder: your schema is TypeScript and every query maps closely to the SQL it sends. Prisma is a higher-level ORM: you write a schema file and get a generated, model-based client. Both are type-safe, and both work well with PostgreSQL and Next.js.

In October 2026 both are in the middle of a major version. Drizzle 1.0 is a release candidate while 0.45.4 is still npm latest. Prisma 8 is a release candidate that npm latest already installs. So I benchmarked all five combinations against the same PostgreSQL 17 database. On simple queries the gap was a tenth of a millisecond. On one common query pattern it was 6-19x, and the cause was the shape of the SQL, not the ORM.

TL;DR: Drizzle or Prisma in 2026?

Pick Drizzle if you think in SQL, deploy to serverless or edge, and want the smallest install and fastest cold start: 30 MB and about 35 ms bundled in my test. Pick Prisma 7 if you want the most guided workflow, a generated client and Prisma Migrate. Wait for GA before moving production to Drizzle 1.0 or Prisma 8.

Drizzle Prisma
Stable line 0.45.4 (npm latest) 7.10.1 (npm prev)
Next major 1.0.0-rc.4 (npm rc) 8.0.0-rc (npm latest)
Schema lives in TypeScript (pgTable) schema.prisma (7) or contract.prisma (8)
Code generation None prisma generate (7), prisma contract emit (8)
Query style SQL builder + relational db.query Model client (7), chained db.orm (8)
Migrations drizzle-kit generate / migrate / push Prisma Migrate
Production install (my test) 21-30 MB, 18 packages 329 MB (7), 130 MB (8)
Bundled cold start (my test) ~35 ms ~100 ms (7), ~370 ms (8 RC)

What is the difference between Drizzle and Prisma?

Drizzle defines tables in TypeScript and gives you a typed SQL builder, so db.select().from(users).where(...) reads like the SQL it sends, with no generate step. Prisma defines models in its own schema language, generates a client and hides SQL behind model methods. Drizzle is closer to the database; Prisma is closer to your domain model.

The same table in each:

```ts title="schema.ts (Drizzle 1.0)"
import { defineRelations } from "drizzle-orm";
import { boolean, index, integer, pgTable, serial, text, timestamp } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const users = pgTable("User", {
id: serial().primaryKey(),
email: text().notNull().unique(),
name: text(),
createdAt: timestamp({ precision: 3, mode: "date" }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export const posts = pgTable("Post", {
id: serial().primaryKey(),
title: text().notNull(),
published: boolean().notNull().default(false),
views: integer().notNull().default(0),
authorId: integer().notNull().references(() => users.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
}, (t) => [index("Post_authorId_idx").on(t.authorId)]);

export const relations = defineRelations({ users, posts }, (r) => ({
users: { posts: r.many.posts() },
posts: { author: r.one.users({ from: r.posts.authorId, to: r.users.id }) },
}));






```prisma title="prisma/schema.prisma (Prisma 7)"
model User {
  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  email     String   @unique
  name      String?
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  posts     Post[]
}

model Post {
  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  title     String
  published Boolean @default(false)
  views     Int     @default(0)
  authorId  Int
  author    User    @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@index([authorId])
}

How do queries compare in Drizzle and Prisma?

All four clients can fetch a user with their posts in one call. Drizzle 1.0 uses object filters in db.query, Prisma 7 uses findMany with include, and Prisma 8 chains .include("posts") on a collection. The type-safety level is the same; the difference is whether the code looks like SQL or like method calls.

These are the exact queries from my benchmark, and all of them type-check under strict:

```ts title="Fetch 20 users with their posts"
// Drizzle 0.45 (RQB v1)
db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true }, orderBy: (u, { asc }) => [asc(u.id)], offset, limit: 20 });

// Drizzle 1.0 (RQB v2)
db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, offset, limit: 20 });

// Prisma 7
prisma.user.findMany({ include: { posts: true }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, skip: offset, take: 20 });

// Prisma 8 RC
db.orm.public.User.include("posts").orderBy((u) => u.id.asc()).offset(offset).limit(20).all();




Drizzle also keeps its plain SQL builder (`db.select().from(posts).innerJoin(...)`) for anything the relational API does not cover. Prisma 7 falls back to `$queryRaw` or TypedSQL, and Prisma 8 has its own SQL builder. I covered Prisma 8's query API in detail in my [Prisma 8 guide](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/prisma-8).

## Is Drizzle faster than Prisma?

For single-row reads and inserts, barely. In my test every client answered a primary-key lookup in 0.12-0.20 ms against local PostgreSQL, and over a network that gap disappears. The real difference was in nested pagination: with `OFFSET`, single-query JSON loading got 6-11x slower than Prisma 7's two-query default.

### Benchmark setup

- PostgreSQL 17.11 on the same machine (8 vCPU Xeon, 15 GB RAM), Node.js 24.22.0, 1,000 users and 10,000 posts with an index on `Post.authorId`.
- Each case: 200 warm-up calls, then 2,000 timed calls. Each client ran 3 times, with inserted rows deleted before each run. The table shows the median of the three per-run medians.
- Versions: Prisma 7.10.1 with `@prisma/adapter-pg`, Drizzle 0.45.4, Drizzle 1.0.0-rc.4 (with and without `jit: true`), and Prisma 8 (`@prisma/orm-postgres` 8.0.0-rc.18).
- "Deep page" means 20 users plus their posts at `OFFSET` 0 to 960.

### Results (median, milliseconds)

| Query | Prisma 7.10.1 | Drizzle 0.45.4 | Drizzle 1.0 rc.4 | Drizzle 1.0 `jit` | Prisma 8 rc.18 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Find user by id | 0.150 | 0.129 | **0.121** | 0.136 | 0.195 |
| First page, 20 users + posts | 0.730 | 0.719 | **0.561** | 0.617 | 1.185 |
| Deep page, 20 users + posts | **0.749** | 4.650 | 5.164 | 5.287 | 8.060 |
| Insert one post | 0.168 | 0.146 | **0.139** | 0.164 | 0.208 |
| Process RSS after run | 289 MB | 251 MB | 295 MB | 296 MB | 404 MB |

Two things stand out. Drizzle 1.0 was the fastest at nearly everything, but `jit: true` made no measurable difference here. Drizzle documents it as "just-in-time compiled row mappers," and mapping 20 rows is not where the time goes. And the deep-page row looks like a Prisma win, but it isn't one, as the next section shows.

## Why are nested queries with OFFSET slow?

Drizzle and Prisma 8 load relations in one SQL statement, using a JSON subquery for each parent row. PostgreSQL applies `OFFSET` last, so it builds the JSON for every skipped row and then throws it away. At `OFFSET 960`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` showed the posts subquery running 980 times to return 20 users.

![Why OFFSET is slow with single-query relation loading: PostgreSQL builds JSON posts for every skipped row before applying OFFSET, while two-query loading and keyset pagination only touch 20 users](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792248750/fabwaseem/blog/drizzle-vs-prisma/diagram-sql.jpg)

This is the SQL Drizzle 0.45 generated (Drizzle 1.0 is nearly identical):



```sql
select "users"."id", "users"."email", "users"."name", "users"."createdAt", "users_posts"."data" as "posts"
from "User" "users"
left join lateral (
  select coalesce(json_agg(json_build_array(...)), '[]'::json) as "data"
  from "Post" "users_posts" where "users_posts"."authorId" = "users"."id"
) "users_posts" on true
order by "users"."id" asc limit $1 offset $2

The PostgreSQL docs warn about this directly: "The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient" (PostgreSQL 17, LIMIT and OFFSET). Here, each skipped row includes a full posts subquery.

Prisma 7 avoided it only because it sent two queries: the 20 users, then SELECT ... FROM "Post" WHERE "authorId" IN (...). When I turned on Prisma 7's relationJoins preview and set relationLoadStrategy: "join", the deep page went from 0.79 ms to 14.8 ms, the slowest result in the whole test. Prisma's relation queries docs say join uses "a combination of LATERAL JOINs and JSON aggregation", which is the same shape.

How do I fix slow nested pagination?

Use keyset (cursor) pagination instead of OFFSET: ask for "the 20 users after id X". PostgreSQL then seeks straight to the right index position and builds JSON for only 20 rows. In my test, Drizzle 1.0 deep pages dropped from 5.16 ms to 0.66 ms and Prisma 8 from 8.06 ms to 1.29 ms.

```ts title="Keyset pagination (both tested)"
// Drizzle 1.0
db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true }, where: { id: { gt: afterId } }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, limit: 20 });

// Prisma 8 RC
db.orm.public.User.where((u) => u.id.gt(afterId)).include("posts").orderBy((u) => u.id.asc()).limit(20).all();

// Prisma 7
prisma.user.findMany({ include: { posts: true }, cursor: { id: afterId }, skip: 1, take: 20, orderBy: { id: "asc" } });




Prisma's [pagination guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/queries/pagination) recommends the same: use cursor-based pagination "when you care more about performance and consistency as the dataset grows." If you need page numbers, run the parent query first and load children with a second `IN (...)` query. That is exactly what Prisma 7's default does.

## Which has a faster cold start, Drizzle or Prisma?

Drizzle, once bundled. With esbuild, importing the client and running the first query took about 35 ms with Drizzle, about 100 ms with Prisma 7 and about 370 ms with Prisma 8 RC. Unbundled, Drizzle was slower than Prisma 7, because Node loaded 425-528 separate Drizzle module files from `node_modules`.

| Median of 5 process starts | Prisma 7.10.1 | Drizzle 0.45.4 | Drizzle 1.0 rc.4 | Prisma 8 rc.18 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unbundled: import + first query | 55 + 89 ms | 400 + 31 ms | 699 + 18 ms | 494 + 30 ms |
| esbuild bundle: import + first query | 21 + 78 ms | 17 + 19 ms | 16 + 18 ms | 342 + 26 ms |
| Bundle size | 5.0 MB | 448 KB | 476 KB | 1.8 MB |

Next.js and most serverless builds bundle server code, so the bundled row is the one that usually applies. Prisma 7's import is fast, but its first query costs about 78 ms; the client ships its query compiler as base64-encoded WebAssembly, which is the likely cost of that first call. Prisma 8 RC's time goes into startup itself. A CPU profile showed the top functions inside arktype's `@ark/schema` and `@ark/util`, which Prisma 8 uses for runtime validation. That is RC behaviour and may change before GA.

## How big is Drizzle vs Prisma in node_modules?

Drizzle installed in 21 MB (0.45.4) or 30 MB (1.0 RC) with 18 packages, including `pg`. With `npm ci --omit=dev`, Prisma 7 came to 329 MB and 345 packages, and Prisma 8 RC to 130 MB and 118 packages. For Docker images and serverless size limits, that is the clearest difference between them.

Where the Prisma weight comes from, according to `npm ls` and `du`:

- **Prisma 7:** `@prisma/client` (72 MB) lists `prisma` and `typescript` as optional peer dependencies. My project had both as devDependencies, so npm kept them in the production tree, along with the CLI, `@prisma/studio-core` (43 MB) and `@prisma/dev`.
- **Prisma 8 RC:** `@prisma/orm-postgres` depends on `@prisma/orm-toolchain`, which brings `typescript`, `prettier` and rolldown into a production install.

If image size matters, bundle the server and copy only the output. My [Next.js AI starter kit](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/nextjs-ai-starter-kit) uses Drizzle partly for this reason.

## How do migrations compare?

Both generate SQL migration files from your schema. drizzle-kit diffs your TypeScript schema and writes plain SQL, and `push` can sync a dev database without a migration file. Prisma Migrate diffs `schema.prisma`, keeps history in `prisma/migrations` and manages a shadow database for `migrate dev`. Both let you edit the generated SQL before applying it.

Drizzle 1.0 changed the folder layout. `npx drizzle-kit generate --name init` created this:



```text
drizzle/
└── 20261017144733_init/
    ├── migration.sql
    └── snapshot.json

There is no meta/_journal.json any more. The Drizzle v1 upgrade guide says this removes "potential Git conflicts with the journal file," and drizzle-kit generate now runs commutativity checks that flag migrations on two branches that change the same thing. Run npx drizzle-kit up once to convert an existing 0.x migrations folder.

Prisma Migrate is still the more guided tool: prisma migrate dev uses a shadow database to detect drift and offers to reset the dev database when history and schema disagree. One Prisma 7 change to know: seeding no longer runs automatically during migrate dev or migrate reset; you run npx prisma db seed yourself. See the Prisma Migrate docs.

What changed in Drizzle 1.0?

Drizzle 1.0 removes the old relational query API (RQB v1) and replaces it with defineRelations() and RQB v2. Filters and ordering become plain objects. Validators move into the package as drizzle-orm/zod and similar, getTableColumns becomes getColumns, and drizzle-kit drops the migration journal. It also adds MSSQL and CockroachDB dialects.

From the official v0 to v1 changes page:

Area 0.x 1.0
Relations relations() per table One defineRelations() call
Filters where: (u, { eq }) => eq(u.id, 1) where: { id: 1 }
Casing drizzle({ casing: "snake_case" }) snakeCase.table(...)
Validation drizzle-zod package drizzle-orm/zod
Migrations meta/_journal.json One folder per migration
push / pull public schema only by default All schemas by default
Introspection ~10 s under 1 s (Drizzle's figure)

The relations v1 to v2 guide covers the query migration step by step. As of October 17, 2026, npm latest is still 0.45.4 (published October 8) and rc is 1.0.0-rc.4 (June 27).

Should I use Prisma 8 or Prisma 7?

For production today, Prisma 7. Prisma 8 is a rewrite with a new contract file, a new runtime package and a chained query API, and it is still a release candidate. In my test it was also the slowest to start and the heaviest per process. Prisma 8 is worth trying on a branch now; plan the switch after GA.

Note that npm install prisma already installs Prisma 8, so pin prisma@7 and @prisma/client@7 in existing projects. The full migration path, with the contract and the new client, is in my Prisma 8 guide.

Which should I choose for Next.js?

Both work in Next.js 16 server components, route handlers and server actions. Choose Drizzle for Vercel functions, edge routes or small Docker images, where cold start and install size matter. Choose Prisma 7 when a team wants one schema file, generated types and Prisma Migrate's guardrails more than they want SQL control.

Your situation Pick
You think in SQL and want queries that map one-to-one Drizzle
Serverless, edge or tight cold-start budget Drizzle
Small Docker image or function size limit Drizzle
Team wants one schema file and a generated client Prisma 7
Guided migrations with drift detection and a shadow DB Prisma 7
Existing Prisma 6/7 app Stay on Prisma 7, pin it, test 8 on a branch
New app starting this month Drizzle 0.45 or Prisma 7, and plan the move to 1.0 / 8
Paginating nested data Either: use keyset pagination, not deep OFFSET

Auth libraries matter here too. Better Auth 1.7 lists both drizzle-orm (0.45.2+ or 1.0 RC) and Prisma (5 to 7) as supported peers, but not Prisma 8 yet.

Common Drizzle and Prisma mistakes

  • Deep OFFSET with nested relations. Both ORMs build JSON for every skipped row. Use keyset pagination or a second query.
  • Turning on Prisma relationJoins everywhere. In my test it was slower for paginated includes. Measure per query.
  • Unpinned prisma installs. latest is Prisma 8 RC. Pin major versions in Prisma 7 projects.
  • Expecting jit: true to fix slow queries. It speeds up row mapping, not the SQL.
  • Running Drizzle unbundled on serverless. It loads hundreds of module files at startup. Bundle the server output.
  • Upgrading to Drizzle 1.0 without drizzle-kit up. Old migration folders must be converted first.

Related: choosing primary keys for these schemas? In UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18 I benchmarked uuidv7() against UUIDv4 and bigint on 10M rows, with tested Prisma and Drizzle setups for a database-side uuidv7() default.

Related: building the API layer with NestJS? My NestJS 12 migration guide covers the v11 to v12 upgrade, Zod validation (28% faster than class-validator in my test) and v11 vs v12 benchmarks.

Key takeaways

  • Drizzle is a SQL-first TypeScript query builder with no code generation; Prisma is a schema-first ORM with a generated client. Both are fully type-safe.
  • On simple queries, all five clients I tested answered within 0.12-0.21 ms of local PostgreSQL, so raw speed rarely decides the choice.
  • Single-query relation loading plus a deep OFFSET was 6-19x slower than two queries, whether it came from Drizzle, Prisma 8 or Prisma 7 with relationJoins. Keyset pagination fixed it.
  • Bundled, Drizzle started in about 35 ms, Prisma 7 in about 100 ms and Prisma 8 RC in about 370 ms.
  • Production installs were 21-30 MB for Drizzle, 329 MB for Prisma 7 and 130 MB for Prisma 8 RC.
  • Drizzle 1.0 and Prisma 8 are both release candidates on October 17, 2026; use Drizzle 0.45 or Prisma 7 in production and pin your versions.

FAQ

Is Drizzle better than Prisma?

Neither is better for everyone. Drizzle suits developers who want SQL-shaped queries, no code generation, small installs and fast serverless cold starts. Prisma suits teams that want one schema file, a generated model client and guided migrations. Both are fully type-safe, and on simple queries their speed was within 0.1 ms in my test.

Is Drizzle faster than Prisma?

Slightly, on most queries. Drizzle 1.0 RC was fastest on lookups, first pages and inserts, but every client stayed between 0.12 and 0.21 ms on simple queries against local PostgreSQL. The bigger differences were cold start (Drizzle about 35 ms bundled vs about 100 ms for Prisma 7) and nested pagination with OFFSET.

Why is my nested query with OFFSET slow?

Drizzle, Prisma 8 and Prisma 7 with relationJoins load relations in one SQL statement, with a JSON subquery per parent row. PostgreSQL applies OFFSET last, so it builds JSON for every skipped row. At OFFSET 960 the posts subquery ran 980 times. Use keyset pagination (WHERE id > lastId) or a second query.

Is Drizzle 1.0 stable?

Not yet. On October 17, 2026, npm latest for drizzle-orm is 0.45.4, published October 8, and the rc tag is 1.0.0-rc.4 from June 27. Drizzle 1.0 replaces relational queries v1 with defineRelations and RQB v2 and changes the migration folder layout, so test it on a branch first.

Should I use Prisma 8 or Prisma 7?

Use Prisma 7 in production for now. Prisma 8 is a release candidate with a new contract file, a new runtime package and a chained query API. In my test it also had the slowest cold start, about 370 ms bundled. Note that npm install prisma already installs Prisma 8, so pin prisma@7 in existing projects.

Which is better for serverless, Drizzle or Prisma?

Drizzle. Bundled with esbuild, importing Drizzle and running the first query took about 35 ms, against about 100 ms for Prisma 7 and about 370 ms for Prisma 8 RC. Drizzle's production install was 21 to 30 MB, while Prisma 7's came to 329 MB with npm ci --omit=dev.

Does Drizzle have migrations like Prisma Migrate?

Yes. drizzle-kit generate diffs your TypeScript schema into SQL migration files, drizzle-kit migrate applies them, and drizzle-kit push syncs a dev database directly. Drizzle 1.0 stores each migration in its own folder with no journal file and checks for conflicting migrations across branches. Prisma Migrate adds a shadow database and drift detection.

Does Better Auth work with Drizzle and Prisma?

Yes, with both. Better Auth 1.7.10 lists drizzle-orm 0.45.2 or newer, including the 1.0 release candidates, and Prisma 5, 6 and 7 as supported peer dependencies. Prisma 8 is not in its supported range yet, so a Better Auth app on Prisma should stay on Prisma 7 for now.

title: A Green Test Suite Can Still Hide a Broken PR: 5 Questions to Ask Before Merging
description:
AI coding assistants can write implementation code and tests in minutes. The problem is that both can look correct while the behavior that matters remains untested.

A passing test suite is useful evidence, but it isn't proof that a change is correct.

I've been thinking about this problem while building a Java-focused, AI-powered pull request reviewer. These are five questions I believe developers should ask before approving a PR, especially when AI helped write the code or its tests.

1. What behavior is this test actually verifying?

Start with the expected behavior, not the number of assertions.

Imagine a service that should reject a payment when the account has insufficient funds. A test might call the service and verify that it returns a response.

But what if the test never checks whether the payment was rejected?

The test can execute successfully without verifying the important business rule.

Ask yourself:

  • What behavior should this test protect?
  • What result would prove that behavior?
  • Would the test fail if the behavior were broken?

If you cannot answer these questions, the test may provide less confidence than its green status suggests.

2. Could this test pass without checking anything meaningful?

Consider this JUnit example:

java
@test
void shouldRejectInvalidPayment() {
paymentService.processPayment(invalidPayment);

assertTrue(true);

}

The test passes as long as execution reaches the assertion. It doesn't establish that the payment was rejected.

A more meaningful test would verify the expected outcome, using the appropriate assertion for the application's behavior.

For example, if the contract requires an exception:

java
@test
void shouldRejectInvalidPayment() {
assertThrows(
InvalidPaymentException.class,
() -> paymentService.processPayment(invalidPayment)
);
}

This is only an illustration. The correct assertion depends on the actual application contract.

The important principle is simple: an assertion should verify the behavior the test claims to protect.

3. Are mocks hiding the behavior we need to verify?

Mocks are valuable when testing dependencies, failure conditions, and isolated units of code. But excessive mocking can make a test appear meaningful while avoiding the behavior that matters.

Suppose a test claims to verify that an order is saved correctly, but it mocks the repository and only verifies that save() was called.

That may establish that a method was invoked. It doesn't necessarily establish that the order was persisted correctly or that the resulting state is correct.

Before approving a heavily mocked test, ask:

  • Is the test checking an outcome or just an interaction?
  • Is the mocked dependency the behavior being tested?
  • Would an incorrect implementation still satisfy the assertions?
  • Should an integration test verify the real interaction between components?

Don't remove mocks indiscriminately. Choose the test boundary that matches the behavior you're trying to protect.

4. Does the test cover the change described in the PR?

A PR can change behavior without changing the test that originally covered it.

For example, a developer might change the conditions under which a user can access a resource. The existing test may still verify the successful access path while failing to check the newly introduced restriction.

Compare the change with the tests:

  • Which behavior changed?
  • Which existing tests exercise that behavior?
  • What new failure scenario could the change introduce?
  • Are the expected outcomes explicit?

This is also where repository context matters. The affected behavior might involve callers or related files that aren't part of the diff.

A reviewer should consider those relationships rather than treating each changed line as an isolated unit.

5. Would the test catch a deliberately broken implementation?

This is a useful thought experiment.

Imagine the implementation contains a defect that violates the requirement. Would the test fail?

If the answer is no, the test may not protect that requirement.

Mutation testing takes this idea further by making deliberate changes to the implementation and checking whether the tests detect them. It can provide stronger evidence than simply counting assertions, although it has its own limitations and costs.

You don't need a full mutation-testing setup to start asking the question during code review. But actually running tests against controlled mutations is a separate validation step, not something a normal passing test run proves.

The practical takeaway

Before merging a PR, especially one produced with AI assistance, ask:

  1. Does the test verify the intended behavior?
  2. Could it pass without a meaningful assertion?
  3. Are mocks hiding the behavior that matters?
  4. Do the tests cover the changed behavior and relevant regression scenarios?
  5. Would the tests detect a broken implementation?

These checks won't guarantee that every defect is caught. They can, however, help identify tests that create confidence without providing enough evidence.

AI can help write code and tests faster. The review process still needs to establish what those tests actually prove.

Disclosure: I'm building CodeGuard AI, a self-hosted AI-powered pull request reviewer for GitHub. It reviews PR changes alongside repository context and supports custom team review rules. It does not currently run mutation testing or guarantee detection of every weak test assertion.

title: We changed one word in a prompt and broke a feature nobody was watching
description:
The change was one word in a system prompt. "Concise" became "brief." The diff was a single line. What broke: a summarization feature that our team judged by vibes — read the output, seems fine, ship it — had started omitting a detail that mattered, and three weeks passed before anyone noticed. Nobody was to blame individually. There was just no mechanism in place that could catch it, because we treated prompts like config when they behave like code.

30-second takeaway

  • 3-week bug discovery window collapsed to 60 seconds with prompt regression guards
  • "Concise" vs "brief" — one-word diff → feature silently broke for 8% of users (my own users)
  • Prompts are code: same regression-test arguments apply, and almost nobody I know actually gates them in CI (my own observation, not a measured rate)
  • CI-native: eval gates run where ships already get gated, no manual checklists

(Confession: I changed one word in a system prompt — "concise" to "brief" — and a summarization feature silently degraded for 8% of users (my own users). Nobody noticed for three weeks. Three weeks! I treated prompts like config when they behave like code. Same arrogance, different medium.)

(Caveat: your eval set is only as good as the cases you pick. Ship broken tests = ship broken prompt. And eval sets drift too — revisit them quarterly.)

Prompts are code without a test suite

Every argument for regression testing applies to prompts: changes have non-local effects, behavior varies across inputs you didn't test, and "it seems fine on the two examples I tried" is exactly the confidence level that produces three-week-late bug reports. But most teams' prompt testing process is a human squinting at a handful of outputs — slow, inconsistent, and not something that runs before every ship.

Eval checklists instead of vibes

TestPilot turns prompt testing into a repeatable gate: paste your prompt and the expected behavior, get an eval checklist and a version regression guard — so "brief" vs "concise" gets compared across a real set of cases before it ships, not discovered by users after. It's aimed at dev and QA teams shipping LLM-powered features, with CI integration so the check runs where ships already get gated, and version compare so you can see what actually changed when you touched the prompt.

The version-compare framing matters. The unit of change in an LLM app is the prompt+model+params combination, and "what did this change affect" is only answerable if you can diff behavior across versions, not just diff the text.

The realistic version of this practice

Full honesty about costs: building an eval set is real work, the checklist you define is only as good as your understanding of what the feature should do, and LLM outputs are probabilistic — expect some eval noise, and design thresholds with that in mind rather than demanding perfect determinism. Start embarrassingly small: ten cases that capture what "correct" means for your feature, including the inputs that broke it before. Ten good cases beat a hundred mediocre ones, and the set grows every time reality surprises you.

What it is not

It doesn't score abstract "quality" — it checks the behaviors you specify, which means the hard part (deciding what correct looks like) stays with you. It won't catch biases or failure modes absent from your case set. And CI integration gates what you run it against; a feature with no eval cases has no guard, just the vibes you started with.

The one-feature start

Pick the single LLM feature whose silent failure would embarrass you most. Write down what it must always do and must never do. Turn that into ten test cases, and run the next prompt change against them in TestPilot before it ships. Free to try — and if the first regression it catches pays for the hour you spent, that's the moment prompt testing stops being an idea and becomes a habit.
