title: Properties Without Witnesses Are Decorations: A Falsifiability Gate for Agent Patches
description:
A property that passes on the patched tree and on the pre-patch tree carries no information. That is the first thing to measure, before you trust any property an agent wrote for you.

Most agent-written property tests fail this way. The agent reads the diff, writes an invariant that the new code obviously satisfies, and the suite goes green in both trees. The test is not wrong. It is simply unable to distinguish the two states, which makes it a decoration, not a check.

This post describes a gate with three rules and one artifact. Properties need a committed witness and a measured detection rate on the baseline. Fixtures must be isolated per sample, verified by transcript hashing. Flaky-frozen tests are forbidden from acting as oracles. The gate is small enough to run on every agent patch.

The three roles, and what each one can lie about

Role What it claims How it lies Gate check
Property "This invariant holds for the domain" Domain is one hand-picked example Fail-rate on pre-patch tree ≥ floor
Fixture "Setup is deterministic" Sample N sees state left by sample N-1 Set of per-sample transcript hashes has size 1
Freeze "This test is temporarily excused" Frozen test becomes the only oracle Freeze list ∩ oracle set = ∅

Each row fails independently. A property with a real domain can still be useless if the fixture leaks state between samples; a clean fixture cannot save an invariant that holds by construction.

Step 1: Commit a witness next to every property

A witness is the concrete input that proves the property can fail. It is not a test case the agent is allowed to invent during the run — it lives in the repository, reviewable, in its own file.

{
  "id": "inv_total_never_negative",
  "seed": 20261018,
  "input": {"lines": [{"qty": 1, "unit_cents": -5}], "discount_cents": 0},
  "expected_on_baseline": "fail",
  "expected_on_patched": "pass"
}

The two expected_* fields are the whole point. On the merge-base tree the witness must reproduce the bug. On the patched tree it must pass. If the witness passes on both, the patch fixed nothing the witness can see, and the review should stop there.

# gate/witness.py — runnable sketch; plugin points are stubbed
import json, subprocess

def replay(tree_dir, prop_id):
    w = json.load(open(f"witnesses/{prop_id}.json"))
    return subprocess.run(
        ["python", "-m", "props.run", prop_id, json.dumps(w["input"])],
        cwd=tree_dir, capture_output=True, text=True,
    ).returncode == 0

Step 2: Measure detection power on the baseline, not on the patch

Passing the witness is necessary and cheap. The expensive question is whether the property generalizes past that one input. Sample the declared domain under a seeded generator on the pre-patch worktree, and count how often the invariant fails.

# gate/power.py
import random

def detection_power(prop, baseline_tree, gen, run_invariant, fixture_hash):
    rng = random.Random(prop.seed)
    fails, transcripts = 0, set()
    for _ in range(prop.samples):
        example, transcript = gen.sample(prop.domain, rng)
        transcripts.add(fixture_hash(transcript))       # rule 2, below
        if not run_invariant(baseline_tree, prop.invariant, example):
            fails += 1
    return fails / prop.samples, transcripts

Set power_floor from your own baseline run, not from this post. A property whose fail-rate on the buggy tree is near zero is a description of the current code, not a check on it. A fail-rate near one usually means the generator produces out-of-domain inputs and the property is failing for the wrong reason.

Rates in between need a human eye. There is no universal threshold; the number is a policy knob your repo owns and reviews.

Step 3: Isolate fixtures per sample and prove it with hashes

Property sampling multiplies whatever your fixture does. If setup writes rows, mutates a module-level cache, or advances a clock, sample 12 is running against sample 11's leftovers — and your fail-rate is measuring ordering, not behavior.

Give each sample a reset hook and hash the setup transcript (touched tables, env keys, temp paths, fake clock value). Across a run, the set of hashes must have exactly one member.

power, transcripts = detection_power(prop, baseline_tree, gen, run_invariant, fixture_hash)
if len(transcripts) != 1:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: fixture state varies across samples → {sorted(transcripts)[:3]}")
if power < prop.power_floor:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: detection power {power:.2f} < floor {prop.power_floor:.2f}")

A set of size greater than one is a deterministic, reproducible red — the kind of failure you can hand back to the agent without a discussion.

Step 4: Freeze the flaky tests, and keep them out of the oracle set

Freezing a flaky test so the suite stays green is a reasonable maintenance move. Letting that frozen test quietly become the only thing validating an agent patch is not.

Pass the freeze list into the property runner explicitly. Any intersection between the frozen set and the tests the property run actually executed is a hard failure, not a warning.

frozen = {l.strip() for l in open("tests/frozen.txt") if l.strip()}
ran    = run_property_suite(patched_tree, prop.id)      # returns test node ids
leaked = frozen & ran
if leaked:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: frozen tests used as oracle → {sorted(leaked)}")

The same list should carry an expiry date per entry. A freeze without an end date silently becomes a permanent hole in coverage.

Step 5: Wire it as one gate with three exit codes

Run the three steps in a fixed order and stop at the first failure. Exit code 0 means the property is falsifiable, its fixture is deterministic, and its oracle is un-frozen. Anything else is a reviewable artifact, not a vibe.

git worktree add ../baseline "$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)"
python -m gate.run --prop inv_total_never_negative \
  --baseline ../baseline --patched . --samples 200 --power-floor 0.10
# 0 = accepted, 1 = property rejected, 2 = harness error
git worktree remove ../baseline

Per-property cost is samples × setup_time. Two hundred samples across a ten-property patch is a few minutes of wall clock on a modest machine — acceptable per pull request, not acceptable on every keystroke.

The proposal side of this loop does not need a frontier model; scanning a diff and drafting invariants is well inside what free model access handles, and running the sampler on the free server option keeps the 200-sample loop off a laptop that is already running the app under test. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Availability of free tiers is not a guarantee — check the current terms on your own account before wiring it into CI, and do not send proprietary code or credentials to a shared runner.

Limitations and who should skip this

  • Property sampling only works on domains you can generate. Stateful protocols and payment flows usually need a hand-built model first.
  • The power floor is a heuristic. It catches decorative properties; it does not prove the invariant is the right one.
  • Suites with heavy fixtures (containers, seeded production snapshots) will spend the whole budget on setup resets.
  • Teams with data-residency constraints should run the harness entirely in-house; the remote runner is a cost convenience, not a requirement.

Start with the witness registry. It is the cheapest file to commit and the fastest way to discover that half of your agent's properties pass on both trees. When the power floor turns out to be the number you have to lower, that lower number is the finding worth writing down.

title: How Factory scaled its cloud backend to one billion monthly requests on Vercel
description:
Factory on Vercel

  • One billion backend API requests served daily

  • 350ms p95 response time

  • Scaled backend, internal tooling, and security without a dedicated infrastructure team

Factory's mission is to bring autonomy to every phase of the software development lifecycle, from signals to production. Not to replace engineering judgment, but to automate the repetitive work around it, giving engineers more time to focus on the decisions that matter most. To deliver this enterprise-grade platform, Factory adopted their ideal operation model internally: remaining lean and agile by deploying Droids to manage routine workloads, so their engineers could focus strictly on building the product.

As Factory scaled from a simple web app into a multi-surface platform, serving everyone from individual developers to enterprises with tens of thousands of engineers, their backend scaled alongside them. Today, a single Next.js backend on Vercel powers every surface, handling one billion daily requests across API routes, middleware, and webhook handlers, without becoming a separate engineering project.

Next.js as a full-stack backend for cloud SaaS: API routes, middleware, and backend logic at scale

Most teams think of Next.js as a frontend framework. Factory runs its entire cloud backend on it:

  • API routes handle the customer-facing API, which launched in its own section of their Next.js app

  • Middleware manages authentication and routing logic across every surface

  • Webhook handlers and log drain pipelines run alongside the web platform, feeding analytics downstream

As Factory grew rapidly, the same backend absorbed every new workload. None of it required standing up separate infrastructure or making a new vendor decision. The only areas that required tuning were memory limits and function duration. Both scaled up without incident. Fluid compute keeps functions warm across requests, removing the cold start penalty that makes traditional serverless a liability for latency-sensitive workloads. The result is a p95 response time of 350ms or below.

Three years in, the trajectory has been smooth growth without the overhead that typically comes with it.

Shipping internal tools without pulling engineers off product

Non-technical teams were bottlenecked on engineering

When an account executive needed an internal analytics dashboard or a solution architect needed to deploy a customer prototype, the request went to engineering. Every context switch cost the team shipping product, and they pointed their own product at Vercel to solve the problem.

Droids hit Vercel's APIs to build and deploy autonomously

Factory's non-technical teams now use their own Droids in the Factory Desktop App or CLI to build what they need and deploy directly to Vercel. Droids reach Vercel programmatically to handle configuration, builds, and deployments end-to-end. Engineers set guardrails and review high-stakes decisions, and Droids handle everything else. That workflow produces dozens of deployments a day across the team, and a growing library of internal tools:

  • Internal analytics dashboards that pull directly from Factory's analytics databases and software tools

  • Tailored, customer-specific demos that solutions engineers can build and deploy in minutes

  • Custom utilities for one-off internal workflows

Securing a consumer-facing product with minimal security overhead

Going self-serve exposed Factory's backend to a new category of threat

When Factory opened self-serve signups, attacks from automated traffic followed. Bots created fraudulent accounts, and requests flooded in from bad IPs. The team needed route-level protection at the network layer quickly.

Observability and WAF handle protection at the network level

Vercel Observability gives the team visibility into what's hitting the API, surfacing traffic patterns and problematic IPs as they appear. The Web Application Firewall handles enforcement: the team blocks bad actors with route-level rules, while rate limiting and DDoS protection run continuously beneath the surface.

What's next

Factory uses their own Droids to build Factory. Every internal automation is a future product feature, stress-tested on their own infrastructure first. That loop is about to run at a different scale.

Factory is growing rapidly as it continues to implement and expand its pioneering vision towards autonomous software factories at scale.

About Factory: Factory is the platform enterprises use to build and operate their software factory: a 24/7 system that continuously turns signals into production software across the entire lifecycle. It's model-agnostic, deploys anywhere from cloud to fully private, and keeps engineers in control as the governance layer. Factory was founded in 2023 by Matan Grinberg and Eno Reyes and is headquartered in San Francisco.

title: Permissions Hadn't Changed, but QA Said 'I Can't Create' — Answering with a Table Uncovered an Unreachable Branch
description:
The question

QA for our internal business system sent me this:

I can't create a project. Did it change so that only executives can create them now?

Short answer: no, the permission rules hadn't changed at all. But the question turned out to be valuable. While building a permission table to answer it, I cross-checked the code — and found a branch that could never execute. Dead code, alive in production. Here's how it happened.

Background: we had just changed how roles are stored

Shortly before this, we changed how job roles are modeled.

  • Before: one role per user
  • After: one role per affiliation (seat) — to support concurrent posts and secondments, a user can hold multiple affiliations, each with its own role

The project-creation rules themselves were untouched:

Role Can create projects in
Chairman / Secretary Entire group
President / Executive Own company
Department head / Section chief / Team leader Own org and below
Team member Nowhere

The "did the system change?" question almost certainly came because of that recent refactor. When a system is being actively changed, every unrelated symptom starts looking like a side effect of "that change."

Trying to answer with a table, I read the code

I could have just replied "nothing changed," but for permission questions, a table is the most reliable answer. To build the table above, I re-read the actual check:

Scope scopeOf(long userSeq, Role role) {
    if (role == CHAIRMAN || role == SECRETARY) return companyWide();
    if (role == PRESIDENT || role == EXECUTIVE) return ownCompany();
    if (role == TEAM_MEMBER) return denied();  // ← early return

    // Per-affiliation branch (added in the refactor):
    // even if the primary affiliation is "team member",
    // a section chief seat elsewhere can create under that org
    for (Affiliation a : affiliationsOf(userSeq)) {
        if (a.role().isLeaderOrAbove()) {
            return orgScope(a.org());
        }
    }
    return denied();
}

See it? The for loop was added during the per-affiliation refactor, precisely to handle "primary affiliation is team member, but section chief somewhere else." But above it, the pre-refactor early return for TEAM_MEMBER was never removed.

Since the role argument carries the primary affiliation's role, any user whose primary role is team member hits return denied() on line 3 — and the loop below it never runs. The code we wrote for concurrent-post users had never executed, not even once.

The compiler can't warn you about this. Syntactically, both branches are reachable. Code written after a return statement triggers an unreachable-code error, but a branch that's unreachable because of how the conditions combine can only be found by a human reading the code — or by a test.

The fix: drop TEAM_MEMBER from the early return

The fix itself was small: stop short-circuiting on "team member," and read the affiliations before judging.

Scope scopeOf(long userSeq, Role role) {
    if (role == CHAIRMAN || role == SECRETARY) return companyWide();
    if (role == PRESIDENT || role == EXECUTIVE) return ownCompany();

    // If any seat is leader-or-above: that org and below. Otherwise: denied.
    for (Affiliation a : affiliationsOf(userSeq)) {
        if (a.role().isLeaderOrAbove()) {
            return orgScope(a.org());
        }
    }
    return denied();
}

I verified with a user whose primary affiliation is a team member but who holds a section-chief seat at another company:

  • the creation-scope API returns allowed: true with the section-chief org
  • a project-creation POST under that section returns 201
  • creation under the primary org still returns 403

One more thing: deployment timing. If the server restarts while QA is in the middle of testing exactly this permission area, they get confused by unrelated errors. I scheduled the release for 14:00, right after lunch break, so the restart landed between test sessions.

Answering QA

The answer to the original question was simple: "The permission rules haven't changed — here's who can create where," with the table attached. And for the cases where creation still fails, I asked three things:

  • which account, and that account's affiliations and roles
  • whether the create button is missing or clicking it errors out (and if so, the exact message)
  • which organization was selected as the creation target

A bare "it doesn't work" is unreproducible for permission bugs, so having these triage questions templated saves a lot of round trips.

Takeaways

  • When you add a branch below an early return, check that the branch is actually reachable. The compiler won't catch condition-level unreachability; only a human read or a test will. If we'd had a concurrent-post user in the test suite from day one, we'd have caught this at refactor time.
  • Answer permission questions with a table. Building the table forces you to re-read the implementation, and mismatches between the rules and the code — like this dead branch — surface along the way.
  • Schedule permission-related deploys outside QA's testing hours. A single restart at the wrong moment costs you trust.

A naive-sounding "did the system change?" ended up unearthing a latent bug. I'm grateful for the question.

title: Anatomy of a Paid AI Video Job: What Happens Between Upload and MP4
description:
A walkthrough of the lifecycle behind a two-photo trend video generator: validation, quotes, credit holds, async rendering and data expiry.

Consumer AI video looks like a single button: upload photos, get a clip. Behind that button sits a long-running, paid, failure-prone job, and most of the product work goes into making that job predictable for someone who just wants a funny video of their friends.

This post follows one job through AIHotelLobby.win, a single-purpose tool that recasts the Hotel Lobby trend video with two uploaded portraits. It makes a good example because its public guides, help page, terms and privacy policy spell out every stage, from upload checks to how long each file lives. Everything below is based on those pages; the snippets are simplified sketches of the behavior they describe.

Stage 1: Reject bad input before anything expensive happens

A GPU minute costs far more than a file check, so the cheapest quality control is at the upload box. Each photo has to be a JPG, PNG or WebP, at least 512 × 512 pixels and no larger than 10 MB, showing one clearly visible adult.

const ACCEPTED = ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'];
const MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024;

function checkPhoto(type: string, bytes: number, w: number, h: number): string | null {
  if (!ACCEPTED.includes(type)) return 'Use a JPG, PNG or WebP image';
  if (bytes > MAX_BYTES) return 'Keep the file under 10 MB';
  if (w < 512 || h < 512) return 'Use an image at least 512 × 512 pixels';
  return null;
}

Two details worth noting. Metadata is stripped when the images are prepared, which removes location data people forget their phones attach. And the docs are explicit that these checks only cover the file: they do not verify identity, age or consent. Being honest about what validation can't do is part of the design.

Stage 2: Keep the draft alive through the login wall

Users can pick both photos, assign left and right, and choose length and sound before creating an account. The draft is kept on the device while they sign in, so the login wall doesn't throw away their work. Signing out clears it.

This is a conversion detail as much as a technical one. The moment someone is asked to sign in is the moment they are most likely to leave, and making them redo the upload afterwards doubles that risk.

Stage 3: Quote first, then hold the credits

After sign-in, the photos upload privately and the server returns a quote: length, format and credit cost. Prices are fixed per length (5 seconds is 30 credits, 10 is 50 and 15 is 70), and the quote is pinned to the task.

type Quote = {
  durationSeconds: 5 | 10 | 15;
  aspect: '16:9';
  audio: 'original' | 'silent';
  credits: 30 | 50 | 70;
  configRevision: string; // the model, template and price recorded for this task
};

The terms make the pinning explicit: prices and models can change for new requests, but an existing task keeps the provider, settings and price recorded in its quote. Confirming the quote reserves the credits. They are captured only after a valid video has been stored, and released if the task definitively fails. Buying credits is a separate flow and never starts a job by itself.

Stage 4: Hand off to the model, then let the user leave

The configured model is Kling 3.0 Omni, accessed through KIE as the API provider. (A second model, Seedance 2.0 Mini, is integrated but not enabled for customers.) The provider receives the two photos, the reference video and the instructions for that task.

From here everything is asynchronous. The published examples list render times from about three to seven and a half minutes, which is far too long to hold a browser tab hostage. The user can close the page; the task keeps running and shows up in My videos on any device signed in to the same account.

The hard case is a timeout during submission: the provider may or may not have accepted the job. Releasing the credits risks giving away a video that will finish anyway; capturing them risks charging for nothing. The answer here is a holding state:

type Job =
  | { state: 'reserved' }
  | { state: 'running' }
  | { state: 'needs_review' } // submission outcome unknown; credits stay held
  | { state: 'completed'; videoKey: string } // credits captured
  | { state: 'failed' }; // confirmed failure; credits released

The page on credits and task recovery tells users what this means for them: losing the connection does not stop generation, an uncertain task keeps its credits reserved while it is checked, and they should follow that same task rather than start a duplicate. Credit returns and cash refunds are also kept separate, which saves a lot of support confusion.

Stage 5: Deliver briefly, then delete

Personal photos are a liability the moment you no longer need them, and the retention schedule reflects that:

Data How long it stays
Validated photos never submitted for a task 24 hours
Photos needed by an active or uncertain task Up to 48 hours
Task inputs after the task reaches a final state Scheduled to expire within 24 hours
Finished videos 7 days
A download link 5 minutes

Downloads use short-lived signed links. Deleting a file stops new links from being issued, though a link already handed out can work until it expires, and the privacy policy says so plainly. It also notes that provider copies and backups follow their own schedules, which is the kind of caveat most products leave out.

What's worth copying

  • Validate cheaply, and say what validation can't check.
  • Let the draft survive authentication.
  • Pin the quote to the task, so a price or model change never rewrites a job already in flight.
  • Model the unknown state explicitly instead of guessing between refund and charge.
  • Publish retention times as numbers, not "as long as necessary".

None of this is specific to trend videos. Any product that runs a slow, paid job on someone's personal media faces the same five stages, and users notice when one of them is handled carelessly.

AIHotelLobby.win is an independent service. It is not an official Kling, Seedance or KIE product and is not affiliated with the artists behind "Hotel Lobby". Details come from its public pages as of October 18, 2026.

title: PhotoCraft Review: I Tested the Free, Open-Source Photoshop Alternative With 4 Real Edits
description:
Photoshop costs $22.99 a month. PhotoCraft costs $0, it's open source, and in under three weeks it passed 66,000 stars on GitHub.

So I put it to work on my Mac mini M4 with four real edits, the kind most of us actually do: cutting someone out, a caption meme, fixing a dull photo, and text for a meme video. Here is what worked, step by step, and what it still can't do.

▶ Full video: https://youtu.be/O4necNCA5D4

What is PhotoCraft?

PhotoCraft is a free copy of Photoshop, rebuilt from scratch in the Rust language. It's part of ArtCraft, a family of open-source clones of creative apps.

  • Open source: all the code is public on GitHub, so anyone can read it, fix it or improve it.
  • Runs everywhere: Mac, Windows, Linux, and even in your web browser.
  • Offline: no account, no subscription, no cloud.
  • Opens real PSD files with your layers still editable.

Install and quick tour

  1. Go to getartcraft.com (or the GitHub releases page) and pick the file for your computer.
  2. On a Mac, open the DMG and drag PhotoCraft into Applications.
  3. Open it. If you've used Photoshop, it will feel familiar: 67 tools on the left (move, select, crop, brush, text…) and layers on the right. Every edit sits on its own layer, like sheets of glass.

Edit 1: Cut out anyone (The Rock eyebrow meme)

  1. Open a frame from the meme.
  2. Press Command + F and search for Subject. PhotoCraft finds the person by itself, in about a tenth of a second.
  3. Layer → Layer Mask → Reveal Selection. The background is gone.
  4. Open any background photo, Select All → Copy, and paste it into the meme.
  5. Layer → Arrange → Send to Back, so it sits behind him.
  6. Add a caption with the Type tool, then give it a Stroke from the fx button so it pops on any background.

Result: a brand-new meme, and every layer is still editable.

Edit 2: The classic caption meme (Surprised Pikachu)

  1. Open a frame from the meme video.
  2. Image → Canvas Size. Anchor at the bottom, make it taller, and fill with white. Now there's room on top for the joke.
  3. Type tool, black text, write the caption. Tip: the best captions fit in two lines.
  4. File → Export as a PNG, and post it.

Edit 3: Make a dull photo pop, the pro way

  1. Layer → New Adjustment Layer → Curves. Bend the line into an S shape for more contrast.
  2. Add a Vibrance adjustment layer to bring the colours back.

Adjustment layers never change your original photo: turn them off and it's untouched. The same two layers work on selfies, product photos and thumbnails.

Edit 4: Text for a meme video

  1. File → New, background Transparent.
  2. Write your caption and give it a stroke and a drop shadow.
  3. Export as PNG. The empty parts stay see-through.
  4. Drop that PNG on top of any clip in your video editor.

Bonus: scripts and AI agents can drive it

Every button in PhotoCraft is also a command, over 500 of them. So scripts, and even AI agents, can run the same edits, with the same engine and the same results.

The honest part

  • PhotoCraft is still early alpha. The team says it's not yet a Photoshop replacement for daily professional work.
  • There's no generative AI yet, some tools are missing, and you will hit bugs.
  • But for memes, thumbnails and quick photo fixes, it already does the job, for free.

Price check (October 18, 2026)

  • Adobe Photoshop: US$22.99/month (annual plan, billed monthly, adobe.com)
  • PhotoCraft: free, open source

Links

  • Full video: https://youtu.be/O4necNCA5D4
  • Download PhotoCraft: https://getartcraft.com/apps/photocraft
  • Source code: https://github.com/storytold/photocraft

Would you switch from Photoshop? Tell me in the comments.

Not sponsored by or affiliated with ArtCraft or Adobe. Adobe and Photoshop are trademarks of Adobe Inc.

This post was written with AI assistance, from my own video and real tests.

title: React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked
description:
I compiled a Next.js 16.4 app with no compiler, the Babel React Compiler and the experimental Rust one, then counted re-renders in Chrome. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes your components and hooks, so you no longer write most useMemo, useCallback and memo calls by hand. In Next.js it is one config flag, reactCompiler: true, stable since Next.js 16.0. Next.js 16.4 adds an experimental native Rust version.

I built a Next.js 16.4.2 test app and compiled it three ways: compiler off, the Babel compiler, and the Rust compiler. Then I counted re-renders in a real browser. With the compiler on, 20 clicks on a counter caused 0 list-row re-renders instead of 20,000, and scripting time fell from about 60 ms to about 7 ms. The Babel version more than doubled compile time. The Rust version cost about a quarter of a second and produced byte-identical output.

TL;DR: should I turn on the React Compiler in Next.js?

Yes, for most App Router projects. Turn it on with reactCompiler: true, run the compiler lint rules first, and try experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler if you build with Turbopack. In my test the compiler removed almost all wasted re-renders for free. It does not replace memo on list items whose parent re-renders, and it skips code that breaks the Rules of React.

Compiler off Babel compiler Rust compiler (experimental)
Config default reactCompiler: true + experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true
Extra install none babel-plugin-react-compiler none
Compile step (median, my app) 2.25 s 5.65 s 2.5 s
Full next build (median) 7.7 s 11.1 s 8.2 s
Client JS, gzip 178,305 B 181,295 B 181,295 B (identical to Babel)
Row re-renders, 20 counter clicks 20,000 0 0
Works with webpack yes yes no (Turbopack only)

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool that rewrites your components so they cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders, and recompute them only when their inputs change. The React Compiler v1.0 announcement calls it "a build-time tool that optimizes your React app through automatic memoization." Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025.

It works with React 17 and later, and on React Native. The introduction docs say that in most cases its memoization "will be as precise, or moreso, than what you may have written." Meta reports that in the Meta Quest Store, "initial loads and cross-page navigations improve by up to 12%, while certain interactions are more than 2.5× faster."

You keep writing plain components. The compiler does the bookkeeping at build time.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js 16?

Install the Babel plugin and set the top-level reactCompiler option in next.config.ts. It moved out of experimental in Next.js 16.0. Next.js does not run Babel on every file: per the reactCompiler docs, "Next.js uses a custom SWC optimization that only applies the React Compiler to relevant files—like those with JSX or React Hooks."

npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

That is the whole setup. New projects can also pick the compiler in the create-next-app prompts.

Can I enable it only for some components?

Yes. Set compilationMode: "annotation" and add the "use memo" directive to the components or hooks you want compiled. This is a good way to start on a large codebase. Add "use no memo" to a component to opt it out in the default mode while you fix it.

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: { compilationMode: "annotation" },
};

export default function Dashboard() {
  "use memo";
  // ...
}

What is the Rust React Compiler in Next.js?

It is a native Rust port of the React Compiler that runs inside Turbopack instead of through Babel in Node.js. It was merged into the React repo in June 2026 (PR #36173) and added to Next.js 16.3 as an experimental option. The Next.js 16.4 release added a fast check that skips files that don't need compiling.

Next.js 16.4 says the Turbopack team's memory changes "reduced the React Compiler's memory usage by 30% and compile time by 15%." To turn it on:

// next.config.ts
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
  experimental: {
    turbopackRustReactCompiler: true,
  },
};

From the turbopackRustReactCompiler docs:

  • It "requires reactCompiler to be enabled". It picks the implementation but doesn't switch the compiler on.
  • It works only with Turbopack. "Using it with webpack will throw an error."
  • You do not need babel-plugin-react-compiler installed.

How I tested it

I wanted numbers from a real Next.js app, not a toy counter, so I measured both build cost and runtime behaviour.

  1. App: Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3.1, Turbopack, Node 24, on an 8-vCPU Linux box. The client dashboard has 1,000 product rows, a filter input, a counter, a stats panel and one deliberately "bad" component. Nothing uses useMemo or useCallback.
  2. Build load: 300 more generated client components on a /gen route, so compile time is measurable.
  3. Three builds: one next.config.ts read an RC_MODE variable (off, babel, rust). I deleted .next before every build, so the Turbopack disk cache never helped, and ran 5 rounds. The tables use the median of rounds 2-5. Round 1 was a cold start: 3.3 s, 12.6 s and 2.9 s of compile time.
  4. Re-renders: each component calls a tiny useRenderCount(name) hook that increments a counter in an effect. Puppeteer drove headless Chrome against next start, and Chrome's ScriptDuration metric measured JavaScript time. I ran each scenario 3 times, and the render counts were identical every run. 
// lib/useRenderCount.ts
"use client";
import { useEffect } from "react";

export function useRenderCount(name: string) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const r = (window.__renders ??= {});
    r[name] = (r[name] ?? 0) + 1;
  });
}

The counter lives in an effect on purpose. Writing to a global during render breaks the Rules of React, and the compiler would skip that component.

Does the React Compiler reduce re-renders?

Yes, dramatically for state that doesn't touch a component's props. Clicking the counter 20 times re-rendered every component on the page with the compiler off: 20,000 row renders. With either compiler, only the two components that actually use the count re-rendered. Rows, stats, the list and even the uncompilable component were all skipped.

Scenario (renders counted) Off Compiler Compiler + memo(Row)
20 counter clicks: Row renders 20,000 0 0
20 counter clicks: JS time 55-62 ms 6-7 ms 6-7 ms
Type "99" in filter: Row renders 290 290 0
Select 10 rows: Row renders 10,000 10,000 19
Select 10 rows: JS time 26-31 ms 14 ms 8 ms

The Babel and Rust builds produced exactly the same render counts, which you would expect from identical output.

The click case is the common one in real apps. Some unrelated state changes high in the tree, and with the compiler off everything below it re-renders.

Why do list rows still re-render with the compiler?

Because the compiler memoizes inside components. It does not turn every component into React.memo. When ProductList must re-render, for example because selectedId changed, its .map() creates new <Row> elements and each row runs. The compiled Row is cheaper to run, since its internals are cached, so JS time still halved from about 28 ms to 14 ms. But all 1,000 rows rendered on each click.

Wrapping the row in memo() fixed it. Selecting 10 rows then rendered 19 rows (1 + 9×2: the newly selected row and the previously selected one).

import { memo } from "react";

function Row({ item, selected, onSelect }: RowProps) {
  return (
    <li style={{ fontWeight: selected ? 700 : 400 }} onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}>
      {item.name}
    </li>
  );
}

const MemoRow = memo(Row); // still worth it for big lists

Without the compiler, the same memo(Row) did nothing: still 10,000 renders. The parent passes onSelect={(id) => setSelectedId(id)} as a new function every render, which breaks memo's prop comparison. The compiler caches that callback automatically. That pairing is what makes memo reliable: compiler for stable props, memo for big lists.

What does the compiled code look like?

The compiler adds a small cache array per component (_c(n) from react/compiler-runtime) and wraps each computation in an "inputs changed?" check. This is what the Babel plugin produced for my Stats component, which totals prices on every render in the source:

function Stats(t0) {
  const $ = _c(10);
  const { items } = t0;
  let onSale, t1, t2, t3;
  if ($[0] !== items) {
    const total = items.reduce(_temp, 0);
    onSale = items.filter(_temp2).length;
    // ...store results in $[1..4]
  } else {
    onSale = $[1]; // reuse cached values
    // ...
  }
  // the returned <p> is cached the same way
}

The expensive reduce and filter run only when items changes. This is the same thing you would do by hand with useMemo, applied to every value in every component.

Does the React Compiler slow down next build?

The Babel version does, the Rust version barely does. In my 300-component app the compile step went from 2.25 s with the compiler off to 5.65 s with Babel, about 2.5 times longer. The Rust compiler took 2.5 s, only 0.25 s more than no compiler at all. Full next build wall time was 7.7 s, 11.1 s and 8.2 s.

Both compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript: the same chunk hashes and the same sizes. Compiled code is larger, because every component now carries cache checks. Raw client JS grew by 213,496 bytes (+28.9%), but after gzip the difference was only 2,990 bytes (+1.7%). The cache checks are repetitive and compress well.

These are numbers from one small app on one machine. Your ratio will differ with codebase size, but the direction should hold: Babel adds noticeable compile time and Rust mostly removes it.

Which code does the React Compiler skip?

Components that break the Rules of React. The compiler checks your code, and if it can't prove a component is safe to memoize it leaves that component uncompiled instead of guessing. The build does not fail. My Bailout component reads and writes ref.current during render, and the Babel plugin's logger reported CompileError: Cannot access refs during render.

export function Bailout({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const renders = useRef(0);
  renders.current += 1; // breaks the rules: ref mutation during render
  return <aside>{label} (render #{renders.current})</aside>;
}

Notice from the render table that Bailout was still skipped on counter clicks. The compiled parent cached the <Bailout label="legacy widget" /> element, so React never re-rendered it. Code the compiler skips simply misses its own internal optimizations. It doesn't break.

How do I find code the compiler can't optimize?

Use the latest eslint-plugin-react-hooks (7.x today). Since React Compiler 1.0, the compiler-powered lint rules ship in the plugin's recommended preset: refs, purity, immutability, set-state-in-effect, set-state-in-render, globals, static-components, incompatible-library and more. You don't need the separate eslint-plugin-react-compiler package any more.

// eslint.config.mjs
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";

export default [
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
];

On my test app, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 flagged the Bailout ref access three times. It also caught a real bug pattern in my generator: 300 components called setState inside useEffect. The rule message says this "can trigger cascading renders". I fixed the generator before benchmarking.

Run the linter before turning on the compiler, fix what it reports, and treat the warnings as a list of components that won't be optimized.

Step by step: adopt the React Compiler in an existing Next.js app

  1. Upgrade. Use Next.js 16.x and React 19.x. The compiler also supports React 17 and 18 through react-compiler-runtime.
  2. Lint first. Add reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended, run eslint . and fix or note the errors.
  3. Install and enable. Run npm i -D babel-plugin-react-compiler, then set reactCompiler: true. On a large app, start with compilationMode: "annotation" and add "use memo" to hot paths.
  4. Try Rust on Turbopack. Add experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true and compare next build times.
  5. Test behaviour. Run your end-to-end tests. Watch effects that depend on memoized values.
  6. Keep memo on big lists. The compiler stabilizes props. memo still decides whether a list item renders.
  7. Remove manual memoization slowly. The React team advises keeping existing useMemo and useCallback or testing carefully before removing them, because removal can change compilation output.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback?

Not in a hurry. For new code, write plain components and let the compiler memoize. In existing code, leave useMemo and useCallback alone until you have tests. The React docs say the hooks "can continue to be used with React Compiler as an escape hatch", for example to keep an effect dependency stable. Removing them can change what the compiler outputs.

Common React Compiler mistakes in Next.js

  • Expecting it to fix big lists alone. It doesn't add React.memo to children. Keep memo() on heavy list items.
  • Mutating during render. Ref writes, global writes or prop mutation make the compiler skip the component, with no build error.
  • Using the Rust flag with webpack. turbopackRustReactCompiler throws with webpack. Remove it or switch to Turbopack.
  • Enabling it without the lint rules. You won't know which components were skipped.
  • Benchmarking with a warm cache. Turbopack's build disk cache hides compile cost. Delete .next between comparison builds.
  • Expecting Server Component wins. The compiler targets components that re-render on the client. Server Components render once per request.

If you are on Next.js 16.4, pair this with the other new client-side features in my guides to React View Transitions in Next.js and the use cache directive.

Related: the React Compiler lint rules from eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7 don't all survive a linter switch. Oxlint ported 12 of 14, Biome none; see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint.

Related: wondering whether to leave Next.js entirely? In TanStack Start vs Next.js I built the same app in both: TanStack Start shipped 111 KB of gzipped JS to Next.js 16.4's 139 KB and built in 1.26 s vs 4.86 s.

Key takeaways

  • React Compiler 1.0 automatically memoizes components and hooks at build time; in Next.js 16 enable it with reactCompiler: true.
  • In my Next.js 16.4.2 test, 20 counter clicks caused 0 row re-renders with the compiler versus 20,000 without, and JS time fell from about 60 ms to 7 ms.
  • The compiler does not make children React.memo; list rows still re-rendered until I wrapped them in memo(), which then cut 10,000 renders to 19.
  • The Babel compiler made the compile step 2.5x longer (2.25 s to 5.65 s); the experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 s.
  • Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript; gzipped size grew only 1.7%.
  • experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler needs reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack, and needs no Babel plugin.
  • Run eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules first; components that break the Rules of React are silently skipped.

FAQ

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes components and hooks. It rewrites your code to cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders and recompute them only when inputs change, replacing most manual useMemo, useCallback and memo calls. Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025, and it supports React 17 and later.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js?

Install babel-plugin-react-compiler as a dev dependency and set reactCompiler: true at the top level of next.config.ts. The option became stable in Next.js 16.0, moving out of experimental. Next.js applies the compiler only to files with JSX or hooks, using an SWC pre-check, to keep build cost down. Use compilationMode: 'annotation' to opt in per component.

What is turbopackRustReactCompiler?

It is an experimental Next.js option, added in 16.3, that runs the native Rust port of the React Compiler inside Turbopack instead of the Babel plugin. It requires reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack and throws with webpack, and needs no babel-plugin-react-compiler install. In my test it compiled in 2.5 seconds versus 5.65 seconds for Babel.

Does the React Compiler make next build slower?

With the Babel plugin, noticeably. In my 300-component Next.js 16.4.2 app the compile step went from 2.25 seconds to 5.65 seconds, and full next build from 7.7 to 11.1 seconds. The experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 seconds to compile and 8.2 seconds in total, so most of the cost disappeared.

Does the React Compiler replace React.memo?

Not for list items. The compiler memoizes inside each component and caches child elements, but when a parent re-renders and maps over data, every child still runs. In my test, selecting a row re-rendered all 1,000 rows with the compiler alone. Wrapping the row in memo() cut 10,000 renders to 19, because the compiler kept its props stable.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback when using the React Compiler?

Not right away. Write new code without them, but keep existing calls until you have tests, because the React team notes that removing them can change compilation output. The hooks still work as an escape hatch, for example to keep an effect dependency stable so the effect doesn't fire repeatedly when its inputs haven't meaningfully changed.

What happens if my code breaks the Rules of React?

The compiler skips that component and leaves it unoptimized; the build does not fail. In my test, a component that mutated ref.current during render produced a 'Cannot access refs during render' compile error in the logger and was left as written. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules report the same problems in your editor.

Does the React Compiler increase bundle size?

Slightly. Compiled components carry cache checks, so in my test raw client JavaScript grew 28.9 percent, by 213,496 bytes, but gzipped size grew only 1.7 percent, by 2,990 bytes, because the generated code compresses well. The Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical bundles in Next.js 16.4.2.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Three things in our app wait for a job to finish, and no two of them poll the same way
description:
CogniPrep has three places where the user is looking at a screen that is not finished yet: a payment that has to be granted, a written exercise whose review is still running, and a recorded interview that is being processed. All three resolve somewhere else, in a webhook or a background job, and all three have to update a page that is already on screen.

They are implemented three different ways. I went looking for the inconsistency to tidy it up and ended up keeping all three, because the differences are each answering a different question: who owns the truth, and what ends the poll.

One: the purchase, which gives up

Every checkout returns the buyer to the thing they bought rather than to a receipt page. That creates a race, because the Stripe redirect is immediate while our webhook may land on a cold function. For a second or two the destination still considers the buyer unentitled, and would otherwise show them the buy panel they have just paid to be rid of.

/** ~30s of polling. Long enough for a cold webhook, short enough to not stall. */
const INTERVAL_MS = 2500;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 12;

useEffect(() => {
  if (granted) return;
  let attempts = 0;
  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    attempts += 1;
    if (attempts > MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
      clearInterval(timer);
      setGaveUp(true);
      return;
    }
    router.refresh();
  }, INTERVAL_MS);
  return () => clearInterval(timer);
}, [granted, router]);

Three things in there matter more than the interval.

granted is a prop, read on the server from the same row every access gate reads. Not from the Stripe redirect, which only says money moved, and not from client state. So router.refresh() is the entire update mechanism: it re-runs the server component, which re-reads the plan, and the parent then renders the real content. There is no second source of truth to keep in step.

The attempt counter exists because this poll has no terminal failure state of its own. If the grant has not landed in half a minute, something is wrong on our side, and an endless spinner is worth less to the buyer than a route to a human:

This is taking longer than usual. Your payment is safe. Reload the page, or contact support and we will activate it for you.

And the one-shot query parameter that brought the buyer here is only dropped once there is nothing left to wait for, because the parent decides whether to render this component from that same parameter. Clear it mid-poll and the next refresh comes back without it.

Two: the exercise review, which has no counter

The written review on a saved exercise attempt uses the same mechanism and deliberately does not count anything:

export function ExerciseReviewRefresher() {
  const router = useRouter();
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => router.refresh(), 5000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [router]);
  return null;
}

Ten lines, renders nothing. What stops it is not in the component at all, it is in the page that mounts it:

/**
 * The attempts route scores written answers inside its own 60 second budget. A
 * review still marked in progress well after that was cut off and will never
 * finish, so it reads as failed rather than as a spinner that never stops.
 */
const REVIEW_STALE_MS = 2 * 60 * 1000;

function toPanelStatus(status: string, updatedAt: Date): AiPanelStatus {
  if (status === 'complete' || status === 'failed') return status;
  if (status === 'pending' || status === 'processing') {
    return Date.now() - updatedAt.getTime() < REVIEW_STALE_MS ? 'processing' : 'failed';
  }
  return 'not_applicable';
}

The route that produces the review has a 60 second limit, so a row still claiming to be in progress two minutes later is not slow, it is dead: the function was killed and nothing will ever write the terminal status. Deriving that on read means the state machine has a failure state even though nothing wrote one, the page stops mounting the refresher, and the poll ends.

This is the version I would reach for first now. A counter in the component bounds the polling. A staleness rule on the server bounds the status, which bounds the polling for every reader of that row, including one who arrives an hour later on a fresh page load and should see "failed" rather than a spinner.

Three: the interview, which actually calls an API

The odd one out does not use router.refresh():

const POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 30_000;

export function useInterviewStatus(interviewId: string | null): InterviewStatusState {
  // fetch(`/api/interview/sessions/${interviewId}`), set state,
  // and stop the interval as soon as status is 'complete' or 'failed'
}

Two reasons it is different. The processing takes long enough that 30 seconds is the right cadence, and refreshing a whole route tree thirty times would re-run far more server work than reading one status. And the status drives client-side UI that is mid-flow, not a server-rendered panel, so the answer has to land in React state rather than in a re-render of the page.

The honest third reason is that this one is older than the other two. Its own comments still carry the requirement numbers from the spec it was built against, which is a nice archaeological marker for which parts of a codebase were written to a document and which were written to a bug.

What the three have in common

One sentence: every poll has a terminal condition that does not depend on the happy path.

An attempt cap, a staleness rule derived from the producer's own time budget, or a status enum with failure in it. Pick whichever you like, but pick one before you ship the interval, because the failure mode of forgetting is not a crash. It is a spinner that spins forever on a screen you will never see, burning a setInterval and one server render every few seconds in a tab somebody left open.

If you want to see the three surfaces these sit behind: the purchase confirmation is on whatever you bought from the pricing page, the reviewed written answers belong to the assessment centre exercises, and the processing one is the mock interview.

title: TypeSafe AI's Jev 1.14 is now available on AI Gateway

Jev 1.14 from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway.

Jev is a decision model for software. You pass it state and a set of questions, and it returns typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers with probabilities instead of free-form text. It answers every question in one request, in parallel, for classification, routing, scoring, and automated verification.

Jev 1.14 accepts images as part of the state, and has an experimental long-context mode for documents, logs, or conversation histories that are too long for a standard request.

Use typesafe-ai/jev-1.14.0 as the model name.

title: 8 Things a Hotel or Villa Website Needs Before Guests Will Book (A Developer's Checklist)
description:
Most guests book their stay from a phone. They often scroll on mobile data, sometimes from an airport gate, and they make up their mind in a few seconds. A hospitality website gets judged by different rules than a portfolio or a company page: it either answers "what will I get, and how do I book it?" right away, or the visitor goes back to a booking platform.

I am a WordPress and Flutter developer in Famagusta, North Cyprus. Many of the small hotels, villas and holiday rentals around me depend on summer visitors from Turkey, the UK, Germany and Russia. Here is the checklist I use when I build or review a hospitality site. If you build sites for clients in tourism, most of it applies wherever you are.

1. Photos that sell the stay, without killing speed

People decide to book by looking. Large, bright photos of the rooms, the pool and the view do more than any paragraph. The technical part is keeping them fast:

  • serve WebP at the size each breakpoint actually needs
  • lazy-load everything below the first screen
  • use a gallery that swipes properly on touch screens
  • put the most convincing photo first, not the reception desk

2. One page per room or villa

Each unit needs its own URL with the essentials visible at a glance: number of guests, beds, bathrooms, distance to the beach, what is included and the price per night or per season. If you can, add an availability calendar. If you can't, a clear "Check availability" button still saves a lot of back-and-forth over email.

3. A direct booking path on every screen

Booking platforms bring visibility, but they take a commission on every booking, and the guest relationship belongs to them. The website's job is to turn returning guests and Google visitors into direct bookings. That means either a booking request form or a connected booking engine, plus one-tap WhatsApp, phone and email buttons. On mobile, a sticky contact bar works well.

4. Every language in its own URL

A Turkish family, a British couple and a German group all trust a booking page more in their own language. For SEO, give each language its own address (/de/, /tr/ and so on), use proper hreflang, and translate menus, forms and confirmation emails as well as the page text. A plugin like WPML handles this in WordPress. Remember that right-to-left languages need their own layout checks.

5. Location and local context

Guests want to know where they'll actually be: how far the beach is, how to get there from the airport, and what's within walking distance. An embedded map, simple directions and a short area guide keep visitors on your site while they plan. They also give Google more local signals to work with.

6. Trust details

Show reviews from past guests and link to your profiles on review platforms. Publish check-in times, cancellation rules and house rules, and show a licence number, a real address and the people behind the business. For a small hotel, this is what makes booking directly feel safe.

7. Speed on mobile data

A heavy theme loses guests before the first photo loads. Page caching, optimised images, fewer third-party scripts and lean CSS let a site look luxurious and still feel fast. On a multilingual WordPress site I helped optimise, the median mobile PageSpeed score went from 51 to 75 on the same page. That shows how much room for improvement most sites have.

8. Local SEO for every season

Write pages for the searches guests actually type, like "villa with private pool in Kyrenia" or "beach hotel near Famagusta". Add Hotel / LodgingBusiness structured data and keep publishing seasonal content, so you show up before travellers settle on a platform.

When an app is worth it

For a larger hotel or a group of villas, a companion app can add digital check-in, room-service requests, local recommendations and return-visit offers. With Flutter, one codebase can share content and APIs with the website, which keeps both in sync.

FAQ

Can the website take bookings directly?

Yes. It can send booking requests to the owner, show live availability or connect to a booking engine. It depends on how many units there are and how many bookings come in.

Do I still need booking platforms?

Usually, yes, because they bring visibility. Your own site works alongside them and turns returning guests into direct bookings.

Can the owner update prices and photos?

With WordPress and Elementor, yes. Seasonal prices, photos and offers can be edited in every language without calling a developer.

Originally published on ehsanabedi.com. Running a hotel or villa in North Cyprus? See my web design services.

title: VaultExam AI: Mock Tests from Your Notes, Without Uploading Them Anywhere
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

VaultExam AI is a 100% local, privacy-first tool that turns a chapter (In any format) into a ready-to-print question paper + answer key and lets you ask questions of the same document with page-cited answers.

Who would pay for it: independent coaching institutes, test-prep tutors, university professors and corporate trainers. Their curated notes and question banks are their intellectual property, and they don't want to upload them to a cloud API. They also spend hours every week typing up mock tests, DPPs and Set A/B variations by hand.

What it does:

  • Upload Notes in any format. It is chunked and embedded locally, and the file is deleted from disk straight after ingestion.
  • Ask the document: answers come only from your notes, with Page citations.
  • Generate an exam: choose the institute name, exam type (Coaching Mock Test, University Mid-Sem, Corporate SOP Quiz), difficulty (Recall, Application, Analytical/Edge Cases) and the number of MCQs, short answers and long answers.
  • Set A/B/C: each set draws on different parts of the document and avoids repeating earlier questions.
  • Answer key included: MCQ answers with explanations, model answers for short and long questions, marking-scheme key points, and the source page for every question so a teacher can verify it.
  • Print or save as PDF straight from the browser.

Demo

Code

https://github.com/ronitsolanki-01/VaultExam.git

How I Built It

Everything runs on the user's own machine. No cloud calls, no per-token fees.

  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Spring AI 2.0.1
  • LLM: an open-weight model (qwen3.5:4b) served by local Ollama
  • Embeddings: nomic-embed-text via Ollama
  • Vector store: PostgreSQL with PGVector (pgvector/pgvector:pg16 via Docker Compose), with metadata filtering by document_id
  • Ingestion: Spring AI's TikaDocumentReader and PagePdfDocumentReader keeps page number on every chunk, then TokenTextSplitter chunks it
  • Frontend: one Next.js page (TypeScript, Tailwind), with window.print() for output

How the exam generator works: it retrieves a sample of chunks from the document, asks the model for MCQs, short answers and long answers in separate structured-output calls, then validates each result (question count, exactly four options, valid answer index) and retries if the local model returns bad JSON. Each set uses a different seeded sample of the document, plus a "don't repeat these questions" list.

Things that bit me on a small local model:

  • Reasoning models like qwen3.5 can spend their whole token budget "thinking" and return an empty answer, which breaks JSON parsing. I fixed it by disabling thinking in the Ollama options.
  • Ollama's default context window silently truncates long RAG prompts, so I set a larger num-ctx and tuned how many chunks each call retrieves.
  • Small models sometimes return a bare JSON array instead of an object, so the parsing and validation code handles that and retries.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A closed API would have made this product impossible to sell to its target customers. A coaching institute's notes are its business, and "send your question bank to a third party" is a dealbreaker.

Open-weight models let the whole pipeline run inside the customer's own machine. That also changes the economics: generating a hundred papers costs electricity, not tokens, so a tutor can regenerate Set B at 11pm without watching a bill. And because the stack is open, institutes can swap the model for a bigger one as their hardware allows.

title: Introducing the new v0 API
description:
Today we're introducing the new v0 API: programmatic, headless access to v0's app-building agent. Send a prompt and v0 generates an app, starts a dev server in a Vercel Sandbox, and gives you a preview URL you can embed in your own UI.

Each chat is an isolated workspace for one app, where v0 can read, edit, and run the files. Follow-up messages continue from the current state. v0 verifies the code running in the Sandbox, so it can catch and fix errors in your app in real time.

The new API is now generally available.

How it works

Create a chat from a prompt, stream its work, and render the live preview, all from your own interface. First, install the v0 SDK.

Then, create a chat. Send a prompt, and v0 generates your app.

Send follow-up messages to the same chat to keep building. Each one continues from the current state.

Then embed the app.

A prompt goes in, a running app comes out. v0 operates the Sandbox, dev server, and preview behind it. When you're ready, deploy to Vercel in one API call. v0 manages the whole pipeline.

What this unlocks

The new API lets you run v0's app builder inside your own product or pipeline. This opens use cases like:

  • A white-labeled app builder: Your users describe an app and get one back.

  • Automated app changes: Trigger v0 from a script, CI job, or webhook to generate a new app or update an existing one.

  • A build tool for your agents: An agent hands back a working app instead of a code snippet.

Below, we break down the API primitives behind this workflow.

Start with a chat

Each chat holds the state for one app, and a repo or Vercel project can have many. Keep each chat's ID and send its follow-up messages to that chat. Metadata lets you group chats by customer, workspace, app, or any key you already use.

Learn more about messages.

Stream the trace

Your interface needs to show what happens between sending a request and seeing the updated preview.

Every message includes ordered parts: text, thinking, file reads and edits, searches, bash commands, tool calls, and agent actions. The same object can drive a one-line status, a changed-files view, or the full trace.

Usage is returned with chat and message responses, so you can account for the work when it finishes.

Choose sync, async, or streaming

Chat creation and messages support synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming responses. Use sync when the caller needs the completed response. Use async to queue the work and receive updates via webhook or poll for v0's response later. Stream the request to render v0's work as it happens.

Work from existing code

You can also create a chat from a repository, ZIP archive, or set of files.

Render the dev server preview

Each chat gets a short-lived preview token. Fetch it from a server route and proxy browser requests through it, so your v0 API key never reaches the browser. When a preview is ready, traffic forwards to it; while the Sandbox spins up, requests fall back to a loading route. Point an iframe at your proxy route and cache the preview details until they expire.

Read more about Accessing Previews in the docs.

Bring your own tools and design systems

Turn on specific MCP servers for a chat, or use the defaults.

Design Systems 2.0 saves a design system as a skill. Include it in a request to load its components, tokens, setup, and starter app.

You can pass up to three skills per request, from team or user memory, skills.sh, or the connected repo, or let the agent pull them in for you.

Use v0 from agents

If you're building an agent, give it v0 as a tool. When the agent needs to produce a working app, it calls v0, and gets back a running preview or deployment to hand to the user. Your agent stays in charge of everything else.

There are three ways to connect it:

MCP

Connect the v0 MCP server to an IDE, desktop assistant, or agent runtime that supports MCP.

The first connection starts an OAuth flow. The MCP server exposes tools for creating chats, listing chats, getting chat details, listing and sending messages, resolving pending tasks, and getting preview URLs.

AI SDK

For TypeScript agents built with AI SDK, use @v0-sdk/ai-tools to expose v0's API operations as tools in the agent's own loop.

The agent decides when to create or continue a chat. Your AI SDK run keeps control of the orchestration and final response.

eve

For eve agents, add an OpenAPI connection file. eve turns the allowed operations into tools and attaches the API key at execution time, out of model context.

Connect a Vercel project

Create a Vercel project for the chat, then manage its environment variables, integrations, and settings through the Vercel API. Your apps get Vercel's security and observability by default.

When you're ready to ship, deploy the chat to Vercel.

Migrate your chats

Chats from the previous version of the v0 API don’t run on the new one, so carry them forward. Pick the version you want to keep, download it as a ZIP, and create a new chat from that ZIP. Store the old identifiers in the new chat’s metadata if you need traceability.

The migration guide covers the full mapping. The main changes:

  • Use https://api.v0.dev/v2 for new requests.

  • The chat holds current app state, and messages hold its history.

  • Replace version workflows with chat file workflows, and v0 Project organization with chat metadata.

  • Use vercelProjectId plus the Vercel API for project operations.

  • Render message parts, not only final text.

Get started

Create an API key in v0 settings and install the SDK.

Or, scaffold a full app.

Read the documentation and migration guide.
