title: FLUX 3 Image Klein: Flagship Image Features on an 8GB GPU
description:
Originally published at: https://toolpilotpro.com/flux-3-image-klein-guide

FLUX 3 Image Klein: Flagship Image Features on an 8GB GPU

Black Forest Labs released FLUX 3 Image Klein on October 15, 2026, and it deserves more attention than it is getting. A 5.6B-parameter image model with open weights, native 4K output, and hardware requirements low enough to run on a mid-range gaming GPU — this is the release that brings serious AI image generation to hardware people already own.

What it is

One set of weights handles three jobs: text-to-image generation, image editing, and multi-reference generation with up to 10 source images guiding a single output. It also does bounding-box layout control — draw a box to tell the model where an element belongs, or restrict an edit to a selected region.

Two checkpoints ship: Klein Base (50 steps, for fine-tuning and LoRA training) and Klein Distilled (16 steps, the fast one behind the API). The INT8 build runs on NVIDIA RTX cards with as little as 8GB of VRAM — BFL measures about 4 seconds per 1MP image on an RTX 5090, under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070.

The pricing

The BFL API serves the distilled checkpoint as flux-3-image-klein, priced per image by resolution: $0.008 at 768px, $0.009 at 1K, $0.011 at 1.5K, $0.014 at 2K, $0.036 at 4K. The full FLUX 3 Image model charges $0.048 and $0.607 for 1K and 4K — Klein is roughly 5x cheaper at 1K and nearly 17x cheaper at 4K. Self-host the weights and the per-image cost drops to electricity.

The license, honestly

Weights are under the FLUX Kommunity License: free commercial use for individuals and businesses under $5M in annual revenue, plus research and non-commercial use. Above $5M, you need a paid self-hosted license or the API. Not MIT-style open source — but effectively free for freelancers, small studios, and indie makers.

How it stacks up

Black Forest Labs claims internal benchmarks beat Qwen-Image 2.1 and Ideogram V4.5 — vendor claims, treat accordingly. The one public third-party blind test (200 tasks, judged by Claude, Gemini, and GPT) scores Nano Banana 2.1 at 7.20 vs Klein's 6.93, with Klein at roughly one-fifth the cost per image. Close on quality, far ahead on price and deployment freedom.

Early testers flag real weaknesses: people and pose generation is noticeably weak, multi-reference compositing gets shaky with complex scenes, and fine text rendering is mixed. If your work is portraits, test before committing.

Getting started

API users keep the same request format as FLUX 3 Image — just switch the endpoint. For local runs, BFL shipped ComfyUI weights and a workflow on day one, plus Diffusers support, a Gradio bounding-box demo on GitHub, and a try-it demo on Hugging Face Spaces. LoRA training works via Diffusers or Ostris AI Toolkit on Klein Base.

For the full spec table, the honest limitations, and who should (and should not) switch, read the complete guide: https://toolpilotpro.com/flux-3-image-klein-guide

title: A Resolved Task Is Not a Resolved Case: Building ReturnTrail with FalkorDB
description:
Two records. One failed pickup. Two different explanations.

“Pickup cancelled by customer.”

“Pickup failed because the courier was unavailable.”

This is a fictional example from ReturnTrail, the project we built for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks.

Finding different words is the easy part. The useful questions come next: do these records describe the same pickup attempt? What did an earlier reply actually explain? If another document arrives, does that old explanation still cover the evidence?

Those questions shaped our graph model, our investigation tools and the way we handle “resolved” tasks.

Try ReturnTrail · Source code and setup

Product capture using fictional records and a local FalkorDB instance. Case API responses were not mocked for this capture.

The job we chose

ReturnTrail helps a shopper prepare an evidence-linked support conversation about a disputed return pickup.

The output is a reviewable brief: original claims, their source connections, follow-up questions and the history of manual explanations. We keep those explanations separate from the records they describe.

Our current prototype uses four seeded fictional cases and bounded fictional text additions. We have not validated customer demand or measured real-world dispute outcomes. The hackathon gave us a focused implementation to put in front of users.

Why the pickup attempt belongs in the graph

An order can have more than one pickup attempt. Different failure reasons on different attempts need not contradict each other.

Our graph connects:

  • A case to its order, item and return request.
  • Each pickup attempt to its return request.
  • Each statement to the pickup it describes and the document that recorded it.
  • Each follow-up action to its reviewed documents.
  • Each manual clarification to its follow-up action.

Here is the evidence query documented in the repository:

MATCH (c:Case {id:$caseId})-[:HAS_ORDER]->(o:Order)-[:CONTAINS]->(i:Item)
MATCH (c)-[:HAS_RETURN]->(r:ReturnRequest)-[:RETURNS]->(i)
MATCH (p:PickupAttempt)-[:ATTEMPTS]->(r)
MATCH (s:SupportStatement)-[:ABOUT]->(p)
MATCH (s)-[:RECORDED_IN]->(d:EvidenceDocument)
RETURN DISTINCT c.id AS caseId, o.id AS orderId, i.id AS itemId,
r.id AS returnId, p.id AS pickupId, s.id AS statementId,
s.claimedStatus AS claimedStatus, s.text AS statement,
d.id AS evidenceId, d.sourceType AS sourceType
ORDER BY evidenceId, statementId;

The backend chooses the authorized workspace graph and binds the case ID. Both ownership paths through the order/item and return/item must match. The API exposes source connections derived from the executed query results.

CASE-002 is our negative example: records describe separate pickup attempts, so the supported rule does not flag them as a same-attempt disagreement.

FalkorDB supplies the evidence traversal and stored workflow context. Java applies explicit rules to the returned records.

What an earlier explanation actually covers

Our most useful design decision was connecting a saved action to the documents it reviewed:

Case → Action → REFERENCES → EvidenceDocument

A manual reply is linked through:

Action → HAS_CLARIFICATION → ClarificationRecord

This lets us ask a more precise question than “Was this task resolved?”

Does the reviewed source set, including its evidence revision, match the current source set?

In our implementation, coverage requires a nonempty current source set, matching evidence IDs and a matching revision. The ContextCoverage implementation exposes reviewed sources, newly added sources, task state and saved-note context.

A later document can therefore require fresh review while the earlier task remains resolved in history. We preserve what happened instead of rewriting the old task as if it had reviewed information that did not exist yet.

A matching source set still does not verify a manual explanation. It establishes its context boundary.

Context lab: preview the missing connection

Context lab lets a user temporarily set aside one source and inspect the result.

For CASE-001, setting aside DOC-001 leaves only the courier-unavailable claim. Our bounded disagreement rule no longer has two conflicting reasons to compare.

The application runs a parameterized, read-only graph query with a source exclusion. It returns the remaining evidence connections and evaluates that result. Original records and saved tasks stay unchanged.

This is a diagnostic preview. It does not establish that the excluded document is false or that the remaining claim is true. It shows how the available evidence changes the supported next question.

CASE-004 extends the demonstration: add a reviewed fictional source to a case with an earlier manual reply, then inspect the changed coverage.

The agent's job is bounded

Our Spring Boot backend exposes four investigation tools:

  1. get_case_evidence
  2. get_case_clarifications
  3. get_case_findings
  4. prepare_followup_action, when a finding is pending

The AI workflow must retrieve the current evidence and saved context before proceeding to findings and a local follow-up action. The backend enforces the sequence and renders the final report from tool results.

These are application tool calls. We did not build an MCP server, and the model does not generate arbitrary Cypher or decide who caused the failed pickup.

A separate Review rules & prepare question action performs the deterministic workflow without a model request. Users can then record an explicit manual outcome and export a fresh brief. The application does not send that draft to a courier or issue a refund.

What we tested—and what those tests establish

We tested the distinctions that could otherwise produce a misleading answer: same versus different attempts, unknown reasons, changed source context, stale writes and workspace isolation.

Recorded check Scope
93 backend tests successful; 2 skipped Hosted default suite at commit 275fb37; zero failures or errors
14 frontend tests passed Domain, draft and public-video input boundaries
Five public API workflow groups passed Actual hosted application and external FalkorDB; synthetic writes, history, retries, version protection and guest isolation
One real hosted AI investigation passed Four model requests, all four required tools in order and one OPEN local follow-up

The validation record distinguishes mocked contracts, actual graph checks and the hosted model request. The twenty labelled synthetic rule fixtures are a regression set, not an accuracy benchmark.

A deployment lesson: readiness has a limited meaning

When we enabled OAuth providers, the graph readiness endpoint stayed UP while the homepage returned HTTP 500.

The authorization resolver was treating an ordinary page path as a possible provider path. At the root URL, that produced an empty registration ID. We reproduced the exception, restricted lookup to OAuth authorization routes and added three regression tests.

That failure changed our release check: we verify the homepage, sign-in shell, provider redirects and a fresh guest workflow alongside database readiness.

The backend and frontend run together on Render; the graph runs on FalkorDB Cloud. The current free preview can lose sessions and graph data. Its database tier has no TLS, persistence or backups, so it is an evaluation environment for fictional data, with no durable-account promise. See hosting boundaries before using or reproducing it.

Try the part that changes the next action

Open the demo as a guest and start with CASE-001:

  1. Compare the original claims in Evidence.
  2. Inspect their paths in Connections.
  3. Set aside one source in Context lab and compare the assessment.
  4. Prepare the question, record a fictional manual outcome and export Case brief.

Then try CASE-002 and CASE-004. The interesting outcome is whether the graph context supports another question, and which sources make that question necessary.

Next, we want to observe nontechnical users completing this brief workflow and speak with support operators about the information they need. We need those observations before claiming that the product saves time or fits an operational process.

The lesson we are taking forward is specific: a saved answer needs a record of the evidence it covered. When that evidence changes, the application should make the boundary visible.

Built by Om Singh Jadon and Ajeet Gadekar for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks, under Agents That Act on Connected Data.

ChatGPT assisted with planning, implementation.

Explore: Live demo · Repository · Cypher queries · FalkorDB documentation

title: A dispatch policy should sort candidates, not filter them
description:
Every dispatcher grows an extension point sooner or later. One operation wants the next job to go to the least loaded courier, another to whoever has been on duty longest, and a third wants a rule nobody has written yet. The obvious shape for that extension point is a hook that picks the courier, and that shape is wrong. A hook that can pick can also reject, and a hook that can reject can also accept something the depot's rules never allowed.

We draw the line somewhere else in shift-planner, our library for planning field courier shifts (https://github.com/shipmindlabs/shift-planner). Eligibility is fixed code inside the dispatcher. The plug-in gets exactly one method, and that method returns a sort key over the shifts that already passed.

Two kinds of rule, two kinds of failure

The distinction worth drawing is about cost, not about taxonomy. A preference that is wrong costs you a worse choice: a courier who was slightly more loaded than the one you would have picked takes the job, and the day comes out marginally less balanced. A constraint that gets bypassed costs you a courier sent to the wrong depot, handed a job past the capacity of their shift, or called again ten minutes after they declined one and were put on a cooldown.

Those two failures differ in size, but what matters more is that they differ in when they show up. If you implement a constraint as a strong preference (rank cooling-down couriers last, rank shifts with no capacity left last) the system behaves correctly for as long as somebody better is available. The moment the shortlist is down to a single candidate, the preference has nothing left to prefer and the violation lands. That is lunchtime, or a storm, or exactly the hour the whole plan exists for. A constraint expressed as a preference is a rule that switches itself off precisely when load is highest.

So what you ask of any plug-in point is not "what does it do when it is written correctly" but "what is the worst a wrong one can do". We want that answer to be a bad ordering, and nothing else.

The filter is fixed code

Dispatcher.candidates builds the eligible list itself. A shift survives three checks, and all three are about the job rather than about preference:

def candidates(
    self, job: Job, taken: Mapping[str, int] | None = None
) -> tuple[Candidate, ...]:
    loads = taken or {}
    eligible = [
        Candidate(shift, loads.get(shift.worker, 0))
        for shift in self.roster
        if shift.location == job.location
        and shift.covers(job.at)
        and not self.cooldowns.locked(shift.worker, job.at)
    ]
    return tuple(
        sorted(
            (candidate for candidate in eligible if candidate.spare_capacity > 0),
            key=self.policy.sort_key,
        )
    )

def assign(
    self, job: Job, taken: Mapping[str, int] | None = None
) -> Candidate | None:
    ordered = self.candidates(job, taken)
    return ordered[0] if ordered else None

Three details in that list carry most of the argument.

The location check is an equality, not a distance. A policy cannot quietly widen it into "nearest depot", because a shift that fails the comparison never becomes a Candidate at all.

covers is the shift's half-open interval test, start <= moment < end, applied to the job's moment rather than to the dispatcher's. No moment in this library comes from the wall clock; every check takes the moment as an argument.

The cooldown gets read at job.at too. A courier who declined a job is held back over the half-open interval [since, until) recorded on the CooldownBoard, and that lock lifts by the passing of time rather than by anybody clearing it. Asking the board about the job's own moment is what makes a replay of yesterday's job stream produce yesterday's answers.

Capacity is the fourth check, and it happens after the list is built, because it depends on something the dispatcher does not own: the load. Candidate.taken is read from the caller's mapping, an absent worker counting as zero, and spare_capacity is max(0, self.shift.capacity - self.taken). A candidate with no spare capacity gets dropped before any ordering happens. Only then does sorted run, and assign returns ordered[0] when the tuple is non-empty and None otherwise.

None is the correct answer to "nobody is eligible". It is also the answer no pick-shaped hook can be trusted to give, because a hook asked to pick one will pick one.

The policy is a sort key and nothing else 

class AssignmentPolicy(Protocol):
    """Orders the candidates for a job; the first one gets it."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LeastLoaded:
    """Prefers the courier with the fewest jobs so far, then the earlier shift."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (candidate.taken, candidate.shift.start, candidate.worker)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EarliestStart:
    """Prefers the courier who has been on duty the longest."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (candidate.shift.start, candidate.taken, candidate.worker)

The Protocol is the whole guarantee. A function from a Candidate to a tuple can reorder what survived the filter. It cannot admit a shift the filter rejected, because it is never shown one. It cannot remove a shift the filter passed, because sorting a sequence returns a permutation of it, and the length does not change whatever the key says.

That bound is worth testing against hostile input rather than reasonable input. Here is a policy nobody should ship, sitting next to one that is a legitimate change of emphasis:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MostSpareCapacity:
    """Prefers the courier with the most room left, then the earlier shift."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (-candidate.spare_capacity, candidate.shift.start, candidate.worker)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Perverse:
    """Deliberately bad: hands the job to the busiest eligible courier."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (-candidate.taken, candidate.worker)

Perverse is about the worst policy anyone can write inside the rules, and the damage it does is this: the busiest eligible courier gets the job. Still at the right location. Still on duty at the job's moment. Still inside their capacity. Still not cooling down.

That is what makes the extension point cheap to review. A reviewer argues about whether a policy expresses a sensible preference, which is an operations judgement, instead of re-deriving whether it is safe, which would be a correctness judgement repeated on every plug-in anyone ever writes.

The key ends in a name

Both built-in policies end their key with candidate.worker, and that last element does more work than you would guess.

Python's sort is stable, so without a final discriminator an exact tie on the leading fields gets settled by the order in which the candidates arrived. In this library that order comes from Roster, which normalises its shifts to a tuple sorted by (start, end, worker). It is deterministic today, and it is still the wrong thing to lean on: it is a detail of how a different class stores its data, and an assignment that quietly depends on it changes behaviour the day that storage changes, with no test anywhere pointed at the thing that moved.

Ending the key with the worker name makes the tie-break a property of the candidates themselves. It also makes the key total, and it is the roster that earns that: two shifts of one worker may never share time. At most one shift per worker can cover job.at, so within a single job's candidate list every worker name appears exactly once. No residual tie is left for arrival order to decide. The same roster, the same taken mapping and the same moment produce the same assignment on every run, in a test, on a laptop, and in production.

This kind of determinism is not an aesthetic preference. It is what lets you argue about a dispatch decision after the fact. When an operations lead asks why this courier and not that one, the answer is a tuple comparison over values that were all passed in as arguments.

What it costs to run

Three things stay your job as the caller, and they are the three that bite.

The load mapping is yours. Nothing in the library ever increments it. Dispatcher.assign reads taken and returns a Candidate; it does not record that the job was handed out, because it does not know whether your transaction committed. In a batch loop you update the mapping yourself, or LeastLoaded will hand every job in the batch to the same courier, each time correctly, each time on the same stale count.

dispatcher = Dispatcher(roster, policy=MostSpareCapacity())
taken: dict[str, int] = {}

for job in jobs:
    chosen = dispatcher.assign(job, taken)
    if chosen is None:
        continue
    taken[chosen.worker] = taken.get(chosen.worker, 0) + 1

Refusals work the same way. The board is immutable, so recording one returns a new dispatcher instead of mutating the one you held:

dispatcher = dispatcher.refuse("anna", job.at)

And candidates walks the whole roster on every call. For a roster drawn over a long horizon that is a linear scan you pay per job, so dispatch against the slice you actually need rather than the full plan.

Close

The rule we apply when a new dispatch rule turns up in review is short. If getting it wrong sends a courier somewhere they must not go, it belongs in the filter, in fixed code, where there is exactly one copy of it. If getting it wrong only costs a worse choice, it belongs in the key. And whatever the key contains, it ends with a name, so that the candidates, and not the order they happened to arrive in, settle the last tie.

title: Build a Reviewable Gemini Form Assistant in React
description:
A person filling out a travel request often already has the information in a message:

Prepare a round trip from SFO to JFK, departing November 12, 2026 and returning November 15, 2026, for one traveler in economy. Purpose: customer workshop.

An AI assistant can turn that brief into form fields. The more interesting problem starts when its response arrives. The person might have changed the dates, corrected the purpose, or opened another request.

I built and maintain Trip Workbench, a React and TypeScript demo with synthetic travel data, to explore that interaction. Its assistance flow lets a person request suggestions, inspect proposed fields and clarification questions, and explicitly apply a change.

The useful unit of work is a proposal tied to a particular draft state. That gives the application something it can validate, display, reject when outdated, and save through its existing API.

Keep generation separate from saving

The feature uses two application operations:

Operation Responsibility
POST /api/trips/:id/proposal Read the authorized draft, ask Gemini for suggested fields, and validate the response
PATCH /api/trips/:id Apply a user-accepted patch after checking authorization, revision, and domain rules

Generating a proposal leaves the saved trip unchanged. Clicking Apply proposed changes sends a separate mutation. In this demo, applying saves the draft; reviewing and submitting the trip request happens afterward.

That distinction should be visible in the interface. A generic “Accept” button is less clear than a label that explains whether the action fills a local form or saves to the server.

The Gemini call runs in the Node backend using @google/genai. The React client sends its brief and draft context to the application API. Google’s API-key guidance recommends keeping production keys out of browser code.

This article follows that embedded assistance flow. Trip Workbench’s separate WebMCP tools provide another entry point for external agents; they are not involved in the Suggest button.

Define what a proposal can contain

A proposal contains two things: a patch and clarification questions.

For the opening brief, this is an illustrative response:

{
  "patch": {
    "origin": "SFO",
    "destination": "JFK",
    "departureDate": "2026-11-12",
    "returnDate": "2026-11-15",
    "tripType": "round_trip",
    "passengerCount": 1,
    "cabin": "economy",
    "purpose": "customer workshop"
  },
  "clarifications": []
}

The patch contains editable trip fields. It has no place for an owner ID, tenant ID, approval decision, or submitted status.

Partial patches are useful. If the brief says “change the destination to JFK,” the assistant should preserve unrelated fields. If the destination is ambiguous, it can return an empty patch and a question.

For example, “Springfield next Friday” needs more context. This demo supports a small airport list. The assistant should explain that limit and ask for a supported destination instead of silently substituting one.

Here is a stricter proposal schema I would use when extending the adapter. It constrains airports at the schema boundary and rejects unknown keys throughout:

import { z } from "zod";
import { AIRPORTS } from "../../domain/types.js";

const Field = z.enum([
  "origin", "destination", "departureDate", "returnDate",
  "tripType", "passengerCount", "cabin", "purpose",
]);

const ProposedTripSchema = z.object({
  patch: z.object({
    origin: z.enum(AIRPORTS).nullable().optional(),
    destination: z.enum(AIRPORTS).nullable().optional(),
    departureDate: z.string().nullable().optional(),
    returnDate: z.string().nullable().optional(),
    tripType: z.enum(["one_way", "round_trip"]).optional(),
    passengerCount: z.number().int().min(1).max(9).optional(),
    cabin: z.enum(["economy", "premium_economy", "business"]).optional(),
    purpose: z.string().max(500).optional(),
  }).strict(),
  clarifications: z.array(z.object({
    field: Field.nullable(),
    kind: z.enum(["missing", "ambiguous", "unsupported"]),
    question: z.string().min(1).max(240),
  }).strict()).max(8),
}).strict();

The date strings still need calendar validation. A string-shaped value does not establish that February 30 exists.

Define patch semantics explicitly, too: omitting a field preserves its value; null clears a nullable field. The model should omit uncertain information and ask a question. It should clear a field only when the requested change calls for that.

Give Gemini the context needed to interpret the brief

The server loads the current saved draft after checking access. It also supplies a reference date, application timezone, and allowed values.

These details affect interpretation. “Next Friday” depends on a reference date and may still require clarification. An airport mentioned in ordinary language might be outside the application’s supported set.

The prompt should describe those limits and ask for only the requested changes. Treat the brief as input data; instructions embedded in it do not grant additional application capabilities.

At commit 4b3f370, the repository pins @google/genai 1.30.0. Its adapter requests JSON using responseMimeType, then parses and validates the result locally. It does not yet pass an output schema to Gemini.

A focused improvement is to supply the schema during generation as well:

const { GoogleGenAI } = await import("@google/genai");
const ai = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: config.geminiApiKey! });

// config and prompt are constructed by the server adapter.
// ProposedTripSchema is the schema defined above.
const response = await ai.models.generateContent({
  model: config.geminiModel,
  contents: prompt,
  config: {
    responseMimeType: "application/json",
    responseJsonSchema: z.toJSONSchema(ProposedTripSchema),
  },
});

if (!response.text) {
  throw new Error("AI_INVALID_OUTPUT");
}

const proposal = ProposedTripSchema.parse(
  JSON.parse(response.text),
);

This excerpt belongs inside the existing adapter, after its API-key check. Its route must translate parsing and validation failures into an application error.

The SDK reference documents responseJsonSchema for this API. It supports a subset of JSON Schema, so keep runtime checks such as string limits and calendar rules even when the schema is supplied to the model. Current Google examples also show the newer responseFormat shape; do not copy fields between SDK generations without checking the version you actually ship.

These examples follow the repository’s models.generateContent path. Google now documents that path under Generate Content API Legacy; its newer Interactions API uses a different request shape. Keep the SDK version and API surface consistent when adapting the code.

The next check is application-specific. Merge the proposed patch with the saved fields and run the existing domain validator. A return date can be a real date and still precede departure. A valid cabin can still require policy review.

Google’s structured-output documentation also calls for application validation. Constraining the response shape does not establish that its values match the person’s intent.

Bind the proposal to the state that produced it

Consider this sequence:

  1. A suggestion request starts with the purpose “customer workshop.”
  2. The person changes the purpose to “leadership meeting.”
  3. The original suggestion arrives with “customer workshop.”

Checking only the server revision misses the problem. The person’s newer text may still be unsaved.

Trip Workbench tracks three versions for this reason:

Version What it tracks
Saved revision Changes persisted by the backend
Client edit version Local form edits
Brief version Changes to the text being interpreted

The server echoes those bindings outside the model-generated proposal. They are application metadata; Gemini does not choose them.

The coordinator’s freshness check includes:

return (
  bound.boundRevision !== state.savedDraft.revision ||
  bound.boundClientEditVersion !== state.editVersion ||
  bound.boundBriefVersion !== state.briefVersion
);

The surrounding implementation also checks the draft identity, session, and editor generation. That prevents a response for one editor context from being treated as a suggestion for another.

Check freshness when the response arrives and again when the person clicks Apply. The second check matters because a proposal can become outdated while someone is reading it.

The simplest policy is to mark the proposal stale and ask for a new suggestion. For eight fields, that is easier to explain than automatically merging an old proposal with new intent. A larger editor might justify more granular conflict handling.

There is another practical detail: this endpoint uses saved fields as model context. Unsaved form edits are not sent to Gemini. The coordinator blocks an agent-style patch while local edits remain unsaved. A clearer UI would ask the person to save or discard those edits before requesting a suggestion.

Version checks protect this particular handoff. They do not, by themselves, prove that every refresh or recovery path in a shared editor preserves local changes.

Make review useful and apply through the existing API

The current React panel lists proposed values and clarification questions. It disables Apply when the proposal is stale or its patch is empty.

For an existing populated form, I would add a current-value column:

Field Current Proposed
Destination BOS JFK
Departure November 10, 2026 November 12, 2026
Purpose Team meeting Customer workshop

That table is a suggested review improvement, not a screenshot of the current demo. It makes the consequences of applying easier to inspect.

Keep clarification questions visible beside the fields. A partial proposal can be useful without being ready for submission. In the current design, the person can refine the brief and request another suggestion.

The Apply handler checks freshness, then delegates to the existing coordinator:

if (coordinator.isProposalStale(proposal)) {
  // Keep the form unchanged and ask for another suggestion.
  return;
}

const result = await coordinator.applyAgentPatch(
  proposal.patch,
  proposal.boundRevision,
  newCommandId(),
);

The backend checks the user’s authority, validates the patch against the current draft, and enforces the expected revision. If another writer changed the draft, the application should require a fresh review before applying a different change.

This second validation is necessary even though the proposal was already checked. The draft can change between generation and application. Client-side review is also not an authorization boundary.

A business-cabin request illustrates the distinction: the patch can save successfully while the later validation step returns a review requirement. Saving the draft does not approve a policy exception or purchase a ticket.

Keep failures understandable

The manual form should remain usable when assistance fails.

A rejected model response should leave the fields unchanged and explain that no suggestion could be prepared. A stale proposal should explain that the brief or draft changed. A revision conflict should lead to reviewing current data before trying again.

For a production feature, also release the “Suggesting” state in a finally block and distinguish provider failures from invalid output. The current adapter maps otherwise unclassified provider exceptions to AI_TIMEOUT; that label alone does not establish that a timeout occurred.

Generation failures and save failures need different treatment. A lost proposal response has not saved a trip. A lost PATCH response may have followed a successful save. The latter requires reconciling the original command’s outcome before creating another mutation.

Evaluate the proposal and the handoff separately

Trip Workbench has disabled, fixture, and live modes. Fixture mode returns canned examples so the interface can be exercised repeatedly. Its SFO–JFK example uses fixed dates, so it does not measure Gemini’s extraction ability.

Use deterministic checks for the application behavior:

Check Expected behavior
Unknown patch key or invalid calendar date Reject the proposal without changing saved fields
Form edit while generation is pending Mark the returned proposal stale
Brief change after generation Prevent applying the old suggestion
Navigation to another draft Discard the old context’s response
Server revision changes before Apply Reject the stale mutation
Network failure during generation Restore usable controls and preserve the form

Then evaluate live Gemini with a complete brief, an ambiguous brief, and a partial update to an existing draft. Run each several times and record the model, prompt, proposed fields, clarification questions, human corrections, and final saved state.

For the partial update, explicitly check what stayed unchanged. A correct destination is not enough if the assistant also overwrote a purpose that the user never asked to change.

The repository’s results document records fixture evidence and leaves live Gemini unverified. These exercises define the next evaluation; they are not a reported success rate.

Finally, compare the complete task with manual entry. Include the time spent writing the brief, waiting, reviewing, and correcting. For a short form, manual entry may be faster. Assistance becomes more interesting when the user already has a longer brief containing the required information.

The question I want feedback on is concrete: can a person understand and correct the proposed change with less effort than entering it themselves?

That is the outcome this design lets us evaluate. The model provides a candidate change, the interface makes it reviewable, and the application decides whether it can be saved.

title: Set the canvas size before configuring the drawing context
description:
If a canvas loses its background on the second render, inspect its size assignments. Look for writes to canvas.width and canvas.height between painting the background and drawing the image.

Assigning either dimension resets the drawing context. The pixels disappear, and settings such as the fill color, transform, and compositing mode return to their defaults. Even assigning the width its existing value causes a reset. MDN documents this behavior in its canvas width reference.

The order that loses the background

Suppose an export should place a transparent image on white. This sequence contains a problem:

const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
ctx.fillStyle = "white";
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
canvas.width = targetWidth;
canvas.height = targetHeight;
ctx.drawImage(image, 0, 0, targetWidth, targetHeight);

The background was painted into the old bitmap. Changing the dimensions clears it before the image is drawn. A preview against a white page may conceal the mistake because the page shows through the transparent canvas.

Set both dimensions first, then establish the drawing state:

canvas.width = targetWidth;
canvas.height = targetHeight;
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
if (!ctx) throw new Error("A 2D context is required");
ctx.fillStyle = "white";
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, targetWidth, targetHeight);
ctx.drawImage(image, 0, 0, targetWidth, targetHeight);

Here image must already be decoded, and the target dimensions must be positive integers chosen by the application. The example assumes their aspect ratio is intentional. Stretching a photograph into a different ratio would be a separate bug.

Make each render complete

Give the render function the source image and the output settings it needs. After setting the dimensions, apply every setting the drawing operation depends on. That makes the second render follow the same path as the first.

For example, if the application uses a transform for rotation, configure that transform after resizing. If it disables smoothing for pixel art, apply that choice after resizing too. A context object remaining in a variable does not mean its earlier settings survived.

Avoid using canvas.width = canvas.width as an unexplained clearing trick. It also resets state, which can make later edits difficult to reason about. If clearing pixels is the intention, a deliberate clearing operation communicates that intention more clearly, with the current transform and clipping region taken into account.

A small regression case

Use a transparent test image with an opaque colored square in the middle. Render it onto a white background, change the output dimensions, then render it again. Inspect a corner that should contain only the background. The corner should remain white after both renders.

Also exercise the case where the second render requests the same dimensions. A test that only checks changes in size can miss an unconditional width assignment in a shared helper. Keep the test focused on the output pixels and the behavior the user needs, rather than asserting which internal helper ran.

When a preview looks correct but an exported file has an unexpected background, inspect the drawing sequence before adjusting compression. An encoder cannot restore a background that was cleared before encoding began. Put both size assignments near the start of the render function so a later edit does not clear work already drawn.

title: Go Scheduled Payment Data Cleanup — Compare 4 Cron Scheduler Latency and Cost Tests
description:
Short answer: choose a cron scheduler for nightly payment reconciliation by testing admission latency, duplicate delivery, missed-run recovery, and execution isolation; the cheapest trigger is a poor bargain if it can silently widen the cleanup backlog.

For a customer-support system, the job is deceptively plain: reconcile yesterday's payment-provider records, repair local status drift, and make corrected state available before agents begin answering billing tickets. The scheduling decision should follow the error budget for that outcome. If agents need corrected data by 06:00 UTC, a trigger at 05:59 with a one-minute runtime has no capacity margin. A trigger at 02:00, feeding bounded workers that can replay partitions, converts a brittle deadline into an observable batch SLO.

Don't optimize the clock first.

How should cost govern a cron scheduler comparison for scheduled data cleanup?

I would run four tests against the whole path, not just the timer: trigger admission latency, duplicate invocation, an intentionally unavailable worker, and a cleanup partition that exceeds its normal runtime. This is a capacity-planning exercise — arrival rate, service rate, backlog age, and deadline are the useful variables. A scheduler's dashboard can show a green invocation while the payment cursor remains twelve hours behind.

The bounded production scenario is one nightly reconciliation with 24 hourly partitions. Each partition reads a stable provider time range, compares external payment IDs with local records, and writes an idempotent result. That number is an example of partition shape, not a benchmark: use enough partitions to replay a narrow failure domain, but not so many that scheduling and database overhead dominate useful work. I'm not sure there is a universal best partition duration; provider rate limits, record skew, and the local write path settle it, and a load test with production-shaped distributions is what resolves the uncertainty.

A useful acceptance sheet is short:

Test Evidence to retain Failure decision
Admission latency Intended time and observed start time Does the remaining window preserve the batch SLO?
Duplicate trigger Two runs with the same logical date Do idempotency keys prevent repeated mutation?
Worker unavailable Trigger accepted while workers are stopped Is work durably recoverable without guessing?
Long partition One partition crosses the next tick Does overlap stay bounded by a lease or concurrency rule?

These tests separate a trigger from a job system. A trigger decides when work becomes eligible. A job system owns durable state, acknowledgements, retry policy, concurrency, and backlog. Combining those responsibilities can be convenient for a small workload, but treating them as the same thing makes incident diagnosis muddy: an absent trigger, a rejected enqueue, and a slow consumer create the same visible symptom — stale support data — while requiring different repairs.

Govern the payment data window before touching the clock

Consider a production incident as a tabletop rather than a claimed war story. The 02:00 trigger fires, the payment provider answers with HTTP 429 for several partitions, and the next run begins before the first has drained. If the job means “delete or update everything older than midnight,” the second run can race the first, retry already-applied writes, or move a shared cursor past records that were never reconciled. The invariant revealed by this scenario is more valuable than any scheduler feature list: each unit of cleanup needs a stable identity, a bounded input interval, and a result that can be applied more than once without changing the final state.

The obvious first model is cron -> cleanup(). It is also where SLOs disappear. The safer model is cron -> create logical run -> enqueue partitions -> workers -> reconcile run; its extra durable state costs storage and operational attention, but it gives on-call engineers a ledger of what should have happened, what did happen, and what remains eligible for retry. This doesn't create exactly-once execution. It makes at-least-once execution tolerable through idempotent effects. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation is useful here because it distinguishes consumer acknowledgements from publisher confirms: the broker accepting a message and a worker completing its effect are separate events.

Here is the preventative boundary in Go. The scheduler calls Start, while the repository enforces uniqueness for the logical date and the queue carries partition identities. Implementations can use a database uniqueness constraint and a durable queue; the interface keeps vendor choice outside the reconciliation rule.

package reconcile

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Partition struct {
    RunDate string
    Start   time.Time
    End     time.Time
}

type RunRepository interface {
    CreateOnce(ctx context.Context, runDate string) (created bool, err error)
}

type Queue interface {
    Enqueue(ctx context.Context, key string, p Partition) error
}

type Starter struct {
    Runs  RunRepository
    Queue Queue
}

func (s Starter) Start(ctx context.Context, runDate string, dayStart time.Time) error {
    created, err := s.Runs.CreateOnce(ctx, runDate)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create reconciliation run: %w", err)
    }
    if !created {
        return nil // A repeated trigger refers to the existing logical run.
    }

    var enqueueErrs []error
    for hour := 0; hour < 24; hour++ {
        start := dayStart.Add(time.Duration(hour) * time.Hour)
        p := Partition{RunDate: runDate, Start: start, End: start.Add(time.Hour)}
        key := fmt.Sprintf("payment-reconcile/%s/%02d", runDate, hour)
        if err := s.Queue.Enqueue(ctx, key, p); err != nil {
            enqueueErrs = append(enqueueErrs, fmt.Errorf("enqueue %s: %w", key, err))
        }
    }
    return errors.Join(enqueueErrs...)
}

One detail matters: after CreateOnce succeeds, failed partition enqueues must remain discoverable in the run ledger so a reconciler can enqueue the missing work. Returning an error is necessary for observability, but it isn't the recovery mechanism. A periodic sweeper can compare expected partition identities with accepted ones and fill gaps; because identities are stable, that repair is safe to repeat.

Slow down here.

Test each trigger boundary with the same harness

GitHub Actions scheduled workflows are attractive when cleanup already lives beside repository automation. Its documentation says scheduled workflows run from the latest commit on the default branch, can be delayed during high load, and may be dropped under sufficiently high load; the shortest interval is five minutes. Those properties can fit a non-urgent maintenance task, but they make the workflow history an inadequate system of record for a deadline-bound reconciliation unless the job also records durable run intent elsewhere. Repository access and workflow permissions also expand the blast radius beyond “wake a worker.”

Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers invoke a Worker's scheduled handler on UTC time. Cloudflare documents that trigger changes can take several minutes, up to 15 minutes, to propagate. This model keeps the trigger close to lightweight edge code, while the execution limits and the need for durable reconciliation state still determine whether the work belongs in one invocation or should be handed to another worker path. It is a boundary choice, not a guarantee that a large batch finishes because the clock fired.

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler exposes one-time and recurring schedules, flexible time windows, retry policy, and dead-letter queue configuration. Those controls make delivery policy explicit, with the trade-off of cloud IAM, target configuration, and another provider-specific control plane. For teams already operating that environment, those dependencies may be normal; for a portable or self-hosted stack, they are lock-in and on-call surface that must earn their place.

BullMQ represents a different boundary. It is a Redis-backed Node.js queue with job scheduling and worker semantics, so choosing it means owning or buying the Redis layer and operating consumers rather than selecting a remote trigger alone. RabbitMQ can supply durable messaging and acknowledgement semantics, but cron eligibility remains a separate concern. These aren't rankings. They are different allocations of responsibility between source control automation, edge execution, a cloud scheduler, and an application-owned queue.

Option shape Best evidence from the four tests Operational cost to count
Repository-scheduled workflow Workflow start history plus external run ledger Repository permissions, variable start time, runner use
Edge cron handler Trigger event plus durable handoff record Execution limits, deployment propagation, state service
Cloud scheduler targeting a worker Delivery attempts, retry policy, dead-letter records IAM, target policy, provider control plane
Application queue with repeatable jobs Queue state, acknowledgements, backlog age Data-store operations, consumers, upgrades, paging

Price should be measured from the current official calculators against expected invocations, execution duration, storage, logs, egress, and on-call ownership; a trigger's sticker price alone excludes most of the system. Published rates and free allowances change, so hard-coding a winner into an architecture review ages badly. The latency side is equally contextual: nightly work rarely needs millisecond admission, but it does need enough recovery time before the support-data deadline.

A Go implementation for idempotent partition admission

The worker needs a lease or equivalent concurrency guard, an idempotency key at the mutation boundary, retry classification, and a checkpoint that advances only after the partition's effects are durable. A 429 response is retryable under the provider's policy; malformed input or an impossible state transition usually needs quarantine and review. Don't turn every error into an immediate retry. Correlated retries can consume the remaining batch window faster than ordinary processing.

For observability, retain logical run date, partition identity, attempt count, intended trigger time, accepted time, worker start time, completion time, and a low-cardinality outcome. From those fields, derive admission delay, queue delay, processing duration, oldest incomplete partition age, success ratio, and projected finish time. Alert on user impact or a threatened deadline rather than on one failed attempt; the retry can be healthy while the backlog trend is not. Logs help explain a partition, metrics show the fleet, and the run ledger answers the awkward audit question: which payment intervals were actually reconciled?

Capacity planning closes the loop. Let W be the available window in seconds, R the sustained records processed per second after rate limiting, and N the expected record count. Require N/R to sit comfortably below W, then test the margin with skew and retries. The exact headroom is an SLO policy decision, not a universal constant. If a provider permits only modest concurrency, earlier scheduling or incremental reconciliation can buy more safety than a larger worker fleet.

Deployment deserves the same skepticism. Pin the cleanup binary or image version, make schema changes backward compatible with in-flight workers, test duplicate and out-of-order partitions, and rehearse replay from the durable ledger. A scheduler configuration change should pass review and emit an auditable event. For a nightly job, a staging clock that runs every few minutes can validate orchestration, but test data must preserve the production invariants: stable external IDs, overlapping updates, pagination, and rate-limit responses.

No mystery metrics.

When should the deployment stay small?

Stick with a simple repository or host cron when the cleanup is disposable, quick, idempotent as a whole, easy to rerun, and has no hard completion deadline. A small cache purge whose next run safely catches up does not automatically justify a queue, run ledger, leases, and another pager. The catch is that “small” must be supported by observed duration and backlog, not by the current row count.

A managed scheduler is not suitable when provider-specific IAM and targets violate portability requirements, while a self-hosted queue is a poor fit when the team cannot own its data store, upgrades, and consumer capacity. An edge handler is the wrong execution home for work that exceeds its documented resource model, though it may still be a clean trigger. Repository automation should remain repository automation when production credentials or unpredictable start delay would breach the service boundary.

The decision rule is deliberately unbranded: define the reconciliation deadline, make run intent durable, test the four failure conditions, and choose the least operational machinery that still preserves the invariant under replay. Cost matters. So do the pages created by the architecture.

References

  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/managing-schedule-flexible-time-windows.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585#section-4

title: What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing
description:
What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing for Chatbots

Sooner or later, every chatbot project hits the same wall: customers don't stay on one channel. A user asks a question on Instagram, follows up on WhatsApp, and expects the Telegram bot to know what happened. If each channel runs its own isolated logic, you end up with duplicated flows, lost context, and replies that arrive twice or not at all.

This is a behind-the-scenes post about how we approached cross-channel message routing for chatbots, the mistakes we made, and the patterns that held up. By the end you'll know how to design a normalized message format, build channel adapters, route messages reliably, and avoid the failure modes that cost us the most time.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • What is cross-channel message routing?
  • Lesson 1: Normalize messages before you route them
  • Lesson 2: Keep channel quirks inside adapters
  • Lesson 3: Build the router around rules, not channels
  • Lesson 4: Make delivery idempotent
  • Lesson 5: Plan for fallbacks and human handoff
  • Mistakes we'd avoid next time
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

You don't need a full production stack to follow along. It helps to have:

  • [ ] Basic familiarity with webhooks and REST APIs
  • [ ] Node.js 18+ and TypeScript (the examples use them, but the ideas are language-agnostic)
  • [ ] An account or sandbox for at least two messaging channels (e.g., WhatsApp Business API, Telegram Bot API, Instagram Messaging)
  • [ ] A queue or job system (Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, or similar)

What is cross-channel message routing?

Cross-channel message routing is the layer that sits between your messaging channels and your bot logic. It receives inbound messages from any channel, decides where they should go (a flow, an AI agent, or a human), and delivers the reply on the right channel in the right format.

Why it matters: without a routing layer, every new channel multiplies your logic. With one, adding a channel means writing an adapter, not rewriting your bot.

Here's the high-level shape:

[WhatsApp] [Telegram] [Instagram]
     \         |         /
      \        |        /
     [ Channel Adapters ]
              |
     [ Normalized Message ]
              |
        [ Routing Engine ]
         /     |      \
   [Flow]  [AI Agent]  [Human]
              |
     [ Outbound Dispatcher ]

Lesson 1: Normalize messages before you route them

Our first version passed raw webhook payloads around. It worked until we added the second channel and every if (channel === "...") branch started leaking into business logic.

The fix was a single internal message schema that every channel converts into:

type Channel = "whatsapp" | "telegram" | "instagram";

interface NormalizedMessage {
  id: string;              // our internal ID
  externalId: string;      // the channel's message ID
  channel: Channel;
  contactId: string;       // stable ID across channels (when known)
  channelUserId: string;   // the user's ID on that channel
  type: "text" | "image" | "audio" | "button_reply" | "other";
  text?: string;
  mediaUrl?: string;
  receivedAt: string;      // ISO timestamp
  raw: unknown;            // keep the original payload for debugging
}

Two small decisions paid off immediately:

  • Keep raw. When a channel changes its payload format, you'll want the original to debug against.
  • Separate contactId from channelUserId. This is what later lets you recognize the same person on different channels.

Lesson 2: Keep channel quirks inside adapters

Every channel has its own rules: message length limits, button formats, media handling, and messaging windows. We moved all of that into adapters with the same interface:

interface ChannelAdapter {
  channel: Channel;
  parseInbound(payload: unknown): NormalizedMessage;
  send(to: string, message: OutboundMessage): Promise<SendResult>;
}

class TelegramAdapter implements ChannelAdapter {
  channel: Channel = "telegram";

  parseInbound(payload: any): NormalizedMessage {
    const msg = payload.message;
    return {
      id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      externalId: String(msg.message_id),
      channel: "telegram",
      contactId: "", // resolved later by the contact service
      channelUserId: String(msg.from.id),
      type: msg.text ? "text" : "other",
      text: msg.text,
      receivedAt: new Date(msg.date * 1000).toISOString(),
      raw: payload,
    };
  }

  async send(to: string, message: OutboundMessage) {
    // Telegram-specific formatting and API call live here
    return { ok: true };
  }
}

Rule of thumb: if a line of code mentions a specific channel, it should live in an adapter.

A useful side effect is that you can test routing logic with a fake adapter and no network calls.

Lesson 3: Build the router around rules, not channels

Our early router asked, "Which channel did this come from?" The better question turned out to be, "What does this conversation need?"

We switched to declarative rules evaluated in priority order:

interface RoutingRule {
  name: string;
  priority: number;
  when: (msg: NormalizedMessage, ctx: ConversationContext) => boolean;
  to: "flow" | "ai_agent" | "human";
  target?: string;
}

const rules: RoutingRule[] = [
  {
    name: "human-takeover-active",
    priority: 1,
    when: (_m, ctx) => ctx.humanAssigned,
    to: "human",
  },
  {
    name: "keyword-support",
    priority: 2,
    when: (m) => /refund|complaint|cancel/i.test(m.text ?? ""),
    to: "human",
  },
  {
    name: "default-ai",
    priority: 99,
    when: () => true,
    to: "ai_agent",
    target: "general-assistant",
  },
];

function route(msg: NormalizedMessage, ctx: ConversationContext) {
  return [...rules]
    .sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority)
    .find((r) => r.when(msg, ctx))!;
}

Because rules don't care about the channel, the same logic works on WhatsApp, Telegram, and Instagram. You can still add channel-aware rules when you need them, such as a rule for a channel's messaging window.

Lesson 4: Make delivery idempotent

Webhooks get retried. Networks fail. If you don't plan for this, users get duplicate replies. Two protections helped us the most:

  1. Deduplicate inbound messages using channel + externalId.
  2. Use idempotency keys on outbound sends so a retried job doesn't send twice. 
async function handleInbound(msg: NormalizedMessage) {
  const key = `inbound:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`;
  const isNew = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 86400, "NX");
  if (!isNew) return; // duplicate webhook, ignore

  await queue.add("route-message", msg, {
    jobId: `route:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`,
  });
}

Acknowledge the webhook fast and do the real work in a queue. Channels penalize slow responses, and long AI calls shouldn't block your HTTP handler.

Lesson 5: Plan for fallbacks and human handoff

Things that will go wrong: a channel API times out, a message is rejected, or the AI isn't confident. Decide the behavior in advance:

  • Retry with backoff for transient errors (timeouts, 5xx).
  • Don't retry permanent errors (blocked user, invalid recipient). Mark them and move on.
  • Hand off to a human when confidence is low or the user asks for one, and make the router respect that state (see the human-takeover-active rule above).
  • Log every routing decision with the rule name, so you can answer "why did the bot do that?" later. 
async function dispatch(adapter: ChannelAdapter, to: string, msg: OutboundMessage) {
  try {
    return await adapter.send(to, msg);
  } catch (err) {
    if (isTransient(err)) throw err;   // let the queue retry
    await markUndeliverable(to, err);  // permanent failure
  }
}

Mistakes we'd avoid next time

  • Routing on raw payloads. Normalize first, always.
  • Treating identity as an afterthought. Decide early how you'll link a user across channels.
  • Skipping decision logs. Debugging a routing bug without them is guesswork.
  • Assuming channels behave alike. Message windows, formats, and rate limits differ more than the docs suggest.

Replace this section with 1-2 real incidents from your build (a bug, a surprising channel behavior, a number you measured) before publishing.

Conclusion

The main takeaways from building cross-channel message routing for chatbots:

  • Normalize every inbound message into one schema.
  • Isolate channel-specific behavior inside adapters.
  • Route on conversation needs using ordered rules, not on channel names.
  • Make both inbound and outbound delivery idempotent.
  • Design fallbacks and human handoff from day one.

These patterns take time to get right, and many teams would rather spend that time on the customer experience than on plumbing. That's the problem platforms like Botsailor aim to take off your plate, with omnichannel automation across WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram, and more, so you can focus on conversations instead of webhooks. If you're building your own, we hope these lessons save you a few late nights.

How do you handle routing across channels? Share your approach or your worst webhook horror story in the comments.

title: My Q4 model said True where BF16 said False, so I diffed them layer by layer
description:
Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 reads this:

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return

and puts 97.9% on False. The Q4_K_M quant of the same model puts 79.1% on True.

That's one token out of 1,282 I scored. Across the whole text, Q4_K_M changes the top token at 11.6% of positions, its mean KL from BF16 is 0.067, and perplexity goes from 7.83 to 8.53. Those numbers tell you the quant drifted. They don't tell you where: which tokens, which layers, which block inside a layer, or whether the weights are even the main cause compared with the KV cache or the batch size.

I built heterodyne to answer that.

zaydmulani09 / heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, and move activations between them to test which layers, and which attention or MLP blocks, carry the divergence. Local, CPU, no API keys.

heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, then move activations between them to test which layers' divergence actually reaches the output.

A quantized GGUF, a quantized KV cache, a different batch size, a fine-tune: each changes what your model says, and the usual answer to "how much, and where?" is one aggregate number. heterodyne runs two configurations of llama.cpp (two arms: a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers) on identical tokens and shows:

  • where the outputs differ: exact full-vocabulary KL(A‖B) and top-1 changes at every position, next to a measured numerical floor;
  • where inside the network the difference appears: the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • which layers carry it to the output: activation transplants that write one arm's residual stream into the other, layer by layer, in llama.cpp's own numerics;
  • attention or MLP…
View on GitHub

Why not the usual interpretability tools

TransformerLens, nnsight and the rest run PyTorch. But on CPU, llama.cpp quantizes the activations to 8 bits before every quantized matrix multiply. A PyTorch model with dequantized weights is a different model from the GGUF you actually run. And llama.cpp's own llama-perplexity --kl-divergence reports aggregates only.

So heterodyne works inside llama.cpp, in the same kernels you deploy.

Two arms, same tokens

An arm is a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers: K and V cache types, flash attention, ubatch size. heterodyne runs arm A and arm B on identical tokens, chunk by chunk, and records:

  • exact KL(A‖B) over the full vocabulary at every position, summed in f64 from raw logits, plus every top-1 change and how confident it was;
  • a numerical floor: arm A re-run with an odd batch split, as a yardstick for how big harmless differences get on this machine;
  • the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • transplants (next section);
  • optionally, every combination of the settings that differ, to attribute the change to one of them.

Everything is saved as an experiment file with provenance (GGUF hashes, llama.cpp commit, build flags) and an integrity hash. heterodyne verify re-runs it and compares every stored number exactly.

The hook

llama.cpp's scheduler accepts an eval callback, cb_eval. When it's set, the scheduler asks for each graph node "do you want this tensor?" and, if you say yes, computes everything up to that node, synchronizes, and hands you the data before anything downstream runs.

A small C++ shim uses that moment to either copy the tensor out or overwrite it. Every consumer of a node comes after it in topological order, so an overwrite is seen by everything downstream. Tensors are addressed by graph name: l_out-N is the residual stream after layer N, ffn_inp-N the residual between layer N's attention and its MLP. The shim counts rows per ubatch and checks that every row of every hooked tensor was seen, so a missing name is an error, not silent zeros. Rust only sees structs I define, so a llama.cpp update can't silently shift a field under the FFI.

Transplants

Denoise: run B, but write A's l_out-N into it, and measure KL(A‖patched B). Noise: the reverse. Do it at every layer and you get a curve. For Q4_K_M vs BF16:

layer   0      4      8      12     16     20     24     26     27
KL    0.062  0.052  0.038  0.029  0.021  0.013  0.006  0.004  0.0013

It falls steadily over all 28 layers: no single layer carries the divergence. The 0.0013 left after the last layer is what the final norm and output head add on their own.

At the is_prime token, writing BF16's residual into Q4_K_M brings that token's KL from 0.48 after layer 6 down to 0.04 after layer 9, and writing Q4_K_M's residual into BF16 reproduces the flip from about layer 12. At that token, the decisive difference forms in layers 6 to 12.

New: attention or MLP?

The obvious way to split a layer is to write A's MLP output into B. The problem: that also erases the MLP's reaction to every difference upstream, so a block with identical weights in both arms can still look responsible.

So heterodyne restores A's whole residual at two points per layer, after attention (ffn_inp-N) and after the MLP (l_out-N), and takes the steps between consecutive points. Attention's share at layer N is the KL with A restored at the layer's input minus the KL with A restored after attention; the MLP's is the next step. The steps telescope: summed over all layers they equal the untouched KL minus what's left after the last layer, so nothing is counted twice.

There's a check with a known answer. If two arms differ only in K-cache type, only attention reads the K cache, so every MLP step must be exactly zero. The tests check that bitwise, and it holds on Qwen3 too.

12 chunks, 1,282 scored positions, 95% intervals over chunks:

attention MLP
restoring BF16 in Q4_K_M (of 0.067) removes 0.030 (0.019–0.041) removes 0.036 (0.024–0.048)
injecting Q4_K_M into BF16 adds 0.026 (0.021–0.031) adds 0.040 (0.028–0.051)

Restoring BF16, the paired difference is 0.006 (−0.011 to 0.022): it spans zero, and attention's part ranges from 20% to 82% across chunks, so on this text the two can't be told apart. Injecting Q4_K_M, the MLPs add more (0.014, 0.005 to 0.023). The largest single step is layer 0's attention, but llama.cpp doesn't name layer 0's input, so that bar also holds any difference in the token embeddings. A few steps are negative (layer 2's attention, −0.0014): restoring that block alone left Q4_K_M further from BF16.

It costs two more passes per layer per chunk; the 12-chunk run took 29 minutes on a laptop i7-1355U.

Other things it turned up

All on Qwen3-0.6B, same text, same laptop:

B mean KL top-1 changed perplexity (BF16: 7.83)
Q8_0 0.0022 2.2% 7.83
UD-Q4_K_XL 0.058 11.3% 8.33
Q4_K_M 0.067 11.6% 8.53
Q3_K_M 0.214 20.8% 9.47
Q2_K 0.780 36.3% 16.75
  • The KV cache matters more than you'd think. Same Q8_0 file twice, B with a q8_0 K and V cache: KL 0.0038. That's further than quantizing the weights from BF16 to Q8_0 (0.0022).
  • llama.cpp's CPU path isn't batch-invariant at every size. With flash attention off, Q4_K_M output was bitwise identical at ubatch sizes that are multiples of 4 and changed at others (ubatch 63: 4.7% of top tokens). The repacked K-quant matmul quantizes activation rows in groups of 4 and sends the remainder down a separate path. That's why heterodyne's numerical floor uses an odd split.

What this is and isn't

  • One small model, one text, one machine. Intervals are 95% t-intervals with a cluster-robust standard error over chunks, because tokens within a chunk are correlated.
  • Transplants are interventions on your input. They say where restoring one model's activations removes the divergence on that text, not which block's weights quantize worse in general.
  • CPU only. GPU kernels compute differently, and nothing here says anything about them yet.

Try it

Grab a binary from the releases (Linux, Windows, macOS arm64) and run:

heterodyne serve --models ~/models

or from the command line:

heterodyne diff --a Qwen3-0.6B-BF16.gguf --b Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --text-file examples/corpus.txt --chunk 128 --max-chunks 12 --components

The experiment files behind every number here are in examples/. If you run it on a bigger model or different prompts, I'd love to see what you get.
