title: Severance: An IAM Security Agent That Explains and Tests Its Fixes
description:
A security finding tells you something is exposed. It rarely tells you which relationship to change without disrupting legitimate access.

In an IAM environment, access can pass through users, groups, roles, and shared policies. A permission that looks harmless in isolation can become dangerous when combined with several other relationships. Removing the first connection you find might block the exposure, but it might also break access that should remain.

We built Severance to investigate that problem for Graph Hacks, entering Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data.

Severance is an AI agent that investigates an IAM graph, explains the path behind an exposure, proposes a specific relationship to remove, and tests that change before asking for approval.

The current implementation operates on an offline FalkorDB model. It does not change AWS permissions.

The graph supplies the evidence

We gave the language model responsibility for selecting tools and explaining their results. Reachability, paths, scores, and proposed changes come from deterministic code and FalkorDB queries.

The graph contains five node types:

Node What it represents
Principal A user, group, service, or modeled untrusted identity
Role An IAM role or an explicit permission-carrier adapter
Policy A managed or inline permission policy
Action An operation scoped to an assessed target
Resource A seeded resource or a concrete permission request

Relationships capture group membership, role access, role assumption, policy attachment, permitted actions, and their targets.

One public-input investigation follows this chain:

Compromised user
  → MEMBER_OF → Group
  → HAS_ROLE → Group permission carrier
  → GRANTS → Policy
  → PERMITS → s3:PutObject
  → TARGETS → Assessed object permission

The permission carrier adapts user and group policy attachments to our existing graph schema. It is not an additional AWS role.

That distinction matters: a graph should make the source data easier to reason about without silently inventing cloud infrastructure.

Where FalkorDB does the work

FalkorDB is the primary operational context layer.

Parameterized Cypher queries find the principals connected to a target through identity and permission relationships. For example, the reachability query follows the policy and action spine backward from a resource, then finds the identities that reach the relevant role:

MATCH (res:Resource {id: $rid})<-[:TARGETS]-(act:Action)
      <-[:PERMITS]-(:Policy)<-[:GRANTS]-(role:Role)
MATCH path =
      (p:Principal)-[:MEMBER_OF|HAS_ROLE|CAN_ASSUME*1..6]->(role)
RETURN p.id AS id,
       p.name AS name,
       p.kind AS kind,
       min(length(path)) + 3 AS hops,
       collect(DISTINCT act.name) AS via_actions

We use algo.SPpaths to obtain shortest exposure paths and sampled betweenness centrality to identify load-bearing roles and policies.

The planner then evaluates candidate relationship removals using GRAPH.COPY. Each candidate is tested on a disposable copy, allowing the same reachability queries to measure its effect.

Without FalkorDB, Severance cannot establish the exposure path, rank candidate fixes, simulate their effects, or apply the selected graph change.

Finding a path is only the beginning

Several different changes can block the same path. Choosing between them requires measuring what each change removes.

Our planner considers edges on the shortest untrusted paths and ranks candidate cuts using:

  • How many untrusted reachers remain.
  • How many existing shortest paths are closed.
  • How much other modeled access is lost.
  • The broker score of the roles or policies involved.
  • Relationship specificity and a stable final tie-break.

This gives us a declared, reproducible decision policy rather than asking the model to choose whichever fix sounds convincing.

The selected fix is simulated again before approval. Severance shows the supporting path, before-and-after measurements, and any collateral impact.

Approval produces a single-use token bound to the specific plan. The agent cannot apply a different edge deletion using that approval. Non-interactive investigations reject changes by default.

An append-only audit trail records tool calls, proposals, simulations, approval decisions, and applied changes.

Moving beyond our own seeded scenarios

We started with four deterministic scenarios containing known vulnerabilities. Those fixtures let us check exact paths and expected fixes.

We also wanted to test whether Severance could work with data maintained outside our project.

For that, we imported the public account-authorization example from Salesforce’s Cloudsplaining repository. The pinned input contains:

  • 44 users.
  • 5 groups.
  • 78 roles.
  • 84 managed policies, alongside inline policies.

The original file, source revision, checksum, and upstream license are included in the repository.

Each import assesses one concrete action/resource request and explicitly identifies a user or role session assumed to be compromised.

One case examines the OverprivilegedEC2 role. Its attached InsecurePolicy grants S3 write operations on wildcard resources. Severance traces that grant and proposes detaching the policy from the role.

Another case follows a user’s group membership to a policy granting s3:*. That investigation produces a five-edge explanation and proposes removing the selected user’s membership.

These are externally sourced example records, not a verified production-account export. The assessed object ARN is a concrete example request, not evidence that an object exists.

What the benchmark showed

We defined six cases from the source records before running the engine:

Case Expected behavior
Role-attached S3 write Find the path and detach the relevant policy
Group-inherited S3 write Find the path and remove the selected membership
Group-inherited object ACL access Find the path and remove the selected membership
Rejected approval Preserve the graph
Allow and deny in one policy Produce no positive exposure path or mutation
Allow and deny across attached policies Respect the explicit deny

The final run passed 30 out of 30 deterministic engine evaluations and six out of six live Sonnet MCP-agent investigations.

Approved cases reduced the assessed untrusted reacher count from one to zero, with no collateral among the supported modeled principals. Each approved run deleted exactly one graph edge. Rejection and deny controls preserved the graph.

The repository also has 113 passing deterministic tests.

These results establish that the selected workflows behave as expected on these fixtures. Six agent calls are not a production accuracy estimate.

Earlier runs exposed resource-name lookup errors and a collision between concurrent benchmark graphs. We retained those results, fixed exact-name handling and graph isolation, and ran the final benchmark again.

The benchmark report and per-call evidence are available in the repository.

The most important limitation is authorization scope

An IAM snapshot is not the complete AWS authorization environment.

Our importer supports unconditional identity-policy allows and explicit denies, wildcard matching, default managed-policy versions, inline policies, and group inheritance.

Relevant conditions, unsupported negations, policy variables, missing policy documents, and permissions boundaries produce an unknown result. An unknown selected identity stops the import. Other unknown identities are reported and excluded from positive paths.

The projection does not evaluate role-trust transitions, resource policies, organization controls, session policies, or actual resource existence.

Consequently, a positive path means a supported identity-policy grant in the imported model. It does not prove that AWS would authorize a live request. Likewise, collateral measurements cover the assessed permission, not every permission or workload.

Keeping those boundaries visible was an important part of building the project.

What we learned

Resource scoping is essential. A globally shared s3:GetObject node could accidentally connect a policy to unrelated resources. Action nodes need to preserve their target scope.

Explicit denies also cannot be treated as ordinary graph edges alongside allows. Their effect must be resolved when constructing the supported permission projection.

Finally, graph-copy simulation made the agent’s proposed actions reviewable. Instead of presenting a recommendation alone, Severance can show what changed in the model and what remained reachable.

That is the interaction we wanted to build: an investigation whose evidence, decision policy, approval, and resulting change can all be inspected.

Explore Severance on GitHub, including local setup instructions, the graph model, essential queries, and benchmark evidence.

View the working-project recording, covering both a seeded investigation and a public-snapshot investigation through approval and application.

title: The Observability Tax: A Forensic Audit of How Your Unified Platform Became a Liability
description:
Observability was sold to the industry as the panacea for system reliability: instrument every trace, log every request header, emit metrics on every function call, and you will achieve total operational omniscience.

Instead, modern observability has become an unchecked tax on gross margins.

In recent forensic audits of scaling SaaS platforms, we routinely find companies spending 22% to 28% of their entire cloud budget on proprietary telemetry platforms like Datadog, Splunk, or New Relic, often paying more for monitoring than for the actual production databases serving customers.

Why does this happen?

High-cardinality tag explosion. Engineers blindly add user_id, session_id, or request_uuid as tags to custom metrics, causing timeseries databases to multiply metrics into billions of discrete streams.

Furthermore, 95% of ingested debug logs are never queried by a human engineer during an incident.

By implementing high-signal telemetry filtering at the edge, converting raw logs to sampled spans, and storing long-tail audit logs in cheap S3-compatible cold storage, we regularly slash observability bills by 60% while dramatically improving incident resolution speed.

Key Takeaways & Architectural FAQs

Q: How do you reduce observability and logging costs before a Series B raise?

By filtering high-signal telemetry at the edge, converting raw logs to sampled spans, and moving long-tail audit logs to cheap cold storage. This has cut observability bills by up to 60% without losing incident-response visibility.

Q: Why does observability spend often exceed the cost of production databases?

High-cardinality tag explosion (per-user or per-request labels on default metrics) and debug logs nobody ever queries compound unchecked over time, until telemetry tooling costs more than the infrastructure it is monitoring.

title: Paid Apps and In-App Purchases in a Google Play Closed Test: What Testers Pay
description:
Disclosure: 12Testers14Day publishes this article and sells Google Play closed-testing help.

If your app costs money, or sells one-time products or subscriptions, a closed test raises a practical question: will your testers be charged? Google's answer depends on the testing track and on whether each tester is a license tester. Getting this wrong can mean testers paying real money, or a 14-day test where nobody ever touches your purchase flow.

The short answer

Based on Google's Play Console Help and Android Developers documentation:

Situation Paid app install In-app purchases and subscriptions
Internal test Free for testers Charged, unless the tester is a license tester
Closed or open test Testers must buy the app Charged, unless the tester is a license tester
License tester on a test track See the note below Test payment methods, no real charge

Google's test setup article says: "Testers must purchase paid apps when participating in open or closed tests. For internal tests, testers can install paid apps for free." It also says internal testers pay for in-app purchases unless you add them to a license testers list.

Google's billing testing guide adds that users "incur actual charges for their test track purchases unless the user is a license tester."

Note on paid apps and license testers: Google's license testing article says your own publishing account can buy your app as a test purchase, and that license testers can buy one-time products and subscriptions without being charged. Before you promise testers a free install of a paid app in a closed test, try it with one license-tester account and check the price shown on the Play Store page.

Why this matters for the 12-tester requirement

If your personal developer account was created after November 13, 2023, Google's testing requirements article says you need a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before you can apply for production access. (See our 12-testers requirement explainer for details.)

That has two consequences for monetized apps:

  • A paid price is a barrier to opting in. Every closed tester has to buy the app. Fewer people will agree, and anyone who doesn't install can't give you much feedback.
  • An untested purchase flow is a launch risk. If testers avoid your paywall because they don't want to spend money, your billing code ships with almost no real-device use.

Option 1: Keep in-app purchases testable with license testers

For a free app with in-app products or subscriptions, add your closed testers as license testers as well.

  1. In Play Console, go to Settings > License testing.
  2. Choose testers with an email list (up to 2,000 addresses per list) or a Google Group (no user limit, according to Google).
  3. Save your changes.
  4. Make sure the same people can receive your release. Being a license tester doesn't put someone on your closed track. They still need to be in the track's tester list and opt in through the opt-in link. Our guide to inviting testers and fixing access problems covers the common opt-in issues.
  5. Make sure your one-time products and subscriptions are published. Google says they must be published before they can be tested.

Once that's done, license testers see test payment methods at checkout. Google's billing guide lists several, including:

  • Test instrument, always approves, for a successful purchase.
  • Test instrument, always declines, for a failed payment.
  • Slow test card, approves after a few minutes and Slow test card, declines after a few minutes, for pending purchases.
  • A test instrument that simulates a user-initiated chargeback.

Things that behave differently for license testers

Tell testers about these so their reports make sense:

  • Subscriptions renew fast. A monthly or weekly test subscription renews about every 5 minutes, and a yearly one about every 30 minutes. Test subscriptions renew at most six times, not counting free trials and introductory periods.
  • Unacknowledged purchases are refunded. Google says a license-tester purchase is refunded after 3 minutes if your app doesn't acknowledge it. If testers report that "the purchase disappeared", check your acknowledgement code first.
  • Resubscribe and pause are always on. Google says these features are always enabled for license testers even if you've disabled them in Play Console.

Google also recommends testing with some non-license-tester accounts, either occasionally or after large changes, so your app doesn't depend on test-only behavior.

Option 2: Decide what to do about a paid app price

If your app has an up-front price, you have a few choices. Each has trade-offs.

  • Ask closed testers to buy it. This matches Google's rules, but expect fewer people to agree, and be clear with them about the cost before they opt in.
  • Use internal testing for early paid-app checks. Internal testers install paid apps free, but an internal test doesn't count toward the 12-tester closed-testing requirement. Google also says people who opt in to internal testing aren't eligible for your closed test, even if they're on its tester list. Our internal vs closed testing guide compares the two.
  • Think hard before making a paid app free. Google's pricing article says you can change an app from paid to free, but "once your app has been offered for free, the app can't be changed to paid." To charge again you would need a new app with a new package name. Moving to a free app with an in-app purchase or subscription is a separate product decision, not a testing shortcut.

A pre-test checklist for monetized apps

  • [ ] Decide whether testers should make purchases, and write it in your tester instructions.
  • [ ] Add every closed tester to License testing if you want purchases tested without real charges.
  • [ ] Publish the one-time products and subscriptions you want tested.
  • [ ] Confirm each tester is on the closed track's tester list and has opted in.
  • [ ] Check that your app acknowledges purchases, so test purchases aren't refunded after 3 minutes.
  • [ ] Give testers specific purchase journeys, such as "buy the monthly plan, cancel, then restore purchases".
  • [ ] Run at least one check with a non-license-tester account before production.

Our free closed-testing checklist covers the rest of the setup.

FAQ

Do closed testers pay for in-app purchases?
Yes, unless they're license testers. Google says users are charged for test-track purchases unless they're license testers.

Do license testers count toward the 12 testers?
License testing and the closed-test tester list are separate settings. Google's requirement counts testers who are opted in to your closed test. A license tester who isn't on the track and opted in doesn't count.

Can testers use promo codes instead?
This article doesn't cover promo codes. Check Play Console Help for the current rules before relying on them.

Does a paid-app closed test affect production access?
Google decides production access based on your testing, your app and your answers. The price alone isn't something this article can predict. What helps is a test where testers actually use the app, including the paid features. See what tester activity looks like.

If you'd rather not recruit testers yourself

12Testers14Day provides Google Play closed-testing help: about 14 testers for about 16 days, as a buffer around Google's 12-tester, 14-day requirement. Packages are one-time ($15 Basic for one app, $29 Premium for two, per the pricing page on October 18, 2026). If your app is paid or you want testers to make test purchases, contact the team before you buy so they can confirm what's possible. You can also read how a testing run works.

Official references: Set up an open, closed, or internal test · Test in-app billing with application licensing · Test your Google Play Billing Library integration · Set up your app's prices · App testing requirements for new personal developer accounts

title: Holdfast: a webhook safety net where Gemma explains what broke and code decides what happens
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

My day job is message queues in containers. The first rule there is boring and absolute: a message isn't acknowledged until it's safely stored. Lose power a millisecond later and it's still there.

Webhooks don't work like that. Stripe or GitHub sends your app a message, and if the app is down, slow, or chokes on a field that was renamed overnight, the message is usually just gone. The person who finds out is the shop owner, two days later, asking why three payments never showed up.

Holdfast is that queue rule, turned into a product for the people who get that phone call: freelance developers and small agencies who look after integrations for a handful of clients. It sits between the provider and the app and:

  1. Saves every webhook to disk before saying "got it".
  2. Checks the signature, and keeps forged or replayed messages aside.
  3. Delivers patiently: retries when the app is down, holds when a retry won't help.
  4. Explains what broke in two voices: a plain sentence the client can read, and a precise fix for the developer. Gemma writes both; code checks every word.
  5. Sends held messages again, never twice.

Who pays: the freelancer who maintains "the Stripe thing" for five small clients. One lost payment webhook is a lost order and an awkward conversation. Holdfast turns that into a note they can forward:

Kabir's ₹1050 payment for Ginger chai, 500 g couldn't reach Chai & Co. because the sender changed how it sends customer information. Holdfast is keeping the message safe, and it can be sent again once the app is updated to expect the new format.

That's a real answer from the deployed site, written by Gemma 3 4B running on Render.

Demo

Live: https://holdfast-o9ba.onrender.com

It has two modes, switchable from the header:

  • Demo (/demo, no sign-up): Chai & Co., a pretend tea shop with made-up customers. Seven buttons break it on purpose: the shop goes down, a field is renamed, a payment arrives twice, a signature is forged, an old payment is replayed. The relay, retries, checks and explanations are the real engine.
  • Live (/live): sign in with GitHub, pick one of your repositories, and Holdfast adds itself as the webhook. GitHub's test ping arrives within seconds. If you don't have an app, deliver to Holdfast's built-in test app and switch it to "Server down" or "Turns messages away" to watch a real webhook get held, explained and resent.

Landing Page:

Demo:

Event Gemma:

One honest note: Gemma runs on two CPU cores, so an explanation takes up to a minute and a half (48 s and 83 s in my last two live runs). The page shows the built-in rules' answer instantly and swaps in Gemma's when it's ready.

Code

Tanay3484 / holdfast

A safety net for webhooks: stores every event, holds what your app fails on, explains why with an open-weight model, and resends safely.

Holdfast

A safety net for webhooks. Holdfast sits between a provider (Stripe, GitHub) and your app. It stores every event before acknowledging it, holds the ones your app fails on, explains why in plain words with an open-weight model, and resends them safely once the problem is fixed.

Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2: Side Hustle.

How it works

provider ──▶ /in/{route} ──▶ check signature ──▶ save to disk ──▶ "got it"
                                                      │
                     deliver to your app ◀────────────┘
                       ├─ accepted      → done
                       ├─ worth a retry → wait a little longer each time
                       └─ won't work    → hold it safely
                                             │
                     code collects the facts ┘  (signature, every try, what changed since the last success)
                     Gemma names the cause from a fixed list and explains it; code checks every word
                     resend: never twice, never anything that failed its signature check
  • Code decides, the model explains.…
View on GitHub

Go, about 5,900 lines plus 1,550 lines of tests (59 tests). Every feature has a spec in specs/ with numbered requirements.

How I Built It

Open-weight model: Gemma 3 4B, served by Ollama in a private service next to the app. Stack: Go standard library, SQLite (pure-Go driver), server-rendered HTML, a little vanilla JS. Hosting: a single Render Blueprint (more below).

Code decides, the model explains

The rule I held to: the model never decides what happens to a message. Retries, holds, duplicate detection and resends are plain, tested Go. Gemma gets the facts code collected (signature result, every delivery attempt, the app's error, what changed in the payload) and does two jobs:

  1. pick a cause from a fixed list of eight, under a JSON schema, and
  2. write the explanation.

Then code checks what it wrote. The client summary is rejected and replaced with the built-in rules' wording if it contains jargon ("HTTP", "payload", "endpoint", an error number) or promises something nobody did. Titles always come from code.

The bug that taught me the most

First version, renamed-field scenario. Gemma got the cause right, but the client summary said:

A payment notification failed to reach the Chai & Co. system. The notification is being kept safe and reviewed.

Nobody was reviewing anything. Worse, the developer note said the app "now requires customer_id", which is backwards: Stripe changed, the app didn't.

The fix wasn't a better prompt alone. It was moving more work into code:

  • Code finds the rename. A shape-diff walks both JSON bodies and spots that data.object.customer_id disappeared while data.object.customer.id appeared. That's one rename, with a direction. Gemma is told "the sender now sends X where it used to send Y; the app did not change" instead of a raw list of paths.
  • The summary has a required shape: what happened to this payment (who, how much), why in everyday words, what happens next.
  • A Promise check rejects "being reviewed", "will resend", "our team is…".
  • The developer fix must name the field that moved, or the rules' fix is used.

After the fix, on the same scenario:

For your developer: The sender now uses data.object.customer.id instead of data.object.customer_id. Change the app to expect data.object.customer.id.

Model size, measured

Model Where Result on the renamed-field case
Gemma 3 1B laptop Wrote "the app will resend the held events" (a promise) and told the sender to change. The checks now catch both and fall back to the rules' answer.
Gemma 3 4B laptop GPU Named the customer and amount, explained the change plainly, and pointed at the exact field. About 16 s.
Gemma 3 4B Render, 2 CPUs Same quality. 92 s for one explanation.
Gemma 3 4B Render, after the fixes below Two live runs, both explained by Gemma: 48 s and 83 s.

On a laptop CPU with two threads, one explanation was 740 prompt tokens read in 15 s and 115 tokens written in 14 s. That's why the page shows a rules answer first.

How I built it: an unlock game

I built this with Claude Code, spec first. The four core pieces started as stubs I had to write by hand, each a "level" with known-answer checks. go run ./cmd/unlock prints a progress board, and while a level was locked, every part of the website it powered showed a "WIP: write this file to reveal how this will look" tile. Writing a file literally revealed part of the site.

Being honest about who wrote what (it's recorded in tasks.md):

  • Level 1, signatures: I wrote GitHub's HMAC check. Stripe's was started by me and finished by Claude.
  • Level 2, retry policy: written by me (backoff, Retry-After, the hold rules), polished by Claude.
  • Levels 3 and 4, shape diff and resend plan: written by Claude at my request. Level 3 was a worked example to teach me recursion, which I'd stalled on, and level 4 was the last night before the deadline.

Two safety details I'm glad I didn't skip

  • Server-side request forgery. Live mode lets you type the URL Holdfast forwards to. Without care, anyone could point it at holdfast-ollama:11434 or a cloud metadata address and read the answers on the event page. Destinations are checked when saved and every connection is checked again at dial time, so a hostname that later resolves to a private IP is still refused.
  • Duplicates. Providers deliver at least once. The resend plan sends each event once, in arrival order, never one that was already delivered, and never one whose signature failed.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The data is the business's customers. Payment webhooks carry names, amounts and addresses. With an open-weight model on the same private network, none of it goes to an AI company, and the freelancer can tell their client that truthfully.
  • No per-message bill. A small shop's integration might send hundreds of events a day. One small model on one server explains every failure for a flat cost.
  • I could look inside the failure. When Gemma promised a review that wasn't happening, I could see exactly what it was given, change what code tells it, and constrain its output with a JSON schema. The fix was engineering, not hoping a vendor's model changes.
  • Swappable. The model is one setting (HF_MODEL). I measured 1B against 4B and chose on evidence.

My Agent Session

Built pair-programming with Claude Code: spec first (brief, requirements, design, tasks, each approved by me), then implementation task by task, with subagents for coaching me on my levels, writing specs, and drafting this post. The coach was told never to write my code, only give hints and review.

Building Holdfast: a webhook safety net with Gemma
You

Status is approved. Set up the rest today: the frontend website, and leave certain things as "WIP: work on this file to reveal how the website will look", something like a game for me, where every file I code, I unlock a bit of the website. Obviously the coding bits are still to be done by me.

Agent

Plan: the four core pieces (signature checks, retry policy, JSON shape diff, resend plan) become documented stubs that return wip.ErrLocked. Each is a 'level' with known-answer checks in internal/unlock. The relay falls back to simpler behaviour while a level is locked, and every part of the site a locked level powers renders a WIP tile naming the file to write. go run ./cmd/unlock prints the board.

▸ Write internal/verify/verify.go (stub + contract + GitHub's documented known answer)
Input
internal/verify/verify.go (stub + contract + GitHub's documented known answer)
Output
File created
▸ Bash go run ./cmd/unlock
Input
$ go run ./cmd/unlock
Output
HOLDFAST · UNLOCK BOARD  0 of 4 levels
[··········]  Level 1  Signature check  LOCKED
  next → open internal/verify/verify.go (H1)

Then the engine: SQLite store that commits before the relay answers 200, a delivery worker with a one-try fallback, rule-based diagnosis plus Gemma via Ollama under a JSON schema, a client note, and the website with a live demo shop (Chai & Co.) that visitors can break on purpose.

▸ Bash fire every demo scenario at the local server, read the dashboard
Input
$ fire every demo scenario at the local server, read the dashboard
Output
3 payments held safely … What happened: the app's server was down.
You

So shouldn't we first have some kind of struct present that will be needed when unmarshalling?

Agent

No struct: Of has to accept any JSON. Unmarshal into any, then a type switch over map[string]any, []any, string, float64, bool and nil tells you what each node is. The rest is a small recursive walk that records the kind at each path.

You

Just write it for me so I can understand what you're trying to tell me. I will do the next one on my own.

Agent
▸ Edit internal/shape/shape.go: walk(s, path, v) records the kind, then recurses int...
Input
internal/shape/shape.go: walk(s, path, v) records the kind, then recurses into object keys (path.key) and array items (path[]); record() marks Mixed when array items disagree; Diff compares two shapes and sorts by path
Output
Level 3 UNLOCKED (7/7 checks)

It is the folder-listing idea: write down what this thing is, and if it contains other things, call walk again for each with a longer path. tasks.md records that I wrote this level at your request.

You

Ok just check and lmk if Function 1 is ok?

Agent
▸ Bash go run ./cmd/unlock -v
Input
$ go run ./cmd/unlock -v
Output
Level 1  Signature check  4/10 checks
✓ GitHub: accepts GitHub's own documented example
✓ GitHub: rejects a body changed after signing
✓ GitHub: reports a missing header
✓ GitHub: rejects a header without sha256=

GitHub is correct, and decoding the hex and comparing raw bytes with hmac.Equal is better than comparing hex strings. The remaining six checks are Stripe's: same seal, but over "t.body", any v1 may match, then a freshness check.

You

Gemma only says: "A payment notification failed to reach the Chai & Co. system. The notification is being kept safe and reviewed." Is this temporary? Because come on it should say more than that.

Agent
▸ Bash read the held event's page
Input
$ read the held event's page
Output
For your developer: The app is now requiring a 'customer_id' field, which was previously absent…  (backwards: the sender changed, not the app)

Not temporary: the prompt only asked for 'two short sentences, no jargon', nothing checked for promises ('reviewed'), and Gemma was handed raw paths and guessed the direction. Fix by moving work into code: detect renames (customer_id → customer.id) and tell the model the sender changed; require what happened / why / what next; a Promise check; and the developer fix must name the moved field or the rules' fix is used.

▸ Bash renamed-field demo again on gemma3:4b
Input
$ renamed-field demo again on gemma3:4b
Output
Nisha's ₹1050 payment … couldn't reach Chai & Co. because the sender changed how they send customer information. Holdfast is keeping the message safe and it can be sent again once the system is updated.
For your developer: The sender now uses data.object.customer.id instead of data.object.customer_id.
▸ Bash same demo on gemma3:1b
Input
$ same demo on gemma3:1b
Output
"The app will resend the held events." / "Ensure the sender updates the customer ID field."  → guards now replace both
You

I want to go 4b since the good answers is what we want. How will we host it on Render though? I want to mimic my Week 1 setup.

Agent

Same shape as Week 1: a public web service plus a private Ollama service with the model baked into its image, now on 2c-4g because gemma3:4b needs about 3.5 GB loaded. Measured on a CPU with 2 threads: 740 prompt tokens in 15 s, 115 output tokens in 14 s, so the page shows the rules' answer at once and swaps in Gemma's when it arrives.

▸ Edit relay: save the rules' diagnosis first (pending), replace with the model's; r...
Input
relay: save the rules' diagnosis first (pending), replace with the model's; resume pending ones after a restart
Output
tests pass
You

Can you do Level 4 for me? And then overhaul the website since it's no longer a game. Can we have two modes, Demo and Live? Live will be for users to connect GitHub. I don't have a Stripe account, so we will be honest about it in our submission.

Agent
▸ Edit internal/replay/replay.go: DedupeKey (GitHub delivery id, Stripe event id, el...
Input
internal/replay/replay.go: DedupeKey (GitHub delivery id, Stripe event id, else sha256 of body); Plan sorts a copy by arrival, sends each key once, never a forged or already-delivered event
Output
Every level unlocked. Holdfast is ready to ship.

Live mode: GitHub OAuth (admin:repo_hook only), Holdfast adds the webhook to the chosen repo, delivery to the user's app or a built-in test app that can be made to fail. Routes become dynamic; user-typed destinations go through a guard that refuses private addresses at save time and again at dial time, so nobody can point Holdfast at its own Ollama service. Tokens and webhook secrets are sealed with AES-GCM. Stripe connects by hand, and the site says so.

▸ Bash go test ./internal/netguard/
Input
$ go test ./internal/netguard/
Output
ok  (refuses 127.0.0.1, 10.x, 169.254.169.254, holdfast-ollama:11434; dial-time check refuses loopback)
You

The GitHub login looks a bit weird. Also there's too much text on the demo and live page. We want it attractive to customers so they will pay.

Agent

The page in the screenshot was rendering with almost no CSS: the stylesheet was linked as app.css?v=dev, so the browser kept an old cached copy. Assets are now linked with a hash of their contents. Then the copy: Live becomes a headline, one line, a dark 'Continue with GitHub' button, three chips and three step cards; Demo becomes 'Break the shop. Lose nothing.' with short button labels.

You

For the how it works section, can we add an animation rather than textboxes? Makes it easier for people to understand.

Agent

A 15-second SVG/CSS loop: a payment travels Stripe → Holdfast → the shop, is saved, checked, finds the shop down, is held, explained, then sent again while a duplicate is crossed out; five captions light up in step. Headless screenshots showed it frozen until I added --disable-threaded-animation: transform and opacity animations run on the compositor, which virtual time doesn't drive.

You

Deployed. GitHub seems to be working fine.

Agent
▸ Bash render logs (holdfast)
Input
$ render logs (holdfast)
Output
WARN model unavailable; used rules err="ollama: Post \"http://holdfast-ollama:10000/api/chat\": dial tcp …:10000: connect: connection refused"
▸ Bash render logs (holdfast-ollama)
Input
$ render logs (holdfast-ollama)
Output
ollama ready with gemma3:4b
Detected service running on port 11434

Ollama is healthy on 11434, but the Blueprint's fromService hostport used Render's default port 10000. The rules answered every held event, so the site stayed usable. Fix: PORT=11434 on the private service.

▸ Bash after the redeploy: send a renamed-field payment to the live site
Input
$ after the redeploy: send a renamed-field payment to the live site
Output
after 92s: Kabir's ₹1050 payment for Ginger chai, 500 g couldn't reach Chai & Co. because the sender changed how it sends customer information…
Explained by Gemma, checked by code.
20 of 20 messages

My First User

My first user is a real app with a real repository: Tasklet, a small todo app I built (source) that turns GitHub issues into todos. It's strict on purpose, like a real handler, and it has a maintenance switch that makes it answer 503. I signed in to Holdfast's Live mode with GitHub, connected Tanay3484/tasklet, and pointed it at Tasklet's webhook address. My coding agent ran the rest from the command line while I was out, and I checked the results when I got back.

Step What happened
Connect the repo Holdfast added the webhook. GitHub's test ping was acknowledged in 0.27 s.
Open issue #1 GitHub → Holdfast acknowledged in 0.82 s. The todo appeared in Tasklet within 4 s.
Tasklet in maintenance, open issue #2 Holdfast tried 5 times in 34 s (waiting 2, 4, 8, 16 s), got 503 each time, and held it. Gemma explained it in 40 s.
Close issue #1 The todo was ticked off within 4 s.
Maintenance off, then "Send all held again" I pressed it in Live mode. Issue #2's todo appeared in Tasklet, once. Nothing was lost while the app was down.

One detail I'll own: Tasklet runs on Render's free plan, which doesn't keep a disk, so its todos reset whenever it falls asleep. That's why issue #1's todo had disappeared by the time I resent #2. Holdfast's copy of every message was still there.

Did anyone pay? No. My first user is me and my own app, so I won't claim a sale. What the run convinced me of is the thing I'd charge for: I switched an app off, opened an issue, and nothing was lost, and I got a sentence explaining why it was held that I could forward to a client. What I'd build next: an email or Slack alert the moment something is held, one-click Stripe sign-in, and a share link for the client note.

Something real from deploy day: on the first deploy, every Gemma call failed with connection refused on holdfast-ollama:10000. Ollama was healthy on port 11434, but Render's service-to-service address used its default port. The rules took over automatically, so the site stayed fully usable, which is exactly the fallback I designed for. One line in render.yaml (PORT=11434) fixed it.

Then two more, the same afternoon:

  • Out of memory. Render killed the Gemma service. Inside the container, llama.cpp sees the whole host (60+ GB, 16 CPUs), not my 4 GB plan, so it kept a prompt cache that could grow to 8 GB and a second, repacked copy of the weights. Three LLAMA_ARG_* settings (no prompt cache, no repack, 2 threads) brought it back under 4 GB.
  • A runaway answer. Some diagnoses ran on for hundreds of tokens and never closed their JSON. I reproduced it on my laptop's CPU with Render's exact settings: in 3 of 5 runs Gemma tried to end a string with a curly quote (”}), which JSON treats as ordinary text, so it never stopped and started repeating itself. A second cause: Go wrote the JSON format's fields alphabetically (cause, fix, summary), so Gemma poured the whole story into the developer's fix and left the owner one line. The fix: length limits on each field, code that cuts a field at the stray ”}, a check that the summary ends like a sentence, and the fields listed as cause, summary, fix. Before: 2 of 5 runs usable. After: 4 of 4, in 16–40 s.

Each time, the visitor still got a correct, plain-language answer from the rules. Gemma makes the explanation better; it was never the thing keeping a payment safe.

What isn't built: one-click Stripe sign-in. Stripe Connect needs a Stripe platform account, which I don't have, so Stripe connects by hand. You paste one address into Stripe's webhook settings and its signing secret into Holdfast. The site says so plainly.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Render. Render is the AI runtime: one Blueprint runs the public Go service (with a persistent disk for the event store) and a private Ollama service with Gemma baked into the image, talking over Render's private network. The model is never exposed to the internet.
  • Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 4B writes every explanation and client note. Its output is constrained to a schema and checked by code, and I measured it against 1B to choose the size.

title: Build a Hiring-Signal Feed from Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and SmartRecruiters (with Python)
description:
"They just opened 6 SDR roles" is one of the strongest timing signals in outbound. If a company is hiring for the team that would use your product, you have a reason to reach out now. Most teams get that signal from LinkedIn scrapes or expensive data vendors. But most tech companies already publish their entire job board as clean JSON through their applicant tracking system (ATS). This tutorial shows how to turn that into a company-level hiring-signal feed you can refresh every week.

The data source: public ATS job-board APIs

Career pages are usually powered by one of a handful of ATSs, and each exposes a public, unauthenticated endpoint meant for embedding job lists:

ATS Public endpoint pattern
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json (EU: api.eu.lever.co)
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}?includeCompensation=true
SmartRecruiters https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/{id}/postings

These are the employer's system of record. Roles show up here first and disappear when they're filled, so the data is fresher and cleaner than most aggregators.

A 20-line DIY version (Greenhouse only) 

import httpx, collections

def greenhouse_signal(slug):
    jobs = httpx.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs",
                     params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30).json()["jobs"]
    by_dept = collections.Counter(
        (j.get("departments") or [{"name": "Other"}])[0]["name"] for j in jobs)
    sales = [j for j in jobs if any(k in j["title"].lower()
             for k in ("sdr", "bdr", "account executive", "sales"))]
    return {"company": slug, "open_roles": len(jobs),
            "sales_roles": len(sales), "top_departments": by_dept.most_common(5)}

print(greenhouse_signal("stripe"))

That works, but a real feed also needs:

  • detection of which ATS a company uses,
  • Lever's EU cluster and SmartRecruiters' paging,
  • seniority classification,
  • salary parsing,
  • memory between runs, so you can say "+11 roles since last week".

That last part is what makes it a signal rather than just a list.

The hosted version: Hiring Signal Feed

Hiring Signal Feed is an Apify Actor that does all of the above. It returns one row per company, with:

  • open_roles, roles_by_department, roles_by_seniority, remote_roles
  • new_roles_7d and new_roles_30d
  • open_roles_change, roles_added_since_last_run and roles_closed_since_last_run, from a snapshot it keeps for you
  • salary_bands and the ats the company uses

Optionally, it also returns normalized job rows. Pricing is $0.01 per company row (or $0.0015 per job row), plus $0.02 per run.

pip install apify-client pandas

import os, pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
accounts = ["greenhouse:stripe", "greenhouse:discord", "ashby:ramp",
            "https://jobs.lever.co/spotify", "notion"]   # bare names are auto-detected

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/hiring-signal-feed").call(run_input={
    "companies": accounts,
    "outputMode": "companies",
    "titleKeywords": ["sales", "sdr", "bdr", "account executive"],
    "snapshotStoreName": "my-sales-hiring-watch",
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
df = df[df.row_type == "company"]
print(df[["company", "ats", "open_roles", "new_roles_30d", "roles_added_since_last_run"]]
      .sort_values("new_roles_30d", ascending=False))

Because titleKeywords is set, every count is computed only on sales roles. So new_roles_30d = 9 means nine new sales jobs this month.

Score and route accounts 

df["score"] = (df.new_roles_30d.fillna(0) * 2
               + df.roles_added_since_last_run.fillna(0) * 3
               + df.open_roles.fillna(0) * 0.2)
hot = df[df.score >= 10].sort_values("score", ascending=False)
hot.to_csv("hot_accounts.csv", index=False)

Get the actual postings for personalization

Run again with outputMode: "jobs" for just the hot accounts. Each job row includes title, department, location, posted_at, salary and the posting url. That's ideal for a first line like "Saw you're hiring a Founding AE in Austin…".

Make it weekly

  1. Save the input as an Apify Task and attach a Schedule (for example, Mondays at 07:00).
  2. Keep snapshotStoreName the same, so each run diffs against the last one.
  3. Pipe results to your CRM:
    • In Clay, use an HTTP API column that calls run-sync-get-dataset-items.
    • In n8n, Make or Zapier, use the Apify app (Run Actor, then Get dataset items, then upsert into HubSpot or Sheets).

cURL for the HTTP column:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/eligible_fame~hiring-signal-feed/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"companies":["{{domain_or_slug}}"],"outputMode":"companies"}'

Signals beyond sales hiring

The same feed answers other questions. A few common ones:

  • Selling data tools: filter for data engineer and analytics.
  • Selling security: watch for security and GRC roles.
  • Investors: track open_roles_change_pct across a portfolio for early momentum or slowdowns.
  • Recruiters: look for companies whose new_roles_7d jumps in your niche.

A sudden spike in manager and lead/principal seniority often means a new team is being built. That's usually a better trigger than one-off backfills.

Limitations to know

  • It only covers companies that use these four ATSs. That's most venture-backed tech, plus many enterprises on SmartRecruiters, but not every employer. If a company isn't found, you get a free error row.
  • posted_at semantics differ between ATSs. Some companies repost roles, so the snapshot diff (roles_added_since_last_run) is the most reliable "new" signal.
  • Salary only appears where the employer publishes it.

Wrap-up

Hiring data is the cheapest high-intent signal there is, because companies publish it themselves. Whether you write the 20-line script or use Hiring Signal Feed, the key is tracking change over time at the company level, not just collecting rows.

title: How to find your Android Advertising ID (GAID) and register a test device
description:
If you work on an Android app with ads, sooner or later someone asks you for your "advertising ID", "GAID" or "AAID". This short guide shows where to find it and how to use it to register a test device, so you can see test ads safely and keep your own clicks out of real traffic.

What is the Advertising ID?

The Android Advertising ID (GAID, also called AAID or Ad ID) is a resettable identifier provided by Google Play services. It is the Android counterpart of IDFA on iOS. Ad networks and attribution tools use it to recognize a device, and most of them let you flag a device as a "test device" by entering this ID.

Option 1: Find it in Settings

On most recent Android versions:

Settings → Privacy → Ads (on some devices: Settings → Google → Ads)

You will see "Your advertising ID" there. Copying it from this screen is not always possible, and the menu location differs between manufacturers.

Note: if you have chosen "Delete advertising ID" (Android 12+) or "Opt out of Ads Personalization", apps receive an ID made of zeros. Test-device registration will not work with a zeroed ID, so turn that option off first.

Option 2: Use a small app

If you need to send the ID to a teammate or paste it into a dashboard, an app that reads the ID and lets you copy or share it is faster. I built GAID for exactly this: open it, tap Copy or Share, done. It also warns you when your device is returning a zeroed ID.

GAID on Google Play

Registering the device as a test device

Once you have the ID, add it in your ad network or attribution dashboard. Common places to look:

  • AdMob: in the AdMob console, Settings → Test devices → Add test device, then enter the advertising ID.
  • AppLovin MAX: the MAX dashboard has a Test Mode section where you add a device by its advertising ID.
  • Unity Ads: the Unity dashboard lets you add test devices by advertising ID in the monetization settings.
  • Attribution tools (for example AppsFlyer or Adjust): their SDK testing / test device pages accept the advertising ID.

Menu names change from time to time, so search the dashboard for "test device" if you cannot find it.

Tip: AdMob's in-code test device setting (RequestConfiguration.setTestDeviceIds) uses a different, hashed ID that the SDK prints to Logcat, not the raw advertising ID. Use the console method above with the advertising ID, or copy the hashed ID from Logcat for the code method.

Why bother?

Clicking real ads on your own device, even by accident, can be counted as invalid traffic and hurt your ad account. Registering a test device is a two-minute job that avoids that risk.

title: iMessage support for eve agents
description:
eve agents can now connect to iMessage through the new Photon channel.

The channel keeps each iMessage conversation in one eve session, verifies incoming webhooks, and marks accepted messages as read.

If more messages arrive while the agent is replying, they steer the in-progress reply instead of each getting a separate answer. The onMessage hook filters which messages the agent handles and adds context to a turn.

Run eve add channel/photon-imessage to add the channel. iMessage delivery runs through Photon, so the command sets up a Photon project, registers your phone number, and scaffolds the channel:

eve uses Vercel Connect to create the connector and configure Photon's webhook. On hosts without Connect support, choose Use portable credentials during setup and the channel reads its credentials from environment variables instead.

title: Server-side lead events with the GA4 Measurement Protocol (and the pitfalls)
description:
Browser tags miss leads. Ad blockers, consent banners, people closing the tab right after submitting, and thank-you pages that never load all mean that the generate_lead event in GA4 is often lower than the number of rows in your CRM. If you optimise paid campaigns on that number, you are optimising on a sample with a bias you cannot see.

A small, honest fix is to send the lead event from your server, at the moment the form submission is actually stored, using the GA4 Measurement Protocol. This post shows a minimal version and the pitfalls that make people give up on it.

What you need

  • A GA4 web data stream, its Measurement ID (G-XXXXXXX) and a Measurement Protocol API secret (Admin → Data streams → your stream → Measurement Protocol API secrets).
  • The visitor's GA client ID, captured in the browser and sent along with the form. Without it, GA4 cannot join the server event to the session that produced it.

Capture the client ID in a hidden field:

<input type="hidden" name="ga_client_id" id="ga_client_id">
<script>
  gtag('get', 'G-XXXXXXX', 'client_id', (id) => {
    document.getElementById('ga_client_id').value = id;
  });
</script>

Send the event when the lead is saved

Node.js 18+ (built-in fetch), called right after your form handler writes the lead to the database:

const MP_URL = 'https://www.google-analytics.com/mp/collect';

export async function sendLeadEvent({ clientId, leadId, formName, value = 0 }) {
  if (!clientId) return { skipped: 'no client id' }; // never invent one
  const url = `${MP_URL}?measurement_id=${process.env.GA4_MEASUREMENT_ID}` +
              `&api_secret=${process.env.GA4_API_SECRET}`;
  const body = {
    client_id: clientId,
    events: [{
      name: 'generate_lead',
      params: {
        form_name: formName,
        lead_id: leadId,          // lets you de-duplicate and reconcile with the CRM
        value, currency: 'AED',
        engagement_time_msec: 1,  // makes the event count toward active users
      },
    }],
  };
  const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(body) });
  return { status: res.status };
}

Keep the API secret in an environment variable on the server, never in front-end code.

Validate before you trust it

The production endpoint returns 204 even for malformed payloads, so a "successful" request proves nothing. During development, post the same body to the debug endpoint, which returns a list of validation messages:

https://www.google-analytics.com/debug/mp/collect?measurement_id=...&api_secret=...

An empty validationMessages array is what you want. After that, confirm in GA4 DebugView, and then in the standard reports a day later.

Pitfalls

  • Double counting. If the browser tag also fires generate_lead, you will count most leads twice. Pick one source for the event. A clean split: the browser keeps form_start and form_submit, and only the server sends generate_lead.
  • Consent. Server-side does not mean consent-free. If a visitor declined analytics, do not send the event. Store the consent state with the lead and check it before calling sendLeadEvent.
  • Timestamps. If you queue events and send them later, set timestamp_micros. GA4 accepts events up to 72 hours in the past.
  • Spam. Send the event after your spam filter, not before. Otherwise the bot traffic you just blocked becomes "conversions".

The payoff

Once the event comes from the same place as the CRM row, the two numbers finally reconcile, apart from consent-declined leads, which you can count separately. That is the number worth importing into Google Ads or feeding to bidding. It is a small piece of the measurement work we do in performance marketing: fix what is counted before spending more on what is counted.

References

  • Google for Developers: Measurement Protocol (GA4)
  • Google for Developers: Validating events
  • Google Analytics Help: Recommended events: generate_lead

title: avoiding race conditions in async cascade deletes for event‑sourced services
description:
you've got an event‑sourced aggregate that emits a UserDeleted event, and several downstream services react by cleaning up related rows in their own stores. the cleanup runs in background workers, so a second request that references the same user can slip through the cracks and hit a foreign‑key violation.

the race condition

in a typical setup each service subscribes to the UserDeleted topic and issues a cascade delete against its own tables. because the subscription processing is asynchronous, a request that arrives after the UserDeleted event is published but before the worker finishes will see stale data. the DB then throws an error, and the client gets a 500 instead of a graceful "not found".

a deterministic approach

the trick is to make the delete operation idempotent and observable before the request reaches the service. one pattern is to store a tombstone flag in a shared cache (e.g. Redis) as part of the same transaction that publishes the event. workers check the flag before proceeding, and request handlers read it to short‑circuit.

// publish + tombstone atomically
await redis.multi()
  .set(`tombstone:user:${userId}`, '1', 'EX', 300) // 5 min TTL
  .publish('user.deleted', JSON.stringify({ userId }))
  .exec();

workers then do:

const flag = await redis.get(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);
if (!flag) return; // nothing to clean up
await db.transaction(async trx => {
  await trx('orders').where({ userId }).delete();
  await trx('profiles').where({ userId }).delete();
});
await redis.del(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);

trade‑offs

  • latency vs consistency – adding the cache lookup adds a few milliseconds to every request, but it eliminates sporadic DB errors.
  • cache eviction – the TTL must be long enough to cover the slowest worker, otherwise a stale request could still hit the DB.
  • failure handling – if the worker crashes after deleting rows but before clearing the tombstone, subsequent requests will be rejected even though the data is gone. a periodic reconciler that scans for orphaned tombstones can mitigate this.
  • testing – simulate the race by issuing a delete and a read in parallel within integration tests; assert that the read returns a 404 rather than a DB exception.

when to apply

if your service experiences occasional 500 spikes after bulk deletions, or if you already use a message broker for domain events, the tombstone pattern is a low‑overhead way to enforce eventual consistency without locking the DB.

anyone using a similar approach with different stores (e.g. DynamoDB streams) or who prefers optimistic concurrency controls instead? how do you keep the delete path safe without sacrificing throughput?

title: A page-turning book in Remotion is one array of leaves, a rotateY and two faces, and the stacking order is the only hard part
description:
The third video ad we built for Nakodo is a book. It drops onto a desk, the cover opens, twenty pages riffle past under a thumb, and it stops on the first of three spreads. It is React, rendered with Remotion, and there is no 3D library anywhere in it.

The thing I expected to be hard, the page turn, is nine lines of CSS. The thing that actually took the afternoon was deciding which page is on top.

A book in a 9:16 frame

The first decision is not an animation one. A book is landscape and a reel is portrait, so an honest drawing of an open book in a vertical video gives you two tiny pages and a lot of desk.

So the spine sits just inside the left edge:

export const BOOK = { left: 70, top: 250, width: 940, height: 1360 };
export const COVER = { left: BOOK.left - 6, top: BOOK.top - 28, width: BOOK.width + 42, height: BOOK.height + 56 };

The right-hand page fills the frame. The left-hand page exists, and is drawn, at left - width, which is off screen. You never see it, but pages have to turn onto something, and the shadow near the spine only reads as a gutter if there is a page under it.

COVER is the same box plus a margin on three sides, because a hardback's boards overhang its pages, and that overhang is most of what makes a rectangle read as a book.

Every leaf is a row in one array 

type Leaf = {
  start: number;
  turn: number;
  ease: (t: number) => number;
  front: (f: number) => ReactNode;
  back?: ReactNode;
  box?: typeof BOOK;
};

The whole book is one array in that shape: the cover first, then twenty riffle pages, then the three content pages, then the call to action.

const LEAVES: Leaf[] = [
  { start: COVER_OPEN, turn: COVER_TURN, ease: easeInOut, front: () => <Cover />, back: <CoverInside />, box: COVER },
  ...Array.from({ length: RIFFLE_PAGES }, (_, k): Leaf => ({
    start: RIFFLE_STARTS[k],
    turn: riffleTurn(k),
    ease: smooth,
    front: () => <Paper><RifflePage k={k} /></Paper>,
  })),
  ...PAGES.map((Page, i): Leaf => ({ start: TURN_AT[i], turn: TURN, ease: easeInOut, front: (f) => <Paper><Page t={f - PAGE_AT[i]} /></Paper> })),
  { start: 1e9, turn: 1, ease: smooth, front: (f) => /* the end card */ },
];

front is a function of the frame, not a node, because the content of a page animates while the page lies there: a word gets pecked and turns into another word. back is a plain node because the back of a page is blank in every case but one.

start: 1e9 on the last leaf is the laziest possible way to say "this one never turns over". It is the last page; the video ends while it is open. A turnsOver: false flag would have been one more branch in the renderer for one row in the data.

The turn 

export function Turning({ angle, front, back, box = BOOK }) {
  if (angle >= 179.5) return null;
  const { left, top, width, height } = box;
  const lift = Math.sin((Math.min(angle, 90) * Math.PI) / 180);
  return (
    <div style={abs({ left, top, width, height, perspective: 4200, perspectiveOrigin: `0px ${height / 2}px` })}>
      <div style={abs({ inset: 0, transformOrigin: "0 50%", transformStyle: "preserve-3d", transform: `rotateY(${-angle}deg)` })}>
        <div style={abs({ inset: 0, backfaceVisibility: "hidden" })}>
          {front}
          <div style={abs({ inset: 0, background: `rgba(20,30,50,${0.16 * lift})` })} />
        </div>
        <div style={abs({ inset: 0, backfaceVisibility: "hidden", transform: "rotateY(180deg)" })}>{back ?? <Paper />}</div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

That is the entire mechanism. transformOrigin: "0 50%" puts the hinge on the spine. rotateY(-angle) swings it, 0 lying flat and 180 turned over. Two children both with backfaceVisibility: hidden, the second pre-rotated by 180 degrees, so exactly one of them faces you at any angle and they swap at upright on their own.

perspectiveOrigin at 0px, height/2 puts the vanishing point on the hinge rather than in the middle of the page, which is the difference between a page turning and a page being swung around like a door.

lift darkens the front as it rises, peaking at upright, using sin of the angle clamped to 90. No lighting model, one multiply.

The early return at 179.5 rather than 180 is a practical detail. A page lying flat on the left page is off screen and perfectly flush with whatever is under it, and leaving it mounted means every landed page contributes another composited layer for the rest of the video.

Which page is on top

This is the part that is not obvious, and it is six lines:

const angles = LEAVES.map((l) => angleOf(l, f));
const open = angles.findIndex((a) => a === 0);
const turning = LEAVES.map((l, i) => ({ l, i, a: angles[i] })).filter(({ a }) => a > 0 && a < 180);
const lowest = turning.length ? turning[turning.length - 1].a : 0;

At any frame a leaf is in one of three states, straight out of its angle: not started (0), turning (0 to 180), or done (180). So:

  • the page you can see lying open is the first leaf that has not started to turn, found with a findIndex for a zero;
  • everything turning is drawn after it, in reverse array order, because a leaf later in the book sits under the ones before it, and the ones before it have turned further;
  • lowest is the angle of the last leaf still turning, which is the one closest to the page below, and that is the angle the cast shadow is drawn from. 
{turning.slice().reverse().map(({ l, i, a }) => <Turning key={i} angle={a} front={l.front(f)} back={l.back} box={l.box} />)}

Nothing in the data says what is in front of what. Z-order falls out of array order plus the angles, which means adding a page to the book is adding an object to an array and nothing else. The first version of this had explicit z-index numbers and I got twenty pages into the riffle before I admitted that I was maintaining a second copy of the ordering by hand.

The riffle is two easing curves, not twenty keyframes 

const gapAt = (k: number) => 2 + 2.6 * (1 - Math.sin((Math.PI * k) / (RIFFLE_PAGES - 1)));
export const RIFFLE_STARTS = Array.from({ length: RIFFLE_PAGES }, (_, k) => k)
  .reduce<number[]>((s, k) => [...s, k === 0 ? RIFFLE_FROM : s[k - 1] + gapAt(k)], []);
export const riffleTurn = (k: number) => 6 + 4 * (1 - Math.sin((Math.PI * k) / (RIFFLE_PAGES - 1)));

A thumb released off a stack of pages is slow at the start, fast through the middle and slows to a stop. Both the gap between pages starting and the time each page takes to turn follow the same half-sine: 4.6 frames apart at the ends, 2 frames apart in the middle.

The starts are a cumulative sum, because what you control is the gap and what the renderer needs is the time. Twenty rows of hand-tuned numbers would have been the obvious thing to write and impossible to retime later; this way the whole riffle is two constants and a curve.

The shadow 

const reach = width * Math.cos((angle * Math.PI) / 180);
const k = Math.sin((angle * Math.PI) / 90) * 0.28;

A lifting page casts a shadow onto the page under it, and the shadow is as wide as the page's own projection: width * cos(angle). At 0 it covers the page exactly, at 90 it has gone.

The darkness uses angle * PI / 90, not /180. That doubles the frequency, so the sine peaks at 45 degrees and returns to zero at 90, which is roughly when a real page is darkest against the one below: not flat, not upright, somewhere in between.

The end card is a whole screen stuffed into a page

The last leaf has to show the same call to action as our other two reels, which is a component laid out against the full 1080 by 1920 frame, not against a 940 by 1360 page.

<Paper>
  <div style={abs({ left: -BOOK.left - 4, top: -BOOK.top - 4, width: W, height: H })}>
    <EndCard t={endT(f)} alcy={false} background={C.paper0} headline={<>Find creators<br />who say yes.</>} />
  </div>
</Paper>

Shift it back by the page's own offset and let Paper's overflow: hidden crop it. The alcy={false} prop exists because the shared end card normally flies our bird in to press the button, and in this reel the bird is already on the page and walks to it instead.

Was the book the right idea

The reel argues three things: that the wrong creator will not film your product, that a DM sinks under everybody else's, and that a guessed fee gets no reply. Those are the same arguments as the written guide to vetting a creator and the sponsorship cost calculator, which is the point: the ad is a trailer for pages that already existed.

A field guide was the right container for "three reasons" because turning a page is a free scene transition that an audience already understands. The cost is this file. If you only need one transition, use a crossfade.

The thing I would take to the next project is the leaf array. Any sequence where things overlap in time and stack in space wants to be one list of objects with a start, a duration and a renderer, with the stacking derived rather than stored. The moment the ordering lives in two places, one of them is already wrong.

title: The Call Order Is the Contract: Trace Fixtures Before a Messy-Repo Extraction
description:
Call order is part of a module's contract. Most extraction refactors keep the output identical and silently change the sequence. The workflow below records an ordered call trace before the move, then diffs it after. You shrink the change until every difference has a name.

Output fixtures answer "same result?". They never answer "same path?". A refactor can call the discount function twice and still return the correct total. It can skip a validation call that only fires on error paths. Byte pinning catches neither of those.

So pin the path. Use the standard library tracer. No plugin, no service, no dashboard.

1. Record on the Commit You Have Not Touched

The "before" trace must come from the current code. Record it first, commit the fixture, then refactor. Recording after the change only proves the new code agrees with itself.

# tools/trace_record.py
import json, os, sys

PKG_ROOT = os.path.abspath("src")
SECRET_KEYS = {"token", "secret", "password", "api_key"}


def _scalar(name, value):
    if name.lower() in SECRET_KEYS:
        return "<redacted>"
    if isinstance(value, (bool, int, float)):
        return repr(value)
    if isinstance(value, str) and len(value) <= 40:
        return repr(value)
    return f"<{type(value).__name__}>"


def record(target, *args, **kwargs):
    events = []

    def tracer(frame, event, arg):
        if event == "call":
            code = frame.f_code
            if os.path.abspath(code.co_filename).startswith(PKG_ROOT):
                n = code.co_argcount + code.co_kwonlyargcount
                names = code.co_varnames[:n]
                fn = getattr(code, "co_qualname", code.co_name)
                events.append({
                    "fn": f'{frame.f_globals.get("__name__", "?")}::{fn}',
                    "args": {k: _scalar(k, frame.f_locals.get(k)) for k in names},
                })
        return tracer

    previous = sys.gettrace()
    sys.settrace(tracer)
    try:
        target(*args, **kwargs)
    finally:
        sys.settrace(previous)
    return {"events": events}

sys.settrace fires for every new frame in the current thread. Filter to your package root or the fixture fills with library noise. Arguments are read from frame.f_locals at call time, which is exactly when they are bound.

Capture scalars only. Objects collapse to <ClassName>. That keeps fixtures diffable and stops repr of large models from leaking data into a committed file.

2. Pick a Corpus You Can Argue About

One operation. Three to six inputs. Include the boring case, one branch case, one failure case.

# tools/record_corpus.py
import json
from pathlib import Path
from trace_record import record

from legacy.billing import build_invoice

CASES = {
    "single_item": lambda: build_invoice({"sku": "A1", "qty": 1}),
    "discount": lambda: build_invoice({"sku": "A1", "qty": 3, "coupon": "TEN"}),
    "empty_qty": lambda: build_invoice({"sku": "A1", "qty": 0}),
}

out = Path("tests/fixtures/trace")
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for name, call in CASES.items():
    trace = record(call)
    (out / f"{name}.json").write_text(json.dumps(trace, indent=1, sort_keys=True))
    print(f"{name}: {len(trace['events'])} events")

Commit tests/fixtures/trace/*.json. Size beats coverage here. A fixture over a few thousand events is slow to diff and slow to review.

3. Normalize Before You Compare

Raw traces are noisy. Four rules tame them.

  1. Drop frames outside src/.
  2. Drop dunders and loggers listed in NOISE (__repr__, __eq__, __hash__, log, debug).
  3. Map moved modules through MODULE_MOVES.
  4. Redact argument names in SECRET_KEYS during recording.

Rule 3 is the honest one. Moving a function to a new module changes key. Declare that move once in the diff tool, and the reviewer sees it as data, not as a surprise.

4. Diff Into Three Buckets 

# tools/trace_diff.py
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path

MODULE_MOVES = {}  # {"legacy.billing": "invoicing.core"}
NOISE = {"__repr__", "__eq__", "__hash__", "log", "debug"}
ALLOW = Path("tests/fixtures/trace/allow.txt")


def load(path):
    keys = []
    for e in json.loads(Path(path).read_text())["events"]:
        module, _, fn = e["fn"].partition("::")
        if fn.split(".")[-1] in NOISE:
            continue
        module = MODULE_MOVES.get(module, module)
        args = ",".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(e["args"].items()))
        keys.append(f"{module}::{fn}({args})")
    return keys


def main(before_path, after_path):
    before, after = load(before_path), load(after_path)
    b, a = set(before), set(after)
    allowed = {
        line.strip()
        for line in ALLOW.read_text().splitlines()
        if line.strip() and not line.startswith("#")
    }
    missing = sorted(k for k in b - a if k not in allowed)
    new = sorted(a - b)
    moved = [k for k in b & a if before.index(k) != after.index(k)]
    print(f"events before={len(before)} after={len(after)}")
    print(f"missing={len(missing)} new={len(new)} moved={len(moved)}")
    for k in (missing + moved)[:20]:
        print("  !", k)
    return 1 if missing or moved else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]))

Three outcomes carry different weight.

Bucket Meaning Policy
missing a call disappeared block, unless a reason is written in allow.txt
new a call appeared review; expected for a declared helper
moved same key, new position block by default

Missing calls block the merge. New calls on a pure extraction are a smell worth reading. Moved calls mean you changed sequencing, which is a behaviour change wearing a cleanup costume.

5. Shrink the Change Until the Diff Is Boring

Use a ladder, not a leap.

Step Change Expected diff
1 rename a local or parameter zero
2 move one function, same module level zero, after MODULE_MOVES
3 extract one helper, called from the same site new only, declared
4 reorder calls or split a loop moved, needs a written reason

Stop at the first step that produces a moved bucket you cannot justify in one sentence. That is your smallest safe change. The rest becomes a second commit with its own trace diff.

This is where the fixture pays for itself. Step 3 usually exposes one hidden coupling: a shared cache, a mutated default argument, a retry that fires twice. Output tests never showed it.

6. Where Free Model Access and a Free Server Fit

Drafting normalization rules is mechanical work. Filtering trace noise by hand costs an hour per repo. MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are relevant there, and only there.

The free model proposes NOISE entries and MODULE_MOVES rows from a sample trace. A human accepts or rejects each line; nothing enters allow.txt unreviewed. The free server option runs the record-and-diff job in a stable environment, so both traces come from the same machine. Laptop-versus-CI comparisons fail for boring reasons.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The method stands on its own. Two small scripts and one committed JSON file are the whole mechanism.

Limitations

  • settrace conflicts with anything that owns the tracer: coverage tools, some debuggers, some profilers. Disable them while recording.
  • C extensions do not appear as Python frames. A parser written in Rust is invisible to this diff.
  • Async and threaded code produces unstable ordering across await points. Keep the corpus single-threaded, or diff per task.
  • Tracing slows call-heavy loops enough to break timeout-sensitive tests. Measure it before you wire it into CI.
  • co_qualname needs Python 3.11+. On older versions the helper falls back to co_name, which loses class context.
  • A clean trace diff proves structure held. It does not prove the refactor is correct.

Who Should Skip This

Skip it when the module fits on one screen. Skip it when the hot path is native code. Skip it when nobody will read the diff, because an unreviewed fixture is decoration with a commit message.

Use it when a repo has thin tests, real traffic, and one function everyone is afraid to move. Record once. Then move exactly one function.

If you have a candidate in mind, start with the smallest case in the corpus and a single operation. The first trace usually reveals a call you did not know existed.
