title: Why You Shouldn't Build Your Own Authentication From Scratch
description:
The cost is not writing it, it is keeping it right

TL;DR: A working login takes an afternoon. What costs money is everything that keeps it correct afterwards: password hashing that has to be tuned, keys that have to rotate, protocol guidance that changes, passkeys and recovery flows, abuse protection and an audit trail. This article lists those ongoing costs with sources, says honestly when building your own is the right call, and shows how to price the alternative.

What "from scratch" actually means

The phrase covers three very different things, and most of the confusion in this debate comes from mixing them up.

Approach What you write What you keep maintaining
Hand-rolled Password hashing, sessions, token issuing, reset flows All of it, including the cryptographic choices
Framework building blocks (ASP.NET Core Identity, OpenIddict) The screens, the policy, the glue, and for a token server, the whole server around the library Configuration, upgrades, keys, recovery, operations
Packaged server or cloud service Client registrations and settings Configuration and upgrades, or a subscription

ASP.NET Core Identity is not "from scratch". Microsoft's documentation describes it as managing users, passwords, profile data, roles, claims, tokens and email confirmation, with support for external providers. If your need is one web application with its own user store, it is a perfectly reasonable foundation, and nothing below argues against it. The argument is about the point where that stops being enough, and about the second row of the table, where you still own a lot.

What sits under the login form

Each item below is a piece of work that does not end when the feature ships.

Password storage that has to be upgraded

OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet covers Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt and PBKDF2, and treats the work factor as something you raise over time as hardware gets cheaper. Its usual approach is to re-hash a password with the new settings the next time the user signs in. ASP.NET Core Identity's default hasher uses PBKDF2 with a default of 100,000 iterations, writes a version marker into every hash so older ones still verify, and can report that a correct password should be re-hashed. A hand-rolled scheme needs that upgrade path designed in from day one, which is easy to skip and hard to add later.

Keys that rotate, persist and survive a deployment

ASP.NET Core's Data Protection system, which protects cookies and many other payloads, creates keys with a default lifetime of 90 days and rolls them automatically. It also documents the trap: unless the environment provides a persistent location, keys are not persisted outside the process, and in a container they should be stored on a volume or in an external provider. Deleting a key makes everything protected with it permanently unreadable. None of this is exotic, but each deployment target needs someone to have thought about it. A token server adds signing and encryption certificates on top, with their own expiry dates and their own rotation.

A protocol that keeps moving

RFC 6749, the OAuth 2.0 core specification from 2012, was updated in January 2025 by RFC 9700, the current best-practice document for OAuth security, which also updates RFC 6750 and RFC 6819. It asks for exact redirect URI matching and PKCE for public clients, advises against the implicit grant and forbids the password grant. An implementation that was reasonable when you wrote it can drift out of line without a single line of your code changing. I walked through the practical consequences in What happens when your authentication is misconfigured.

Passkeys, second factors and the recovery question

.NET 10 added passkey support to ASP.NET Core Identity, which is a real step forward, and its documentation is candid about the edges. Passkeys are treated as a primary sign-in factor, not as a second factor. Attestation statements are not validated by default. Only the Blazor Web App template includes passkey support out of the box. For apps that allow passkeys as the only credential, recovery is left to you: the documentation suggests recovery codes, email-based flows or requiring several passkeys. It also notes that you may need to revoke credentials if a particular authenticator model turns out to be vulnerable. Microsoft's multi-factor authentication documentation adds that SMS as a second factor is no longer recommended, pointing to NIST's digital identity guidelines. Choices like these are product decisions that someone has to own and revisit.

Abuse protection and an audit trail

Lockout, rate limiting and detection of credential stuffing are not features you build once. They need tuning against real traffic, and OWASP keeps a separate cheat sheet on credential stuffing prevention for a reason. When something does go wrong you want to answer who signed in, who failed, which account was locked and which tokens were revoked. That means recording security events deliberately, from the start, in a form you can query.

💡 The pattern behind the list

Every item has a build cost, which is visible, and a maintenance cost, which is not. The maintenance cost is paid by whoever is on the team in two years' time, usually without having seen the original decision.

When building it yourself is the right call

It is a short list, but it is not empty:

  • One application, one user store, no third-party clients. ASP.NET Core Identity alone is enough, it is maintained by Microsoft, and adding an OpenID Connect server would be over-engineering.
  • Authentication is your product. If you are building an identity provider, you own all of it by definition.
  • A constraint that rules out third-party components. Some environments do not allow them. Then the maintenance list above is the budget you are signing.
  • Learning. Building a small authorization server once is the best way to understand one. Just do not point real users at it. What changes the answer is growth in the requirements: a second application that should share the sign-in, a mobile client, an API consumed by someone else, partners who need tokens. At that point you are no longer adding a login to an app, you are operating a token server, and the second row of the table above becomes a project.

Buying is not free of work either

A packaged server or a cloud service moves the maintenance, it does not remove it. You still configure it, upgrade it and watch what it does. And you take on vendor risk, which is real: IdentityServer4's end of life left many teams with an unpatched server in front of their login. Before you choose anything, check who maintains it, how recently it was updated and what happens to you if that stops.

For a .NET team that wants a self-hosted token server with the work above already done, IdentitySuite (which I build, so weigh this part accordingly) is one option. It is built on OpenIddict and ASP.NET Core Identity, and the settings files that ship with it include:

  • Passkey sign-in, switched on in the shipped templates, alongside authenticator-app two-factor authentication and recovery codes.
  • Sign-in with Google, Microsoft, Facebook, GitHub, LinkedIn and Apple.
  • Lockout after repeated failures and rate limiting per endpoint class, both enabled in the templates.
  • Built-in signing and encryption certificates that are rotated automatically as they near expiry, with an expiry alert, instead of keys you manage by hand.
  • A security audit log with sign-in successes and failures, lockouts, two-factor events, passkey events and token revocations. It does not remove the maintenance entirely: you still run it, configure it and keep it updated, and it is a younger product with a smaller ecosystem than the established ones. If you want to see what adopting it looks like, the Authentication Made Easy article adds authentication to a single-page app with it.

How to price the decision

I will not invent a number of person-months for you; it depends on your team and your requirements. The comparison is easier than it looks, though. List the capabilities above that you need, estimate the first build and the yearly upkeep for each in hours, and multiply by your own hourly cost.

Then compare that with the price of the alternative. IdentitySuite's Standard plan is €349 per year. As an illustration only, at an assumed €60 per hour that is under six hours of one developer's time. The question is whether you would spend more than that in a year on key rotation, upgrades, checking security guidance and reading audit logs, before writing any feature at all. Use your own rate; the shape of the answer rarely changes.

If you want to see what each plan includes, the pricing page has the details.

title: Five concepts to learn before you build with LLMs
description:
If you can ship ordinary software, you can start building with large language models. I would not start in the API console. I would learn five ideas in this order: machine learning, what an LLM is, generative AI versus older predictive AI, prompting, then evaluation. Each one has a small thing to try in code before you depend on a vendor SDK.

What should I learn before I call a model?

In traditional software, a programmer writes the rules. Machine learning works the other way: you show a model many examples, and a training process adjusts it until its predictions match those examples. The rules end up in learned parameters, not in a document you can read.

Deep learning is the branch that uses neural networks with many layers, and it sits behind almost all recent AI progress. Large language models are deep learning models trained on text. The practical consequence is the same as for any machine learning system: the model is only as good as the data it learned from, and it can be confidently wrong on cases unlike its training data.

What to try: encode the fraud-style rule from that definition (amount over a threshold and a new country), then replace the rule with a weighted sum you chose by hand. You are not training a model. You are seeing that the "decision" is numbers, and those numbers only mean something relative to examples.

What is an LLM actually doing?

A large language model reads text as tokens and, given everything so far, predicts the next one. Repeat that and you get a paragraph. "Large" refers to the size of the neural network, measured in parameters, and to the amount of text it learns from in pre-training. Post-training then teaches it to follow instructions and hold a conversation.

Because the model is built to produce plausible text, it can be fluent and wrong at the same time. On its own it also does not know about events after its knowledge cutoff, or about your private data. Most useful products wrap the model in more: retrieved documents, tools, memory, and checks.

Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition, argues that what people are using are plausibility engines: they assemble plausible outputs token by token. That is a strong way to get a prototype, and a weak way to get behavior you can guarantee.

What to try: give yourself a four-word vocabulary and a function that returns the highest-scoring next token. Loop it ten times from a fixed prefix. Read the string you get and notice that nothing in the loop checked the sentence against a source of record.

How is generative AI different from predictive AI?

Much of the AI in business before 2022 was predictive: a model looked at an input and gave back a label or a number, such as fraud or not fraud, or a demand forecast. Generative AI produces something new instead: a paragraph, an image, a song, a block of code. Large language models generate text. Image, audio, and video models generate media, and multimodal models handle several of these at once.

Generative AI and agentic AI are related but not the same. A generative model produces content when asked. An agent uses a generative model to plan and take actions toward a goal, calling tools and checking results along the way. I would get comfortable with the generator before I tried to build the agent.

What to try: take one short support ticket and return two values from separate functions. One is a label, such as billing or access. The other is a drafted reply. The label is the older predictive job. The draft is the generative job. If you mix them in one return value, you will start treating a guess at a category as if it were a finished answer.

What should I practice in the prompt?

Prompt engineering is the craft of the instruction itself: how you phrase the task, what examples you include, what format you ask for, and how you structure the request. A clearer prompt produces better output. It is the first lever everyone reaches for, and it still matters.

I would not treat clever wording as the place your system wins. As models got better at understanding intent, wording stopped being a durable advantage. It is table stakes. The work that used to hide inside slogans moved outward, to the documents, history, and tools you supply, and to what the system remembers across tasks. Learn the names later: context, and memory. Do the prompt exercises anyway. Then leave the thesaurus alone.

Dan Klein's description of prompting as a control surface matches that limit. A prompt has no precise semantics and no guarantee. If the model ignores you, rewriting, capital letters, and extra exclamation points are weak recourse.

What to try: one task, three prompts. A bare instruction. The same instruction plus one example. The same instruction plus a required format, such as one JSON object with two fields. Save all three outputs. You are practicing phrasing, examples, format, and structure, which is the whole craft named above.

How do I know the answer is good enough to keep?

Dan Klein argues that "how many of these scenarios did I get right" is the wrong shipping question. He wants to know, for how many scenarios, the system gets it right every time, including a hundred times in a row. A system at about 80% or 90% right is still, in his view, unshippable if one in ten customers is told a flight was booked when it was not. A system that gets 70% of scenarios right every single time is more valuable, because that is consistency you could put in a product.

He also argues that putting a second model on top to check the first is a weak fix. Both can be wrong, and they tend to fail on the same hard cases, so in his estimate 80% checking 80% ends up around 82%. Add more checkers and the stack gets expensive and slow.

Your first check can be smaller than a benchmark suite. Freeze the input. Run the call several times. Record whether the outputs agree, and whether they match a fact you already know. Fluency is not that check.

On the reading list, the AI, decoded pages are grouped in five levels. If you are building, skim Level 1 (how a large language model works, why it costs what it costs, and why it makes things up), then Levels 4 and 5, where evaluation shows up as a builder's problem. After that, use Start here: five episodes on agents, evals, agent memory, AI infrastructure, and shipping AI in a real product.

# Sketch for practice only. Not a client, and not a system any guest or lab runs.

def rules_flag(amount: float, new_country: bool) -> bool:
    return amount > 1000 and new_country

def learned_score(amount: float, new_country: bool, w: tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    return w[0] * amount + w[1] * float(new_country)

def next_token(scores: dict[str, float]) -> str:
    return max(scores, key=scores.get)

def draft_prompt(task: str, example: str, fmt: str) -> str:
    return f"Task: {task}\nExample: {example}\nFormat: {fmt}"

def same_every_time(run, n: int = 5) -> bool:
    outs = [run() for _ in range(n)]
    return len(set(outs)) == 1

Checklist

  • Treat machine learning as examples and parameters, and expect confident errors off that data.
  • Read a paragraph as repeated next-token prediction, with hallucination, a knowledge cutoff, and no private data unless you supply it.
  • Keep a predictive label and a generated draft in separate functions.
  • Practice phrasing, one example, and a fixed format, then move on to context and memory.
  • Repeat one frozen input and compare it to a known fact before you trust a single fluent answer.

title: Next.js 16.3 support on Vercel
description:
Yesterday the Next.js team announced the release of Next.js 16.3, with leaner prefetching, immutable static assets, and instant navigations. As part of this release, we worked with the Next.js team to fully support 16.3 on Vercel, including better performance and additional observability. Applications that have upgraded have seen:

  • Fewer prefetch requests: Apps upgrading from 16.2 to 16.3 saw 45% fewer prefetch requests on average, with some seeing reductions over 70%.

  • Lower static asset costs: With immutable static assets, upgraded apps saw 17% fewer CDN requests and 24% fewer bytes transferred for static content, and up to 60% global TTFB reductions for frequently deployed projects.

  • Faster routing at scale: Routing metadata improvements in the critical serving path deliver ~2x faster p99 route resolution for large sites.

Platform improvements

Next.js 16.3 ships leaner prefetching and enables immutable static assets by default. Supporting both meant changing the platform too, in how it caches static assets, resolves routes, and surfaces what happened in production.

Immutable static assets

Vercel now supports reusing immutable static assets across deployments for Next.js. Immutable static assets can't suffer from version skew, even for projects without Skew Protection enabled, and the browser cache survives redeploys. Because Next.js uses query-parameter-based Skew Protection, this change cut CDN requests by 17% and bytes transferred by 24% for static content. Deployments also complete up to 30% faster on average, since unchanged assets skip re-upload. In Next.js 16.3, immutable static assets are enabled by default.

Next.js 16.3 outputs immutable content-addressed static assets under the public path /_next/static/immutable/*. The Vercel CDN uses this prefix to differentiate immutable static assets from other static assets.

If you're a framework author and want to implement this in your own toolchain, see the immutable static files section of the Build Output API docs.

Faster routing at scale

Next.js 16 introduced an optimization where common parts of an application are prefetched once and reused across navigations, rather than fetched again for every link. To make that reuse work, each shared segment has to be fetchable on its own, so Next.js generates many more paths for the same application.

Those extra paths add up on the platform side. Frameworks like Next.js deploy to Vercel through the Build Output API, and for each path the framework generates a metadata file that describes how to serve it, such as its prerender configuration. The Vercel CDN reads that metadata in the path of every request, so each lookup has to finish in milliseconds or less, and it caches the metadata to stay under that budget. Globally, that's 5 million lookups per second. As Next.js 16 applications shipped more paths, the cache held more entries, hit rates dropped, and we saw p99 TTFB increase for larger applications.

To fix this, we improved the layer that serves route metadata, making it ~2x faster with ~10x fewer cache misses. Instead of storing each segment's metadata as its own cache entry, we now combine entries into JSONL-formatted shards, and we optimized in-process and remote caching around those shards. Fewer, larger entries mean better hit rates, and the JSONL format still lets the CDN find the right entry inside a shard quickly.

This improvement is implemented in the platform and already live for every deployment, so other frameworks that deploy through the Build Output API automatically benefit from it as well.

Improved observability

Next.js 16.3 includes improvements to prefetching that resulted in a 45% reduction in prefetch requests. You can now query whether a request was a prefetch in Vercel Observability and Runtime Logs, or in the query builder with Observability Plus.

We have also heard from users who want more visibility into Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) revalidations. The ISR observability page now prominently displays time-based and on-demand revalidations, we expose cache reasons and ISR write utilization, and we published a guide on how to reduce ISR revalidations.

Today, we are also launching observability for Partial Prerendering (PPR). PPR serves the static parts of a page immediately and then streams dynamic content, such as personalization or experimentation. Under the hood, it combines ISR and Vercel Functions into one system so applications benefit from both at the same time. Next.js 16 applications that use Cache Components get PPR automatically when deployed to Vercel.

In the Vercel dashboard, the PPR Observability page shows which requests are serving static content, dynamic content, or a combination of the two. Use it to confirm static shells are working, catch routes that have regressed to fully dynamic, and see when your functions run.

If you need to dig in, click through to the ISR or Functions observability pages for details about cache revalidations or function executions.

Upgrade today

Next.js 16.3 is available today. Upgrade to take advantage of the new features:

pnpm add next@16.3.0

Read the Next.js 16.3 announcement for the full release notes or learn more about Next.js on Vercel.

title: 12 developers are not 12 testers per app. The small mistake that breaks a Google Play testing group.
description:
You find 12 Android developers. Everyone agrees to test everyone else's app.

Problem solved?

Each app has 11 other people available to test it. The owner isn't an extra tester.

I got this wrong in an earlier Dozena post. A reader pushed me to explain the dropout math more clearly. Here's the model I'm building now — including where it can fail.

The group size is not the tester count

Assume each developer brings one app and tests every other app:

Developers in the group Other developers per app Margin above 12
12 11 Below the minimum
13 12 None
15 14 Two

The formula is simply testers per app = participating developers − 1.

These are potential testers, not confirmed opt-ins. The table only holds if everyone actually joins each relevant test. Fifteen names in a group chat aren't fourteen testers in Play Console.

The calendar matters as much as the headcount

For personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023, Google's current requirement includes at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before applying for production access. Meeting that threshold doesn't guarantee approval.

Google's official testing requirements

Consider an app starting with exactly 12 eligible testers:

  • Day 1: all 12 opt in.
  • Day 9: one opts out.
  • Day 9: a new person joins.
  • Day 14: the newcomer has not accumulated 14 consecutive days.

The replacement hasn't inherited the departing person's history.

That doesn't mean the remaining testers lose their own history. It means this app no longer has the required twelve people with the necessary continuous opt-in history at that point.

Starting with 14 confirmed testers can absorb two opt-outs if the remaining twelve stay continuously opted in. That's a buffer, not a promise that people won't leave.

Attendance still isn't useful feedback

A counter can't tell you whether onboarding makes sense.

One reader suggested asking for the screen name and what the tester expected to happen. That's much more actionable than collecting “looks good” until a text box reaches its character minimum.

For a testing round, I'd want to know:

  • Which flow did you try?
  • Where did the result differ from what you expected?
  • What changed after the developer fixed it?

The aim is to improve the apps, not just exchange names on a list.

Why I'm building Dozena

Dozena is my attempt to organize this into synchronized rounds of 13–16 developers, targeting 15: a shared setup period, the same testing window, check-ins and private feedback.

It's still in development. The public site explains the format and accepts waitlist signups. I haven't completed a real pilot yet. The MVP will be free and open source.

It won't sell testers, ask for public Play Store ratings or promise Google approval.

If your Android app is approaching closed testing, and you're willing to test other developers' apps too, join the Dozena waitlist.

I'm the developer behind it. The math above is useful whether you use Dozena or organize your own group.

title: 'useMemo' Hook in React
description:
When building React applications, components can re-render many times. During re-rendering, some calculations may run again even when the data has not changed. To avoid unnecessary calculations, React provides a Hook called useMemo.

What is useMemo?

useMemo is a React Hook that remembers, or caches, the result of a calculation. React can reuse the previous result when its dependencies have not changed.

For example:

import { useMemo } from "react";

const result = useMemo(() => {
  return number * number;
}, [number]);

Here, number is the dependency. If its value stays the same, React can reuse the cached result instead of recalculating it.

Why Do We Need useMemo?

Imagine a college application that displays student results. The application filters thousands of student records to find students who scored above 80 marks.

const topStudents = useMemo(() => {
  return students.filter(
    student => student.marks >= 80
  );
}, [students]);

Here, React can reuse the filtered student list when the students dependency remains unchanged. If the student data changes, React recalculates the list.

Understanding the Dependency Array

The dependency array tells React which values the calculation depends on.

const total = useMemo(
  () => price * quantity,
  [price, quantity]
);

If either price or quantity changes, React recalculates the total. If neither changes, React can reuse the previous result.

When Should We Use useMemo?

We can use useMemo when performing expensive calculations, filtering large datasets, sorting records, or processing complex data.

However, we should not use it for every small calculation. For simple operations, using useMemo may add unnecessary complexity without providing much benefit.

It is also important to understand that useMemo does not prevent a component from re-rendering. It only helps avoid unnecessary recalculations.

Conclusion

useMemo is a useful React Hook for improving performance when calculations are expensive. It caches a calculation result between renders and recalculates it when its dependencies change.

title: A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox
description:
Running untrusted code safely requires more than separating it from the host. You also have to control what that code can reach.

This matters more as AI agents gain the ability to read files, execute commands, install packages, and generate programs of their own. A microVM can prevent that code from accessing the host or another workload. By itself, it cannot stop the code from exfiltrating data, probing internal services, attacking systems elsewhere on the internet, or using credentials available inside the environment.

Isolation without egress control contains the process, not its consequences.

A complete sandbox therefore needs both compute isolation and control over the authority available through its network: where code can connect, which credentials it can use, and how those permissions change throughout the workload’s lifecycle. These controls are part of the security boundary, not protections to bolt on later.

A sandbox has more than one boundary

Compute isolation answers one important question: what can this program access on the machine where it runs? Network isolation answers another: what can it access, or attack, through the network?

Consider an agent that reads a repository and runs generated code. A prompt injection hidden in an issue, log entry, dependency, or source file might instruct it to upload private data. The generated program does not need to escape its microVM. With unrestricted outbound traffic, it can simply send anything it can read to an external server.

The same access can be used to scan internal networks, exfiltrate data and credentials, or call an authenticated API. From the attacker’s perspective, crossing the VM boundary may be unnecessary. Without a network boundary, it is only half a sandbox.

A network bypass can be a sandbox escape

Recent security research has made one pattern clear: untrusted code does not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment. It only needs one network path that the security model failed to account for.

That path might be a DNS resolver left available in an otherwise disconnected environment, an empty allowlist that fails open, a hostname interpreted differently by a policy engine and a proxy, or a trusted package service turned into a relay. Any one of them can give untrusted code a channel to exfiltrate data, receive instructions, or move toward more sensitive infrastructure.

These are not compute escapes. The kernel, VM, or container boundary may continue working exactly as designed while containment still fails. The practical security boundary also includes DNS, proxies, identity services, internal networks, and every intentionally permitted destination.

Whether we call the result an escape or a bypass, the requirement is the same: a sandbox must account for every path by which untrusted code can communicate.

Useful sandboxes need selective connectivity

Completely disconnecting a sandbox closes the network path, but it also makes many workloads impractical. An agent may need to clone a repository, install a dependency, call an AI model, query a database, or upload its result.

Unrestricted internet access is not the only alternative. A useful sandbox should grant only the connectivity a workload requires:

  • Allow an AI provider, but no other public destination.

  • Allow one object storage bucket, rather than an entire cloud network.

  • Reach a private service, while blocking the rest of the private address space.

  • Install dependencies during trusted setup, then remove registry access before generated code runs.

  • Authenticate an API request without placing the API key inside the sandbox.

A practical policy model should support fully open access, complete network isolation, and granular policies that deny unmatched traffic by default. Those policies should be able to combine domain rules with allowed and denied address ranges.

Domains and CIDRs solve different problems. Domain policies are precise enough for modern services whose IP addresses change or serve many unrelated hostnames. CIDR policies work across protocols and provide control over fixed infrastructure and private networks.

Connectivity should also be temporary. A workflow can begin with access to a package registry, narrow access before untrusted execution, briefly permit an output destination, and finish with no outbound access, all without restarting the workload.

How Vercel enforces the network boundary

The Vercel Sandbox firewall runs on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it.

Linux networking transparently redirects outbound TCP connections and DNS queries through the firewall. Workloads do not need to configure a proxy, and the firewall retains each connection’s original destination.

For domain-restricted connections, the firewall inspects the beginning of the TLS handshake and extracts the Server Name Indication, or SNI. This identifies the requested hostname before the firewall opens an upstream connection. It checks that hostname against the sandbox’s domain policy and also checks the destination address against its CIDR policy.

Ordinary allowed TLS connections pass through without decryption. The firewall reads only the unencrypted handshake information required to enforce the policy, then connects the workload directly to its destination.

Some policies need to inspect or modify the HTTP request itself. For those configured domains only, header injection and request forwarding selectively terminate TLS using a certificate authority unique to the sandbox. The firewall can then match requests by hostname, path, method, query, or headers before injecting a credential or forwarding the request to an endpoint that you trust.

DNS traffic is filtered using the same domain policy. Together, these layers control both where a sandbox can connect and what authority a particular connection receives.

Keep credentials outside untrusted compute

An agent often needs to call an authenticated service, but a credential stored in an environment variable or file is a transferable bearer credential. Every program inside the sandbox can read it. Malicious code can copy it to a third-party service, where it can be retained and used long after the sandbox stops.

Vercel Sandbox instead injects credentials at the host network boundary. The firewall creates a dedicated certificate authority just in time for the sandbox and adds it to the sandbox’s trusted certificates. For a configured destination, it selectively terminates TLS, adds or replaces the authentication header, then establishes a new TLS connection to the upstream service.

The credential never enters the microVM. It never leaves the host unencrypted. The certificate authority is unique to the sandbox and is disposed when the sandbox stops.

Injection also limits where the credential can be used. The firewall sends it only to its configured destination, so uploading the sandbox’s files or environment to another service does not transfer that authority. Matchers can restrict it further by path, method, query, or request headers. Generated code might receive permission to submit results to one endpoint without receiving permission to read other resources from the same API.

Injected credentials should still follow the principle of least privilege, with access limited to the specific operations the workload requires.

Put your own policy in the path

Static allowlists cannot express every security requirement. Some workloads need to inspect payloads, enforce business rules, record an audit trail, or make an authorization decision using context only you have.

Request forwarding sends selected HTTPS requests through a proxy that you control. The proxy receives the original request along with a Vercel-issued OIDC token identifying the team, project, and sandbox that originated it.

That proxy becomes a programmable policy layer. It can:

  • Redact sensitive fields before a request leaves the environment.

  • Enforce per-user or per-sandbox authorization.

  • Route package downloads through supply-chain scanning and block artifacts that fail organizational policy.

  • Record requests and responses for compliance workflows.

  • Exchange a sandbox identity for a narrowly scoped credential.

  • Reject an operation that does not match organizational policy.

The policy and its secrets remain outside the sandbox, even when the code being governed has full root access inside its microVM. You can read more about request proxying in the Sandbox documentation.

Security belongs in the baseline product

We believe a sandbox should not require a payment method before it can safely handle untrusted code.

Every Vercel Sandbox includes both compute isolation and a complete firewall for defining what code inside it can communicate with.

The goal is not to make every sandbox completely offline. It is to make authority explicit:

  • Which destinations can this sandbox reach?

  • Which private address ranges are unavailable?

  • Which requests can use credentials?

  • Which operations must pass through additional policy?

  • When should all communication stop?

These are fundamental properties of the execution environment, not security controls to add after a workload reaches production. We believe so strongly in this that we have made our full egress firewall capabilities available to all Sandboxes.

Getting started

The following policy allows outbound connections to one API and injects a credential only for one operation. Other destinations are denied by default, and the credential remains outside the sandbox.

The same policy can be replaced while the sandbox runs:

A sandbox is not defined only by where its code runs. It is defined by what that code can reach, what authority it receives, and which boundaries still hold when the code itself is hostile.

The network is part of the sandbox.

Further reading

  • Vercel Sandbox firewall documentation

  • Understanding Vercel Sandboxes

  • Security boundaries in agentic architectures

title: css-ghost: find and delete orphaned CSS selectors with zero config
description:
You've been there. You rename a component, move a file, or quietly migrate from one styling approach to another – and the old CSS stays behind. Nobody complains, the build doesn't break, and the dead selectors quietly accumulate.

css-ghost is a small Node.js CLI tool I built to solve that problem. Point it at a folder and it tells you every CSS class defined in your style files that isn't referenced anywhere in your components.

What it does

css-ghost scans your style files (.css, .module.css, .scss, .sass, .less, MUI makeStyles, vanilla-extract), extracts every class selector, then cross-references them against every component file it can find (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, .vue, .svelte).

Anything defined but never actually used gets reported as an orphan – with its line number and the full CSS rule printed inline, so you can see what it does before deciding to delete it.

It also catches orphaned CSS custom properties (--my-token: value defined but never consumed via var(--my-token) anywhere in the codebase), reported in a separate 🔮 section.

Run it now

No install required:

npx css-ghost ./src

Or install globally for repeated use:

npm install -g css-ghost
css-ghost ./src

Interactive folder picker

Run css-ghost with no arguments and an interactive directory picker opens. Navigate with ↑↓ (or j/k), press Enter or → to go into a folder, ← to go back up, [a] to add the current directory to the scan, then [d] when done:

css-ghost

Useful when you're not sure which subfolder to target, or want to scan multiple directories in one pass.

Dynamic class detection

If a component accesses classes dynamically – styles[variable], styles[\${variant}] – css-ghost can't resolve the class name statically. Rather than silently skip those files or report false positives, it flags them with a ⚠️ warning per file:

✅ src/components/Alert/Alert.module.css

   ⚠️  Dynamic class references detected – results may be incomplete.
   Dynamic references in: src/components/Alert.jsx

   👻 .hidden (line 30)
      .hidden { display: none; }

All statically resolvable patterns are still analysed: string literals, ternaries, cx({ active: isOn }) object keys, array literals, and both branches of ternaries.

Deleting orphans

Once you're happy with the report, pass --delete to remove every flagged selector from its source file:

css-ghost ./src --delete

css-ghost prints the full report first, lists what it's about to delete, then asks for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt in CI:

css-ghost ./src --delete --yes

Tip: commit or stash first. There's no undo.

Other useful flags

Flag What it does
--ghost-trail Show the last git commit that touched each orphan
--strict Exit with code 1 when orphans exist (CI / pre-commit)
--install-hook ./src Write a pre-commit hook that blocks commits with orphans
--output <path> Custom path for the markdown report
--ai Append a plain-English AI summary (needs free OpenRouter key)

Ghost trail

Pass --ghost-trail to fetch the last git commit that changed each orphan's occurrence count:

css-ghost ./src --ghost-trail

   👻 .iconRight (line 28)
      🕵️  b5c6efb · Roland Levy · 3 weeks ago – "Refactor Button component"
      .iconRight {
        margin-left: 6px;
      }

Handy for tracking down when and why a class went dead.

Pre-commit hook 

css-ghost --install-hook ./src

Writes .git/hooks/pre-commit (executable, chmod 755) that blocks commits whenever orphaned selectors exist. Remove it with rm .git/hooks/pre-commit.

How is it different from PurgeCSS?

PurgeCSS is a build-time bundler – it hooks into webpack or PostCSS to strip unused CSS from your production output. It's designed for frameworks like Tailwind or Bootstrap where you use a fraction of the utility classes.

css-ghost is a source code auditor – it finds dead selectors in your actual codebase, with no build step and no config file.

PurgeCSS css-ghost
Works on source files ❌ Build output only ✅
Zero config, no build step ❌ ✅
CSS custom property orphans ❌ ✅
Git history per orphan ❌ ✅
Pre-commit hook ❌ ✅
Deletes dead code for you ❌ ✅
Safe with dynamic classes ❌ Silently removes them ✅ Flags with ⚠️

The two tools are complementary – PurgeCSS for trimming framework output at build time, css-ghost for auditing your own hand-written CSS throughout development.

The source is on GitHub and the package is on npm. PRs and issues welcome.

title: How Sandstone grew 40x in 147 days on Vercel
description:
Sandstone on Vercel

  • 1,000+ legal requests managed daily across customer teams

  • 7-app turborepo monorepo deployed seamlessly to multiple Vercel projects

  • Multi-step agentic legal workflows built end-to-end with AI SDK

When in-house legal teams get a request from their business, it kicks off a manual process of pulling data from multiple systems. In a typical workflow, lawyers will pull deal details from Salesforce, review past contracts, and chase account teams for missing context, all before they start the legal work itself.

Sandstone automates this data gathering process, and centralizes requests into a single platform. When a request is created, Sandstone automatically ingests context from every system, including messaging and email tools. By the time the lawyer sees it, they have all of the information they need to get to work.

The founding team includes a McKinsey legal tech veteran, a lawyer-turned-engineer, and cybersecurity founder. At Sandstone, that mix shows up directly in the product: legal professionals work alongside engineers, catching the workflow details and legal nuances that only someone who has practiced law would notice. That is how Sandstone ships fast and correctly for one of the most demanding buyers in enterprise software.

That attention to detail has paid off: in less than 6 months after their launch, their revenue grew 40x. Three things made their growth possible on Vercel:

  • Preview deployments fast enough to win enterprise trust

  • An AI layer flexible enough to ship agentic workflows in minutes

  • Secure Compute that makes security a one-sentence answer

Vercel deployments turned a Sunday request into a five-minute fix

For Sandstone's customers, trust is built on responsiveness, and lawyers are trained to notice small details. Liam Germain, Co-Founder and CTO, puts it simply: when a customer asked for a scrollbar accessibility change on a Sunday, he had it live in production in five minutes. On any other platform, he said that same change would have taken five or ten times longer.

Vercel deployments help with more than just fixes. Preview branches with inline commenting mean Sandstone's head of marketing can leave a note on a live landing page with Vercel Toolbar, which is configured to automatically creates a Linear issue and assigns it to engineering. What used to take an afternoon happens in a single comment.

Vercel Flags runs feature flags across all applications, giving the team dynamic control over what is live, what is demoed, and what is still in progress, without touching a deployment.

Sandstone runs a monorepo of over seven applications across multiple Vercel projects with clean environment variable linking and a custom CLI built on top of Vercel's API layer, and every push on every repo generates a preview of production.

Without the right foundation, complexity kills velocity

Sandstone's product started as smart triage, routing requests to the right lawyer. But the bigger opportunity was what happened when a request landed: every lawyer was still manually gathering context before they could act, pulling relevant details from a handful of separate systems, every time, for every request. Shipping a system that could handle that automatically required infrastructure capable of keeping pace with the product vision.

AI SDK unlocks faster agentic workflows

Sandstone has evolved into an AI system that executes complex, multi-step legal workflows end-to-end, searching through thousands of procurement agreements, surfacing the most at-risk agreements, alerting owners via Slack, and notifying legal when responses come in.

Vercel's AI SDK is what makes those workflows composable enough for a small team to keep pace with a rapidly expanding product surface.

The composability shows up across the entire stack. Chat SDK powers the Teams integration. Emulate SDK handles integration testing for Slack and Okta. Agent Browser SDK runs agentic testing locally. Flags SDK drives the toolbar integration. One SDK, four workflows, zero separate infrastructure.

Vercel Secure Compute makes security a one-sentence answer

Sandstone uses Vercel Secure Compute to establish private communication between Vercel and its data layer. The setup was straightforward to implement and well-architected enough that it became a point of confidence rather than friction in every enterprise conversation. When the security question comes up with customers and prospects, and it always does, the answer is simple: all communication between Vercel and Sandstone's data layer is private and never touches the public internet.

Sandstone chooses platforms they believe will be ahead of the market in three to five years, a vendor evaluation framework they apply to both frontier model providers and core infrastructure.

Sandstone connected with the Vercel team through the Sequoia startup partnership. Within ten days of starting the company, the program gave them a shared Slack channel and access to engineers who could help think through architecture decisions in real time.

What’s next

Less than 6 months after launch, Sandstone had grown revenue 40x and landed customers across technology, manufacturing, and ecommerce, leading to a $30M Series A led by Lightspeed. The team is already shipping fast, so the goal for using that capital is straightforward: get Sandstone into more legal departments.

The vision they are building toward is a Legal Relationship Management platform that not only manages intake but also connects every workflow to the business context behind it, flags issues before they surface, and operationalizes legal knowledge through supervised agents. Sandstone describes this as a system of action for the legal department of the future.

For a team shipping with speed toward that ambition, the infrastructure underneath the product has be a competitive advantage, not a burden, and that's why Sandstone runs on Vercel.

About Sandstone: Sandstone was born out of the acute frustration experienced by in-house legal teams who spend more time on process than progress due to fragmentation across disparate business systems. The platform provides a comprehensive solution for intake, triage, execution, fulfillment, and measurement of legal work, designed to run across email, messaging, and the business tools teams already use.

title: How My NVR Cuts Recording Storage by 75% — Without AI, and Without Dropped Frames
description:
A few third-party write-ups about MiBeeNvr — review sites, aggregator posts — describe its adaptive recording as "motion-aware, saves disk" and stop there. I'm the author. This post is the full mechanism: what signal decides when to record, why the switch drops zero frames, which cameras break it, and where AI fits (and deliberately doesn't).

If you run Frigate, Blue Iris, Surveillance Station or just a camera on a Raspberry Pi, the design trade-offs below should map onto things you already know.

TL;DR

95% of the time, nothing happens in front of your cameras — but continuous recording writes full-rate video anyway. MiBeeNvr's adaptive recording:

  • drops to time-lapse-grade sparse writes (one keyframe every 30s) when the scene is quiet;
  • snaps back to full frame rate the instant activity is detected, with zero dropped frames at the switch;
  • measures -75% disk on a static 2K/H.265 scene (~2700 → ~688 MB/h), and ~34× less during fully-empty periods;
  • decides "is something happening?" from P-frame sizes in the compressed domain — no decoding, no model, near-zero CPU;
  • keeps AI out of the core on purpose, and puts it where the hardware is (MiBeeVision, released today).

Background: why "activity" is visible in the byte count

You don't need a video-codec background for this section, but it's the foundation for everything else.

A camera's H.264/H.265 stream is cut into GOPs. Each GOP starts with an I-frame (a complete picture, independently decodable), followed by P-frames that only store the difference from the previous frame.

The key property: the quieter the scene, the smaller the P-frames. An empty corridor produces P-frames of a few KB. Someone walks through, and the encoder has to describe their outline, motion and shadows — the same P-frame balloons to hundreds of KB. So the sequence of P-frame sizes is already an activity curve. You can see it without decoding a single frame.

Measured on a 2K H.265 camera pointed at a mostly-static studio (documented, not estimated):

The third bar is derived: a sparse segment of 5.6 MB / 248 s ≈ 81 MB/h, versus ~190 MB of full-rate video for the same wall-clock window — about 34× less.

The one enemy of this trick

If the camera's bitrate is flattened — roughly the same bytes per second whether or not anyone is there — P-frame sizes stop correlating with activity. Some smart-encoder cameras behave exactly like that. That's the blind spot of compressed-domain gating; my fallbacks are pixgate and tiered recording.

The hardware constraint, and why AI stays out of the core

MiBeeNvr's design baseline is a 1 GB low-end ARM board (Raspberry Pi 3B), with a 512 MB process budget, a single static binary and zero runtime dependencies. Every feature has to fit that budget.

A resident inference model doesn't fit. It would either eat the memory or force you onto Coral/GPU hardware — which would break the premise of "an old device that runs today". So the core recording path deliberately contains no model. That's a trade-off, not a capability gap.

Where does AI go instead? Two places, both outside the budget line:

  • Browser-side: detection runs on the viewer's device (ONNX Runtime Web + WebGPU). Many viewers share the load; the server never pays. The cost is that it isn't a 7×24 unattended pipeline.
  • External Vision: a separate process on hardware you actually have room for. The NVR stays light and dumb; the AI runs where the silicon is; conclusions come back over an API. Full architecture in the MiBeeVision section.

This is also why the storage design works at all: the cheaper the activity decision, the more often you can afford to make it — and the denser you can make "nothing is happening" writes. Three layers, cheapest first: compressed-domain signals (near-zero cost), pixgate classic CV (under 2% of one core), external Vision (someone else's hardware).

Core mechanism: gating in the compressed domain

The NVR never decodes the picture. It watches each P-frame's size against a rolling baseline — the typical P-frame size of that stream recently, maintained with MAD (median absolute deviation, a statistic that resists jitter). A P-frame suddenly several times the baseline (default 5×) means "activity": switch back to full frame rate immediately.

Conversely, if the scene stays quiet for 60 seconds, drop into sparse mode: one keyframe every 30 seconds, audio paused.

In config terms, that's all there is (every value below is the default):

cameras:
  - id: "studio"
    recording_mode: "adaptive"    # default "continuous" = full frame rate
    adaptive:
      calm_threshold: "60s"       # how long quiet must last before downgrading (10s–30m)
      timelapse_interval: "30s"   # keyframe spacing in sparse mode (5s–10m)
      spike_factor: 5.0           # activity sensitivity (1.5–20, lower = more sensitive)
      gop_buffer_bytes: 33554432  # GOP pre-buffer ceiling (1–64MB)

In the web UI it's Camera → Edit → Recording mode: Adaptive (motion-aware).

Five signals, any one of which restores full frame rate

Signal What it is Requirement
Video spike P-frame size deviates from baseline by more than spike_factor× Any H.264/H.265 camera; the default path
Audio trigger Loudness (dBFS) over a 1-second window — breaking glass, shouting, alarms G.711 audio from the camera
pixgate Sampled sub-stream decoded and run through classic CV: "is there real, persistent foreground motion?" ffmpeg + reachable sub-stream
Camera-side ONVIF event Subscribe to the camera's MotionAlarm; the camera itself says something moved Camera support, enabled
External semantic trigger Any external system POSTs to an API — e.g. "your AI backend saw a person" An external system

The GOP ring buffer: why the switch drops zero frames

The biggest risk of a "don't write everything" strategy isn't saving too little — it's the first frames of an event missing from disk. Here's the insurance.

While in sparse mode, a 32 MB ring buffer in memory always holds the most recent complete GOP. The moment an activity spike appears:

  1. the buffered GOP (the continuous footage right before the spike) is flushed to disk;
  2. then the recorder switches back to full frame rate, and everything after lands on disk as usual.

The switch point contains no gap. Playback doesn't artifact, doesn't skip.

Blue Iris has a pre-trigger buffer, Synology has 5–300 s pre-recording — same family of idea: get the seconds before the trigger back onto disk. The difference is only the source: their pre-roll comes from deciding to record in advance; mine comes from what the buffer happens to be holding. No hierarchy, just different constraints.

What sparse mode writes, and what playback looks like

Empty periods are stored as compressed time. During merge, dwell samples longer than 2 s are squeezed to 0.1 s frame spacing. A 122-second sparse segment becomes 0.4 seconds in the file — playback fast-forwards through empty stretches and runs real-time through active ones, automatically, inside the same file.

The database row keeps the wall-clock axis, and the playback timeline's seek goes through a timeline_map to land at the right offset inside the product.

Synology's Smart Time Lapse and Blue Iris' Periodic mode do the same family of thing — fewer bytes for longer empty time. I folded it into the everyday recording stream instead of shipping it as a separate switch.

pixgate: the pixel-domain gate

Why it exists

Compressed-domain gating has a blind spot that is principled, not a bug: rain hitting a puddle, leaves in the wind, a person walking past — all are real pixel motion, all inflate P-frames. The bitrate domain cannot tell "rain" from "person".

A second class of cameras is worse: smart encoders flatten the bitrate, so P-frame sizes decouple from activity entirely. Compressed-domain gating simply stops working on those streams.

So there's a pixel-domain layer: sample, decode, and use classic computer vision to ask "is there a coherent, persistent foreground object?" This layer isn't novel — ZoneMinder's zones, Shinobi's regions and Blue Iris' motion zones are all this idea. Here's my implementation.

The pipeline, and what each stage fixes

Stage by stage, in plain language:

Stage The failure it fixes
① Background model (EMA) "A person standing still for a few minutes gets absorbed into the background" — foreground learns at 1/5 the background rate, so a stationary person is still recognized
② Adaptive diff threshold Night gain produces full-frame grain noise — the threshold tracks the sensor-noise median, so grain isn't read as foreground
③ Illumination-step suppression Headlights sweeping a wall, IR-cut flips — a single step is suppressed; only "the light really stayed on" rebuilds the background
④ Connected-component min area Rain vs. person: rain is many small, short-lived blobs; a person is one large, persistent blob (a mid-distance person on a 480p sub-stream covers ~2–8% of the grid)
⑤ ROI mask Sky, water, streets — areas that "always flicker" — are excluded with normalized polygons
⑥ Ghost absorption Static new foreground (lights on, a parked car, a water droplet on the lens) merges into the background after 5 minutes and stops triggering. Moving objects keep drifting centroids and are never absorbed
⑦ Persistence hysteresis 2 consecutive active samples to confirm, 3 consecutive quiet samples to release — single-frame noise can't trigger

Costs and prerequisites, stated plainly

  • Requires ffmpeg (the same optional dependency transcoding uses). If missing, the gate disables itself with one warning; nothing else is affected.
  • Requires a reachable sub-stream (rtsp / onvif / gb28181 cameras — GB/T 28181 is a Chinese national standard, relevant only if you have such devices; not applicable to srt / rtmp push cameras).
  • Cost: 480p-class sub-stream at 1 fps, roughly 10–20 ms/frame of software decode per camera — under 2% of one core.
  • While a PTZ camera is moving, the gate goes blind (anti-false-trigger) and rebuilds the background afterwards.
  • Decisions are published on the event bus as pixgate.activity (with area_pct / centroid / flood / ghost fields) for UI and automations; Prometheus exposes nvr_pixgate_samples_total / nvr_pixgate_triggers_total.

Its designed partner: video_exit: false

With video_exit: false, video spikes never exit sparse mode — rain can pour and the camera stays in time-lapse. Only pixgate, audio, camera events or the external API restore full rate. For doorways and corridors where "no human, no full frame rate" is the rule.

Tiered recording: a safety net for flattened bitrates

For cameras whose bitrate is flattened, single-layer adaptive may never downgrade. Tiered recording walks on two legs:

  • the sub-stream records 24/7 as a layer=1 baseline — 480p-class, 60-second segments, low bitrate, never misses anything;
  • the main stream keeps its adaptive density — paired with video_exit: false + pixgate, the main stream records events only, at full quality.

Sub-layer segments live in the same directory tree with a sub_ prefix, are born terminal (merge_status='sublayer'), never merge, and follow ordinary retention. The recordings API takes ?layer=1 / ?layer=0 to toggle visibility.

Blue Iris' "sub-stream continuous + main on trigger" (direct-to-disc BVR, sub-stream upsampled on playback) and Synology's Advanced Continuous Recording (low-res continuous, high-res on event) are the same family. Their trigger comes from configured rules; mine comes from automatic compressed-domain/pixgate decisions — plus sub-layer segments can feed external AI directly (next section).

Noise engineering: the three knobs

All three exist because of real user reports:

Setting What it treats
noise_floor_bytes At night the encoder can starve the bitrate down to a few hundred bytes/frame, and the relative-multiple metric catches jitter as activity — "the log says activity, the playback shows nothing". An absolute byte floor below which a P-frame never counts as a spike
auto_noise_floor (default on) Self-calibrating from time-lapse dwell frames: sparse-mode frames are static by construction, so their p99 size × 1.25 is this camera's own noise ceiling. Only engages on bitrate-starved streams; healthy streams behave identically
video_exit: false Permanent time-lapse: video spikes never exit sparse mode; only pixgate / audio / camera events / external API escalate. Treats rain, water, foliage

Explicit floor and self-calibrated floor take the larger value — the explicit value sets a hard minimum, the self-calibration raises it further on starved streams.

Activity scores, heat timelines, content-aware cleanup

Every segment gets an activity score from the compressed-domain analyzer, queryable in the recordings library: filter by "has activity / quiet / scene change", set a minimum score, or color the timeline by activity (green = quiet → red = busy).

Two anti-distortion measures since v0.13:

  • Absolute-bitrate confidence: purely relative metrics fabricate high scores on bitrate-starved streams. Confidence is anchored to the segment's median P-frame bytes in absolute terms (~400B → 0, ~1200B → full trust, linear between). Rankings and cleanup read "activity score × confidence".
  • Pixel-first routing: with pixgate enabled, if the pixel-domain foreground series covers a segment sufficiently, the score is synthesized from pixels (0.8 × foreground duty cycle + 0.2 × area amplitude), immune to night-gain noise and encoder refresh frames.

When the disk hits its watermark (default 85%), cleanup deletes the lowest-activity quiet segments first — the same disk holds more "something happened" footage. Frigate's retain ladder decides by type what to keep; I order deletions by content within a type. Same idea, two directions.

eval-replay: tuning without touching production

The gate is a pure function of "P-frame size sequence + config", so a finished recording can answer "what would this parameter set have done?" — no camera, no decoding:

# scorer replay: activity score + confidence per segment
mibee-nvr eval-replay --corpus corpus.json

# gate replay: default vs candidate parameters, side by side
mibee-nvr eval-replay --corpus corpus.json --gate --videoexit=false
mibee-nvr eval-replay --corpus corpus.json --gate --spike 8 --noisefloor-bytes 600

A corpus is a JSON array whose label field is conventionally rain / lowbitrate / static / active, aggregated into per-label means.

MiBeeVision: AI where the hardware is

Architecture

How data flows

The NVR watches segment-completed events, checks the Vision consumer's heartbeat, and pushes the segment in the window after it lands on disk but before merge (push_mode: notify lets the consumer pull; upload pushes bytes).

Why push at all: early Vision polled the NVR for recordings, and 78% of those requests hit 404 — the segment had already been merged or cleaned up before Vision arrived. With push, the video is in Vision's hands before the merge process touches it.

Heartbeat timeout (default 60 s) pauses pushing; on recovery, missed segments are re-pushed with bounds — a 2-hour window, max 500 segments, 200 ms pacing — so a recovery burst can't hammer the consumer or the disk.

Multi-instance routing

vision.instances supports several consumers at once, each with its own address, identity and on/off switch; cameras select instances via vision_targets (empty = all). Different instances can run different models, routed by scenario:

vision:
  enabled: true
  url: "http://192.168.1.20:9091"      # single-instance shorthand
  heartbeat_timeout_secs: 60
  push_mode: "notify"                   # notify = consumer pulls
  skip_cameras: ["cam-mjpeg-1"]         # pushing MJPEG cameras is pointless
  sub_layer_cameras: ["cam-4k-yard"]    # on-demand sub-stream analysis segments (not in the recordings library)
  tiered_cameras: ["cam-smart-codec"]   # layer=1 segments for semantic gating

cameras:
  - id: "cam-gate"
    vision_targets: ["jetson-yolo", "coral-tpu"]   # multi-instance routing

Feeding AI low-resolution segments: decode cost cut to 1/4–1/16

Two low-res channels (shipped in v0.12.0, issues #512–#537):

  • Sub-layer analysis (sub_layer_cameras): the NVR pulls the sub-stream on demand and records short-retention analysis segments — outside the recordings library, never merged, deleted once consumed;
  • Tiered sub-layer segments (tiered_cameras): reuse the formal library's layer=1 rows; main-stream segments step aside and are no longer pushed.

4K main-stream recording is untouched. For the consumer, judging a 480p segment is an order of magnitude cheaper than judging 4K.

How conclusions come back

Two paths, both ending in the same action — pulling the main stream back to full frame rate:

  1. Vision writes AI events back to the NVR (AI tags in the recordings list + events), visible during playback;
  2. any external system (Vision itself, home automation, your scripts) calls the trigger API: 
curl -u admin:password -X POST \
  http://192.168.1.50:9090/api/cameras/cam-gate/adaptive/trigger \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"source": "vision", "hold": "30s"}'

hold is how long full frame rate is maintained; each new confirmation restarts the clock.

MiBeeVision Lite v0.1.0 — released today (2026-10-18)

  • What it is: MiBeeNvr's AI detection component — object detection and tracking over NVR-recorded video, event generation from area / line-crossing / loitering rules, results written back to the NVR.
  • Shape: single Linux binary (x86_64 / aarch64) with YOLOv8n and ONNX Runtime 1.17.1 (CPU) built in. Lite = single camera, CPU inference.
  • Deploy: web UI on port 9092 — enter the NVR address, paste an API key, pick a camera, draw rule zones.
  • Auth: API keys are mbv_-prefixed; the web session token (mbs_) returns 401 on write-back.
  • Transport: http_download when Vision runs on a different machine; local_file requires a shared recordings directory.
  • License: closed-source proprietary, © Mi-Bee Studio, distributed free with MiBeeNvr; the bundled YOLOv8n is Ultralytics AGPL-3.0.
  • Versioning: independent of MiBeeNvr's vX.Y.Z line.

Lite is the first footprint on this path: one camera, CPU. It changes none of the NVR's budgets — it runs on your other machine, and the NVR pays at most some push bandwidth.

Same table, different bets

A framework: six places to save storage

F is the load-bearing one: an NVR's storage ceiling is set first by which signal it uses to decide "record now".

Where each project spends its effort

Project Quiet-period behavior Detection domain Signature move
MiBeeNvr sparse keyframes (30s/frame) compressed + pixel + audio + ONVIF + external GOP ring buffer; activity-score cleanup
Frigate event segments (10s granularity, no motion = discarded) semantic (object detection) + pixel motion mask retention ladder by type; review UX
Blue Iris sub-stream continuous, or nothing pixel zones + optional AI + DIO sub-continuous + main-on-trigger in one BVR
Synology SS low-res stream, or nothing camera-side or SS-side pixel + person/vehicle Advanced Continuous Recording; Smart Time Lapse
ZoneMinder nothing (Modect writes events only) pixel zones (five zone types) event maturity; external triggers (Nodect)
Shinobi nothing (Watch-Only + Trigger Record) pixel regions + optional OpenCV/YOLO per-user storage quotas; flexible event config

In prose, because the table flattens things:

  • Frigate has the strongest server-side AI event recording in the category — object detection driving retention, the review interface, Home Assistant integration depth. It asks for Coral/GPU and Docker; that's the cost of the route, not a flaw. On "AI decides, then store the event", I'm clearly behind it.
  • Blue Iris ships "sub-stream continuous + main on trigger" as a mature feature (direct-to-disc BVR + pre-trigger buffer), works out of the box on Windows, and has a rich trigger ecosystem. Its storage measurement (1 hour: 3.90 GB → 120 MB) is the most persuasive community data point I've cited.
  • Synology Surveillance Station is the NAS-native surveillance hub — Advanced Continuous Recording, Dual Recording, Smart Time Lapse, edge recording, plus its licensing model. If you already run a Synology, it's the lowest-friction path.
  • ZoneMinder is one of the oldest open-source NVRs; its event system is mature and its zone types (Active/Inclusive/Exclusive/Preclusive/Inactive) were my reference for ROI masks. The LAMP stack is heavy on low-end hardware — again, route cost.
  • Shinobi is Node.js with flexible event-driven recording (Trigger Record + Buffer Time) and multi-tenant storage quotas as a standout. Pure event recording simply isn't in the same lane as mine on continuity.

Camera-side smart codecs

H.265+ (Hikvision), Smart H.265+ (Dahua), Ultra H.265 (Uniview), Zipstream (Axis), WiseStream (Hanwha) cut baseline bitrate with background modeling, dynamic GOP and ROI encoding. Vendor claims: 20–40% below standard H.265 at equal quality, more in favorable scenes. They complement NVR-side gating; they don't replace it.

Two traps I've written about (in Chinese):

  1. Smart codecs are proprietary extensions, not standards — cross-brand they usually degrade to standard H.265. Don't count their savings in cross-brand capacity planning.
  2. A flattened smart-encoder bitrate breaks every compressed-domain activity signal — not just mine. For those cameras, go tiered + pixgate.

My honest limits

# Limit Consequence Mitigation
1 Sparse-mode playback is compressed time Slow changes during empty periods are gone; the product file is far shorter than wall-clock and can look "corrupt" Documented behavior; a real trade-off against real-time sub-stream continuity (Blue Iris / Synology route)
2 No server-side AI chain Can't answer "how many cats yesterday?" unattended like Frigate MiBeeVision + external trigger API
3 Compressed domain fails on flattened bitrates May never downgrade tiered + pixgate
4 Push cameras (RTMP/SRT) can't use tiering or pixgate Single-layer adaptive only Video spike + audio + external trigger still apply
5 MJPEG has no compressed-domain signal; AAC/Opus can't trigger audio Adaptive degrades on these cameras MJPEG gets dark-frame filtering + AVI containers; audio needs G.711
6 GOP pre-buffer is 32 MB resident per camera Many cameras = redo the memory math 1–64 MB configurable; must hold one full GOP
7 Single-maintainer project Long-term maintenance risk is a real selection variable Docs and engineering depth — judge for yourself

Try it 

# one-line install: downloads the binary, creates the nvr system user,
# generates a config, installs a systemd service and starts it
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mi-Bee-Studio/MiBeeNvr/main/install.sh | sudo bash
# Web UI on http://localhost:9090, data in /var/lib/mibee-nvr

# or Docker (recordings on an external drive: edit the volume mount + NVR_DATA_DIR)
docker compose --project-directory . -f deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

Then set any camera to Recording mode: Adaptive and watch the storage trend on the dashboard. eval-replay lets you tune parameters against recordings you already have.

  • Repo: https://github.com/Mi-Bee-Studio/MiBeeNvr
  • Docs: https://www.mlsbs.top/projects/mibeenvr
  • My blog (mostly Chinese): https://blog.mickeyzzc.tech
  • MiBeeVision Lite v0.1.0: see the repo's releases page

Glossary

Term Plain meaning
I-frame / keyframe A frame decodable on its own; starts a GOP
P-frame Stores only the difference from the previous frame; the quieter the scene, the smaller it is
GOP The run of frames between two I-frames; 1–30 s is typical in surveillance
Bitrate Bytes per second; bitrate × time ≈ disk usage
VBR / CBR Variable vs. constant bitrate; VBR saves when quiet, CBR is predictable
Compressed domain Reading frame sizes and types without decoding
Pixel domain Decoding and comparing pixels (background differencing, connected components)
Semantic domain AI models deciding "that's a person" — most expensive, most accurate
Pre-buffer Memory holding recent video so the trigger's lead-in isn't lost
Sub-stream The camera's second, lower-resolution output
MAD Median absolute deviation — a statistic resistant to outlier jitter
EMA Exponential moving average — a "slowly learning" background model
Connected component Adjacent foreground pixels merged into a blob, judged by area and lifetime
ROI Region of interest; a mask is the opposite — an excluded region
Ghost A static new foreground (parked car, lens droplet) being absorbed into the background
Hysteresis N consecutive active samples to confirm, M consecutive quiet samples to release
timeline_map The wall-clock ↔ offset-in-product lookup that makes seek land correctly

Mechanisms described against v0.13.0 docs and source comments; comparison data from each project's public docs and community measurements as of 2026-10; storage figures marked as measured are from my own documented runs, the rest are estimates or vendor claims. Diagrams are the SVG files in the diagrams/ folder next to this markdown — upload them to your publishing platform (dev.to: drag each into the editor) or host them on your own domain and update the paths.

title: Vercel Sandbox now runs on Vercel Managed Images
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel Managed Images (VMI), a set of versioned, open-source base images you can use as-is or extend. The source for every image lives in the public vercel/sandbox repository.

Managed images replace Sandbox runtimes, which are now deprecated. Starting with version 3 of the Sandbox SDK, new sandboxes default to vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. It ships with Node.js, Python, common coding agents and standard utilities, so most users never build a custom image or install packages at boot.

The universal image switches our default operating system from Amazon Linux to Ubuntu, a lighter and more widely used system across the industry.

Secure by default

Every managed image gets a nightly release. Rolling tags such as latest and the major-version tags pick up operating system and dependency updates automatically, including security patches and new releases of Node.js, Python, and the preinstalled coding agents.

Within each release, dependencies are pinned to specific versions wherever possible, so a given image version stays consistent.

If you need a fully immutable, reproducible environment, pin to an image digest (SHA). Digest-pinned images opt out of automatic updates.

Choose a managed image from the catalog

Each managed image targets a different starting point:

  • vercel/sandbox/universal:latest is the new default, a rolling release on Ubuntu 26.04 with Node.js 24, Python 3.14 with uv, the opencode, claude-code, codex, and pi coding agents, and utilities including git, vim, nano, tmux, ripgrep, jq, and fzf.

  • vercel/sandbox/node:22, node:24, and node:26 provide Node.js versions on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/python:3.14 provides Python on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/ubuntu:latest provides base Ubuntu 26.04 with no extra tooling.

  • vercel/sandbox/arch:latest provides Arch Linux, regularly updated, with no Node.js or Python preinstalled. Its large package repository makes it useful for agents that install tools on the fly.

Reference an image and migrate from runtimes

Sandboxes can use an image from any repository in your project, a repository which has been shared with your team or any public repository.

Images are addressed by their full path, team-slug/project/repo:tag, for example vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. The SDK types the image property so built-in images autocomplete while any string is still accepted. The previous runtime property is deprecated, not removed, so existing code keeps working.

Amazon Linux runtimes are not part of the managed image catalog, so teams that need AL2023 can stay on runtime. Managed images run as the default ubuntu or arch user with passwordless sudo, rather than the vercel-sandbox user.

Open an issue or a pull request to improve them, and read the Vercel Sandbox images documentation to get started.
