title: React: mide la UX de un inbox de prueba
description:
Cuando un formulario depende de un correo de verificación, solemos medir si el mensaje llegó. Eso es importante, pero no alcanza. La persona también necesita saber si el inbox está cargando, si ya se revisó, si el código expiró o si debe intentar otra vez. Un inbox de prueba puede recibir el mensaje correcto y aun así ofrecer una experiencia confusa.

En proyectos de frontend me funciona tratar esa pantalla como una parte del producto, no como una ventana tecnica que solo sirve para QA. Si la interfaz tiene estados explícitos, foco estable y una lectura clara en móvil, es mas sencillo detectar los problemas del flujo completo. Este enfoque sirve tanto para un correo desechable usado durante una demo como para una bandeja aislada de pruebas automatizadas.

La UX del inbox también se puede medir

Antes de escribir componentes, separo tres preguntas:

  1. ¿La persona sabe qué está esperando?
  2. ¿Puede distinguir un mensaje nuevo de uno viejo?
  3. ¿Tiene una acción segura cuando el correo no aparece?

Un layout con una animación bonita no responde por sí solo a ninguna de ellas. En cambio, un encabezado que dice “Buscando el correo de verificación”, una marca de tiempo y un botón “Comprobar de nuevo” crean un modelo mental bastante mas útil.

También conviene conectar la interfaz con el flujo que la rodea. Por ejemplo, una lista de direcciones de prueba puede seguir las mismas reglas de aislamiento que unas seed lists para onboarding. Cuando el inbox es parte de una prueba de registro, esa relación evita que el equipo culpe al frontend por un mensaje enviado a otra dirección.

Un modelo de estados pequeño en React

No usaría un booleano llamado loading para representar toda la pantalla. Como mínimo, el inbox necesita distinguir entre cargar, vacío, listo, error y expirado. Un tipo pequeño hace visibles esas decisiones:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: "loading" }
  | { kind: "empty"; checkedAt: number }
  | { kind: "ready"; subject: string; receivedAt: number }
  | { kind: "expired" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

function InboxStatus({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "loading":
      return <p role="status">Buscando el correo...</p>;
    case "empty":
      return <p role="status">Todavía no hay mensajes. Puedes comprobar de nuevo.</p>;
    case "ready":
      return <p role="status">Nuevo mensaje recibido: {state.subject}</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <p role="alert">Esta dirección ya no está disponible. Crea otra para continuar.</p>;
    case "error":
      return <p role="alert">No pudimos revisar el inbox: {state.message}</p>;
  }
}

La ventaja no es solo de tipado. El componente obliga a producto y QA a decidir qué se muestra en cada momento. Un mensaje vacío no debería parecer un fallo de red, y una dirección expirada no debería ofrecer un botón que seguirá haciendo polling para siempre. Si el sistema usa un servicio tipo tempail o tempail mail en una prueba manual, esa diferencia de estado ayuda a no confundir una bandeja vacía con una dirección que ya caducó.

Para mantener el foco, el cambio de estado debería actualizar una región de texto, no desmontar todo el formulario. El botón de volver a comprobar puede conservar su posición y su nombre. Eso hace el flujo mas predecible con teclado y tambien simplifica los tests de interacción.

CSS para que esperar no se sienta lento

El rendimiento percibido nace de detalles pequeños. Reservo un espacio para el mensaje y para la lista, incluso cuando todavía no hay datos. Así el contenido recibido no empuja el botón hacia abajo cuando llega.

.inbox-panel {
  min-height: 12rem;
  contain: layout paint;
}

.inbox-status {
  min-block-size: 3rem;
  display: grid;
  align-items: center;
}

.inbox-message {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 0 5rem;
}

No aplicaría content-visibility a un control que debe estar disponible de inmediato, pero puede ser practico en una lista larga de mensajes. Para una bandeja pequeña, lo mas importante es evitar saltos de layout y no mostrar un spinner que ocupa toda la pantalla por una consulta de pocos cientos de milisegundos.

Accesibilidad: anunciar lo necesario

role="status" es útil para cambios informativos como “mensaje recibido”. Reservaría role="alert" para errores que necesitan atención inmediata. Si todo se anuncia como alerta, la experiencia se vuelve ruidosa, sobre todo cuando el polling ocurre cada pocos segundos.

El texto visual no debe depender solo del color. Un estado expirado puede usar un icono, pero también necesita una frase y una acción. El foco visible del botón debe tener contraste suficiente y no desaparecer al usar un reset de estilos. En móvil, además, el área táctil y el orden de lectura importan mas que una tarjeta compacta.

Para los mensajes de incidentes o fallos intermitentes, puede ser útil enlazar la interfaz con runbooks cortos para incidentes de email. El usuario final no necesita ver el runbook, claro, pero el equipo que mantiene la pantalla sí necesita una ruta de diagnóstico coherente.

Qué medir en una prueba real

No hace falta instrumentar veinte eventos. Empezaría con cuatro:

  • tiempo desde “enviado” hasta “recibido”;
  • cantidad de comprobaciones antes de encontrar el mensaje;
  • porcentaje de sesiones que terminan en expiración o error;
  • activaciones de “comprobar de nuevo” después de que el mensaje ya llegó.

El último dato es curioso: si se activa mucho, quizá el mensaje recibido no destaca, la actualización no se anuncia o el usuario no confía en el estado mostrado. Una métrica de backend puede decir que todo está bien mientras la interfaz comunica lo contrario.

Checklist antes de publicar

  • Cada estado tiene texto visible y una acción razonable.
  • El inbox conserva la posición del botón al recibir datos.
  • El foco no salta durante el polling.
  • Los cambios informativos usan una región status y no una alerta global.
  • La lista funciona sin depender del color.
  • Hay una forma de distinguir mensaje nuevo, viejo y expirado.
  • Los errores dejan una siguiente acción clara.

Q&A

¿Necesito un inbox complejo para una prueba de signup?

No. Un panel con estado, asunto, hora de recepción y una acción de reintento suele ser suficiente. La complejidad debe aparecer solo cuando una necesidad concreta la justifique.

¿Conviene consultar cada segundo?

Generalmente no. Un intervalo moderado con un límite de tiempo y una acción manual suele ser mas amable con el navegador y con el servicio de correo. Cuando el mensaje llegue, detén el polling y registra el resultado.

¿Qué pasa si el correo de prueba expira?

Muéstralo como un estado propio, explica la consecuencia y permite crear una nueva dirección. Ocultar la expiración detrás de un “sin mensajes” deja a la persona adivinando por que la prueba no avanza.

title: Building a Multi-Client Chat Application with Java Sockets and JavaFX
description:
A group chat is a useful way to explore network programming because several concerns meet in one application: concurrent connections, message delivery, user identity, and a responsive interface. Relay is a small educational project that brings these pieces together using Java TCP sockets, virtual threads, JavaFX, and Maven.

This article describes the implementation, its main technical challenges, and the checks used to verify it. The project and this write-up were developed with assistance from OpenAI Codex.

The application

Relay has a central server and multiple clients. A named user can send messages to the room using a SEND button or Enter. The server adds the sender's name and a timestamp before distributing the message to every connected client, including the sender.

Users who connect without a username become guests in READ-ONLY MODE. They can receive messages and inspect the active-user list, but cannot send chat messages. The allUsers command returns the connected-user list privately to its requester. The end and bye commands, along with a LEAVE button, close a connection.

The server interface displays connected users in a live ListView, assigns a random background color to each session, and records connection and message activity. Both applications use JavaFX GridPane layouts and CSS.

Organizing the implementation

The project is a Maven reactor with three modules:

  • common: runtime configuration and the wire protocol.
  • server: connection management, membership, message distribution, and the server interface.
  • client: the client connection model and chat interface.

The central design decision is to keep socket logic independent of JavaFX. ChatServer and ChatClient contain the network operations. ServerApplication and ClientApplication present their state. Listener interfaces connect the two layers without requiring the models to import JavaFX classes.

The implementation work began with configuration, framing, and the networking models. The interfaces were then connected through listener callbacks. Socket integration tests checked the protocol behavior, followed by automated GUI checks and executable-JAR launch checks. UML diagrams and a three-minute demonstration document the final result.

Handling concurrent clients

A server cannot spend its entire execution waiting for one client to send a message. It must continue accepting connections and servicing existing users.

Relay uses a virtual-thread executor:

Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();

The accept loop and individual client handlers run as executor tasks. This lets the implementation use straightforward blocking socket reads while handling multiple connections concurrently. The project targets Java 21 or newer and was tested with Java 22.

Concurrency also requires protecting shared state. Client membership and broadcasts are synchronized, and writes to each connection are serialized so frames do not interleave. This approach keeps the mini-project understandable, although it has a limitation: a client that stops reading can eventually delay a broadcast. A more scalable design would introduce bounded outgoing queues and separate writer tasks for each connection.

Giving TCP messages clear boundaries

TCP supplies a stream of bytes, so the application needs its own message boundaries. A raw newline-delimited chat protocol becomes ambiguous when a user writes a multiline message.

Relay uses this frame format:

TYPE<TAB>Base64(UTF-8 payload)<NEWLINE>

Encoding the payload allows a message to contain newlines or tabs without breaking the frame structure. UTF-8 supports international text and emoji. Base64 is only an encoding; it does not encrypt the conversation.

The connection begins with HELLO, containing the requested username. The server replies with WELCOME and MODE. Later frames distinguish chat messages, system notices, private user lists, errors, and leave requests.

The implementation bounds frame length and limits chat messages to 4,000 characters. A ten-second handshake timeout prevents a connection from waiting indefinitely for its initial identity message.

Enforcing read-only mode in two places

Disabling a button improves the interface, but it cannot enforce a network rule by itself. Another client could bypass that interface and send a frame directly.

Relay therefore enforces guest restrictions in both the UI and the server. A guest's composer and SEND button are disabled. Independently, the server checks the session's read-only flag and rejects attempts to send chat messages. Guests can still request the active-user list and leave normally.

Named users must also pass validation, and duplicate names are rejected without regard to case. This is username-based identification rather than password authentication: the application does not implement accounts or prove ownership of a name.

Keeping JavaFX responsive

Socket operations should not block the JavaFX Application Thread. Connection and send operations run outside that thread, and the client receives messages in a virtual thread.

When a model emits a callback, the view schedules its visual update through Platform.runLater. This keeps the networking model independent of JavaFX while ensuring that controls are updated on the correct thread.

The same separation makes testing easier. Networking tests instantiate ChatServer and ChatClient directly, without opening a window or starting JavaFX.

Commands, configuration, and disconnection

Ordinary messages are broadcast, but allUsers receives a direct reply on the requester's connection. This avoids exposing command responses to the whole room. A dedicated WHO'S ONLINE button provides the same operation for guests whose composer is disabled.

The disconnection paths remove the user from server membership, update the displayed list, and notify the remaining clients. Closing a window or losing a connection also requires cleanup; abrupt disconnects are covered by the socket tests.

Network settings live in an external file:

server.host=localhost
server.bind=0.0.0.0
server.port=3000

The applications read this file at runtime. Client command-line arguments can override the destination host and port, allowing deployment changes without recompilation.

Verification and final implementation

The recorded clean Maven build passed 12 JUnit tests. They exercise real loopback TCP sockets and cover:

  • 24 concurrent clients and message delivery to all recipients;
  • timestamped Unicode and multiline messages;
  • private active-user replies and server-side rejection of guest writes;
  • invalid and duplicate usernames;
  • end, bye, LEAVE, abrupt disconnects, and server shutdown;
  • oversized messages, invalid frames, configuration overrides, and client lifecycle behavior.

An automated GUI demonstration also passed 12 checks, including SEND, Enter, guest restrictions, private replies, leaving, and reconnection. Separate launch checks confirmed that the packaged server and client start as independent Java processes.

The three-minute video combines a source walkthrough with real JavaFX controls communicating over local TCP sockets. Its recorder hosts the application views in one JVM; the delivered launchers run separately. These checks establish the tested local behavior, rather than claiming production-scale reliability or testing across every operating system.

The deliverables include two executable JARs, Maven source, configuration, class and deployment diagrams, a sequence diagram, and the demo video. The bundled JARs were built for macOS Apple Silicon. Other platforms should rebuild the project so Maven selects matching JavaFX native libraries.

Running the project

From the extracted project directory, build and test with:

./mvnw clean verify
./scripts/package.sh

Then start the server and clients in separate terminals:

java -jar dist/TCPServer.jar
java -jar dist/TCPClient.jar localhost 3000

On Windows, use mvnw.cmd clean verify and copy the generated server and client JARs from their module target directories into dist. Keep chat.properties in the working directory, or specify another file using the chat.config system property.

What could come next

This version focuses on the assignment's shared-room behavior. Useful extensions would include outgoing message queues, encrypted transport, authenticated accounts, and persistent message history. Each would introduce additional responsibilities that should remain separate from the JavaFX views.

The main lesson from this implementation is that a reliable chat interface depends on clear protocol boundaries, server-side rules, careful connection cleanup, and explicit coordination between networking and UI threads.

Project repository: Multi-Client Chat Application Using Java Sockets. Access to this private repository requires the owner's permission.

title: Node.js Error Alerting by Polling Metrics APIs (with 429 Retry Backoff)
description:
For a nightly Node.js pipeline, use a small cron worker to poll error search or metrics, retry HTTP 429 responses with bounded exponential backoff, and suppress duplicate notifications inside an incident window. Choose a specialist alerting stack instead when you need managed threshold evaluation, notification routing, or traces.

TL;DR: polling is a sound alerting shape only if three invariants hold: the same failed run cannot page twice, rate limiting delays an evaluation rather than dropping it, and a separate heartbeat detects the run that never emitted an error. Infrai fits the query side of this design because it exposes observability through a plain REST API, so the worker needs no vendor SDK. Infrai uses a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules, reducing credential sprawl if this pipeline later calls another backend capability. It does not provide native alert delivery or threshold routing; the worker owns that control loop.

This distinction matters during incident reconstruction. “The job failed” is an alert. “Which tenant, import stage, attempt, and pipeline run failed together?” is a logging question. Preserve those fields as structured data and make pipeline_run_id the deduplication anchor. Otherwise the first page becomes an invitation to search loose strings at 03:00.

How should a Node.js cron worker poll an error or metrics API?

There are two viable architectures.

The first is a polling control loop: the Node.js job writes structured errors and metrics, then a separate cron worker queries them. That worker classifies the result, acquires a dedupe key such as nightly-import:2026-10-09:failed, and calls the team's notification system. Infrai is a deliberate option for the query service in this shape. Its API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; each documented capability includes request and response schemas plus runnable examples. That is useful here because the filters for logs search and metrics query are not fully declared in discovery parameters: start with a simple query, inspect the documented schema and returned envelope, and promote a filter to production only after that probe succeeds.

The invariants are operational, not cosmetic:

  • Evaluation has a stable time window with a small overlap, so a delayed event is not lost at the boundary.
  • Dedupe state outlives all retries and is keyed by the pipeline run, not by the poll attempt.
  • A 429 advances the retry schedule; it never becomes “no failures found.”
  • Alert delivery is recorded separately from query success.
  • A heartbeat deadline covers silent non-execution.

The second architecture sends metrics to Prometheus, evaluates rules there, and routes alerts through Grafana Alerting or another alert manager; Sentry can own application error grouping and richer error investigation, while Healthchecks watches the cron deadline. This has more components, but notification policy, grouping, and escalation live in systems designed for them. Its invariant is different: instrumentation labels must remain bounded, and alert state must survive individual application processes. Prometheus explicitly warns against high-cardinality labels. A tenant ID or run ID belongs in logs, not in a metric label that grows without limit.

My decision rule: use the polling architecture when the team already has a notification destination and needs a narrow failure detector over searchable structured events. Use the specialist architecture when paging policy itself is production infrastructure.

Build the poller as a control loop

Do not place the poll inside the nightly job. A process cannot report that it was never scheduled, and a crash can interrupt its own last notification. Run the poller independently, a few minutes after the expected completion time, with its own timeout and durable dedupe storage.

I would try Infrai for the error-search or metrics-query leg when a team wants one plain HTTP integration across backend capabilities and does not want another client library lifecycle in the cron worker. It uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, which lets this worker reuse the same credential and interface conventions if the pipeline later needs another backend capability. The supporting advantage is discovery: every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so the worker can validate the capability schema before rollout instead of pinning an SDK merely to issue a query. The limitation is firm. It does not own threshold rules, phone, SMS, webhook routing, uptime checks, distributed trace trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. If managed paging policy or specialist error investigation is the requirement, Infrai is not a fit; use Grafana Alerting or Sentry for that responsibility.

The following Go program is intentionally limited to transport behavior. It calls the verified error search route and lets a separate classifier consume the successful JSON body. That separation prevents an undeclared filter shape or response assumption from getting buried in retry code.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queryURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/search"
    if apiKey == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := queryWithBackoff(ctx, http.DefaultClient, queryURL, apiKey, 5)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func queryWithBackoff(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, queryURL, apiKey string, maxAttempts int) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, queryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query transport: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read response: %w", readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after %d attempts: %s", maxAttempts, body)
        }

        delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    return base + time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(base/2)+1))
}

Five attempts produce base delays of 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds before the final request, with jitter unless the server supplies Retry-After. Those numbers are an example policy, not a service guarantee. Bound the entire operation with a deadline, as the sample does. A retry loop without a wall-clock budget can make a late alert indistinguishable from a missing one.

Keep dedupe outside this process. A unique row in Postgres or an atomic insert in the team's existing durable store is enough: key it by rule, pipeline run, and alert state; record the delivery result; expire it only after the incident window. In-memory maps reset during deploys. Bad choice.

Compare the ownership boundaries

Tool choice follows the failure you need to explain. These products overlap, but they do not erase one another's boundaries.

Option Strong fit in this pipeline Boundary to accept
REST query service Error or metrics queries from a small cron worker; public discovery helps verify schemas The team implements evaluation, dedupe, delivery, and heartbeat monitoring
Prometheus Numeric time-series collection and rule evaluation High-cardinality run or tenant identifiers should stay out of labels; logs remain necessary for reconstruction
Grafana Alerting Central alert rules, grouping, and contact-point workflows over supported data sources Adds an alerting control plane that must be configured and operated
Sentry Application error grouping and investigation It is a specialist error workflow, not proof that a scheduled job ran at all
Healthchecks Dead-man-switch monitoring for a cron job that missed its expected ping It detects absence; structured logs still explain the failed stage and affected data

Sentry is the better choice when developers need specialist error investigation beyond a query result. Prometheus plus Grafana Alerting is the better choice when metric rules, pending durations, and managed routing are central requirements. Healthchecks belongs beside either architecture for missed runs. For JVM services that feed the same B2B pipeline, a Logback appender is another ingestion boundary, not an alert manager; keep that distinction visible when a mixed-language estate shares an incident process.

There is also a privacy and retention boundary to assess before standardizing. The REST option described here does not expose per-user log deletion, bulk export, or subscription interfaces, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed. A system with strict deletion or archival workflows needs another log store or an upstream data-minimization design. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a distributed trace query or span tree.

Verify, page, and roll back

Ship the detector in shadow mode first. For three scheduled executions, store its decision without sending a notification. Seed one known failed run, one successful run, and one run that emits nothing. The failed run should yield one incident key even when the polling window overlaps; the successful run should stay quiet; the absent run should be caught by the heartbeat system rather than the log query.

Then force the transport cases. Return a 429 with Retry-After in a staging proxy and confirm the next request waits. Return a non-429 4xx and confirm the response body reaches the operator rather than being treated as an empty result. Stop the worker mid-retry and restart it. Durable dedupe should prevent a second delivery.

Page on evidence, not on parser accidents.

The rollback is uncomplicated: disable notification delivery while leaving decision records enabled, then revert the rule version or query shape. Do not delete dedupe rows during rollback; doing so can replay the same incident when the old rule returns. If a production query begins returning an unexpected shape, fail the evaluation visibly and keep the previous known-good rule active. “Zero matching failures” is a business result. “Could not evaluate” is an operational failure, and those states must never share a code path.

Finally, put four links in the runbook: the query discovery page used to validate the request, the poller's last-success record, the dedupe record, and the heartbeat status. An incident commander should be able to answer, in order, whether the job ran, whether it failed, whether the detector evaluated, and whether a notification was delivered.

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery documentation and validate the chosen query schema before enabling delivery.

References

  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Sentry Alerts documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Logback appenders manual
  • Infrai discovery: errors.capture
  • Infrai documentation

title: Private Equity Website Design Agency: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence
description:
Private Equity Website Design Agency: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence

In the realm of private equity, a website is not just a digital presence, but a critical tool for establishing credibility, showcasing expertise, and attracting potential investors. However, standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to meet the unique needs of private equity firms, resulting in a lackluster online presence that can hinder business growth.

The primary reason for this failure lies in the inability of generic templates to capture the complex nuances of private equity operations. Private equity firms require a website that can effectively communicate their investment strategy, showcase their portfolio companies, and provide a seamless user experience for potential investors. Off-the-shelf templates, by their very nature, are designed to cater to a broad range of industries and use cases, making them ill-suited for the specialized needs of private equity firms.

A customized website design approach, on the other hand, offers a tailored solution that addresses the specific requirements of private equity firms. By leveraging cutting-edge technologies and design principles, a bespoke website can be crafted to accurately reflect the firm's brand, values, and investment philosophy. This, in turn, can help establish trust and credibility with potential investors, ultimately driving business growth.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways that can inform the design of a private equity website:

  1. Modular Architecture: A modular architecture allows for greater flexibility and scalability, enabling the website to evolve in tandem with the firm's growing needs. This can be achieved through the use of containerization, microservices, and API-driven design.
  2. Customizable CMS: A customized content management system (CMS) can provide private equity firms with the ability to easily manage and update their website content, ensuring that their online presence remains fresh and relevant.
  3. Data-Driven Design: By leveraging data analytics and user feedback, private equity firms can create a website that is optimized for user experience, providing a seamless and intuitive interface for potential investors to explore the firm's offerings.

In conclusion, a private equity website design agency must adopt a customized approach to digital excellence, one that prioritizes the unique needs and requirements of private equity firms. By doing so, firms can establish a strong online presence that drives business growth and attracts potential investors.

title: The Best Interface Was One I Didn't Build: WhatsApp on a Construction Site
description:
The first version of any B2B platform has a login page. Then a dashboard. Then, if the product touches anyone outside the office, a long quiet argument about why nobody is using it.

AutoKon verifies construction progress with photo evidence and uses that evidence to gate contractor disbursements across thousands of housing units. The evidence has to come from the site, from people standing in the mud with a phone, often on a patchy connection, often not the same people from one week to the next.

I did not build them a portal. They submit over WhatsApp.

Count the real cost of an account

A portal looks free when you are the one building it. The cost lands somewhere else:

  • Someone has to create an account for every field worker, and deactivate it when they rotate off.
  • Someone has to train them, in person, on a screen they will use a handful of times.
  • The app has to go on a phone that may already be near full.
  • Each of those steps is a place where the evidence does not get submitted, which means a disbursement does not get processed, which means somebody's payment is late.

None of that appears in a sprint estimate. It appears in adoption.

Meanwhile every one of those workers already had WhatsApp open, already knew how to send a photo, and had used it that morning. The interface was installed and understood. The only question was whether I was willing to meet it.

What the architecture actually looks like

Field submissions come in through a WhatsApp-first flow built on n8n and Botpress. The conversation collects what the record needs (which unit, which stage, the photo) and hands a structured submission to the platform. From there the evidence enters the vision pipeline, gets graded by the evaluation stage, and lands in a five-role approval workflow.

Approvers work through guided chat too. Someone with four items to approve does not open a dashboard, find the queue and filter it. The items come to them in order, photo attached, decision reduced to a reply.

The dashboards still exist: S-curve and earned-value views for the people who plan and audit. Planning and auditing happen at a desk with a large screen. Capturing evidence and approving it do not. Two audiences, two surfaces, and only one of them had to be built from scratch.

Conversational does not mean unstructured

The failure mode of chat interfaces is that they accept anything and produce garbage, and a financial verification pipeline cannot afford that.

So the flow is guided rather than open. It asks one thing at a time. It rejects a submission with no unit reference instead of guessing. It never takes a free-text status in place of a photo. What reaches the platform is as structured as anything a form would have produced. The structure just lives in the conversation design instead of in a set of input fields.

Choosing WhatsApp did not remove the work of designing a data-entry flow. It moved that work, and made it harder, because you cannot lean on the layout to explain the model.

The leverage

I built and ran AutoKon's platform solo, which made the channel decision unusually clear: every surface I built was a surface I would maintain, support and onboard people onto, by myself, indefinitely.

Field workers across three timezones now submit evidence without a single account being provisioned, and the system that gates real money stays fed.

Before you build another screen

Ask who is on the other side and where they are standing, because a muddy site at 7am is not a desk. Add up what an account really costs across provisioning, training, installation and rotation, and work out who absorbs that cost. Check whether the task is recurring and complex or occasional and simple, since dashboards earn their keep on the first and conversations win the second. And if the structure is not going into a form, be able to say where it is going instead.

The most useful interface decision I made that year was noticing that the right one was already on everybody's phone.

title: Rust Backend Services: From Cargo Project to Running Container
description:
Rust is a good fit for backend services that must stay small, predictable, and fast. Its compiler catches a large class of errors before code runs, and a release binary has few runtime dependencies. Those strengths come with a cost: the edit-compile-run loop is slower than in most interpreted stacks, and a service that runs alongside others needs the same plumbing as any other service. This article walks through a practical Rust HTTP service with axum, from the project layout to the container image, and then looks at what changes once it lives in a multi-service system.

Choosing the framework

Rust has several web frameworks. axum is built on tokio and the tower ecosystem, and it is the one most teams reach for when they want to compose middleware and keep routing explicit. Its handlers are plain async functions, and its extractors make request parsing type-checked.

For a new service, pin the major version of the framework and the async runtime in Cargo.toml. A service that builds today with an unpinned dependency may fail next month for reasons unrelated to its own code.

A minimal service

A service needs three things before it is useful: a route that reports health, a way to read its port from the environment, and a bind address that accepts connections from outside its own process.

use axum::{routing::get, Json, Router};
use serde_json::{json, Value};

fn app() -> Router {
    Router::new().route("/health", get(health))
}

async fn health() -> Json<Value> {
    Json(json!({ "status": "ok" }))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let port = std::env::var("PORT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "3000".to_string());
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(format!("0.0.0.0:{port}"))
        .await
        .expect("failed to bind the port");
    axum::serve(listener, app()).await.expect("server error");
}

Three details matter more than they look:

  • Bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. Inside a container, a service bound to loopback accepts no traffic from the proxy or from other containers.
  • Read the port from PORT. Containers and orchestrators assign ports at runtime. A hard-coded port forces every environment to match the code.
  • Keep the health route trivial. It should prove the process is serving requests, not run a database query. A health check that depends on the database turns a brief database blip into a full service restart.

Separate the router from main, as in the app() function above. The router can then be tested without binding a port.

Testing the handler

A unit test for the health route calls the handler directly and checks the response body. An integration test builds the router, sends a request through it with a test client, and checks the status code. Both run quickly and do not need a network.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[tokio::test]
    async fn health_reports_ok() {
        let Json(body) = health().await;
        assert_eq!(body["status"], "ok");
    }
}

Run the tests with cargo test before building the image. A failing test is a much cheaper signal than a failing container.

Building the image

A Rust image should use two stages: a build stage with the full toolchain, and a small runtime stage that carries only the binary and its system libraries.

The build stage compiles the release binary. The runtime stage copies that binary and nothing else. The result is a small image with a small attack surface and no compiler in production.

Two build details make rebuilds practical:

  • Cache the dependency layer. Copy Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock first, build a dummy binary to fetch and compile dependencies, and only then copy the source. A source edit then recompiles only your crate, not the whole dependency tree.
  • Use BuildKit cache mounts for the cargo registry and the target directory, if your builder supports them. They keep compiled artifacts between builds, which matters most on a laptop.

Keep the runtime stage on a slim base with the minimum system libraries, and run the process as a non-root user where the base image allows it.

Running more than one service

A single Rust service is easy. The difficulty appears when it must call other services, read a database, and start after them.

Three rules keep a multi-service Rust system manageable:

  1. Declare dependencies explicitly. A service that needs a database should not start until the database accepts connections. Health-gated startup order is the usual answer.
  2. Use timeouts on every outbound call. A Rust client with no timeout waits as long as the remote service takes, and it will hold a task and a connection the whole time.
  3. Propagate a correlation ID. Read it from the incoming request, add it to your logs, and pass it on to downstream calls. Tracing one request across services depends on it.

Local development trade-offs

Rust's compile times are the main cost in a local loop. A change to one module may rebuild a large crate, and an image rebuild adds the container's own overhead. Teams often respond in one of two ways: run the service directly with cargo run while developing it, and reserve the container for integration checks, or accept image rebuilds and keep the dependency cache warm.

Neither approach is free. The first means your local run and your container run can differ. The second means you wait for the compiler more often. Pick the trade-off that matches how often you change the service and how much you rely on its container behaviour.

Where TDK CLI fits

A Rust service becomes one resource in a larger local system. TDK CLI can scaffold that resource with tdk resource <name> --type backend --language rust. The scaffold uses axum 0.8 and tokio, serves GET /health, reads PORT, binds 0.0.0.0, and includes a unit test. The engine generates the image with a rust:1-slim-bookworm build stage, a cargo test stage, and a small debian:bookworm-slim production stage with a health check. Like the other compiled languages it has no live update, so Tilt rebuilds the image when a watched file changes. tdk up then starts the service with the rest of the stack, and tdk status --json reports whether it is ready.

The provider's docs describe Rust as an opt-in language. Omitting --language still produces the default Bun and Hono scaffold, so existing projects are unaffected.

title: Gaming Password Reset Email API 429 Rate Defense (An Incident Playbook)
description:
Route every password-recovery request through one account-scoped admission gate, then retry an accepted send only after Retry-After or exponential backoff says it is due. Short answer: a transactional email API fits this job when the application owns the reset token, resend cooldown, queue deduplication, and retry budget. A gaming support form should route the player to the account-recovery queue with the existing recovery-operation ID; it should never become a second, hidden send button.

The page I want is “eligible recovery operation exhausted its delivery budget.” A page that says only “429 count is high” confuses controlled backpressure with player harm, and it gives the responder no failed transition to inspect. Dashboards are especially good at smoothing away the oldest stuck job, which is often the one that matters.

This boundary is unavoidable. The email surface has no managed OTP API, so the game must issue and validate its own single-use reset token or code. There is no SMTP relay, either; the delivery adapter must use HTTP directly. Those are reasonable constraints if they are explicit before an incident rather than discovered during one.

How should a password reset email API handle 429 rate limits?

A cooldown and a retry policy regulate different actors. The cooldown limits new intent from a player, a support agent, or an automated contact-form workflow. The retry queue controls attempts for intent that the application already accepted. Combining them creates a nasty failure mode: changing the user-facing cooldown during an incident also changes transport pressure, or a transport retry accidentally generates a fresh reset token.

Imagine one player clicking resend four times, opening the account-access form, and asking an agent to resend while the first request is waiting. Six entry points must converge on one logical operation. Store a non-secret operation ID, account ID, token expiry, cooldown deadline, attempt count, and next-attempt time. Do not put the email address, token, or reset URL in routine logs.

Use a small state machine: admitted, queued, attempting, deferred, accepted, and exhausted. The contact-form router can inspect that state. accepted routes to ordinary account-recovery support, deferred keeps the case attached to the same operation, and exhausted raises the priority because delivery has actually failed its policy.

No second send.

That is the control loop.

The admission transaction should atomically create an operation only when the account's cooldown has elapsed. A repeated request returns the same neutral UI response and does not enqueue work. Keep the reset token single-use and independently expiring; an unknown network outcome is not evidence that a new token is needed.

Turn 429 into a scheduled state transition

Retry-After can be delay-seconds or an HTTP date. Parse both forms, use exponential backoff when it is absent or invalid, cap attempts, and persist the next attempt rather than sleeping inside an HTTP handler. A 429 is scheduling information. Most other 4xx responses are correction work, not retry work.

The Go code below isolates the decision that a durable worker needs. It deliberately accepts a SendFunc instead of inventing an email payload schema. The production adapter must call the provider's documented send operation with an explicit HTTP method, bearer credentials from an environment variable, a stable idempotency key, and full status checking. The policy values here are application examples, not provider limits.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand/v2"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Result struct {
    Status int
    Header http.Header
}

type SendFunc func(context.Context, string) (Result, error)

type Decision struct {
    RetryAt time.Time
    Done    bool
}

func infraiSender(client *http.Client, baseURL, key string, body []byte) SendFunc {
    return func(ctx context.Context, operationID string) (Result, error) {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/")+"/email/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return Result{}, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", operationID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return Result{}, err
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        if readErr != nil {
            return Result{Status: resp.StatusCode, Header: resp.Header}, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return Result{Status: resp.StatusCode, Header: resp.Header},
                fmt.Errorf("send status=%d body=%q", resp.StatusCode, responseBody)
        }
        return Result{Status: resp.StatusCode, Header: resp.Header}, nil
    }
}

func retryAfter(value string, now time.Time) (time.Duration, bool) {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second, true
    }
    when, err := http.ParseTime(value)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, false
    }
    if when.Before(now) {
        return 0, true
    }
    return when.Sub(now), true
}

func attempt(ctx context.Context, operationID string, attemptNumber int, send SendFunc, now time.Time) (Decision, error) {
    result, err := send(ctx, operationID)
    if err == nil && result.Status >= 200 && result.Status < 300 {
        return Decision{Done: true}, nil
    }
    if result.Status != 0 && result.Status != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("permanent send failure: status=%d: %w", result.Status, err)
    }
    if attemptNumber >= 4 {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("delivery budget exhausted: %w", err)
    }

    base := 500 * time.Millisecond * time.Duration(1<<attemptNumber)
    wait := base + time.Duration(rand.Int64N(int64(base/4)+1))
    if result.Status == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        if advised, ok := retryAfter(result.Header.Get("Retry-After"), now); ok {
            wait = advised
        }
    }
    return Decision{RetryAt: now.Add(wait)}, nil
}

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("EMAIL_REQUEST_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || len(body) == 0 {
        panic("set INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and EMAIL_REQUEST_JSON")
    }
    send := infraiSender(&http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, baseURL, key, body)
    decision, err := attempt(context.Background(), "reset-01JAZ8YF4Q", 0, send, time.Now())
    if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("done=%t retry_at=%s\n", decision.Done, decision.RetryAt.Format(time.RFC3339))
}

The stable operationID must survive every attempt and become the idempotency identity used by the transport adapter. That matters when the provider accepts a request but the connection fails before the application receives the response. Queue deduplication cannot resolve that ambiguity by itself. Infrai, for example, specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window; the application retry horizon must stay within the deduplication guarantee it relies on.

Do not retry in a tight loop. Four attempts and the 500-millisecond base in the example are starting policy choices that need testing against token lifetime, queue delay, and the provider contract. A durable worker should record RetryAt, release the job, and let other accounts progress.

Compare the incident boundary before choosing a sender

Provider selection should start with the page that fires and the evidence available after it fires. SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Amazon SES, and Infrai can all sit behind an application-owned recovery state machine, but they expose different operational boundaries.

Option Boundary worth testing Practical fit
SendGrid API rate-limit behavior plus Event Webhook handling Teams already operating SendGrid's event and suppression workflow
Mailgun HTTP sending, domain configuration, and event retrieval Teams willing to make region and domain setup part of the runbook
Postmark Transactional message streams and bounce processing Workloads centered on explicitly transactional mail
Amazon SES Sending quotas, throttling, and AWS identity controls Services whose incident access and governance already live in AWS
Infrai Direct HTTP sending with email event state retrieved by polling Teams that value one key across a broad backend surface and can tolerate pull-based observation

The relevant Infrai advantage is breadth behind a consistent surface: its live discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the public discovery surface requires no key; every documented capability also ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That lets an incident responder inspect the current request and response schemas without production credentials instead of trusting an old runbook at 3 a.m. Adding a later backend capability is another HTTP integration under the same contract. Infrai uses one plain REST API over pure HTTP, requires no SDK installation, and can be called from any language or runtime with an HTTP client; for this Go worker, that reduces dependency and credential work when the recovery service also gains another backend function. It does not make email delivery provider-independent, and it does not erase the application's cooldown or token responsibilities.

The explicit limitation is more important than the route count. Email delivery and bounce events have no push webhook and must be polled, so Infrai is not suitable when an immediate bounce must trigger another channel; SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark should be evaluated for their documented event-webhook paths instead. Email also has no hosted OTP flow, and the pending Tencent email vendor cannot support a domestic-compliance claim. This is a real trade-off. If push delivery events, SMTP relay, or that compliance evidence is a hard requirement, choose a provider whose documented boundary supplies it.

Polling loses immediacy.

This comparison is intentionally not about the lowest unit price. Rate-limit recovery depends on admission control, observable state, and safe replay; a cheap request that causes two reset emails is still an operational defect.

Verify the page, not merely the happy path

Run the test with one eligible request, four clicks inside the cooldown, a simultaneous contact-form submission, and an agent action. Confirm that all of them resolve to one operation and one reset token. Then inject a network timeout after an ambiguous send, an ordinary 429, each legal form of Retry-After, an invalid Retry-After, a permanent 4xx, and an exhausted retry budget.

The assertions should be blunt:

  1. Cooldown rejection creates no queue job.
  2. Every retry preserves the operation ID and token.
  3. A permanent response does not enter the retry queue.
  4. The worker schedules a future attempt instead of blocking a request handler.
  5. Support sees delivery unknown while observation is pending, not a fabricated failure or success.

Polling needs its own load test. Store provider acceptance separately from observed delivery, choose the polling interval from the support queue's tolerance for stale state, and never interpret a missing event as permission to send again. Pull-only observation also means real-time fallback orchestration is constrained; record that as a design boundary, not a surprise in the postmortem.

Now test the alert. Can the responder find the oldest eligible operation, its last status, next attempt, and remaining budget without averaging across every player? Can they distinguish cooldown rejection from provider deferral? If the answer is no, the dashboard may look calm while account recovery is stuck.

Page on exhausted recovery operations or dangerous queue age, not healthy throttling. A rise in 429 responses is useful context, but it should be a ticket or warning while the queue is making bounded progress. The postmortem should name the failed transition: duplicate admission, ignored Retry-After, unsafe replay, late polling, or an alert that measured the provider instead of the player.

Roll back while preserving recovery state

Pause new delivery jobs first, but keep cooldown records, operation IDs, tokens, and queued work. Drain or quarantine by operation ID. Clearing cooldown storage reopens the floodgate; generating replacement tokens creates a synchronized wave of mail and invalidates links players may already be opening.

Switching providers is not a string substitution. Map the replacement's idempotency behavior, accepted response, rate-limit headers, and event model before replaying ambiguous operations. Resume a small partition, watch queue age and exhaustion, then widen. The rollback is complete when existing operations have a known owner and new account-recovery forms route correctly, not when the aggregate error chart turns green.

Keep the final decision simple: use a direct transactional email API for password recovery when the application can own admission, tokens, retries, and delayed delivery observation. Select a webhook-capable provider when immediate event-driven fallback is part of the promise. Either way, the support queue should receive the state of one recovery operation, because the player asked to regain an account, not to benchmark your email vendor.

References

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, Retry-After
  • Twilio SendGrid: Event Webhook reference
  • Mailgun: Events API
  • Postmark: Webhooks overview
  • Amazon SES: Managing sending quotas
  • RFC 8058: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers

title: What connects two returned products? Building ReturnTrace with FalkorDB
description:
When a product’s return rate rises, the first question is usually straightforward: what went wrong?
Answering it is harder.
A returns dashboard might show that two headphone models have unusually high return rates. But it may not explain whether those products share a manufacturing batch, a component supplier or a courier. Investigating those possibilities means moving between records and comparing groups that don’t always appear together.
That was the problem I chose for ReturnTrace, my project for the WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB hackathon.
I wanted to build something that went beyond summarizing a dashboard. The idea was to help a returns analyst follow the evidence, decide what deserves inspection and use the inspection outcome in the next investigation.
Starting with a question, not a chatbot
The question behind ReturnTrace is:
Which connection best explains this return pattern, and what should someone investigate next?
That gave the project a clear workflow:

  1. Select a product with elevated returns.
  2. Compare its batches, couriers and warehouses.
  3. Follow relevant connections to other products.
  4. Propose an inspection task.
  5. Record the inspection outcome.
  6. Include that evidence in future investigations. I used synthetic data with deliberately different scenarios. This let me check whether the application could distinguish a shared-component lead from a courier handling pattern and whether it could stop when the evidence was insufficient. That last case mattered. An investigation tool shouldn’t always produce a confident explanation just because the interface expects an answer. Why I used a graph The useful information in this problem sits between records. An order contains a unit. That unit belongs to a product and comes from a batch. The batch uses a component lot supplied by a supplier. Another batch, for another product, might use that same lot. ReturnTrace stores those relationships in FalkorDB. Its investigation tools execute Cypher queries to follow them. The main demo starts with Aura Pro. One batch has 32 returns from 80 orders, compared with eight returns from 160 orders elsewhere. That is a lead, but it isn’t enough to explain the cause. Following the batch’s component lot, DSP-X17, reaches another product: Lyra. Lyra also has elevated returns associated with that lot. The application then compares the pattern across courier groups rather than immediately blaming the shared component. The resulting inspection scope covers 160 orders, including 56 returns, across two products. Those numbers describe the connected group worth investigating. They do not mean that 160 units are defective, or that the component has been proven responsible. That distinction shaped much of the project. Counting returns wasn’t enough One of my biggest learnings was that a convincing-looking number can still be misleading. A batch with more returns may simply have more sales. Looking only at returned orders removes the denominator needed to understand the rate. The graph queries therefore include orders that were not returned. They also use distinct counts to avoid counting an order multiple times while traversing relationships. The same principle applies when connecting products. Sharing a component is common in manufacturing. ReturnTrace checks whether the connected products each show an elevated rate relative to their own comparison groups before strengthening the shared-component lead. The graph finds the connection. The comparisons help decide whether that connection deserves attention. The most useful part was what happened after the investigation Finding DSP-X17 made a good demonstration of graph traversal. But I didn’t want the workflow to end with a finding on a screen. ReturnTrace creates a reviewable inspection task. A person can approve it and record an outcome- confirmed, refuted or inconclusive. That outcome becomes evidence for later investigations. For the demo, I recorded a clearly labeled simulated inspection of 12 units, with zero reproducing the suspected failure. No physical inspection took place. When the product is investigated again, the return pattern remains. The application doesn’t rewrite the historical data. Instead, it recognizes that the inspection challenges the original lead and changes the recommendation to independent review. This became the clearest way to explain the project: New evidence should change a decision without changing the facts that led to the original suspicion. It also made memory more useful than simply saving previous answers. An inspection connected to a shared component can matter when investigating another product that uses it. Giving the model a limited role ReturnTrace uses Groq for language model assisted tool selection. The tools expose scoped graph queries through MCP. I kept the model’s role separate from the numerical calculations and decision rules. It can help select eligible follow-up checks, but it cannot skip the mandatory initial checks. Application code calculates the metrics and applies the evidence policy. This made the results easier to inspect. The interface exposes the tool run log, retrieved source records and relevant queries. I wanted someone reviewing a finding to be able to ask, “Where did this number come from?” and find an answer beyond a generated paragraph. What didn’t go smoothly Local setup took more effort than expected. I initially used Docker, but later ran into a Docker Desktop installation registration problem that prevented the engine from starting. I moved the working demo to FalkorDB Cloud That experience made me appreciate having a cloud option, but it also highlighted how much onboarding depends on clear connection details and useful error messages. Testing was another important part of the process. The project passed 24 automated tests, a real FalkorDB integration check and a four scenario synthetic evaluation Those checks helped verify the intended behavior. They are not evidence of real-world diagnostic accuracy. The dataset was designed for the demo, and a production system would need much broader validation. Building with AI assistance I used OpenAI Codex extensively for implementation, interface design, debugging, testing and documentation. My contribution included choosing and developing the returns-investigation use case, directing the workflow and visual revisions, configuring the services and practicing the demonstration. Working this way made technical understanding especially important. A functioning screen isn’t enough: I need to understand how the graph connects the records, why the comparisons use order denominators and why an inspection changes the recommendation. AI assistance helped build the project, but it didnt remove that responsibility. What I’d improve next The next step would be to test the workflow against a more realistic, permissioned dataset. I would also improve how inspection methods are captured. A small sample that fails to reproduce a problem doesn’t necessarily disprove it. Recording how units were selected, what conditions were tested and who reviewed the result would make the evidence more useful. Any claim about reduced investigation time or fewer returns would need measurement. For now, ReturnTrace demonstrates the workflow rather than claiming those outcomes. Building it taught me that a useful investigation agent needs more than a plausible answer. It needs connected evidence, visible reasoning steps, a human review point and a way to reconsider its recommendation when new information arrives. That is what I tried to build with ReturnTrace.

title: actix-web: When Throughput Is the Requirement
description:
actix-web has been one of Rust's most widely used HTTP frameworks for years, and it regularly appears near the top of community benchmarks of raw request throughput. That reputation is earned, but it is also easy to over-read. Throughput is one requirement among several, and the framework's design has trade-offs worth understanding before you commit to it.

Where its design comes from

actix-web grew out of the actix actor framework. Its core is built on an actor-style runtime, and its worker model runs one event loop per thread, with each worker handling many connections. The result is low per-request overhead and good scaling across cores.

For most services this detail is invisible. You write handlers, register routes, and the runtime decides how work is spread across threads. It becomes relevant when you need to reason about shared state, long blocking calls, or how the worker count interacts with your database connection pool.

What it does well

  • Throughput under load. For services that are CPU-bound on request handling, the framework adds little overhead on top of your code.
  • A mature extractor system. Typed extractors pull JSON bodies, path parameters, and query strings into your handler signatures, and they reject malformed input before your code runs.
  • Middleware and guards. Authentication, logging, and CORS are expressed as composable middleware, and route guards keep routing rules readable.
  • Stable and well documented. Its documentation and examples cover most common cases, which shortens the path from a new project to a working endpoint.

Where to be careful

  • Shared state needs thought. Per-worker state and shared state behave differently. Work that must see one consistent value across all workers needs an explicit shared structure, usually behind a lock or a channel.
  • Blocking work belongs off the request path. A blocking database driver or a CPU-heavy function inside a handler stalls the worker it runs on. Move that work to a blocking thread pool or a dedicated task.
  • The actor vocabulary can confuse newcomers. You do not have to use actors to use actix-web, but the documentation mentions them, and the terms can make the first week harder than it needs to be.

When it is the right choice

Pick actix-web when throughput per core is a stated requirement, when your team is comfortable with async Rust, and when you value a long track record. It is a sound default for APIs that serve many concurrent clients.

If your priority is developer ergonomics above raw speed, or your service is small and mostly I/O bound, a framework with a gentler learning curve may serve you better. Performance differences rarely decide a project; the database and the network usually do.

Testing and deployment

Build the router as a function, as you would with any Rust framework, so the same routes can be tested without binding a port. Use a test client to send requests through the app and assert on the response. Build a release binary in a multi-stage container image, and run the process as a non-root user.

Running it with other services

actix-web services follow the same rules as any other service in a system. They need a health route, a port read from the environment, a bind address that accepts traffic from outside the process, and timeouts on every outbound call.

TDK CLI scaffolds Rust backends with axum rather than actix-web. If you want to run an actix-web service inside a TDK stack, you can build it as a container and register it as a bring-your-own resource, which handles the routing and health check for you.

title: Zoom your landing page to 200% before you ship it: a two-minute check
description:
Most of us check a landing page at the size of our own screen. Plenty of visitors don't see it that way: they zoom in, use a larger default font, or browse on a small window. Here is a short check that catches the most common breakage.

The check

  1. Open the page in a desktop browser.
  2. Press Ctrl and + (Cmd and + on a Mac) until you reach 200%.
  3. Scroll the whole page, top to bottom.
  4. Zoom further, to 400%, and scroll again.

Two WCAG success criteria cover this:

  • 1.4.4 Resize Text: text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
  • 1.4.10 Reflow: content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without scrolling in two dimensions, at a width of 320 CSS pixels. W3C notes that this is the same as a 1280 pixel wide window at 400% zoom. Parts that need a two-dimensional layout, such as data tables, maps and diagrams, are an exception. A single column is a common way to meet it, but the requirement is the lack of sideways scrolling and of lost content, not a specific layout.

What usually breaks

  • Fixed-height hero sections. If the hero has height: 600px, big text spills over the next section. Use min-height instead.
  • Text that gets clipped. Buttons or cards with a fixed width and overflow: hidden cut off labels. Let them grow.
  • A sticky header that eats the screen. At 200%, a tall fixed header can cover half the viewport. Check that you can still reach the content under it.
  • Sideways scrolling. Usually one wide element, like a pricing table or a code block, pushes the page past the viewport. Wrap it in its own scroll area.
  • Font sizes in px. If someone sets a larger default font in their browser, px text ignores it. Using rem for body text respects it.

A quick way to find the culprit

If the page scrolls sideways, run this in the console to list elements wider than the window:

[...document.querySelectorAll('*')].filter(
  (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().right > document.documentElement.clientWidth
);

The first few results are normally the cause.

One fix worth making today

Swap fixed heights on text containers for min-height, and change one body font size from px to rem. Both are small edits and both help at any zoom level.

What's the first thing that broke when you zoomed one of your own pages?
