title: Frontend Testing: Confidence Without Brittleness
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Test behavior, not implementation, and your suite stops breaking on every refactor. Follow the testing trophy to put effort where it pays, write component tests that survive change, and reserve end-to-end for critical flows.

Contents

  • The suite that broke on every refactor
  • The one principle that fixes most of it
  • The testing trophy: where effort should go
  • Choosing the right layer for each test
  • A component test that survives refactors
  • Behavior over implementation, in practice
  • End-to-end: the critical-flow crown
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The suite that broke on every refactor

Here is a story you have probably lived. Your team has 600 frontend tests and a green checkmark on every pull request. Then one day you rename a prop from onSubmit to onConfirm and clean up some internal state, pure refactor, zero behavior change. Forty tests go red. They were asserting that a useState hook held a certain value, that a child got a specific prop, that a function was called with exact arguments. None of those things matter to a user. You spend the afternoon updating tests to match the new internals.

The cruel twist: a week earlier, that same 600-test suite shipped a checkout button that did nothing when clicked. The handler was wired to the wrong element. Every test passed. The suite was loud about things that did not matter and silent about the one thing that did.

That is the central tension of frontend testing. Tests coupled to how a component is built break constantly and protect nothing. Tests coupled to what the user experiences survive refactors and catch the bugs that reach production. This article is about deliberately writing the second kind.

📌 Who this is for: Frontend engineers who write tests but feel they are paying a tax without getting safety in return. You know the tools (Jest, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright) but want a model for what to test, at which layer, and what to leave alone. Comfort with React and TypeScript is assumed; the principles apply to any component framework.

The one principle that fixes most of it

Test what the user does, not how the component is built. The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you.

The Testing Library philosophy, paraphrased

Every decision downstream, which queries to use, what to mock, where to draw the line, falls out of this one idea. A user does not know your component uses a reducer. They click a button labeled "Add to cart" and expect the cart count to go up. So your test should find the button by its label, click it, and assert the count went up. If you can swap the reducer for a signal and the test still passes, the test was measuring the right thing.

In the real world In tech
Test-driving the car: turn the key, it starts; press the brake, it stops Behavior test: render the UI, click the button, assert what the user now sees
Opening the hood to check the exact spark-plug part number Implementation test: assert a specific hook value or internal prop name
A new model with a redesigned engine still passes the test-drive A refactored component still passes the behavior test
The part-number check fails the moment the supplier changes, even if the car drives fine The internals test fails on every refactor, even when nothing user-visible broke

Two ways to verify a car works, one survives every redesign, one breaks on a new model year.

The testing trophy: where effort should go

The old advice was a pyramid: a wide base of unit tests, fewer integration tests, a thin cap of end-to-end. For frontends, that shape underinvests in the layer where most user value, and most bugs, actually lives: components wired together. The modern shape is the testing trophy: a sliver of static checks, a modest band of pure-unit tests, a fat middle of component/integration tests, and a focused crown of end-to-end.

The testing trophy, width hints at relative volume. Cheap static checks at the base, a fat component layer in the middle, a focused E2E crown on top.

Read the trophy top to bottom as a cost gradient. Static analysis is nearly free and runs as you type, a typo or a wrong prop type is caught before a test ever executes. Unit tests cover logic with no DOM: a currency formatter, a date helper, a reducer. Component tests render real UI in a fake DOM (jsdom) and interact with it, this is where you spend most of your effort because it most resembles real use while staying fast. End-to-end drives a real browser through a whole flow; slow and occasionally flaky, so reserve it for the handful of journeys that must never break.

  1. Let the type checker and linter run first: tsc --noEmit and ESLint catch a whole class of bugs, undefined props, unhandled null, wrong shapes, with zero test code. Treat them as the base of the trophy and run them in CI on every push.
  2. Unit-test the logic with no UI: Extract pure functions (formatting, validation, calculations) and test them directly. Fast, deterministic, no rendering. If a piece of logic is hard to unit-test, that is a hint it should be extracted from the component.
  3. Component-test the user-facing behavior: Render the component, query by what the user sees (role, label, text), interact, and assert the resulting DOM. This is your highest-leverage layer, aim most of your test count here.
  4. End-to-end the critical flows only: Pick the 5-10 journeys that, if broken, cost real money or trust, sign-in, checkout, the core create-action. Run them in a real browser with Playwright or Cypress against a deployed-like build.

Choosing the right layer for each test

When you are unsure where a test belongs, match the thing you are protecting against the layer that catches it most cheaply. Push tests down the trophy whenever a cheaper layer can catch the same bug, but never so far down that you stop testing real behavior.

Test type What it catches Cost / speed When to reach for it
Static (TS, lint) Type errors, undefined props, dead code, unsafe access Free, instant Always on, the default safety net for every change
Unit Wrong logic in pure functions, edge cases in helpers and reducers Very cheap, milliseconds Non-trivial logic you can isolate from the DOM
Component Broken rendering, wiring, conditional UI, accessibility of interactions Cheap, fast (jsdom) The default for anything a user sees or clicks, most of your suite
End-to-end Whole-flow breakage: routing, real network, auth, cross-page state Expensive, seconds, occasionally flaky A small set of business-critical journeys only

Pick the cheapest layer that still catches the bug you care about.

A component test that survives refactors

Here is a component test the right way: it renders the real component, finds elements the way a user (or a screen reader) would, by role and text, never by class name or test-id-on-everything, interacts, and asserts the visible outcome. Notice there is not a single reference to internal state, hook names, or child props.

AddToCart.test.tsx

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { AddToCart } from "./AddToCart";

test("adds an item and reflects it in the cart count", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<AddToCart productName="Wireless Mouse" price={29} />);

  // Query the way a user perceives the UI: by role + accessible name.
  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /add to cart/i });
  expect(screen.getByText(/cart: 0 items/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

  await user.click(button);

  // Assert the user-visible outcome, not internal state.
  expect(screen.getByText(/cart: 1 item/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
  expect(
    screen.getByRole("status", { name: /added wireless mouse/i })
  ).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test("disables the button while a request is in flight", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<AddToCart productName="Wireless Mouse" price={29} />);

  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /add to cart/i });
  await user.click(button);

  // The user sees a disabled, busy button, we never inspect a loading flag.
  expect(button).toBeDisabled();
});

Two things make this test durable. First, queries by role and accessible name mean the test only passes if the markup is actually accessible, a free accessibility check baked into every test. Second, userEvent simulates real interaction (focus, key events, the works) rather than firing a synthetic click, so you exercise the same path a person would. Rename the internal state, swap the styling, move logic into a custom hook, as long as the button still says "Add to cart" and the count still updates, the test stays green.

💡 Query priority: Reach for queries in this order: getByRole (with a name), then getByLabelText / getByText, then getByPlaceholderText. Use getByTestId only as a last resort for elements with no accessible handle. If you cannot find an element by role or text, that is often a sign the markup itself is not accessible.

Behavior over implementation, in practice

The rule "test behavior, not implementation" sounds obvious until you are mid-test and tempted to peek at internals. A quick litmus test: would this assertion break if I refactored the component without changing what the user sees or does? If yes, you are testing implementation. Asserting a useState value, that a specific function was called, or that a child received a named prop, all break on refactor and protect nothing.

Implementation tests also lie in the dangerous direction. A test that checks setLoading(true) was called will pass even if the spinner never actually renders because of a CSS bug or a missing conditional. A behavior test that asserts the spinner is visible catches that. Always assert the outcome the user perceives, not the mechanism you hope produces it.

Mocking the network, at the boundary, not inside

Components fetch data, and tests should not hit a real server. The brittle approach is to mock your fetch wrapper or stub a hook's return value, that couples the test to your data-fetching internals. The durable approach is to intercept at the network boundary with a tool like MSW (Mock Service Worker). You declare what the endpoint returns; your component does its real fetching, parsing, and error handling against that fake server. Swap fetch for axios for React Query and the test does not care.

ProductList.test.tsx

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { ProductList } from "./ProductList";

const server = setupServer(
  http.get("/api/products", () =>
    HttpResponse.json([{ id: "1", name: "Wireless Mouse", price: 29 }])
  )
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test("renders products from the API", async () => {
  render(<ProductList />);
  // The component does its real fetch; we wait for the user-visible result.
  expect(await screen.findByText("Wireless Mouse")).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test("shows an error state when the API fails", async () => {
  // Override just this test's response to exercise the error path.
  server.use(
    http.get("/api/products", () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 }))
  );
  render(<ProductList />);
  expect(
    await screen.findByText(/couldn't load products/i)
  ).toBeInTheDocument();
});

The same MSW handlers can back your component tests and your Playwright end-to-end runs, and even power local development with a mock backend. One source of fake truth, reused everywhere, far better than a thicket of per-test jest.mock calls.

End-to-end: the critical-flow crown

Component tests run in jsdom, a simulated DOM with no real layout, no real browser quirks, no real navigation. For the journeys that absolutely cannot break, you want a real browser. Playwright (and Cypress) drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through a complete flow: load the page, fill the form, click through, assert what renders. It catches things component tests structurally cannot, broken routing, a real network round-trip, auth redirects, a button hidden behind a z-index bug.

checkout.spec.ts

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("a user can complete checkout", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/products");

  // Same philosophy as component tests: locate by role and text.
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /add to cart/i }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole("link", { name: /view cart/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /checkout/i }).click();

  await page.getByLabel(/card number/i).fill("4242 4242 4242 4242");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /pay now/i }).click();

  // Assert the user-visible success outcome.
  await expect(
    page.getByRole("heading", { name: /order confirmed/i })
  ).toBeVisible();
});

Notice the queries look almost identical to the component test, by role and accessible name. That consistency is the payoff of the behavior-first philosophy: the same mental model scales from a single component up to a full browser flow. Keep this layer small. A handful of E2E tests for your money-making journeys gives enormous confidence; a hundred of them gives you a slow, flaky pipeline nobody trusts.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Testing implementation details. Asserting hook values, internal state, or that a function was called with exact args. These break on every refactor and pass even when the UI is visibly broken. Assert what the user sees instead.
  2. Snapshot overuse. A wall of auto-generated snapshots becomes noise: people update them blindly when they go red, so they catch nothing and just nag. Reserve snapshots for small, stable, intentional outputs, and review every diff.
  3. No end-to-end for critical flows. Component tests in jsdom cannot catch broken routing, real auth, or a button buried under an overlay. If sign-in or checkout breaking would be a disaster, it needs at least one real-browser test.
  4. Over-mocking. Mock the network boundary, not your own modules. When you stub the very code under test (the fetch wrapper, the hook, the child component), you are testing your mocks, not your app, green tests, broken product.
  5. Querying by class or deep test-ids. container.querySelector('.btn-primary') couples tests to styling and bypasses accessibility. Prefer role and text; the test doubles as an a11y check.
  6. Chasing 100% coverage. Coverage measures lines executed, not behavior verified. Test the paths that matter, error states, edge cases, the happy path, and let trivial getters go untested.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • Test what the user does, not how the component is built, that one rule prevents most brittleness.
  • Follow the testing trophy: a little static, some unit, a fat layer of component tests, a focused crown of E2E.
  • Static checks (TypeScript, ESLint) are the cheapest layer, let them catch a whole class of bugs for free.
  • Query by role, label, and text; touch internals never. Accessible markup falls out for free.
  • Mock at the network boundary (MSW), not inside your own modules, reuse the handlers across unit, component, and E2E.
  • Reserve end-to-end for the few money-making journeys; keep that layer small to keep it trustworthy.
  • A green suite that breaks on refactors and misses real bugs is worse than fewer, behavior-focused tests.

Where to go next

Testing rides on top of how your components are structured and how your state flows. Well-factored components with clear inputs and accessible markup are dramatically easier to test, so the testing payoff is also an architecture payoff.

  • Component Architecture & Design Systems, composable, accessible components are the ones that test cleanly by role and text.
  • State Management in Frontend Apps, predictable state flow is what makes behavior assertions stable across refactors.
  • See how this fits the broader role on the Frontend Engineer path.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: AZ-500 practice, week 1: 4 questions
description:
Four exam-style questions I wrote this week (PIM, Key Vault, storage, NSG), answers hidden, explanations in plain words.

How to use these: read the question, pick your answer before you open Answer, and write it down (or in the comments). Then check the "why not the others" part even if you got it right: that is where the exam traps live. Every scenario, name and number is made up by me; only the question formats follow the real exam.

Table of contents

  • Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval
  • Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret
  • Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later
  • Q004: NSG rules with application security groups
  • Cheat sheet
  • Coming next

Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval

Identity and access · Single choice · standalone page

Your helpdesk lead, Mai, sometimes needs the User Administrator role to fix accounts. Your security team says: "Fine, but only when she asks for it, for at most 4 hours, and someone has to say yes first."

What should you configure?

  • A. A permanent active assignment of User Administrator, plus a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA
  • B. A Privileged Identity Management (PIM) eligible assignment of User Administrator, with role settings: activation maximum duration 4 hours and require approval to activate
  • C. An access review on the User Administrator role that runs every 4 hours
  • D. An administrative unit that contains Mai's account

Answer

B. "Eligible" means Mai does not hold the role until she activates it. In the PIM role settings, the activation maximum duration can be anything from 1 to 24 hours (so 4 is fine), and "Require approval to activate" makes at least one approver say yes first.

Why not the others:

  • A gives her the role 24/7. MFA proves it is really Mai, it does not make the role go away after 4 hours.
  • C checks who has access, after the fact. An access review every 4 hours would mostly annoy the reviewers.
  • D limits which users she can manage, not when she can manage them.

Source: Configure Microsoft Entra role settings in Privileged Identity Management

Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret

Identity and access · Yes/No series ("Does this meet the goal?") · standalone page

Yes/No series: same scenario, a different solution each time. Some scenarios have several right solutions, some have none.

An app on the Azure VM vm-lab-01 must read a database password stored in the key vault kv-lab-01. The vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Goal: no password, key or certificate is stored in the app code or on the VM.

Solution: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on vm-lab-01 and assign it the Key Vault Secrets User role on kv-lab-01.

Does this meet the goal?

  • A. Yes
  • B. No

Answer

A. Yes. The VM gets its own identity in Microsoft Entra ID, so the app asks Azure for a token instead of keeping a secret in a config file. Key Vault Secrets User can read secret contents, and it works here because the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model.

Other solutions you might see in the same series:

  • "Store a client secret for an app registration in appsettings.json" → No. That is a secret sitting on the VM, the exact thing the goal forbids.
  • "Assign the managed identity Key Vault Reader" → No. Reader sees the vault and the names of its secrets (metadata), but it cannot read the secret values. Close, but no password for you.

Source: Provide access to Key Vault keys, certificates, and secrets with Azure role-based access control

Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later

Compute, storage and databases · Hot area · standalone page

Someone set one container in the storage account stlabdata01 to "Container (anonymous read access)". Your boss wants no anonymous reads in any container of this account, now and later, even if someone changes a container setting again next week.

Pick the right value for each line:

Where Setting Your choice
Storage account stlabdata01 › Settings › Configuration Allow Blob anonymous access ▢ Enabled ▢ Disabled
Each container Anonymous access level ▢ Must be changed to Private one by one ▢ Nothing more to do

Answer

Disabled / Nothing more to do. The account setting (property AllowBlobPublicAccess) overrides the container settings: once it is off, containers that were set to anonymous access are no longer reachable anonymously. Flipping containers to Private one by one is nice tidying, but it is not what stops the leak, and the next person can flip a container right back.

Why not the other values: Enabled leaves every container in charge of its own fate. Changing containers one by one only fixes today, not "later".

Bonus: to do this for every storage account at once, use the built-in Azure Policy "Storage account public access should be disallowed" (Audit or Deny). One gotcha: a static website's $web container stays public no matter what, because that is its job.

Sources: Remediate anonymous read access to blob data · Azure Policy built-in definitions for Azure Storage

Q004: NSG rules with application security groups

Networking · Drag and drop · standalone page

The virtual network vnet-shop has one subnet with the network security group nsg-shop attached. The VMs web01 and web02 are in the application security group asg-web. The VMs api01 and api02 are in asg-api. Everything is in the same virtual network.

You need to meet these rules:

  1. People on the internet can reach the web VMs on HTTPS.
  2. Only the web VMs can reach the API VMs, on TCP 8443.
  3. Nothing else inside the virtual network can reach the API VMs. (Yes, that includes the test VM someone "temporarily" created in March.)

Drag the right value into each numbered box. Each value can be used once, more than once, or not at all.

Values: Internet · VirtualNetwork · AzureLoadBalancer · asg-web · asg-api · 443 · 8443 · 3389

Inbound rules on nsg-shop:

Priority Name Source Destination Port Action
100 allow-https-web [1] [2] 443 Allow
200 allow-web-to-api [3] [4] [5] Allow
300 deny-vnet-to-api [6] asg-api Any Deny

Answer

[1] Internet · [2] asg-web · [3] asg-web · [4] asg-api · [5] 8443 · [6] VirtualNetwork

Application security groups let you write rules against "the web VMs" instead of a list of IP addresses, and they work as both source and destination. Rule 300 is the one people forget: the default rule AllowVNetInBound (priority 65000) lets every machine in the virtual network talk to every other one. You cannot delete default rules, but a custom rule with a lower number wins. Rules are checked from the lowest number up and stop at the first match, so the web VMs still get in through rule 200 before rule 300 says no to everyone else.

Why not the other values:

  • AzureLoadBalancer in [6] would block the load balancer health probes, not your test VM. Your API would go "unhealthy" and you would get a very confusing afternoon.
  • VirtualNetwork in [3] would let any VM in the network call the API, which breaks rule 2.
  • 443 in [5] or 3389 anywhere: wrong port. Nobody asked for RDP from anywhere.

Gotcha: all network interfaces in one application security group must be in the same virtual network, and when a rule uses an ASG as both source and destination, both groups must be in that same virtual network.

Sources: Application security groups · Network security groups overview

Cheat sheet

The same four ideas in plain words, for the manager who asks "so what?". Share it with them.

Coming next

Monday and Tuesday bring a SAS question for storage accounts with key access switched off, and a just-in-time RDP question for Defender for Cloud. All questions live in the AZ-500 practice folder.

Got one wrong? Good. That is one fewer surprise in the exam room. Drop your answers in the comments.

title: Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis
description:
title: "Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-11T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [nodejs, redis, backend, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Producers And Consumers: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Delayed And Recurring Jobs: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency Control: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Exponential Backoff Retries: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Producers and consumers, delayed and recurring jobs, concurrency control, exponential backoff retries, and monitoring queue health with Arena."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: What jstack Misses When Your Java Service Uses Virtual Threads
description:
Take a Spring Boot service with virtual threads enabled, a HikariCP pool of 10 connections, and roughly 5,000 requests in flight. Latency is climbing. You grab a thread dump and find 43 platform threads, most of the scheduler workers waiting in ForkJoinPool.awaitWork, and very little CPU activity.

If you used jstack, the requests you're looking for may never have made it into the file. On JDK 21 through 25, the traditional dump doesn't list virtual threads. You can spend quite a while reading the scheduler's stacks without seeing the requests waiting for your database.

I'll use that connection-pool scenario throughout this article. The numbers and dump excerpts are illustrative. I run ThreadMine, and its support for these formats needs some explanation too; I'll get to that after the commands.

The carrier can be idle while the request waits

jstack and jcmd <pid> Thread.print show platform threads. That includes the carriers, the scheduler workers on which virtual threads run. When a virtual thread unmounts to wait for I/O or another resource, its carrier is free to run something else.

If most requests are waiting, there may be very little for the carriers to do. Low CPU and idle workers are entirely compatible with a large backlog.

The scheduler uses a ForkJoinPool, with default parallelism based on the processors available to the JVM. You can change it with jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, but I'd leave that alone until I knew what the requests were waiting for. More workers won't help requests queued behind the same ten database connections.

A carrier with a virtual thread mounted can include this line in the traditional dump:

Carrying virtual thread #212

From JDK 24 on, the dump also prints that virtual thread's own stack right below the carrier, under a Mounted virtual thread #212 line. Either way it's useful for identifying the mounted thread. For the thousands of unmounted threads, you need another dump.

Use Thread.dump_to_file

This command has been available since JDK 21:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/dump.txt

The JVM writes the file, so /tmp/dump.txt is a path in the target process's filesystem. This matters in containers. The process also needs permission to write there; the capture guide covers those details.

Plain text is the default. For JSON:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json

The documented format names are plain and json. Existing files aren't overwritten unless you pass -overwrite. Use a new filename for each capture so there's something to compare later.

The output also depends on the JDK version. JDK 21 through 24 give you the thread ID, name, a virtual marker, and the stack. JDK 25 adds state, timestamps, and lock information. A shortened JDK 25 entry might look like this:

#412 "" virtual WAITING 2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z
    at java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:582)
    ...
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:179)
    at com.example.orders.OrderRepository.load(OrderRepository.java:48)
    ...

There's the request, waiting to acquire a connection. The empty name is common for virtual threads; an application can assign a name if it needs one.

For our example, suppose the file contains 5,004 virtual threads and 4,962 occurrences of HikariPool.getConnection. You can check those counts without loading the dump into anything:

grep -cE '^#[0-9]+ ".*" virtual' dump.txt
grep -c 'HikariPool.getConnection' dump.txt

The second command counts matching lines. Open a few of the stacks to check the call path, especially if the method occurs more than once per thread.

At this point, I'd look at connection hold time. If each request holds a connection for 18 ms, ten connections would take roughly nine seconds to clear a backlog of 5,000 requests, with no new arrivals. That gives us a plausible scale for the delay. It doesn't calculate p99, but it tells us where to investigate.

Check slow queries and transaction scope before changing the pool size. A connection held during an unrelated HTTP call, for example, reduces the capacity available to every request behind it. The database may support more concurrency, or it may already be struggling. The dump helps locate the queue; pool and database metrics help explain it.

Virtual threads make waiting cheaper. The database still has to do the work.

What I'd compare in the next dump

For a slowdown that lasts minutes, take another capture after about 30 seconds. Look at the large stack groups and compare thread IDs within them.

If the same requests are still waiting in the same place, investigate why they aren't progressing. If the IDs have changed but the group stays large, requests may be completing while new ones refill the queue. Those situations can look almost identical if you only compare totals.

I wouldn't read much into 5,004 threads becoming 5,011. I'd be more interested in whether connection acquisition time is rising and whether throughput has stopped keeping up with arrivals. I've been fooled by a single dump more than once, and the second one has always been cheap.

The state labels need the same treatment. WAITING is expected in a service doing I/O, and it doesn't tell you by itself whether a virtual thread released its carrier. RUNNABLE doesn't establish CPU saturation either. Start with the stack and the resource involved, then check the metrics that could explain the wait.

JSON helps when there are several executors

For a single pile of requests waiting on HikariCP, the text file is enough to get started. JSON becomes useful when you need to separate work created by different executors or structured-concurrency scopes. It groups threads into containers.

On JDK 25, an entry for a mounted virtual thread can also include its carrier's ID. Here's a reduced container with one thread:

{
  "container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@3f1e7a2c",
  "parent": "<root>",
  "owner": null,
  "threads": [
    {
      "tid": "412",
      "time": "2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z",
      "virtual": true,
      "name": "",
      "state": "RUNNABLE",
      "stack": ["..."],
      "carrier": "37"
    }
  ],
  "threadCount": "1"
}

Run these against the complete JDK 25 JSON file to count virtual-thread entries with a carrier and list the container sizes:

jq '[.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[] | select(.virtual == true and .carrier != null)] | length' dump.json
jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threadCount)\t\(.container)"' dump.json

The dump is collected while threads keep running. That carrier count therefore isn't a measurement of how many carriers were busy at one instant. The container breakdown is what I'd use first to find where the threads are accumulating.

Keep the JDK version with the file. Some fields used here aren't available in older releases. Also check for -Djdk.trackAllThreads=false, which can leave some virtual threads out of the dump.

Pinning depends on the JDK version

A request waiting for a connection and a virtual thread blocking its carrier call for different investigations. For the second case, look for VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread: it's the path where a virtual thread parks while retaining the carrier.

On JDK 21 through 23, this code can take that path when the HTTP call blocks:

synchronized (lock) {
    return httpClient.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
}

The relevant part of the stack can look like this:

#37 "" virtual
      java.base/jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(VirtualThread.java:675)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:593)
      ...
      com.example.price.PriceService.lookup(PriceService.java:32)

With JDK 24 and JEP 491, holding a monitor no longer causes this pinning. Native frames and class initialization can still be involved in other cases. Check the runtime version before recommending changes to synchronized code.

For pinning that comes and goes, I'd use JFR. The jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event has been enabled by default with a 20 ms threshold since JDK 21. A recording gives you frequency and duration, which a couple of dumps can easily miss. The old jdk.tracePinnedThreads option was removed in JDK 24.

Finding parkOnCarrierThread is useful evidence of that particular parking path. Its absence doesn't rule out every form of pinning. There's more on the version differences in the pinning reference.

A note on ThreadMine

ThreadMine reads the text file that Thread.dump_to_file writes, in both shapes it has had so far: the JDK 21 to 24 one, with no state in the header and no at on the frames, and the JDK 25 one, which has both. Virtual threads come through as virtual threads, empty names stay empty, and a thread sitting in parkOnCarrierThread is flagged as pinned. I'll be honest about how recent that is: until this week the parser silently dropped every #22 "" virtual line, and I only found out while checking this article against real dumps from JDK 21 through 25. The JSON form is still not accepted, so paste the text; the per-container counts are the one thing jq still does that the analyzer doesn't.

The change I'd make to a team's incident runbook is straightforward: when the service uses virtual threads, capture Thread.dump_to_file as well as the traditional dump. You want the request stacks available before anyone starts drawing conclusions from idle carriers.

Felipe Maschio is the founder of ThreadMine, a free JVM thread dump analyzer.

References

  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads
  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
  • JDK 25 jcmd command reference
  • JDK 25 release notes: thread dump lock information
  • Virtual threads in JDK 25

title: Node.js Export Authorization: Temporary User Downloads with Private Object Storage
description:
The operational constraint is simple: an export link is a bearer credential, so it must outlive neither the user's need nor your authorization decision. Short answer: generate exports on the server, keep the bucket private, authorize the export in your application, and mint a short-lived signed download URL only after the file is ready. Start with a five-minute policy, then measure how long real clients take to begin downloads.

That choice is different from putting a public URL in a job result. A signed URL limits exposure, but it does not identify the person using it. Anyone who obtains the link can use it until expiry. Your app still has to decide who may receive one.

Five minutes.

What should a Node.js SaaS flow check before signing an export?

Treat the database row as the authorization record. A request should carry an opaque export ID, not a bucket and key selected by the browser. The Node.js handler authenticates the session, checks tenant and user ownership, confirms status == "ready", and reads the object key stored with that record. Only then does it ask storage to sign a read. If generation is still running, return its job state; if it failed, return an application-level failure without exposing storage details.

This ordering prevents a confused-deputy bug in the design: a valid user cannot persuade your signer to bless another tenant's key. It also fits notebook-to-prod work. A worker writes to an exports/ prefix, commits the row as ready after the write completes, and the web process creates a fresh link on demand. I would not put that URL in a durable email, analytics event, or model trace, and I don't cache it in a shared CDN. The query string is the credential.

For a plain-HTTP provider such as Infrai, this signer can be called from a Node.js service without installing a storage SDK. One API contract works for any language that can send an HTTP request. The app remains the policy owner; the provider only creates the bounded read URL.

Here is a minimal Python version of that provider call. The same request shape is straightforward to issue from Node.js with fetch; I keep this example in Python because my eval harness runs beside the worker.

import os
import time
import requests


def presign_export(bucket: str, key: str, expires_seconds: int = 300) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    payload = {"op": "get", "expires_seconds": expires_seconds}

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
            json=payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        response.raise_for_status()
        body = response.json()
        return body["url"]
    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear")

Use the returned URL without adding the provider's Authorization header. Check the response body in your integration test and keep the bucket and key server-controlled. A presign operation is a read of policy state, so a retry does not create a second object; export creation itself should still use an application idempotency key.

How do expiration, lifecycle cleanup, and export size fit together?

Separate two clocks. URL expiry controls access to a ready object; lifecycle cleanup controls how long that object remains in storage. I usually test 60, 300, and 900 seconds as candidate link lifetimes, using the p95 time-to-first-byte and the slowest supported client as inputs. A mobile browser that suspends a tab changes the answer. Your mileage may vary.

My eval checks invariants before it checks a vendor: an unauthorized caller gets no URL, a non-ready export gets no URL, the caller cannot choose the key, and the issued TTL stays within policy. Then I replay representative CSV and PDF sizes and record download-start latency. For example, I run the same export through a fast desktop connection, a throttled mobile profile, and a backgrounded browser tab; I record when the link is minted, when the first byte arrives, whether the user retries after a transient 429, and whether the object is deleted on schedule. A five-minute URL that works for a 2 MB CSV may be too short for a 900 MB archive, while a one-hour URL leaves a much larger bearer window when a support ticket includes the full address. This is more useful than a synthetic “URL works” test because it makes the expiry decision observable.

Keep exports in a dedicated bucket or prefix so usage accounting and deletion rules are obvious. Lifecycle rules are a backstop, not a substitute for an application deletion deadline. The storage lifecycle minimum is one day, so it cannot enforce a 15-minute retention promise; delete sensitive artifacts from your worker or database-driven cleanup job as well. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup plan.

Which storage option fits a private export pipeline?

The providers below all support private-object patterns, but their operational trade-offs differ. I would choose based on the rest of the system, not on a link-lifetime number.

Option Good fit Trade-off to validate
Amazon S3 Deep IAM, lifecycle, and multipart tooling More configuration and SDK surface across services
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API with an edge-oriented deployment Check egress behavior and regional needs for your users
Google Cloud Storage Teams already standardized on Google IAM and buckets A separate cloud's identity and network controls add work
Infrai storage A mixed-language stack that wants one plain REST signer No public-read URLs, object versioning, object lock, or self-service CORS; vendor coverage is r2/s3/oss/cos rather than gcs/b2

Infrai is a reasonable fit when “no SDK to install” matters: a Python worker and a Node.js API can share an HTTP contract, with one key and billing surface for the platform's capabilities. It is not suitable for static website hosting, permanent public links, or a finance-grade immutable archive. There is no If-Match conditional write, cross-region automatic replication, or batch cross-cloud migration tool, so strict concurrency and disaster-recovery requirements belong in your database, queue, or an external storage design.

Browser-direct upload is also a poor default for this export workflow. Bucket CORS rules are not self-service here, and exports are normally produced server-side anyway. If your product later accepts large user uploads, compare a server proxy with S3 multipart upload rather than assuming a single browser PUT will scale.

A small launch checklist

Before shipping, I want an authorization test for every tenant boundary, a ready-state test, and a check that logs redact the complete query string. I also want a refresh path: an authorized user can request a new URL without regenerating the export. Track issuance count, expiry-before-start rate, object age, and cleanup lag; those metrics tell you whether five minutes is conservative or wasteful.

The catch is that a signed URL cannot revoke a copy already downloaded. For highly sensitive exports, shorten the TTL, add watermarking, or stream through an authenticated application endpoint. Stick with a provider that offers immutable retention and conditional writes when those are contractual requirements, even if its SDK is heavier.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.set_lifecycle
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/

title: S3 Lifecycle Rules, Step by Step: Move Old Data to Cheaper Storage Without Surprise Fees
description:
Most S3 buckets start the same way. Someone creates a bucket, an app writes files into it, and nobody looks at it again. Months later the bucket holds years of logs, old exports and copies of files nobody remembers. Every byte sits in the default storage class, S3 Standard, and every byte is billed at that rate.

S3 Lifecycle rules fix this. A lifecycle rule tells Amazon S3 to move objects to a cheaper storage class after a number of days, or to delete them when they are no longer needed. You write the rule once, and S3 applies it every day.

The catch is that cheaper classes come with conditions. Some charge for a minimum number of days. Some charge to read data back. Some charge per object moved. A careless rule can cost more than it saves. This guide from CloudSkill Consulting LLC walks through S3 lifecycle rules one step at a time, so you can lower storage cost without surprise fees.

Step 1: Learn the storage classes in plain words

A storage class is a price plan for an object. Each object in S3 has one. The data is the same; what changes is the price to store it, the price to read it, and how fast you can get it back.

Here are the classes this guide uses, in order from "used often" to "almost never used":

  • S3 Standard (STANDARD): the default. No minimum storage time and no retrieval fee. Best for data you read often.
  • S3 Standard-IA (STANDARD_IA): "IA" means infrequent access. Cheaper to store, but there is a fee each time you read data, a 30-day minimum storage charge, and a 128 KB minimum billable size (see the S3 pricing and storage-class pages linked in Sources).
  • S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (GLACIER_IR): for data read about once a quarter, still with millisecond access. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (GLACIER): archive storage. You must restore an object before you can read it, and that takes minutes to hours. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive (DEEP_ARCHIVE): the lowest-cost archive, with restores measured in hours. It has a 180-day minimum.

There is also S3 Intelligent-Tiering (INTELLIGENT_TIERING). It watches how each object is used and moves it between tiers for you, for a small monitoring fee per object. It has no retrieval fees. It is a good choice when you honestly don't know how often data is read.


Figure 1: Each step down is cheaper to store, but has a longer minimum stay and slower or paid reads.

Step 2: Find out what is in the bucket before you write a rule

Never write a lifecycle rule from memory. Look at the data first. Two questions matter:

  1. How big are the objects? Small objects behave differently. By default, S3 Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class. AWS explains why: you pay a transition request for each object, so for small objects the request cost can outweigh the savings.
  2. How often is each prefix read? A prefix is the start of an object key, like logs/ or exports/2025/. Logs written once and almost never read are good candidates. Product images that a website loads all day are not.

AWS gives you tools for this. S3 Storage Class Analysis watches access patterns on a bucket or prefix and helps you decide when to move data from Standard to Standard-IA. S3 Storage Lens shows storage use across buckets. Turn one of them on and give it time before you choose your day counts.

A good habit: write down each prefix, who owns it, how often it is read, and how long it must be kept. "How long it must be kept" is a business question, not a technical one. Ask the data owner.

Step 3: Understand the three rules that cause surprise fees

These three rules are where most lifecycle mistakes come from.

Rule A: minimum storage duration. Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum, Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval have 90 days, and Deep Archive has 180 days (minimum storage charges, per the S3 pricing and storage-class pages). If you delete, overwrite or move an object out before that time, you are charged for the rest of the minimum. A rule that moves logs to Glacier Flexible Retrieval and then deletes them 30 days later still pays for 90 days.

Rule B: small objects. Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill each object as at least 128 KB. Objects archived to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive also carry about 40 KB of extra metadata each: 8 KB billed at the Standard rate and 32 KB at the archive rate. Millions of tiny files can cost more after archiving than before.

Rule C: reads cost money and time. IA and Glacier classes charge per GB retrieved. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects are not readable until you restore them, and while restored you pay for both the archive copy and a temporary Standard copy.


Figure 2: Check every lifecycle rule against these three conditions before you turn it on.

Step 4: Write a first rule that is hard to get wrong

Start with one prefix that is clearly "write once, read rarely", such as application logs. Here is a full lifecycle configuration in the JSON format the AWS CLI expects. It has three rules.

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "logs-tier-then-expire",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 120, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 400 }
    },
    {
      "ID": "old-versions-cleanup",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {
        "NoncurrentDays": 30,
        "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3
      }
    },
    {
      "ID": "abort-stuck-uploads",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

Here is what each part does, in plain words:

  • logs-tier-then-expire applies only to keys starting with logs/. After 30 days the objects move to Standard-IA. After 120 days they move to Glacier Flexible Retrieval. After 400 days they expire. The gaps are chosen on purpose: 90 days in Standard-IA is more than its 30-day minimum, and 280 days in Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more than its 90-day minimum. No early-deletion charge applies. Since July 2026 you can move objects to Standard-IA from day 0. We wait 30 days because new logs are read most often in their first weeks.
  • old-versions-cleanup matters only if versioning is on. When you overwrite or delete an object in a versioned bucket, the old copy stays as a noncurrent version, and you keep paying for it. This rule permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent, but always keeps the 3 newest ones. Be sure that matches your recovery needs, because deleted versions can't be brought back.
  • abort-stuck-uploads cleans up multipart uploads that started but never finished. Their parts are stored and billed, yet they don't appear as normal objects. AWS notes that expiration rules don't remove incomplete multipart uploads; you need this separate action.

An empty Filter ({}) means "every object in the bucket".

S3 rounds lifecycle timing to the next midnight UTC. An object created at 10:30 AM UTC with a 3-day rule becomes eligible at midnight UTC four days later. Transitions to Glacier also run in the background, so the physical move can lag behind the date. You are still billed at the destination rate from the date the rule is met.


Figure 3 (example rule): One object's life under the logs/ rule, with each stay longer than that class's minimum.

Step 5: Apply it safely with the AWS CLI

First, save any rules that already exist. This step matters. The AWS CLI documentation says put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration replaces the whole existing configuration. Any rule you leave out of your file is gone.

# 1. Back up the current configuration (an error here usually means none exists yet)
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data > lifecycle-backup.json

# 2. Check your new file is valid JSON
jq . lifecycle.json

# 3. Apply the new configuration
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

# 4. Read it back and compare
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket example-app-data

If an older rule existed, merge it into lifecycle.json before step 3. A bucket has one lifecycle configuration with up to 1,000 rules.

To see stuck uploads before and after, list them:

aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket example-app-data

Step 6: Check the result, then widen slowly

Lifecycle rules don't act the moment you save them. Give it a few days, then check:

  1. Billing: in AWS Cost Explorer, group S3 cost by usage type. Storage cost for the moved classes should rise while Standard storage falls.
  2. Request and retrieval costs: watch for a jump in transition requests (many small objects) or in retrieval fees (data that is read more than you thought).
  3. Complaints: if someone needs an archived object, they will find it isn't instantly readable. That tells you the day count was too short for that prefix.

When the first prefix looks right, add the next one as a new rule. One prefix at a time keeps every change easy to undo: set its Status to Disabled and apply again.


Figure 4: Grow your lifecycle configuration one prefix at a time.

A short checklist

  • Know each prefix's size, read pattern and required retention.
  • Leave small objects in Standard or Intelligent-Tiering.
  • Make every stay longer than the class's minimum duration.
  • Add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to every bucket.
  • On versioned buckets, decide how many old versions to keep, then expire the rest.
  • Back up the current configuration before every put.

At CloudSkill Consulting LLC, we test lifecycle rules like this on a small prefix before applying them to a whole bucket. Storage tiers are often the first place a cloud bill can shrink. We do this kind of FinOps check for teams on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. If a rule here behaves differently in your account, write to info@cloudskillconsulting.com.

Sources (official documentation, checked Oct 17, 2026)

  • Amazon S3 storage classes and comparison table (minimum storage duration charges): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html
  • Transitioning objects using S3 Lifecycle (128 KB default, minimum durations, archive overhead, billing timing): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html
  • Lifecycle configuration elements (filters, noncurrent versions, multipart uploads, midnight UTC timing, 1,000 rules): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intro-lifecycle-rules.html
  • AWS CLI put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI list-multipart-uploads: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/list-multipart-uploads.html
  • Amazon S3 pricing (minimum storage duration charges): https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • AWS What's New, Jul 16, 2026: S3 removes the 30-day minimum before lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/07/s3-removes-30-day-transitions-standard-ia-one-zone-ia/

title: GLM 5.3 now available on AI Gateway
description:
GLM 5.3 from Z.ai is now available on AI Gateway.

GLM 5.3 has improvements vs. GLM 5.2 at complex software engineering and at agent tasks that run across many steps, and it reaches those results while producing fewer output tokens than GLM 5.2 did at the same effort level.

Z.ai also reports stronger vulnerability discovery, including reasoning across the successive stages of an exploitation chain. DeepsecBench measures that work directly, scoring how reliably a model finds security vulnerabilities in application code and what a run costs, and it covers GLM-5.3 at both high and max effort.

GLM 5.3 takes text input, with a 1M token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens, both unchanged from GLM 5.2. It supports function calling, structured output, streaming, and context caching.

To use the model, the slug is zai/glm-5.3:

To use it in a coding agent, run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Pi, and more, then select zai/glm-5.3 inside the agent.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

title: Deploy Cursor Origin repositories with Vercel in public beta
description:
You can now connect Origin repositories to Vercel.

Once connected, pull requests on Origin will automatically generate Preview deployments on Vercel, and merging will trigger a Production deployment.

You can connect Origin through Team settings, Project settings, or by clicking "Continue with Origin" when creating a new project.

You can also connect Vercel to a repository from within Origin by adding Vercel in the repo's Apps tab.

Vercel's integration is in public beta and Origin is in early beta. Origin repositories are subject to Vercel's existing private repository policy.

Learn more about connecting Origin in the Git integration documentation.

title: Privacy Budgets for Test Email in Web Apps
description:
Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. In a web application, it is closer to a small data store: messages can contain personal-looking addresses, sign-in links, verification codes, and enough context to explain what a user did. When a test fails, that data may then be copied into CI logs, screenshots, artifacts, or a developer's laptop.

A useful pattern is to give test email a privacy budget. The budget is not a single number. It is a set of limits for who owns a fixture, how long it lives, what evidence may be retained, and which parts of a message can be exposed to a test. This makes Privacy a design property of Web Development, rather than a cleanup task at the end.

Why test email deserves a privacy budget

Browser and API tests need realistic signals. A signup flow may need to prove that a message is delivered, that the correct link changes account state, and that a second click is rejected. But a test does not need to preserve the entire email forever to prove those things.

Without explicit limits, a shared inbox can let one parallel run read another's message, a failed assertion can print a verification URL into a long-lived log, and a retry can reuse an address or token. A cleanup job can also remove the message before a developer understands the failure.

The first question are not “which temporary inbox is cheapest?” It is “what is the smallest piece of email evidence that proves this behavior?” Search phrases such as tempmailso and temp mail mail may appear in product or test discussions, but the engineering decision should be based on isolation, retention, and access control.

Define the budget before choosing an inbox

Start with the assertion. If the test only checks that a verification message arrived, a receipt may be enough:

{
  "run_id": "ci-1842-attempt-2",
  "fixture_id": "signup-7f31",
  "message_id": "msg-9081",
  "received_at": "2026-10-18T02:20:00Z",
  "subject": "Verify your account",
  "result": "matched"
}

If the test must follow a link, grant the browser step temporary access to the link while keeping it out of ordinary logs. The test helper can return a short-lived value in memory, then replace it with a token identifier once the assertion finishes.

This separation matters because message metadata and authentication material have different sensitivity. A subject and timestamp are useful for diagnosing delivery. A complete URL with a bearer token may be enough to sign in as the test account. It also make the failure record much safer to share with a teammate.

The budget should answer four questions: who owns the fixture, how long the raw message lives, what the test can read, and what survives cleanup. The answers should favor one run attempt per address, bounded retention, narrow access, and a redacted receipt instead of the whole message.

Keep ownership and retention explicit

Give every fixture a run id and attempt number. A retry should get its own address, message correlation value, and token. It is tempting to retry a failed fetch against the same inbox, but that makes old and new messages indistinguishable. A retry should get it's own evidence trail.

The provider adapter should own fixture creation, message lookup, short-lived link claims, and release receipts. The application test should own expected behavior. This division makes it possible to change from a hosted temporary inbox to a local mail capture service without rewriting every test. The runner requests release in a finally-style cleanup step; a janitor removes expired fixtures, and repeated cleanup returns an ordinary “already released” result.

For old fixtures, even a query string like temp gamil com can reveal how legacy test data was generated. A phrase such as temp org mail may also be present in search or compatibility cases. Keep these typo keywords as plain test data only; do not use them as selectors, links, or supported domain examples.

Collect evidence without collecting secrets

Good CI evidence is specific enough to explain a failure and small enough to be safe. A layered receipt works well:

  1. Correlation: run id, attempt, fixture id, and environment.
  2. Delivery: message id, received time, and a normalized subject hash if needed.
  3. Consumption: token id, response status, and whether the token was accepted, expired, or already used.
  4. Cleanup: expiry time, release status, and janitor outcome.

Avoid printing the complete HTML body, query strings, authorization headers, or screenshots of the inbox. Redact before logging, not in a dashboard query after the value has already been copied to several systems. A small allowlist of fields is easier to review than a large blocklist of secret-looking fields.

There is a related lesson in turning API tests into useful CI receipts: the result should describe what happened, not preserve every input. For signup flows, idempotent signup email handling provides another useful boundary. A receipt can say that an event was handled once without retaining the triggering message.

A small implementation contract

Teams do not need a large platform to start. They need a few invariants that are tested alongside the application:

  • A fixture belongs to one run attempt and one environment.
  • A message is accepted only when its recipient and correlation value match.
  • A verification token is single-use, purpose-bound, and short-lived.
  • A retry creates new fixture and token identifiers.
  • Logs contain identifiers and outcomes, never raw links or message bodies.
  • Cleanup is repeatable and a janitor handles crashes.
  • Access to message content is narrower than access to test receipts.

These rules reduce flakiness as well as exposure. The boundary stay understandable when a provider changes or a browser test runs in parallel. It is a modest contract, but it turns email from hidden shared state into an owned test resource.

Review checklist

Before adding an email-dependent test, ask: can two runs claim the same message; does a failure expose a clickable URL; does every retry have a new fixture and token; is raw data deleted after a crash; can a developer diagnose delivery from a redacted receipt; and are screenshots covered by the same retention policy?

If the answers are explicit, the test is checking both product behavior and the safety of its own evidence. That prevent a common failure mode: a green test suite that quietly creates a growing archive of sensitive email.

Questions teams usually ask

Should every test use a hosted temporary inbox?

No. A local mail capture service is often best for application semantics; use a provider-like fixture when delivery integration itself is under test. Keep the same ownership and retention contract in both cases.
