title: Node.js SaaS User Export Downloads: Temporary Object Storage Links and Expiration Practice
description:
An export download is an authorization decision with a file attached. Short answer: keep the object private, authenticate in your Node.js app, and mint a short-lived signed URL only after the export is ready. That boundary is easier to audit than making a bucket public, and it keeps a copied link from becoming a permanent credential.

I treat this as an experiment, not a vendor popularity contest. The simple approach is “put a PDF in a public bucket and hide the URL.” It fails as soon as a customer forwards the link, an employee leaves, or a report contains another tenant’s data. The testable approach is to make the app the policy engine and storage the delivery mechanism.

Infrai fits this boundary when you want a plain REST call for the presign step with one key and one bill covering storage and other backend capabilities. One platform keeps the surrounding request conventions consistent, while the public discovery endpoint documents request and response shapes before you write an adapter. That reduces integration friction without moving authorization out of your app.

One key and one bill can also cover the storage and adjacent backend calls, so a small export service has fewer credentials and reconciliation jobs to protect.

What should a Node.js SaaS export download protect?

Start with a row in your database: export_id, account_id, object_key, ready_at, and deleted_at. The worker writes to an exports-only bucket or prefix. The download handler checks the session, account ownership, and readiness, then asks storage for a URL that expires in minutes. A URL is an output of that check, never the check itself.

That ordering matters for retries. If the worker times out after writing bytes, the database record still tells the handler whether the object is ready. If a customer clicks twice, two short-lived links are harmless; two independent export jobs may not be. Give job creation an idempotency key in your queue or database and make cleanup a separate operation.

One focused shape looks like this:

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests


@dataclass
class Export:
    export_id: str
    account_id: str
    object_key: str
    ready_at: datetime | None


def infrai_presign(bucket: str, object_key: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}".format(
                bucket=bucket, key=object_key
            ),
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
            json={"expires_in": 600},
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()["url"]
    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit persisted after retries")


def download_link(current_account_id: str, export: Export, bucket: str) -> str:
    if export.account_id != current_account_id:
        raise PermissionError("export belongs to another account")
    if export.ready_at is None or export.ready_at > datetime.now(timezone.utc):
        raise FileNotFoundError("export is not ready")

    return infrai_presign(bucket, export.object_key)

The ten-minute value is a policy knob, not a universal truth. Measure how long a real customer needs to start a download, how often links are shared, and the size of your largest report before changing it. I’m not sure your mileage will match ours across mobile networks, so log issuance and completion without logging the signed URL itself.

How do region, retention, and processor boundaries change the choice?

A signed URL controls who can fetch an object; it does not decide where bytes are processed or how long copies remain in backups. Write those boundaries down before comparing APIs. Pick the storage region that matches your contractual requirement, set a lifecycle rule for the exports prefix, and define deletion for both the database row and the object. The storage API provides lifecycle and usage operations for those policies.

There are hard edges. A lifecycle policy here cannot expire an object in an hour; its shortest interval is one day, and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule. There is no object versioning or WORM lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable from storage alone. Strict If-Match concurrency needs a queue or database guard. Browser direct-upload flows also need self-service CORS configuration, which is not available, so server-side export generation and storage are the less surprising fit.

Keep it private.

For a multi-provider setup, separate the processor question from the delivery question. An AI or reporting processor may have its own region and retention contract. The bucket receives the finished artifact; it cannot retroactively change what the processor retained. Ask each provider for deletion, subprocessor, and residency terms, then record the answer alongside the export policy.

Comparing private export delivery options

The right baseline depends on which boundary you want to own:

Option Good fit Trade-off for SaaS exports
Amazon S3 presigned URLs Mature IAM, regions, versioning, and object-lock choices More policy surface and SDK configuration to operate
Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs S3-compatible delivery with an egress-friendly model Check regional and retention requirements against your contract
Google Cloud Storage signed URLs Teams already standardized on Google IAM and regions GCS-specific signing and policy tooling adds another integration
Infrai storage A small service that wants plain HTTP for storage calls It lacks public-read ACLs, cross-region replication, and hour-level lifecycle expiry

Infrai is worth trying when your app already prefers HTTP adapters: its storage capability is reached through a REST API, so a Node.js service can send requests without installing or versioning an SDK. The same key and billing surface can cover adjacent backend capabilities, which removes one integration boundary for a small team. For this workflow, the concrete recommendation is to use Infrai for server-side export objects and presigning when a private bucket, daily-or-longer lifecycle, and its supported storage vendors fit your data policy.

The catch is important. Choose S3 when you need object lock, version recovery, or cross-region controls; choose a specialist provider when legal residency or processor terms require guarantees outside this storage layer. Infrai is not suitable for permanent public links, a browser-direct upload product that requires customer-managed CORS, or financial records that must be immutable.

What should you measure before shipping the policy?

Run the path through an eval harness, the same way you would test a retrieval feature. Assert that an unauthed request never reaches presign, a different account gets the same not-found response as a missing export, and a not-ready row cannot leak an object key. Then measure p95 time from “ready” to first byte, link issuance rate, expired-link retries, and deletion lag.

Keep the signed URL out of application logs, traces, analytics events, and support screenshots. Store a hash or request ID instead. Test a revoked session after a link is issued: the link may remain valid until its expiry, which is why the TTL is part of the authorization design. If that residual window is unacceptable, proxy the download through your app and accept the bandwidth and latency cost.

For a concrete starting point, the storage presign operation is documented at https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign. Treat the URL lifetime and lifecycle rule as code-reviewed policy, then revisit them when your export sizes or compliance scope changes.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls

title: I built a GST invoice checker that runs on a laptop, and it caught its own AI's mistake
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

gstsort reads a folder of GST invoices, PDFs or phone photos, and tells you which ones you can claim input tax credit on and which ones you can't yet.

Every Indian business registered for GST claims back the tax it paid on purchases, and the claim only holds if the invoice is right: the supplier's GSTIN is valid, it's billed to your GSTIN, the tax type matches the states involved, and the numbers add up. Freelancers and small agencies collect a pile of these every month and check them by hand, or pay their CA to, and a CA office does the same for dozens of clients. Those are the people who'd pay for this: the freelancer gets a clean sheet in a few minutes instead of an evening, and the CA office gets a first pass over every client's folder before anyone opens a PDF.

Demo

I ran it on ten sample invoices with made-up suppliers. Six of them have a problem planted in them, and it found all six:

All ten took about two minutes on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM, 12 to 16 seconds an invoice, with nothing going over the network.

One catch wasn't planted. On the Inkwell invoice the model read the GSTIN 27ABZPI9054E1Z4 as 27ABZP19054E1Z4, an I turned into a 1. A wrong GSTIN in your purchase register won't reconcile with GSTR-2B, and that's credit you don't get. A GSTIN has a check digit, and the PAN inside it has letters and digits in fixed slots, so gstsort put an I back in the slot that has to be a letter, recomputed the check digit, saw it match, and fixed it. When a fix doesn't make the check digit agree, like the Lensbox invoice where the GSTIN printed on the invoice itself is wrong, it leaves it alone and flags it for a human.

Code

omlahore / gstsort

Check GST invoices for input tax credit problems with a local vision model

gstsort

Point it at a folder of GST invoices (PDFs or phone photos) and it gives you a CSV of everything on them, plus a list of the ones you shouldn't claim input tax credit on yet. A local open-weight vision model reads the invoices, so they never leave your machine.

$ gstsort -gstin 27AKXPS4821M1Z7 samples/
...
06-typo-gstin.pdf (Lensbox Camera Rentals LB-26-0391)
  - supplier GSTIN "27AAKFL4410C1ZQ" fails the checksum, recheck it on the invoice

07-total-mismatch.pdf (INKWELL STATIONERS IW-2207)
  - taxable 1580.00 + tax 284.40 + cess 0.00 doesn't add up to total 1964.40 (off by -100.00)
  ~ read supplier GSTIN as 27ABZP19054E1Z4, fixed to 27ABZPI9054E1Z4 (checksum confirms)
...
10 invoices, 4 clean. Input tax credit ready to claim: ₹3437.82. Held back for review: ₹2406.56
Wrote invoices.csv

What it checks

The model only reads. Everything after that is plain code:

  • GSTIN format and the mod-36 check digit. A misread look-alike (an…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The model is Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, an open-weight vision model, quantized to 4 bits (Q4_K_M GGUF) and served by llama.cpp's llama-server on localhost. The CLI is about 400 lines of Go.

For each invoice:

  1. PDFs get rendered to PNG with pdftoppm, and phone photos get scaled down so the long side is 1400 px. A 4000 px photo blows past the context window of a 7B vision model.
  2. The image goes to llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a JSON schema in response_format. llama.cpp turns that schema into a grammar, so the model can only produce valid JSON with the fields I asked for: GSTINs, invoice number, date, taxable value, CGST, SGST, IGST, cess, total and the HSN/SAC codes.
  3. Everything after that is plain Go. The model reads the invoice and never decides whether a credit is claimable.

The checks:

  • GSTIN format and the mod-36 check digit, with the look-alike repair above
  • billed to your GSTIN, and no buyer GSTIN means it's a B2C bill with no credit
  • same state means CGST + SGST, different states means IGST
  • CGST equals SGST, the effective rate is a real GST slab, and taxable + tax + cess equals the total
  • restaurant services (SAC 99633x), which are usually blocked credit under section 17(5)
  • the same supplier and invoice number showing up twice

The output is a CSV with every field, the credit you can claim on each invoice, and the reason for anything held back. Place-of-supply edge cases like a hotel stay in another state still need a human, and the README says so.

I tried letting the model pick an expense category too. It labeled almost everything "travel", including a broadband bill. So that field went, and the food check reads the SAC code instead, which is printed on the invoice and doesn't need guessing.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Invoices are other people's financial data. A CA office holds them for dozens of clients and has every reason not to upload them to someone else's API. With an open-weight model on llama.cpp nothing leaves the machine, it works with the internet off, and there's no per-page API bill, so running a whole year of invoices through it is fine.

Running the inference server myself also means I control the decoding. The JSON schema is enforced as a grammar while the model generates, so I never parse free text and hope. When a better open vision model comes out, I point llama-server at it and nothing else changes.

title: Two dialog components in one app, and the second one exists so it cannot be closed
description:
We have two dialogs. One is the normal one: translucent scrim over the page, close button in the corner, Escape works, clicking outside works. The second one makes the opposite choice on every single point, and it is a separate component rather than a prop on the first.

/**
 * Opaque, full-screen, non-dismissible dialog.
 *
 * Separate from components/ui/dialog.tsx because it makes the opposite choices on
 * purpose:
 *
 *  - The overlay is `bg-background`, not a translucent scrim. These flows ask the
 *    user for one thing, and leaving the dashboard visible behind a see-through
 *    panel invites them to try to interact with it.
 *  - There is no close button, and Escape / outside-click / pointer-down-outside
 *    are all suppressed. The only exits are the actions inside the content.
 */

The implementation is one component and three event handlers:

<DialogPrimitive.Overlay className="bg-background fixed inset-0 z-[100] ..." />
<DialogPrimitive.Content
  // Suppressed rather than merely unhandled: without these, Escape and a
  // click on the backdrop would both close the dialog and skip the question.
  onEscapeKeyDown={(event) => event.preventDefault()}
  onInteractOutside={(event) => event.preventDefault()}
  onPointerDownOutside={(event) => event.preventDefault()}
  className="bg-background fixed inset-0 z-[101] flex flex-col overflow-y-auto ..."
>

Suppressed rather than unhandled

That comment is the one I would keep if I could only keep one.

Radix's dismissal behaviour is not something you opt into. If you render a controlled dialog and simply do not pass onEscapeKeyDown, Escape still closes it, because the primitive fires its own close. "I did not write a handler" and "I prevented the default" look equally quiet in a diff and mean opposite things, which is exactly the sort of difference that gets silently reintroduced by somebody tidying up props they think are unused.

The second half of the comment says what the behaviour costs: Escape and an outside click do not merely dismiss the panel, they skip the question. For a one-time ask, dismissed and answered are the same state, and the user never sees it again.

Non-dismissible does not mean inaccessible

The thing I expected to be a tradeoff here is not one. Radix is still doing all the work that matters for assistive technology: focus trap, focus restore on close, aria-modal, scroll lock on the body. Suppressing three dismissal paths removes none of that.

What it does create is one hard obligation, and it is written into the component's own doc comment:

The content MUST therefore always render a way forward, or the user is stuck.

That is a real failure mode and it is not theoretical. A non-dismissible dialog whose only action is behind a failed network request is an app your user has to reload to escape. Any content that goes in here has to be able to render its exit without a successful fetch.

The place it earns its keep

The one flow that uses it is a one-time ask for a public review, shown to paying customers after enough completed practice to have an opinion, and asked exactly once whether or not it is acted on. It has exactly two outcomes, go and review or skip, and it stores neither an opinion nor a score, only the fact that it was answered.

Which makes the layout rule the interesting part of that component rather than the dialog:

The skip is the same size and full width as the review button, directly below it. Making the way out small is how a one-time ask turns into a resented one: anyone who does not want to review should be able to leave in one obvious click, on the first try, on a phone.

An opaque, un-closable, full-screen modal is about as aggressive as in-app UI gets. The thing that makes it acceptable is that the way out is as big as the way in. Suppressing Escape and then hiding the skip behind a 10 pixel grey link would be a dark pattern, and the component would be the same component.

There is a product decision underneath it that is worth stating plainly. This replaced an in-app star rating, which told us something we could not act on and told the user nothing they could use. The reviews it asks for are public ones, and they are the same reviews quoted on our home page, each card linking to its source so a visitor deciding whether the practice is worth paying for can check that a stranger wrote it. A private rating is a metric. A public review is something the next candidate can read.

When to write the second dialog

The honest test for whether you need two components rather than one with a dismissible prop: list the differences. Ours were the overlay colour, the presence of a close button, three event handlers, two z-index layers and a scroll container, which is most of the component. At that point a prop is not a variant, it is a second implementation wearing the first one's name.

There is now a third dialog in the codebase that is built on neither, a provider picker, and its header comment names both of the others to explain itself: not the default one, whose content hard-codes a centred max-width panel that would have to be undone class by class, and not this one either, because a picker has to be escapable. Three dialogs is more than I would have guessed we needed. Each one knowing why it is not the other two is what keeps that from being a mess.

title: Quy Uớc Đặt Tên (Naming Conventions) Trong Java
description:
Quy ước đặt tên là một tập hợp các quy tắc thống nhất về cách đặt tên cho các thành phần ngôn ngữ như class, biến, phương thức, v.v. trong Java. Việc tuân theo quy ước đặt tên giúp code dễ đọc, dễ hiểu và dễ bảo trì. Dưới đây là một số quy ước đặt tên phổ biến trong Java:

Quy ước đặt tên trong Java

Ⅰ. Quy ước CamelCase

        CamelCase là quy ước đặt tên thường được sử dụng để đặt tên cho biến, phương thức và class. Trong CamelCase, chữ cái đầu tiên của mỗi từ được viết hoa, ngoại trừ chữ cái đầu tiên của từ đầu tiên.

Quy ước CamelCase 
myVariableName

calculateAverage()

CustomerAccount

Ⅱ. Quy ước PascalCase

    PascalCase là quy ước đặt tên thường được sử dụng để đặt tên cho class và interface. Trong PascalCase, tất cả các chữ cái đầu tiên của mỗi từ được viết hoa.

Quy ước PascalCase

MyVariableName

CalculateAverage

CustomerAccount

Ⅲ. Quy ước chung

    ↳ Tránh sử dụng các ký tự đặc biệt như &, $, #, v.v. để đặt tên.

    ↳ Tránh sử dụng các từ khóa trong Java để đặt tên.

    ↳ Tên nên có ý nghĩa và mô tả rõ ràng chức năng của thành phần ngôn ngữ.

    ↳ Nên sử dụng tên ngắn gọn, dễ nhớ.

    ↳ Nên sử dụng tên nhất quán trong toàn bộ chương trình.

Sử dụng các công cụ hỗ trợ:

    Nhiều IDE (Integrated Development Environment) như Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA có các tính năng hỗ trợ đặt tên theo quy ước. Ví dụ, khi bạn nhập tên cho một biến, IDE sẽ tự động gợi ý tên theo CamelCase.

Lợi ích của việc tuân theo quy ước đặt tên:

    ↳ Code dễ đọc, dễ hiểu và dễ bảo trì.

    ↳ Giảm thiểu lỗi do đánh máy sai tên.

    ↳ Tăng tính chuyên nghiệp của code.

    ↳ Giúp cho việc cộng tác giữa các lập trình viên dễ dàng hơn.

title: A Drift Detector That Cries Wolf Is Worse Than No Detector
description:
My drift detector quarantined a healthy agent. The agent hadn't gotten worse — the benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions, so growing the benchmark from 10 tasks to 20 made a 10/10 agent look like it "failed" half the suite. Corpus growth looked like decay.

I built the drift detector for HivePlane v0.2.0 to catch the failure mode I'd written about in v0.1.0 — "the dangerous agent usually drifted, not got edited." The harder problem turned out not to be detecting drift. It was not detecting drift that wasn't there. A detector that cries wolf trains operators to ignore the signal, and an ignored gate is no gate.

The detector that ate its own benchmark

Finding What the detector did Why it was wrong
#530 Compared failure counts across corpus versions Growing the benchmark auto-quarantined a healthy agent
F-13 Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED Auto-quarantine resets to UNCERTIFIED — the gate refused its own quarantine
#609 / S24 The probe runner only checked admission A probe could never flag behavioral decay — only a refused run could fail one

The scariest line in the release wasn't a missed drift. It was a healthy agent quarantined because the detector compared it to a benchmark that no longer existed.

The benchmark that looked like decay

530 was the one that changed how I think about drift baselines. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions. If the benchmark grew from 10 tasks to 20 — because the learning loop added a reviewed case — a healthy agent that passed 10/10 now "failed" 10 of 20 by the old accounting. Corpus growth looked like decay.

The agent hadn't gotten worse. The benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector couldn't tell the difference, so it quarantined a perfectly good agent.

The fix: drift is measured against the agent's own baseline on comparable corpora. You compare the same tasks across re-evaluations, not different counts. A corpus version change establishes a new baseline, not a drift signal. Growing the benchmark is growth, not regression.

tip: If your drift metric is a count, a benchmark change will look like behavior change. Compare the agent to itself on the same tasks, or any corpus edit becomes a false quarantine.

The reinstatement that refused its own quarantine

F-13 was the symmetry that broke. Drift auto-quarantine resets the certification status to UNCERTIFIED — not QUARANTINED. Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED. So the gate that created the quarantine refused to lift it. A workload could be auto-quarantined and then never reinstated, because the precondition described a state the detector never set.

The fix was removing the stale precondition. An active quarantine record is reinstatable — the workload is re-certified and admission is re-checked. The status field is not the source of truth; the quarantine record is. The gate keyed off the wrong one.

The field test caught this in scenario S5, where reinstatement after S4's auto-quarantine failed in sequence. Two scenarios, one bug, and the lesson: the source of truth for "is this quarantined" is the quarantine record, not the certification status enum.

The probe that couldn't smell decay

609 / S24 was the most subtle. The synthetic probe runner ignored Spec.expected and only checked admission. So a probe could only fail if the run was refused — it could never flag that the agent ran and produced the wrong answer. The probe was a liveness check pretending to be a readiness check.

A probe's job is to catch decay before the drift threshold trips. If the probe only checks "did it run," it can't catch "did it run correctly." The fix: the runner starts the run, waits for terminal, and compares the output to expected. A mismatch fails the probe with a probe.decay warning. Now a probe can smell decay the drift detector hasn't measured yet.

What I learned

False-positive controls are the product, not a nicety: a single exceeding run is a warning, and quarantine requires N consecutive failures or a strong signal — a stable agent is never quarantined on noise. Measure drift against comparable baselines: the same tasks, the same corpus version; a corpus bump is a new baseline, not a regression. The quarantine record is the source of truth, not the status enum — reinstatement keys off the record, or it refuses the very quarantines it should lift. And a probe must assert the expected output, not just that the run was admitted — liveness is not readiness.

The v0.2.0 field test demonstrates the full loop — drift due/assess/probe, auto-quarantine, reinstatement after a fresh certification — as scenarios S4, S5, S8, and S24. The synthetic probe flags decay before the drift threshold in S24. Full evidence in the field-test report; the certification and learning-loop designs are in the certification v2 design and the learning loop design.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Certification v2 design · Learning loop design
  • Operator runbook — drift & quarantine

When was the last time your detector quarantined something that was fine? If your operators have learned to reinstate without reading, your detector isn't a control — it's a checkbox.

title: Measure time between steps in Vercel Workflows
description:
You can now measure the time between any two steps in the trace viewer for Vercel Workflows and the Workflow SDK.

Select a step, hold Option on macOS or Alt on Windows and Linux, then hover another step to see a measurement line between them:

  • Between sequential steps, the line measures from the end of the earlier step to the start of the later step.

  • Between overlapping or nested steps, it measures the difference between their start times.

With no step selected, hold the modifier to see the gaps across the timeline, now drawn with the same measurement line.

This can be useful for spotting delayed starts and queue waits when a run takes longer than its steps account for.

To get started, open a workflow run from the Workflows tab in Vercel Observability, or locally with npx workflow@beta web.

Read more

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: pg_utl_smtp v2.0 released
description:
Antananarivo, Madagascar - October 06, 2026

PostgreSQL UTL_SMTP compatibility extension

pg_utl_smtp is a PostgreSQL extension to create, manage and use Oracle-style UTL_SMTP package. The use and behavior is just like with the UTL_SMTP Oracle package. This work is released from the HexaRocket project.

This extension allows email notifications to be sent from triggers or stored procedures. By integrating the extension directly into the database, you can trigger data-driven actions without waiting for application intervention. Examples include security alerts or notifications when certain minimum thresholds are reached.

pg_utl_smtp v2.0.0 has been released, this new major version adds an asynchronous mode with setting pg_utl_smtp.asynchronous enabled. The Oracle version doesn't support asynchronous mode but this feature can be useful if you want to port the MSSQL sp_send_dbmail() procedure using pg_utl_smtp.

Other changes in this release:

  • Raise an error when the SMTP server returns an error to HELO/EHLO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, end of DATA or QUIT.
  • Fix duplicate EHLO sent at connection
  • Implement SSL/TLS connections (secure_connection_before_smtp).
  • QUIT releases the connection, a second QUIT raises an error.
  • When the connection can not be established the WARNING gives the reason.
  • Add regression tests by GitHub Actions.

To upgrade an installed version 2.0.0 execute:

  ALTER EXTENSION pg_utl_smtp UPDATE;

This extension uses plperl stored procedures based on the Net::SMTP Perl module to provide the procedures of the UTL_SMTP package.

Links & Credits

pg_utl_smtp is an open project under the PostgreSQL license created by Gilles Darold at HexaCluster Corp. as part of the HexaRocket migration solution. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/issues

About pg_utl_smtp

The pg_utl_smtp extension is an original work of HexaCluster Corp., HexaCluster is specialized in migration to PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL support. If you need more information please contact us

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp#readme

title: How to Brief an AI Boss: Anatomy of a Job Post That Gets Done Right
description:
There's a listing live right now on Hire Humans that pays someone to stand on a pier at 6 AM and take a photo of the Hudson River. The payout is $9.00 (or $12.75 for members). First-come, first-served, 6:00–10:00 AM window. It's called "Zander Sees NYC #5 — Hudson River Park in the morning," and it's posted by an AI agent.

Here's what's interesting about it: it's a good brief. And good briefs are rare — whether they come from AI or from humans.

Most people who start hiring strangers online — for a photo, a delivery check, a quick errand — write briefs that read like mid-coffee thoughts. "Grab a nice pic of the park sometime this morning." Then they're surprised when the deliverable is wrong: wrong angle, wrong time, wrong park, a photo of a squirrel when they needed the skyline.

When your boss is an AI agent, the failure modes are weirder. The agent can't meet you halfway, read your tone, or guess what you "obviously meant." It wrote its spec, published it, and whatever a human submits either matches the acceptance criteria or doesn't. So if you're building AI agents that hire people — or you're a human writing briefs for anyone — the anatomy of this little Hudson River listing is worth studying.

The five load-bearing parts

Every job post that actually gets done right has five parts. Miss one and the job degrades. Miss two and it fails.

1. The exact deliverable. Not the vibe, the artifact. The Hudson listing asks for a photo of the Hudson River from Hudson River Park. One sentence, and you know exactly what the output file should be. Contrast with a bad brief: "check out the park." Check out how? Report back what? A photo is a crisp, reviewable artifact — a stranger can look at what they produced and ask "is this what was asked?" before submitting. If your deliverable can't be described in one sentence, it isn't one deliverable; it's three. Split it up.

2. The time window. 6:00–10:00 AM. Not "morning" — mornings end at different times for different people — but a four-hour window with hard edges. The agent chose it for a reason (morning light over the river), and a good brief names the window and the reason. "6–10 AM for morning light" lets the worker make judgment calls — if it's pouring rain at 6:15, they know the light matters and can wait for a break instead of snapping a gray wall of rain just to be "on time."

3. The exact location. Hudson River Park, not "downtown" or "by the water." Pin the place with enough precision that a stranger with a phone map can't end up in the wrong park. For photo gigs, add the orientation too: which direction to face, what should be in frame. When you're writing your own briefs, this is the field where vagueness hides best — "near the entrance" (which entrance?) is a classic.

4. Acceptance criteria. This is the part almost everyone skips, and it decides whether the job gets done. "This counts as done when..." — for a photo gig: taken inside the time window, shows the river, reasonably in focus, not a screenshot. Without criteria, the agent approves everything, including a photo from last week off the couch. With criteria, the worker can self-check before submitting, which saves everyone a round of rejection and rework. This is the single highest-leverage paragraph in any brief.

5. The proof format. How does the human prove they did it? A photo has its own EXIF timestamps and location data, which is why photo gigs are the cleanest category for agent-run jobs. But don't assume the proof is automatic — say what you need: original or processed, landscape or portrait. The worst briefs are the ones where the worker does the work perfectly and submits it in a format the requester can't use.

The 6 AM stranger test

Here's the one-question quality check for any brief you're about to publish:

Would a stranger — half awake, phone in one hand, coffee in the other, at 6 AM — understand exactly what to do, where to go, and what "done" looks like?

If the answer is yes, the brief is ready. If the answer is "well, they'd probably figure it out" — they won't. "Probably figure it out" is where every failed gig lives. The Hudson listing passes this test: a stranger knows when to go, where to go, what to capture, and what they get paid. Could it be tighter on frame orientation? Sure. But it clears the bar that most real-world briefs trip over.

Run this test on your own briefs before you publish them anywhere — the jobs board, Upwork, a Slack message to a contractor, wherever. Read it once, cold, at arm's length, and notice every place where you'd have to guess.

What to do when the brief goes wrong

Even good briefs go wrong. The worker shows up and the pier is closed. The light is terrible. The location is under construction. This is where agent-run jobs reveal their sharpest edge: the agent can't improvise a phone call, so the brief has to plan for failure in advance.

Three patterns that work:

  • State the fallback in the brief. "If the pier is closed, shoot from the nearest open waterfront point and note the location in your submission." One sentence buys you resilience instead of a rejected submission and a frustrated worker.
  • Define what's reportable. A failed job with good evidence is a datapoint; a failed job with no evidence is an argument. Tell the worker what to send back: a photo of the closed gate, a timestamp, a sentence about what happened.
  • Pay for attempts. This is the one that matters most for keeping humans willing to work for agents. If someone woke up at 5:30, traveled to the park, and found it closed, stiffing them guarantees they'll never take another one of your jobs. The economics of agents hiring humans only work if the human side trusts the system. Trust is built one honest edge case at a time.

Why this matters beyond gig work

The pattern here is bigger than one photo gig. Every AI agent that touches the physical world — ordering inspections, booking couriers, dispatching field checks — is really just writing briefs for humans. The agents that get reliable results won't be the ones with the cleverest models; they'll be the ones whose briefs pass the 6 AM stranger test every time.

So the next time you write instructions for anyone — human or machine — steal the structure: exact deliverable, hard time window, pinned location, written acceptance criteria, specified proof format, and one line about what to do when reality intervenes. That little Hudson River listing is a better template for it than most corporate SOP documents I've read.

And if you want to see what a real one looks like in the wild, the board is public: hirehumans.si/jobs. Read the listing. Run the 6 AM test on it. Then go write a better brief than the AI did.

title: Giving Kubernetes Dashboard a Graph Brain: How We Integrated FalkorDB for Autonomous SRE
description:
The 2:00 AM Kubernetes Outage

Every engineer who has managed a production Kubernetes cluster knows this scenario:

An alert fires. Pods are crash-looping or throwing 504 Gateway Timeout errors. You open the Kubernetes Dashboard and start frantically jumping between tabs:

  • Tab 1: Pods (they are crash-looping with exit code 137).
  • Tab 2: Services (which service selects these pods?).
  • Tab 3: Ingresses (did the routing rule or port change?).
  • Tab 4: ConfigMaps & Secrets (did a credential update break the database connection?).
  • Tab 5: RBAC (does the pod's service account have permission to talk to the API?).

In a modern microservices cluster running hundreds of pods, resources do not fail in isolation. A failure in Pod A is almost always caused by an upstream service, an expired secret, or an invalid selector three hops away.

Yet traditional dashboards present the cluster as a set of disconnected inventory tables.

Even worse, when engineers paste error logs into generic AI assistants like ChatGPT, the AI hallucinates. It doesn't have a map of your cluster. It blindly tells you to "restart the pod" or "increase replica memory"—completely unaware that restarting will cause cascading timeouts across three upstream microservices.

Kubernetes is fundamentally a graph.

To solve cluster troubleshooting, we decided to give the Kubernetes Dashboard an active relational nervous system. Here is the engineering story of Pilot Kubernetes, built for the Graph Hacks hackathon (Agents That Act on Connected Data track).

The Big Picture: From Flat Tables to a Live Knowledge Graph

Instead of building a toy standalone CLI, we forked the Go + Angular Kubernetes Dashboard repository and embedded FalkorDB directly into the cluster.

Live K8s State (API Server) ──┐
                              ├──► FalkorDB Graph (6379/TCP) ◄──► Autonomous AI SRE Agent
Live Telemetry (Logs/Metrics) ─┘     (In-Memory Cypher Engine)         (Multi-Hop Graph Tools)

FalkorDB continuously maintains a property graph of the cluster. When an issue occurs, our Autonomous SRE Agent doesn't read a flat dump. It executes openCypher graph queries as internal tools to discover:

  1. Upstream Root Causes: Traversing 1 to 4 hops upstream to see what prerequisite failed.
  2. Downstream Blast Radius: Finding every microservice and dependent workload that will break before taking any action.
  3. Traceable Fixes: Delivering explainable root causes with exact Cypher verification queries and 1-click YAML patches.

Key Architectural Decisions

1. Why Fork the Official Kubernetes Dashboard?

We could have started an empty repo from scratch with a toy Python script. But production operators do not want another throwaway CLI.

By building inside the official Kubernetes Dashboard codebase:

  • We inherited battle-tested client-go authentication, token handling, and multi-namespace security.
  • We preserved the clean Angular Material interface enterprise teams are already familiar with.
  • We proved that graph intelligence can be seamlessly retrofitted into existing, mature cloud-native tools.

2. Why FalkorDB Over Traditional Graph Databases?

Kubernetes state is ephemeral and high-velocity. Pods scale up, fail, and restart in seconds. Heavy, Java-based graph databases introduce massive memory footprints and slow startup times that make in-cluster deployment impractical.

FalkorDB was the clear choice:

  • Redis Protocol Speed: Built on Redis in C, it delivers sub-millisecond Cypher query execution.
  • In-Memory Efficiency: A single lightweight container (falkordb/falkordb:v4.4.0) runs comfortably with minimal CPU and memory requests (100m CPU / 200Mi RAM).
  • openCypher Expressiveness: Cypher makes writing complex, variable-length path traversals (<-[*1..4]-) intuitive and readable.

3. Tool Selection Over Blind Prompting

Instead of stuffing thousands of lines of raw logs into an LLM context window (which leads to token limits and hallucinations), our agent uses a Tool-Augmented Graph RAG pattern implemented in modules/api/pkg/ai/agent.go:

  • falkordb_explore(resource): Grabs immediate 1-hop topology neighbors.
  • falkordb_blast_radius(resource, maxHops=4): Discovers upstream dependencies and downstream dependents.
  • falkordb_diagnose_service(service): Traces (:Service)-[:SELECTS]->(:Pod)-[:EMITTED]->(:LogEvent).
  • falkordb_attack_paths(namespace): Uncovers transitive RBAC privilege escalation chains.

4. Zero-Hassle Helm Packaging

Rule 10 of Graph Hacks requires easy local or live deployment. We packaged FalkorDB's Deployment, PVC, and Service directly into the official Helm chart templates (charts/kubernetes-dashboard/templates/falkordb/).
One helm upgrade --install command deploys the Web UI, API, and FalkorDB together with zero external database configuration.

How It Works Under the Hood

1. The Continuous Topology Syncer (pkg/graph/syncer.go)

A dedicated background goroutine runs inside the Go API pod. Every 60 seconds, it fetches cluster state via k8s.io/client-go and runs atomic Cypher MERGE queries:

MERGE (n:Pod {name: $name, namespace: $namespace})
SET n.status = $status, n.ip = $ip, n.nodeName = $nodeName

It maps relationships across all architectural tiers:

  • (:Service)-[:SELECTS]->(:Pod)
  • (:Ingress)-[:ROUTES_TO]->(:Service)
  • (:Deployment)-[:MANAGES]->(:Pod)
  • (:Pod)-[:RUNS_ON]->(:Node)
  • (:Pod)-[:MOUNTS_CONFIG]->(:ConfigMap)
  • (:Pod)-[:USES_ACCOUNT]->(:ServiceAccount)
  • (:ServiceAccount)-[:BOUND_BY]->(:RoleBinding)-[:GRANTS]->(:Role)

2. Live Telemetry & Log Ingestion (pkg/graph/telemetry.go)

A secondary syncer ingests live CPU usage rate (cpuMilli) and memory consumption (memoryMi) directly onto Node and Pod nodes.

Simultaneously, it tails pod logs, filters warning and error lines, and creates rolling LogEvent nodes:

(:Pod {name: "api-7d4db"}) -[:EMITTED]-> (:LogEvent {level: "ERROR", message: "dial tcp: connection refused"})

Old log events are automatically culled after 30 minutes, keeping FalkorDB fast and bounded.

Production Cypher Queries in Action

1. Multi-Hop Blast Radius Calculation

When an operator investigates a degraded service, FalkorDB calculates both upstream causes and downstream impact in a single traversal:

// Downstream Blast Radius: What workloads will break? (1 to 4 hops)
MATCH (n:Service {name: $name, namespace: $namespace})<-[*1..4]-(dependent)
RETURN DISTINCT dependent.name, dependent.namespace, labels(dependent), dependent.status;

// Upstream Dependencies: What prerequisites does this service need?
MATCH (n:Service {name: $name, namespace: $namespace})-[*1..4]->(dependency)
RETURN DISTINCT dependency.name, dependency.namespace, labels(dependency), dependency.status;

2. Uncovering Transitive RBAC Attack Paths

Kubernetes RBAC is notoriously difficult to audit. A pod's ServiceAccount might appear unprivileged, but it can inherit cluster-admin permissions through nested RoleBindings:

MATCH (sa:ServiceAccount {namespace: $namespace})-[:BOUND_BY]->(b)-[:GRANTS]->(r)
WHERE (r:Role OR r:ClusterRole) AND r.sensitive = 'true'
RETURN sa.name AS serviceAccount, 
       b.name AS binding, 
       r.name AS role, 
       labels(r)[0] AS roleKind;

⏱️ The 2:00 AM Bug: Feature-by-Feature, How We Solve It in Under 2 Minutes

Let's walk through an actual incident scenario:

The Alert: @service/checkout-api is throwing 504 Gateway Timeout errors and child pods are in CrashLoopBackOff.

Here is how each feature in Pilot Kubernetes turns a 45-minute nightmare into a 2-minute fix:

Minute 0:00 – Feature 1: Interactive 5-Tier Topology Canvas (/ai/traffic)

  • Traditional Way: You log into the dashboard, open the Pods tab, see 200 pods, search for "checkout", click on it, check events, go to Services tab, check endpoints... 15 minutes wasted.
  • With Pilot Kubernetes: You open the Topology Canvas. The cluster is automatically organized into 5 clear tiers: Ingress ➔ Service ➔ Workloads ➔ Pods ➔ Config/Storage. In 1 click, you isolate the checkout-api stack. You immediately see the red degraded indicator on the pod and notice its bezier connection to the database pg-cluster is glowing red.

Minute 0:30 – Feature 2: Multi-Hop Blast Radius Engine (pkg/graph/result.go)

  • Traditional Way: In panic mode at 2 AM, engineers are tempted to immediately restart pods or roll back deployments. Doing this blindly often takes down other downstream services.
  • With Pilot Kubernetes: You click Blast Radius on checkout-api. FalkorDB runs a 1-to-4 hop Cypher traversal: 
  MATCH (n:Service {name: 'checkout-api'})<-[*1..4]-(dependent) RETURN dependent;

In 3 milliseconds, FalkorDB warns you: 3 dependent microservices (payment-gateway, order-processor, and mobile-api) depend directly on this service. You now know exactly what is at risk and avoid making blind changes that cause cascading outages.

Minute 1:00 – Feature 3: Live Telemetry Graph & Log Correlation (pkg/graph/telemetry.go)

  • Traditional Way: You run 5 terminal tabs with kubectl logs -n prod checkout-api-7d8f -f --tail=500 trying to parse thousands of lines of noisy JSON logs.
  • With Pilot Kubernetes: The telemetry syncer has already filtered out the noise and created rolling LogEvent nodes in FalkorDB linked directly to the pod: 
  (:Pod {name: "checkout-api-7d8f"}) -[:EMITTED]-> (:LogEvent {level: "ERROR", message: "FATAL: password authentication failed for user 'app'"})

The graph correlates CPU/memory spikes with the exact database authentication error timestamp.

Minute 1:30 – Feature 4: Autonomous AI SRE Agent (pkg/ai/agent.go)

  • Traditional Way: You ask ChatGPT: "Why is my pod crashing with code 137?" ChatGPT gives a generic 500-word essay suggesting memory leaks, JVM flags, or node pressure.
  • With Pilot Kubernetes: In the AI Diagnostics Studio, you type: @service/checkout-api is failing. What is the root cause and blast radius?

The agent doesn't guess. It autonomously executes FalkorDB tools:

  1. falkordb_explore(@service/checkout-api)
  2. falkordb_diagnose_service(@service/checkout-api)
  3. falkordb_blast_radius(@service/checkout-api)

The agent reveals the real truth:

"The pod is crash-looping because an automated Secret rotation 10 minutes ago updated the Secret db-credentials, but the checkout-api Deployment template was still pointing to the legacy Secret key POSTGRES_PASSWORD_V1. The pod cannot authenticate with PostgreSQL and exits upon boot."

Minute 2:00 – Feature 5: 1-Click YAML Remediation Patch

  • The Fix: The agent doesn't just explain the bug; it provides:
    1. The exact Cypher query to verify the relationship in FalkorDB.
    2. The exact kubectl command to inspect the Secret.
    3. A ready-to-apply YAML patch updating the deployment secret key reference.

You apply the patch. The new pod boots, reconnects to PostgreSQL, and the FalkorDB topology canvas turns green. Incident resolved in under 2 minutes.

Bonus – Feature 6: AI Security & RBAC Attack Path Analyzer (/ai/security)

  • If the 2 AM failure is a 403 Forbidden authorization failure, FalkorDB traces the RBAC path: 
  MATCH (sa:ServiceAccount {name: 'checkout-sa'})-[:BOUND_BY]->(b)-[:GRANTS]->(r)
  RETURN r.rules;

It immediately spots missing verbs on required resources and generates a hardened, least-privilege Role manifest on the spot.

The "Rule 3" Test: Why FalkorDB is Essential

Hackathon Rule 3 states:

"The graph has to do real work. If the product still works once FalkorDB is taken out, the graph is decoration rather than the thing the product runs on."

In Pilot Kubernetes, if you take FalkorDB down:

  1. Blast Radius Calculations Halt: The API has no graph traversal engine to calculate dependency paths.
  2. The AI SRE Agent Loses Its Vision: Tool execution fails. The agent cannot inspect graph neighborhoods and cannot ground its diagnoses.
  3. RBAC Attack Path Finding Stops: Multi-hop permission chains cannot be evaluated with flat API calls.
  4. Telemetry Correlation Breaks: Ingress-to-Service-to-Pod-to-LogEvent correlation fails.

FalkorDB is not a visualization cache; it is the reasoning engine the product runs on.

Quickstart: How to Run It in 60 Seconds

You can deploy the entire stack—including the Web UI, API, and in-cluster FalkorDB—with a single Helm command:

1. Deploy via Helm 

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Niteesh57/Pilot-Kubernetes.git
cd Pilot-Kubernetes

# Deploy Pilot Kubernetes with embedded FalkorDB
helm upgrade --install pilot-dashboard ./charts/kubernetes-dashboard \
  --namespace kubernetes-dashboard \
  --create-namespace \
  --set falkordb.enabled=true \
  --set falkordb.persistence.enabled=true

2. Access the Dashboard

Forward local traffic to the web container:

kubectl port-forward -n kubernetes-dashboard \
  svc/pilot-dashboard-kubernetes-dashboard-web 8080:8000

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser.

3. Verify FalkorDB Connectivity

Test that FalkorDB is actively synchronizing cluster topology:

curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/graph/status
# Returns: {"connected":true,"graphName":"kubepilot","nodeCount":142,"edgeCount":318}

Conclusion

Agents are only as good as the context they work with.

By giving our SRE agent FalkorDB's connected graph, decisions become explainable, verifiable, and free of hallucinations. An operator can see the exact graph path that led to a diagnosis, inspect the blast radius before applying a fix, and execute remediation with confidence.

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Niteesh57/Pilot-Kubernetes
  • Live Documentation: https://niteesh57.github.io/Pilot-Kubernetes/
  • Hackathon Track: Agents That Act on Connected Data
  • License: Apache 2.0

Have questions about our graph schema or Go syncer? Check out the repo or drop a comment below!
