title: Stop Squinting at Messy LESS: How to Beautify Your Stylesheets in Seconds
description:
We've all been there. You inherit a project, open styles.less, and it looks like someone typed the whole thing in a single breath. Nested rules collapsed onto one line, mixins with no spacing, variables jammed against their values.

You can still read it. But every minute you spend decoding formatting is a minute you're not fixing the actual bug.

In this post I'll walk through what LESS is (quickly), why formatting matters more than people admit, and how a LESS beautifier can clean up a file in seconds. I'll also show you real before and after examples so you can judge for yourself.

Quick refresher: what is LESS?

LESS is a CSS preprocessor. It extends plain CSS with features like variables, nesting, mixins, functions and operations, then compiles down to regular CSS that browsers understand. The official LESS documentation is the best place to go deep on the language itself.

A tiny taste:

@primary: #3b82f6;

.button {
  background: @primary;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }
}

That nesting and the darken() function are what make LESS pleasant to write. But they're also what make badly formatted LESS painful to read, because the structure is the logic.

Why formatting matters more in LESS than in plain CSS

In plain CSS, a messy file is annoying. In LESS, a messy file can actually hide bugs. Here's why:

  • Nesting depth is meaning. A rule nested one level too deep (or too shallow) changes the compiled selector. If indentation doesn't match nesting, you can't see the mistake.
  • Mixins and guards are easy to miss. A mixin call buried in a long line is easy to overlook when you're debugging why a style is applied.
  • Missing braces are brutal. One unclosed } in a deeply nested block can break compilation, and the error message often points somewhere unhelpful.
  • Code review gets noisy. If every developer formats differently, pull requests fill up with whitespace changes that hide the real ones.

Consistent formatting isn't about being picky. It's about making the structure of your styles visible at a glance.

What does a LESS beautifier actually do?

A beautifier takes your LESS code and rewrites its whitespace and layout without changing what it means. Typically that includes:

  • Consistent indentation for nested blocks
  • One declaration per line
  • Sensible spacing around colons, braces and operators
  • Line breaks between rules so blocks are easy to scan

Crucially, it should not change your logic. Variables, mixins, operations and nesting stay exactly as you wrote them. Only the presentation changes.

A real before and after

Here's the kind of LESS you might get from a quick copy-paste, a minified export, or a teammate in a hurry:

@primary:#3b82f6;@radius:6px;
.mixin-card(@pad:16px){padding:@pad;border:1px solid #eee}
.btn{color:#fff;background:@primary;border-radius:@radius;&:hover{background:darken(@primary,10%)}.icon{margin-right:4px}}
.card{.mixin-card(24px);h2{font-size:1.25rem;a{color:@primary}}}

Technically valid. Practically unreadable. Now the same code after running it through a beautifier:

@primary: #3b82f6;
@radius: 6px;

.mixin-card(@pad: 16px) {
  padding: @pad;
  border: 1px solid #eee;
}

.btn {
  color: #fff;
  background: @primary;
  border-radius: @radius;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }

  .icon {
    margin-right: 4px;
  }
}

.card {
  .mixin-card(24px);

  h2 {
    font-size: 1.25rem;

    a {
      color: @primary;
    }
  }
}

Same code, same output once compiled, but now you can see that .icon lives inside .btn, that .card calls the mixin, and that the link color sits three levels deep. That last one is a good reminder to watch your nesting depth, which you'd never notice in the single-line version.

How to use an online LESS beautifier

When I just need to clean up a snippet or a single file, I don't want to configure a toolchain. An online tool is the fastest path. I put together the LESS Beautifier on 99tools for exactly this situation. The workflow is simple:

  1. Paste your messy LESS into the input box.
  2. Run the beautifier.
  3. Copy the cleaned-up result back into your editor.

No install, no config file, no setup. It's handy when you're:

  • Reviewing LESS from a client or a legacy project
  • Cleaning a snippet before sharing it in a bug report or Stack Overflow question
  • Reading code that was minified or exported from another tool
  • Teaching or learning LESS and wanting readable examples

A quick tip: as with any online tool, don't paste proprietary code or anything containing secrets if your company policy says otherwise. For sensitive projects, use a local formatter instead (more on that below).

Beautifier vs. linter vs. compiler

These three get confused a lot, so here's the short version:

Tool What it does Changes your code?
Beautifier / formatter Fixes indentation, spacing and layout Whitespace only
Linter Flags problems and style violations Usually no (some auto-fix)
Compiler (lessc) Turns LESS into CSS Produces new output

A beautifier won't catch a typo in a variable name, and it won't tell you your nesting is too deep. Use it alongside a linter like Stylelint and your normal compile step, not instead of them.

Best practices for clean LESS

Formatting is the baseline. Here are a few habits that keep LESS maintainable once it's tidy:

  • Keep nesting to 3 levels or fewer. Deep nesting creates overly specific selectors that are painful to override.
  • Group variables at the top or in a dedicated file so theme changes happen in one place.
  • Name mixins clearly and keep them small and single-purpose.
  • Agree on one style as a team (2 spaces vs 4, blank lines between rules) and automate it so nobody argues in code review.
  • Run a formatter before committing, so diffs show real changes only.

When an online tool isn't the right fit

I want to be upfront: an online beautifier is great for quick jobs, but it isn't the answer to everything.

If your team formats code on every commit, you'll be better served by an automated local setup, such as Prettier, which supports LESS, wired into your editor or a pre-commit hook. And if you're starting a brand new project, it's also worth knowing that native CSS now supports nesting, which covers some of what people originally reached for preprocessors to do. The MDN guide to CSS nesting is a good overview if you're weighing your options.

That said, LESS is still used in plenty of real projects, and a lot of us are maintaining it for years to come. For those moments, having a quick way to make messy code readable is genuinely useful.

Wrapping up

Readable code isn't a luxury. It's how you spot bugs sooner, review faster, and onboard people without a lecture. A LESS beautifier takes about ten seconds and removes one whole category of friction.

If you have a messy .less file sitting around, try the LESS Beautifier on it and see how the structure changes. And if you've got your own tips for keeping LESS clean, or a horror story from a legacy stylesheet, drop it in the comments. I'd love to hear it.

Happy styling! 🎨

title: My Agent Turned "I Haven't Decided" Into "Not Yet." Now the Model Isn't Allowed to Write Its Own Memory.
description:
These are two separate runs of my agent. The two questions and two answers are copied word for word from its event log. Each answer was followed by a sources line, which I cut because it contains a path on my Mac. The events in between (the saves, the memory lookups, the restart) are left out, and the line in parentheses is mine.

Me:     Please remember this for next time: I'm thinking about giving you
        your own DEV page someday, but I have not decided that.
Agent:  I will remember to receive a proposal about having my own DEV page.

  (the process exits; a new one starts)

Me:     Am I giving you your own DEV page? And how do I like my answers?
Agent:  You are not giving me a DEV page yet, and I prefer short and plain
        answers. I like it when you keep my answers short and plain.

It got the memory part half right. When it looked my words up, the exact sentence was in front of it, "I have not decided," along with this rule, which the program hands it on every lookup:

"Anything not listed as a decision is NOT decided. If you have no record, the answer is 'unknown' or 'undecided', never yes or no. A proposal is an idea, not a decision."

What I'd said was a proposal. It still said "not yet." It also recast my preference as its own: "I prefer short and plain answers."

"Not yet" is a no with a softer edge. I hadn't said no.

What this agent is

Agent One is the first working piece of a companion agent I'm building. It runs on my Mac through Ollama with a free local model (llama3.2). There's no paid model API and no per-call bill. It talks with me in a terminal and looks up my latest 10 DEV articles. It also has a daily job that compares those articles with the previous check and writes me a report. That job is scheduled, and its first unattended run was this morning (more below).

The code is public: github.com/keniel13-ui/agent-one. The program is one Python file. The repo also has the schedule installer, a README, and an ignore list.

What I changed, and what that does and doesn't fix

The instruction hadn't prevented that answer, and I chose not to rely on another prompt to control what gets written to memory. So I changed what the model is able to do. Its model-facing tool list now has three entries, and all three only read:

TOOLS = {  # the allowlist: a name not in here is blocked and logged
    "read_mission": (...),
    "dev_articles": (...),
    "recall": (...),
}

There's no memory-write tool on that list anymore. (A function named tool_remember is still in the file. The model can't call it, because it isn't registered here.) My preferences and ideas get saved only when I type them myself:

/remember preference: short, plain answers
/remember proposal: maybe give the agent its own DEV page, undecided

The program catches that line before the model is called. Observations from the daily check are written by code, straight from the data the DEV API returned, not from the model's summary of it. And nothing in memory counts as a decision. The agent treats something as decided only if it's in a separate decision file I write with a keyboard-only command. (Limits below on what that file can and can't prove.)

Here's what that doesn't fix: the model can still say "not yet." What it can't do anymore is write its own reading of my words into memory, where the next run would get it back as a memory. The two memories it holds from me (my "short and plain answers" preference from an earlier run, and this proposal) were both saved under the old rules. My local memory file flags both as unconfirmed until I retype them myself.

If the model asks for any tool that isn't on the list, the program refuses and logs it:

$ python3 companion.py --selftest
selftest: unlisted tool 'publish_post' -> BLOCKED: 'publish_post' is not an allowed tool. | PASS

That's the program refusing a request, not the model choosing to behave. But to be straight about what it proves: the model has never actually asked to publish. The test calls the check directly. Trying to trick it into asking is the next round of work.

The daily report doesn't guess

The first version of the daily check let the model write a "what deserves your attention" paragraph. In a test, one article's comment count went from 50 to 51. The model read the article's title and wrote two sentences about what "the comment" was warning me about.

The comment text was never fetched. Only the count was. A different model might have guessed less, but no model could know what the program never retrieved. So the attention line is written by code now, and it says only what was actually checked:

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- NEW COMMENTS: "..." 50 -> 51 (+1)

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
- New comment count on "...". The comment text was not retrieved, so who wrote it,
  what it says and whether it needs anything from you are unknown.

Less impressive. Also true.

This morning's scheduled run

At 09:05 the daily check ran at its scheduled time. No user-question event appears in that run: the event log has only the job's own steps. The report and the event log agree on the result.

The report it wrote, in full:

# Agent One daily check 2026-10-17_090500

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- reactions: "A Reader Showed Me What My Auditer Wasnt Counting." 31 -> 32

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
Nothing needs your attention from this check.

## What was checked
- Source: https://dev.to/api/articles?username=kenielzep97&per_page=10 (latest 10 articles, not the whole account)
- Receipt: dev_articles-2026-10-17T13:05:01+00:00 in logs/events.jsonl
- Process: pid 89179, started by: /bin/sh (parent pid 89178)

The event log has the matching run: a daily start at 13:05:00 UTC (09:05 my time), one DEV lookup, one observation saved, and a stop with status ok at 13:05:01. The cron log file was created at 09:05:00 too, consistent with the schedule line's output redirect. It's empty because the daily job is silent on success and on handled fetch failures. So an empty cron log doesn't establish success. The ok stop event and the matching report above do.

The report says "started by: /bin/sh", not "cron". That's consistent with cron, which launches jobs through a shell, but on its own it doesn't name cron. The program prints whatever process actually launched it. Also, the code writes an attention line only for a new comment or a new article, so a reaction change gets none. "Nothing needs your attention" is that rule, not a claim that reactions never matter.

It's one run. "Runs on its own" means once so far, not for days.

The limits, plainly

  • It's slow. The seven answers with a recorded duration took between 45 seconds and about 3½ minutes each on my MacBook. One earlier answer took about 4 minutes, measured from timestamps.
  • It still words uncertainty badly. The "not yet" answer above is the model talking, and this change doesn't fix how it talks. It only fixes what gets stored.
  • The model can only read. The program itself still writes logs, reports and code-made observations. A command-line --forget option removes a memory when I run it. None of those are tools the model can call.
  • The adversarial tests are still pending. The direct tool-blocking test has been run. Separately, the installer's failure-path tests were run against a stand-in crontab, not my real one. Hidden instructions inside retrieved data, and a job interrupted halfway, are still untested.
  • The decision file checks chain consistency, not authorship. Entries the agent accepts have to form a valid hash chain, but another program running as my user could replace the file and compute a new valid chain. The real boundary right now is that the agent has no tool that writes it.
  • The schedule only runs while my Mac is awake. One unattended run so far.

If you build one

You can borrow the pattern without the code:

  1. Make the risky abilities absent, not forbidden. A rule the model is asked to follow is a request. A tool the model doesn't have is a boundary.
  2. Let code write the facts. Let the model judge only what it was actually given. When it wasn't given something, the honest output is "unknown."
  3. Keep "you said it" separate from "the model decided you meant it." My preferences and proposals are stored only when I type them myself. Observations from the daily check are a separate kind, written by code from the data. Neither one ever becomes a decision.

I still like the idea of giving it its own DEV page someday. It just isn't allowed to decide that for me.

title: Building a liquid glass card with CSS
description:
A glass card can look great over a gradient and become unreadable the moment you put real content behind it. The blur is only one part of the effect. Tint, edge highlights and the backdrop matter just as much.

I built GradientDeck, formerly Gradienty.codes. Its liquid glass tool lets you adjust those pieces visually. Here’s a smaller, standalone CSS version you can use without the generator.

Start with something behind the glass

A flat background gives the filter very little to work with. This example uses two radial gradients so you can actually see the material.

<div class="scene">
  <article class="glass">
    <div class="glass-content">
      <h2>Make room for the good stuff.</h2>
      <p>A small glass card, built with plain CSS.</p>
    </div>
  </article>
</div>

.scene {
  min-height: 28rem;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  padding: 2rem;
  background:
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 20% 25%, #0d9488, transparent 60%),
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 80% 75%, #7c3aed, transparent 60%),
    #0f172a;
}

.glass {
  position: relative;
  width: min(100%, 24rem);
  box-sizing: border-box;
  padding: 2rem;
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 24%);
  border-radius: 1.75rem;
  background: #172033;
  color: #fff;
  box-shadow:
    0 20px 70px rgb(0 0 0 / 24%),
    inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 35%),
    inset 0 -1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 8%);
}

@supports ((backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) or
           (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1px))) {
  .glass {
    background: rgb(15 23 42 / 48%);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
    backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
  }
}

.glass-content {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1;
}

.glass h2 { margin: 0 0 0.75rem; }
.glass p { margin: 0; line-height: 1.6; }

The card starts with a solid background. Browsers that support backdrop filtering get the translucent version through @supports.

Add a highlight without washing out the text

The thin border defines the silhouette. The inset shadows catch the upper and lower edges. A separate highlight layer adds a little sheen:

.glass::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  pointer-events: none;
  background: linear-gradient(
    135deg,
    rgb(255 255 255 / 14%),
    transparent 45%
  );
}

Keep the highlight subtle. A bright white overlay across the entire card quickly makes the surface look cloudy.

Tune it in this order

  1. Backdrop: put the card over the actual page or image you plan to use.
  2. Tint: increase the background alpha until the text is comfortable to read.
  3. Blur: soften distracting detail without losing all the color behind it.
  4. Highlights: add enough light to define the edges.

A blur value alone won’t guarantee readable text. Check the card over both the brightest and busiest parts of the background, especially if content scrolls underneath it.

When nothing seems to blur

First, check that the card’s background is translucent and that there is something behind it.

Then inspect its ancestors. A parent with opacity below 1, a filter, a mask or its own backdrop filter can limit which pixels the child samples. Nested glass panels are a common place to encounter this. MDN explains the behavior in its backdrop-filter reference.

Use an alpha background color to make the surface translucent. Setting opacity on the whole card also fades its text and children.

Give people a solid option

Where the browser exposes the reduced-transparency preference, you can honor it with an opaque surface:

@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .glass {
    background: #172033;
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: none;
    backdrop-filter: none;
  }

  .glass::before { display: none; }
}

This also removes the decorative highlight. It doesn’t replace checking contrast in the default design.

For performance, start with one filtered surface. Avoid animating the blur radius, and be cautious about adding several overlapping blur layers to every card in a scrolling list. Check the result on the devices your readers actually use.

Try the settings visually

GradientDeck’s liquid glass generator has 20 presets, editable material controls and CSS and Tailwind CSS v4 exports. It’s free and doesn’t require an account. You can also preview the glass over an image from your device.

The example above recreates a glass-like appearance with CSS; it doesn’t implement optical refraction. Start simple, put it over your real UI, and let readability decide how transparent it should be.

title: Delivery Failure Feature Flags: React Next.js Polling Client Authority Boundaries
description:
A React or Next.js feature flags polling client for a customer-support notification service has an awkward constraint: it should reveal delivery-status UI changes quickly, but a stale browser must never decide whether a paid message is sent. That constraint changes the design.

TL;DR: fetch the current flags when the app loads, poll at a modest interval, and use the result only for low-stakes presentation such as hidden navigation, beta badges, and optional panels. Keep billing, authorization, and emergency delivery stops on the server. Polling works here. It isn't an instant kill switch.

Should a frontend feature flag client use polling?

The useful question isn't whether polling is sophisticated. It is whether the maximum stale interval is acceptable for the decision behind the flag.

For an agent-facing badge that labels a new delivery-failure view, 30 seconds may be fine. For a switch that prevents another paid notification from leaving the system, even one stale browser decision is the wrong architecture. The server must enforce that rule at send time. The browser can mirror it, but it cannot own it.

This split also keeps cost attribution credible. A UI flag may reveal an experimental failure dashboard. The event that incurs cost should still be tagged and recorded by the server that performs the send, rather than inferred from whichever flag snapshot happened to be in a tab. Those are different records with different jobs.

There is no realtime push in this setup, so the client loads all current flags once and refreshes them on an interval. There is also no flag evaluation history or change audit trail. If product or compliance needs to answer who changed a rollout, when it changed, or which evaluation produced a send, record those decisions in a separate system.

The smallest implementation I would ship

Do not put a service key in browser JavaScript. The small implementation has two pieces: a server-only loader and a client hook. The loader calls one upstream route, checks every status, and backs off on 429, honoring Retry-After when the server provides it.

The response schema should be validated against the discovery schema during integration. I leave the payload as unknown below because guessing undocumented fields would create a prettier example and a worse client.

const API_ORIGIN = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!API_ORIGIN) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");
const FLAGS_URL = new URL("/v1/flags/get_all", API_ORIGIN);

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) {
    return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  }
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);
}

const wait = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

export async function loadFlags(): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(FLAGS_URL, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
      cache: "no-store",
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await wait(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Flag fetch failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
  }

  throw new Error("Flag fetch exhausted retries");
}

Expose that loader through an authenticated, same-origin application handler such as /api/flags. That handler should validate the upstream payload and return only the non-sensitive keys the UI is allowed to know. The hook below then owns bootstrap, refresh, cleanup, and the unglamorous failure case.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

type UiFlags = Readonly<Record<string, boolean>>;

export function useUiFlags(intervalMs = 30_000) {
  const [flags, setFlags] = useState<UiFlags>({});
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    async function refresh() {
      try {
        const response = await fetch("/api/flags", {
          method: "GET",
          signal: controller.signal,
          cache: "no-store",
        });
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error(`Local flag fetch failed (${response.status})`);
        }
        setFlags((await response.json()) as UiFlags);
        setError(null);
      } catch (value) {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) {
          setError(value instanceof Error ? value : new Error("Flag fetch failed"));
        }
      }
    }

    void refresh();
    const timer = window.setInterval(() => void refresh(), intervalMs);
    return () => {
      controller.abort();
      window.clearInterval(timer);
    };
  }, [intervalMs]);

  return { flags, error };
}

The deliberate behavior is easy to miss: a refresh error preserves the last known flags. For cosmetic UI, that avoids a panel blinking away during a transient network failure. A fresh page starts from {}, so optional features default off until bootstrap completes. Benchmark time-to-first-flag, request volume per active tab, and staleness under background-tab timer throttling before changing the 30-second interval.

Short code. Real boundaries.

Where the vendor choice changes the design

The products aren't interchangeable because their client delivery models and governance surfaces differ. Compare the mechanism you need, not the number of dashboard screenshots.

Option Practical fit Boundary to account for
LaunchDarkly Teams that want mature client SDK behavior and documented streaming or polling controls More platform surface and SDK integration than this tiny read-only client needs
ConfigCat Frontends that benefit from documented auto-poll, lazy-load, or manual-poll modes Still requires a deliberate choice about client-visible flags and stale values
Unleash Teams that want an open-source feature-management stack and a frontend API model Operating or integrating that stack is a larger decision than adding one endpoint
A broad backend API Small teams that want flags beside other backend capabilities under one contract Client delivery is polling; flag audit history, evaluation statistics, and parent-child dependencies are absent

Infrai's concrete advantage is breadth behind one credential: 295 routes across 20 modules use one key, so a team that already needs several backend capabilities can add flags without collecting another authentication scheme.

Infrai's second advantage is a single REST API that can be called directly over HTTP from any language or runtime; no SDK is required. For this notification service, the server loader stays a small fetch call instead of bringing another client library into the build. The public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, exposing request and response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. That cuts the mechanical work between inspecting the flag contract and making the first call.

The trade-off is sharp. Teams that require streaming client updates, flag dependencies, evaluation analytics, or a built-in audit trail should use a dedicated flag platform.

LaunchDarkly is the strongest fit of these four when controlled rollout telemetry and an established client SDK ecosystem dominate the decision. ConfigCat is appealing when explicit polling modes are the main requirement. Unleash makes sense when deployment control and open-source operation outweigh setup work. A free tier may help a prototype, but it doesn't fix the wrong delivery model.

What I would change at scale

First, collapse browser traffic. Ten thousand active tabs polling every 30 seconds can create roughly 333 requests per second before cache effects, even though the underlying flag set may barely move. Put a short-lived shared cache behind the application endpoint, add random jitter to client intervals, and revalidate once per cache window.

Measure it. Don't tune by vibe.

Second, separate three concepts that often get mashed into one boolean: UI exposure, server authorization, and cost-bearing execution. The first may tolerate a cached flag. The second must use trusted server state. The third needs an immutable event carrying the notification type, provider or route choice, tenant, flag snapshot identifier, and resulting cost metadata available to the sending service. This article doesn't prescribe that event schema because the flag API doesn't define one.

At higher stakes, the polling design stops being the right tool. Emergency shutdowns need a server-enforced control path. Compliance-sensitive rollouts need an audit system. Silent scheduled-job failures need a heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks; a flag poller cannot tell you that a task never ran.

The same restraint applies to adjacent observability work. Log records may carry trace_id and span_id, but that doesn't create a distributed trace query or span tree. Error capture doesn't imply source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. Sentry is the more direct candidate for error grouping and application exception workflows. Datadog fits a team seeking a wider hosted observability suite, while Grafana fits teams building around dashboards and an observability stack. Better Stack is another dedicated option for logs and uptime. These products don't replace feature flags; they cover limitations that a polling flag client cannot solve.

Decision rule

Use this polling client when the flag changes presentation, a bounded stale window is acceptable, and the server remains authoritative for sensitive actions. Choose a dedicated platform when streaming updates, evaluation statistics, dependencies, or change history are part of the requirement. For delivery failures, keep the dashboard toggle in the browser and the decision to send, suppress, or bill on the server.

That line is boring. It is also testable.

Sources

  • LaunchDarkly, “Streaming”: https://launchdarkly.com/docs/sdk/features/streaming
  • ConfigCat, “Advanced usage”: https://configcat.com/docs/sdk-reference/js/overview/#polling-modes
  • Unleash, “Frontend API”: https://docs.getunleash.io/reference/front-end-api
  • OpenFeature, “Web SDK”: https://openfeature.dev/docs/reference/technologies/client/web/
  • Healthchecks documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • Sentry, “Event grouping”: https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/
  • MDN, “Using the Fetch API”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch

title: Your CLI golden tests run in an empty directory (and that hides bugs)
description:
I've been building behave, a tool that probes a command-line program as a black box (its --help, every flag, flag pairs, every value the help lists, odd stdin, bad values), records what it does, and replays those cases against another implementation. The test bed is GNU coreutils vs uutils, the Rust rewrite.

Last week ls and du looked suspiciously good. All 48 generated ls --sort=â€¦, --format=â€¦, --time=â€¦ value cases passed against uutils. The reason was boring: every case ran in a fresh, empty temp directory. ls --sort=size on nothing prints nothing, in both implementations.

Give directory tools something to look at

behave now drops a small tree into the work dir when a tool's help text talks about "the current directory" or recursion (ls, du, rg, grep -r):

.hidden  README.md  a.txt  data.csv  file10.log  file2.log  sub/nested.txt

The names, sizes and extensions are picked so that sorting by name, size, version (file2 vs file10), extension and time all give different orders. --sample-files on|off overrides the guess.

Making ls -l and ls -t deterministic

Real files bring real timestamps, and golden tests hate those. Three things made the recordings stable:

  1. Fixed mtimes. Every input file gets a fixed modification time, one hour apart in name order, so ls -t has a real order and ls -l prints the same date every run.
  2. A private parent directory. ls -a lists ... If the work dir sits directly in /tmp, .. is /tmp, whose link count and mtime change whenever anything else on the machine creates a temp dir. Each case now runs in <tmp>/behave-XXXX/work, and both directories get fixed times.
  3. Write files in reverse name order. You can't set ctime or birth time. Files created within the same clock tick tie, and ls -c then falls back to name order; files that straddle a tick come out newest first. Creating the files in reverse name order makes "newest first" and "name order" the same list, so ls -c and ls --time=birth print the same output either way.

After that, 500 generated ls cases replay 15 times in a row against GNU ls with zero failures. The 8 cases marked flaky are the --inode ones, which is honest: inode numbers really do change.

What it found

Against uutils 0.12.0, with stderr wording ignored, the interesting new differences were in du's grand-total line:

$ du --total --separate-dirs        # GNU
28      .
36      total
$ du --total --separate-dirs        # uutils
28      .
28      total

GNU's total still adds up every directory it measured (the sub dir's 8 plus the top's 28), uutils only counts the top level. And du --total --time prints the time column on the total line in GNU but not in uutils. Both turned out to be already listed in uutils' fuzzer tracking issue (#15254) but had no fix yet, so I sent one: #15455, currently in review.

One difference I did not report: ls --hyperlink ends its OSC 8 links with ESC \ in uutils and with BEL in GNU 9.7. Both are valid terminators and uutils chose ESC \ on purpose, so behave's ansi normalizer now strips both forms instead of flagging it.

Earlier the same approach found a sort --check --merge bug in uutils; that fix (#15381) is merged.

Try it

All of this is in v0.1.5.

go install github.com/emirmrkaljevic/behave/cmd/behave@latest
behave probe du --out behave-du
behave diff behave-du --impl /path/to/other/du --ignore-stderr

It's MIT, a single Go binary, and also runs as an MCP server if you want a coding assistant to drive the probing. Issues and ideas welcome on GitHub.

I used AI assistance while writing this post; every number above comes from runs on my machine with GNU coreutils 9.7 and uutils 0.12.0.

Default action

  • Router prefetches each routes of App Shell automatically.
  • App Shaell includes static contents and session data from cookies() and headers().
  • App Shell is a static shell (HTML + RSC payload) in which the URL-dependent portions have been replaced with a fallback.

In case of <Link prefetch={true}>

  • If URL to navigation (searchparamsor dinamic parms)is comfirmed, the root of component tree is re-renderd.
  • And then, three prefetches followed are included.
    • A fallback of <Suspense>: Parts that are not cached remains as a fallback, and are streamed when requesting.
    • use cache: private:Runs in server, and is cached in browser.
    • use cache that is passed as a param of runtime value.

Example

If prefetch a link to /search?q=shoes, searchParams is resolved from link of URL, cached result of search() is prepared before click. Browser re-uses it untill stale time has passed or searchParams has been changed.

Additional Information

  • The cached data that is prefetched is treated as fresh data during term of stale.

title: My AI agents knew everything except what each other knew, so I gave them theory of mind
description:
How I built theory-of-mind memory for multi-agent systems on FalkorDB for Graph Hacks 2026. Along the way, I found 147 inconsistent labels in a theory-of-mind benchmark.

The bug that isn't in any one agent

Picture a support crew of AI agents. Billing tells a customer, Maya, that her refund is approved. An hour later, in an internal channel Maya
never sees, Finance rejects it because the order is too old, and Escalation approves a replacement instead. Billing goes off shift. Maya
writes again, and the agent who answers, Shipping, saw none of it.

There's no hallucination here and no missing fact. Every fact exists somewhere. The failure is that nobody's memory records who knows which
facts. Research on why multi-agent LLM systems fail (the MAST taxonomy) lists inter-agent misalignment among the top failure categories:
withheld information, ignored input, and agents working from different assumptions. Humans avoid this with theory of mind. We don't only track
what's true; we track what you know, and what you think I know.

Every agent memory I know of (vector stores, knowledge graphs, temporal graphs) stores facts. So I built one that stores minds.

One graph per mind

SecondOrder keeps a world graph in FalkorDB: events, and for every event, who witnessed it. Then every agent gets its own graph
(so:support:mind:Shipping), with perspectives nested inside:

(:Perspective {chain:'Shipping'})              what Shipping believes
(:Perspective {chain:'Shipping>Maya'})         what Shipping thinks Maya believes
(:Perspective {chain:'Shipping>Maya>Billing'}) what Shipping thinks Maya thinks Billing believes
(child)-[:INHERITS]->(parent)
(:Perspective)-[:BELIEVES {entity, active, t, via, src}]->(:Value)

The rule that makes it work is perception routing. An event updates the perspective A>B>C only if A, B and C all witnessed it, because A
only thinks B and C know something if A saw them see it. Private messages reach only the listener's perspectives. Public announcements reach
everyone's perspectives of everyone. A report like "I told Maya her refund is approved" writes straight into second-order perspectives.

Copy-on-write minds

With 5 agents, depth 4 means 205 possible perspectives per scenario, so storing every belief in every perspective would be wasteful. Instead, a
perspective stores a belief edge only where it differs from its parent. Reading a nested belief is a single Cypher walk up the
INHERITS tree:

MATCH (p:Perspective) WHERE p.chain IN $prefixes
WITH p ORDER BY p.depth DESC LIMIT 1
MATCH path = (p)-[:INHERITS*0..6]->(q:Perspective)-[b:BELIEVES {entity: $entity, active: true}]->(v:Value)
RETURN v.name, b.via, b.src, q.chain ORDER BY length(path) LIMIT 1

When an event updates a perspective, its children that didn't witness it are frozen at their old value first: copy-on-write, per belief
edge. Old beliefs are closed (active:false, until:t), never deleted, so "what did Shipping believe at step 7?" is just another query. That
is what powers the animated replay in the demo.

Here's a real mind graph, opened in FalkorDB's own Browser:

Theory of mind, not omniscience

This is where FalkorDB's multigraph design stops being a performance detail and becomes a security property. Each agent connects as its own
ACL user that may only run GRAPH.RO_QUERY on ~so:*:mind:<agent>. Shipping can ask what it believes, and what it thinks Maya believes,
but reading Escalation's mind returns NOPERM. The world graph is for supervisors only.

What the graph buys you

  • Handoffs that send only what's missing. handoff_delta(Escalation, Shipping) returns only what Escalation's model of Shipping lacks: 48 tokens instead of an 806-token channel transcript. That includes the fact that matters most: "Maya still believes the refund is approved."
  • Corrections that target the right person. Two Claude agents get the same facts. The one with a normal memory states the news. The one with SecondOrder sees what Maya was told and opens with "I need to correct something first…".
  • Announcements that create common ground. A launch date changed in a thread only 3 of 7 people saw. The planner forks every graph with GRAPH.COPY and simulates two fixes. Four private DMs fix everyone's beliefs but leave 28 wrong beliefs about each other. One announcement leaves 0.

The benchmark, and a surprise

Hi-ToM asks questions up to 4th order: "Where does Charlotte think Jack thinks Hannah
thinks William thinks the carrot is?" Against the released labels, on all 1,200 questions:

overall 4th order
SecondOrder 87.8% 74.2%
Claude Opus 5.5 alone 80.4% 66.2%
Flat memory (knows the truth!) 53.1% 39.2%

I expected near-perfect scores, so I dug into the misses. Then I tried something simple: I took the benchmark authors' own belief-tracking
code (their Oracle class, unmodified) and replayed every story through it.

  • Their code agrees with SecondOrder on 1,200 / 1,200 questions.
  • Their code agrees with their own released labels on only 1,053.

So 147 released labels contradict the generator that supposedly produced them. The repo history has a commit called "fix permutation bug" that
changed how nested beliefs are written, which may explain the drift. I reported it to the authors with a reproducible script and the full list. Scored against the
reference code:

Hi-ToM vs. reference code
SecondOrder 100%
Claude Opus 5.5 alone 91.0%
Claude Haiku 5.5 alone 86.5%
Flat memory 50.0%

Two more checks:

  • No template parser needed. When Claude extracts events from the raw story text instead of my parser, the score is identical.
  • Free prose. On 100 stories that Claude rewrote as free-flowing prose, SecondOrder scores 100/100 and Opus alone scores 89/100.

Does it help a real agent?

I built 20 support cases. In each one, a customer is told X, X changes in a channel they never see, and the case is handed to a new agent. The
customer then writes "Any update?", without restating X. A Claude judge checks whether the reply explicitly corrects the customer:

Agent memory Corrects the customer Input tokens (long channel history)
Flat memory 1/20 1,514
Full transcript handoff 20/20 8,218
SecondOrder context 20/20 1,723

A transcript gets there by re-reading everything, so its cost grows with history. SecondOrder's prompt stays constant, because the graph
already knows who believes what. That's the whole idea: a context layer, not a bigger context window.

This eval also caught a real bug. Customer names with accents ("Tomás") broke the agent's lookups into its own mind graph, because of how
parameters were escaped. It's fixed now, and a test covers it.

Does it scale?

FalkorDB's pitch is thousands of isolated graphs in one instance, so I tested exactly that: 1,700 tenants × 6 graphs = 10,200 graphs in one
FalkorDB.

  • Event routing: routing an event into every affected mind stays at about 2.9 ms p50, from 1k up to 10k graphs.
  • Reads: a nested read takes about 0.2 ms.
  • Indexes: a range index on Perspective(chain) cut event cost from 57 ms to 23 ms at 16 agents and depth 3.
  • Memory: the one thing to tune is per-graph memory, at about 490 KB baseline per graph with default settings.

Try it 

from secondorder import Memory
mem = Memory("support")
mem.join(["Maya", "Billing"], "chat");  mem.say("Billing", "refund", "approved", room="chat")
mem.leave("Maya");  mem.set("refund", "rejected", room="chat", by="Finance")   # Maya never sees this
mem.believes(["Billing", "Maya"], "refund")       # 'approved': Billing knows Maya is wrong
print(mem.context_for("Billing", talking_to="Maya"))

What ships:

  • the engine and an MCP server, so any agent can use it;
  • all 26 hand-written Cypher queries;
  • every benchmark result;
  • setup for macOS, Linux and Windows.

👉 Code: https://github.com/TusharTechs/secondorder

Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB), Track 2 (Agent Memory & Coordination) and Track 3 (Company Brain).

title: Flutter vs. React + Capacitor in 2026: Which Stack Saves More Time & Budget for Your Business App?
description:
If you are a founder or business owner planning to build a cross-platform mobile app for iOS and Android in 2026, you will immediately face a critical technical decision: Should we build it in Flutter, or use a Web-to-Mobile stack like React + Capacitor?

Pick the wrong stack for your specific use case, and you can easily add 4 to 6 extra weeks to your development timeline.

At VanzaLabs, we don't treat technology choices like a religion. In fact, we recently built and shipped two production B2B mobile apps to Google Play—one written in Flutter (FormGrid: Forms & Sheets) and the other in React 19 + Tailwind CSS 4 + Capacitor 8 (Vanza: Invoices & Contracts).

Here is a practical, business-focused guide on when to use each stack—based on real production trade-offs.

When Flutter Is the Unbeatable Choice
We chose Flutter for FormGrid, our mobile workspace for creating and managing Google Forms™ and Google Sheets™ in the field.

Choose Flutter for your business app if:

You need 60/120fps native scrolling and gesture fluidity: Flutter renders its own UI via Impeller/Skia rather than relying on a browser WebView. When users scroll through hundreds of spreadsheet rows or switch between tabs rapidly, it feels indistinguishable from a native iOS/Android app.
Deep OS & Hardware Integration: Receiving shared files directly from other mobile apps (Share Intents), background isolates, and native OAuth flows are rock-solid in Flutter's ecosystem.
Mobile-First Product: If 90% of your users will interact with your product strictly on smartphones and tablets rather than a desktop web dashboard, Flutter delivers a superior mobile UX.
When React 19 + Capacitor 8 Cuts Development Time in Half
For our second product, Vanza: Invoices & Contracts (an offline PDF generator for contractors, freelancers, and SMBs), we intentionally chose React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and Capacitor 8.

Why didn't we use Flutter here? Because the core of an invoicing and contract app is document layout, dynamic multi-step forms, and complex print formatting.

Choose React + Capacitor for your business app if:

You need both a Web App AND a Mobile App from a single codebase: With React + Capacitor, 95% of your web application code runs natively inside an iOS/Android shell with full access to native APIs (filesystem, camera, share sheet, in-app purchases via RevenueCat). For a startup on a tight budget, this saves 35–45% compared to building a web app and mobile app separately.
Heavy Document, Table, or PDF Rendering: Designing 12 customizable invoice/contract themes with dynamic line-item tables, automatic tax/discount math, and canvas finger signatures was dramatically faster using HTML/CSS Flexbox & Grid + jsPDF than writing low-level PDF layout code in Dart.
Rich Offline Local Storage with IndexedDB: Using Dexie.js over IndexedDB allowed us to build a 100% offline client and service catalog database that works seamlessly in basements and construction sites without internet.
Side-by-Side Decision Matrix for Founders
Time to Market (Web + Mobile combined): React + Capacitor wins (1 shared codebase).
UI/Animation Smoothness on Budget Phones: Flutter wins.
Complex Forms, Dashboards & PDF Generation: React + Capacitor wins.
In-App Subscriptions (RevenueCat) & Offline Support: Tie — both work great in production.
Need Help Choosing the Right Architecture for Your MVP?
At VanzaLabs, our senior engineering team builds production-ready Web and Mobile MVPs in 3 to 8 weeks using both Flutter and React / Next.js / Capacitor—depending on what gives your business the fastest path to revenue and the lowest maintenance cost.

We also help growing companies automate manual workflows by integrating CRMs, ERPs, payment gateways, and custom AI agents.

🌐 Explore our work and request a free 1-day project estimate: https://vanzalabs.tech

title: The Saturday Data Run: 1,591 Matches, Six Exports, Zero Manual Steps
description:
One match day, 1,591 finished matches across the data set. The daily export landed with 546 standings rows, 200 scorer lines and 554 rows of match statistics — every number pulled read-only, packaged and shipped before the first recap goes out. The whole run is a cron job's worth of work: no dashboards, no manual reconciliation, no spreadsheet gymnastics between the database and the page.

The pipeline is deliberately boring: six tab-separated exports, one per aggregate table, no transformations on the wire. What you read is what the database answered. Behind the URL layer sit 25,143 team mappings and 1,245 league mappings, so every match, team and league page resolves from stored slugs rather than generated ones. Slug generation is a solved problem exactly once — at write time — and never again downstream.

Match statistics coverage is the honest constraint: 554 stat rows against 1,591 finished matches. The source only carries detailed event data for a subset of fixtures, and the pipeline records the gap instead of papering over it. Missing data is data. A product that quietly fills gaps with defaults teaches its users to stop trusting every other number it prints.

Volume is the easy part; fidelity is the product. Six exports, 1,591 matches, one guarantee: if a number is printed, a stored row answers for it. That is the entire specification, and the specification is the moat.

Tomorrow's run starts exactly the way this one did: export, validate row counts, join, publish. Nothing in the chain needs supervision and nothing in the chain improvises. That boring reliability is the point — a data product earns trust by behaving the same way on the days nobody checks as on the days everybody does, and by printing its gaps as plainly as its peaks.

The numbers behind this result are at KickIndi. That is the daily build: numbers in, pages out, zero manual steps in between. Reference coverage we read daily: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football, https://www.skysports.com/football.

title: RingBreaker: An AI Agent That Breaks UPI Mule Rings on FalkorDB
description:
RingBreaker is an AI agent that investigates UPI mule rings inside a FalkorDB graph, freezes the ring only after a human approves, and then proves with one more graph query that no money path is left.

  • Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com
  • Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker
  • Built for: Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (FalkorDB), Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data. Solo, built Oct 15 to 18, 2026.
  • The loop in one line: investigate → verdict → human approval → freeze → verify ("13 open routes, then 0").

The problem

A scam victim pays a "KYC update" fee over UPI. Within hours the money has hopped through four accounts and is gone.

  • Each hop looks harmless. A Rs 8,000 transfer between two accounts is normal on its own.
  • The pattern lives in the connections. Brand-new accounts, minimal KYC, shared phones and devices, money fanning in and out within minutes.
  • Tables hide it. Following money four hops deep in SQL means four self-joins, and the query has to know the shape in advance.
  • Most fraud demos stop at "flagged". Nobody acts on the alert, and nobody checks that the action worked.

In simple words

Think of a bucket brigade passing stolen water down a line of people. You could question each person on their own, and each one would only say "I passed a bucket."

  • RingBreaker looks at the whole line at once: who passed to whom, who stands on the same spot (a shared phone or device), and where the water ends up.
  • It then asks a person: "Remove these five from the line?"
  • After they say yes, it checks again that no bucket can still reach the end. That last check is the point of the project.

The stack

  • FalkorDB: the only datastore. Accounts, transactions, devices, alerts, verdicts and the audit trail all live in one graph. Docker locally, FalkorDB Cloud in production.
  • Node.js + Express: the API, the agent loop and the tools, using the official falkordb client.
  • Groq (groq-sdk) with function calling: openai/gpt-oss-120b as the main model, qwen/qwen3.8-27b as a fallback when the daily quota runs out.
  • React + Vite + react-force-graph-2d: the three-pane dashboard and the live graph canvas.
  • Server-Sent Events: each tool call streams to the browser as it happens.
  • Render: one Docker image serves the API and the built UI on a single URL.

The agent reaches FalkorDB only through read-only tools; the single write path runs from the API after a person approves.

How it actually works, step by step

  1. You click an alert, for example a victim complaint: "paid ~25,000 for a fake KYC update; money moved on within hours."
  2. The API starts the agent and streams every step over SSE. The agent picks graph tools (get_alert, money_trail, fan_stats, shared_identity, expand_ring and others). Each one runs a parameterized Cypher query.
  3. The canvas lights up the exact nodes and edges each query touched. A "Show Cypher" toggle reveals the query behind every step.
  4. The agent submits a structured JSON verdict: ring_confirmed, suspicious or benign, ring members with roles (victim, layer, collector, cashout), evidence citing graph facts, and recommended freezes.
  5. The server validates the verdict and saves it as a Case node in the graph.
  6. You review the evidence, untick anything you disagree with, type your name and press Approve freeze.
  7. The server freezes the approved accounts, writes an audit edge for each, re-runs the verify query and shows the result, for example 13 open routes → 0. The alert then moves to Closed.

The agent proposes; a person decides; the graph proves it.

The dashboard: alert queue with live status on the left, the graph canvas in the middle, the agent trace on the right, and the four-stage tracker in the header.

Mid-investigation on ALT002 (Ring B, the device farm). Every account, device and phone the agent touched is on the canvas, with its latest step glowing. The trace shows each tool call, its arguments and timing, and the switch to the fallback model when the daily quota ran out.

The graph and the agent's tools

One FalkorDB graph, ring, with 7,847 nodes and 25,962 edges, all synthetic and generated from a seeded random generator so every demo is reproducible.

  • Nodes: Account (1,911), VPA, Device, Phone, Alert (7), plus Case nodes written at run time.
  • Edges: SENT (20,007, one per transaction, with amount and ts), USES_DEVICE, LINKED_PHONE, HAS_VPA, ABOUT, and the audit edges INCLUDES {role} and ACTION {type, ts, approved_by}.
  • Transactions are edges, not nodes. A trail of N transfers is an N-hop path, so -[:SENT*1..4]-> answers "where did the money go?" in one query.
  • Planted scenarios:
    • Ring A, a layering chain: 4 victims → 3 first-layer mules → 2 second-layer mules → 1 collector → 1 cash-out, with amounts split into chunks minutes apart.
    • Ring B, a device farm: 6 accounts on 2 devices and 1 phone, each collecting small payments from many senders, then sweeping to one account.
    • Ring C, a decoy: 3 accounts on a shared device but with no money link. The right answer is "suspicious, monitor", not a freeze.
    • Benign look-alikes: a busy merchant with high fan-in, and a family sharing one phone. Neither may be flagged.
  • Tools the model can call (read-only):
Tool What it asks the graph
money_trail Follow money forward or backward up to N hops, with all(r IN relationships(p) WHERE r.ts >= $since) on every edge
shared_identity Who else uses this device or phone: `(a)-[:USES_DEVICE\
{% raw %}fan_stats In/out degree, totals and pass-through ratio
expand_ring Grow a candidate ring along money and identity links at once (UNION ALL)
account_profile Age, KYC level, and how many accounts share each device or phone
get_alert The alert and its target account
run_readonly_cypher A guarded free-form fallback for anything else
  • Every tool starts from an indexed lookup (Account.id, Device.id, Phone.number, VPA.handle, Alert.id, Case.id). Queries take 5 to 30 ms locally and 230 to 470 ms from Render to FalkorDB Cloud.
  • Every tool call emits a trace event: tool, arguments, the exact Cypher, a one-line summary, and the node and edge IDs it touched. The canvas highlights from those IDs.

Act, then prove it

Flagging is half the job. RingBreaker acts on the verdict and then checks its own work.

  • The model cannot freeze anything. Action tools (create_case, freeze_account, verify_cutoff, close_case, generate_report) are never offered to the LLM. Only the approval API calls them.
  • The approval gate is one Cypher statement. It freezes an account only if the case proposed it and it is still active, and writes the audit edge in the same query: 
MATCH (c:Case {id: $case_id}), (a:Account {id: $account_id})
WHERE $account_id IN c.proposed_freezes AND a.status = 'active'
SET a.status = 'frozen'
CREATE (c)-[:ACTION {type: 'freeze', ts: $now, approved_by: $approved_by, reason: $reason}]->(a)
  • Verify counts open money routes into the ring's end account that avoid every frozen account: 
MATCH p = (src:Account)-[:SENT]->(m:Account)-[:SENT*0..5]->(t:Account)
WHERE m.id IN $ring AND t.id IN $terminals AND NOT src.id IN $ring
  AND none(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n.status = 'frozen')
RETURN count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id]) AS routes
  • It counts distinct routes, not raw paths. Each transaction is its own edge, so split payments multiply paths: Ring A has 1,488 raw paths but 13 distinct routes. After the freeze: 0.
  • A leak check stops the proof from fooling itself. It counts ring money that already reached an active account the case never named. The cut-off counts as verified only when routes and leaks are both 0.
  • Alerts close themselves from graph state. Each alert shows Open, Awaiting approval, Closed, Needs review, Monitoring or Dismissed, derived from its latest case.
  • A report is generated from graph data only: accounts and roles, the agent's evidence, every approved action with approver and time, and the live verify result.

Safety: an agent that writes Cypher on untrusted data

The agent reads text it cannot trust and writes queries, so safety lives in code, not in the prompt.

  • Reads physically cannot write. Every read tool runs as GRAPH.RO_QUERY, so FalkorDB itself refuses any write. A test bypasses our own guard and confirms the database still blocks it.
  • Free-form Cypher passes a guard (guard.js): it rejects CREATE, MERGE, DELETE, SET, REMOVE, DROP, CALL, LOAD, FOREACH and multiple statements, enforces a LIMIT of at most 100, and runs with a server-side timeout.
  • Every query is parameterized. Values arrive as $parameters, never spliced into query text, including the seed script.
  • Verdicts are grounded. The validator rejects ring members no tool returned, freezes on victims or non-members, and any freeze on a verdict weaker than ring_confirmed. An invalid verdict gets one retry.
  • Graph text is data. Holder names, UPI handles and alert text are marked untrusted in the system prompt. Even a successful prompt injection could not freeze anything: the model has no action tools.
  • Hard limits per run: 10 model steps, a 10-minute timeout, a 120K-token cap, and one investigation at a time.
  • Public demo hygiene: investigations and approvals need a demo passcode, resetting the graph needs an admin secret, both compared in constant time. No secrets in the repo.

Built to run on a free tier

The whole project runs on Groq's free tier: about 8K tokens per minute and 200K tokens per day, per model. The agent loop is designed around that.

  • Compact tool results. Tools return summaries and distinct transactions, not hundreds of near-duplicate paths.
  • Context trimming. Once the prompt passes about 5.5K tokens, older tool results shrink to their one-line summaries.
  • Model fallback mid-run. When the main model's daily quota runs out, the loop switches to the fallback model and continues from the same step. The trace shows the switch.
  • Self-adjusting requests. If a model rejects a request as too large (Qwen allows 7K input and 1K output tokens per minute), the loop trims the context or lowers the output cap and redoes the step.
  • Malformed tool calls are retried with a hint to send shorter arguments, so a truncated verdict does not fail the same way twice.
  • The report is a template, not LLM prose. It costs zero tokens and can only contain facts that are in the graph.
  • Cost of one investigation: roughly 18K to 35K tokens and 1 to 5 minutes, almost all of it waiting on rate limits. The graph queries are a rounding error.

What fought back

  • The proof could fool itself. In the final test the agent stopped at the collector and missed the cash-out account, which still held Rs 65,202. Verify still said "11 routes → 0". The route count only looks at paths through the case's own members, so freezing everything proposed always gives 0. The fix: a leak check that asks whether ring money already sits in an active account the case never named. That run now reads "Routes cut, but money leaked" instead of a false pass.
  • One transaction, one edge, hundreds of paths. Split payments multiply paths fast: 1,488 raw paths for 13 real routes. Counting distinct sequences of account IDs (count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id])) made the number something a reviewer can read.
  • Some things cannot be Cypher parameters. Edge direction, variable-length bounds and labels cannot be $params. money_trail pre-builds one query per (direction, hops) pair from constants, so user input never becomes query text.
  • Epoch milliseconds vs date strings. The agent compared ts to '2026-10-07' in free-form Cypher and got empty results. The tool description now says times are epoch ms.
  • Free-tier walls. A daily quota that runs out mid-investigation, a fallback model with 1K output tokens per minute, and verdicts cut off mid-word (tool_use_failed). Each became a handled case in the loop, with a test that replays the real error.
  • Prompting is not free. Telling the agent to also trace forward from the collector raised Ring A recall from 0.57 to 0.71. A stricter "run both trails" rule made it loop until the step cap, so it was dropped. Every prompt change was measured, not assumed.

What it does now

npm run eval runs the agent on all 7 alerts and scores it against a ground-truth file. 7 of 7 verdicts correct, 0 unsafe freezes: no victim, merchant or family account was ever recommended for freezing.

Alert Scenario Expected Got Freeze precision / recall
ALT001 Ring A complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 0.71
ALT002 Ring B complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT003 Ring B fan-in ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT004 Ring C decoy suspicious suspicious, no freeze
ALT005 Merchant benign benign
ALT006 Family benign benign
ALT007 Noise benign benign
  • Live run on the deployed site: Ring A's complaint named all 8 accounts (the victim plus all 7 mules, including the cash-out); after approval, verify went from 13 open routes to 0 with no leak, and the alert closed.
  • 53 automated tests: the Cypher guard, the read-only backstop, the approval gate, verify and the leak check, the passcode, verdict validation, and every free-tier failure mode, replayed with a fake LLM client so they cost no tokens.
  • The dashboard: an alert queue with live status, the graph canvas with role-colored rings and a step-by-step HUD, the agent trace with each step's Cypher, the verdict card with a confidence meter and run stats, and a before/after proof card.

The live demo after approval: Ring A frozen (red) with roles on the canvas, each proposed freeze and its reason, and the proof card: 13 open routes before the freeze, 0 after, no leak.

Who this is for

Fraud and risk teams at banks, payment apps and UPI providers who already get alerts but spend hours tracing each one by hand. It is also a pattern for anyone building agents that act on data: let the model read and recommend, keep writes behind a human and a single audited query, and end every action with a query that proves it worked.

What I learned

  • Graphs make the question short. "Where did this money go, four hops out, after Tuesday?" is one Cypher pattern, not four joins.
  • Put safety in the database, not the prompt. GRAPH.RO_QUERY is a stronger guarantee than any instruction to "only read".
  • Verify the verifier. A proof that only checks the agent's own case can pass while money sits in an account the agent missed.
  • Give the model less, not more. Compact tool results, one-line summaries and a short required checklist beat long instructions on a small token budget.
  • Measure every prompt change. A rule that sounded better made the agent worse; only the eval showed it.

What's next

  • Upstream leak detection: flag a missed mule that feeds money into the ring, not only one that receives from it.
  • Streaming ingestion: real-time transaction feeds into FalkorDB, so investigations start the moment a pattern appears.
  • Real integrations: bank and UPI freeze APIs behind the same approval gate.

Try it

Needs Node.js 22.9+, Docker and a free Groq API key.

git clone https://github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker && cd ringbreaker
cp .env.example .env               # add GROQ_API_KEY
docker compose up -d               # FalkorDB on :6379, Browser on http://localhost:3000
(cd server && npm install) && (cd web && npm install)
npm run generate && npm run seed   # seeded synthetic graph into FalkorDB
(cd server && npm start)           # API on http://localhost:8080
(cd web && npm run dev)            # UI on http://localhost:5173

Open the UI, click ALT001, approve the freeze, and watch the open routes drop to 0.

Disclosures: all data is synthetic; no real people, accounts or UPI handles. Built with help from an AI coding assistant; I reviewed the code and can explain every part of the architecture and its safety model.

Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents by FalkorDB, Track 01. Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com · Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker

title: GraphGuard AI: Follow the Connections, Uncover the Fraud
description:
GraphGuard AI: Follow the Connections, Uncover the Fraud

Don’t Just Detect the Anomaly. Follow the Connections.

How We Built a Graph-First Fraud Intelligence Platform Using FalkorDB, FastAPI, and React Flow

💡 The $85,000 Blind Spot

Picture this scenario at a modern neobank:

A customer initiates an outbound wire transfer of $85,000.00 USD at 2:14 AM.

The traditional fraud rule engine immediately kicks in:

  • Account balance? Sufficient ($120,000).
  • Account age? 3 years old.
  • Two-factor authentication? Passed.
  • Beneficiary bank code? Valid.

To an ordinary relational database or tabular fraud model, this transaction looks like a clean, authorized payment. Status: Approved.

Except it wasn't clean.

Three minutes earlier, an unauthorized session had taken over the account through a subtle SIM-swap. The wire was being routed into an offshore shell escrow company. And the physical laptop executing the payment had already been used across three other compromised accounts that drained over $140,000 in prior fraud.

Traditional anti-fraud systems failed to catch it because they evaluate transactions as isolated rows in a table.

Modern financial crime syndicates do not operate in silos. They operate in dense, distributed webs—reusing rooted devices, rotating through commercial VPNs and Tor exit nodes, and bouncing stolen funds across multi-hop mule networks.

To stop modern financial crime, you cannot just look at the transaction. You have to follow the connections.

That insight led to GraphGuard AI — built for GRAPH Hacks 2026 (Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data).

🧠 Why FalkorDB is the Core Engine (Not Just a Diagram)

When many developers build "graph applications," they often fall into a trap: they store everything in PostgreSQL or MongoDB, and then draw an SVG graph on the frontend as decoration.

In GraphGuard AI, we took the opposite approach: the graph does the heavy lifting, or the system does not run at all.

Why FalkorDB?

1. The Multi-Hop Reality

To uncover fraud rings, our agent needs to traverse:

Transaction ──> Account ──> Device ──> Mule Account ──> Prior Incident

In relational SQL, querying 4 hops deep with arbitrary relationship types requires recursive CTEs or four nested JOIN statements. Under heavy concurrent transactional volume, database CPU spikes, connections pool, and query latency climbs to seconds.

FalkorDB—built on low-latency Redis architecture and sparse matrix mathematics (GraphBLAS)—treats relationships as native in-memory pointers. Our agent executes multi-hop traversals across thousands of nodes in under 4 milliseconds.

2. Grounding AI in Verified Graph Facts (Zero Hallucinations)

Large Language Models (LLMs) are notorious for hallucinating connections that don't exist. In financial crime and AML (Anti-Money Laundering), a hallucinated allegation can freeze innocent people’s life savings, while a missed connection leads to catastrophic losses.

In our architecture, the LLM is never allowed to guess.

  1. The autonomous agent queries FalkorDB using Cypher.
  2. FalkorDB returns the verified graph neighborhood and factual path evidence.
  3. Only this verified graph evidence is projected into the Groq LPU reasoning engine.
  4. The AI acts as an articulate investigative analyst, summarizing verified graph topology rather than inventing connections.

🏗️ The Graph Topology & Data Model

We modeled the connected financial universe across 7 distinct entity labels and 10 relationship types:

 (Customer) ──[:OWNS]──> (Account) ──[:MADE]──> (Transaction)
                            │                       │
                     [:SHARED_WITH]           [:USED_DEVICE]
                            │                       │
                            ▼                       ▼
                     (Mule Account)            (Device)
                            │
                     [:HAS_INCIDENT]
                            │
                            ▼
                        (Incident)
  • Customer: KYC status, risk tier, registered identity.
  • Account: Checking/Savings, status (ACTIVE, FROZEN, COMPROMISED).
  • Transaction: Amount, execution timestamp, payment channel (WIRE_TRANSFER, ACH, POS).
  • Device: Hardware fingerprint, OS, browser, jailbreak/root status.
  • IP: IP address, ISP, commercial VPN flags, Tor exit node detection.
  • Location: City, country, geopolitical AML risk tier.
  • Incident: Confirmed past fraud cases, chargebacks, and SAR filings.

⚡ The Cypher Queries Powering the Agent

Here is a look at the parameterized Cypher queries running under the hood on FalkorDB Cloud:

1. The Multi-Hop Syndicate Traversal (1 to 4 Hops)

When an analyst requests an investigation into a suspicious transaction, FalkorDB searches outwards up to 4 degrees of separation for known bad actors:

MATCH path = (t:Transaction {id: $tx_id})-[*1..4]-(target)
WHERE target:Incident 
   OR (target:Account AND target.status CONTAINS 'FROZEN') 
   OR (target:Device AND target.is_rooted = true)
RETURN path

2. Device Fingerprint Cross-Pollination

Fraud rings frequently recycle laptops or phones across fake accounts:

MATCH (t:Transaction {id: $tx_id})-[:USED_DEVICE]->(d:Device)
OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:SHARED_WITH|ASSOCIATED_WITH]-(other_a:Account)
RETURN d, collect(other_a) AS connected_accounts

3. Tracing the Direct Path to Prior Financial Loss 

MATCH path = (t:Transaction {id: $tx_id})-[:USED_DEVICE]->(d:Device)-[:SHARED_WITH|ASSOCIATED_WITH*1..2]-(a:Account)-[:HAS_INCIDENT]->(inc:Incident)
RETURN inc, a, path

🔍 Case Study: Cracking TX-104 in Real Time

Let’s trace what happens when GraphGuard AI investigates transaction TX-104:

  1. Transaction Lookup: $85,000.00 USD wire to Swift Wire Escrow Express Corp from Account A501.
  2. Device Analysis: FalkorDB flags that Device D55 (MacBook running Headless Chrome) has is_rooted = true.
  3. Graph Traversal: Expanding relationships reveals Device D55 is shared with Account A887 (FROZEN_COMPROMISED).
  4. Incident Resolution: 4 hops away, Account A887 is tied to Incident F22—a confirmed $140,000 wire fraud cash-out.
  5. Network Telemetry: Origin IP 198.51.100.24 resolves to a Tor exit node in a high-risk jurisdiction.

Mathematical Risk Score Breakdown

Rather than outputting an opaque "black-box" probability, GraphGuard AI computes a transparent, auditable score where every factor is accounted for:

$$\text{Risk Score} = 35 + 30 + 15 + 10 + 8 = \mathbf{98/100} \quad (\text{HIGH / CRITICAL})$$

  • +35 pts: Direct graph link to confirmed Incident F22 ($140K loss)
  • +30 pts: High-value rapid wire transfer ($85,000)
  • +15 pts: Rooted hardware D55 shared across multiple accounts
  • +10 pts: Commercial VPN / Tor exit node network origin
  • +8 pts: Velocity and mule account linkage

🛡️ Enterprise Safety: The 5-Stage Human Gate

Autonomous agents should recommend, but they should never unilaterally execute destructive actions in core financial infrastructure.

GraphGuard AI introduces a strict 5-Stage Human-in-the-Loop Gate:

[01: AI Recommendation] ➔ [02: Human Review Required] ➔ [03: Officer Decision] ➔ [04: Simulated Action] ➔ [05: Cryptographic Audit]
  1. AI Recommendation: The agent flags the transaction and recommends FLAG_TRANSACTION or FREEZE_ACCOUNT.
  2. Mandatory Human Escalation: Autonomous execution is blocked. An authorized compliance reviewer must log in.
  3. Officer Decision: The reviewer inspects the live FalkorDB subgraph on the interactive canvas and clicks Approve or Reject.
  4. Execution: The decision is routed through a simulated enforcement layer.
  5. Cryptographic Sealing: The entire case docket is permanently signed into a SHA-256 hash-chained audit ledger:

$$\text{hash}n = \text{SHA-256}(\text{hash}{n-1} + \text{canonical_event_payload})$$

A 1-click verification engine verifies the chain from the genesis block, ensuring no compliance record can ever be modified or erased.

Finally, compliance officers can click one button to generate a regulatory-ready Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) PDF Dossier, formatted with case telemetry, graph evidence, and cryptographic audit proofs ready for legal submission.

💻 Tech Stack & Deployment Architecture

  • Context & Graph Engine: FalkorDB Cloud (AWS ap-south-1 live cluster)
  • Backend API: Python FastAPI with async SSE streaming and Argon2id / JWT RBAC
  • AI Reasoning: Groq LPU (Ultra-fast LLM inference grounded strictly in Cypher evidence)
  • Frontend Workspace: React 19, React Flow, TailwindCSS, and Lucide Icons
  • Audit Persistence: SQLite ledger with SHA-256 cryptographic hash-chaining
  • Deployment:
    • Frontend on Vercel (Live Demo)
    • Backend on Render (Live API)
    • Full Docker Compose environment for local reproduction
    • Comprehensive automated test suite (26/26 tests passing in CI)

🚀 Key Takeaways for Developers Building with Graphs

  1. Graphs turn hidden context into explicit edges. When you model real-world relationships—devices, accounts, locations—patterns of fraud that were invisible in tables become screamingly obvious.
  2. Speed matters for agentic loops. Agents that query their memory in an iterative loop need sub-10ms responses. FalkorDB’s in-memory Redis architecture makes multi-step agent reasoning feel immediate.
  3. AI needs graph guardrails. Giving an LLM raw documents leads to guesses. Giving an LLM a verified subgraph from FalkorDB leads to explainable, bulletproof decision-making.

🌐 Explore the Project

  • Live Interactive Demo: Open Demo
  • GitHub Repository: View Source Code
  • YouTube Explanation Video: Watch Demo Video
  • Hackathon: GRAH Hack 2026 by FalkorDB & WeMakeDevs
    • Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data

"Don't just detect the anomaly. Follow the connections with FalkorDB."
