title: Hono vs Express vs Fastify (and NestJS) in 2026: Real Benchmarks on Node 24, Node 26 and Bun
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Hono vs Express in 2026 is a closer race than the benchmark charts you've seen suggest. On Node.js 24, Hono served 1.44× as many JSON requests per second as Express 5 in my tests, and Fastify was right next to it. But Fastify beat Hono on route parameters and POST bodies, and NestJS added 21 to 23% overhead on top of whichever engine it ran on. The biggest jump didn't come from the framework at all: moving Hono from Node to Bun gave another 1.6×.

I benchmarked seven setups (raw node:http, Hono, Express, Fastify with and without response schemas, and NestJS 12 on both its Express and Fastify adapters) across three workloads, two Node versions and Bun. Here's every number, how I got it, and which framework I'd pick for which job.

TL;DR: Hono vs Express vs Fastify, which is fastest?

On Node, Hono and Fastify are tied for first, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express. Hono won the plain JSON test, Fastify won route parameters and POST bodies. Express 5 is the slowest of the three but still served 50,000 requests per second on two CPU cores, which is more than most APIs will ever see. On Bun, Hono pulls clearly ahead at 118,000 requests per second.

Node 24.22, 2 cores, requests/s (median) JSON Route param POST JSON body Startup to first response Install size
node:http (no framework) 78,870 73,049 41,917 76 ms none
Hono 4.13.13 73,067 70,128 36,553 94 ms 3.9 MB, 2 packages
Fastify 5.12.7 71,786 76,746 38,936 153 ms 14.4 MB, 48 packages
Express 5.3.0 50,744 48,335 28,569 116 ms 4.3 MB, 65 packages
NestJS 12.1.3 + Fastify 56,434 59,499 33,418 425 ms n/a
NestJS 12.1.3 + Express 38,893 35,829 23,011 320 ms 22.4 MB, 98 packages

My pick: Hono for new APIs, especially anything that might run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or another edge runtime. Fastify for Node-only services where you want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express when the team and middleware already exist, because it's fast enough. NestJS when the codebase is big enough that structure matters more than 20% of throughput, and then put it on the Fastify adapter.

What are Hono, Express and Fastify?

All three are HTTP frameworks for JavaScript and TypeScript, and they come from different eras.

  • Express is the 2010 original and still the default. Express 5 finally shipped native promise support in route handlers and dropped a lot of legacy API. It has the largest middleware ecosystem by far: 145 million npm downloads in the week of October 6 to 12, 2026.
  • Fastify was built for speed on Node. It compiles JSON schemas into fast serializers and validators, has a strict plugin system with encapsulation, and logs with Pino by default. 15.4 million downloads that week.
  • Hono is built on web standards: handlers take a Request-like context and return a Response. The same app runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda and Vercel. It's tiny and has zero dependencies. 74 million downloads that week, partly because other tools bundle it.
  • NestJS isn't a fourth HTTP engine. It's an application framework with modules, dependency injection and decorators that runs on top of Express (the default) or Fastify. I covered the latest release in my NestJS 12 upgrade guide.

The code looks similar for a simple route. Here are the three handlers I benchmarked:

// Hono
app.get('/users/:id', c => c.json({ id: c.req.param('id'), fields: c.req.query('fields') ?? null }))

// Express 5
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

// Fastify 5
app.get('/users/:id', async req => ({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

How I benchmarked them

Benchmarks of web frameworks are easy to get wrong, so here's exactly what I ran.

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB of RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3.
  3. Versions. Hono 4.13.13 with @hono/node-server 2.1.5, Express 5.3.0, Fastify 5.12.7, and NestJS 12.1.3 with @nestjs/platform-express and @nestjs/platform-fastify. These were the latest npm releases on October 17, 2026.
  4. Workloads. GET /json returns {"message":"Hello, World!"}. GET /users/42?fields=name reads a route parameter and a query string. POST /echo parses a 907-byte JSON body and returns a count.
  5. Fair settings. No logging. ETags off in Express and in NestJS on Express, and x-powered-by off in Express. Fastify ran twice, once without schemas and once with response schemas. Every app returns the same JSON.
  6. Method. Each run started a fresh server, warmed it up for 4 seconds, then measured for 10 seconds. I ran 3 rounds per setup and report the median. Four setups had one noisy round, so I re-ran those with 5 rounds. That's 32 setups and more than 65 million measured requests, with a 100% success rate.

Absolute numbers depend on hardware. The ratios between frameworks are what transfer to your servers.

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. On Node 24, Hono handled 1.44× Express's throughput on plain JSON (73,067 vs 50,744 requests per second), 1.45× on route parameters and 1.28× on POST bodies. Latency followed: p99 on the JSON test was 1.50 ms for Hono against 2.12 ms for Express.

Two details matter more than the headline:

  • Hono came within 8% of raw node:http on the JSON test. There's very little left to optimize in the framework itself.
  • Hono's lead shrinks on POST. On Node, Hono goes through @hono/node-server, which turns Node's request into a web-standard Request before your handler sees it. Parsing a body through that layer costs more than Fastify's native parser. On Bun, where Request is native, the same Hono app did 80,749 POST requests per second, 2.2× its Node result.

Express 5 pays for its flexible middleware pipeline and the extra properties it adds to every request and response. It's still not slow. Fifty thousand requests per second on two cores is about 4 billion requests a day. Your database will give out long before Express does.

Hono vs Fastify: which is faster?

It depends on the route. On Node 24:

Requests/s, Node 24 Hono Fastify Fastify + response schema Winner
JSON 73,067 71,786 74,567 tie (within 4%)
Route param + query 70,128 76,746 75,526 Fastify, +9%
POST JSON body 36,553 38,936 39,045 Fastify, +7%

Fastify's router is a radix tree (find-my-way), and it beat even my hand-written node:http router on the route parameter test (76,746 vs 73,049), because my raw version builds a URL object per request. Adding response schemas, which Fastify compiles into a serializer with fast-json-stringify, was worth only about 4% on these small responses. The bigger value of schemas is validation and documentation, not speed.

So on Node, call it a draw. Pick between them on design: web standards and portability (Hono), or schemas, plugins and Node depth (Fastify).

Fastify vs Express: is it worth switching in 2026?

On raw speed, Fastify was 1.41× faster on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST. Its p99 latency was 25 to 40% lower too.

Whether that justifies a rewrite depends on where your time goes. If a typical request spends 20 ms in Postgres and 0.3 ms in the framework, cutting the framework's share in half changes nothing a user can feel. Switch when profiling shows the framework near the top, when you want schema validation built in, or when you're starting fresh anyway. Don't switch because of a chart, including this one.

How much overhead does NestJS add?

NestJS adds a layer of decorators, guards, pipes and interceptors on top of the engine. In my tests that cost 23% of Express's throughput (38,893 vs 50,744 on JSON) and 21% of Fastify's (56,434 vs 71,786). It also used more memory: about 100 MB idle versus 65 MB for plain Express.

The fix is easy and well documented in the NestJS performance guide: NestJS on Fastify was 1.45× faster than NestJS on Express on JSON and POST, and 1.66× faster on route parameters. It was also faster than plain Express on every test. If you use NestJS and none of your middleware is Express-specific, the Fastify adapter is the cheapest performance win available.

Do Node 26 and Bun change the ranking?

Node 26 made every framework faster without code changes. On the JSON test, Express and Fastify gained about 12%, NestJS 10%, Hono 6% and raw node:http 7%.

JSON requests/s Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Hono 73,067 77,454 118,432
Fastify 71,786 80,220 86,269
Express 50,744 56,627 72,479
NestJS + Express 38,893 42,923 not tested

On Bun, the ranking changes. Hono uses Bun's native server directly, so it ran 1.62× faster than on Node 24 and opened a 37% lead over Fastify. Express and Fastify also got faster on Bun (1.43× and 1.20×) but they run through Bun's node:http compatibility layer instead of calling Bun.serve directly. If you plan to run on Bun, Hono is the obvious choice. I compared the runtimes themselves in Bun vs Node.js in 2026.

Memory, startup time and install size

Throughput isn't the only cost. Startup matters for serverless and autoscaling, and install size matters for container images and cold deploys.

Node 24 Startup to first 200 Peak RSS at startup RSS idle Peak RSS under JSON load
node:http 76 ms 62 MB 58 MB 97 MB
Hono 94 ms 67 MB 63 MB 104 MB
Express 116 ms 75 MB 65 MB 97 MB
Fastify 153 ms 78 MB 72 MB 105 MB
NestJS + Express 320 ms 100 MB 98 MB 143 MB
NestJS + Fastify 425 ms 109 MB 106 MB 138 MB
Hono on Bun 14 ms 24 MB 20 MB 43 MB

Startup is the time from launching the process to the first successful response, measured with hyperfine over 20 runs. Hono on Bun was ready in 14 ms, which is why it's popular for serverless functions. NestJS needed about 2.8 times as long as the plain framework underneath it, because it scans modules and builds its dependency graph at boot.

Install size, measured in a fresh folder with npm: Hono plus its Node adapter is 2 packages and 3.9 MB. Express 5 is 65 packages but only 4.3 MB. Fastify is 48 packages and 14.4 MB. A minimal NestJS app on Express (core, common, platform-express, reflect-metadata, rxjs) is 98 packages and 22.4 MB. If you ship Docker images, my Next.js Dockerfile guide has the same multi-stage tricks that keep a Node API image small.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

If you need... Pick Why
A new API with the fewest moving parts Hono Within 8% of raw Node, zero dependencies, web-standard code
To run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda Hono Same app everywhere; 118k req/s on Bun
The best Node throughput on real routes Fastify Won route params and POST; schemas and plugins built in
An existing team and Express middleware Express 5 50k req/s is plenty; huge ecosystem; easy hiring
Structure for a large team (modules, DI) NestJS on Fastify 1.45 to 1.66× faster than NestJS on Express
End-to-end typed clients Hono (RPC) or Fastify with TypeBox Types flow from routes to clients

Two more points rarely show up in benchmark posts:

  • Ecosystem. Express still has the most middleware, tutorials and Stack Overflow answers. Fastify's plugin ecosystem covers most production needs. Hono's middleware set is smaller but growing, and anything built on web standards tends to just work.
  • Typed clients. Hono's RPC mode lets a frontend import the API's types directly. If your frontend is Next.js, also check whether you need a separate API at all; I covered that in Server Actions vs Route Handlers.

How do I migrate from Express to Hono or Fastify?

You don't need a big-bang rewrite. Both frameworks can sit next to Express while you move routes.

// Fastify: run existing Express middleware during a migration
import Fastify from 'fastify'
import expressPlugin from '@fastify/express'
const app = Fastify()
await app.register(expressPlugin)
app.use(legacyExpressMiddleware)

// Hono: same handler shape on every runtime
import { Hono } from 'hono'
const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', c => c.json({ ok: true }))
export default app // Bun, Workers, Deno; use @hono/node-server on Node

A safe order: move health checks and read-only routes first, measure them in production, then move the routes that write data. Keep the request and response shapes identical so clients never notice. Watch for Express habits that don't carry over: mutating req from middleware, res.locals, and error handlers with four arguments.

Common mistakes when benchmarking web frameworks

  • Running the load generator on the server's cores. Pin them apart, or you measure contention.
  • Benchmarking only /hello. Hono won plain JSON, Fastify won routes with parameters and bodies. One endpoint gives you one answer.
  • Leaving logging on. Fastify with a logger and Express with morgan are both much slower. Compare like with like.
  • Trusting a single run. Four of my 32 setups had one round 10 to 20% below the others. Take the median of several runs.
  • Comparing frameworks on different runtimes. "Hono is 2× faster than Express" is often Hono on Bun versus Express on Node.
  • Ignoring where time actually goes. Profile one real request. The framework is rarely the bottleneck.

Related: if your API is meant for AI agents, read MCP vs API before choosing a framework, because the protocol choice changes more than the framework does.

Key takeaways

  • On Node 24, Hono (73,067 req/s) and Fastify (71,786) are tied on JSON, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express 5 (50,744).
  • Fastify won route parameters (+9% over Hono) and POST bodies (+7%). Hono won plain JSON and came within 8% of raw node:http.
  • NestJS costs about 21 to 23% throughput and about 2.8× the startup time. On the Fastify adapter it's 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express.
  • Node 26 sped every framework up by 6 to 12% with no code changes.
  • On Bun, Hono jumped to 118,432 req/s, 1.62× its Node result, with 14 ms startup and 43 MB under load.
  • Hono installs as 2 packages (3.9 MB). Express is 65 packages (4.3 MB), Fastify 48 (14.4 MB), and NestJS 98 (22.4 MB).
  • Even Express handled 50,000 requests per second on 2 cores. Pick on design and ecosystem first; the framework is rarely your bottleneck.

FAQ

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. In my October 2026 benchmark on Node 24, Hono 4.13.13 served 73,067 JSON requests per second against 50,744 for Express 5.3.0, which is 1.44× faster. It was 1.45× faster on route parameters and 1.28× faster on POST bodies, with lower p99 latency.

Is Hono faster than Fastify?

On Node they're tied. Hono won plain JSON by 2%, but Fastify won route parameters by 9% and POST bodies by 7%. On Bun, Hono pulls ahead: 118,432 requests per second versus 86,269 for Fastify, because Hono uses Bun's native server directly.

Is Fastify faster than Express in 2026?

Yes. Fastify 5.12.7 was 1.41× faster than Express 5.3.0 on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST bodies, with 25 to 40% lower p99 latency. Express still handled about 50,000 requests per second on two cores, which is enough for most APIs.

How much slower is NestJS than Express or Fastify?

NestJS 12.1.3 cost about 23% of Express's throughput and 21% of Fastify's on the JSON test, used about 100 MB of memory at idle, and took about 2.8× as long to start. Using the Fastify adapter made NestJS 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express, and faster than plain Express on every test.

Should I switch from Express to Hono or Fastify?

Only if you have a reason beyond a benchmark. Switch when profiling shows the framework is a real cost, when you want built-in schema validation (Fastify), or when you need to run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or other runtimes (Hono). If most request time is spent in the database, a faster framework won't be noticeable.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

Hono for new APIs and anything that may run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda. Fastify for Node-only services that want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express 5 for teams with existing middleware and experience. NestJS on the Fastify adapter for large codebases that need modules and dependency injection.

Does Node 26 make Express, Fastify and Hono faster?

Yes. With no code changes, Node 26.12 improved JSON throughput over Node 24.22 by about 12% for Express and Fastify, 10% for NestJS, 7% for raw node:http and 6% for Hono.

How did you benchmark Hono, Express and Fastify?

Each server ran on 2 pinned CPU cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM, with oha 1.16.0 on the other cores at 64 connections. Every run started a fresh server, warmed up for 4 seconds and measured for 10 seconds. I report the median of 3 rounds, or 5 rounds for setups with a noisy round, across 32 setups on Node 24.22, Node 26.12 and Bun 1.4.3.

title: Runevault - Hardware Authenticator Platform!
description:
Inspiration
In most companies, sending a large payment can be incredibly risky when only a username and password stand in the way. One shared login or compromised account can lead to a costly transfer that's hard to undo. Approving a six-figure payment often takes just one click.

We wanted every high-value payment to be approved on purpose, by the right person, with something you can hold, and not rely on the internet for.

We drew inspiration from the Poneglyphs in One Piece: ancient stone tablets that guard secrets only the right reader can unlock. Runevault is a security key disguised as one of those relics. Every important transfer must be sealed by hand before it sets sail.

What it does
📜 Physical Sign-Off: The approver enters a glyph sequence on the Runevault tablet. It creates a unique signature for that exact transfer, with lights confirming each step. 🔐 Verification: The backend checks that the signature is genuine, matches the transfer, comes from the registered tablet, and has never been used before. 🧭 AI Risk Review: Gemini turns the glyphs into ancient lore and gives a risk score with a plain-English explanation. Gemini advises while our backend rules make the final call. If anything looks off, or Gemini fails, the transfer is blocked. ⚓ Secure Transfers: Only after every check passes does Runevault send the transfer through Capital One's Nessie API and show a receipt. 👑 Role-Based Access: Employees can create requests, Department Heads approve up to $10,000, the CFO up to $250,000, and the CEO any amount. 🗺️ Live Captain's Log: The dashboard updates in real time with status, risk gauges, lore, receipts, and an approvals vs. blocks chart.

How we built it
Our dashboard uses Angular and TypeScript, styled with weathered stone, parchment, and ocean tones. It holds a primarily navy and gold color palette.

The physical key is a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 running MicroPython. It signs each transfer with HMAC-SHA256 and saves a counter to block replays. A bridge sends approvals over USB to our backend.

Our Java and Spring Boot backend runs every transfer through one pipeline:

Verify the signature, device, counter, and rate limits.
Send only transfer metadata to Gemini, which returns schema-enforced JSON.
Apply our rules: confidence of at least 0.8 and risk of at most 30.
Call Nessie and build the receipt.
Push each step live over Spring WebSockets and log it in Tiger Data (TimescaleDB).
Auth0 handles login, MFA, and roles. Everything runs in Docker on a Vultr server behind Caddy, at our GoDaddy Registry domain, sailthedeal.fishing.

Link to Demo Video

Challenges we ran into
The key and backend had to produce identical signatures down to the byte. Tiny formatting differences broke valid approvals until we wrote a shared signing spec.

We started with two approval flows and merged them into one, so no transfer can skip a check.

We had to keep Gemini helpful without letting it make security decisions. Deploying in less than basically 12 hours was tough, as DNS, HTTPS, Auth0 redirects, and WebSockets all had to line up on a brand-new domain.

Accomplishments that we're proud of
Runevault was able to work*end to end*, even though we had our fears about being unable to integrate the hardware and software together. A press on one of the buttons travels over USB, gets verified, reviewed by Gemini, sent through Nessie, and shown live on the dashboard.

We covered most of the edge cases, allowing fails in a safe manner such as transfers being blocked if Gemini does not respond, a time limit set for entering your generated glyph sequence, etc. Bad signatures, replays, high risk, and AI outages all are addressed and stopped, never leading to any accidental payments.

Our biggest accomplishment was turning payment approval into something that feels like uncovering an ancient artifact, and for trying something new that was not purely software! We were really glad to see that this could be an amazing possibility for keeping authentication safer if it's physical and does not rely on WiFi and other factors.

What we learned
Hardware Security: Signatures, counters, and replay protection, and how strict byte-level protocols are. Responsible AI: Getting reliable JSON from Gemini, and letting AI advise rather than decide. Identity & Access: Building role-based access with Auth0 and enforcing it on the backend. Time-Series Data: Using TimescaleDB hypertables and aggregates for live charts. Cloud Deployment: Going from localhost to a live HTTPS domain on Vultr.

What's next for Runevault
If we were to continue expanding on Runevault, our next steps include: Multi-Step Approvals: Big transfers that need both a Department Head and the CFO. Our project is currently designed a way that makes it possible for scalability and for real multi-step pipelines that might happen in companies. More Custom Glyphs: We would have liked to incorporate more combinations than the 3 glyphs we have as of now, and to incorporate more potential stories that Gemini could tell. Banking Integrations: Bringing the physical seal to real corporate banking platforms. Hardware Prototype: Designing the Runevault token to be compact and likely lightweight so it would not be an inconvenience to bring it around.

We had so much fun building this project! #mlhacks.

title: Why do finance teams reject black-box AI in revenue accounting?
description:
Controllers, outsourced accounting partners and QoE analysts keep evaluating "AI for technical accounting" tools and keep going back to spreadsheets. The reason is accountability: their name is on the workpapers, and the vendor isn't in the room when the auditor asks how an allocation was determined.

The audit problem with black boxes

  • Unverifiable rationale: "The model suggested this split" is not an audit workpaper.
  • Re-verification overhead: if someone has to re-read the whole contract to check the tool, it added a step instead of removing one.
  • Reproducibility: a calculation that cannot be re-run to the same cent cannot be a reliable audit schedule.

Worked example: what "ties out" means

A $100,000 contract bundles three obligations. Total SSP is $180,000, so the $80,000 discount is spread in proportion.

Obligation SSP Engine allocation
Implementation $30,000 $16,666.67
Premium support $30,000 $16,666.67
Platform subscription $120,000 $66,666.66
Total $180,000 $100,000.00

Round each line on its own and the three allocations sum to $100,000.01. The engine's allocation sums to exactly $100,000.00 because one obligation absorbs the rounding residual. The exported workbook carries the page and excerpt for each obligation plus a SHA-256 hash, so re-running the same inputs gives the same cents.

What makes it reviewable is the order of operations: a human confirms the obligations and prices, the arithmetic is integer and deterministic, and the evidence (page plus verbatim excerpt; on uploaded text-layer PDFs, a highlight box on the cited line) travels with the number.

Try your own numbers in the free SSP allocation calculator.

Read the full worked example on soluqube.com

title: Your Desktop Apps Deserve Updates Straight from the Source
description:
When we install software on our computers, we rarely think about the journey a new version takes before reaching us.

We download applications from websites, install package managers, add third-party repositories, or wait for someone else to package the latest release. These approaches can be convenient, but they also introduce another question:

Why should updating an open-source application depend on someone other than its original developer?

For desktop applications distributed through GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo, and similar platforms, the release artifacts are often already available. Developers publish binaries, attach them to releases, and make them accessible to anyone.

Yet discovering and downloading those files can still be a surprisingly manual process.

That's the problem I'm exploring with Updainium.

The Desktop Update Problem

Consider a simple scenario.

You use an open-source application that you downloaded six months ago. The developer has released three new versions since then, including security fixes and improvements.

How do you find out?

Perhaps you bookmarked the repository. Maybe you follow the developer on social media. Or perhaps you periodically open the application's website to check whether a new version is available.

Now imagine doing this for ten, twenty, or fifty applications.

The problem isn't that downloading software is difficult. It's that keeping track of independently maintained applications becomes tedious when every project has its own release page, naming conventions, and distribution methods.

Package managers solve part of this problem, but they aren't always the ideal solution for every project.

Some applications aren't available in your package manager. Others depend on community-maintained manifests or repositories. And sometimes, you simply want the binary published by the project's own maintainers.

Package Managers Aren't the Enemy

Let's be clear: package managers are excellent tools.

Homebrew, APT, winget, and other package management systems make software installation and maintenance much easier. They provide convenient workflows and, depending on the ecosystem, additional verification and dependency management.

However, they introduce a distribution layer between the original project and the user.

Depending on the package and ecosystem, that layer might involve a third-party maintainer, a separate release schedule, or a packaging process that doesn't perfectly match the upstream project's releases.

That's not necessarily a bad thing. It's simply a different distribution model.

But there is another option: let users discover and download release files directly from the source.

Meet Updainium

Updainium is an open-source desktop application inspired by Obtainium, adapted for desktop software distribution.

Instead of manually checking every repository, you can use Updainium to track public projects across supported Git hosting platforms.

The idea is straightforward:

  1. Add a public repository.
  2. Configure the file extension you want to download.
  3. Let Updainium check the project's releases.
  4. Download the matching release asset when you need it.

For example, depending on the assets published by a project, you might look for .dmg files on macOS, .exe installers on Windows, or .AppImage packages on Linux.

You don't need every project to follow the same naming convention or distribute its software through a single centralized store. You choose the artifact type that fits your workflow.

The goal is to make upstream releases easier to discover and download.

Why I Built It with Tauri, Rust, and Svelte

Updainium is built with Tauri, using Rust for its backend and Svelte for its interface.

I wanted a desktop utility that could remain lightweight while still providing a native application experience.

Rust handles backend operations, including application logic and file handling. Svelte powers the user interface, while Tauri connects the two without requiring a traditional heavyweight desktop application stack.

This combination is a practical fit for a tool whose job is to monitor releases and download files rather than run a large collection of background services.

It also keeps the project hackable. The source is available under the GPL-3.0 license, so developers can inspect how it works, modify it, and contribute improvements under the terms of that license.

Direct Downloads Don't Automatically Mean More Security

There is an important distinction between downloading directly from a project's release page and knowing that a file is safe.

A direct download doesn't automatically guarantee authenticity, integrity, or security.

A compromised maintainer account, malicious release, or vulnerable application can still put users at risk. Likewise, downloading a binary from an upstream repository doesn't necessarily mean it has been independently audited.

That's why software distribution should be transparent about what it does and what it doesn't guarantee.

Updainium focuses on discovering releases and downloading matching files. It isn't a substitute for signature verification, checksums, reproducible builds, or a project's security practices.

Whenever a project publishes checksums or signed artifacts, users should take advantage of those verification mechanisms.

The point isn't to blindly trust the source. It's to give users a more direct route to the software they have chosen, while leaving room for independent verification.

What About APIs and Web Scraping?

Not every Git hosting service exposes the same information through a standardized API.

Some sources provide structured release data, while others may require Updainium to gather information from their web pages.

That creates a limitation worth acknowledging: scraping depends on the structure of the website. If a platform changes its HTML or release page layout, tracking can break until compatibility is restored.

This is an engineering trade-off, not something that should be hidden behind marketing language.

The long-term goal is to make release tracking reliable across supported platforms while remaining transparent about compatibility limitations.

A Different Philosophy for Desktop Software

Updainium isn't intended to become another platform that controls how you develop, distribute, or maintain software.

Its development follows a deliberately simple set of principles:

  • No AI features.
  • No telemetry.
  • No subscriptions.
  • No automatic installation or updates.
  • No Contributor License Agreements (CLAs).
  • No proprietary server components.

These aren't claims that every other software project should follow the same rules. They're decisions about the kind of tool I want to build and maintain.

For me, an update manager should help users stay informed and obtain software, not take control of their machines.

That's why Updainium doesn't automatically install updates. Discovering a new release and deciding to install it should remain separate actions.

Automation is useful, but it shouldn't eliminate user consent.

What's Next?

Updainium is still evolving.

The project is open to improvements that make release discovery, downloading, configuration, and everyday desktop use more reliable.

I'm particularly interested in feedback from developers who maintain desktop applications and users who prefer obtaining their software directly from upstream projects.

If you've ever had to maintain a collection of manually downloaded applications, I'd like to hear how you currently handle updates and what you'd improve about that workflow.

Try Updainium

You can explore the source code, inspect the implementation, report bugs, and follow development here:

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/livrasand/Updainium
  • License: GPL-3.0

If you find the project useful, consider starring the repository or contributing a human-reviewed improvement.

Desktop software distribution doesn't need to be complicated to be useful.

Sometimes, the best improvement is simply making it easier to get the software you already trust—from the people who actually build it.

title: BlastShield AI: an evidence-first incident commander built on FalkorDB
description:
The safest cloud response starts with a path, not a prompt

BlastShield AI: an evidence-first incident commander built on FalkorDB

When a cloud incident starts, the first instinct is usually to find the red service and restart it.

That is often too late, too broad, or simply wrong.

A compromised Kubernetes pod may be connected to an authentication service. That service may assume an IAM role. The role may read a secret. The secret may unlock a database. The database may replicate into another environment.

The visible failure is one node. The real incident is the path behind it.

We built BlastShield AI for the Graph Hacks challenge by WeMakeDevs and FalkorDB to answer a more useful question:

Given a compromised node, what can it reach, where can we contain it, and what evidence supports that decision?

BlastShield stores a synthetic cloud-infrastructure topology in FalkorDB, gives an AI incident commander named KIMO controlled tools to inspect that graph, and requires explicit human approval before any remediation mutation is applied.

Live demo: blast-shield-ai.vercel.app

Source code: github.com/sandman-sh/BlastShield-AI

Contents

  • The problem
  • The idea: walk from the incident to the containment point
  • How a containment candidate is selected
  • What the demo measured
  • Fixing it safely
  • Seeing the graph
  • What we learned
  • What is not done yet
  • If you keep one thing
  • Sources

The problem

Most incident tools are very good at answering:

  • Which service is returning errors?
  • Which container is using too much CPU?
  • Which deployment happened most recently?
  • Which log line contains the exception?

They are less good at answering:

  • What can this compromised component reach?
  • Which relationship makes the incident dangerous?
  • Which node can be isolated without taking down everything else?
  • What remains reachable after containment?

That gap matters because cloud infrastructure is connected.

A dashboard may show that pod-auth-x92 is compromised. It does not automatically show whether the pod can reach an IAM role, which can read a JWT secret, which can reach the users database.

An LLM-only incident assistant has a different problem. It can summarize an incident fluently, but it may invent a dependency, use stale context, or recommend an action without proving the path behind it.

BlastShield was designed around a simple rule:

The model can explain the decision, but the graph must provide the evidence.

The idea: walk from the incident to the containment point

BlastShield models infrastructure as a typed property graph in FalkorDB.

The graph contains entities such as:

  • APIGateway
  • LoadBalancer
  • K8sPod
  • Service
  • Database
  • IAMRole
  • Secret

The relationships are operationally meaningful:

  • CALLS
  • CONNECTS_TO
  • ASSUMES
  • PERMITS
  • READS_SECRET
  • HOSTS
  • REPLICATES_TO

This lets the application distinguish a service call from an authorization edge or a secret access path.

The incident pipeline is:

Incident source
    → FalkorDB multi-hop traversal
    → Candidate articulation points
    → Reachability comparison
    → Human-readable recommendation
    → Explicit approval
    → FalkorDB mutation
    → Audit record and agent memory

The core traversal is executed against FalkorDB through the Redis protocol using GRAPH.QUERY.

MATCH path = (source {id: $sourceNodeId})-[*1..6]->(downstream)
RETURN downstream, length(path) AS hops
ORDER BY hops ASC

The returned paths become evidence for the incident report. They are not replaced by a generated explanation.

How a containment candidate is selected

BlastShield does not use a fixed rule such as:

If a pod is compromised, shut down the pod.

Instead, it combines several pieces of graph evidence.

1. Find downstream impact

The system traverses outward from the incident source and records the reachable downstream entities and the number of hops to each one.

For example:

pod-auth-x92
  └── HOSTS → auth-service
        └── ASSUMES → iam-auth-token
              └── READS_SECRET → sec-jwt-private
                    └── CONNECTS_TO → users-db

2. Find articulation points

BlastShield retrieves the current topology and runs Tarjan's articulation-point algorithm.

An articulation point is a node whose removal disconnects part of a graph.

In a cloud topology, that can represent a choke point where isolation may stop a cascade without disabling unrelated infrastructure.

3. Compare reachability before and after isolation

For each selected candidate, BlastShield measures:

Reachable nodes before containment
Reachable nodes after candidate isolation
Remaining reachable Tier-1 paths

This turns a vague recommendation into a measurable trade-off.

The system can explain not only what it wants to isolate, but also what the graph predicts will remain available.

4. Let KIMO explain the evidence

KIMO is the tool-calling AI incident commander inside BlastShield.

The model does not independently calculate the topology. It calls application tools that read FalkorDB and return structured results.

The main tools are:

inspect_topology
analyze_blast_radius
recall_memory
propose_remediation
apply_remediation
reset_topology

KIMO is instructed to use tools before making claims about nodes, counts, paths, or safety.

The language model writes the explanation after the graph analysis has already produced the evidence.

What the demo measured

The current demo uses a deterministic synthetic infrastructure graph. It is designed to be reproducible and safe for a hackathon demonstration.

After seeding the graph, the baseline topology contains:

  • 21 infrastructure nodes
  • 24 relationships
  • Services, databases, pods, IAM roles, and secrets

For the demonstration incident, pod-auth-x92 was treated as the compromised source.

The live analysis produced:

  • 2 impacted downstream entities
  • 2 hops of downstream impact
  • 2 candidate articulation points in the current topology
  • 19 ingress-reachable nodes before isolation
  • 17 ingress-reachable nodes after the selected cut
  • 13 reachable Tier-1 paths protected after the analysis

These are results from the deterministic demo topology, not a production benchmark. The purpose of the scenario is to show that the graph is performing the analysis and that the remediation decision is based on the current topology.

The important result is not a universal number.

The important result is that the system can show the path, calculate the candidate cut, compare the graph before and after isolation, and preserve the decision as an audit record.

Fixing it safely

An incident assistant should not turn a conversational sentence into an uncontrolled mutation.

BlastShield separates planning from execution.

When the operator asks for an analysis, KIMO can inspect the graph and propose a remediation.

The proposal does not mutate FalkorDB.

The operator must explicitly approve it before apply_remediation is allowed to run.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Operator
    participant KIMO
    participant FalkorDB
    participant Audit

    Operator->>KIMO: Analyze compromised node
    KIMO->>FalkorDB: Inspect topology
    FalkorDB-->>KIMO: Nodes and relationships
    KIMO->>FalkorDB: Traverse blast radius
    FalkorDB-->>KIMO: Impact paths
    KIMO->>KIMO: Run articulation analysis
    KIMO-->>Operator: Explain and propose
    Operator->>KIMO: Explicitly approve
    KIMO->>FalkorDB: Quarantine and mutate graph
    FalkorDB->>Audit: Persist action hash and memory
    Audit-->>Operator: Show result

The remediation flow can:

  • Quarantine the selected node
  • Sever dangerous permission relationships
  • Select a healthy database candidate for failover
  • Persist a SHA-256 audit hash
  • Store an episodic memory for KIMO
  • Return the new graph state to the console

The safety boundary is:

AI proposes
Human approves
Graph mutates

The current project simulates infrastructure changes inside the FalkorDB topology. It does not claim to directly modify a user's AWS account or Kubernetes cluster.

Seeing the graph

The first useful UI decision was to make the topology visible without making the operator understand the database internals first.

The command console exposes:

  • FalkorDB connection status
  • Node and edge counts
  • The visual topology
  • Incident selection
  • Blast-radius results
  • KIMO's evidence summary
  • Cypher query execution
  • Approval-gated remediation
  • Audit history
  • Agent memory

The command console brings the live graph, incident controls, and agent conversation into one view.

The graph is also useful because it gives the operator something to challenge.

If KIMO says a database is at risk, the operator can inspect the highlighted path and see which relationships connect the source node to that database.

The highlighted path shows why a downstream entity was included in the blast-radius report.

The audit view closes the loop.

The proposed action is visible before approval, and the resulting mutation is recorded afterward.

Memory that stays connected

Incident memory is more useful when it keeps its topology context.

BlastShield stores AgentMemory nodes in FalkorDB with information such as:

  • Incident category
  • Source node
  • Learned containment strategy
  • Confidence
  • Success rate
  • Timestamp
  • Related audit hash

That gives KIMO a path from a previous incident to the action that was taken:

graph LR
    I[Incident] --> S[Source Pod]
    I --> M[Agent Memory]
    M --> A[Remediation Action]
    A --> H[Audit Hash]
    S --> T[Current Topology]

The long-term question is not only:

What happened?

It is also:

What did we do?
Did it preserve the right paths?
What should we consider next time?

What we learned

The graph was the product, not the decoration

At first, it is tempting to build a graph because graphs look impressive in a demo.

That is not enough.

The graph became valuable only when every important feature depended on it:

  • Blast-radius analysis reads graph paths.
  • Cut-vertex analysis reads graph structure.
  • Remediation mutates graph state.
  • Audit records are stored in the graph.
  • Agent memory is stored in the graph.

If the graph is removed, the main product behavior disappears.

Deterministic analysis should come before fluent explanation

We learned to keep the language model away from the parts that should be reproducible.

The graph traversal, articulation-point analysis, reachability calculation, and mutation rules are application logic.

KIMO's job is to choose the appropriate tool, summarize the result, explain the evidence, and ask for approval.

The safest action may be smaller than the obvious action

The obvious response to a compromised pod is often to disable the whole service.

The graph can reveal a smaller containment point that breaks the dangerous path while preserving more healthy connectivity.

That is the difference between reacting to a red node and reasoning about a connected system.

Approval is not the opposite of autonomy

An autonomous agent can investigate independently and prepare a high-quality action plan without silently changing production state.

The approval gate made the system more trustworthy because the operator can inspect the evidence before the mutation occurs.

Synthetic data can still demonstrate real architecture

We used synthetic infrastructure data so the demo is public, reproducible, and safe.

That does not make the graph behavior fake. The topology, queries, traversal, analysis, mutation, audit, and memory flows are real application behavior.

It does mean we are careful not to claim that this version is already a production AWS or Kubernetes controller.

What is not done yet

There are important limitations.

No live cloud ingestion yet

The current graph is seeded from a deterministic synthetic topology.

The next version should ingest authorized data from Kubernetes, AWS IAM, cloud databases, service meshes, and deployment systems.

Remediation is graph-level simulation

The current remediation changes the FalkorDB representation and records the action. It does not execute kubectl, AWS SDK calls, or cloud-provider mutations.

That is appropriate for the hackathon demo, but a production version would need provider-specific connectors, permissions, rollback, and policy enforcement.

No production multi-tenancy yet

A real SaaS version would require tenant isolation, role-based access control, secret rotation, encrypted connections, per-project credentials, and a detailed authorization model.

The demo is not a benchmark

The numbers in this post come from the deterministic demo scenario. We have not presented them as a general production accuracy benchmark.

That distinction matters because trustworthy incident tooling should report what it has measured, not what sounds impressive.

If you keep one thing

The safest incident response starts with a path, not a prompt.

The path tells you what the compromised component can reach.

The graph tells you where a cut may contain the incident.

The algorithm compares the consequences.

The agent explains the evidence.

The human approves the change.

That is the design behind BlastShield AI.

Technology

BlastShield AI uses:

  • FalkorDB
  • Next.js
  • TypeScript
  • React
  • OpenCypher
  • Redis wire protocol
  • OpenRouter-compatible AI APIs
  • Tarjan articulation-point analysis
  • SHA-256 audit hashes
  • Docker Compose
  • Vercel

Sources

  • BlastShield AI source repository
  • BlastShield AI live demo
  • FalkorDB

AI Assistance Disclosure

AI coding assistants were used for implementation assistance, debugging, documentation, and testing support.

The project team reviewed, tested, and understands the submitted code, graph model, queries, architecture, security boundaries, and product decisions.

title: Pricing Flag Incident Reconstruction — Node.js Uptime Failure Alerts from Health Endpoint Metrics API
description:
For a Node.js pricing rollout, use regional health polling for reachability, a metrics poll for bad outcomes, and a heartbeat for missing work; page only when the evidence agrees, but retain every signal under one rollout identifier for reconstruction. The deciding constraint isn't how quickly one probe can turn red. It's whether an engineer can later answer which flag variant, region, and pricing-rule revision produced a wrong checkout result.

Short answer: a simple uptime alert should combine an outside-in health endpoint, outcome metrics, and a scheduled heartbeat, because each observes a different failure boundary and none can reconstruct a flagged pricing incident alone.

This is an experiment note, not a vendor ranking. The tempting first pass is one poll against /health and one alert on any failure. That approach is easy to demo, yet it confuses transport trouble with pricing correctness and creates almost no evidence for an evaluation harness. The better experiment treats the rollout as the unit of analysis: every observation carries a synthetic checkout case, flag variant, rule revision, region, and timestamp. Then the alert links to the observations that justified it.

No magic here.

The incident record we need to reconstruct

A process-level health endpoint can prove that a caller reached the service and received the expected response shape. It cannot, by itself, prove that a flagged pricing rule selected the intended price. A metrics API can show the count or ratio of evaluated outcomes, but aggregation can hide one region or variant. A heartbeat can show that a scheduled synthetic checkout ran, while saying nothing about whether its assertion was correct unless the payload records that assertion.

The useful question is therefore not “is the app up?” It is “what claim does each signal support?” For this rollout, the external poll supports reachability, the outcome poll supports behavioral change, and the heartbeat supports evaluator liveness. An alert becomes actionable when it names the failed claim and preserves the dimensions needed to replay it.

I first reach for the smallest possible signal set because every label and event has storage and review cost. But prompt-cost awareness offers a useful analogy: dropping context makes an evaluation cheaper until the result can no longer be explained. Observability has the same cliff. Removing rule_revision or flag_variant may reduce cardinality, but it also makes two different pricing behaviors look identical during an incident.

Use a compact event contract before choosing a monitor:

Signal Claim it supports Required reconstruction context Misleading green state
Regional health poll The public path answered as expected region, observed status, latency bucket, rollout ID Pricing output is wrong but the route responds
Outcome metrics poll Evaluated results remain within the rollout's tested bounds variant, rule revision, region, evaluation window Aggregation masks a narrow failure
Evaluator heartbeat The scheduled check completed run ID, expected cadence, last completion, rollout ID The check ran but asserted the wrong thing

That table is also an alert review checklist. If a page cannot identify its supported claim, it probably belongs in a dashboard or deployment record instead.

How should a Node.js health endpoint poll metrics API and heartbeat monitor work?

Run the synthetic evaluator from at least the two deployment geographies named in the rollout plan, EU and US in this example. Each run calls the public Node.js health endpoint, evaluates one fixed cart against the active pricing flag, reads the corresponding aggregate outcome window, and emits a completion heartbeat. The evaluation input must be stable enough to replay: currency, item identifiers, quantities, expected variant, and rule revision belong in the test fixture, while secrets and customer data do not belong in logs.

The collector below is Python because notebook-to-prod work benefits from keeping the evaluation record explicit. It uses only the standard library, accepts observations from generic adapters, and returns an alert decision plus the evidence that produced it. Network calls are intentionally outside the function; the hard part is the decision contract, not an SDK.

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Iterable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Observation:
    region: str
    rollout_id: str
    flag_variant: str
    rule_revision: str
    health_ok: bool
    pricing_assertion_ok: bool
    completed_at: datetime


def evaluate_rollout(
    observations: Iterable[Observation],
    expected_regions: set[str],
    now: datetime,
    heartbeat_window: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=5),
) -> dict:
    recent = [
        item
        for item in observations
        if now - item.completed_at <= heartbeat_window
    ]
    seen_regions = {item.region for item in recent}
    missing_regions = sorted(expected_regions - seen_regions)
    failed = [
        item
        for item in recent
        if not item.health_ok or not item.pricing_assertion_ok
    ]

    return {
        "alert": bool(missing_regions or failed),
        "missing_heartbeats": missing_regions,
        "failed_observations": [asdict(item) for item in failed],
    }


decision = evaluate_rollout(
    observations=[
        Observation(
            region="eu",
            rollout_id="pricing-rule-42",
            flag_variant="candidate",
            rule_revision="r7",
            health_ok=True,
            pricing_assertion_ok=True,
            completed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        ),
        Observation(
            region="us",
            rollout_id="pricing-rule-42",
            flag_variant="candidate",
            rule_revision="r7",
            health_ok=True,
            pricing_assertion_ok=False,
            completed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        ),
    ],
    expected_regions={"eu", "us"},
    now=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
)

The focused failure is deliberately boring: EU completes and passes; US completes but fails the pricing assertion. The heartbeat is healthy, so labeling this “monitor down” would destroy information. The health check is also healthy, so labeling it “uptime failure” alone would send the responder toward networking rather than the flagged rule. The decision keeps all three facts and points at candidate, r7, and pricing-rule-42. That is enough to compare the exact fixture against the control variant and the deployment record without guessing which aggregate moved first.

This example doesn't prescribe the pricing threshold. That number must come from the rollout's eval cases and business invariant, and I'm not sure a global percentage can represent mixed currencies, promotions, and tax paths without more domain evidence. Your mileage may vary. Resolve that uncertainty before deployment by defining expected outputs for representative carts, then make the online assertion use the same versioned fixtures.

A pricing flag failure, replayed backward

A single failed poll should become an observation, not automatically a page. Require a policy that accounts for repeated failure, regional agreement, or a pricing assertion failure tied to the candidate flag. The exact threshold is an operational choice; inventing a universal retry count would hide differences in poll interval, traffic, and recovery objectives.

This matters during a flag rollout because causality is easy to overstate. A health probe might fail near the same moment that a pricing metric changes, yet timestamps alone do not prove the rule caused the probe failure. Preserve the raw observations, clock basis, rollout ID, and deployment event. Then let the incident timeline show what happened rather than embedding a causal claim in the alert title.

Keep the page compact — region, failed claim, first and latest observation, variant, revision, and a link to the retained evidence are enough. Keep the evidence richer. OWASP's logging guidance warns that logs may contain sensitive information and calls for attention to data handling, so synthetic identifiers are safer than customer details for this check. Cart fixtures should be designed for evaluation, not copied from production requests.

There is a second privacy surface in the monitoring toolchain itself. Command-line telemetry should respect the DO_NOT_TRACK convention when supported, especially in local eval and CI workflows where an engineer may reasonably disable ancillary usage reporting. This doesn't replace a data inventory. It makes the intent machine-readable at one boundary.

Privacy and operational boundaries

The simplest architecture is a scheduler, two regional runners, an append-only observation store, and a small decision worker. A free or cheap SaaS may host one or more of those pieces, but price should not choose the evidence model. Free tiers, retention, regional execution, and alert routing can change; verify current terms directly before adopting any service.

The catch is that an external hosted monitor is not suitable when policy forbids sending endpoint metadata or evaluation dimensions to a third party. Use a self-hosted runner and store in that case. Conversely, stick with a hosted check when the team cannot operate an independent scheduler reliably; putting the monitor on the same failure boundary as the application creates a blind spot. For strict data residency, confirm where checks execute and where event data is stored rather than treating an “EU region” label as proof of the whole data path.

Do not force all signals into one retention class. High-volume outcome observations may need short detailed retention plus longer aggregates, while alert decisions and rollout metadata are small and valuable for later review. Also budget label cardinality before exposing metrics: rollout_id and bounded variants are useful, but cart or request identifiers can explode the series count. Detailed per-run context fits an event record better than a metric label.

This architecture is intentionally replaceable. The scheduler, probe adapter, metric reader, and notifier meet at plain records, so a team can move between self-hosted and SaaS components without rewriting the evaluation rule. That's more important than finding one service that claims to cover every box.

The pre-rollout scorecard

Before making this pattern the default, measure detection delay by failure class, the fraction of pages with enough context to identify a variant and revision, duplicate pages per incident, evaluator completion rate, and storage volume by dimension. Also replay known-good and deliberately failing fixtures through the decision function in CI. An alert pipeline without an eval harness is still untested application logic.

Track cost as an engineering constraint, not a victory metric. Poll frequency multiplies requests, regional runners multiply them again, and high-cardinality evidence changes storage. Start from the maximum acceptable detection delay and the incident reconstruction window, then calculate the required cadence and retention. Don't choose a one-minute poll merely because a UI defaults to it.

Finally, run a paper reconstruction after the first staged rollout. Give another engineer only the page and retained evidence, and ask them to identify the affected region, flag variant, rule revision, missing or failed signal, and replay fixture. If they must search chat history or infer a revision from wall-clock time, the experiment failed even if every notification arrived.

Ship the signal contract first.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://consoledonottrack.com/

title: The Geometry of Shadows: What a Bridge Railing Taught Me About the Mathematics of LLMs
description:
While running one morning, I found myself staring at the shadows cast by a stone bridge railing. The railing had a series of identical, carved镂空 (hollowed-out) structures. As I ran past, the angle of the sun shifted, and the shadows on the ground transformed.

At one moment, the shadow looked like a swimming fish; a few steps later, it looked like a rolling wave; later still, it was just an abstract, elongated blob.

It struck me that I was witnessing a perfect physical metaphor for how human language—and Large Language Models (LLMs)—generate meaning.

The stone bridge hole is the concept. The sunlight is the context. The shadow on the ground is the utterance.

This realization perfectly mirrors the "Central Problem" of language modeling, beautifully stripped of its usual jargon in Joseph L. Breeden’s paper, The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models.

The Problem of the Single Shadow

In his paper, Breeden highlights a fundamental flaw in early AI approaches: treating words as static, unchanging symbols. He uses the classic example of the word "bank":

  1. "I deposited money at the **bank." (a financial institution)
  2. "We walked along the river **bank." (the land beside a river)
  3. "The plane **banked* sharply left."* (tilted)

If we assign a single, fixed vector to the word "bank" in a high-dimensional space, we are essentially trying to capture all three meanings in one static shape. But as Breeden points out, a fixed vector for "bank" cannot simultaneously be close to "money," "river," and "tilt."

In my running metaphor, a single, fixed vector is like looking at the bridge hole only at exactly high noon. You get one specific shadow. But language is dynamic. The meaning of "bank" depends entirely on the "angle of the light" provided by the surrounding words.

The Mathematics of Light: Learned Weighted Averaging

How does an LLM solve this? Breeden explains that the core mechanism of a Transformer is not magic; it is Learned Weighted Averaging.

Let’s map Breeden’s mathematics to the bridge railing:

1. The Bridge Hole (The Token Embedding, $e$)
Before any context is applied, the word "bank" is just an initial embedding vector ($e$). It is the physical stone structure itself. It contains the potential for all its meanings, but it is currently unshaped by the environment.

2. The Angle of the Sunlight (Influence Scores, $a_i \cdot b_j$)
To determine what the shadow will look like, we need light. In an LLM, the "light" comes from the surrounding words (the context).
Breeden explains that the model computes an influence score between the target word and its context. It does this by projecting the vectors through learned matrices ($W^A$ and $W^B$).

  • When the context is "deposited money," the "light" hits the bridge hole from a financial angle.
  • When the context is "river," the light hits it from a geographical angle. The dot product ($a_i \cdot b_j$) measures how perfectly the angle of the light aligns with the shape of the hole.

3. The Shadow on the Ground (Context-Dependent Representation, $h_i$)
Finally, the light passes through the hole and casts a shadow. Mathematically, the model takes a weighted average of the context vectors (using the content projection $W^C$), resulting in a brand new vector ($h_i$).
This new vector is the shadow. It is a context-dependent representation. The "bank" in the first sentence is mathematically pulled toward the geometry of finance; the "bank" in the second sentence is pulled toward the geometry of nature. They are the same material, but entirely different products.

Why This Metaphor Matters

What makes Breeden’s explanation so profound is that it removes the anthropomorphic jargon of "Queries," "Keys," and "Values." There is no little homunculus inside the computer "looking up" information in a database.

There is only geometry and light.

When an LLM reads the sentence "The plane banked sharply left," it doesn't "know" what a plane is. Instead, the high-dimensional vectors for "plane" and "sharply left" act as a specific angle of light. This light passes through the "bank" bridge hole and casts a shadow that aligns perfectly with the geometric region of "physical motion" in the model's latent space.

Furthermore, this explains the difference between languages. In English, "bank" is a single, multi-purpose bridge hole that requires complex, dynamic lighting (Attention mechanisms) to cast the right shadow. In Chinese, the language has already carved three separate, distinct bridge holes: 银行 (bank), 岸 (riverbank), and 倾斜 (to tilt). The Chinese model requires less "light manipulation" because the physical structures themselves are already disentangled.

Conclusion: Meaning is a Projection

As I finished my run, I realized that the bridge railing wasn't just casting shadows; it was performing a physical projection.

Large Language Models do not store a dictionary of definitions. They store a high-dimensional geometry of concepts. Meaning is not a static object you can hold in your hand; it is a projection. It is the dynamic, mathematical shadow cast when the light of context passes through the structure of language.

And just like the shadows on the pavement, the beauty of language lies not in the stone itself, but in how it changes with the light.

References:
Breeden, J. L. (2026). The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models. CRC Working Papers.

title: AI Gateway logs now have a dedicated page
description:
AI Gateway now has a dedicated Logs page listing every request your team sends through the gateway, newest first, with cost, token counts, duration, and the model, provider, and region that served it. Open any request to see how it was routed. It's available at the team scope and per project.

Filter and search

Filter by provider, model, modality, credentials, or status, or search by model, provider, or request ID to jump straight to one request. Every filter is stored in the URL, so you can share a filtered view by copying the address. A chart above the table shows request counts over the selected range, and you can drag across it to zoom into a narrower window.

You can also export the current view as CSV or JSON, with your filters applied.

Drill into a request

Click any row to open its details next to the list: total cost, a token breakdown across input, output, reasoning, and cache reads and writes, duration, time to first token, and whether Zero Data Retention and region restrictions were applied.

The fallback path lists every provider attempt for the request in order. Each attempt shows the model, provider, status code, credentials, and how long it took, and failed attempts include the reason, such as a provider timeout or an exhausted routing budget.

To learn more about AI Gateway logs, read the documentation.
