title: Building Resilient LLM Data Pipelines: Rate Limiting and Circuit Breaking with Crawl4AI
description:
The Problem: When Your LLM Pipeline Becomes a DDoS Attack

Last quarter, our content ingestion pipeline for LLM fine-tuning crashed three times in production. The root cause? Unbounded retry loops in our web scraping layer created accidental DDoS attacks against upstream targets, triggering IP bans that cascaded into a 6-hour data blackout.

We were using Crawl4AI to convert documentation sites into LLM-ready markdown for our RAG system. The library itself is solid—clean markdown extraction, JavaScript rendering, and structured output. But we had wrapped it in naive retry logic that amplified transient network blips into infrastructure fires.

War Story: The Thundering Herd

The incident timeline:

  1. T+0m: Upstream CDN hiccup caused 3% request failure rate
  2. T+2m: Our scraper retried failed requests immediately, no backoff
  3. T+5m: Retry storm overwhelmed both the target and our Redis rate limiter
  4. T+12m: Target firewall banned our entire IP block
  5. T+6h: Manual intervention to rotate IPs and rebuild scrape queue

The fix required three layers of defense: exponential backoff with jitter, distributed rate limiting with atomic Lua scripts, and a circuit breaker to fail fast when targets are genuinely down.

Implementation: Resilient Crawl4AI Client Wrapper

Here's the production-grade wrapper we built. Copy-paste ready for TypeScript projects:

import axios, { AxiosError } from 'axios';

interface RetryConfig {
  maxRetries: number;
  baseDelayMs: number;
  maxDelayMs: number;
}

class ResilientCrawler {
  private failureCount = 0;
  private lastFailureTime = 0;
  private readonly circuitThreshold = 5;
  private readonly circuitResetMs = 60000;

  constructor(
    private crawl4aiEndpoint: string,
    private retryConfig: RetryConfig = {
      maxRetries: 3,
      baseDelayMs: 1000,
      maxDelayMs: 32000
    }
  ) {}

  private calculateBackoff(attempt: number): number {
    const exponential = Math.min(
      this.retryConfig.baseDelayMs * Math.pow(2, attempt),
      this.retryConfig.maxDelayMs
    );
    const jitter = exponential * 0.1 * Math.random();
    return exponential + jitter;
  }

  private isCircuitOpen(): boolean {
    if (this.failureCount < this.circuitThreshold) return false;

    const elapsed = Date.now() - this.lastFailureTime;
    if (elapsed > this.circuitResetMs) {
      this.failureCount = 0;
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }

  async scrape(url: string): Promise<string> {
    if (this.isCircuitOpen()) {
      throw new Error(`Circuit breaker OPEN: ${this.failureCount} consecutive failures`);
    }

    for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= this.retryConfig.maxRetries; attempt++) {
      try {
        const response = await axios.post(
          `${this.crawl4aiEndpoint}/crawl`,
          { url, markdown: true },
          { timeout: 30000 }
        );

        this.failureCount = 0;
        return response.data.markdown;

      } catch (error) {
        const isRetryable = this.isRetryableError(error as AxiosError);

        if (!isRetryable || attempt === this.retryConfig.maxRetries) {
          this.failureCount++;
          this.lastFailureTime = Date.now();
          throw error;
        }

        const backoffMs = this.calculateBackoff(attempt);
        await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, backoffMs));
      }
    }

    throw new Error('Retry exhausted');
  }

  private isRetryableError(error: AxiosError): boolean {
    if (!error.response) return true;
    const status = error.response.status;
    return status === 429 || status >= 500;
  }
}

Layer 2: Distributed Rate Limiter with Redis

For multi-worker deployments, client-side backoff isn't enough. You need atomic rate limiting at the infrastructure layer:

-- rate_limit.lua (Redis atomic sliding window)
local key = KEYS[1]
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, now - window)
local current = redis.call('ZCARD', key)

if current < limit then
  redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now)
  redis.call('EXPIRE', key, window)
  return 1
else
  return 0
end

# Python middleware using the Lua script
import redis
import time

class RedisRateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, redis_client: redis.Redis, script_path: str):
        with open(script_path) as f:
            self.script = redis_client.register_script(f.read())

    def allow(self, key: str, limit: int, window_sec: int) -> bool:
        now_ms = int(time.time() * 1000)
        return bool(self.script(
            keys=[f"ratelimit:{key}"],
            args=[limit, window_sec * 1000, now_ms]
        ))

Lessons from Production

  1. Jitter is non-negotiable: Without randomization, synchronized retries create secondary thundering herds
  2. Circuit breakers need memory: Track failure rate across requests, not just individual call stacks
  3. Atomic rate limits: Redis INCR is not atomic for sliding windows—use Lua scripts or sorted sets
  4. Fail fast on 4xx: Only retry transient errors (5xx, timeouts, network), never client errors

Integration with Crawl4AI Cloud

If you're using Crawl4AI Cloud instead of self-hosted, wrap the API client with the same resilience patterns. The cloud endpoint handles JavaScript rendering and gives you one-key access, but upstream rate limits and transient failures still require client-side defense.

The production deployment serves 2M pages/day for our LLM training pipeline with zero unplanned downtime since implementing these patterns.

References

  • Crawl4AI: github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai
  • Redis rate limiting: redis.io/commands/incr
  • Circuit breaker pattern: Martin Fowler's original post

No affiliates. No sponsors. Just infrastructure that doesn't catch fire at 3am.

title: How we migrated the database behind every Vercel build
description:
Every build on Vercel starts in the build warm pool, which is a set of standby containers that let builds begin without waiting for new compute. The pool runs on state that tracks which containers are ready, the tokens each one uses to authenticate, and the mapping that ties every running build back to the deployment that gets billed for it. When we built the pool, we put all of that in Redis, which was fast and made sense at the time.

Over the years, though, that state turned into a liability. Tokens and container statuses can be rebuilt if they get lost, but the billing mappings can't, and all of it was sitting in a store that we ran as an ephemeral cache. That state needed to live somewhere durable, which is why we decided to migrate it to DynamoDB.

The problem is that the pool never stops. Containers are coming up, polling, picking up work, and expiring around the clock, which meant we couldn't pause the world, copy the data, and restart. The migration had to happen live, under production traffic, in phases, each one behind a flag with a rollback ready if we needed it.

Durable state in an ephemeral store

Redis was a good home for it at first. It was fast, familiar, and efficient for the access patterns the pool started with. But over time the state became more important than the store holding it. If Redis became unavailable or lost data, the pool could no longer reliably authenticate containers, track which of them were ready, or resolve the work in flight.

Lose a token and the pool rebuilds it within about ten minutes. Lose a mapping and the build is never billed, because nothing else records which deployment it belonged to.

We wanted it in durable storage and landed on DynamoDB. On-demand scaling fits bursty deployment traffic, TTL is native, and there are no connections to manage at high concurrency. But what it did not promise was Redis's latency.

What Redis made cheap

Inside Redis, the pool's state looked like this:

  • Tokens lived in a set so we could check membership, and in a sorted set so we could expire them

  • Each lifecycle status (pending, polling, building) had its own sorted set, which meant a status change was a removal from one set and an add to the next

  • A string tied each working container to its deployment

All of these operations were cheap, about a millisecond each, and the code grew to lean on that speed. A single run of the supply loop, which is the loop that refills each warm pool in turn, would make hundreds of count calls just to tally up the pending and polling containers.

That's how the warm pool grew, one easy write at a time, until data we needed to keep was sitting in structures built for speed. Untangling that layout was where the migration started.

Designing the schema from the access patterns

Most migration plans treat the database as the thing being replaced. You map the access patterns, copy the data, and verify that the two stores agree. We planned ours that way too, so before designing any schema, we listed everything the code actually asked of that state:

  • Verify a token when a container polls for work

  • Add a token when a new container comes up

  • Expire tokens past their deadline

  • Count tokens to size the pool

  • Move a container between lifecycle statuses

  • Count containers by status

  • Look up the deployment behind a container's callback

  • Remove expired containers

Almost every operation already knows which container it's touching, and only polling ever starts from a token. So we put the container at the center of the model. The container ID became the sort key, and the token became just a field on the record, stored as a hash so that reading the table never hands you a usable credential. Verifying a token now just means looking up its container and comparing the hashes.

Two of the access patterns couldn't be served by a key lookup alone. Status counts had to skip containers that were already past expiry, which takes a time-aware index. And the deployment lookups feed billing, so they needed consistent reads, and the mapping got a small table of its own.

Reading a container's state, moving its status, and clearing its token all became direct key lookups. Counting a status became a single read against the time-aware index, one query per status with expired containers already filtered out.

Where Redis had let the data structures imply what we needed, DynamoDB made us spell out keys, indexes, conditional writes, and TTL behavior. So instead of carrying the Redis structures forward, we modeled the container and added the indexes that its access patterns needed.

Shadow mode validated every write

The rollout ran as feature-flagged phases: Redis-only, then dual writes, shadow reads, DynamoDB-primary, and finally DynamoDB-only. Every phase kept a rollback open for as long as possible. The last step, which removed the Redis writes, was the only one without an easy rollback, but any lingering token expires within ten minutes anyway.

We started by baselining the existing Redis operations, their counts and their latencies, so that the dashboards had a normal to compare against. The new DynamoDB methods merged days before anything actually called them. Dual writes went out next, with Redis still the source of truth and DynamoDB failures logged instead of fatal. Then came shadow reads, which queried both stores and compared the results. And then primary reads flipped, with the Redis writes kept on until the new path had proven itself.

What the comparisons told us was whether the two stores agreed on the stored values, which is something tests alone couldn't. They said nothing about timing. We checked that every write landed in both stores, that expiration kept moving forward as containers changed status so stale state never piled up, that clearing a token left the rest of the container's record intact, and that the counts stayed close enough to steer the pool.

On top of the comparisons we built dashboards that watched match rates, write errors, per-query latency, and expiration counts while Redis was still serving production. That way any divergence surfaced while it was still cheap to investigate, instead of showing up as a cutover failure. Every mismatch got chased down to a real bug, a dual-write race, or an expected difference before we moved on. Those dashboards decided when each phase advanced, and every time the numbers held steady under production traffic, the next step felt safer.

Two failures along the way

In March, one region's builds went down, and the investigation pointed at our own comparison machinery, which was the added load of checking two stores against each other. The scenario had actually come up in review, and we had throttled the comparisons for exactly that reason, but the throttling wasn't enough. Four days later, a pull request citing the incident added the index that the status counts needed. Without it, every count was O(n) work, and the comparisons were counting constantly. With the index in place, the rollout continued.

Later that month, the Redis infrastructure that we were migrating off actually went down. The warm pool and its token handling stayed up, because both of them were already reading from DynamoDB as the source of truth. Builds still felt the outage, but through services further up the pipeline that hadn't moved yet. The failure we'd been migrating away from arrived before the migration was even finished, and the state that had already moved survived it.

The supply loop stalled on slower reads

In April, the supply loop began to stall. The shadow data had looked healthy when we advanced primary reads, and the per-query latency had looked acceptable on the dashboards. What failed was a behavior that neither one measured.

We drew the loop to see where the time was going.

At P95 on getWarmPoolTokenCount, that check measured 1.29ms on Redis and 5.13ms on DynamoDB. At the time we shorthanded it as two to three times slower per query, which turned out to be an underestimate.

A few extra milliseconds cost nothing when you only pay them once. But the loop was paying them before every container, hundreds of times per run, and that stretched runs out to minutes at their worst, which meant the pool couldn't stay ahead of demand. The loop was an N+1 query, and Redis had just simply been fast enough to hide it.

No one wrote "this loop requires millisecond reads" anywhere. But the assumption lived in the design, and at a millisecond per check, nothing had ever made us stop and look.

We rebuilt the loop around the new latency

DynamoDB was never going to match Redis's millisecond, so instead of chasing it, we designed the requirement out.

The first attempt was batching, which is the shape drawn at the bottom of the sketch. The size of the gap depends on which percentile you look at, and at P90, where it was widest, the gap was about 17x. So the batch design checked state once per 17 containers, with one read amortized across the whole batch, and that constant was lifted straight from the measurement. But the constant was also the reason we walked away from it. It hard-coded a latency ratio that would drift with load, which meant one more unwritten dependency on the store's speed. Concurrency didn't need a constant at all.

What shipped instead let the loop's supply calls run concurrently, so each warm pool was no longer waiting behind the one before it, and each call worked from the last state it saw. Overlapping the reads bought us the same thing that batching would have, which is that no run serialized on any single read. The worst case is a few extra containers created from a stale picture of the pool, and that went into the pull request as an accepted cost. The redesign meant we could keep the more durable store without compromising the thing users actually care about, which is builds starting quickly and reliably. The fixes landed the same way the rollout did, one measured step at a time. As one of us put it, "we have less risk on each iteration because we've corrected for a previous misestimation."

It turned out the loop had stalled under Redis too, sometimes for a minute or more, and we only learned that while we were diagnosing DynamoDB. The evidence had been in our telemetry the whole time, but because the pool sits ahead of demand rather than in any request path, nothing had ever forced us to go look until the migration did. And the redesign ended up removing a flaw that was older than the project itself.

Migrating the assumptions

The migration completed in April, with the Redis calls gone from the warm pool paths. Copying the data turned out to be the easy part. The real work was finding the assumptions that had been built on top of the store, and then redesigning the loop that had held them. The state that every build depends on now lives in a store that was built to keep it, and the loop that manages it no longer serializes on any single read.

The April retrospective put the lesson in one sentence. "Even a 1ms-to-15ms query time degradation on P90 could bring down our warm pool management logic." Nobody had written that sentence in February, when the migration started.

title: I Replaced runc with a Rust Container Runtime (youki) for a Week
description:
The Boring Layer That Matters Most

Every container you've ever run — docker run hello-world included — went through a tiny binary called runc before it became a process. It creates the namespaces, sets up the cgroups, drops privileges, and hands off to your entrypoint.

You never think about it. And that's the problem.

runc is written in Go + C (yes, C — for the nsenter and pivot_root bits that Go can't handle cleanly). It's been the reference implementation since 2014. It's also the layer where CVE-2024-21626 (a container escape) lived.

What if that layer was memory-safe by construction?

Enter youki — a container runtime written entirely in Rust, now a CNCF Sandbox project.

What Is youki?

youki (Japanese for "container") is an OCI runtime-spec implementation in Rust. It's a drop-in replacement for runc: same CLI, same spec, same integration path through containerd, Podman, or Docker.

Fact Detail
Language Rust (pure, except a libseccomp-rs FFI shim being replaced)
CNCF status Sandbox (accepted Oct 17, 2024)
GitHub youki-dev/youki
Stars ~7,300
License Apache 2.0
Adopters Azure Kubernetes Service, Docker, containerd/runwasi
Contributing orgs Microsoft, Docker, Red Hat

The key differentiator vs. runc: no Go runtime startup, no C nsenter binary, no mixed-language memory safety boundary. The entire create → start → delete lifecycle lives in one Rust binary with compile-time safety guarantees.

The Benchmarks (Honest Version)

The headline number from youki's own repo:

Runtime Time (mean ± σ)        Range (min … max)    vs youki
youki   111.5 ms ± 11.6 ms     84.0 ms … 142.5 ms   100%
runc    224.6 ms ± 12.0 ms     190.5 ms … 255.4 ms  200%
crun     47.3 ms ±  2.8 ms     42.4 ms …  56.2 ms   42%

Youki is ~2× faster than runc for create → start → delete. But crun is ~2.5× faster than youki.

Here's the honest context:

Scenario Does it matter?
Single long-lived container No. 100ms of startup is noise over a 7-day uptime.
Serverless: 10k containers/min Yes. A 100ms savings × 10k = 1,000 CPU-seconds per minute reclaimed.
K8s pod churn (CI/CD, spot nodes) Moderately. Image pull + CNI + scheduling dominate; runtime is ~5–10% of total.
Edge/embedded (tight RAM) Yes. youki's binary is smaller and RSS is lower per instance.

The real win isn't raw speed — it's the Rust safety guarantee. You're not betting your node's security on a C memcpy in nsenter.

Setup: Replacing runc on a K8s Node

Prerequisites

  • Kubernetes 1.28+ with containerd (not Docker Engine)
  • Linux kernel 5.10+ (youki drops older kernel support to use modern features)
  • cargo / just for building from source (or use a pre-built binary)

Step 1: Build youki 

git clone https://github.com/youki-dev/youki.git
cd youki
just build
# Binary: ./target/release/youki

Or grab a release binary from GitHub Releases.

Step 2: Register with containerd

Edit /etc/containerd/config.toml (or use containerd config path):

[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.youki]
  runtimeType = "io.containerd.youki.v1"

Then install the shim (youki ships a containerd-compatible shim):

sudo cp target/release/youki /usr/local/bin/
sudo cp target/release/containerd-shim-youki-v1 /usr/local/bin/

Restart containerd:

sudo systemctl restart containerd

Step 3: Create a RuntimeClass 

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: youki
handler: youki
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/arch: amd64

kubectl apply -f runtimeclass-youki.yaml

Step 4: Run a Pod with youki 

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: youki-test
spec:
  runtimeClassName: youki
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "32Mi"
        cpu: "10m"

kubectl apply -f youki-pod.yaml
kubectl get pod youki-test -o wide
# youki-test   1/1   Running   0   2s

Verify it's actually using youki:

kubectl exec youki-test -- cat /proc/1/cgroup
# Confirms cgroup v2 hierarchy managed by youki

Step 5: Run It for a Week (What I Noticed)

I ran a 3-node k3s cluster with a mix of workloads:

  • 20 long-lived API pods (Go, ~50 MB each)
  • A CI pipeline spawning 50–200 short-lived pods/day
  • A cron job that scales a batch processor 0 → 10 → 0 every hour

What went well:

  1. Zero crashes, zero OOMs in the runtime itself. The Rust error handling is visible in logs — when something goes wrong, you get a structured Error with context, not a segfault.
  2. Short-lived pods were noticeably snappier. My CI pods (build → test → delete) came up ~30–50ms faster than runc. Not dramatic per-pod, but across 200 pods/day it added up.
  3. Rootless mode was cleaner. youki create with --rootless worked without the newuidmap/subuid gymnastics that runc sometimes needs.
  4. Binary size. youki: ~8 MB. runc: ~12 MB. crun: ~3 MB. On an edge node with 512 MB RAM, every MB counts.

What was rough:

  1. cgroups v1 support is there but v2 is the path of least resistance. If your distro still defaults to v1 (looking at you, CentOS 7), you'll hit edge cases.
  2. No --checkpoint/--restore (CRIU) yet. If you rely on live migration or pause/resume, you're stuck on runc.
  3. Docs are thin. The user docs cover the basics but there's no "migrating a production cluster from runc to youki" guide. You're on your own.
  4. One C dependency remains. libseccomp-rs is an FFI wrapper around the C libseccomp. The team is working on a pure-Rust replacement, but it's not done.

youki vs. runc vs. crun: Where Each Wins

Dimension runc crun youki
Language Go + C C Rust
Memory safety ❌ (C portion) ❌ ✅ (99% — one FFI shim)
Create→delete (benchmark) 224 ms 47 ms 111 ms
Binary size ~12 MB ~3 MB ~8 MB
cgroups v2 ✅ ✅ ✅
Rootless ✅ ✅ ✅ (cleanest)
CRIU (checkpoint/restore) ✅ ✅ ❌ (roadmap)
Wasm support ❌ ❌ ✅ (first-class)
CNCF governance ❌ (OCI) ✅ (Sandbox) ✅ (Sandbox)
Production battle-testing 10+ years 5+ years ~3 years
Best for Default, compatibility Max performance, minimal footprint Safety + Wasm + future-proofing

The honest takeaway: If you need maximum raw speed today, crun wins. If you need the safest runtime with a path to Wasm workloads, youki is the pick. runc remains the "it just works" default.

The Wasm Angle (Why This Matters More Than You Think)

Here's the part that excites me: youki is the low-level runtime that powers runwasi (the containerd shim for Wasm workloads) and, by extension, SpinKube.

The architecture:

containerd
  └── containerd-shim-runwasi (Rust)
        └── youki libcontainer (Rust) ← shared library
              └── Wasmtime / Wasmer / WasmEdge

Youki's libcontainer crate is used as a library by other Rust container tools. That means the same memory-safe, OCI-compliant primitives that run your nginx:alpine pod also run your Wasm modules. One codebase, two workload types, same security guarantees.

This is the "Rust container stack" taking shape:

Layer Rust project Role
Runtime youki OCI container lifecycle
Shim runwasi Wasm on containerd
Orchestrator SpinKube Wasm on Kubernetes
Image tooling naftiko Build OCI/Wasm images
Spec oci-spec (Rust crate) The spec itself, in Rust

Youki is the foundation. If it's not solid, nothing above it is.

What's Missing (and Where Funding Helps)

youki is in CNCF Sandbox — the earliest maturity level. The project is healthy (active commits, 80+ contributors, backing from Microsoft/Docker/Red Hat) but under-resourced for what it needs to do:

  • Pure-Rust seccomp (eliminate the last C dependency) — significant engineering effort
  • SELinux in Rust — needed for RHEL/CentOS production adoption
  • CRIU support — checkpoint/restore is table-stakes for production
  • OCI conformance test suite — a dedicated, automated compliance harness
  • Docs and migration guides — "how do I move a 500-node cluster from runc to youki?"
  • Security audit — a formal audit would be a major trust signal for enterprise adoption
  • Conference presence — KubeCon, RustConf, containersc — the project needs more visibility

No LFX Crowdfunding campaign is active yet. If you use or evaluate youki, the highest-impact things you can do:

  1. Contribute — even docs, test cases, or bug reports. GitHub
  2. Run it in production and report what breaks (or doesn't)
  3. Write about it — this article is a start, but we need more "I ran youki in a real cluster" content
  4. Watch for an LFX Crowdfunding launch — CNCF funding page

TL;DR

Question Answer
Is youki production-ready? For new, non-critical workloads: yes. For a 500-node cluster: not yet.
Is it faster than runc? ~2× for create/delete. Yes, but crun is faster still.
Is it safer than runc? Yes — memory-safe Rust eliminates the C nsenter attack surface.
Should I switch today? If you're running Wasm workloads or want to be early on the Rust container stack: yes. Otherwise: watch this space.
What's the risk? It's a Sandbox project. The API could shift. CRIU is missing. Docs are thin.

Final Thought

The container runtime is the most underappreciated layer in the stack. It's the thing that's always running, that touches every syscall, that sits between your workload and the kernel. For a decade, that layer was a Go binary with a C sidecar.

Now there's a Rust option with CNCF governance, major-company backing, and a clear path to being the foundation for the next generation of container workloads (including Wasm).

I ran it for a week. It didn't break. It was faster. And the Rust error messages in the logs were genuinely pleasant to read.

That's about as good as "boring infrastructure" gets.

Have you tried youki in production? What broke? What didn't? Drop your experience in the comments — I'm especially curious about anyone running it alongside runwasi or SpinKube.

If you want to support the project, the best things right now are **contributing code/docs* and writing about your experience. The CNCF funding infrastructure is ready when the project is.*

title: Edge Config is now Global Config
description:
Edge Config is now Global Config. This rename better reflects that it is a globally replicated data store with ~1ms reads in every region, built for the configuration that applications read at runtime, such as feature flags, redirects, and experimentation settings.

Global Config stores can now hold up to 1 MB on every plan, and Pro and Enterprise teams can create unlimited stores with more writes per day. The rename also ships with a new server-side SDK, @vercel/global-config, and a new environment variable.

What changed

  • Name: Global Config is the new name for Edge Config. The store itself is unchanged.

  • Package: @vercel/global-config replaces @vercel/edge-config as a drop-in replacement.

  • Environment variable: Connecting a Global Config store to a project creates a GLOBAL_CONFIG environment variable instead of EDGE_CONFIG.

  • Limits: Raised on every plan. Pricing is unchanged.

What you need to do

  • Existing projects: no action required. Deployments, connected stores, and the EDGE_CONFIG environment variable continue to work.

  • Upgrading proactively is safe. The new SDK reads GLOBAL_CONFIG by default and falls back to EDGE_CONFIG, so it works with stores connected before and after the rename. You can switch packages today without touching your stores.

  • Creating stores and pushing new config values work without upgrading. Neither depends on which SDK version your project uses.

  • Upgrade before connecting new stores to a project. Connecting a store now creates a GLOBAL_CONFIG environment variable, and the legacy SDK only reads EDGE_CONFIG by default. A project still on @vercel/edge-config cannot read a newly connected store.

To upgrade, install the new package and update imports:

New limits

Limit

Hobby

Pro

Enterprise

Stores

1 (unchanged)

Unlimited (was 3)

Unlimited (was 10)

Writes

250/month (unchanged)

100/hour (was 480/day)

100/hour (was 480/day)

Store size

1 MB (was 8 KB)

1 MB (was 64 KB)

1 MB (was 512 KB)

Pricing is unchanged at $3 per 1,000,000 reads and $1 per 100 writes.

See the Global Config migration guide for custom setups and the full list of changes.

title: Trust Is a Feature: Verification Lessons From Building the Calendrz Mobile Backend
description:
Trust was everywhere in my LinkedIn feed last week. LinkedIn is testing a feature that lets verified members confirm their connections’ work and school history, with enough confirmations earning a profile badge. Its engineering team also explained how it detects low-quality AI content. And in Europe, the AI Act’s transparency rules had their first real effect: OpenAI said it will add invisible watermarks to text generated in the EU.

Each of those is a different problem, but the theme is the same. “Trust me” isn’t good enough any more. Platforms are being asked to prove things: that a person really worked where they say, that a piece of text really came from where it claims, that an account is really who it says it is.

I’ve spent the last couple of weeks on a less glamorous version of the same problem: preparing the Calendrz backend for native iOS and Android apps. Most of that work wasn’t about features. It was about making sure that the thing calling our API really is who it claims to be, and that the trust stops when it should.

Why mobile apps make trust harder

A web app has an easy setup: a session cookie, on a domain you control, in a browser that enforces a lot of rules for you. A mobile app is a public client. It runs on a device you don’t control, it can’t keep a secret (anything shipped in an app binary can be extracted), and it stays signed in for weeks. If a token leaks, you need to know, and you need to be able to shut it down.

Calendrz holds access to people’s work and personal calendars. That’s sensitive data: who you meet, when, and often why. So the bar here isn’t “good enough for a to-do app”.

What we built: verification at every hop

Here’s a quick tour of the trust-related pieces that landed in the Calendrz backend over the past couple of weeks.

1. Proof of who’s calling: PKCE public clients

The iOS and Android apps are registered as first-party OAuth clients with no secret, because a secret in an app isn’t really secret. They sign in with PKCE instead, which proves that the app finishing the login is the same app that started it. A malicious app that intercepts the redirect can’t do anything with the code it grabbed.

2. Proof that the link is really ours: Universal Links and App Links

When a login finishes, the browser has to hand control back to the app. Custom URL schemes can be claimed by any app, so we serve the Apple and Android “well-known” verification files from our own domain. That’s how the operating system knows a link to calendrz.com really belongs to the Calendrz app. If an environment isn’t configured, the files return a 404, so a misconfigured server can never claim links it shouldn’t.

3. Detecting stolen tokens: refresh-token reuse detection

This is the one I’m proudest of. The mobile apps get short-lived access tokens (60 minutes) and a refresh token that rotates: every time it’s used, it’s replaced. The catch is that a plain rotation setup only knows about the current token. If an attacker copied an older one, the server just sees an unknown token and rejects it, but never notices that something is wrong.

So we now keep a record (a SHA-256 hash, never the token itself) of every refresh token that has been rotated out. If one of those shows up again, that’s the signature of a stolen token chain, as described in the OAuth security best-practice RFC (RFC 9700). Calendrz then revokes the whole authorization, so both the attacker and the legitimate app have to sign in again, while the user’s other sessions are left alone. Refreshes for a given authorization are serialized at the database level, so two refreshes racing each other can’t be mistaken for an attack, and can’t undo a revocation.

4. Trust that ends when it should: revoke on account deletion

When you close your Calendrz account, or unlink one of your connected calendar accounts, every OAuth authorization tied to that identity is now removed. That covers the mobile apps and any AI assistants you’ve connected over MCP. Their refresh tokens die with the account. The revocation runs only after the deletion has committed, so a failure can’t leave you half-deleted.

5. Failing honestly instead of failing quietly

A smaller one, but it’s the same idea. When the new mobile event endpoints can’t load your calendar from Google or Microsoft, they now return an explicit “service unavailable” error instead of an empty list. An empty calendar is a claim (“you’re free all day”), and an app or agent would act on it. If we can’t verify the answer, we say so.

Trust is a feature, even if nobody sees it

LinkedIn’s colleague vouching will show up as a badge on a profile. Most of the work I’ve described won’t show up anywhere. Nobody opens an app and thinks “great refresh-token rotation”. But it follows the same principle: don’t take identity on faith; verify it, and be able to revoke it.

There’s also a lot of AI in this story. Much of this backend work was planned, written and code-reviewed with AI agents, and several of the review rounds caught real issues: a race between two concurrent refreshes, a revocation that could have been rolled back, a log line that leaked more than it should have. As more code gets written this way, having automated checks verify the work before it ships is the engineering version of the trust problem LinkedIn and the EU are trying to solve for content.

The Calendrz mobile apps are still in progress, but most of the trust layer underneath them is already in place. That felt like the right order: build the part people need to rely on before the part they’ll see.

Calendrz keeps your work and personal calendars in sync, privately and securely. Find out more at calendrz.com.

title: AI Is Redrawing the US Data Center Map
description:
Power access is shaping where new campuses rise, when they come online, and the networks connecting them.

October 18, 2026

In June 2024, construction began on the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas. Within a year, its first two buildings had been energized. By September 2025, Crusoe said the site was running early training and inference workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The planned campus would eventually contain eight buildings. Crusoe’s account captures both the speed of the AI infrastructure boom and its defining complication: large campuses become useful in stages.

That progression is changing the geography of computing. Developers need sites where land, electricity and equipment can come together on a workable schedule. As established markets fill up, new locations become attractive, and connecting distant facilities becomes an engineering problem of its own.

The spending curve shows how quickly this has become a national construction story. In November 2022, private US data center construction was running at an annualized pace of $13.9 billion. By August 2026, that rate had reached $85.0 billion, roughly six times as much. These Census Bureau figures cover data centers broadly and measure construction work, including fixed electrical and mechanical systems. They exclude racks and servers, whose costs sit on top of the building investment.

Figure 1. Monthly construction spending expressed as a seasonally adjusted annual rate, in current dollars. The August figure is a spending pace, rather than money already spent during 2026. Source: US Census Bureau.

Construction spending was already increasing before ChatGPT’s launch. Because the figures are in current dollars, the curve combines changes in construction prices with changes in the amount being built. It establishes the growing scale of spending without measuring computing capacity.

The next question is where that work can happen. In its August report, JLL placed 77% of North American data center capacity under construction in frontier markets, highlighting West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and the Carolinas. Its market analysis describes a buildout extending well beyond the industry’s established hubs.

Texas illustrates the shift. JLL reported 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity across the state, compared with 13 GW in Virginia. Northern Virginia remained the largest individual market, with nearly 7 GW of inventory. The state totals show the direction of investment while including projects that still have to become operating facilities.

Figure 2. State totals combine existing capacity and capacity under construction, including hyperscalers’ own facilities. They do not measure electricity currently being consumed. Source: JLL, Midyear 2026.

A large pipeline creates a planning problem for utilities. They must decide how much infrastructure to build before they know which projects will arrive, when their servers will be installed, or how quickly customer workloads will fill them. A speculative request can therefore influence planning long before it becomes a substantial electricity load.

AEP Ohio’s experience shows how that pipeline changes as commitments become binding. Its new tariff required developers to advance through paid studies and financial commitments. About one-fifth of the initial requested capacity reached signed contracts. AEP attributed the narrowing to the filtering of speculative or uncertain projects. The utility still had 17.9 GW of total contracted data center projects, including earlier contracts, scheduled to come online progressively through 2035. AEP’s February update distinguishes those future obligations from operating demand.

Figure 3. Successive stages of one AEP Ohio intake cohort, as reported in February 2026. The final bar excludes contracts signed before the tariff. Source: AEP Ohio.

Texas faces its own version of the credibility problem. ERCOT’s September board update documented a pause in energization approvals for relevant new data center and cryptocurrency facilities of at least 75 MW while verification and community-impact reviews proceeded. Projects received provisional classifications; those classifications did not constitute final permission to connect. The operator expected to publish its community-impact report by December 10.

For developers, that makes the location of available power consequential to computing design. Microsoft offers a concrete example. Its Fairwater facilities in Wisconsin and the Atlanta area are linked through a dedicated network intended to let sites cooperate on large AI workloads. Microsoft explicitly identifies land and power availability as reasons to spread work across locations. Its description of the architecture connects the choice of geography to the need for new networking infrastructure.

Distance introduces costs of its own. Large training jobs require frequent communication among processors; slow exchanges can leave expensive hardware waiting. Microsoft describes dedicated fiber and changes to network protocols designed to reduce bottlenecks between sites. Finding land and power therefore creates another task: making the resulting facilities operate efficiently together.

There are also ways to change the terms on which a facility receives electricity. In a report published October 14, the International Energy Agency examines connection agreements that allow consumption to be curtailed, phased in or adjusted to grid conditions. Such arrangements can help projects connect sooner by changing the reliability or timing of their access.

The tradeoff is practical. Interrupting expensive AI hardware can be costly, and a facility operator may have limited control over customers’ workloads. The IEA’s analysis identifies coordination among computing customers, facility operators and electricity networks as a condition for greater flexibility. Onsite generation also brings equipment lead times and engineering requirements of its own.

The buildout is consequently creating an architecture that extends beyond each campus. Transmission studies, substations, fiber routes and electricity agreements increasingly influence where AI work can run. Abilene’s first buildings became useful when several of those pieces came together. Repeating that achievement across a much larger pipeline will determine how quickly the new map translates into computing capacity.

Data: Figures use the research snapshot checked October 18, 2026. Each chart retains its source’s geography, period and definition. Charts are original graphics based on the cited figures.

title: Download mode explained: how to enter it, what each screen means, and how to exit safely
description:
If you have ever plugged a Samsung phone into a flashing tool and watched it sit there unrecognized, Download mode is usually the missing piece. It is a low-level state that lets a computer talk to the phone before the normal system starts. That is why tools such as Odin need it: they are not installing an app, they are writing system software, and they need a stable channel to do that work.

What Download mode actually does

Download mode, also called Odin mode, puts the phone in a waiting state. The phone is not booting into its home screen, and it is not running your apps. Instead, it listens for instructions over USB and accepts a firmware package when a trusted tool sends one. When the connection is working, the flashing tool can see the phone, check that it is ready, and start the transfer.

That also explains why the phone can look almost blank in this mode. It is not frozen, and it is not broken. It is simply holding still so the computer can do its job without the normal system getting in the way.

How to enter Download mode on newer Galaxy phones

On most newer Galaxy phones without a physical Home button, use this sequence:

  1. Power the phone fully off.
  2. Press and hold Volume Up and Volume Down at the same time.
  3. While still holding both buttons, plug in a USB cable connected to a computer.
  4. Keep holding the buttons until the warning screen appears, then let go.

If the phone starts charging or boots normally, you probably released the buttons too early or plugged the cable in after the phone had already started. Power it off and try again, keeping both volume buttons held as the cable goes in.

How to enter Download mode on older models

On older models with a physical Home button, the combination is different:

  1. Power the phone fully off.
  2. Press and hold Volume Down, Home, and Power at the same time.
  3. Keep holding them until the warning screen appears, then let go.

The idea is the same on both kinds of phone: start from powered off, hold the right buttons, and wait for the warning screen rather than the normal logo animation.

What the warning screen means and how to continue

The first screen is a warning. It tells you that installing unofficial or custom software can cause problems, and it asks you to confirm that you understand the risk. That warning is there for a reason. Flashing the wrong package, or stopping halfway, can leave the phone unable to boot normally.

Read it, pause, and only continue if you are sure about what you are about to flash. To continue into Download mode, press Volume Up. To cancel and restart the phone instead, press Volume Down. Do not rush this step. If you are unsure, backing out is the safer choice.

What the downloading screen shows

After you press Volume Up, you should see the main Download mode screen. It usually shows the word Downloading, a large icon, and a short block of device details such as the model, product name, and current binary status. On some phones it also shows whether the bootloader is locked or unlocked and whether the device has been modified.

Those details matter. Before you flash anything, check that the model shown matches the phone in your hand and the firmware you prepared. If something looks off, stop and check your files before you connect a flashing tool.

At this point the phone is ready. A flashing tool on the computer should now detect it, and you can load the firmware package you already checked.

How to exit safely

If you have not started a flash, leaving Download mode is simple.

  • Hold Volume Down and Power together until the phone restarts.
  • On some models, a long press of the Power button alone will also restart the phone.

Let the phone restart on its own and reach the normal lock screen. Do not pull the battery on a phone with a sealed battery, and do not force a restart in the middle of a transfer.

If a flash is already in progress, do not exit. Wait until the tool reports that it finished and the phone restarts by itself. Interrupting a transfer is one of the fastest ways to cause a boot problem.

Common mistakes to avoid

Entering Recovery mode by accident

Recovery mode uses a different button combination and shows a menu with options such as reboot, wipe, and apply update. If you see that menu, you did not enter Download mode. Power off and try the Download mode combination again, paying close attention to which volume button you held.

Unplugging the phone mid-flash

Once a flash starts, the cable is part of the process. Unplugging the phone, closing the tool, or letting the computer sleep can break the transfer. Keep the phone still, keep the cable connected, and wait for the tool to finish.

Using a bad cable or loose port

A cable that only charges, a worn connector, or a loose port can drop the connection at the worst moment. Use a good-quality data cable, plug it directly into the computer rather than through a hub when you can, and check that the phone is detected before you start. If the tool keeps losing the phone, swap the cable and try another USB port before you blame the firmware.

A short safety note

Back up anything you cannot afford to lose before you flash. Flashing can wipe data, and it can fail even when you follow the steps carefully. Also use firmware made for your exact model and CSC, which is the region and carrier configuration code. A package for a similar-looking model is not close enough. Check the model number on the phone, check the CSC, and only then start.

Download mode is not something to fear, but it is something to respect. Enter it with the right buttons, read the warning, confirm the details on the screen, and leave it the clean way. If you want a place to check firmware details before you start, SamFware keeps things organized, and you can return to SamFware whenever you need to double-check a model or CSC before flashing.

title: Accelerator certification speeds VLA models 10
description:
Bounding the risk of acceleration‑induced failure lets practitioners reap order‑of‑magnitude speedups on vision‑language‑action agents. The twist is that a formal guarantee can coexist with those gains, overturning the common belief that safety and performance are mutually exclusive.

Prior VLA accelerators have chased raw latency reductions—action chunking, visual‑token pruning, and similar tricks—while reporting only average task success. Those metrics hide failures that only manifest over closed‑loop trajectories, because a single misstep can cascade into an episode‑level collapse that the average numbers never reveal.

CARE certifies 9.0–10.8× faster inference while guaranteeing that at least 85.8 % of reference‑solved episodes remain successful with 95 % confidence, even under a user‑specified failure budget [1].

The certification process itself requires roughly five times fewer rollouts than exhaustive testing. “care also has the lowest evaluation cost, using 5,263 rather than 25,000 rollouts ( fewer) and reducing H1 evaluation from 1,000 to 113 rollouts.” [1]

The method’s guarantees rely on a static calibration set and have only been demonstrated on four LIBERO suites and two agents (Qwen3.5‑9B, Llama‑3.1‑8B), leaving open how it scales to larger, continually evolving deployments or to online adaptation scenarios [1].

Future VLA benchmark runs should replace naïve latency baselines with CARE‑certified selectors as the default evaluation protocol, and deployment pipelines ought to employ failure‑triggered reference rollouts instead of exhaustive pre‑deployment testing.

References

  1. CARE: Certifying Acceleration for Vision-Language-Action Inference

title: Retrieval Platform vs Specialist Candidate Search: 4 Failure-Recovery Rules (My Choice)
description:
Short answer: for a game studio's recruiting search, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. A general retrieval platform is a good fit for the web-context stage; a specialist search service is the better choice when regional residency, deletion SLAs, or contractual processor boundaries are the deciding requirement.

The bill is usually not the first thing to model. The dominant term is the work you repeat: fetching the same public page, embedding unchanged candidate material, and reranking a wide result set after a timeout. Keep raw pages and embeddings only as long as your recruiting policy permits, then delete them deliberately. The trade-off is real: a deleted snapshot cannot help explain a decision made six months ago.

That loss is deliberate.

Start with a retrieval contract, not a vendor

For a game hiring team, “find a gameplay engineer with console networking experience” is an answer contract, not an implementation. Define the fields the UI can show, the maximum number of candidates, and the evidence each hit must carry. The contract should require tenant ID, access-control labels, source URL or document ID, fetch time, and a deletion deadline on every indexed item.

Use two collections: one for public web context and one for first-party candidate records. They have different owners and retention rules. A web result may be refreshed; a candidate resume may need immediate deletion when a person withdraws consent. Mixing them makes an innocent rerank request cross a trust boundary.

Infrai fits the public-context leg because it exposes web and vector capabilities through plain REST, without making the recruiting system install and track a client SDK. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and needs no key, so an integration check can read the request schema, response schema, and runnable examples before a protected request crosses the boundary. Infrai uses a single API key and one bill across the platform's capabilities; for this workflow, that means one credential policy across the fetch and index stages instead of separate key rotation and invoice reconciliation. Those are two concrete maintenance advantages when several services participate in recovery.

The recovery path is intentionally boring. Search a bounded slice, record which stage answered, and return citations with the context. If web search reaches its timeout, the first-party collection can still produce a useful answer that clearly identifies the stages used. This is preferable to silently blending stale pages into a confident shortlist, especially when the user is an internal recruiter who will act on the ordering rather than inspect every source. Preserve the source URL or document identifier in each result so a reviewer can trace what contributed to the result without assuming the indexed copy is still authoritative.

How should retrieval architecture handle candidate search failure recovery?

Use a short, explicit state machine: fetch, normalize, index, retrieve, rerank, and cite. Each transition gets a timeout and a retry budget. A retry must not create a second vector record, so the upsert key is derived from the source document ID and content version. Standard queues are at-least-once; consumers therefore need the same idempotency rule.

Before wiring protected requests, this runnable check confirms that discovery advertises the web-search entry route. It sends an explicit method, handles rate limits, checks status, and makes no assumptions about undeclared request fields.

import os
import time
import requests

url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

for attempt in range(3):
    response = requests.request(
        method="GET",
        url=url,
        headers=headers,
        timeout=8,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        delay = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
        time.sleep(delay * (2**attempt))
        continue
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
    advertised = {item["path"] for item in response.json()["capabilities"]}
    required = {"/v1/web/search"}
    missing = required - advertised
    if missing:
        raise RuntimeError(f"routes unavailable: {sorted(missing)}")
    print("retrieval routes available")
    break
else:
    raise TimeoutError("discovery retry budget exhausted")

The important invariant is that tenant and access-control metadata never disappear during normalization. Treat a retry as a scheduling decision rather than a reason to widen the query: honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, back off exponentially, and keep the total attempt count bounded. For writes, derive an idempotency key from the source document ID and content version. Then a repeated upsert represents the same fact instead of duplicating context. If a source cannot supply the required tenant and access labels, stop at fetch; don't guess.

Small budgets win here.

Retention is part of relevance quality

Deletion changes recall. Set a retention clock per collection, delete expired source text and vectors together, and retain only the minimum audit record allowed by policy: document ID, tenant, decision timestamp, and the source pointer needed for review. The exact record depends on the recruiting policy and processor contract. Do not retain a public page forever just because it was easy to crawl.

One key can cover the web and vector calls while the specialist provider remains the system of record for candidate data. This reduces credential rotation and reconciliation work across the two retrieval stages. It does not collapse their retention policies into one, and it is not a promise that a routing layer supplies residency or contractual deletion guarantees.

The catch is important. If your legal team requires a named processor in a specific region, an auditable deletion SLA, or private networking into the applicant-tracking system, choose the specialist service that can sign those terms. A unified API does not replace that contract.

Four options under the same failure budget

The comparison below is about operating boundaries, not a popularity contest. Measure retrieval quality and tail latency with your own candidate queries before committing.

Option Retrieval and recovery shape Trust-boundary fit Choose it when
Elasticsearch Mature filters, analyzers, and shard-level controls; you own retry and replay logic. Strong control in your deployment, with more operational surface. You need deep boolean filtering beside vector search.
OpenSearch Familiar Lucene lineage and self-managed deployment choices. Useful for teams that require infrastructure ownership. You already operate AWS-compatible search clusters.
Pinecone Managed vector index with simple scaling model. Verify region, deletion behavior, and processor terms for your data. You want a vector specialist and can keep sensitive records elsewhere.
Infrai web + vector routes Staged web and vector calls over one REST surface; bounded requests and your own collection policy. Good for public or low-sensitivity context; residency and contractual guarantees remain with the specialist provider. You want HTTP-only integration for the context leg and a separate system of record for candidate data.

Do not compare these on a single top-20 score. A retrieval miss caused by a deleted document is a policy outcome, while a miss caused by a low-quality embedding is a relevance problem. Log them separately. I’m not sure any off-the-shelf benchmark captures that distinction for your hiring corpus; your mileage may vary with language mix, stale profiles, and access rules.

A practical decision rule

Run a two-week replay of anonymized queries. Cap web fetches, cap vector candidates, and inject timeouts into each stage. Track answer coverage, citation coverage, p95 latency, and the number of records removed by tenant or ACL filters. Then ask one uncomfortable question: can an auditor reconstruct why this candidate appeared without restoring deleted personal data?

Try Infrai for the public web-context portion if the answer is yes and your team values a plain HTTP integration across languages. Keep a specialist search backend for restricted candidate records when region, retention, or processor language is non-negotiable. That split preserves failure recovery without pretending every backend has the same trust boundary.

Further reading

References: Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper, Elasticsearch reference, OpenSearch documentation, and Pinecone documentation. If this public-context boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's reranking guide.

title: npm Supply-Chain Attacks: What the Chalk and Shai-Hulud Incidents Mean for Your App
description:
In September 2025 attackers poisoned some of the most widely used packages on npm, the public registry almost every modern web app is built from. This is a software supply-chain attack: rather than break into your company, attackers compromise code you depend on. In the worst of them, the Shai-Hulud worm, the prize was developers' cloud and GitHub keys.

Below: the two biggest npm supply-chain incidents, why they matter even if you've never heard of npm, and a checklist to protect your product. Much of it belongs in your build pipeline, which our CI/CD pipelines service sets up with reproducible builds and least-privilege secrets.

What happened in the 2025 npm attacks

September 2025: Chalk, Debug and 16 other packages

On 8 September 2025, an attacker phished the npm account of a well-known maintainer and published malicious versions of 18 widely used packages, including chalk and debug: small utilities that sit deep inside a huge number of projects. Together they are downloaded billions of times a week.

The injected code tried to intercept and redirect cryptocurrency wallet transactions in the browser. The bad versions were removed within hours, but any project that installed during that window pulled them in automatically.

September 2025: the Shai-Hulud worm

A week later came something worse: Shai-Hulud, a self-replicating worm. When a developer installed an infected package, the malware:

  1. searched the machine for secrets: GitHub tokens and cloud keys for AWS, Google Cloud and Azure;
  2. sent them to the attackers and published them in a public GitHub repository named "Shai-Hulud";
  3. used the developer's own npm access to inject itself into other packages they maintained, and published those, so it spread on its own.

On 23 September 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) reported that over 500 packages had been compromised. GitHub, which runs npm, removed the infected packages and blocked uploads carrying the malware's signatures. Later waves of the campaign hit hundreds more.

Why this matters to a business, not just to developers

  • Your app can be infected without anyone writing bad code. A routine npm install on a developer laptop or build server was enough.
  • The target was your keys. Cloud credentials stolen from a developer machine can open your production servers, databases and customer data.
  • Front-end code reaches your customers. A poisoned package in your website's JavaScript runs in your visitors' browsers, as the Chalk attack tried to exploit.
  • It's not a one-off. One widely used package reaches thousands of victims at once, so attackers will keep trying.

What changed afterwards

GitHub then announced a plan to tighten npm publishing, including:

  • publishing only through 2FA-protected local publishing, short-lived granular tokens or trusted publishing;
  • deprecating legacy classic tokens;
  • moving from authenticator-app codes (TOTP) to phishing-resistant FIDO-based 2FA;
  • expanding trusted publishing, which publishes straight from CI with short-lived OIDC credentials instead of long-lived tokens.

These changes make maintainer accounts harder to hijack. Every team still has to protect its own projects.

How to protect your app from npm supply-chain attacks

For every project

  • [ ] Commit your lockfile (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml or yarn.lock) and install from it in CI (npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile). Builds should never quietly pick up a newer version.
  • [ ] Don't upgrade dependencies the moment they're released. Most malicious versions are caught within hours or days. Renovate and Dependabot can wait a few days before proposing one.
  • [ ] Review install scripts. Many attacks run during installation; pnpm, for example, can block dependency lifecycle scripts unless you allow them.
  • [ ] Turn on automated alerts: Dependabot security updates and GitHub secret scanning cost nothing on most plans.
  • [ ] Remove what you don't use. Every dependency is attack surface; audit them once or twice a year.

For developer machines and CI

  • [ ] Use phishing-resistant 2FA (security keys or passkeys) on GitHub, npm and your cloud console. CISA specifically recommends this.
  • [ ] Keep long-lived secrets off laptops. Use short-lived credentials (such as AWS SSO sessions), not permanent access keys in config files.
  • [ ] Give CI only what it needs. A build job that runs tests shouldn't hold production deployment keys.
  • [ ] Use trusted publishing if you publish packages yourself, so there's no npm token to steal.

If you think you were affected

CISA's guidance, summarised:

  1. Check your lockfiles (including nested dependencies) and cached packages against published lists of compromised versions.
  2. Pin to known-good versions.
  3. Rotate every credential a developer or CI machine could have exposed: GitHub tokens, npm tokens, cloud keys, API keys.
  4. Review GitHub for unexpected repositories, workflows, apps, webhooks or secrets.
  5. Check network logs for connections to unfamiliar endpoints.

Questions to ask whoever builds your software

If an agency or freelancer maintains your product, these five questions reveal a lot (for the wider hiring decision, see choosing a dedicated developer or an agency):

  1. Do you install from a committed lockfile in every build?
  2. How quickly do you adopt new dependency versions, and how do you review them?
  3. Who has npm, GitHub and cloud access, and is it protected with phishing-resistant 2FA?
  4. Where are our production secrets stored, and who or what can read them?
  5. If a dependency we use is compromised tomorrow, how would we find out, and what would you do?

Good answers are short and specific; vague ones are a reason to dig deeper.

The bottom line

Open-source packages are still the right way to build software; nobody should write their own date library. But the 2025 incidents made the supply chain a primary target. Lock your versions, slow down upgrades, protect developer credentials and make sure someone is watching: cheap habits that turn a potential breach into a non-event. Built your app with an AI tool? Our checklist for vibe-coded apps covers the other gaps.

Not sure how exposed your project is? Book a free consultation and we'll go through your build setup with you.

Frequently asked questions

What was the Shai-Hulud worm?

Self-replicating malware that spread through npm in September 2025. It stole GitHub tokens and cloud keys from developer machines, published them in public GitHub repositories, and used the victim's npm access to infect their other packages. CISA reported over 500 packages compromised.

How do I prevent npm supply-chain attacks?

Install from a committed lockfile in CI, wait a few days before adopting new versions, block unapproved install scripts, use phishing-resistant 2FA on GitHub, npm and your cloud console, and keep long-lived secrets off laptops.

What is npm trusted publishing?

It lets a package be published straight from a CI system using short-lived OIDC credentials instead of a long-lived npm token. With no stored token, there is nothing to steal.

Sources

  • CISA, "Widespread Supply Chain Compromise Impacting npm Ecosystem" (23 September 2025): https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/09/23/widespread-supply-chain-compromise-impacting-npm-ecosystem
  • GitHub Blog, "Our plan for a more secure npm supply chain" (22 September 2025): https://github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/our-plan-for-a-more-secure-npm-supply-chain/
  • AWS Security Blog, defending against supply chain attacks like Chalk/Debug and the Shai-Hulud worm: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/defending-against-supply-chain-attacks-like-chalk-debug-and-the-shai-hulud-worm
  • Trend Micro, "What We Know About the NPM Supply Chain Attack": https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/npm-supply-chain-attack.html
  • ReversingLabs, "Shai-Hulud npm supply chain attack: What you need to know": https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm

title: Why Client Feedback Loops Are Broken (And How We Built a Zero-Login DOM Overlay to Fix Them)
description:
If you’ve ever built a website for a client, you know the exact pain cycle:

  1. You spend two weeks building a pristine frontend in Webflow, Framer, or custom code.
  2. You send the staging link over for review.
  3. The client responds with: "Hey, can you move that thing over there a bit? Also, the heading looks weird on mobile." (Accompanied by a 14MB screenshot taken on an outdated device with a giant red arrow drawn in MS Paint).

As developers, our immediate instinct is to look for a review tool. But almost every existing feedback widget forces the client to create an account, log in, or install a browser extension just to leave a comment.

And what do clients do when forced to create a password or sign up? They give up, close the tab, and text you a screenshot instead.

The Technical Challenge

We wanted to build something fundamentally simpler for a project we’ve been working on tweak : a visual feedback overlay that requires zero client-side installation or authentication.

The architecture needed to solve three core problems:

  1. Zero Auth Friction: The client opens a staging URL and can immediately click anywhere on the DOM.
  2. Element Targeting & Selector Mapping: Capturing the precise DOM element and CSS selector relative to the viewport so the developer gets an actionable task card, not just a vague coordinate.
  3. Payload Routing: Bundling the note and DOM snapshot, then dispatching it instantly to a central dashboard.

How We Solved It (Without Bloating the Staging Site)

Instead of forcing a heavy widget or client login wall, we used a lightweight script tag injected into the <head> of the staging build.
