title: 12,534 MCP and Agent Skill Repositories, One Conclusion: This Ecosystem Has No Middle Class
description:
Originally published at MCPMarkets. Live numbers and methodology: mcpmarkets.com/insights.

A full-catalog data analysis of the MCP server and agent-skill ecosystem — snapshot: October 17, 2026

We crawled public GitHub data for every MCP server and agent skill we could find, classified it, and measured what the ecosystem actually looks like — not what the launch posts say it looks like. The catalog held 13,598 published entries at snapshot time; this analysis covers the 12,534 deduplicated entries we could pull and verify (5,945 MCP servers, 6,589 agent skills) — about 92% coverage.

The picture that emerges is not a healthy long tail. It is a very tall, very narrow head, a wide lukewarm plain, and a ravine in between.

Three findings up front:

  1. The head is far narrower than most people assume. The top 1% of repositories by stars hold 47.5% of all server-side stars (41.7% on the skill side). The top 10% hold roughly 83%. Gini: 0.867 for servers, 0.882 for skills.
  2. The middle is nearly empty. 62.8% of MCP servers have fewer than 100 stars. Median: 64. Mean/median ratio: 8.4×.
  3. Skills are hotter than servers — and it isn't close. Median stars 160 vs 64 (2.5×); 84.6% of skill repos were pushed to within the last six months, versus 64.2% of servers. One in five servers has been dormant for a year or two.

By the numbers

Metric MCP servers Agent skills
Entries analyzed 5,945 6,589
Total stars 3,211,236 14,168,570
Median stars 64 160
Repos under 100 stars 62.8% 37.1%
Repos under 1,000 stars 93.1% 78.1%
Pushed within 6 months 64.2% 84.6%
Repos with ≥ 10,000 stars 54 256
Gini coefficient 0.867 0.882

Method

Data comes from the MCPMarkets catalog (mcpmarkets.com), sourced from GitHub's public API: stars, license, primary language, last push date, and README content. Three things stated plainly, because they matter for how far to trust the numbers:

  • Snapshot: 2026-10-17. The catalog kept growing while we were pulling it (~690 new entries in a three-hour window), so pagination over a live dataset drifts at the boundaries. We ended up with 12,534 deduplicated entries — about 92% of the 13,598 published at snapshot time. Distribution metrics are barely affected; absolute counts run slightly low.
  • The server/skill split is heuristic. It comes from keyword and README-feature rules at ingestion time. See Limitations for what that costs us.
  • Stars are a proxy for attention, not quality. They follow HN threads, Twitter posts, and awesome-list cross-promotion, not production usage.

Finding 1: Ten repositories hold about a fifth of the sky

Server side: 5,945 repositories, 3,211,236 stars. Here is how those stars are distributed:

Percentile Stars
p25 36
Median 64
p75 166
p90 631
p99 8,841
Max 96,415

Mean over median is 8.4×, which almost always means a handful of extreme values dominate — and they do. The top 10 repositories hold 18.1% of all server-side stars. The top 1% hold 47.5%. Gini: 0.867.

The leaderboard needs a footnote. #1 is punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers at 96,415 stars — an awesome list, which our keyword rules filed as a server (more on this in Limitations). Behind it: headroomlabs-ai/headroom (75,471) and sansan0/trendradar (62,923).

The skill side is more lopsided at the very top: its ten largest repos hold 15.6% of all skill stars, and the single largest repository in the entire catalog is a skill repo — openclaw/openclaw at 392,124 stars, four times the server-side leader. Then vinta/awesome-python (327,970, another awesome list) and obra/superpowers (299,876).

One leaderboard entry is worth pausing on: anthropics/skills — 181,394 stars, no license field set. The company that created the protocol never licensed its own official example repo. That is a thread we pick up in Finding 4.

Finding 2: 62.8% of servers live below 100 stars

The back side of the head story is the long tail. Server-side star histogram:

Star range Entries Share
0 229 3.9%
1–5 122 2.1%
6–10 27 0.5%
11–50 2,072 34.8%
51–100 1,301 21.9%
101–500 1,490 25.1%
501–1,000 296 5.0%
1,001–5,000 292 4.9%
5,001–10,000 62 1.0%
> 10,000 54 0.9%

(Bands are inclusive of their upper bound, so "≤ 100" sums to 63.1%; the 62.8% figure above is strictly under 100.)

This is not a smooth long tail. It is a wide lukewarm plain with a ravine: a third of all servers sit in the 11–50 band, a second cluster at 101–500, a noticeably smaller notch at 51–100 in between, and then a deep gap before the four-digit head.

93.1% of servers have under 1,000 stars. About one in sixteen (6.3%) has under ten, and only 229 (3.9%) have zero. So "nobody looked at it" is the minority case. The typical MCP server is in use, but barely starred — a production dependency for one team, invisible to everyone else.

The skill-side distribution has the same shape, shifted one bracket up: 37.1% below 100 stars, 78.1% below 1,000, median 160.

Finding 3: Skills are the crowded end of the ecosystem

This is the one we did not expect going in: skill repositories are visibly hotter than server repositories.

  • Median stars: 160 (skills) vs 64 (servers) — a 2.5× gap
  • Total stars: 14,168,570 vs 3,211,236 — 4.4×
  • Pushed within the last six months: 84.6% vs 64.2%
  • Dormant for 1–2 years: ≈0% vs 20.4%
  • The ≥ 10,000-star club: 256 skills vs 54 servers

Two explanations, probably both true. Authoring a skill has a lower barrier — a SKILL.md is the deliverable; there is no protocol layer to implement. And skills arrived later, straight into the agent hype cycle.

The practical read is counter-intuitive: the server side looks less crowded to enter, but its median survival environment is colder. If you ship a server, "being genuinely maintained" is already a differentiator (see Finding 6).

Finding 4: Licenses are boringly permissive — the problem is no license at all

Server-side license distribution:

License Share
MIT 58.4%
Apache-2.0 13.5%
Unlabeled (unrecognized by GitHub) 16.1%
NOASSERTION (no match) 5.7%
AGPL-3.0 2.1%
GPL-3.0 1.8%
Other GPL/LGPL/MPL/EPL variants ~2%

Grouped: permissive licenses (MIT, Apache, BSD, ISC, CC0, Unlicense…) account for 73.2% of servers. Copyleft with teeth — AGPL and GPL together — totals just 5.0%. Skills look similar: MIT 53.5%, Apache-2.0 11.6%, permissive 66.4%, copyleft 2.9%.

For anyone consuming these tools, that is good news: closed-source use, commercial embedding, and redistribution rarely hit a license wall.

The real hazard is ambiguity: unlabeled + NOASSERTION together cover 21.8% of servers and 30.4% of skills. "No license" is a question every user has to answer for themselves — and most will answer it wrong. A directory that surfaces the field verbatim, per entry, is doing a small but real service.

Finding 5: Installation is the ecosystem's weakest link

This finding came out of parsing READMEs. For every server, we tried to extract one runnable install command (something like npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-xxx) and one copy-paste-ready mcpServers JSON block:

  • Only 28.7% of servers yield an executable install command.
  • Only 34.5% contain a usable config snippet.

Put plainly: for more than seven in ten MCP servers, the install path is broken. A reader finishes the README and still doesn't know the one command to run — the README links to the source repo, or buries the config in 300 lines of prose, or waves at npm install and moves on.

Skills, by contrast, hit 100% on install-command extraction — because the install path is uniformly npx skillfish add owner/repo/path. One convention, zero ambiguity.

If you maintain a server, this is the cheapest available edge: hoist the install command and the JSON config to the top of the README, in their own fenced blocks. Ten minutes of work. It is the difference between a user and a bounce.

Finding 6: Two-thirds actively developed, one-fifth asleep

By last upstream push (as of 2026-10-17):

Window Servers Skills
< 6 months 64.2% 84.6%
6–12 months 15.3% 13.6%
1–2 years 20.4% ≈0%
No record 0.1% 1.7%

One in five servers hasn't been touched in a year or two. Given that MCP's client config formats and transports have changed more than once in that window, a meaningful share of them are dead on arrival — yet they still sit in every directory's listing, often near the top, because directories rank by stars.

"Maintained" is a more useful filter than "popular." It is also cheap to surface: that is why every entry in our catalog carries a last-push date next to its star count.

What this means if you're building here

Three practical takeaways, in order of expected impact:

  1. Don't target stars. 62.8% of servers live below 100, and the median is 64. A server at 40 stars is not a failure; it is the norm. Optimize for the one team that adopts it, not the timeline.
  2. Fix your install command first. Seven in ten repos ship it broken. A copy-pasteable command plus a ready mcpServers block is the highest-leverage ten minutes in this ecosystem.
  3. Just stay maintained. One in five server repos is asleep. If you ship a real server and keep it working, you are already in the top quintile of "will still work next quarter" — and you can say so, because it shows up in your commit dates.

And one meta-lesson for people reading ecosystem data: the head is a list, the tail is the market. The top repos by stars are, in significant part, curated lists and aggregators (two of the top five across both sides are awesome-lists). The actual supply of working software lives in the 11–50 and 101–500 bands — the part nobody writes launch posts about.

Limitations

Stated plainly, so you can judge how far to push the conclusions:

  1. Classification noise. Entries were ingested by keyword heuristics, and some obvious lists slipped in (punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers as a server; vinta/awesome-python as a skill). This inflates the head numbers; the tail shape is unaffected.
  2. Stars are not quality. They are driven by exposure, not usage. A 30-star server can be a team's production dependency.
  3. Single source. No npm/PyPI download data, so "starred" and "used" cannot be separated.
  4. Snapshot drift. ~92% coverage, as described in Method; absolute counts are conservative.
  5. Our taxonomy is early. 89% of server entries currently land in a single category (developer tools), and skills have no useful category split yet — so no category-level analysis is offered here.

Every number above is reproducible from the public catalog. If you find a discrepancy, tell us — we would rather correct it than defend it.

Explore the data

  • Live numbers & methodology: mcpmarkets.com/insights — the same metrics, recomputed on demand with the page's Refresh button, with daily snapshots you can cite
  • Browse the catalog: MCP servers and agent skills
  • Browse by category: e.g. developer tools — the server list has a category filter
  • Every entry carries install command, quality score, last-push date, and license

This is the first in what we intend to be a quarterly MCP and Agent Skill Ecosystem Report. Next edition: category-level analysis and install-command coverage trends.

About MCPMarkets. We crawl, classify, and maintain a multilingual (EN/ZH/JA/KO/RU) directory of MCP servers and agent skills — 13,000+ entries with install commands, quality scores, and maintenance signals. The point is not to list everything; it is to make the one useful thing findable, with the fields that actually decide adoption.

Data: public snapshot of the MCPMarkets catalog, 2026-10-17. Written by the MCPMarkets team.

title: ChaosProxy: Bulletproof Your Microservices with Automated Fault Injection and Network Chaos Testing
description:
Modern distributed architectures are inherently fragile. Microservices, multi-region database clusters, third-party payment gateways, and external SaaS dependencies fail continuously, unpredictably, and silently.

Most engineering teams rely on unit tests, integration tests, and staging environments to validate reliability. Yet, traditional testing paradigms suffer from a fatal assumption: the network is reliable. The first of the eight fallacies of distributed computing continues to trigger multimillion-dollar outages across the tech sector.

When a downstream payment processor suddenly introduces a 4,500ms tail latency spike, does your service timeout gracefully, or does it saturate connection pools, trigger cascading thread starvation, and bring down your entire ingress tier?

Enter ChaosProxy—the lightweight, programmable, high-performance fault-injection reverse/forward proxy engineered to simulate real-world network turbulence before it hits your production revenue.

The Chaos Engineering Imperative: Why Unit Tests Lie

In modern cloud computing, standard synthetic tests run under pristine local network conditions. In production, your microservices face:

  • Jitter and bufferbloat across cross-zone cloud boundaries.
  • Intermittent HTTP 502/503/504 errors during rolling deployments.
  • Malformed payloads and truncated responses caused by abrupt connection resets.
  • TCP half-open connections that bypass simplistic health-check implementations.

Without real-world validation, your resilience mechanisms—circuit breakers (e.g., Resilience4j, Envoy retries), dead-letter queues, and fallbacks—are merely untested theoretical constructs.

ChaosProxy bridges the gap between static testing and chaotic production realities.

What is ChaosProxy?

ChaosProxy is an ultra-low-latency, zero-dependency proxy built for engineers and platform teams who need deterministic failure testing. Positioned inline between your service and upstream/downstream dependencies, ChaosProxy dynamically manipulates network traffic based on declarative rules or dynamic API calls.

+------------------+         +------------------+         +----------------------+
|  Your Service    | ------> |    ChaosProxy    | ------> |  Target Dependency   |
| (API/Worker/K8s) |         | (Fault Injection)|         | (DB/Gateway/REST/gRPC|
+------------------+         +------------------+         +----------------------+
                                      ^
                                      | Dynamic Rules via REST / CLI
                             +------------------+
                             | Chaos Controller |
                             +------------------+

Whether deployed as a local Docker container in continuous integration pipelines, a Kubernetes sidecar, or an edge interceptor, ChaosProxy allows developers to inject chaos deterministically with microsecond accuracy.

Core Capabilities of ChaosProxy

1. Deterministic Latency Injection & Tail-Jitter

Simulate real-world network delays using granular mathematical models:

  • Fixed Latency: Force exact delays (e.g., 350ms) to verify timeout configurations.
  • Normal & Pareto Distributions: Simulate tail latency (p95, p99, p99.9) to detect thread exhaustion and queuing vulnerabilities.
  • Jitter: Add variance buffers to uncover synchronization and race condition bugs.

2. Protocol-Level Fault Simulation (HTTP, gRPC, TCP)

  • Status Code Forcing: Intercept outgoing calls and return arbitrary status codes (500 Internal Server Error, 429 Too Many Requests, 503 Service Unavailable).
  • Connection Resets & Drops: Sever the TCP stream mid-transmission (RST packets) to verify how clients handle dropped sockets.
  • Truncated Responses: Deliver partial HTTP response bodies to test parser resiliency and deserialization error handling.

3. Bandwidth Throttling & Packet Manipulation

  • Emulate constrained cellular or satellite environments (e.g., 2G/3G/4G bandwidth caps).
  • Corrupt arbitrary byte sequences across network payloads to validate cryptographic checks and defensive schema validation.

4. Headless Dynamic Control via REST API

Manage chaos on the fly without restarting pods or containers. Integrate directly into CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to fail PRs that violate recovery SLAs.

Technical Deep Dive: Implementing ChaosProxy

Quickstart Deployment via Docker

Run ChaosProxy alongside your local service stack with zero overhead:

version: '3.8'

services:
  web-api:
    image: my-company/web-api:latest
    environment:
      - PAYMENT_GATEWAY_URL=http://chaos-proxy:8080
    depends_on:
      - chaos-proxy

  chaos-proxy:
    image: ghcr.io/chaosproxy/engine:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080" # Proxy Port
      - "9090:9090" # Control API Port
    environment:
      - TARGET_UPSTREAM=https://api.stripe.com
      - PROXY_PORT=8080
      - CONTROL_PORT=9090

Injecting Faults Dynamically via API

Once running, programmatically trigger network anomalies using a simple REST request:

Example: Injecting a 2.5-second p99 Latency Spike with 30% Probability 

curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "fault": "latency",
    "target_path": "/v1/charges",
    "params": {
      "delay_ms": 2500,
      "jitter_ms": 500,
      "probability": 0.30
    }
  }'

Example: Simulating Upstream Gateway Collapse (HTTP 503) 

curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "fault": "http_error",
    "target_path": "/v1/charges",
    "params": {
      "status_code": 503,
      "body": "{\"error\": \"Service Temporarily Unavailable\"}",
      "probability": 1.0
    }
  }'

Automated CI/CD Integration (GitHub Actions)

Add continuous resilience testing directly to your pull requests:

- name: Run Chaos Proxy Resilience Suite
  run: |
    # 1. Start test environment
    docker compose up -d

    # 2. Inject 5000ms latency on downstream dependencies
    curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
      -d '{"fault": "latency", "params": {"delay_ms": 5000, "probability": 1.0}}'

    # 3. Execute End-to-End Test (Must gracefully fallback within 500ms)
    npm run test:resilience

Architectural Comparison: Why ChaosProxy?

Feature Standard Mocks Linux tc / netem Chaos Mesh / Gremlin ChaosProxy
Layer Application OS / Kernel Kubernetes Cluster Application / L7 Proxy
Privileges Unprivileged Root Required Root / Cluster Admin Unprivileged / App Level
Granularity Static endpoints Network interface Pod/Container level HTTP Route / Payload / Header
CI/CD Fit Easy (but blind) Complex Too Heavy Instant / Native
Dynamic API No No Complex CRDs Simple JSON REST API

Unlike low-level kernel tools like iptables or tc netem, ChaosProxy requires zero elevated root permissions, making it completely secure for shared enterprise CI/CD runners and restricted cloud deployments. Unlike heavyweight cluster tools, ChaosProxy starts in under 15 milliseconds with less than 20MB of memory overhead.

The Economic ROI of Chaos Engineering

Downtime is not an abstract engineering metric—it is a direct financial loss.

  • The average cost of enterprise downtime ranges between $5,600 to $9,000 per minute (Gartner).
  • 70% of enterprise microservice failures are caused by unhandled cascade effects rather than root-cause logic bugs.

By identifying fragile downstream calls, misconfigured timeouts, and missing fallbacks during development, ChaosProxy:

  1. Reduces MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) by 60% through deterministic bug reproduction.
  2. Eliminates cascading outages before code reaches production environments.
  3. Validates SLAs with concrete empirical data before signing upstream vendor agreements.

Supercharge Your Resilience Engineering Today

Do not wait for a midnight PagerDuty incident to discover that your circuit breakers don't trip properly. Build systems that embrace entropy, absorb downstream failures, and guarantee 99.99% availability under adverse network conditions.

Get immediate, production-grade access to the enterprise-ready ChaosProxy suite:

👉 Access ChaosProxy Enterprise & Tooling Now

Arm your engineering organization with the infrastructure required to build fault-tolerant, antifragile cloud architectures today.

title: Invalid Password Reset Email Requests Explained — 4 Malformed Node.js Payload Checks
description:
A healthtech signup flow has an awkward operational constraint: sending the verification or password-reset link is only half the job; the team also needs evidence of what it asked the provider to send and what happened afterward. TL;DR: verify the sending domain and DKIM first, validate template variables against the backend payload before making the API call, then retain the message ID and poll message and event status. A malformed-request response is usually a sender-domain or template-contract problem, not proof that Node.js serialized JSON incorrectly.

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the service should call a plain REST API without installing or tracking a provider SDK. Its public discovery surface exposes request JSON Schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so the application can validate the current contract instead of copying a payload from an old post. Every documented capability ships a runnable example in 10 languages. I would try it for the transactional-email leg of a healthtech signup flow when one auditable HTTP boundary and per-call metadata reduce integration and reconciliation work.

The supporting advantage is single-key access: Infrai uses one credential and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this workflow, that removes another secret rotation and invoice reconciliation path if the service later adds a backend capability. The qualification matters: this is a pull-based design, not an event-driven one.

What page should fire first?

Start with the invariant: a user must receive a single usable, time-bounded link, while the incident record must distinguish a rejected request from an accepted message that later encountered a delivery problem. Those are different failure domains. Paging on a generic "email failed" counter throws away the distinction before anyone reaches the incident.

For a bounded production scenario, consider 186 signup attempts in a healthtech service. That number is a workload model, not a benchmark. The useful accounting is: 186 payload validations, up to 186 send requests, and status polling only for accepted sends that have not reached a terminal state. Record the internal signup ID, template version, sending domain, provider request or message ID, request time, and the final observed state. Do not put the reset token, full link, or other secrets into logs merely to make the dashboard look complete.

The first page should therefore identify the broken invariant: request rejection rate, accepted-but-unresolved messages beyond the service objective, or confirmed delivery failure. It should also include the sending domain and template version. A total-send graph cannot tell the responder which page fired, and I do not trust it to reconstruct that answer at 3 a.m.

Short pages win.

Why is my password reset email request invalid or malformed?

First, inspect the sending domain. An unverified domain or a DKIM setup error can stop transactional email before template rendering is relevant. DomainKeys Identified Mail binds a signing identity to the message through DNS-published key material; RFC 6376 is the protocol reference, while the provider's domain-verification result is the operational evidence. Keep that result with the deployment or configuration record.

Second, treat the template as a versioned contract. Preview it when the template changes, and compare every reset-link variable with the fields the backend will send. A template expecting reset_link while a backend produces reset_url is not an email mystery. It is schema drift. The prevention is a testable application-owned payload type plus a preview gate, rather than a late-night search through JSON logs. Third, validate the JSON locally before the network call. Confirm required values, parse the link, require HTTPS, restrict the host to the account site, and reject an expired link. This catches application mistakes early without pretending to reproduce the provider's complete schema. Fourth, separate submission from delivery evidence. After an accepted send, retain its identifier and poll the email message and event endpoints for status. This platform has no webhook event push for these namespaces, so polling cadence, timeout, and backoff belong in the workload and compliance design. Polling every second for every message inflates downstream traffic and still does not make the evidence better; use a bounded schedule tied to the delivery objective.

Contract drift is ordinary.

A preventative Go path, not a guessed provider payload

The exact provider request should come from live discovery because its schema is public and self-describing. Use that schema to construct a JSON file, then pass it to the small Go sender below. The program is runnable with the standard library; it calls the real send route, but deliberately treats the schema-controlled body as json.RawMessage rather than inventing vendor fields in this article.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    requestID := os.Getenv("RESET_EMAIL_REQUEST_ID")
    if key == "" || requestID == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY and RESET_EMAIL_REQUEST_ID are required")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    payload, err := io.ReadAll(os.Stdin)
    if err != nil || !json.Valid(payload) {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "stdin must contain valid JSON built from live discovery")
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", requestID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "request failed:", err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "response read failed:", readErr)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "send failed (%d): %s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "send remained rate-limited after retries")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Before this code runs, the Node.js application should still validate its own reset-link rules and validate the mapped body against the discovered provider schema. The sender uses an explicit method, a bearer key from the environment, a stable idempotency key, non-2xx error bodies, and bounded HTTP 429 retries. The platform convention has a 24-hour default deduplication window, so the request ID must remain stable across retries; generating a new one per attempt defeats the control. Those rules address duplicate application, hidden validation errors, and rate-limit storms. Another HTTP wrapper doesn't.

Which provider boundary fits the workload?

There is no universal winner. The comparison that matters is not a per-message price leaderboard but the effective operating bill: integration maintenance, evidence collection, retry safety, polling or webhook infrastructure, and the downstream requests produced by status checks.

Option Boundary to evaluate for this incident Better fit when Limitation to price into the design
Infrai Plain REST API with public discovery and a consistent idempotency convention One HTTP contract and consolidated per-call metadata reduce SDK and reconciliation work Email events are pull-only; there is no SMTP relay or hosted email OTP
Amazon SES Direct email service boundary The system is already governed and operated inside AWS Account, identity, event, and application evidence still need to be joined into the incident record
Twilio SendGrid Specialist email boundary Existing mail operations are built around SendGrid's email tooling A separate vendor contract and integration remain part of total ownership
Postmark Specialist transactional-email boundary The team wants a narrowly focused transactional email service It does not remove the application's responsibility for reset-link and template-contract validation

The last three are real alternatives, and their official documentation should be reviewed against the same evidence checklist before selection. The table does not claim that a logo supplies compliance. It never does. Run a representative workload through each candidate, count the application changes and follow-up status operations, and verify how the resulting records enter retention and audit controls.

Choose a specialist or direct provider when SMTP relay is mandatory, webhook-driven event handling is a hard latency requirement, or the organization already has mature evidence pipelines around that provider. This consolidated option also does not provide hosted email OTP, a cancellation operation for scheduled email, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS. A domestic email vendor shown as pending cannot serve as evidence for domestic compliance. Those are architecture boundaries, not footnotes.

The postmortem test

A useful postmortem can answer four questions without opening a provider dashboard: Was the domain verified? Which template version and variable names were used? Did the provider reject or accept the request? What final status did polling observe, and when? If any answer depends on memory, the control failed even when the email eventually arrived.

The decision rule is compact. Use a plain REST boundary when avoiding another SDK, validating against discoverable schemas, and collecting consistent call metadata lower the full operating burden enough to justify polling. Use a specialist or direct provider when its event model or existing organizational controls remove more work than consolidation does. Price can be evidence in that workload model, but it should not decide it.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability schema before implementing the provider mapping.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Infrai discovery: domain verification
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • RFC 6238: TOTP Time-Based One-Time Password
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Twilio SendGrid documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation

title: I open-sourced Commune: a TypeScript MERN community platform you can fork and build on
description:
I wanted a full-stack project that goes beyond a todo app, something with real
authentication, real data modeling and a structure other developers could learn from.
So I built Commune, an open source community platform on the MERN stack, and I'm
releasing it today.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/Haseeb-MernStack/commune.git

What it is

Commune is a TypeScript monorepo with a React frontend, an Express + MongoDB backend
and a shared package for validation and types.

What's inside

  • Secure auth: short-lived JWT access tokens plus rotating httpOnly refresh cookies. Refresh tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes with a TTL index.
  • Posts, comments and likes: with cursor-based pagination and a database-enforced one-like-per-user rule.
  • Shared Zod schemas: the same validation runs in the browser and on the server, so the two never drift apart.
  • Hardening: Helmet, CORS, rate limiting, body size limits and centralized error handling.
  • Tooling: Docker Compose for MongoDB and the API, plus a GitHub Actions workflow.

Tech stack

React 18 · Vite · TanStack Query · Express · Mongoose · Zod · TypeScript · Docker

Run it locally 

git clone https://github.com/Haseeb-MernStack/commune.git
cd commune
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d mongo
npm install
npm run dev

The API runs on localhost:4000 and the web app on localhost:5173.

Where I'd love your help

  • Follows and a personalized feed
  • Image uploads
  • Real-time notifications
  • Moderation tools
  • More tests, especially database-backed ones

I've labeled a few issues good first issue so it's easy to jump in. If you're
looking for your first open source contribution, this is a friendly place to start.

Feedback welcome

What would you build first? What would you change in the architecture? Tell me in the
comments, and if the project is useful to you, a ⭐ on GitHub means a lot.

title: pg_hint_plan v1.9.0 Released
description:
The pg_hint_plan development team is pleased to announce pg_hint_plan 1.9.0. This release of pg_hint_plan adds compatibility with PostgreSQL 19, and includes various improvements and bug fixes. For more details, see the release notes. This new major version includes support for path generation strategies (PGS).

pg_hint_plan is a PostgreSQL extension that offers the possibility to tweak PostgreSQL execution plans using so-called "hints" in SQL comments. For more information, see the project page.

The documentation of the project is published at this page, and is synced up automatically from the source repository.

A new set of minor releases is available down to PostgreSQL 14, each marked with the following versions:

  • pg_hint_plan 1.8.1, compatible with PostgreSQL 18.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.7.2, compatible with PostgreSQL 17.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.6.3, compatible with PostgreSQL 16.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.5.4, compatible with PostgreSQL 15.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.4.5, compatible with PostgreSQL 14.

This is the last release planned for PostgreSQL 14.

Notable changes in this set of releases include the following bug fixes, where applicable:

  • Fix infinite loop with hint parser and multi-query strings
  • Add CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() in get_hints_from_comment()
  • Ignore indexes without a name, like hypothetical indexes
  • Fix server crash when HintStateDump[2] throws an ERROR
  • Restore query ID after SPI execution in get_hints_from_table()
  • Correct schema-qualification of operators for hint table query
  • Add PG_MODULE_MAGIC_EXT
  • Update Japanese documentation

title: A Kotlin Data Class Works as a HashMap Key. In a TypeScript Map It Never Matches
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

A Kotlin grid keyed by Point is about as ordinary as code gets: a cell type and a map from cell to whatever lives there.

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val labels = hashMapOf(Point(1, 2) to "spawn")
    println(labels[Point(1, 2)]) // spawn
}

Two different Point instances, one lookup, a hit. The Kotlin compiler derives equals() and hashCode() from every property in the primary constructor, so the second Point(1, 2) lands in the same bucket as the first and compares equal. Java gives you the same deal with records, final since JDK 16.

Now you port it to TypeScript. The compiler is happy, and the lookup returns undefined with no error anywhere.

Why the Map can't see your Point

Here is the port, as most JVM developers write it on day one:

type Point = { readonly x: number; readonly y: number };

const labels = new Map<Point, string>();
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");

labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // undefined
labels.size;                // 1

const seen = new Set<Point>();
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.size;                  // 2

JavaScript's Map compares keys with the SameValueZero algorithm. MDN spells out what that means for objects: "for object keys, equality is based on object identity. They are compared by reference, not by value." Two object literals with the same fields are two objects, so they are two keys. Set works the same way, which is why your "deduplicated" set holds the same point twice.

The JVM reflex is to add an equals method and move on. It does nothing here:

class Pt {
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  equals(o: Pt): boolean {
    return this.x === o.x && this.y === o.y;
  }
}

const m = new Map<Pt, string>([[new Pt(1, 2), "spawn"]]);
m.get(new Pt(1, 2)); // undefined

There is no equals/hashCode protocol in JavaScript collections. Map never calls your method, and there is no hook to make it. On the JVM, the Object contract says equal objects "must produce the same integer result" from hashCode, and HashMap is built on that promise.

The type checker won't save you either. TypeScript's type system is structural: any { x, y } is a valid Point, so labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }) type-checks perfectly.

One more trap while you are here. If you reach for a plain object as a dictionary instead, every property name gets coerced to a string, and every plain object becomes "[object Object]". Now every point matches every other point. You traded "never matches" for "always matches".

Fix 1: derive a string key

The smallest fix is to stop using the object as the key and use a string computed from it:

const keyOf = (p: Point): string => `${p.x},${p.y}`;

const grid = new Map<string, string>();
grid.set(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
grid.get(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"

Strings are primitives, and SameValueZero compares primitives by value, so this works. For numeric fields the comma is safe because a JavaScript number never stringifies with a comma in it.

String fields are where this goes wrong. With a naive template, { org: "a,b", name: "c" } and { org: "a", name: "b,c" } both produce "a,b,c". Encode the fields as a JSON array in a fixed order instead:

type Member = { readonly org: string; readonly name: string };

const memberKey = (m: Member): string =>
  JSON.stringify([m.org, m.name]);

JSON escaping makes the encoding unambiguous, and the array fixes the order. Don't call JSON.stringify(m) on the whole object: property order follows Object.keys(), which is insertion order for string keys, so { org, name } and { name, org } give you two different keys for the same member.

The cost of Fix 1: the map now holds strings. Iterate it and you get "1,2" back, not a Point. And nothing stops a teammate from calling grid.get("1, 2") with a stray space.

Fix 2: a KeyedMap that takes a key function

If you miss HashMap<Point, V>, write the small wrapper that moves hashCode out of the class and into a function you pass in. It keeps the original key next to the value, so iteration hands you real Point objects:

class KeyedMap<K, V> {
  readonly #entries = new Map<string, [K, V]>();
  readonly #keyOf: (key: K) => string;

  constructor(keyOf: (key: K) => string) {
    this.#keyOf = keyOf;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): this {
    this.#entries.set(this.#keyOf(key), [key, value]);
    return this;
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    return this.#entries.get(this.#keyOf(key))?.[1];
  }

  has(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.has(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  delete(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.delete(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.#entries.size;
  }

  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    return this.#entries.values();
  }
}

Using it reads like the Kotlin version again:

const labels = new KeyedMap<Point, string>(keyOf);
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");
labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // "spawn"

for (const [point, label] of labels) {
  console.log(point.x, point.y, label);
}

One JVM rule carries over unchanged. The java.util.Map docs warn that "the behavior of a map is not specified if the value of an object is changed in a manner that affects equals comparisons while the object is a key in the map." Here, if you mutate a key after set, the stored string is stale and the entry is unreachable by its new value. Keep key types readonly, as Point is above.

Fix 3: branded value types

Fixes 1 and 2 still let anyone pass a raw { x, y } or a hand-built string. Branding closes that door at compile time. The TypeScript playground's nominal-typing example intersects a type with a __brand property, a convention that makes a plain value unassignable to the branded type.

Start with the key string. Brand it, and make one function the only way to produce it:

type PointKey = string & { readonly __brand: "PointKey" };

const pointKey = (p: Point): PointKey =>
  `${p.x},${p.y}` as PointKey;

const spawns = new Map<PointKey, string>();
spawns.set(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
spawns.get(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"
// spawns.get("1,2"); // compile error: not a PointKey

The brand exists only in the type system: at runtime a PointKey is an ordinary string and the map behaves exactly as in Fix 1, while a hand-typed "1, 2" is rejected by the compiler because it has no brand.

You can go one step further and brand the value itself. If a factory hands out one canonical frozen object per coordinate, reference equality becomes value equality, and the plain Map from the first snippet starts working:

type GridPoint = Point & { readonly __brand: "GridPoint" };

const pool = new Map<string, GridPoint>();

function gridPoint(x: number, y: number): GridPoint {
  const key = `${x},${y}`;
  let p = pool.get(key);
  if (p === undefined) {
    p = Object.freeze({ x, y }) as GridPoint;
    pool.set(key, p);
  }
  return p;
}

const owners = new Map<GridPoint, string>();
owners.set(gridPoint(1, 2), "spawn");
owners.get(gridPoint(1, 2));       // "spawn"
gridPoint(1, 2) === gridPoint(1, 2); // true
// owners.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // compile error: no brand

This is interning: one shared instance per distinct value. The brand is what makes it safe: a Map<GridPoint, V> refuses object literals, so the day-one bug from the first section can't compile. The trade-off is memory. The pool keeps every point it ever created alive, so use it for bounded domains like grid cells, currency pairs or enum-like tuples, not for arbitrary user input.

Records and Tuples will not fix this for you

For years the answer to "when will JavaScript get value-equal objects?" was the Records and Tuples proposal, with its #{ x: 1, y: 2 } syntax. That proposal is gone. At the TC39 plenary on April 14, 2025, the committee reached consensus to withdraw it; it "was at stage 2 and unable to gain further consensus for adding new primitives to the language." The inactive-proposals list records the rationale as "Subsumed by Composites".

The Composites proposal is the successor, and it is listed at Stage 2 as of October 2026. Its pitch is this exact problem. Composite({ x: 1, y: 4 }) returns an interned, frozen object, so two composites built from the same values are the same object, === is true, and they work as Map and Set keys. It is the gridPoint factory above, proposed as a language feature.

Read the fine print before you wait for it. Stage 2 in the TC39 process means "refining the solution": the design is a draft that may still change significantly. The README mentions experimental implementations and a polyfill, not a shipping engine. Nested plain objects are compared by reference, so Composite({ v: {} }) !== Composite({ v: {} }). Composites can't be WeakMap keys. And every object you get from JSON.parse, a database driver or an HTTP client will still be a plain object, so you'd convert at the boundary anyway, which is what Fix 3 already does.

Which fix to pick

Reach for Fix 1 when the key is used in one function and never iterated. KeyedMap is the one to pick when you want HashMap<K, V> ergonomics and need the original keys back. Use branded keys or interned values when the map crosses module boundaries and you want the compiler, not code review, to catch the raw object literal.

If this was useful

Map keys are one of those places where Kotlin and Java instincts compile cleanly in TypeScript and then fail quietly at runtime. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript walks through these translation gaps one by one: variance, null safety, sealed classes to unions, coroutines to async/await. If you came to TypeScript from the JVM, it's the one to start with.

The rest of the collection, so you can see which one or two fit you:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript stands in for them if you think in JVM terms, and The TypeScript Type System is where branded types like PointKey get the full treatment. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work. Browse all five on the collection page.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: How to accept crypto payments in Node.js (Express) in 5 minutes
description:
Adding crypto as a payment option sounds like a lot of work: running nodes, generating addresses, watching the
blockchain, handling confirmations, converting prices. With a payment gateway, it comes down to two endpoints on your
server:

  1. Create a payment and send the customer to a hosted checkout.
  2. Receive a signed notification when the payment confirms, and mark the order as paid.

In this tutorial we build both with Node.js and Express, using CigalPay
(disclosure: I'm part of the team building it). It's plain HTTP, so the same flow works in any language.

What you need: Node.js 18 or later (for the built-in fetch), and a CigalPay account. Your account ID and
your notification signing secret are in the merchant dashboard, under Settings.

1. Set up the project 

mkdir crypto-checkout && cd crypto-checkout
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express

Put your credentials in environment variables, never in the code:

export CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID="your-account-id"
export CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET="your-notification-signing-secret"
export PUBLIC_URL="https://your-app.com"   # where CigalPay can reach your server

2. Create a payment

When the customer clicks "Pay with crypto", your server creates a payment and redirects them to the checkout.
The price is in USD or EUR; the customer chooses the coin on the checkout, and the rate is locked while they pay.

// server.js
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const { CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID, CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET, PUBLIC_URL } = process.env;

// A tiny in-memory "database" for the demo.
const orders = new Map();

app.post('/checkout/:orderId', async (req, res) => {
  const orderId = req.params.orderId;
  const order = { id: orderId, amount: 49.9, currency: 'USD', status: 'pending' };
  orders.set(orderId, order);

  const response = await fetch('https://coins-api.cigalpay.com/api/pre-invoice', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      accountId: CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID,
      amount: order.amount,
      currency: order.currency,              // USD or EUR
      description: `Order #${orderId}`,      // shown to the customer
      extraId: orderId,                      // your reference, sent back in the notification
      lang: 'en',                            // checkout language: en, fr, es, de
      callback: `${PUBLIC_URL}/thank-you`,   // where the customer returns
      ipn: `${PUBLIC_URL}/cigalpay/ipn`,     // where the signed notification goes
    }),
  });
  if (!response.ok) return res.status(502).send('Could not create the payment');

  const { chargeLink } = await response.json();
  res.redirect(303, chargeLink);
});

That's the whole integration on the "pay" side. The customer lands on the checkout, picks a coin (Bitcoin, USDT,
Ethereum and many others), scans the QR code or copies the address, and pays.

3. Verify the signed notification

When the payment status changes, CigalPay sends a POST with a JSON body to your ipn URL. The x-cigalpay-sig
header holds an HMAC-SHA512 signature of the body, computed with your signing secret over the JSON with its
top-level keys sorted.

Never mark an order as paid from the customer's redirect to /thank-you: anyone can open that URL. Only trust the
notification, and only after checking its signature.

function isSignatureValid(body, received) {
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac('sha512', CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET)
    .update(JSON.stringify(body, Object.keys(body).sort()))
    .digest('hex');
  return (
    typeof received === 'string' &&
    received.length === expected.length &&
    crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(received), Buffer.from(expected))
  );
}

app.post('/cigalpay/ipn', express.json(), (req, res) => {
  const payment = req.body;
  if (!isSignatureValid(payment, req.get('x-cigalpay-sig'))) return res.sendStatus(401);

  const order = orders.get(payment.extraId);
  if (!order) return res.sendStatus(404);

  switch (payment.status) {
    case 'CONFIRMING':
      // Seen on the network, not final yet: show "payment pending", don't ship.
      order.status = 'confirming';
      break;
    case 'CONFIRMED':
    case 'FINISHED':
      // Final: fulfil the order. Notifications can arrive more than once,
      // so make this step idempotent.
      if (order.status !== 'paid') {
        order.status = 'paid';
        console.log(`Order ${order.id} paid`);
      }
      break;
    case 'PARTIALLY_PAID':
    case 'EXPIRED':
    case 'FAILED':
      order.status = payment.status.toLowerCase();
      break;
  }
  res.sendStatus(200);
});

app.get('/thank-you', (_req, res) => res.send('Thanks! Your payment is being confirmed.'));

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000'));

A few details worth knowing:

  • Constant-time comparison. crypto.timingSafeEqual avoids leaking how much of the signature matched.
  • Idempotency. The same status can be delivered more than once; check the current order state before acting.
  • CONFIRMING is not paid. The transaction is on the network but not confirmed yet. Ship only on a final status.
  • Other coins. If the customer paid with a coin that was converted at checkout, the notification also contains swapFromCurrency, swapFromNetwork and swapFromAmount, so you can show what they actually sent.

4. Test it end to end

Your notification URL must be reachable from the internet. Locally, a tunnel does the job:

node server.js
# in another terminal
npx localtunnel --port 3000     # or ngrok, cloudflared...

Set PUBLIC_URL to the tunnel's address, restart, then:

curl -i -X POST "$PUBLIC_URL/checkout/1042"

Open the Location URL from the response, pay a small amount (a real $1 payment is the best test), and watch your
terminal: Order 1042 paid.

Wrapping up

The whole integration is two routes:

Route Job
POST /checkout/:orderId Create the payment with POST /api/pre-invoice, redirect to chargeLink
POST /cigalpay/ipn Verify x-cigalpay-sig, update the order from status and extraId

No nodes, no wallets to run, no blockchain polling. If you'd rather not write code at all, the dashboard can also
create a payment link you can send by message or show as a QR code.

  • Docs and API reference: cigalpay.com/developers
  • Pricing: 1% per transaction, no monthly fee.

Questions about confirmations, underpayments or wrong-network deposits? Ask in the comments, happy to help.

title: The Failure Mode No Dashboard Shows
description:
Every few months, a hyperscaler experiences a major regional outage: AWS US-East-1 DNS degradation, Azure active directory authentication failure, or Cloudflare edge routing anomaly.

Instantly, half the modern internet stumbles. Food delivery apps stop taking orders, airline check-in kiosks freeze, and smart home thermostats disconnect.

Yet during the first two hours of these disruptions, the hyperscaler's public status dashboard invariably shows a calming sea of green checkmarks.

The failure mode no dashboard shows is Blind Upstream Trust.

Modern engineering teams have outsourced fundamental resilience to third-party cloud guarantees. They assume that because a managed database promises 'four nines of availability,' they do not need to engineer offline caching, regional failover, or graceful degradation.

When the hyperscaler wobbles, their applications collapse immediately because they have forgotten how to survive in degraded operational modes.

True resilience is sovereign: your critical workflows must be capable of operating in local, degraded, or cached modes even when the broader cloud is dark.

Key Takeaways & Architectural FAQs

Q: Why does a hyperscaler status page show green during an outage that is breaking real applications?

Public status dashboards reflect the provider's own control-plane health checks, not whether downstream applications that depend on it can still function. Teams that outsourced resilience entirely to the provider's uptime promise collapse the moment that promise wobbles.

Q: How do you build real resilience against a cloud provider outage?

Engineer critical workflows to operate in local, degraded, or cached modes, with offline caching and regional failover, rather than assuming a managed service's "four nines" guarantee removes the need for it.

title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.
