title: Google Didn't Break Physics: Why AI Exposes the Cloud's Silent Limits
description:
Every few months, marketing departments at cloud hyperscalers announce breakthroughs that supposedly defy the laws of computational physics. Custom silicon, bespoke optical interconnects, and planetary networking fabrics are heralded as the end of latency.

Do not be deceived. Google didn't break physics. Neither did Amazon or Microsoft.

As enterprise AI workloads transition from toy prototypes to continuous production inference, they run squarely into the immutable constraints of thermodynamics, memory bandwidth walls, and speed-of-light propagation across fiber optic networks.

Training and serving large frontier models requires massive parallel tensor communication. The moment data must traverse distributed cluster topologies, interconnect bottlenecks and memory bus saturation immediately assert themselves.

Architects who design AI stacks relying on hypothetical hyperscaler magic find themselves blindsided by staggering latency spikes and eight-figure egress invoices.

Engineering excellence requires designing with physical reality in mind: co-locating data with compute, pruning unnecessary tensor dimensions, and enforcing strict locality of reference.

Key Takeaways & Architectural FAQs

Q: Why do AI workloads expose cloud infrastructure limits that normal apps never hit?

Training and serving large models requires massive parallel tensor communication. The moment data crosses distributed cluster boundaries, interconnect bottlenecks and memory bandwidth walls assert themselves, limits no hyperscaler marketing claim removes.

Q: How do you avoid surprise latency and egress costs when scaling AI infrastructure?

Design with physical reality in mind: co-locate data with compute, prune unnecessary tensor dimensions, and enforce strict locality of reference, rather than assuming hyperscaler custom silicon eliminates the constraint.

Canonical Publication & Systems Archive. Permanent canonical reference at shashwat.si. Syndicated discussion authored by Dr. Shashwat Bishwen.

title: We localise prices for 58 countries from a header, and both our PDF exporters are hard-coded to A4
description:
PubTrivia prints things. Players join by scanning the code on their table, so a venue's first task is to produce a card per table, print it once and reuse it every week. There are two pieces of code that make the printable sheet: one in the dashboard that exports every table's code at once, and a free one on the marketing site that will do it for any web address at all, with no sign-up and no request leaving the browser.

Both of them begin like this:

// A4 dimensions in mm
const A4_WIDTH_MM = 210
const A4_HEIGHT_MM = 297
const PAGE_MARGIN_MM = 15

const doc = new jsPDF({
    orientation: 'portrait',
    unit: 'mm',
    format: 'a4',
})

Elsewhere in the same repository there is a module whose whole job is to notice where the visitor is:

return currencyForCountry(headerList.get('x-vercel-ip-country'))

That map holds 58 countries and 24 currencies, so the pricing page quotes a venue in Mexico in pesos and a venue in Sweden in krona. The same two-letter code, available in the same request, would also answer a question nobody asked it: what size is the paper in that country.

The numbers, because they decide how bad it is

A4 is 210 by 297mm. US Letter, officially ANSI A, is 8.5 by 11 inches, which is 215.9 by 279.4mm, and it is the usual office size in the United States, Canada and the Philippines, with Mexico and Panama mostly using US sizes too. Our country map contains the US, Canada, Mexico, Panama and Puerto Rico.

So an A4 sheet against Letter is 5.9mm narrower and 17.6mm taller. Width is not the problem. Height is: printed at actual size, the bottom 17.6mm falls off the page, and with 15mm margins and a 4-up grid, the thing living in that strip is the label under the bottom row of codes. Printed with "scale to fit", which most drivers default to, everything shrinks to 279.4 / 297, or about 94%, and comes out with an uneven bottom margin.

Neither outcome breaks a quiz night. A QR code at 94% of 82mm still scans from across a table, and the label is the table number, which the person cutting up the sheet already knows. That is exactly why this sat there: the failure is cosmetic, it happens in somebody else's printer dialog, and nobody files a bug that says "my table cards are 6% small".

What the exporter actually does with the space

The dashboard version offers five layouts and derives everything else:

const LAYOUTS: Record<string, LayoutConfig> = {
    '1': { cols: 1, rows: 1, label: '1 per page' },
    '2': { cols: 1, rows: 2, label: '2 per page' },
    '4': { cols: 2, rows: 2, label: '4 per page (recommended)' },
    '6': { cols: 2, rows: 3, label: '6 per page' },
    '9': { cols: 3, rows: 3, label: '9 per page' },
}

const cellWidth = printablWidth / cols
const cellHeight = printableHeight / rows
const cellPadding = 4
const labelHeight = 8 // mm reserved for label text
const qrSize = Math.min(cellWidth, cellHeight - labelHeight) - cellPadding * 2

(Yes, printablWidth. It has been there since the first version and it is spelled that way in both places it is used, which is the only reason it still compiles.)

Because the size is derived rather than fixed, swapping the page format really is a two-constant change. With a 15mm margin, 4-up on A4 gives an 82mm code: width is the binding constraint, so the cell is 90mm wide and the code is that minus two lots of 4mm padding. The same layout on Letter gives about 85mm, because Letter is the wider sheet. The sheet that loses height gains code size, which is a pleasing result and entirely an accident. Everything downstream, including the font size ladder, follows the cell:

doc.setFontSize(perPage === '9' ? 7 : perPage === '6' ? 8 : 10)

Three font sizes, chosen so that nine codes on a page still have a readable number under them. This is the part of the file I would keep unchanged in any rewrite: the layout is a function of the paper, so the paper is the only thing a new size has to change.

The two things I would copy from this exporter

First, jsPDF is imported at the moment the button is pressed, not at the top of the file:

const { jsPDF } = await import('jspdf')

The dashboard page that renders the button is loaded by every host before every quiz. The PDF library is loaded by the subset of them who are printing table cards this week, which is close to all of them once and almost none of them again.

Second, there is no network call in the export, and that is a schema decision rather than a clever bit of client code. Each table row carries its code as a data URL:

doc.addImage(table.qr_code_url, 'PNG', qrX, qrY, qrSize, qrSize)

The images are already in the page's props, so exporting 50 tables is 50 addImage calls and no requests. The free tool on the marketing site reaches the same place from the other direction: it generates the code in the browser with qrcode, so the address you type is never sent anywhere, which is a promise the page makes and the absence of a backend keeps.

The filename is built from what the file contains, too, which costs one line and saves a support thread:

doc.save(`QR_Codes_${activeTables.length}_tables_${perPage}pp_${totalPages}page${totalPages !== 1 ? 's' : ''}.pdf`)

Why the fix is not just adding a dropdown

The obvious change is a page size selector next to the layout selector. I do not think that is the right one, or at least not the first one.

A venue owner printing table cards does not want a choice between ISO 216 and ANSI A. They want the sheet to come out of the printer that is in the room. The country code is already in the request, the paper size follows from it for every country we quote a price in, and the sensible default is the one the request implies, with an override for the minority who are printing for somewhere else. Which is exactly the pattern the pricing page already uses, including the part where the guess is coarse and the override is cheap.

The general shape, and the reason this is worth 1,000 words about paper: we had already decided that locale is something you infer and offer rather than ask about. Then we wrote a feature that produces a physical object and never asked the same question. Internationalisation work tends to stop at currency, language and date format, because those are the three a framework hands you. The list is longer than that, and paper is on it, along with address formats, phone number shapes and which day a week starts on.

Our own audit is now one question per output: for everything this app produces that leaves the screen, which of its properties are facts about the user's country rather than facts about us? The prices got that treatment a month ago. The PDFs are getting it this week.

title: Go 1.27 Finds Leaked Goroutines With the Garbage Collector. Here's What It Misses
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

When researchers pointed a prototype detector at one of Uber's production Go services, it found hundreds of previously hidden partial deadlocks: goroutines parked on a channel or a lock that nothing would ever release. Each one kept its stack and everything that stack pointed to. None of them raised an error.

That detector now lives in the Go runtime. Go 1.26 shipped it as an experimental profile behind GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile. Go 1.27, released on 19 August 2026, made the goroutineleak profile generally available and deleted the experiment flag. You read it from runtime/pprof or from the /debug/pprof/goroutineleak endpoint.

The interesting part is how it decides that a goroutine is leaked. There are no timers and no "blocked for more than ten minutes" heuristics. The runtime asks the garbage collector a reachability question. Once you see the question, you can predict which leaks it will report and which ones it will never notice.

What "leaked" means to the runtime

The release notes define it precisely: a leaked goroutine is one "blocked on some concurrency primitive (channels, sync.Mutex, sync.Cond, etc) that cannot possibly become unblocked."

Think about what it takes to wake a goroutine stuck on ch <- v. Some other goroutine has to run <-ch. To do that, it needs a reference to ch. If no goroutine that could ever run again holds a pointer to that channel, the send can never complete. And "who holds a pointer to what" is exactly what the garbage collector computes on every cycle.

The Go blog post on leak profiles states the rule inductively. A goroutine is live if it is not blocked, or if at least one primitive blocking it is referenced by another live goroutine. Everything else is leaked.

The primitives covered are channel sends and receives (nil channels included), blocking select (empty select {} included), sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.WaitGroup and sync.Cond, per the same post. A goroutine blocked on file or network IO, a raw system call, or a hand-rolled primitive that is not built on those is never reported.

How the mark phase answers "can anything wake this up?"

In a normal GC cycle, every goroutine's stack is a root. A leak-detection cycle changes that. The design document by Georgian-Vlad Saioc and Milind Chabbi lays out the loop:

  1. Treat only runnable goroutines as goroutine roots.
  2. Mark everything reachable from the roots.
  3. Check each unmarked, blocked goroutine. If the primitive it waits on was marked, some live goroutine can reach it, so this goroutine is "eventually runnable." Add it as a root.
  4. Resume marking from step 2. Stop when no new goroutine gets promoted.
  5. Every blocked goroutine that never became a root is leaked. Mark from those too, so the heap ends up marked the same way a regular cycle would mark it, then sweep as usual.

That final step matters for what you expect in production. The profile reports leaks; it does not reclaim them. The blog says the last round lets the GC "mark all the memory it would have marked during a regular run."

There is one wiring problem the loop has to solve. A blocked goroutine is attached to its channel through a sudog, the runtime's record for "a g in a wait list." In runtime2.go, the sudog's channel field is a maybeTraceableChan and its data field is a maybeTraceablePtr. Sudogs are reachable from the global goroutine list and the semaphore table, according to the design doc. If the GC traced those fields normally, every channel with a waiter would be marked through the waiter itself, and nothing would ever look leaked.

So the pointer is stored twice: once as a uintptr (vu, the "source of truth") and once as an unsafe.Pointer (vp, "for liveness only"). When a leak-detection cycle starts, the runtime makes the vp half of every sudog untraceable, so the GC cannot follow the pointer while the address stays recorded. When the cycle ends, it makes them traceable again. The waiter still knows which channel it is parked on, and that knowledge no longer counts as a reason to keep the channel alive.

The blocked goroutine's own stack gets the same treatment by construction. It is not a root until it gets promoted, so the ch variable sitting in its closure does not mark the channel either. A goroutine that survives the whole loop ends up in a new status, _Gleaked, which runtime2.go documents as "a leaked goroutine caught by the GC."

A leak it catches

Here is the classic timeout leak. The worker sends on an unbuffered channel, the caller gives up first, and the send blocks forever.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "runtime/pprof"
    "time"
)

func fetch(ctx context.Context) error {
    ch := make(chan error) // unbuffered: the bug
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        ch <- nil // nobody receives after a timeout
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-ch:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

func main() {
    for range 3 {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
            context.Background(), 10*time.Millisecond)
        _ = fetch(ctx)
        cancel()
    }
    time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond) // senders block

    p := pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak")
    if p == nil {
        fmt.Println("needs Go 1.27, or 1.26 with " +
            "GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile")
        return
    }
    p.WriteTo(os.Stdout, 1)
}

On Go 1.27, go run . is enough. On Go 1.26, build with GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile go run .. Writing the profile triggers a leak-detecting GC cycle and waits for it, as the design doc describes, and debug=1 gives you the text format with function names and line numbers.

Walk through it with the loop above. After each fetch returns, main's frame no longer holds ch. The only remaining references live in the sender's closure and in its sudog. The sender is blocked, so its stack is not a root. The sudog's channel pointer is hidden for the cycle. Nothing marks the channel, so none of the three senders gets promoted, and all three should land in the profile with stacks pointing at the ch <- nil line. I haven't run this exact snippet, so treat that as what the mechanism predicts, not pasted output.

The fix is the one the Go blog gives for its own timeout example: give the channel a buffer of size 1. Then make(chan error, 1) lets the late sender drop its value and exit.

A leak it cannot see

Now move the channel to package level.

var results = make(chan error) // package-level

func fetchGlobal(ctx context.Context) error {
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        results <- nil // same leak as before
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-results:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

The leak is the same: every timed-out call can strand a sender. Sharing the channel also adds a second bug, because a later call can now receive an earlier call's stale result. The profile stays quiet.

Package-level variables are always roots. In step 2 the GC marks results straight from the global, the blocked senders look "eventually runnable" in step 3, and they never reach the leaked set. The Go 1.26 release notes spell this out: "the runtime may fail to identify leaks caused by blocking on concurrency primitives reachable through global variables or the local variables of runnable goroutines."

The second half of that sentence catches more real code than the first. A long-lived worker goroutine that keeps a map of per-request channels in a local variable, and never reads some of them, keeps every one of those channels marked. So does a struct of channels hanging off a server object that a running goroutine still references. The design doc puts it plainly: the detector's "effectiveness is reduced the more heap resources are over-exposed in memory."

That gives you a design rule the detector rewards. Create channels as close to their use as you can, scope them to one request or one call, and do not park them in registries that outlive the work. The narrower the reachability, the more the GC can prove.

Running it in production and in tests

If a service already imports net/http/pprof, Go 1.27 adds the endpoint with no code change. The blog's workflow, with the address left as a placeholder:

# ADDR: wherever net/http/pprof listens in your service
curl "$ADDR/debug/pprof/goroutineleak" > leak.prof
go tool pprof leak.prof

Inside pprof, list fetch (or whatever function spawned the goroutine) shows the blocked line in context.

On cost, the Go 1.26 notes say the feature is designed "to not incur any additional run-time overhead unless it is actively in-use." When you do request it, there is a worst case. The blog describes a leak-free "daisy chain" where runnable G0 references the primitive blocking G1, G1 references the one blocking G2, and so on. Each link only proves live after the previous one, which serializes marking and gives O(n²) steps for one GC cycle, with n the number of goroutines. The blog's answer is to profile periodically, every 4 hours in its example, since a leak that can be observed once stays observable.

The design doc calls the approach "theoretically sound, i.e., there are no false positives," and the blog describes it as "precise" with "little-to-no false positives," so treat a goroutine in the report as a strong signal that it is stuck. The detector also only sees leaks that have already happened. The blog recommends pairing it with goleak in test suites, which flags goroutines still running when a test ends, and with testing/synctest, whose fake clock lets a timeout path run deterministically.

When the profile comes back empty and memory still climbs, check your package-level channels first.

If this was useful

The leak profile makes sense once you know what the runtime does underneath your code: how goroutines park on channels and what the garbage collector treats as a root. The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers the runtime and its concurrency primitives with that picture in mind, including the channel and context patterns that keep a goroutine from getting stranded in the first place.

title: Go error handling patterns that scale: wrapping, unwrapping, sentinels
description:
Go's error handling gets a lot of criticism from developers coming from exception-based languages. But the real problem isn't if err != nil — it's the patterns that get built on top of it. Most tutorials show you bare error returns and call it a day. In a production codebase, you end up with errors that tell you something failed but not where, why, or what caller context led there.

The Problem with Bare Error Returns

Here's the code you write when you're moving fast:

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &u, nil
}

This compiles fine. It even works. But when the error reaches your HTTP handler and you log it, you get:

sql: no rows in result set

That's all. No package name, no function name, no request ID, no context about what was being fetched. Multiply this by 50 functions across 15 packages and you have a log that's useless for debugging.

Wrapping Errors with fmt.Errorf and %w

Go 1.13 introduced the %w verb for fmt.Errorf, which wraps an error while preserving the original for later inspection:

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, err)
    }
    return &u, nil
}

Now the error travels up the stack with context attached at each layer:

handler: processRequest: getUser(id=abc123): sql: no rows in result set

The rule I follow: always wrap at the point of origin, never in the middle without adding information. Wrapping fmt.Errorf("getUser: %w", err) inside a loop that calls getUser ten times just adds noise.

One subtle gotcha: %w creates a chain. fmt.Errorf("context: %w", fmt.Errorf("inner: %w", originalErr)) gives you three levels. That's fine — errors.Unwrap navigates the chain, and errors.Is/errors.As traverse it automatically.

Sentinel Errors: When to Use Them

A sentinel error is a package-level variable that callers can compare against:

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")
var ErrUnauthorized = errors.New("unauthorized")

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, ErrNotFound)
        }
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, err)
    }
    return &u, nil
}

The caller can now do:

user, err := getUser(id)
if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {
    http.Error(w, "user not found", http.StatusNotFound)
    return
}

This works because errors.Is traverses the entire error chain — even though ErrNotFound is wrapped inside fmt.Errorf, errors.Is finds it.

When to use sentinels: when callers need to make branching decisions based on the error type. Not found, permission denied, rate limited — these are meaningful categories that affect control flow.

When not to: for every internal error. Package io has io.EOF because it's a legitimate signal, not just a failure. Your internal database timeout doesn't need to be a sentinel unless callers genuinely need to handle it differently.

Custom Error Types for Structured Data

Sometimes you need to carry structured data in an error — an HTTP status code, a field name that failed validation, a request ID for correlation. That's where custom error types come in:

type ValidationError struct {
    Field   string
    Message string
}

func (e *ValidationError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("validation failed on field %q: %s", e.Field, e.Message)
}

func validateEmail(email string) error {
    if !strings.Contains(email, "@") {
        return &ValidationError{Field: "email", Message: "must contain @"}
    }
    return nil
}

The caller uses errors.As to extract the structured data:

err := validateEmail(input)
var ve *ValidationError
if errors.As(err, &ve) {
    respondWithFieldError(w, ve.Field, ve.Message)
}

errors.As also traverses the chain, so if validateEmail's error gets wrapped by an outer function, errors.As still finds it.

The combination of custom types and wrapping lets you do something powerful: an HTTP handler can catch a *ValidationError and return 400, catch ErrNotFound and return 404, and return 500 for everything else — without knowing the internals of the packages it calls.

Unwrapping: errors.Is, errors.As, and the Chain

Here's the mental model that makes all of this click:

  • errors.Is(err, target) — walks the chain calling == at each step. Use for sentinel comparison.
  • errors.As(err, &target) — walks the chain looking for a type match. Use for custom types.
  • errors.Unwrap(err) — returns the next error in the chain. Rarely call this directly. 
// Chain: wrapErr → ErrNotFound
wrapErr := fmt.Errorf("some context: %w", ErrNotFound)

fmt.Println(errors.Is(wrapErr, ErrNotFound))   // true
fmt.Println(wrapErr == ErrNotFound)             // false — never use == on wrapped errors

This is the most common mistake I see in Go codebases: using == to compare errors after wrapping. It always returns false. Always use errors.Is.

One more thing: if you implement a custom error type that wraps another, implement Unwrap() error to make the chain traversable:

type AppError struct {
    Code    int
    Message string
    Err     error
}

func (e *AppError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("[%d] %s: %v", e.Code, e.Message, e.Err)
}

func (e *AppError) Unwrap() error {
    return e.Err
}

Without Unwrap, errors.Is and errors.As stop at AppError and can't see what's wrapped inside it.

Sanitizing Errors at the API Boundary

For security-hardened applications, consistent error handling isn't just about debuggability — it's about not leaking internal details to API consumers while still giving operators enough context to diagnose issues.

A pattern I've used in production:

type internalError struct {
    Op  string
    Err error
}

func (e *internalError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("op=%s: %v", e.Op, e.Err)
}

func (e *internalError) Unwrap() error { return e.Err }

// At the HTTP boundary, sanitize before responding
func sanitizeError(err error) string {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound):
        return "resource not found"
    case errors.Is(err, ErrUnauthorized):
        return "unauthorized"
    default:
        log.Printf("internal error: %v", err) // full chain logged internally
        return "internal server error"
    }
}

The internal error carries full context for your logs. The API caller gets a safe, generic message. The operator log has everything needed to trace the failure back to its source.

The Takeaway

Go error handling scales when you follow three rules consistently:

  1. Wrap with context using fmt.Errorf("op: %w", err) at every layer that adds meaningful information.
  2. Use sentinels only for errors that callers genuinely need to branch on — not for every internal failure.
  3. Use custom types when you need structured data alongside the error message, and always implement Unwrap() when your type wraps another error.

The errors.Is and errors.As functions handle chain traversal automatically. Once you internalize that model, Go error handling stops being a boilerplate tax and starts being a precise contract between layers.

title: React: estados accesibles para email de prueba
description:
Una pantalla de email de prueba parece sencilla: un botón envía el mensaje, un inbox muestra el resultado y una alerta confirma lo ocurrido. En la practica, esa pequeña interfaz mezcla asincronía, estados visuales, lectores de pantalla y cambios de layout que pueden hacer sentir lenta la aplicación.

La solución no es agregar más spinners. Es modelar con claridad qué sabe la interfaz en cada momento. Un usuario debería distinguir entre “todavía estamos esperando”, “llegó un mensaje”, “la búsqueda expiró” y “algo falló”. Si todos esos casos usan el mismo texto, el flujo se vuelve confuso aunque el backend funcione bien.

El problema no es solo esperar un email

Un inbox temporal o de prueba suele tener este recorrido:

  1. El usuario solicita un email.
  2. React muestra que la solicitud está en progreso.
  3. El servidor acepta el evento, pero el mensaje todavía no es visible.
  4. El mensaje aparece y puede abrirse o copiarse.
  5. La espera termina por timeout o por un error recuperable.

Cada paso necesita una señal distinta. “Cargando” no explica si el mensaje fue enviado, si el inbox está consultando o si la conexión se perdió. En pruebas de frontend, también conviene separar el estado del request del estado del mensaje: una respuesta HTTP correcta no garantiza que el email ya pueda leerse.

Este enfoque se parece a diseñar alertas de trial que sí orientan: el copy debe decir qué pasó y cuál es el siguiente paso, no solo mostrar un color verde.

Modela los estados antes de escribir JSX

Un union type pequeño evita que el componente dependa de varios booleanos que pueden entrar en combinaciones imposibles:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: 'idle' }
  | { kind: 'waiting'; startedAt: number }
  | { kind: 'received'; subject: string; receivedAt: string }
  | { kind: 'expired'; retryable: boolean }
  | { kind: 'error'; message: string };

Con isLoading, hasMessage, hasError y isExpired es facil terminar con una alerta de éxito y error al mismo tiempo. Un estado discriminado obliga a que la vista elija una sola lectura principal. También hace más simple probar las transiciones: idle → waiting → received, o waiting → expired.

El texto debe ser concreto. “Esperando confirmación” ayuda más que “Procesando”. Para un timeout, “No vimos el email en 60 segundos; puedes volver a intentar” ofrece contexto y una acción. Si el usuario usa un lector de pantalla, esa diferencia es todavía más importante.

Un componente React con layout estable

El feedback no debería empujar el botón ni mover el inbox cuando cambia. Reserva una región con altura mínima y usa aria-live solo para cambios relevantes:

function InboxStatus({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  const text = {
    idle: 'Listo para comprobar el inbox.',
    waiting: 'Esperando el email de prueba.',
    received: 'El email ya está disponible.',
    expired: 'La espera terminó; puedes reintentar.',
    error: 'No pudimos consultar el inbox.'
  }[state.kind];

  return (
    <p className="status" role="status" aria-live="polite">
      {text}
    </p>
  );
}

.status {
  min-block-size: 1.5rem;
  margin-block: 0.75rem;
  color: var(--text-muted);
}

.status:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

role="status" anuncia el cambio sin interrumpir cada acción del usuario. No conviene poner un contador que se actualiza cada segundo en esa misma región: un lector de pantalla podria repetirlo demasiado. Muestra el tiempo restante en otra parte, con una etiqueta visible y un ritmo de actualización razonable.

Un botón deshabilitado durante la espera debe conservar una explicación. El texto “Comprobando…” es mejor que dejar solo un icono. Para conexiones lentas, evita reemplazar todo el contenido; conserva el contexto del inbox y actualiza la parte que cambió.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en la misma revisión

La accesibilidad no es un paso posterior al rendimiento. Un árbol pequeño, mensajes estables y menos renders suelen beneficiar a ambos. Calcula el copy del estado en el componente y evita recrear listas grandes del inbox cuando solo cambió la etiqueta.

También reviso estos puntos:

  • El contraste del estado secundario sigue siendo legible en modo oscuro.
  • El foco no desaparece cuando llega el mensaje.
  • El título del email y el timestamp tienen nombres accesibles.
  • La respuesta de error no depende solo de rojo o verde.
  • El polling se cancela al desmontar el componente.
  • prefers-reduced-motion evita animaciones innecesarias.

Para un flujo de CI, los límites de confianza para emails de CI también sirven como recordatorio de que cada ejecución debe tener un contexto claro. En la UI, eso significa mostrar el inbox o identificador de la ejecución, sin exponer datos que no corresponden al usuario.

Checklist para una interfaz de email de prueba

Antes de dar por terminado el componente, comprueba:

  1. ¿Existe un estado explícito para espera, éxito, expiración y error?
  2. ¿El layout mantiene su espacio cuando aparece el feedback?
  3. ¿El mensaje importante se anuncia una sola vez?
  4. ¿El foco y el teclado siguen funcionando después de un reintento?
  5. ¿El polling termina cuando el componente se desmonta?
  6. ¿El inbox se identifica con un nombre entendible, y no como “dummy e mail”?

Si el flujo necesita un buzón aislado para una comprobación manual, un temp mail puede ser parte del entorno de prueba. El enlace no arregla la UX por sí solo: la interfaz aún debe explicar quién está esperando, qué llegó y qué puede hacer la persona después.

Cierre

Una buena interfaz de email de prueba convierte la asincronía en información útil. En React, un modelo de estados claro, una región de feedback estable y una revisión conjunta de accesibilidad y rendimiento suelen ser suficientes para evitar gran parte de la fricción.

No hace falta llenar la pantalla de indicadores. Hace falta elegir palabras precisas, respetar el foco y mantener el contexto cuando el servidor tarda. Ese detalle pequeño se nota mucho cuando el flujo se usa en una prueba real, con una conexión lenta o con tecnologías de asistencia.

title: Collections.unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf in Java
description:
Quick Answer: Collections.unmodifiableList in Java creates a read-only view wrapper over an existing collection rather than an immutable copy. If the underlying collection mutates, those changes immediately reflect in the unmodifiable view. To create a true, isolated snapshot of your data that resists changes to the original source, use List.copyOf() introduced in Java 10.

When you pass a list to another component in your application, you usually want to guarantee its state won't change unexpectedly. You might call Collections.unmodifiableList(), hand over the reference, and assume your work is done. But there is a subtle trap in this approach that leads to unexpected side effects in production.

What is the difference between an unmodifiable view and an immutable list in Java?

An unmodifiable view prevents callers from mutating a list through that specific reference, but it remains linked to the original collection. An immutable list, by contrast, is completely decoupled from the original data source and cannot be altered by any reference.

If you pass around an unmodifiable view, you are essentially placing a clear glass shield over a whiteboard. The consumer holding the view cannot write on the glass, but if another thread or service writes directly on the whiteboard behind it, the consumer sees those changes instantly.

How does Collections.unmodifiableList handle underlying mutations?

When you pass a collection into Collections.unmodifiableList(), Java wraps your original list in a lightweight decorator. Any attempt to call write operations like add() or remove() on this wrapper throws an UnsupportedOperationException.

However, because it remains a view, any direct modification to the underlying collection updates what the view renders.

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Alice", "Bob"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(names);

names.add("Charlie"); // Modifying the underlying list

System.out.println(view.size()); // Prints 3, not 2!

If you hand this view to a service expecting a stable collection, background updates to names will leak through, potentially causing silent bugs or race conditions.

How do you create a true snapshot list in Java using List.copyOf?

Introduced in Java 10, List.copyOf() creates an unmodifiable list containing a shallow copy of the source collection's elements. Because this operation creates a brand-new backing store, subsequent modifications to the source collection have zero effect on the copied list.

It is vital to remember that List.copyOf() creates a shallow copy. While the list structure itself is completely immutable and isolated, the objects contained inside it are not cloned. If you store mutable objects inside the list, their internal properties can still be modified elsewhere.

The same concept applies across languages. If you are working in C#, calling .AsReadOnly() on a list produces a ReadOnlyCollection<T>, which behaves exactly like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList() by acting as a view over the backing list.

Comparison of Read-Only and Snapshot Collections

Method / API Type Decoupled From Source? Language Version
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) Read-Only View No Java 1.2+
List.copyOf(list) Immutable Snapshot Yes Java 10+
list.AsReadOnly() Read-Only View No .NET Framework 2.0+

Frequently Asked Questions

Does List.copyOf create a deep copy of objects in Java?

No, List.copyOf() performs a shallow copy of the collection elements. The reference structure of the list becomes immutable and decoupled from the source collection, but the individual elements inside still refer to their original object instances in memory.

Why does Collections.unmodifiableList throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime?

Java's collection framework uses unified interfaces like List for both mutable and read-only structures rather than separate interface hierarchies. Calling mutation methods on read-only wrappers triggers a runtime UnsupportedOperationException to enforce the contract without breaking interface consistency.

How does C# handle read-only list wrappers compared to Java?

C# uses the .AsReadOnly() extension method on List<T>, which returns a ReadOnlyCollection<T>. Just like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList(), this wrapper provides a read-only interface but remains a live view over the underlying list.

Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

title: Supabase SECURITY DEFINER RPC Callable by anon: Revoke It
description:
The short version

PostgreSQL grants EXECUTE to the PUBLIC role by default the moment CREATE FUNCTION runs. SECURITY DEFINER is the modifier that makes a function run with the privileges of the role that owns it rather than the role that called it. Create a write function with that modifier and leave it without an explicit REVOKE, and it becomes directly callable from the anon (unauthenticated) or authenticated role through Supabase's PostgREST layer.

  • Even with no GRANT written anywhere, EXECUTE for PUBLIC is there from the start
  • RLS policies on the table are irrelevant, because a SECURITY DEFINER function runs as the owner
  • Closing it means writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC explicitly and re-GRANTing only to the roles that need it

What it looks like

We created a function to push records for asynchronous delivery into a table called sync_outbox. Its definition pins search_path. search_path is the schema search path deciding which schema an unqualified object name resolves from inside a function, and pinning it to public is standard practice to stop a caller rewriting it so that a fake same-named object outside public resolves first.

create table if not exists public.sync_outbox (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  kind          text not null,
  ref_id        uuid,
  payload       jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
  status        text not null default 'pending'
                check (status in ('pending','sent','failed','dead')),
  attempts      int  not null default 0,
  -- (omitted)
);

alter table public.sync_outbox enable row level security;
create policy sync_outbox_staff_read on public.sync_outbox
  for select using (public.is_staff());

create or replace function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(p_kind text, p_ref_id uuid, p_payload jsonb)
returns uuid language sql security definer set search_path = public as $$
  insert into public.sync_outbox (kind, ref_id, payload)
  values (p_kind, p_ref_id, coalesce(p_payload, '{}'::jsonb))
  returning id;
$$;

The table's RLS says only "allow SELECT for the staff role". There is no policy anywhere permitting INSERT for anon. The function was written on the premise that only the app's backend (a cron worker) calls it. Pinning search_path was handled, but that guards a different kind of attack and does nothing for the problem here.

But this function is SECURITY DEFINER, and EXECUTE for PUBLIC is granted by default the instant CREATE FUNCTION runs. Supabase's PostgREST automatically exposes functions in the public schema at /rest/v1/rpc/<name>. It connects as anon or authenticated depending on the JWT the caller sends, and both roles inherit PUBLIC's privileges, so any function not explicitly revoked can be called directly by anyone.

That is what the review flagged. The table's RLS correctly narrowed reads to staff, and the function's execute privilege had never been narrowed at all.

Why

Three facts stack up.

① SECURITY DEFINER runs with the function owner's privileges

Not the calling role's privileges but those of the role that owns the function. That much is as specified.

② CREATE FUNCTION grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default

Even with no GRANT ever written, the function is callable by anyone the moment it is created. This is the opposite of tables, whose GRANT is closed by default (nobody can touch them without explicit permission): functions are open by default.

③ PostgREST automatically exposes public schema functions as RPCs

anon / authenticated are the connection roles Supabase provides, and they inherit PUBLIC's privileges as they are. With not a single GRANT on the table, one forgotten REVOKE on a SECURITY DEFINER function leaves a write path open that bypasses RLS entirely.

table GRANT        → closed by default → nobody touches it without explicit permission
function EXECUTE   → open by default   → anyone calls it unless explicitly revoked

This asymmetry is the cause of the oversight. Look only at the table and conclude "RLS protects this", and the hole on the function side goes unseen.

Fixing it

Strip the default PUBLIC privilege and re-allow only the roles that need it.

-- Close the SECURITY DEFINER write function to direct calls from anon/authenticated
-- (via PostgREST). Strip the default PUBLIC EXECUTE, allow only the backend (service_role).
revoke all on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) from public;
grant execute on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) to service_role;

REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC cuts off every inheritance source including anon / authenticated, and GRANT EXECUTE returns it to service_role alone, which actually needs to call it. The function definition itself is unchanged. All that happened is an open door was closed, with no effect on the intended calling path from the backend.

Checking it

Joining pg_proc and pg_roles gives you a function's owner and its execute privileges.

select p.proname, r.rolname as owner, p.proacl
from pg_proc p
join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner
where p.proname = 'enqueue_sync_outbox';

Look for EXECUTE for PUBLIC remaining in proacl (notation like =X/<owner>). Unless this check is run on every new SECURITY DEFINER write function, the same path opens once per function whose revoke was forgotten.

Making it not recur

This fix went in as an addition of revoke / grant to the existing migration file rather than recreating the function. Unless writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC paired with every SECURITY DEFINER function becomes the rule, the next write function added opens the same path.

  • Write REVOKE / GRANT directly beneath the creation SQL for any SECURITY DEFINER write function, so that adding only one of them is structurally impossible
  • Include the function's EXECUTE privilege in the same review item as the table's RLS review (on the premise of the asymmetry: tables closed by default, functions open by default)
  • Verify whether something is anonymously writable by actually querying pg_proc.proacl, not by reading the wording of a policy

However carefully the RLS policies are written, it means nothing if another door — the function's execute privilege — stands open. Another case shaped as an overlooked SECURITY DEFINER is in The function owner and the migration role. That one is about an intended bypass ceasing to work; this one about an unintended bypass working. Both start from the same property: SECURITY DEFINER behaviour is decided by who created the function, not by who called it.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: Mastering Advanced PostgreSQL: A Comprehensive Guide to Hospital Data Intelligence
description:
Introduction

Modern healthcare systems generate vast amounts of relational data daily, from patient admissions and doctor shift schedules to treatment costs and departmental expenses. Transforming this raw data into meaningful clinical and financial insights requires more than basic SQL queries. Database administrators and data analysts must leverage advanced querying techniques to uncover patterns, improve operational efficiency, and support data-driven decision-making.

This article explores four essential PostgreSQL concepts: Window Functions, Joins, Common Table Expressions (CTEs), and Subqueries. Using a realistic Hospital Management Dataset, each concept is demonstrated through practical SQL examples that illustrate how to analyze healthcare data and extract actionable insights.Each concept is explained using practical scenarios based on the hospital management database, which contains the following tables: doctors, department, diagnosis, wards, patients, procedures, and visits.

SQL Window Functions

SQL window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows that are related to the current row, without collapsing the result set into a single summary row. Unlike standard GROUP BY operations which merge rows to give you a single total, window functions preserve the identity of each individual row while appending the calculated aggregate or analytical value right next to it.

Understanding OVER(), PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, and window frames

These elements define how a window function evaluates rows.

The OVER() Clause

The OVER() clause specifies the window of rows used by a window function. Depending on the function and query, it can contain a partition, an ordering, and a window frame.


Result:

What it does: Calculates the average bill across all visits and displays that same average alongside every visit.
Why it is useful: Analysts can compare individual bills with the overall hospital average without losing the individual visit records.

The PARTITION BY Clause

PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for a window calculation without collapsing them into summary rows.

Result:

What it does: Calculates the average bill separately for each patient.
Result: Each visit remains in the output, with an additional column showing that patient's average bill across their recorded visits.
If you had used a standard GROUP BY patient_id, PostgreSQL would have collapsed your rows down to just one row per patient, losing the individual visit_id and total_bill_kes details.

The ORDER BY Clause

Within OVER(), ORDER BY determines the sequence in which rows are evaluated for functions such as ROW_NUMBER(), LAG(), and running totals.

Result:

What it does: Numbers each patient's visits from earliest to latest. visit_id provides a tie-breaker when visits have the same date.
Result: Each patient's first recorded visit receives number 1, the second receives number 2, and so on.

Window Frames

A window frame determines which rows SQL should include when performing a calculation for the current row. It is commonly used with functions such as SUM() and AVG() to calculate running totals and moving averages.
Think of it this way: as SQL moves through hospital visits one row at a time, a window frame tells it which rows to include in the calculation for each visit.
Example: Calculating running hospital revenue

For each row, SQL adds the current bill to all the bills before it.

  • ROWS specifies that the frame is based on rows.
  • UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means start from the first row.
  • CURRENT ROW means stop at the current row. Therefore, the first row includes only its own bill, the second includes the first and second bills, and the third includes all three bills. In summary: A window frame tells SQL how far back or forward to look when calculating a value for each row. It is particularly useful for running totals, moving averages, and calculations involving a specific number of preceding or following records.

Ranking window functions

Ranking functions assign positions to rows according to an ordering criterion. They are useful for identifying the most experienced doctors, highest-cost visits, or patients with the most visits.

ROW_NUMBER()

Purpose: Assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition.
Hospital scenario: Number each patient's visits in chronological order.

Result:

Result: A patient with four visits receives sequence numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4. Numbering restarts at 1 for the next patient.
Even when two visits share the same date, visit_id helps establish a consistent order.

RANK()

Purpose: Assigns the same rank to tied values but skips subsequent rank numbers.
Hospital scenario: Rank doctors by years of experience.

Result:

Result: If the highest experience values are 20, 15, 15, and 10 years, their ranks are 1, 2, 2, and 4.
This function is useful when tied doctors should share the same competitive position.

DENSE_RANK()

Purpose: Assigns equal ranks to ties without leaving gaps.
Difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK(): RANK() skips numbers after ties, while DENSE_RANK() continues with the next consecutive rank

NTILE()

Purpose: Divides ordered rows into a specified number of approximately equal-sized groups.
Hospital scenario: Segment visits into four billing tiers.

Result:

Result: Visits are distributed among four groups. Group 1 contains the highest bills, while group 4 contains the lowest bills, assuming descending order.
This can help the hospital identify visits with comparatively high billing amounts.
NTILE(4) creates four groups of roughly equal numbers of rows, not four groups with equal billing values.

Value Window Functions

Value functions retrieve values from particular rows within a window. They are especially useful for analyzing changes in patients' visits and identifying first or last recorded events.

LAG()

Purpose: Retrieves a value from a preceding row without requiring a self-join.
Hospital scenario: Compare each patient's current bill with their previous visit bill.

Result:

Result: The first visit for each patient has NULL in previous_visit_bill because no earlier visit exists. Subsequent visits show the preceding bill.
For example, patient 1 has bills of KES 3,500 and KES 4,200, so the previous-bill values are NULL and 3,500.

LEAD()

Purpose: Retrieves a value from a following row in the window.
Hospital scenario: Examine the bill recorded for a patient's next visit.

Result:

Result: Each visit is displayed alongside the next recorded visit's bill for that patient. The last visit has NULL because no later visit exists.
Difference between LAG() and LEAD(): LAG() looks backward; LEAD() looks forward.

FIRST_VALUE()

Purpose: Returns the value from the first row in the window frame.
Hospital scenario: Display the bill from each patient's earliest visit alongside every visit.

Result:

LAST_VALUE()

Purpose: Returns the value from the last row in the window frame.
Hospital scenario: Display the bill from each patient's latest recorded visit alongside all their visits.

Result: Every visit for a patient displays the bill from that patient's latest recorded visit.
Important: LAST_VALUE() can be confusing because its result depends on the window frame. With an ordered default frame, it may return the current row's value or the last value among its peers rather than the final value in the entire partition. Specifying UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ensures that the frame extends to the partition's final row.

Aggregate Window Functions

Aggregate window functions calculate summaries while preserving individual rows. They can support hospital revenue analysis, cost monitoring, and patient utilization reporting.

SUM()

Purpose: Adds values within a window.
Hospital scenario: Calculate the cumulative billing revenue generated by visits.

Result:

As shown in the results, starting with visit 1,001 (3,500 KES), the cumulative revenue accumulates chronologically row by row—adding visit 1,002 (2,500 KES) to reach 6,000 KES, visit 1,003 (28,000 KES) to reach 34,000 KES, and so on,allowing hospital management to track financial growth alongside individual visit bills.

AVG()

Purpose: Calculates the average of values within a window.
Hospital scenario: Compare every visit's bill with the average bill for that patient's visits.

Result:

As shown in the results, since Patient 1 has bills of 3,500 and 4,200, the average amount (3,850) is displayed across both of their rows, allowing hospital staff to track individual visit bills alongside each patient's average treatment cost.

COUNT()

Purpose: Counts rows or non-NULL values within a window.
Hospital scenario: Count the recorded visits for each patient.

Result:

As shown in the results, since Patient 1 has two recorded visits (1,001 and 1,011), the total count of 2 is repeated next to both rows, allowing hospital staff to view granular visit logs alongside lifetime patient visit frequency.

COUNT(*) counts rows, including rows containing NULL in individual columns. By contrast, COUNT(column_name) counts only rows where that column is not NULL.

MIN()

Purpose: Returns the minimum value in the window.
Hospital scenario: Identify the lowest recorded bill for each patient.

Result:

As shown in the results, Patient 1 has bills of 3,500 and 4,200, so the lowest amount (3,500) is displayed across both of their rows, allowing hospital staff to track individual bills alongside each patient's lowest overall cost.

MAX()

Purpose: Returns the maximum value in the window.
Hospital scenario: Identify the highest recorded bill for each patient.

Result:

As shown in the results, since Patient 1 has bills of 3,500 and 4,200, the maximum amount (4,200) is displayed across both of their rows, allowing hospital staff to track individual visit bills alongside each patient's peak treatment cost.

SQL Joins

SQL joins combine related data from two or more tables using a specified condition. Hospital databases commonly store patient details, doctors, departments, and visits separately to reduce duplication and maintain data consistency.
For example, the visits table contains identifiers such as patient_id, doctor_id, and department_id. Joins allow an analyst to retrieve meaningful names and department information instead of working only with identifiers.

INNER JOIN

Purpose: Returns only rows with matching values in both joined tables.
Hospital scenario: Retrieve visits with the corresponding patient details.

Result:

What it does: Matches every visit to the patient with the same patient_id.
Result: Visits with matching patient records appear in the output. Visits without a matching patient record are excluded.
This is useful when an analysis requires complete matches between the tables.

LEFT JOIN

Purpose: Returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table. Where no match exists, right-table columns contain NULL.
Hospital scenario: Find all registered patients, including those who have never visited.

Result:

Result: All patients are retained. Patients without visits have NULL for visit_id and visit_date.
This is useful for identifying patients with no recorded visits and checking the completeness of hospital records.

RIGHT JOIN

Purpose: Returns every row from the right table and matching rows from the left table.
Hospital scenario: Retain every visit record, including visits without a matching patient record.

Result:

Result: Every row from visits appears. Where a visit has no matching patient record, the patient columns contain NULL.
This can help audit inconsistent records, although a properly enforced foreign key should ordinarily prevent such orphaned visits.
A RIGHT JOIN can often be rewritten as a LEFT JOIN by reversing the table order.

FULL OUTER JOIN

Purpose: Returns all matching rows plus unmatched rows from both tables.
Hospital scenario: Audit patient records and visit records to identify unmatched entries on either side.

Result:

This is useful for data-quality investigations and reconciliation.

CROSS JOIN

Purpose: Returns every possible combination of rows from two tables, producing a Cartesian product.
Hospital scenario: Generate all possible combinations of departments and wards for planning or review.

Result:

This query performs a CROSS JOIN between the department and wards tables, producing a Cartesian product where every single department is paired with every available ward. As shown in the results, each of the four departments (Cardiology, General Medicine, Orthopedics, and Pediatrics) is combined with all four ward IDs (100, 200, 300, and 400), creating 16 total combinations that allow hospital planners to evaluate every possible department-to-ward pairing.
Caution: A cross join can produce a very large result when the tables contain many rows.

SELF JOIN

Purpose: Joins a table to itself using different aliases.
Hospital scenario: Find pairs of doctors with the same number of years of experience.

The query performs a SELF JOIN on the doctors table by aliasing it as doc1 and doc2, attempting to pair doctors who share the exact same number of experience years while eliminating duplicate reverse pairs using doc1.doctor_id < doc2.doctor_id. As shown in the results, because all four doctors in the dataset currently possess unique experience years (12, 9, 15, and 8 yearsrespectively), no records satisfy the matching condition, resulting in an empty result set with zero rows returned.

Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

What is a CTE?

A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a named result set defined using the WITH clause. It exists for the duration of the SQL statement and can make complex queries easier to understand, organize, and maintain.
In hospital analytics, CTEs are useful for calculating department revenue, identifying high-cost visits, summarizing patient activity, and breaking complex reports into smaller logical steps.

Basic CTEs

Purpose: Give a query result a temporary name so it can be referenced by the main query.
Hospital scenario: Identify visits with bills exceeding KES 10,000.

What it does: The CTE selects visits whose total bill exceeds KES 10,000. The main query retrieves those records from the named result set.
The CTE is not a permanent table. It is defined within this statement and can be referenced by the statement that follows it.

Multiple CTEs

Purpose: Break a complicated analysis into multiple named steps.
Hospital scenario: Calculate total billing revenue for each department and return departments with revenue above KES 10,000.

Result:

How it works:

  1. department_visits joins department details to individual visit billing records.
  2. department_revenue groups the records by department and calculates total revenue.
  3. The final query filters the summary to departments exceeding KES 10,000 and sorts them by revenue. Result: A list of qualifying departments, with their total billing revenue ordered from highest to lowest. This structure is easier to maintain than placing every operation in one deeply nested query.

Recursive CTEs

Purpose: A recursive CTE repeatedly references its own result to process hierarchical data or generate sequences.
Hospital scenario:Generate a calendar containing every date between the hospital’s earliest and latest recorded visits. This helps identify days when patients visited the hospital and days when no visits were recorded

CTEs combined with joins and aggregations

CTEs can work with joins and aggregate functions to produce multi-stage hospital reports.
Hospital scenario: Count visits and calculate total billing revenue for each department.

Result:

What it does: The CTE summarizes visit activity for each department. The outer query joins those summaries to the department table.
Expected result: Every department is listed, including departments without visits. Departments without visits display zero for total_visits and NULL for the revenue and average-bill fields.
COALESCE() replaces a NULL value with a specified alternative; here, it ensures that departments without recorded visits display zero visits.

SQL Subqueries

What is a subquery?

A subquery is a query embedded within another SQL statement. It can appear in the SELECT, FROM, or WHERE clause and can return a single value, a single column of values, or a table-like result.
In hospital analytics, subqueries can identify patients with emergency visits, doctors with above-average workloads, and visits whose bills exceed specified benchmarks.

Scalar Subqueries

Purpose: Return a single value: one row and one column.
Hospital scenario: Display each visit alongside the average bill across all visits.

The inner query calculates the hospital-wide average bill. The outer query displays that value alongside each individual visit.
Result: Each visit retains its own bill and has an additional column containing the overall average.
A scalar subquery that returns more than one row causes an error when used in a scalar context.

Non-correlated Subqueries

Run independently of the outer query; they do not reference columns from that query.
Hospital scenario: Identify visits whose bills exceed the hospital-wide average.

How it works: The inner query calculates the average once conceptually as an independent expression. The outer query compares each visit's bill with that average.
Result: Only visits with bills greater than the overall average appear.

Correlated Subqueries

Purpose: Reference a column from the outer query, making the inner query dependent on the current outer row.
Hospital scenario: Count the total recorded visits for each doctor.

What it does: For each doctor, the subquery counts records in visits that have the same doctor_id.
Result: Every doctor appears with their recorded visit count. Doctors without visits receive a count of zero.
The reference d.doctor_id connects the inner query to the current doctor in the outer query. This is what makes the subquery correlated.

Nested Subqueries

Purpose: Place a subquery inside another subquery to perform multiple levels of filtering or calculation.
Hospital scenario: Find visits whose bills exceed the average bill for visits belonging to patients who have had at least two recorded visits.

How it works:

  1. The innermost query groups visits by patient and identifies patients with at least two visits.
  2. The middle query calculates the average bill across visits belonging to those patients.
  3. The outer query returns visits whose bills exceed that calculated average. Result: A list of visits with bills above the average for the specified group of patients. This query demonstrates nested filtering, although a CTE might make the same logic easier to read in a larger reporting task.

Subqueries using IN

Purpose: Test whether a value matches any value returned by a subquery.
Hospital scenario: Find patients who have had an emergency admission.

What it does: The inner query identifies patients with an emergency visit. The outer query retrieves their demographic information.
Result: Patients with at least one matching emergency visit are returned. A patient with multiple emergency visits still appears only once in this outer query because the outer table is patients.

Subqueries using EXISTS

Purpose: Test whether a subquery returns at least one row.
Hospital scenario: Find patients who have at least one recorded visit.

What it does: For each patient, the subquery checks whether a matching visit exists.
Result: Only patients with at least one recorded visit are returned.

Subqueries using ANY

Purpose: Compare a value with the results of a subquery and return true if the comparison is true for at least one returned value.
Hospital scenario: Find visits whose bills exceed at least one bill recorded for a particular patient, here patient ID 1.

What it does: Returns visits whose bills are greater than at least one non-NULL bill belonging to patient 1.
Result: A visit qualifies if its bill exceeds at least one bill in the comparison set.
For example, if patient 1 has bills of KES 2,000 and KES 5,000, a bill of KES 3,000 satisfies > ANY because it exceeds KES 2,000, even though it does not exceed KES 5,000.
If the subquery returns no rows, the ANY comparison is false.

Subqueries using ALL

Purpose: Compare a value with every value returned by a subquery.
Hospital scenario: Find visits whose bills exceed every non-NULL bill recorded for patient 1.

What it does: Returns visits whose bills are greater than the highest bill in the comparison set, provided the set is nonempty.
Result: If patient 1's bills are KES 2,000 and KES 5,000, a visit with a bill of KES 6,000 qualifies, but a bill of KES 3,000 does not.
If the subquery returns no rows, the ALL comparison is true by definition. This is an important difference to consider when writing filters.

Subqueries in SELECT, FROM, and WHERE

Subqueries can be positioned in different parts of a SQL statement depending on the type of result.

Subquery in SELECT

A scalar subquery can provide an additional calculated column.

Subquery in FROM

A subquery in the FROM clause creates a derived table that the outer query can process.
Hospital scenario: Calculate each patient's total billing, then find the average total billing per patient.

What it does: The inner query calculates total bills for each patient. The outer query averages those patient-level totals.
Result: A single value representing the average total billing per patient among patients represented in the derived table.
This differs from the average individual visit bill because each patient is first represented by their cumulative billing total.

Subquery in WHERE

A subquery can filter records based on a comparison or membership condition.

Return visits meeting a condition derived from another query, such as exceeding the overall average bill.

Conclusion

Advanced PostgreSQL techniques enable healthcare analysts to transform relational data into meaningful operational and financial insights.
Window functions support ranking, comparisons, and cumulative calculations while preserving individual records.
Joins combine related information across tables and help identify unmatched records.
CTEs organize complex queries into manageable stages and support recursive processing. Subqueries allow filtering and calculations based on the results of other queries.
The most effective SQL solution depends on the question being asked, the structure of the data, and the expected output. Understanding not only how to write a query but also why it works is essential for producing reliable and useful analysis.

title: Kimi K3 and Kimi K3 Fast with ZDR and US-based providers now on AI Gateway
description:
Kimi K3 from Moonshot AI and its faster serving path, Kimi K3 Fast, are now available from US-based providers on AI Gateway, including Baseten and Fireworks. Zero Data Retention (ZDR) is also supported for both models.

Running Kimi K3 on US-based providers lets teams with data residency and compliance requirements use the model on US infrastructure. Because AI Gateway serves the models from multiple providers, it automatically routes across them for failover, higher uptime, and more available throughput than any single provider offers. You call the same moonshotai/kimi-k3 model ID, and the gateway handles provider selection and fallback.

Kimi K3 Fast trades a higher per-token cost for lower latency. Request it with the speed option on the base model, which stays on moonshotai/kimi-k3 and falls back to standard speed when the fast tier is unavailable. Alternatively, use moonshotai/kimi-k3-fast. The fast variant costs ~50% more than the base model.

To use Kimi K3, set model to moonshotai/kimi-k3 in the AI SDK:

US inference

To route Kimi K3 requests to use only US data centers for inference, set inferenceRegion. Regional pricing is ~10% more than the regular variant.

Zero Data Retention

Zero Data Retention for Kimi K3 is also available. Turn on Zero Data Retention for every request from the AI Gateway dashboard settings, or set it per request with zeroDataRetention:

Providers and endpoints

To see every provider serving Kimi K3, along with per-provider pricing, supported parameters, uptime, throughput, and latency, call the model endpoints API:

Model prices vary by provider and variant type.

Use Kimi K3 in your coding agent

Run vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup and select Kimi K3. This will detect the agents on your machine, provision an AI Gateway key, and write their config. See how to set it up via the Vercel CLI.

Try Kimi K3 in the model playground.

title: Give your eve agent a browser
description:
Your eve agent can now navigate the web like a human with agent-browser.

The @agent-browser/eve extension gives any eve agent a full set of browser tools: navigate pages, read content, click, fill forms, take screenshots, and inspect console and network activity. Everything runs inside the agent's sandbox.

Install the extension:

Then mount it under agent/extensions/:

Your agent gets namespaced tools like browser__navigate, browser__snapshot, browser__click, browser__fill, and browser__screenshot. Snapshot refs such as [ref=e12] become @e12 selectors, so the agent can inspect a page, then act on exactly what it saw.

The extension includes:

  • Sandbox isolation: Chromium and agent-browser run in the eve sandbox, not your app. Pre-install them in your sandbox template so sessions start warm, or let the extension install them on first use.

  • Domain allowlist: Restrict navigation and subresources with allowedDomains, and control output size, screenshot handling, proxy use, and session naming through extension options.

  • Credential protection: Cookie, storage, and saved-auth-state commands are never exposed to the model. Use eve extension overrides to disable tools, require approvals, or add app-specific guarded tools.

See a complete Next.js eve app with the extension mounted in the example, or read the documentation to get started.
