title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

Read more

title: Node.js Feature Flag Rollouts: Reversible Releases for US and EU Tenants
description:
A percentage rollout is useful only if a bad release can be stopped before noisy telemetry hides the real failure. For a Node.js backend that searches structured logs from a nightly gaming data pipeline, use a flag as a release-control boundary: start off, admit internal traffic, then raise exposure in deliberate steps across US and EU tenants.

TL;DR: keep flag evaluation behind a small application interface, assign tenants deterministically, and record every control-plane change in your own admin log. Infrai is a practical fit when simple percentage rollout is enough and one key and one bill across backend services reduces operational sprawl. It is not a substitute for an experiment platform, an audit system, or a missed-job monitor.

How should a SaaS staged rollout use a percentage feature flag?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. In a nightly pipeline, those two outcomes make percentage releases more dangerous than they first appear: a rollout may change which tenants can search fresh logs, while the underlying job can fail silently or deliver the same batch twice. A flag answers "who receives this code path?" It does not answer "did tonight's job run exactly once?"

That distinction is the invariant. Release control, workload correctness, and observability are separate controls even when one incident touches all three.

Three controls. Three owners.

For this gaming system, I would keep the initial flag off. Internal accounts go first. A small, stable tenant slice follows, then larger percentages only after comparing useful search results, empty-result rates, errors, and latency by region. Signal quality is the decision axis: more events are not automatically more evidence. A flood of successful searches can conceal the handful of EU tenants whose nightly index is stale.

The rollout should also be boring to reverse. Store a stable tenant identifier, flag key, evaluated variant, region, and release identifier with each search event. Do not log raw query text unless its data classification permits that. When the dashboard turns red, the operator needs to correlate exposure with the pipeline run without reconstructing state from memory.

A contract that survives the next provider

The application should not import vendor-specific flag types throughout route handlers. Give the Node.js service one narrow contract: evaluate a Boolean flag for a stable subject, fail closed for this risky search path, and return enough context to annotate telemetry. The provider adapter owns polling, authentication, and response translation.

This is where one combined backend API can earn a place in the design. The verified flag surface includes POST /v1/flags/rollout/{key} and reads for flag state, while the public, unauthenticated discovery surface exposes request and response schemas. That concrete REST boundary matters during migration: an adapter can target plain HTTP, without installing an SDK or spreading its objects through business logic. Infrai also groups 295 routes across 20 backend modules under one credential and one bill, which removes key rotation and invoice reconciliation work when the same team operates several services.

Teams running a straightforward US/EU tenant rollout should try Infrai for the release-control layer when a discoverable REST contract and fewer service credentials matter more than experimentation analytics.

Keep the boundary honest. These flags have no built-in change audit trail, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or recycle bin for deletion, and clients poll. If release governance matters, write actor, old value, new value, reason, and release ID to your own append-only admin log. If you need conversion analysis, exposure-event analysis, or complex dependencies, choose a specialist.

The same separation applies to observability. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but this surface has no distributed trace query or span tree. There are no alert or notification routes, synthetic checks, or heartbeat monitoring. Use a Healthchecks-style monitor for "the nightly job never started," and connect alerting to the metrics system that owns your service-level signals. Do not ask log search to prove absence.

Deterministic rollout without sticky surprises

Percentage assignment must be stable. Random evaluation on every request makes one tenant bounce between old and new behavior, contaminates comparisons, and turns rollback analysis into guesswork. A Node.js service should obtain remote state through its narrow adapters, then keep provider response types out of route handlers. This runnable Go probe exercises the adjacent log-search HTTP boundary during a migration rehearsal, where operators inspect rollout evidence. It uses a verified read route, never embeds a key, handles rate limiting, and treats every non-success response as evidence rather than silently assuming 200. No filters are appended because the discovery parameters for log search are not declared; guessing them would produce a persuasive-looking sample with an unsupported contract.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func searchLogs(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (map[string]any, error) {
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        var result map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    result, err := searchLogs(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    encoded, _ := json.MarshalIndent(result, "", "  ")
    fmt.Println(string(encoded))
}

The probe deliberately prints the response instead of asserting fields that are not in its application contract. A production adapter should decode only fields declared by the live discovery schema and reject malformed responses. The flag adapter needs the same discipline. During a provider migration, run both flag adapters against a fixed corpus of internal, US, and EU tenant contexts; compare decisions without serving the shadow result. If two providers use different native bucketing, preserve assignment in the adapter or accept the reshuffle as an explicit release event. Never discover that difference on live traffic.

Coarse targeting deserves separate keys when the operational decision differs. A US rollout and an EU rollout may advance independently because data residency, pipeline completion time, and on-call coverage differ. A beta cohort or tenant tier can also have its own key. Resist encoding every combination into one clever rule tree; it becomes hard to inspect under pressure.

One trap remains. The sample computes assignments locally, while a hosted provider may evaluate them remotely or publish configuration for polling. Pick one authority. Two evaluators with superficially similar percentages can disagree at the tenant boundary, so migration tests should use a fixed corpus of tenant IDs and compare decisions before traffic moves.

How the real alternatives differ

LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat are credible flag alternatives, not fallback names on a checklist. Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack belong in the adjacent log-search decision. Evaluate them with the same failure modes and governance requirements. The useful comparison is architectural, not a price grid that will age badly: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or ConfigCat can own feature evaluation while Datadog, Grafana, or Better Stack owns richer investigation and alerting. That split adds credentials and operating surfaces, but a specialist is the right trade when its deeper control plane or query workflow is required.

Option Best fit in this decision Boundary to verify before committing
Combined REST backend Simple percentage release through a discoverable REST surface, especially when one backend credential already covers other services Supply your own audit log and evaluation analytics; clients poll
LaunchDarkly Teams shopping for a dedicated feature-management product and willing to adopt its evaluation model Test exportability of flag definitions and tenant assignments in a migration rehearsal
Unleash Teams that want a specialist feature-flag system and value deployment control over the flag service Budget for operating ownership and verify strategy parity with the current rollout
ConfigCat Teams that prefer a focused hosted flag service with client-facing integration choices Confirm polling behavior, cache staleness, and deterministic targeting across regions

Those boundaries should be proved with a thin adapter and contract tests, not inferred from a feature matrix. Create the same flag, run a fixed set of tenant contexts, record decisions, disable the provider, and observe the fallback. Then export or recreate the configuration with a second provider. A reversible choice is one you have rehearsed.

Rehearse it quarterly.

For this particular workload, the combined API is the smaller control-plane choice when basic rollout is the whole requirement. A specialist is better when the release team needs native evaluation analytics, governed change history, sophisticated targeting, or experimentation workflows. Direct ownership may also be rational for a tiny number of flags, but then the team owns storage consistency, polling, access control, audit history, and every edge case around concurrent changes.

The rollout runbook

Start at 0%. Enable internal tenants and verify that their structured searches return the expected pipeline run, not merely HTTP success. Move to a small regional cohort only after the nightly completion signal is green.

At each step, compare old and new paths using a release identifier. Watch result usefulness, empty results, error rate, and latency separately for US and EU tenants. Pause on a signal-quality regression even if aggregate availability looks healthy. If evidence is ambiguous, hold the percentage. Fast movement is not the objective.

Silence is not success.

Every change gets an operator, timestamp, previous percentage, new percentage, reason, and ticket or release ID in the admin log. Use optimistic concurrency when the provider contract exposes it so two operators cannot silently overwrite each other. Deletion should require an explicit retirement procedure because there is no recycle bin.

Rollback is one control-plane change, but recovery may require more. Turning the flag off stops new exposure; it does not repair a stale index, retract duplicate pipeline output, or notify anyone that a scheduled job did not run. Keep an idempotency key at the batch boundary, make consumers safe for repeat delivery, and let the heartbeat monitor page on absence.

Small steps. Clear evidence.

When this pattern is the wrong tool

Do not use a percentage flag to answer a causal product question. Without built-in evaluation analytics, exposure data and outcome analysis belong elsewhere, and an experiment platform is the clearer choice. Do not use it as a regional compliance boundary either; percentage assignment is release control, not proof of residency or authorization.

It is also the wrong primary control for an emergency that demands instant propagation if clients only poll. Measure the configured polling interval and worst-case staleness, then put that delay in the runbook. For destructive changes, database migrations, or incompatible event schemas, use an expand-and-contract migration so both code paths remain valid during the rollout.

The practical standard is simple: a flag limits who sees a change, telemetry tells you what happened, and independent scheduling checks tell you whether the work happened at all. Keep those jobs separate and vendor replacement stays a planned exercise instead of an incident project.

If this boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery contract and generate the adapter from the live schema rather than guessing request fields.

Sources

  • Infrai flag discovery: request and response schema
  • OpenTelemetry metrics signal concepts
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

title: My First Post
description:
Hey DEV Community! 👋 I'm Shamil — A Developer Who Loves Building Things

Hello everyone! 👋

I'm Shamil TP, a developer from Kerala, India, and a first-year MCA student at St. Joseph's College (Autonomous), Devagiri.

I enjoy exploring technology, building projects, solving problems, and figuring out how things work behind the scenes. For me, programming isn't just about writing code — it's about turning ideas into something real.

And this is my first post on DEV! 🚀

💻 What I Work With

I'm interested in both frontend and backend development, and I enjoy exploring different technologies rather than limiting myself to one ecosystem.

Some of the technologies I've been working with include:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Next.js
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Django, Node.js, Express
  • Databases: PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis
  • Programming languages: Python, JavaScript, C
  • Tools & technologies: Git, GitHub, Linux, Docker, and CI/CD

I'm also interested in embedded systems and IoT. Experimenting with Arduino, ESP32, and Raspberry Pi boards has made me curious about connecting hardware with websites, APIs, and real-world applications.

🛠️ I Like Building, Not Just Learning

I believe the best way to understand a technology is to build something with it.

Whether it's developing a web application, deploying a backend service on Linux, experimenting with databases, or connecting a microcontroller to a web dashboard, I enjoy learning through practical projects.

I'm especially interested in building applications that are fast, lightweight, useful, and accessible.

I also enjoy exploring SEO and web performance because building a website is only part of the journey — helping people discover it matters too.

🧠 What I'm Exploring Right Now

Technology moves fast, and there's always something new to learn.

Currently, I'm interested in:

  • Full-stack development and choosing the right tools for each project.
  • Linux, self-hosting, and home lab experiments.
  • DevOps, Docker, CI/CD, and deployment workflows.

title: Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial — Complete Guide
description:
Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial — Complete Guide

A practical, in-depth guide to Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial with examples.

INTRO

Modern APIs are expected to be stateless, scalable, and secure out of the box. Yet, every time you spin up a new Spring Boot service, you end up wrestling with session cookies, CSRF tokens, and a maze of configuration classes just to protect a single endpoint. The result is brittle code that either over‑exposes resources or locks down everything, forcing developers to write ad‑hoc filters that are hard to test and maintain.

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide a clean solution: a self‑contained, signed token that travels with each request, allowing the server to stay stateless while still enforcing fine‑grained access control. The challenge isn’t the concept—it’s wiring JWT correctly into Spring Security’s filter chain, handling token refresh, and mapping claims to authorities without turning your configuration into a spaghetti mess. This guide cuts through the noise, delivering a production‑ready setup you can drop into any Spring Boot project.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

  • How to generate and sign JWTs with asymmetric keys, keeping private keys out of source control.
  • Configuring Spring Security’s filter chain to validate tokens, reject tampered requests, and populate Authentication objects automatically.
  • Mapping JWT claims to Spring GrantedAuthority objects for role‑based access control.
  • Implementing a refresh‑token endpoint that rotates tokens safely and mitigates replay attacks.
  • Testing the security layer with MockMvc and integration tests to guarantee your endpoints behave as expected.
  • Common pitfalls (e.g., token expiration handling, clock skew, and insecure token storage) and how to avoid them.

A SHORT CODE SNIPPET 

@Component
public class JwtAuthenticationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

private final JwtProvider jwtProvider;
private final UserDetailsService userDetailsService;

public JwtAuthenticationFilter(JwtProvider jwtProvider,
UserDetailsService userDetailsService) {
this.jwtProvider = jwtProvider;
this.userDetailsService = userDetailsService;
}

@Override
protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
HttpServletResponse response,
FilterChain filterChain) throws ServletException, IOException {
String token = jwtProvider.resolveToken(request);
if (token != null && jwtProvider.validateToken(token)) {
String username = jwtProvider.getUsername(token);
UserDetails userDetails = userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(username);
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken auth =
new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(userDetails, null, userDetails.getAuthorities());
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
}
filterChain.doFilter(request, response);
}
}

The snippet shows the heart of a JWT‑based security filter: extracting the token, validating its signature and expiration, then building a Spring Authentication object that downstream code can rely on.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Stateless security is achievable with Spring Security – By delegating authentication to a JWT filter, you eliminate server‑side sessions and simplify horizontal scaling.
  • Never hard‑code secrets – Use environment variables or a secret manager for signing keys; the guide demonstrates loading RSA keys from a keystore.
  • Claims drive authorization – Store roles or permissions inside the token and translate them to GrantedAuthority objects, keeping your business logic clean.
  • Refresh tokens are a must – Short‑lived access tokens reduce attack windows, while refresh tokens let clients stay logged in without re‑authenticating.

👉 Read the complete guide with step-by-step examples, common mistakes, and production tips:
Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial — Complete Guide

title: The H100 Rental Trap: Why $2.13 per GPU-Hour Is Not the Price You Pay
description:
An eight-hour H100 fine-tune looks like a $21.52 line item at $2.69 per GPU-hour. Then you discover the cheapest listing is a two-GPU bundle, the dataset sits in storage for a week, the job checkpoints twice, and the instance is interrupted at hour six. The bill is not $21.52, and the headline rate was never the price.

This is a practical teardown of GPU cloud pricing using live catalogue rates observed on 2026-10-17. The point is not that one provider is always cheaper. The point is that the advertised GPU-hour is a component price, and your budget needs the fully loaded number.

What the advertised rate includes

Most GPU marketplaces quote compute only:

  • The GPU and its host memory.
  • The container or VM while it is running.
  • Sometimes local disk, sometimes not.
  • Sometimes network, sometimes not.

Storage, egress, taxes, idle time, and restart overhead are usually separate. Multi-GPU offers may require you to rent the whole bundle even if your job can only use one GPU. Community or interruptible capacity may be cheaper because the inventory is not reserved and can disappear.

That is why a rate table is a starting point, not a budget. The useful unit is cost per useful GPU-hour: the total bill divided by the GPU-hours that actually produced work you can keep.

What the market actually listed on 2026-10-17

The public GPU index samples RunPod's catalogue and Vast.ai's verified on-demand bundles. These are live catalogue observations, not negotiated quotes. Inventory is not guaranteed, and storage and network are extra.

Provider GPU Tier $ / GPU-hour 100 GPU-hours Bundle constraint
RunPod H100 SXM 80GB Community $2.690 $269.00 Single GPU
RunPod H100 SXM 80GB Secure $3.990 $399.00 Single GPU
Vast.ai H100 SXM 80GB Verified on-demand $2.134 $213.40 2-GPU bundle at $4.269/hour
RunPod H100 PCIe 80GB Community $1.990 $199.00 Single GPU
RunPod H100 PCIe 80GB Secure $2.890 $289.00 Single GPU
Vast.ai H100 PCIe 80GB Verified on-demand $2.268 $226.80 2-GPU bundle at $4.537/hour
RunPod A100 80GB SXM Community $1.390 $139.00 Single GPU
RunPod A100 80GB SXM Secure $1.790 $179.00 Single GPU
Vast.ai A100 80GB SXM Verified on-demand $1.056 $105.60 Single GPU
RunPod A100 80GB PCIe Community $1.190 $119.00 Single GPU
RunPod A100 80GB PCIe Secure $1.790 $179.00 Single GPU
Vast.ai A100 80GB PCIe Verified on-demand $1.001 $100.10 2-GPU bundle at $2.002/hour
RunPod RTX 4090 24GB Community $0.340 $34.00 Single GPU
RunPod RTX 4090 24GB Secure $0.890 $89.00 Single GPU
Vast.ai RTX 4090 24GB Verified on-demand $0.429 $42.90 2-GPU bundle at $0.857/hour

Two things stand out. First, the H100 SXM spread between the cheapest verified listing and the secure RunPod listing is $1.856 per GPU-hour, or 87% more for the secure tier. Second, the cheapest headline rate on the board is not always the cheapest job, because of the bundle minimum.

The two-GPU minimum is a commitment

Take an eight-hour fine-tune that fits on one H100 SXM.

At RunPod's community rate, the compute cost is:

8 hours * $2.69 = $21.52

At Vast.ai's H100 SXM rate, the listing is a two-GPU bundle at $4.269 per hour. If the job cannot use the second GPU, you still pay for it:

8 hours * $4.269 = $34.15 for 16 GPU-hours

You paid for 16 GPU-hours to do 8 GPU-hours of useful work. The effective cost is $4.269 per useful GPU-hour, not $2.134. The bundle is only a discount if you can run two single-GPU jobs in parallel or split the workload across both cards.

That is the first rule of GPU shopping: a two-GPU minimum is not a lower price, it is a larger commitment. Compare the smallest rentable unit, not the per-GPU rate.

Community versus Secure is not a 10% upsell

The tier names vary, but the trade-off is consistent: community or interruptible capacity is cheaper because the provider does not reserve it; secure or on-demand capacity costs more because it is isolated and more likely to stay up.

The observed premiums are large:

GPU Community / standard Secure / reserved Premium
H100 SXM 80GB $2.690 $3.990 +48.3%
A100 80GB SXM $1.390 $1.790 +28.8%
RTX 4090 24GB $0.340 $0.890 +161.8%

A 48% premium on an H100 is $1.30 per GPU-hour. On a 100-hour job, that is $130. Whether it is worth it depends on what a lost hour costs you.

If the job checkpoints every 15 minutes and can resume automatically, community capacity can be a rational choice. If the job is a deadline-bound inference service or a multi-day training run without checkpointing, the secure tier may be cheaper than the recovery work. The premium buys availability and isolation, not necessarily raw speed.

Utilization is the multiplier that never appears in the rate

You do not pay for useful GPU-hours. You pay for billed GPU-hours. If the GPU is waiting on data loading, a stuck download, or a serial preprocessing step, you still pay.

For 100 useful GPU-hours:

Utilization Billed GPU-hours Vast.ai H100 SXM at $2.134 RunPod Community H100 SXM at $2.690
100% 100.0 $213.40 $269.00
80% 125.0 $266.75 $336.25
60% 166.7 $355.67 $448.33

At 60% utilization, the effective cost of a useful H100 SXM hour is $3.56 on the cheaper listing and $4.48 on the more expensive one. Neither number appears on the pricing page.

This is where data engineering matters more than GPU shopping. A fast NVMe path, a pre-tokenized dataset, and a loader that keeps the GPU fed can be worth more than a $0.50 rate difference. Measure tokens per second or images per second on your actual pipeline, not just the GPU model.

What 100 GPU-hours actually cost

On paper, Vast.ai's H100 SXM listing is $55.60 cheaper than RunPod's community listing for 100 GPU-hours:

$269.00 - $213.40 = $55.60

That is a 20.7% saving. Now add one operational incident. A 45-minute interruption at a $65 per hour engineering cost is $48.75. That single incident consumes 88% of the saving. Two incidents and the cheaper listing is more expensive.

The arithmetic is not an argument against the cheaper listing. It is an argument for checkpointing, monitoring, and a restart budget. If your job can tolerate interruption and you have automated recovery, the saving is real. If every failure requires a human, the saving is a subsidy for your future self.

Storage and egress can add smaller but real amounts. Using explicit assumptions of $0.10 per GB-month for storage and $0.05 per GB for egress, a 500GB dataset kept for seven days costs about $11.67, and 200GB of egress costs about $10.00. Those are illustrative rates, not quotes. The point is to put them in the model instead of discovering them on the invoice.

The only number to put in the budget

Use this formula:

effective $ / useful GPU-hour =
  (hourly rate * billed hours + storage + egress + restart cost)
  / useful GPU-hours

Example: 100 useful hours on the Vast.ai H100 SXM listing at 80% utilization.

billed hours = 100 / 0.80 = 125
compute = 125 * $2.134 = $266.75
storage + egress + restart = $15 + $10 + $20 = $45
total = $311.75
effective rate = $311.75 / 100 = $3.12 per useful GPU-hour

The headline rate was $2.134. The budget number is $3.12, about 46% higher. Run the same calculation for the secure tier and for your own utilization. The ranking can change.

A decision guide that survives real workloads

Workload Sensible first test Why
Single 8-hour fine-tune RunPod Community H100 SXM or A100 80GB No bundle minimum; $21.52 or $11.12 for eight hours at observed rates
Long, checkpointable batch Vast.ai verified on-demand Lowest observed $/GPU-hour, but budget restarts and verify the bundle
Production inference Secure or on-demand with capacity Availability and isolation matter more than a $0.50 difference
Multi-GPU training Compare bundle price and interconnect A two-GPU bundle can fit, but verify NVLink and topology
Cost-sensitive small models RTX 4090 24GB Lowest $/hour, but 24GB VRAM is not an H100 substitute

The RTX 4090 row is a reminder that the cheapest GPU-hour is not always the right GPU-hour. If the model does not fit in 24GB, a $0.34 rate is irrelevant. If it does fit, the same 100 GPU-hours cost $34 on RunPod Community versus $269 on H100 SXM. The workload decides.

What I would do with a $200 budget

Do not start with 100 GPU-hours. Start with 20 to 40 GPU-hours on the smallest rentable unit that fits the model. Measure throughput, not just latency to first token. Checkpoint every 15 minutes. Log the cost per useful GPU-hour, including storage and egress.

Then compare the effective rate, not the advertised rate. A provider that is 20% cheaper per GPU-hour but interrupts twice as often may lose. A provider that is 20% more expensive but keeps the GPU fed may win.

The public index and the underlying observations are here:

  • GPU cloud price index: gpu.mybskm.top
  • Pricing methodology: GitHub repository
  • Scraping API cost calculator: scrape.mybskm.top

Disclosure: Some outbound links on this page are affiliate links. If you buy a service through them, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Rates are catalogue observations, not quotes, and inventory changes. Verify current pricing, storage, egress, and interruption policy with the provider before committing budget.

Data note: GPU rates observed 2026-10-17T12:50:44Z from RunPod's GraphQL catalogue and Vast.ai's bundles API. Secure and community availability is not guaranteed. Storage, network, taxes, and restart overhead are excluded from the headline rates.

title: Node.js SaaS Structured JSON Logs (Attributing Cost Without User PII)
description:
Short answer: treat application logs as an append-only experiment ledger, not a diary. For a small Node.js SaaS comparing an AI tutoring experiment across school-tenant cohorts, emit one JSON event per model attempt with opaque request and user references, source-reported usage units, assignment version, outcome, and a deliberate level; redact PII before the logger receives it. Recompute cost later against a versioned rate table. That preserves the evidence needed for attribution without turning logs into a second student-record system.

The key decision is event grain. One browser request can trigger retrieval, a model call, an eval rejection, and a retry. Charging the request once hides work; adding usage again on the final response double-counts it. I want the production stream to answer the same question as the Python eval notebook: for each tenant and cohort, what usage did completed attempts consume, and what outcome did the learner see?

Make those two grains explicit.

How can a small Node.js SaaS evaluate structured JSON logging across cohorts?

The data flow is short enough to sketch in prose. Node.js creates a request_id at the trusted ingress, reads a previously assigned experiment cohort, and emits an attempt event after each model call. The event carries opaque tenant_ref and user_ref values, but no prompt, answer, name, email, authorization header, or raw body. A separate attribution job reads those events, joins a versioned rate card, and produces tenant-cohort totals. The terminal request event records the learner-visible outcome; it does not repeat attempt usage.

Here is a runnable Python version of the attribution step. The sample events are illustrative fixtures, not benchmark results. Keeping this beside the eval harness makes notebook-to-prod review concrete: a schema change must still produce the expected cohort totals before deployment.

from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

events = [
    {
        "schema_version": 1,
        "event": "model_attempt_completed",
        "level": "info",
        "request_id": "req_a91f",
        "attempt_id": "att_01",
        "tenant_ref": "tenant_7c2a",
        "user_ref": "user_18d4",
        "cohort": "baseline",
        "assignment_version": "exp_math_03",
        "model_class": "tutor_standard",
        "input_units": 620,
        "output_units": 140,
        "outcome": "accepted",
    },
    {
        "schema_version": 1,
        "event": "model_attempt_completed",
        "level": "info",
        "request_id": "req_b04e",
        "attempt_id": "att_01",
        "tenant_ref": "tenant_7c2a",
        "user_ref": "user_b118",
        "cohort": "retrieval_a",
        "assignment_version": "exp_math_03",
        "model_class": "tutor_standard",
        "input_units": 810,
        "output_units": 175,
        "outcome": "accepted",
    },
]

rates = {
    "tutor_standard": {
        "input_per_unit": Decimal("0.000001"),
        "output_per_unit": Decimal("0.000002"),
    }
}


def attribute_cost(rows, rate_table):
    totals = defaultdict(lambda: {"attempts": 0, "cost": Decimal("0")})
    seen_attempts = set()

    for row in rows:
        attempt_key = (row["request_id"], row["attempt_id"])
        if attempt_key in seen_attempts:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate attempt: {attempt_key}")
        seen_attempts.add(attempt_key)

        rate = rate_table[row["model_class"]]
        cost = (
            Decimal(row["input_units"]) * rate["input_per_unit"]
            + Decimal(row["output_units"]) * rate["output_per_unit"]
        )
        group = (row["tenant_ref"], row["cohort"], row["assignment_version"])
        totals[group]["attempts"] += 1
        totals[group]["cost"] += cost

    return totals


cohort_totals = attribute_cost(events, rates)
assert cohort_totals[("tenant_7c2a", "baseline", "exp_math_03")] == {
    "attempts": 1,
    "cost": Decimal("0.000900"),
}

The rate values exist only to make the fixture executable. Production rates need their own effective date and review path; don't freeze currency inside an application event. Usage units are evidence from the attempted operation, while money is an interpretation that can change with a contract, model class, or rounding rule. Keeping them apart also lets an analyst replay old events after correcting an attribution rule without rewriting the log archive.

This is the first hard boundary: attempt events carry usage; terminal request events carry user-visible outcomes. The request ID joins the story, but it isn't the accounting grain.

Implement the event contract around invariants

An application logger should receive a small allowlisted dictionary. Passing a request object and asking a formatter to clean it later is risky because serializers, exception handlers, and fallback sinks may observe the original object. OWASP advises excluding or masking data such as access tokens, passwords, connection strings, and sensitive personal data. In an edtech application, I would extend that deny category to student names, email addresses, free-form questions, generated answers, and uploaded lesson content. The allowlist is stronger than a growing collection of regexes because an unrecognized field stays out by default.

The minimum useful attempt event has a timestamp, stable event name, schema version, level, request ID, attempt ID, opaque tenant and user references, cohort, assignment version, operation, model class, outcome, latency, and raw usage dimensions. Each field earns its place by supporting a join, an aggregation, or an operational decision.

Contract area Required fields Invariant
Identity request_id, attempt_id The pair is unique per attempt
Assignment tenant_ref, cohort, assignment_version Values stay fixed throughout one request
Usage model_class, input_units, output_units Appears on attempt events only
Result outcome, latency_ms Describes this attempt, not a later retry
Control event, level, schema_version Uses typed, reviewable values

assignment_version matters because a label like retrieval_a can silently acquire new meaning after experiment logic changes. attempt_id matters because retries share a request ID. schema_version makes a breaking change visible instead of leaving an analyst to infer it from missing columns.

No prose parsing.

Use event="model_attempt_completed" and outcome="accepted", for example, rather than hiding both facts in message="Tutor call was fine". A human-readable message can help during an incident, but the cost query should group typed fields. Keep trace identifiers separate from request IDs when distributed tracing exists: a request ID names the application interaction, while trace context can cross service boundaries. Conflating them works in a single process and becomes ambiguous as soon as a queue or background evaluator enters the path.

User IDs deserve the same precision. user_ref should be an application-generated opaque reference, not an email address and not a hash of an email address. A deterministic hash still supports correlation and may be guessable when the original value comes from a small, known domain. Store the mapping in the system that already governs identity, apply its access and deletion controls there, and let the log retain only the reference for the period the experiment actually needs.

The tempting design is one giant context object. It feels flexible in a notebook, then becomes impossible to review: cardinality grows, field meanings drift, and a prompt can arrive under a tenant-defined key nobody anticipated. A flat, versioned measurement contract is less clever. Good.

Operate log levels as action contracts

Levels aren't a measure of how surprising a line of code felt. debug is disposable diagnostic detail that can be disabled or sampled. info records expected lifecycle facts such as an assignment or completed attempt. warn marks a recoverable condition that deserves attention, and error records an operation that failed and requires an owner, retry policy, or alert decision.

Log a failure once at the boundary that owns its outcome. Repeating the same exception in a model adapter, service layer, and route handler inflates cohort failure counts and makes alerts noisy. Expected input rejection should follow the application's response policy rather than automatically becoming error; the operational question is whether the system failed to do its job, not whether a branch returned early.

Keep stack traces away from the accounting event. They can reveal arguments, paths, query strings, or serialized state, so send a sanitized error class and internal error code with the same request ID to a separately controlled diagnostic event. I'm not sure one universal redaction expression can cover tenant-defined school data — the field names and free-form values vary too much. Resolve that uncertainty with representative fixtures from the actual data classification, then fail the contract test when a forbidden key or value pattern appears.

Govern user IDs and PII before serialization

Start with a constructor that copies known-safe values into a new object. Validate types and bounds there. Then serialize. This order means a raw authorization header or student response never enters the logger's buffer, child context, transport fan-out, or exception fallback. Sink-side masking remains useful as defense in depth, but it cannot prove that an earlier sink did not receive the unredacted event.

Test the negative space — fields that must never appear — as aggressively as required fields. A useful fixture set includes an accepted first attempt, a retry with two distinct attempt IDs, an input rejection, and an event containing every forbidden key the application knows about. Parse each emitted line as JSON; reject duplicate attempt keys; require the current schema version; reject direct identifiers and content fields at any nesting depth; and confirm that a terminal event contains no usage dimensions. That last assertion prevents double attribution even when both events are individually valid.

Cost-aware logging also needs a field budget. High-cardinality identifiers are justified when they enable a controlled investigation or cohort join, but putting entire prompts into message adds storage, privacy exposure, and token-sized payloads without improving the aggregate. Sample debug events, set retention by event class, and restrict access to identity references. The exact retention window depends on school agreements and applicable policy, so the engineering contract should name an owner and configuration point rather than inventing a universal number.

There is a subtle eval failure worth guarding against. If cohort assignment is looked up after a model attempt, a concurrent experiment update can label the usage with a different variant from the one that shaped the request. Capture cohort and assignment version at request start, carry them unchanged to every attempt, and assert their equality during aggregation. The logger isn't the experiment allocator; it records the allocator's decision.

Carry the contract through the deployment pipeline

This ledger is not suitable for full conversation replay, safeguarding review, legal discovery, or detailed learning analytics. Those jobs need a purpose-built content store with stricter access, deletion, and audit controls. Link to such a record only when policy permits, and don't copy its payload into observability data. Likewise, stick with metrics rather than per-user logs when the team cannot operate access reviews, retention, schema ownership, and deletion handling for high-cardinality references.

The catch is that privacy and attribution pull in opposite directions. Remove attempt identity and retries become hard to count; retain personal content and an operational store acquires obligations it was never designed to carry. Opaque references, narrow event grains, and short purpose-based retention don't eliminate that trade-off. They make it reviewable.

Before release, run the JSON fixtures through the same Python evaluator used by the notebook, replay one request with two attempts, and confirm it yields two attempt charges but one terminal outcome. Verify that changing a rate table changes the computed total without changing stored events. Inspect rejected events for PII, check that every error has an owner-facing action, confirm debug sampling cannot remove accounting events, and have someone outside the feature branch explain the grain back to you. If that explanation is fuzzy, the dashboard will be worse.

Ship the contract first.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/

title: TIL: GBase Database Default Character Set Can Cause Chinese Text Issues
description:
I recently ran into a character encoding issue while testing GBase Database (GBase 8s). The installation completed successfully, and the database was running normally. However, when I inserted Chinese text, the characters did not display as expected.

The problem wasn't necessarily the SQL statement or the application. It could be related to the database locale and character encoding configuration.

Why Does This Happen?

A typical GBase Database installation is designed to help users get an instance running quickly. However, its default locale settings may not be suitable for every language requirement.

For example, an environment using en_US.8859-1 may not be appropriate for an application that needs to store and process Chinese text.

Character encoding issues can occur when the database locale, client locale, and application encoding are incompatible. Depending on the configuration, symptoms may include garbled Chinese characters, conversion errors, or unexpected text output.

The important lesson is that a successful installation does not guarantee that the default character set meets your application's requirements.

Step 1: Check the Locale Configuration

Before changing anything, check the relevant environment variables:

echo "$DB_LOCALE"
echo "$CLIENT_LOCALE"

These commands show the values currently set in your shell. Keep in mind that they do not independently confirm the actual locale of an existing database.

You should also verify the database's locale configuration and check which locale values are supported by your GBase Database installation.

Step 2: Set the Locale Before Creating a Database

If you're setting up a new database, one approach is to configure the appropriate environment variables before creating it.

For example:

export DB_LOCALE=<supported_chinese_locale>
export CLIENT_LOCALE=<compatible_client_locale>

Replace the placeholders with locale values supported by your installation and compatible with your application. A value such as zh_CN.utf8 may be worth evaluating, but do not assume it is available or appropriate for every environment.

After setting the variables, create the database using the intended locale configuration.

Then test the complete workflow:

  • Insert Chinese text.
  • Query the stored text.
  • Confirm that the results display correctly in your client.
  • Verify that your application uses compatible encoding settings.

This approach is particularly useful when preparing a new development or test environment because you can establish the required locale before creating the database.

Step 3: Recreate the Database if Its Locale Is Unsuitable

What if the database has already been created with an unsuitable locale?

In some situations, recreating the database with the correct configuration is a practical solution, especially for a test instance that contains no important data.

The general process is:

  1. Back up any data that needs to be retained.
  2. Confirm the supported locale values and required configuration.
  3. Set the relevant environment variables.
  4. Create a new database with the intended locale.
  5. Restore or migrate the required data.
  6. Test Chinese text insertion, retrieval, and application compatibility.

Important: Changing environment variables alone does not automatically change the locale or character set of an existing database. If the database contains production data, plan the migration carefully and verify whether data conversion is required.

Step 4: Verify the Entire Encoding Path

Even after creating the database with the intended locale, don't stop at checking a single environment variable.

Confirm that the following components work together:

  • Database locale: Determines the database's locale and character-handling behavior.
  • Client locale: Affects how the client handles character data exchanged with the database.
  • Application encoding: Must be compatible with the data being sent and received.
  • Terminal or display settings: Can affect how text appears when viewed through command-line tools.

Testing both insertion and retrieval is important. Text that looks correct in one tool may still display incorrectly in another if their encoding configurations differ.

Final Takeaway

GBase Database (GBase 8s) makes it convenient to get an instance running, but default installation settings aren't necessarily suitable for every application.

If your application needs Chinese text, check the locale configuration early. For a new database, setting the appropriate environment variables before creation may be sufficient. If an existing database uses an unsuitable locale, recreating it and migrating the data may be necessary.

A few minutes spent validating the locale can save hours of troubleshooting later.

Have you encountered Chinese character encoding issues in GBase Database? Did you solve them by adjusting environment variables, recreating the database, or changing your client configuration? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Building GoRoute: An Ultra-Lightweight (<15MB RAM) LLM Gateway in Go
description:
Most developers using terminal coding agents like Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, or Cursor end up running an LLM router in the background to handle rate limits, multiple accounts, and model failovers.

Popular tools like OmniRoute and LiteLLM work, but running a full Node.js or Python runtime 24/7 just to proxy HTTP requests consumes 150MB to 300MB of RAM and introduces cold-start latency.

I wanted something that idles at < 6MB RAM, starts instantly, and never panics. So I built GoRoute.

What is GoRoute?

GoRoute is a zero-dependency, compiled LLM gateway and multi-agent router written in Go.

It acts as a local reverse proxy (http://127.0.0.1:8128) sitting between your developer agents and AI providers.

+-------------+       +-------------------+       +-----------------------+
| Claude Code | ----> |                   | ----> | Google Antigravity    |
| OpenCode    | ----> | GoRoute (Go Proxy)| ----> | OpenAI / Anthropic    |
| Codex/Cursor| ----> |   (<15MB RAM)     | ----> | Custom Endpoints      |
+-------------+       +-------------------+       +-----------------------+

Key Capabilities

  1. Sub-15MB Memory Footprint: Compiles to a single 16MB binary with zero external dependencies. Idles under 6MB RAM.
  2. Automatic 429 Failover & Round-Robin: Automatically rotates accounts and instantly fails over across keys if rate limits are hit.
  3. Dual Protocol Translation: Speak OpenAI (/v1/chat/completions) or Anthropic Messages API (/v1/messages) seamlessly.
  4. 1-Click Agent Setup: Automatically configures Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, Cursor, Aider, and Cline with a single command: 
   goroute setup all
  1. Seamless OmniRoute Migration: If you already have OmniRoute configured, import your existing credentials and routes in 1 second: 
   goroute import-omniroute

Installation & Quick Start

You can install GoRoute directly via curl:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ziuus/goroute/main/install.sh | bash

Or run via npm:

npx goroute setup all

Once installed, check status:

goroute status

Check out the GitHub repo here: https://github.com/ziuus/goroute

I'd love to hear your feedback, feature requests, or questions!

title: Chat SDK now supports reactions and ephemeral messages on Teams
description:
Chat SDK's Microsoft Teams adapter now supports reactions and ephemeral messages through the same API as other adapters.

Bots can add and remove reactions on Teams messages, and call thread.postEphemeral() or channel.postEphemeral() to send native, targeted messages that only the intended user sees, like permission prompts.

This release also adds:

  • Author emails: Incoming Teams messages include the author's Microsoft Graph email, with their user principal name as a fallback.

  • Custom token factory: Pass a token function in TeamsAdapterConfig to supply your own access tokens, so bots on runtimes without Azure IMDS can authenticate without a static client secret.

  • Native DM status: Progress messages now show as a native Teams status in direct messages.

  • Conversation routing: Group conversations are no longer misidentified as direct messages, so they're always handled correctly.

  • Mention conversion: Email addresses, @handles inside URLs, and mentions inside code spans are no longer turned into Teams mentions.

Read the Teams adapter documentation to get started, or learn more about ephemeral messages and reactions.

Special thanks to onmax for their contributions to this release.

title: I worked like the company was mine. Here is what two and a half years at a Silicon Valley startup taught me.
description:
I was a frontend engineer at Sybill from May 2024 to September 2026.

Founders do not wait for a ticket. For two and a half years, neither did I.

In May 2024 I joined Sybill, a Silicon Valley startup that builds AI for sales teams. I was hired as a frontend engineer. Over the next two and a half years I built a large part of Ask Sybill, our AI chat, from its first version to the day I left. A strong backend team built the AI brain behind it. My job was everything around that brain, so that people enjoyed using it every day.

If something hurt our users or the company, I treated it as my problem, even when nobody had put it on my list. This is the story of what that looked like, day by day.


My GitHub stats from my last two years at Sybill.

It started on day one

On my first day, the browser's developer tools were slow on our app. I wanted to know why. The cause was in our CSS: the same block of style values was copied into the page again and again, once for every file that used it. I removed the copies, the app shipped less CSS, and the tools were fast again. Nobody had asked me to look.

In my first week I moved our build to Vite, a much faster build tool, and a few days later the tests followed. I pushed the team toward TypeScript, which catches mistakes before the code runs, and I started refactoring right away. I did it because I cared about the software we all worked in every day. If the floor creaks, you fix it today.

I gave every screen the same building blocks

Six months in, I noticed that every screen in our app had built its own buttons, modals and menus. Some existed twice. Most of them I would not have approved in a code review. So every new feature started by building the same basic pieces again.

AI could not help much with this yet. When I joined, we used GitHub Copilot in VS Code, and it mostly finished the line you were typing. Then we moved to Cursor with Sonnet 3.5, and its Composer, a chat window that could edit code for you, felt like a huge jump. It could write a function. It could not write good UI that matched the rest of our app.

The old way to go faster was to reuse code. In a product like ours, most screens have to be made for their own job, so you cannot share much of the high-level code. But the small pieces can be shared. A button, a modal and a menu should work the same everywhere.


A Sybill app screen. Buttons, menus and chips like these are the small pieces a shared library gives every screen.

I had wanted a component library for months, so when our CTO mentioned the idea, I was ready. In December 2024 I created syb-ui. I built it with the compound components pattern before I even knew the pattern had a name. It just felt like the natural way to do it. It was also not my first time. I had built component libraries twice before, both in Svelte: once as an open-source side project I never finished, and once at work at Altice.

It paid off. The UI became consistent, we had fewer UI bugs, and new screens were faster to build because we could take an existing screen as a reference. For months I was the only one working on it. Then other engineers started adding to it, and it became a team effort. To me, that was the real sign it worked.

We built an AI chat before the tools for it existed

In January 2025 we started Ask Sybill. Today there are popular frameworks for building an AI chat. Back then they were young and few teams used them, so we built it all ourselves: answers that stream in word by word, a stop button, retries, and a way to manage the huge amount of state an AI chat needs to work.


Sybill's AI agent answering a user query.

For months, almost the whole chat lived in one file. By September 2025 it was about 4,800 lines long. Most people would tell you to split a file like that early. I chose not to. One file kept the total amount of code small, and there were no layers to dig through to understand one click.

It also helped in a way I did not plan. For most of 2025, AI tools did not get much better. Anthropic's models were the best we had. The most expensive models, like Opus and OpenAI's o1 and o3, cost a lot and were not worth it for our daily work. With tools that weak, one big file was a gift: the AI could see everything important in one place. A big file is fine. A big file nobody understands is not.

The right moment to split came when we put Ask Sybill in a sidebar too. The core of the chat moved into one shared piece that both screens used. Each screen kept its own wiring, the code that connects that core to its buttons and lists. About 70% of the two screens behaved the same, but the other 30% had to be different, because the screens did different jobs. With separate wiring, neither screen could break the other. I only connect two parts of the code when the product connects them.

From there, the chat grew up with the rest of the market. At the start, every AI chat was simple: you ask, it answers. Then they learned to run many conversations at once, keep working in the background and use outside tools. Ask Sybill followed the same path. I started with the simplest design that worked and made it more advanced only when the product needed it. The models grew up too. GPT 5 was the first GPT model I really liked, and later Opus 4.5 was another big step.

To keep up, I improved the code all the time. Every time I touched a part of the app, I tried to leave it faster and simpler than I found it. I was known for two things: making the product better, and breaking some of it on the way. During one big refactor of the AI chat, I introduced bugs. I knew it could happen. Refactoring is risky and nobody thanks you for it: when it works, nobody notices, and when it breaks, everybody does. I did it anyway, because I knew what I was doing and better software is worth the risk.

I never let slow or broken things slide

I used our product every day and watched it closely. I watched session recordings of real users and checked our metrics. This was never perfect. We always had more work than time, so these fixes came in small steps, whenever I had a chance. But when something was slow or broken, I did not wait for it to reach the roadmap.

Long chats are a good example. Very few users had them, but for those few, opening a long chat could freeze the app for about 20 seconds. They just stared at the greeting screen, wondering if anything was happening. The code made it clear that this would only get worse as people used the chat more, and I do not like leaving edge cases like that open.

The usual answer is virtualization: draw only the messages you can see on the screen. Virtualization is a fine tool, but it brings its own problems, and I like to understand the root cause first, in code and in life. So I went through the code one function at a time and made each one faster, to raise our baseline. My rule is simple: make the code truly fast first, and add virtualization only when you reach a size where nothing else works.

Then I brainstormed with GPT 6 Astra, and it came up with a clever use of a React feature called startTransition. React uses it to mark an update as not urgent, so the screen stays responsive, for example while you switch tabs. We used it to build a long chat in small pieces: the newest messages show up at once, and the older ones are added quietly in the background. That one idea did about 80% of the job. The freeze went from about 20 seconds to about 1.4 seconds.


Opening a very long chat: newest messages first, older ones in the background.

I thought about the product, not only the code

Fixing what is slow is engineering. Deciding what to build is product. Any product that wants to be good needs both.

Users kept telling us that cutting video clips from their recorded meetings was painful. It took too many steps, it was not clear what to click, and sometimes people lost their work. It was not on the roadmap, and nobody asked me to fix it. So I watched the recordings, read the feedback and designed a new page myself. For ideas, I looked at classic video editors like Sony Vegas, with a real timeline where you can see and shape every clip. Our designer polished the look, and I shipped it. Customers praised it to me directly. That story gets its own article.

We had also wanted, for a long time, to let Ask Sybill build small apps, like dashboards, that run right in the user's browser. That is powerful, but risky: the AI writes code, and that code runs on the user's screen. Our first version was very naive. I started a new project for it, and with a teammate I studied how Claude runs the code it writes. I already had some ideas of my own. In the end we built a sandbox that keeps the code safe and still lets the AI do useful work. For the dashboards we picked shadcn/ui instead of our own library, because Claude already writes it well without any guidance.

I worked on the company, not only in it

We were always running. There was always more to build than time to build it, so I guarded time like money. Every minute lost to bureaucracy or a meeting with no clear point was a minute we paid back at night or on the weekend.

That is why I pushed to keep our processes lean, and sometimes to have almost no process at all. The biggest waste I saw was the distance from our customers. There were too many steps between a customer and an engineer. Feedback got lost on the way, and people forgot how customers really felt. We were fast compared to many companies, but we could be faster. I wanted a key customer to ask for something and get it in one or two days.

So I pushed engineers to talk with customers directly in Slack, to ask the sales team what they were hearing, and to look at the analytics themselves. When one customer asked to sort their data in a new way, we shipped it in a day. That push was mostly mine, and I was still at it when I left.

Saving money was part of the same work. Our end-to-end tests had been broken for six months and still cost about $200 a month to run. We paid about $1,000 a month to store large files in our build pipeline that we did not need. And we sent so much useless noise to Sentry, our error tracking tool, that it cost about another $1,000 a month. Together that is more than $26,000 a year spent on nothing. None of it was my job. If the company were mine, I would want someone to fix it, so I fixed it.

I pushed AI everywhere (when it made sense)

I never treated AI like a religion. Online, the hype was loud long before the tools were good, and I did not let it move me. I watched the tools instead. Each time they got better, I noticed early and put them to work.

In the beginning, AI was only a small help. Still, in September 2024, a few months after I joined, I wrote our first rules file for AI tools: a short guide that tells the AI how we write code. Later I added skills, short guides for specific tasks. With them, anyone could quickly understand a complex component, or take a piece of existing code and turn it into new UI much faster.

Over time, more of the work became agentic, which means AI agents doing whole tasks on their own. We used them for debugging, performance profiling and analytics, and even to click through the app in a real browser to test it.

I pushed AI into places few teams had tried yet. I used it for handoffs and documentation, and I even added an AI step to our hiring process. I said it all the time: documentation is not for people, it is for AI. People rarely read docs. AI reads every word, and then it explains the code to people when they ask.

Then Fable 5 arrived, and my output roughly doubled. For the first time I was not buried in frontend work and tech debt, so I finally had time for the backend too. When a feature needed a backend change, I made it myself instead of waiting. As a team, we moved faster than the roadmap, which left room for the work nobody had planned.

What I would do differently

The first thing is people. There were moments of stress and frustration that could have been fun, with more frank and friendly talk. Today I try to let people be the main character of their own work. I cheer their choices even when I do not agree, and I put being welcoming before being right. It worked with some people and not with others. With some teammates it grew into a strong bond that made both of us happier and more productive, and that is one of the things I am proudest of. What I learned is that it has to start on day one.

The second is tests. I would not have spent time on end-to-end tests, the tests that click through the whole app like a real user. For a long time they did not pay off. They took a long time to write and run, and they kept breaking while the product changed every week. Nobody wanted to take time from features to fix them, so ours sat broken. Fable 5 changed that. It writes a decent test from a short description, so a new test costs almost nothing, and tests that were never worth it suddenly are. Another team brought them back.

The third is cleanup. In August 2026 we spent a week as a team deleting dead code. With Fable 5 we removed a lot of unused code. We tested everything ourselves, and no production issue showed up for a long time after. Still, I think cleanup belongs in every change. A special cleanup week teaches people to wait for the next one.

I left Sybill in September 2026. The lesson I take with me is simple:

Act like the company is yours, even when your title says otherwise.


This is me.
