title: TanStack Start vs Next.js in 2026: Same App, Real Benchmarks
description:
I built the same small store in TanStack Start 1.0 and Next.js 16.4 and benchmarked both on one machine. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

TanStack Start vs Next.js got a lot more interesting on October 13, 2026, when TanStack Start 1.0 went stable. I built the same small store in both frameworks, with the same routes, data, components and Tailwind styles, and measured them on one machine. TanStack Start served 2.9× more server-rendered list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more JSON API calls per second than Next.js 16.4. It also shipped 20% less JavaScript and built 3.9× faster. Next.js still won where it was designed to win: a prerendered page, and a far bigger set of built-in tools.

Here are the numbers, how I got them, and how I'd choose between the two in 2026.

TL;DR: is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes, by a wide margin in my tests. Every route that rendered per request was 2.9× to 8.6× faster on TanStack Start, with much lower tail latency. On the client the gap is smaller: 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript against 135 KB, and an interactive button 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU. Next.js led only on its prerendered home page, because it serves static HTML while Start rendered that page on every request.

Same app, Node 24.22, 2 cores Next.js 16.4.2 TanStack Start 1.169.3 Difference
Home page, req/s 3,220 (static) 2,920 (SSR) Next +10%
Product list, 100 items, SSR, req/s 220 637 Start 2.9×
Product page, SSR, req/s 512 2,341 Start 4.6×
JSON API route, req/s 2,165 18,515 Start 8.6×
p99 latency, product list 754 ms 194 ms Start 3.9× lower
Server memory at idle 94 MB 60 MB Start −36%
Client JS on /products, gzip 135 KB, 7 files 109 KB, 3 files Start −20%
Interactive button, 4× CPU throttle 324 ms 289 ms Start −35 ms
Production build 4.86 s 1.26 s Start 3.9×
Dev server, first page 2.96 s 1.52 s Start 1.9×
Deploy output 38 MB 1.4 MB Start 27× smaller

If you mostly ship content that can be cached, these server numbers matter less. If you run a dashboard, an API-heavy app or anything that renders per user, they matter a lot.

What is TanStack Start?

TanStack Start is a full-stack React framework built on TanStack Router. It adds server-side rendering, streaming, typed server functions, server routes for raw HTTP and middleware, and it builds with Vite (or Rsbuild). The 1.0 announcement calls it ready for production after a long release-candidate phase, and the first stable package was @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0.

The big design difference from Next.js is the component model. In Next.js App Router, pages and layouts are React Server Components by default and you opt into client code with "use client". In Start, components are ordinary React components that render on the server and hydrate on the client. You put work on the server explicitly with createServerFn() or a route loader. Server Components in Start exist, but they are experimental and off by default, so treat them as a preview, not a reason to pick it.

How I benchmarked TanStack Start and Next.js

I wanted a fair app, not a hello world. Both apps have:

  • Home page: a heading and a link. Next.js prerenders it as static HTML; Start has no static prerender by default, so it renders it per request.
  • Product list: 100 products rendered on the server on every request, with a timestamp so neither framework can cache it. In Next.js that's an async Server Component with await connection(). In Start it's a route loader calling a GET server function.
  • Product page: one product plus a client-side "Add to cart" counter, so both frameworks must hydrate interactive code.
  • JSON API: a route returning 20 products. A Next.js route handler with dynamic = "force-dynamic", and a Start server route.

Versions: Next.js 16.4.2 with Turbopack and React 19.3.0, TanStack Start 1.169.3 with Vite 8.3.4, Nitro and React 19.3.1, Tailwind 4 in both. Both ran on Node 24.22 in production mode: Next.js as its standalone server.js, Start as its Nitro Node output. A quick check with next start gave the same results (2,377 req/s on the API, 534 on the product page).

The server was pinned to 2 CPU cores with taskset, and the load generator oha ran on 6 other cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM. Each run used 64 connections for 10 seconds after a 4 second warm-up, and every number is the median of 3 runs on a fresh server process. All runs returned 100% HTTP 200. Client metrics came from Playwright and Chromium: script bytes on each page (gzip level 6), and the time from navigation to a working button click with a 4× CPU slowdown, median of 6 runs.

This is a small synthetic store, not your app. Your database, auth and caching will usually dominate. Treat these as the cost of the framework layer itself.

Server performance: how many requests can each handle?

Server-rendered pages. The product list is where per-request rendering cost shows. Start served 637 pages per second with a p99 of 194 ms; Next.js served 220 with a p99 of 754 ms. On the lighter product page, Start served 2,341 per second versus 512. My reading is that Next.js does more work per request: it renders the Server Component tree to the RSC payload and then renders HTML from it, and it embeds that payload in the page. You can see that in the HTML: the 100-item list was 92 KB raw in Next.js and 60 KB in Start (8.5 KB versus 6.4 KB gzipped).

API routes. This was the biggest gap. A Start server route answered 18,515 requests per second; a Next.js route handler answered 2,165. That's 8.6×. Start's server routes are close to a plain handler on Nitro, while every Next.js request goes through the full Next server and router. For context, Hono on raw Node served 73,000 JSON requests per second on the same 2 cores in my Hono vs Express benchmark, so neither framework is the right place for a hot, high-volume API.

Static pages. Next.js led here: 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second. Next serves the prerendered HTML file, while Start rendered the home page with React each time and still came within 10%. This is the important caveat for Next.js: anything you can make static or cache, with "use cache" or prerendering, skips most of the per-request cost. I covered how to do that in Next.js "use cache".

Memory. Next.js idled at 94 MB and peaked at about 504 MB under the SSR list load. Start idled at 60 MB and peaked at 363 MB. Both are fine for a small VPS, but on a 1 GB box running several apps, Start leaves more room.

Bundle size, hydration and client navigation

On /products, Next.js loaded 7 script files totalling 135 KB gzipped (453 KB raw). Start loaded 3 files totalling 109 KB gzipped (337 KB raw). Most of both is React and React DOM, so the difference is framework runtime: about 26 KB gzipped.

With Chromium's CPU throttled 4×, the "Add to cart" button on a fresh product page became interactive in 289 ms on Start and 324 ms on Next.js. Client-side navigation from the list to a product took 160 ms on Start versus 182 ms on Next.js. Start made 2 requests per navigation (the route chunk and the server function), while Next.js made about 10.

So on the client, Start is faster, but not dramatically. On a real app with a large component library, your own code will outweigh this 26 KB.

Build time, dev server and deployment

Production build: Next.js took 4.86 s (5 clean runs, including its TypeScript check) and Start took 1.26 s with Vite. Running tsc --noEmit separately on the Start app took another 1.54 s, so even with a type check added, Start's build was about 1.7× faster.

Dev server: from launching the dev command to the first fully rendered /products page, Next.js took 2.96 s cold and 2.91 s warm. Start with Vite took 1.52 s cold and 1.45 s warm.

Deploy output: Next.js standalone output was 38 MB because it traces and copies the parts of node_modules it needs, including Next itself. Start's Nitro output was 1.4 MB, fully bundled. In a Docker image that difference is real, but small next to a Node base image. My Next.js Dockerfile guide shows how to keep the Next.js side lean. Installed node_modules were 354 MB for the Next.js app and 152 MB for Start.

Developer experience: what's different day to day?

Numbers aside, the daily work feels different:

  • Data loading. Next.js fetches data inside async Server Components. Start uses route loaders and server functions, usually with TanStack Query for client caching. If you already use TanStack Query, Start will feel natural.
  • Server code. Next.js has Server Actions and route handlers; I compared them in Server Actions vs Route Handlers. Start has createServerFn() with validators, GET or POST, and middleware that runs on both client and server.
  • Type safety. Start's router generates types for every path, param and search param, so a broken link is a type error. Next.js has opt-in typedRoutes, which covers links but not validated search params.
  • Caching. Next.js has a framework cache (Cache Components, "use cache", cacheLife). Start has no server data cache: you use HTTP headers, a CDN, or your own store. That's simpler to reason about and more work for content sites.
  • Built-ins. Next.js ships next/image, next/font, metadata APIs and a huge ecosystem of examples. In Start you bring your own image and font handling.
  • Hosting. Next.js runs best on Vercel and works anywhere with Node or Docker, as I do with Coolify. Start deploys through Nitro or plugins to Node, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

One gotcha I hit in Next.js: my generated project wired Tailwind 4 through a turbopack.rules entry for *.css in next.config.ts (the @tailwindcss/turbopack loader). When I overwrote the config to add output: "standalone", the CSS came out empty and the Tailwind compiler ended up in the client bundle: 280 KB of gzipped JavaScript instead of 135 KB. If you edit that file, keep the rules block, and check your bundle after config changes.

Should I switch from Next.js to TanStack Start?

Pick TanStack Start if:

  • your app renders per user or per request (dashboards, SaaS, internal tools), so server cost matters
  • you want typed routes and search params, explicit server functions and no framework-level cache
  • you like Vite, or want to deploy to Cloudflare Workers or a small VPS without Vercel
  • you already use TanStack Query, Router or Table

Stay with or pick Next.js if:

  • your site is mostly content that can be prerendered or cached, where Next served static pages fastest
  • you rely on React Server Components today, or on next/image, next/font and the metadata API
  • hiring, templates and third-party SDK examples matter more than raw speed
  • you host on Vercel and want its integration

For an existing, healthy Next.js app, I wouldn't rewrite just for these numbers. Cache what you can first. For a new interactive app, Start 1.0 is now a serious default. The official TanStack Start vs Next.js page has a fair feature-by-feature comparison too.

How do I migrate from Next.js to TanStack Start?

The rough steps I'd follow, based on building the same app in both:

  1. Move app/ routes to src/routes/ files using createFileRoute. Dynamic segments change from [id] to $id.
  2. Replace data fetching in async Server Components with a route loader that calls a createServerFn().
  3. Remove "use client" directives. Every component in Start is a normal component.
  4. Turn route handlers into server routes with server: { handlers: { GET } }.
  5. Replace Server Actions with POST server functions, and add an input validator.
  6. Replace next/link with TanStack Router's Link (to plus typed params), and next/image and next/font with your own components or plain tags.
  7. Add Nitro (or a hosting plugin) to vite.config.ts for your deploy target.

Migrate one representative route end to end first, including auth and a mutation, before committing the whole app.

Common mistakes when comparing Next.js and TanStack Start

  • Comparing a static Next.js page to an SSR Start page and calling Next faster. Make the rendering mode the same on both sides, or report it, as I did for the home page.
  • Forgetting to copy .next/static into the standalone folder. Next's standalone server doesn't serve client assets without it, so hydration silently never happens. My first client test showed a 30 second timeout for exactly this reason.
  • Benchmarking dev mode. Always build and run with NODE_ENV=production.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores as the server. Pin them apart or your numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Leaving devtools in production. Check that router and query devtools aren't in your client bundle.

Key takeaways

  • TanStack Start 1.0 went stable on October 13, 2026, and its Server Components support is still experimental.
  • On the same app and 2 cores, Start served 2.9× more SSR list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more API calls than Next.js 16.4.
  • Next.js won on its prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 req/s, so caching closes the gap for content you can cache.
  • Start's p99 on the 100-item SSR page was 194 ms versus 754 ms, and it idled at 60 MB versus 94 MB.
  • Start shipped 20% less client JavaScript (109 KB vs 135 KB gzipped) and became interactive 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU.
  • Start built in 1.26 s versus 4.86 s and its dev server answered in 1.5 s versus 3.0 s.
  • Choose Start for per-request, interactive apps and typed routing; choose Next.js for cacheable content, RSC and its built-ins.

Related: if you're weighing other parts of your toolchain too, see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint and React Compiler in Next.js.

FAQ

Is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes in my tests. With the same app on 2 CPU cores, TanStack Start 1.169.3 served 637 server-rendered list pages per second versus 220 for Next.js 16.4.2, 2,341 product pages versus 512, and 18,515 API requests versus 2,165. Next.js was faster only on a prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second.

Is TanStack Start stable and production ready?

Yes. TanStack Start 1.0 was announced as stable on October 13, 2026, with @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0 as the first stable release. Its React Server Components support is still experimental and off by default.

Does TanStack Start ship less JavaScript than Next.js?

Somewhat. On the same product list page, TanStack Start loaded 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript in 3 files and Next.js loaded 135 KB in 7 files. Most of both is React itself, so the framework difference was about 26 KB gzipped.

Does TanStack Start support React Server Components?

Yes, but experimentally. You opt in with @vitejs/plugin-rsc and rsc: { enabled: true } in the tanstackStart plugin, and the docs say the feature will stay experimental into early v1. Start's normal SSR, loaders and server functions don't need Server Components.

Should I migrate my Next.js app to TanStack Start?

Not just for speed if the app is healthy. Cache or prerender what you can in Next.js first, since static pages were Next's fastest case. Consider Start for new interactive apps, apps that render per user, or teams that want typed routes and search params, Vite and simple hosting.

How much faster does TanStack Start build than Next.js?

In my test app, vite build for TanStack Start took 1.26 s and next build took 4.86 s, averaged over 5 clean runs. next build includes a TypeScript check; adding tsc --noEmit (1.54 s) to the Start build still left it about 1.7× faster.

Can TanStack Start be self-hosted?

Yes. It builds through Nitro to a self-contained Node server, which was 1.4 MB in my test versus 38 MB for the Next.js standalone output. It also deploys to Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

What is the difference between Next.js Server Actions and TanStack Start server functions?

Next.js Server Actions are tied to forms and React's pending and error states. TanStack Start server functions are typed RPC calls created with createServerFn, can use GET or POST, accept an input validator and compose middleware that runs on both client and server. Both need runtime validation and server-side authorization.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React
description:
title: "Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-10T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [webdev, react, nodejs, websockets]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Websocket Protocol Handshakes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Broadcasting Cursor Positions And Canvas Events: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Operational Transformation Basics: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Managing Reconnects: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: WebSocket protocol handshakes, broadcasting cursor positions and canvas events, operational transformation basics, and managing reconnects."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: I Trusted My Own Safety Documentation. Then I Read the Test Suite.
description:
James Coombs is a design engineer who built a 3-layer safety architecture for AI code agents after running into 7 real bypass incidents. He maintains a 60-component design system and has run controlled ablation studies on AI code generation governance.

My documentation said the guard scripts were protected from agent edits, "enforced at the tool layer." My test suite contained a passing assertion that they were not:

check "Write to normal hook file → ALLOW" "ALLOW" "$OUT"

The file that assertion targets is the largest guard in the system. The assertion was green, and it was correct. No hook enforced that protection. The only thing stopping an agent from rewriting a guard was the permission classifier's judgment, and my own documentation describing that as tool-layer enforcement was false.

The dates are the uncomfortable part. That assertion went in on day 16 of the project and had been passing for 77 days. The sentence claiming tool-layer enforcement went in on day 72. So for 21 days the repository contained a document and a test that directly contradicted each other, and the test was the one telling the truth.

I wrote about the seven bypass incidents that built this architecture in I Gave an AI Agent Unrestricted Shell Access. Every one of those was handed to me: the agent did something, I noticed, I fixed it. This one was different. I found it by sitting down to audit the guards deliberately, and the audit turned up a category the incidents never did. Not a guard bug, not an agent bypass. A control that was real in the prose and absent in the code.

What the gate actually was

The protection is called a self-modification gate. Its purpose is narrow and important: an agent should not be able to weaken the thing that constrains it. If the agent can edit guard-destructive.sh, every other layer is decoration.

The intended enforcement was the permission classifier, a model that evaluates each tool call in the permissive mode I run in. Ask it to edit a guard script and it refuses, correctly, even when I asked for the change in conversation. That behavior is real. I had watched it work dozens of times, which is exactly why I never checked whether anything else backed it up.

Two properties of that arrangement matter, and I had thought about neither.

The classifier only runs in one permission mode. Drop out of that mode and nothing consults it. The gate does not weaken; it ceases to exist.

Leaving that mode is not exotic. It is the documented workaround when the classifier is unavailable, which happened to me mid-audit: the model backing it went down, every tool call started failing, and the remedy was to switch modes and keep working. So the control was absent precisely when I was already working around a failure, at the moment I was least likely to notice.

That is an asymmetry worth naming. The gate fails closed on an outage and open on a mode change. An unreachable classifier denies everything, which is the correct direction. A mode change silently permits everything, with no message and no log line. Same control, opposite failure, and only one of them announces itself.

The fix is unglamorous. Six regex patterns in the hook that already gates writes, covering the 11 files that decide, mint, release or execute an approval, and deliberately not the test suite, which has to stay editable or the whole test-first workflow becomes impossible. Three of the 11 had never been in the gate list at all, including the script that mints the approval tokens. 18 assertions now cover it: every protected file denied, Edit denied as well as Write so there is no second route in, the test suite still permitted, unrelated hooks still permitted, and the existing escape hatch preserved.

Then I verified it the only way that counts. I switched out of the classifier's mode, so the layer I had been relying on was off, and tried to write a guard file myself. The hook refused. That refusal is the first evidence I have ever had that this control exists.

If you have a security control you have never seen fire, you do not have evidence it works. You have a habit of not testing it.

The audit also found the credential was too weak

The same pass turned up a second problem, in a mechanism I was more confident about. I described the approval nonce and its content-binding fix in I Gave an AI Agent Unrestricted Shell Access; what that piece did not say is that I found the flaw the same way I found the missing gate, by auditing rather than by being bitten.

The nonce proved the wrong proposition. It established that an approval had happened in the last 300 seconds. It never established that the approval was for this command. That gap is exploitable without breaking anything: write a payload to the staging path when nothing is watching, wait, and the next routine approval executes it. The credential was a bearer token: possession proved recency, not intent.

The fix binds a SHA-256 digest of the exact command to the live nonce, and the detail that matters is the failure path: a mismatch consumes the nonce anyway, deliberately, so a rejected attempt cannot be retried against a different payload.

Ask what your credential proves, not how hard it is to forge.

Why the audit found more than the agent did

The agent found seven things in 44 days. The audit found more than that in three, and the difference is not effort.

The agent only probes paths it needs. It routes around a boundary when the boundary blocks a task, which means it exercises the parts of the system that get in its way. The parts that never get in its way are never tested, and a control that does not exist never gets in anybody's way. That is why the missing gate survived: an agent that can freely edit a guard has no reason to attempt anything clever, so there is no incident to notice.

The second reason is less comfortable. I ran the audit with blind reviewers, separate agent sessions given the changed files and none of my reasoning, a technique I argued for in Context Is a Contaminant. Two review rounds on one change document returned 23 findings I then verified against the code. All 23 were real. I had self-caught none of them.

The shape of my own errors was consistent enough to be embarrassing. Counting across the whole audit, not just those 23, twelve defects were the same species: an artifact asserting something other than what was there. Seven of the twelve were specifically an assertion that could not fail. A test whose grep read the wrong constant, so it passed by coincidence. A count of a literal that stays identical when you extract that literal into a named constant, because the constant's own definition contains it, so the test cannot detect the change it exists to verify. A comment describing the state of three other files, which one commit falsified.

Every one of those looked right when I wrote it. Every one passed. Nothing about care or attention would have caught them, because the failure was structural: each artifact asserted something other than what was there, and a passing test looks the same either way.

There is one technique that did work, and it is narrow enough to be worth stealing. When a change is already applied and its test passes, run that test against the previous version from source control. If it passes there too, it covers nothing. That check caught the last two instances before any reviewer saw them, and it is the only thing in this piece I would call a method rather than a lesson.

What I would tell someone who has already built this

Audit the layer you trust most. Not the newest one, not the one you are least sure of. The control you stopped thinking about is the one whose documentation has drifted furthest from its code, because nothing has forced you to reread either.

Write down what each control actually enforces and where. Then go read the code and check. The prose and the mechanism drift apart silently, and there is no test for "the README is lying." I wrote the false sentence and the assertion that contradicted it, 56 days apart, and never put them side by side.

Trigger every control once, from the position of the thing it constrains. Not in a unit test. Attempt the action it forbids and watch it refuse.

Ask what your credentials prove rather than how strong they are. "Single-use, time-limited, session-scoped" describes the token's lifecycle and says nothing about what it authorizes.

Do not let an assertion into the suite until you have seen it fail. The version of the file before your change is sitting in source control, and it costs nothing to run the test against it.

The seven incidents in the original piece all arrived as symptoms, and symptom-driven hardening is honest work. It is also bounded by what the agent happens to try. Everything expensive I found this month was sitting in a path nothing had reason to walk.

The numbers

  • 1 control documented as enforced, enforced by nothing, across all 93 days of the project
  • 77 days that a passing test asserted the permissive behavior, 21 of them alongside a document claiming the opposite
  • 6 patterns and 18 assertions to make it real
  • 11 approval-machinery files now write-protected at the hook layer, 3 of which had never been in the gate list
  • 23 findings across 2 blind review rounds, 23 verified real, 0 self-caught
  • 12 defects of one species (an artifact asserting something other than what was there), 7 of them an assertion that could not fail
  • 361 assertions in the bash regression suite (as of 2026-08-19)
  • 4 independent time windows in the system, all 4 unnamed literals before this pass, 3 of them named by it. Enumerating them for this list is what surfaced the fourth, a 5-second anti-replay cooldown the audit itself had walked past.

title: Vercel Sandbox supports forking
description:
Vercel Sandbox now supports forking with Sandbox.fork().

The fork starts from the source's current snapshot and inherits its config and environment variables. If the source is running, it forks the latest saved state, not the live in-memory state. If the source has no snapshot, it falls back to a fresh create, using the source's runtime and config. Any parameter you pass overrides the inherited value.

A fork takes about the same time as creating a sandbox, with the same limits. Use it to branch an agent from a shared base, give each tenant its own copy of a template, or run variations of one setup in parallel.

title: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant: Benchmarked for RAG in 2026
description:
I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings into pgvector and Qdrant and measured recall, latency, index build and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its docs only, since I didn't run it. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that stores embeddings in a vector column and searches them with HNSW or IVFFlat indexes, next to your normal tables. Qdrant is an open-source vector database you run yourself or use as a managed cloud. Pinecone is a fully managed, serverless vector database you only reach through an API.

For a RAG app, the real question is whether you need a separate vector database at all. I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings (1,536 dimensions) into pgvector 0.8.7 on PostgreSQL 18.6 and into Qdrant 1.19.2 on one machine. Then I measured recall, latency, build time and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its official docs and limits only, because I didn't run it and I won't invent numbers for it.

TL;DR: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant, which should I use?

Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres and have up to a few million vectors. One database, SQL joins, transactions and backups you already have. Choose Qdrant when vector search is the core workload and you need the best recall per millisecond or heavy filtering. Choose Pinecone when you want zero infrastructure and accept a managed service with usage pricing.

pgvector Qdrant Pinecone
What it is Postgres extension Vector database (open source) Managed vector database (closed)
Hosting Anywhere Postgres runs Self-host or Qdrant Cloud Pinecone's cloud only
Index HNSW, IVFFlat HNSW per segment Managed (serverless, object storage)
Max indexed dims 2,000 vector, 4,000 halfvec 1,536 tested here 20,000 dense
Filtering SQL WHERE (post-filter, iterative scans) Payload indexes + filter-aware HNSW Metadata filters (40 KB per record)
Consistency Transactional (ACID) Upserts readable after wait=true Eventually consistent
Recall@10 at ~2.6 ms, my test 0.978 (ef_search 100) 0.985 (hnsw_ef 40) not tested
Cost to start Your Postgres Free binary / free cloud tier Free Starter; Standard $50/month minimum

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Usually not at first. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, pgvector adds vector search without a second system to deploy, secure, back up and keep in sync. In my test it answered top-10 queries over 100,000 OpenAI embeddings in 1.5-4 ms, with 95-99% recall. A dedicated database starts to pay off at very large scale, under heavy filtering, or when search load needs to scale separately.

The hidden cost of a separate vector store is synchronisation. Every document insert, update and delete has to reach two systems, and a failed write leaves them disagreeing. With pgvector the embedding sits in the same row and the same transaction as the document it describes.

What is pgvector?

pgvector is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec types, distance operators like <=> (cosine) and <-> (L2), and approximate HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. Per the pgvector README, it "performs exact nearest neighbor search, which provides perfect recall" by default. An index trades a little recall for speed.

CREATE EXTENSION vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
  id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id int NOT NULL,
  content   text NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- top 5 chunks for a question, inside one tenant
SELECT id, content
FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 5;

Index limits matter for model choice. HNSW can index a vector of "up to 2,000 dimensions" and a halfvec of "up to 4,000 dimensions". A 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large needs a halfvec index or a shorter output size.

What are Qdrant and Pinecone?

Qdrant is an open-source vector search engine written in Rust. It stores points (vectors plus a JSON payload), builds an HNSW index per segment, and adds payload indexes so filters run inside the graph search. You can run a single binary, Docker or Qdrant Cloud.

Pinecone is a managed, serverless vector database. Per its architecture docs, "all your vector data is stored in highly efficient, distributed object storage." Pinecone "separates write and read operations into different paths, with each scaling independently based on demand." There is no self-hosted version.

How I benchmarked pgvector and Qdrant

  1. Data. The first 100,000 rows of the public DBpedia OpenAI embeddings dataset: 1,536-dimension text-embedding-ada-002 vectors of Wikipedia entities, a typical RAG shape. 1,000 held-out rows from the same dataset served as queries.
  2. Ground truth. Exact cosine top-10 for every query, computed with NumPy. Recall@10 is the share of those 10 that each engine returned.
  3. Machine. One 8-vCPU, 15 GB Linux box, everything on localhost, no Docker.
  4. pgvector. PostgreSQL 18.6 with pgvector 0.8.7, shared_buffers = 2GB, maintenance_work_mem = 2GB. HNSW with defaults (m = 16, ef_construction = 64), loaded with binary COPY through psycopg 3.
  5. Qdrant. The Qdrant 1.19.2 release binary, cosine distance, m = 16 and ef_construct = 64 to match pgvector, default optimizer settings (it made 4 segments). Loaded with the official Python client over gRPC from a single process.
  6. Queries. One client, sequential, 50 warm-up queries, then 1,000 timed queries. Latency includes the Python client round trip on both sides.
  7. Filters. Every vector got a random category from 0 to 9, about 10% of rows each. Filtered queries asked for the top 10 inside one category.

Is pgvector fast enough? Recall and latency results

Yes, at this scale both engines are fast. pgvector reached 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms median with default settings, and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with hnsw.ef_search = 200. Qdrant reached 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms median and 0.999 at 5.4 ms. At roughly equal recall (about 98.5-98.8%), Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster: 2.6 ms against 4.0 ms.

Engine and setting Recall@10 p50 latency p95 latency Queries/s (1 client)
pgvector, ef_search = 40 (default) 0.948 1.45 ms 2.16 ms 683
pgvector, ef_search = 100 0.978 2.60 ms 3.70 ms 389
pgvector, ef_search = 200 0.988 4.02 ms 5.82 ms 249
pgvector halfvec index, ef_search = 100 0.973 2.33 ms 3.30 ms 433
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 40 0.985 2.63 ms 3.56 ms 368
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 100 0.997 3.73 ms 4.66 ms 255
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 200 0.999 5.37 ms 6.99 ms 176
pgvector exact (no index) 1.000 380 ms 445 ms 3
Qdrant exact (no index) 1.000 24.7 ms 32.6 ms 39

Why does Qdrant get higher recall at the same ef? It splits the collection into segments (4 here) and searches each one with that ef, so it explores more candidates in total. Compare the engines at equal recall, not equal settings.

How fast do they load and index?

Qdrant indexed faster: 30.8 seconds from the first upload to a fully indexed collection, with the upload itself taking 20.2 s from one Python process. pgvector loaded the rows with COPY in 3.9 s, then needed 69.1 s to build the HNSW index with the default 2 parallel workers.

pgvector Qdrant
Load 100k vectors 3.9 s (COPY) 20.2 s (Python client, gRPC)
Build HNSW index 69.1 s included, indexed at 30.8 s
Table / data size 798 MB —
HNSW index size 781 MB (vector), 391 MB (halfvec) —
Server memory after test Postgres buffers + OS cache 1,293 MB RSS

Use the halfvec trick in pgvector: indexing embedding::halfvec(1536) halved the index from 781 MB to 391 MB and cost about half a point of recall (0.973 against 0.978 at ef_search = 100). Query the index with the same cast:

CREATE INDEX ON documents
  USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(1536)) halfvec_cosine_ops);

SELECT id FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding::halfvec(1536) <=> $1::halfvec(1536)
LIMIT 10;

How does filtered vector search compare?

Qdrant handled filters best. With a payload index on category, filtered top-10 queries returned 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms median. pgvector gave three very different results depending on the plan Postgres picked, so you need to know how its filtering works.

Filtered query (10% of rows match) Rows returned (of 10) Recall@10 p50
pgvector, planner's choice (B-tree on category, exact sort) 10 1.000 44.2 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = off 3.92 0.389 1.77 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = strict_order 10 0.915 3.62 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = relaxed_order 10 0.953 3.37 ms
Qdrant, payload index 10 0.993 2.11 ms

Why does pgvector return fewer rows with a filter?

Because HNSW filters after the index scan. The README explains: "If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average." I measured 3.92. Since pgvector 0.8.0, iterative index scans keep walking the graph until enough rows match.

-- once per session or per transaction (SET LOCAL)
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

SELECT id, content FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 10;

Postgres often picks the exact plan by itself for a selective filter. In my test it used the category B-tree and sorted about 10,000 rows exactly: perfect recall, but 44 ms instead of about 3 ms. That is fine for one tenant with a few thousand chunks. For large tenants, check EXPLAIN and turn on iterative scans. If one filter dominates, consider a partial index or partitioning by tenant.

What does Pinecone offer that pgvector and Qdrant don't?

Fully managed, serverless scaling with nothing to run. Reads and writes scale separately, storage lives in object storage, and you never tune ef or m. The trade-offs are documented:

  • Eventual consistency. The known limitations page says "Pinecone is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records are available to query."
  • Operation limits. Per the operation limits: dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions, 40 KB of filterable metadata per record, 1,000 records or 2 MB per upsert batch, and top_k up to 10,000.
  • Plans. The object limits give the free Starter plan 2 GB of serverless storage and 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Pinecone pricing lists the Standard plan at a $50/month minimum.
  • Network hop. Every query leaves your VPC. Expect your cloud region's round-trip time on top of search time. My localhost latencies are not comparable to Pinecone and I did not measure it.

When should I choose each one?

Decide by what you already run and what dominates your workload. The pgvector default is strong for product teams. Move when you measure a reason, not before.

  1. Choose pgvector when your data lives in Postgres, you need joins, row-level security or transactions with your embeddings, and you have up to a few million vectors per index. Add pgvectorscale (StreamingDiskANN) if the index outgrows RAM.
  2. Choose Qdrant when search is the product: tens of millions of vectors, many filters, multi-vector or hybrid search, or quantization to cut memory. Its quantization guide says scalar quantization achieves "4x compression with minimal accuracy loss."
  3. Choose Pinecone when nobody on the team should run a database, traffic is spiky, and a usage bill plus eventual consistency are acceptable.

How do I move from pgvector to Qdrant later?

Keep embeddings and IDs portable from day one. Use the same primary key in both systems, store the embedding model name and dimensions with each row, and write a re-sync job that streams rows by ID. Qdrant accepts integer or UUID point IDs, so a UUIDv7 primary key maps across directly.

Then run both side by side, compare recall on a fixed set of real queries, and switch reads before you stop writing to Postgres.

Common mistakes with vector search in production

  • Indexing 3,072-dimension vectors as vector. HNSW on vector stops at 2,000 dimensions. Use halfvec or a smaller output dimension.
  • Forgetting iterative scans. Filtered HNSW queries in pgvector can silently return fewer than LIMIT rows.
  • Comparing engines at equal settings. ef means different work in different engines. Compare at equal recall.
  • Measuring recall on random vectors. Use real embeddings from your model. Random data hides graph quality.
  • Creating Qdrant payload indexes after loading. The indexing docs say payload indexes should be created before ingesting data, so filter-aware HNSW edges get built.
  • Ignoring re-embedding cost. Switching embedding models means re-embedding everything, whichever store you use.

If you want a working starting point, my open-source Next.js AI starter kit, Forgekit, ships RAG on pgvector. For self-hosting Postgres or Qdrant next to your app, see self-hosting Next.js with Coolify.

Key takeaways

  • With 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector 0.8.7 hit 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms with defaults and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with ef_search 200.
  • Qdrant 1.19.2 hit 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms, about 1.5x faster than pgvector at roughly equal recall.
  • pgvector's HNSW filters after scanning: a 10% filter returned only 3.92 of 10 rows until iterative scans were enabled.
  • Qdrant's payload index gave the best filtered search in my test: 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms.
  • A halfvec HNSW index halved pgvector's index size (781 MB to 391 MB) for about half a point of recall.
  • Pinecone is serverless and eventually consistent, supports 20,000-dimension vectors, and its Standard plan has a $50/month minimum.
  • Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres; move to Qdrant or Pinecone when measurements show a need.

FAQ

Is pgvector as good as Pinecone or Qdrant?

For most RAG apps up to a few million vectors, yes. In my test of 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector reached 0.988 recall@10 at 4.0 ms median, and Qdrant reached 0.985 at 2.6 ms. Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster at equal recall and better at filtered search, but pgvector keeps embeddings in the same transactional database as your data.

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Not usually at the start. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, the pgvector extension adds vector columns and HNSW indexes without a second system to deploy, back up and keep in sync. Consider a dedicated vector database when you reach tens of millions of vectors, need heavy filtering at low latency, or need to scale search separately.

Why does pgvector return fewer results than my LIMIT?

Because pgvector's HNSW index applies WHERE filters after scanning the index. With a filter matching 10 percent of rows and the default ef_search of 40, about 4 rows match on average; I measured 3.92. Set hnsw.iterative_scan to relaxed_order or strict_order, available since pgvector 0.8.0, so the scan continues until enough rows match.

How many dimensions can pgvector index?

pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat indexes support the vector type up to 2,000 dimensions, halfvec up to 4,000 and bit up to 64,000. For a 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large, index the column as halfvec or request a smaller output dimension. Pinecone supports dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions.

Is Qdrant faster than pgvector?

In my single-machine test, yes, at equal recall. Qdrant 1.19.2 returned 0.985 recall@10 at 2.6 ms median against pgvector's 0.988 at 4.0 ms, and indexed 100,000 vectors in about 31 seconds against pgvector's 69-second HNSW build. With default settings, pgvector was faster per query but at lower recall, 0.948 at 1.45 ms.

How much does Pinecone cost?

Pinecone has a free Starter plan with 2 GB of serverless storage and up to 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Its Standard plan for production has a $50 per month minimum, after which you pay as you go for usage, according to Pinecone's pricing page. Qdrant's open-source build and pgvector are free to self-host.

What is halfvec in pgvector?

halfvec is pgvector's half-precision vector type, storing each dimension in 2 bytes instead of 4. Indexing an expression like embedding::halfvec(1536) halves the HNSW index size; in my test it shrank from 781 MB to 391 MB with recall dropping from 0.978 to 0.973. It also raises the indexable limit to 4,000 dimensions.

Is Pinecone eventually consistent?

Yes. Pinecone's documentation states that it is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records can be queried, and suggests checking index stats to confirm counts. pgvector writes are transactional and visible on commit, and Qdrant upserts sent with wait=true are applied before the call returns.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?
description:
Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?

For months, the artificial intelligence trade seemed unstoppable. Giant chipmakers, cloud providers, and data-center builders lifted Wall Street to one record after another. This week, the music stopped — at least temporarily — as a brutal sell-off swept through the technology sector and forced investors to confront a question they had been happy to ignore: what happens if the most expensive technology bet in history stops paying off?

A Week of Red Numbers

The damage was fast and broad. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite posted its first weekly loss in five weeks, and the S&P 500 logged its worst week since June. Chip stocks — the engine of the AI boom — took the hardest hits. Micron Technology fell more than five percent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped over five percent, Broadcom slid more than four percent, and Intel lost close to six percent on Friday alone. AI data-center infrastructure company CoreWeave, a major Nvidia customer, plunged more than seven percent after a double-digit decline earlier in the week.

The rout was global. Seoul's tech-rich Kospi briefly triggered a trading halt after diving more than eight percent, with Samsung sinking over nine percent and SK hynix down more than eleven percent. Tokyo shed close to five percent, dragged down by chip-linked names like Advantest and Kioxia as well as investment giant SoftBank.

Why Now? Inflation and the Cost of Money

The immediate trigger was economic, not technological. US inflation data came in hotter than expected, with the consumer price index jumping to 3.7 percent in September and wholesale inflation surging 6.3 percent year-on-year — its biggest jump since 2022. Those numbers stoked fears that the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in September for the first time in three years, may have to tighten further, with futures markets now pricing in a high probability of another hike by December.

Higher rates matter more to AI companies than to almost anyone else. Tech giants have financed an unprecedented infrastructure spree — data centers, GPU clusters, and power-hungry compute farms — largely through debt markets. With bond yields climbing to their highest levels in years, the cost of financing that buildout is rising exactly as patience with unprofitable AI ventures is wearing thin. A week before the crash, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had called AI "the most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime. Investors this week appeared to decide that consequence cuts both ways.

The IMF's Warning Shot

The market turmoil coincided with an uncomfortable warning from the International Monetary Fund. At the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the fund released a report projecting that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028, and cautioned that "weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction."

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva did not mince words: if confidence evaporates and "money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks" that "would be felt across the world." Yet the same meetings underscored how central AI already is to the global economy. The fund noted that global trade grew 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025 — a figure that would have been closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem put it bluntly: "It is here, and it's just the beginning."

Bubble or Growing Pains?

Not everyone reading the sell-off sees a bubble bursting. The Dow Jones actually rose on Friday, suggesting investors are rotating out of tech rather than abandoning equities altogether. Earnings expectations for the quarter remain strong, and companies at the heart of the AI supply chain — from TSMC to memory makers — have continued to report robust demand. Nvidia shares, though down more than five percent for the week, remain up dramatically over the longer arc of the AI era.

The bear case, though, is no longer fringe. Critics point to debt-financed capital expenditure, stretched valuations, and monetization that still lags the hype. Analysts this week cited "worries about the AI buildout, bubbly valuations, lower-than-expected earnings growth at leading US frontier labs, and Chinese competition" as compounding pressures. Moody's Analytics economists added that a prolonged Middle East conflict, by pushing up energy prices and interest rates, could "puncture" the AI boom by straining the economics behind AI investment.

What to Watch

Three signposts will matter in the coming weeks. First, the Fed's October 28 policy decision, landing a week before the US midterm elections — a hawkish surprise could renew the pressure on rate-sensitive tech names. Second, the ongoing earnings season, where markets will demand evidence that AI revenue is catching up to AI spending. Third, and hardest to measure: confidence. As Georgieva noted in Bangkok, "if there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities."

Whether this week proves to be a healthy correction in a long structural boom or the first crack in a bubble, one thing is clear: the era of unquestioned AI enthusiasm on Wall Street is over. From now on, the market will want receipts.

title: Introducing Agent Plugins
description:
Today, Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is publicly available. Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for plugins that extend AI agents.

Agent Skills provide reusable instructions and resources for AI agents. MCP servers connect agents to tools and services. Both can be reused across clients, but clients often package and discover them differently.

Agent Plugins gives compatible clients a common format: a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for its components. The format is intentionally small and easy to implement, and it leaves installation, distribution, policy, user experience, and client-specific capabilities to each client.

One package for the portable parts

Extension authors often adapt the same component to several client formats. Even though the underlying Skill or MCP server is identical, clients often expect different top-level metadata, discovery paths, or MCP configuration.

Agent Plugins gives those shared components one predictable, structured home:

A minimal JSON manifest (plugin.json) identifies the specification version and names the plugin:

Those two fields are the minimum requirement for the manifest, and the rest of the contract is represented in the file structure of the directory itself. A reusable component should not need to be repackaged for every client, so the format specifies only what a client needs to discover and load what is inside.

Every compatible client checks for plugin.json at the plugin root. Clients that support Skills discover them under skills/. Clients that support MCP servers read their configuration from mcp.json. A client can support either component type or both. After the client validates the manifest, components are validated independently, so one invalid component does not disable unrelated ones.

For plugin authors, that means fewer client-specific conventions for the same component. For client implementers, the specification defines a small, deterministic contract for discovery, validation, and loading.

Small on purpose

Agent Plugins defines the portable contract for a plugin and leaves the behavior of the client up to each client.

Version 1 focuses that contract on two component types: Agent Skills and MCP servers. Both already have specifications and meaningful adoption of their own, and Agent Plugins does not attempt to redefine them. Agent Plugins provides a shared definition of how clients find the components together in a distributable plugin.

Other components, such as commands, hooks, and agents, remain with clients. The Technical Steering Committee may consider additional component types in future versions as semantics converge and a demonstrated portability need emerges.

Keeping the boundary small makes the format easier to implement and gives the ecosystem room to converge before adding more portable surface area.

Clients retain flexibility

Clients need freedom to innovate while a shared format evolves, so Agent Plugins includes a namespaced extension mechanism for client-specific data and files.

Extensions remain outside the portable contract. Each client defines its own namespace, and other clients ignore it. This prevents client-specific behavior from leaking into the common format or blocking adoption of the shared components. A client-specific capability can remain client-specific until there is reason and consensus to standardize it.

An open, multi-vendor project

Vercel initiated the proposal, which representatives from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anysphere, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel refined collaboratively into Agent Plugins 1.0.0.

The initial Technical Steering Committee includes Core Maintainers from AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel.

The project is openly licensed, and its maintainers, contribution process, and technical decisions are public. No single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction.

Build with Agent Plugins 1.0.0

The specification, its JSON Schemas, and guides for plugin authors and client implementers are available at agent-plugins.org. Governance and the contribution process live in the Agent Plugins specification repository on GitHub.

If you author agent extensions, you can use the specification to package Skills and MCP servers behind one portable manifest. If you build an agent client, the specification's conformance checklist defines the minimum requirements for discovering and loading Agent Plugins.

At launch, Agent Plugins are supported across:

  • ChatGPT and Codex

  • Cursor

  • GitHub Copilot

  • Kiro

  • VS Code

Plugin authors can package components once, and their plugin will automatically carry between supporting clients.

Agent Plugins is a contract between the authors who build extensions for agents and the clients that load them. That contract is now defined and open for both sides to shape.

title: We went Edgemaxxing and FalkorDB mogged Joins
description:
Here is how we did it, Edgemaxxing is really good (for performance).

Background you need first

What is a graph database?

A graph database stores two things:

  • Nodes: things. For example: a paper, a finding, a hypothesis.
  • Edges: connections between two things. For example: "this finding is evidence for this hypothesis".

Both nodes and edges can hold properties, which are small pieces of data such as year: 2026 or stance: "refutes".

FalkorDB is a graph database. You talk to it with a query language called Cypher. A Cypher pattern looks like a drawing:

(finding)-[:EVIDENCE_FOR]->(hypothesis)

That reads as "a finding, connected by an EVIDENCE_FOR edge, to a hypothesis".

Terms

These are relevant to the problems we are solving so its good to know, But it should work generally for other use cases as well!

Word Meaning Example
Question What the user types "creatine on intelligence vs muscle gain"
Hypothesis One testable claim from the question H2: "Creatine increases muscle gain in adults"
Paper A published article Chen 2026 (a meta-analysis)
Study One experiment inside a paper An RCT with 15 vegans
Finding One measured result from a study "Skeletal muscle mass: no change"
Concept A topic or measurement "lean mass"

Part 1: Edgemaxxing begins

The problem

Lets look at an example "Lean mass increased by 0.37 kg."

  • For a hypothesis H2 (creatine increases muscle gain), this finding supports it.
  • For a different hypothesis, such as "creatine harms kidneys", it is not relevant.

So "supports" is not a fact about the finding alone. It is a fact about the finding together with one hypothesis.

The bad solution

Store stance: "supports" on the finding node. Then the second hypothesis breaks: it sees "supports" too, which is wrong. You would have to copy the finding once per hypothesis, and the copies would drift apart.

What we did

We put the stance on the edge between the finding and the hypothesis i.e Edgemaxxing:

(Finding: "Lean mass ↑ 0.37 kg") -[:EVIDENCE_FOR {stance: "supports", weight: 0.67}]-> (H2)
  • There is one finding node.
  • There is one edge per hypothesis, and each edge has its own stance.

On the finding, “supports” can't say which hypothesis it means. On the edge, it can.

Relevant bit: many databases can't store properties on a connection, or make it awkward. FalkorDB is a property graph, so edges can hold data just like nodes can. This one feature makes the whole design possible.

Why this matters

Papers and findings are shared across all questions. When a new question needs a paper that was already read, the app does not read it again. It only adds new EVIDENCE_FOR edges. That saves LLM cost and time.

Part 2: Make each contradiction an edge, tied to one hypothesis

The problem

Two findings can disagree for one hypothesis and not for another.

  • For a hypothesis H2, "lean mass ↑" (Naddafha 2026) and "skeletal muscle mass: no change" (Chen 2026) disagree.
  • For a kidney hypothesis, the same two findings say nothing, so there is no disagreement.

What we did

Edgemaxxing again! A contradiction is an edge between two findings, and it records which hypothesis it belongs to:

(Naddafha finding) -[:CONTRADICTS {hypothesis: "H2", reason: "different population",
                                   explained_by: "postmenopausal women vs all women"}]-> (Chen finding)

The query:

MERGE (a)-[e:CONTRADICTS {hypothesis:$k}]->(b)
SET e.reason = ..., e.severity = ..., e.explained_by = ...

Relevant bit: MERGE means "create it only if it does not exist yet".

The index

To show the contradictions for H2, the app asks: "give me every CONTRADICTS edge where hypothesis = H2". Without help, FalkorDB would have to check every contradiction edge in the whole graph.

So we created an index on that edge property:

CREATE INDEX FOR ()-[r:CONTRADICTS]-() ON (r.hypothesis)

Relevant bit: an index is like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page, you jump straight to the right page. Most databases only index nodes or rows. FalkorDB can also index edges, which is what makes this lookup fast.

Part 3: Recognise the same outcome under different names

The problem

Paper A says "fat-free mass". Paper B says "lean body mass". Paper C says "FFM". These are almost the same measurement. If the app only matched exact words, it would miss real disagreements between these papers.

What we did

  1. Each Concept node has a synonyms list (other names for the same thing).
  2. When the Stance agent (an LLM) judges a finding, it also answers: "does this finding measure the hypothesis's outcome, even under another name?" (same_outcome: true/false).
  3. If yes, the code adds a special edge from the finding to the hypothesis's own outcome concept: 
   (Finding: "FFM ↑ 1.15 kg") -[:MEASURES {hypothesis: "H2"}]-> (Concept: "muscle gain")
  1. The code also adds the finding's wording to the concept's synonyms. Next time, "FFM" is already known as a name for that outcome, with no LLM needed.

Relevant bit: this MEASURES edge also carries hypothesis, for the same reason as Part 2: "FFM counts as muscle gain" is true for H2, but maybe not for some other hypothesis. It has an edge index too. Again Edgemaxxing!!!!!

Why this matters

The graph learns names over time. Every question makes the synonym lists better for the next question.

Part 4: Contradiction camps with algo.WCC

What it does

Imagine the contradiction edges as strings tied between findings:

  • If A contradicts B, and B contradicts C, then A, B and C are all tied together.
  • Each group of tied-together findings is one "camp": one area where the evidence argues with itself.

WCC ("weakly connected components") is the standard algorithm that finds these groups.

Relevant bit: FalkorDB ships graph algorithms built in, so the app calls CALL algo.WCC(...) inside the database. It doesn't have to download the whole graph and run the algorithm in Python.

The query:

CALL algo.WCC({nodeLabels: ['Finding'], relationshipTypes: ['CONTRADICTS']})
YIELD node, componentId
MATCH (node)-[e:EVIDENCE_FOR]->(h:Hypothesis)<-[:ASKS]-(:Question {id:$q})
WITH h, componentId, count(DISTINCT node) AS findings, collect(DISTINCT e.stance) AS stances
WHERE findings > 1
RETURN h.statement AS hypothesis, componentId AS camp, findings, stances

In plain words: find the camps across all findings, then keep only the ones in this question, and show each camp's size and stances.

One limitation: WCC runs over all CONTRADICTS edges, for every hypothesis. If one finding has contradictions under two different hypotheses, those two camps can join into one.

How it all fits together 

Paper ─DESCRIBES→ Study ─FOUND→ Finding ─EVIDENCE_FOR {stance}→ Hypothesis
                                   │
                                   ├─MEASURES {hypothesis}→ Concept {synonyms}
                                   │
                                   └─CONTRADICTS {hypothesis, reason, explained_by}→ Finding

Parting Notes

Edges are the core feature of graph dbs. Using them effectively can make your life easier (and faster!!!).

title: MgntUtils Stacktrace Filtering in Real-World Use: The Soffa Project
description:
Introduction

This article explores the real-world use of the stacktrace filtering feature in MgntUtils. I am the author and maintainer of the MgntUtils open-source library, and I have written about the library and this particular feature in previous articles. The feature itself is described in detail in Java Stacktrace Filtering Utility.

One of the most frustrating aspects of maintaining an open-source library is trying to track its real-world adoption. Most companies, especially commercial ones, keep their source code in private repositories. As a result, even when they use your library, it is often difficult to know about that usage.

Even when tools allow you to identify projects or organizations that depend on your library, you generally cannot see which specific features they use or how they integrate them into their systems.

Occasionally, however, a project hosted on a public platform such as GitHub provides a rare opportunity to look beyond the dependency declaration and examine the actual implementation.

One such project is Soffa, which uses MgntUtils - and, more specifically, its stacktrace filtering feature. Discovering this project was a lucky break for me as an open-source maintainer.

In this article, I will examine the project's source code to show how the feature was integrated into its logging infrastructure.

About the Soffa Project

Soffa is an open-source Java project associated with LaStartupStation, a Morocco-based organization that promotes collaboration between technology startups and large corporations across Africa, including work involving government agencies. The project is associated with Titus Gahissy, a contributor to its codebase.

Soffa's publicly available source code offers a valuable opportunity to examine how MgntUtils' stacktrace filtering was integrated into a project's logging infrastructure.

Actual Stacktrace Filtering Feature Usage

Let's look at the actual code.

In my previously mentioned article, Java Stacktrace Filtering Utility, I described an integration approach that replaces logging statements such as:

logger.info("Message", e);

with

logger.info("Message" + TextUtils.getStacktrace(e));

However, replacing logging statements throughout an existing commercial codebase can require a massive refactoring effort.

The Soffa project took a different approach: it centralized stacktrace filtering in a shared utility class, so that the filtering logic could be invoked from a common infrastructure layer rather than repeated throughout the codebase.

This functionality is implemented in ErrorUtil.java. The two relevant methods are:

  • public static void setRelevantPackage(String pkg) (line 22)
  • public static String getStacktrace(Throwable e) (line 29)

The getStacktrace method is the single point where the project directly invokes MgntUtils' stacktrace filtering logic:

TextUtils.getStacktrace(e, true, defaultErrorPackage);

This establishes a centralized integration point for stacktrace filtering. Other components do not need to invoke MgntUtils directly; they can delegate to ErrorUtil.getStacktrace() instead.

The next layer of this logging infrastructure is Logger.java. Built on top of ErrorUtil, this class provides the logging interface used by the project. Its error method (line 134) relies on the shared stacktrace handling functionality.

The resulting architecture separates the filtering implementation from the logging interface: ErrorUtil encapsulates the direct interaction with MgntUtils, while Logger builds on that utility to provide a common logging layer for the rest of the project. In this way, stacktrace filtering becomes part of the project's shared logging infrastructure rather than a responsibility that every application component must implement independently.

History of MgntUtils Usage in Soffa

The Soffa project used MgntUtils over a span of several years. According to Maven Central, the earliest version of MgntUtils that appeared as a dependency in a Soffa project was version 1.5.1.2. This MgntUtils version was released on February 4th 2021. Various versions of Soffa Foundation projects appear in the Maven Central dependents list for MgntUtils 1.5.1.2.
However, the earliest GitHub commit I found that declares the dependency uses MgntUtils version 1.6.0.1. In this commit by Titus Gahissy from March 9, 2022, the file foundation-commons/build.gradle.kts (line 14) declares the dependency as api("com.github.michaelgantman:MgntUtils:1.6.0.1"). The entire file from this commit can be seen here.
Since then, the MgntUtils dependency has been upgraded to newer versions very shortly after each new release.
The latest upgrade was to MgntUtils version 1.7.0.3 In the December 16, 2025 commit by Titus Gahissy (See build.gradle.kts (line 14)).

In summary, the available evidence indicates that the Soffa project used MgntUtils' stacktrace filtering feature from approximately February 2021 through the end of 2025, using versions ranging from 1.5.1.2 to 1.7.0.3.

Latest Developments in Stacktrace Filtering Integration

As shown above, the Soffa project developed its own infrastructure layer to encapsulate stacktrace filtering for centralized use throughout the project. Since then, I have developed an integration approach that significantly simplifies adoption. The feature can be integrated at the logging-infrastructure level as custom functionality for Logback or Log4j2. This allows users to integrate the feature without making changes to application-level logging calls, rather than having to implement a project-specific abstraction like the one used by Soffa. Detailed integration instructions for Spring Boot are available in Zero-Code-Change Stacktrace Filtering for Spring Boot: An Infrastructure-Level Integration article

title: The $20M AWS Bill That Would Have Killed a Startup Before Series B
description:
Every startup pitch deck hides architectural skeletons. I know, because I have frequently been brought in by lead investors to dissect platforms that look like commercial rocketships from the outside, only to find extreme financial fragility underneath.

In one notable case, an AI-powered enterprise analytics platform had grown from zero to $10M ARR in fourteen months. They were preparing a massive Series B round at a $150M valuation.

When we opened their cloud infrastructure billing telemetry, the lead partner's jaw dropped.

Their projected AWS invoice for the following eighteen months exceeded $20,000,000. Why? Because every user search triggered unindexed, full-corpus vector embeddings against on-demand GPU clusters running at 8% utilization.

The company was literally subsidizing cloud hyperscalers on every single contract. Had they closed the round without fixing the architecture, the entire investment would have been incinerated in cloud hosting bills before Series C.

We spent three weeks refactoring their search pipeline: introducing quantized local embeddings, implementing hierarchical caching, and migrating inference to reserved instances.

The monthly cloud bill plummeted by 82%. The company preserved its capital, achieved genuine gross margin profitability, and closed the Series B from a position of undeniable operational strength.

Key Takeaways & Architectural FAQs

Q: How can unoptimized AI infrastructure threaten a startup before its next funding round?

Unindexed, full-corpus vector embeddings run against on-demand GPU clusters at low utilization can project an infrastructure bill in the tens of millions over 18 months, effectively subsidizing the cloud provider on every customer contract until the round itself cannot cover it.

Q: What fixes typically cut runaway AI infrastructure costs before a Series B?

Quantized local embeddings, hierarchical caching, and migrating inference to reserved instances. In one engagement this cut the monthly cloud bill by 82% and let the company close its round from a position of operational strength.

title: Why my Electron renderer can't change anything itself
description:
In my Electron app the main process owns the data. It holds the SQLite database, runs git and talks to the network. The renderer, the React side, never does any of that and holds only a read-only copy of the state.

The copy works like this. On connect, the renderer asks for a full snapshot. After that, main sends batches of changes, each with a sequence number, and the renderer applies them in order. Main collects changes for a short moment and sends them as one batch to every window.

The rule I'm glad I made: if a sequence number is skipped, the renderer throws its copy away and takes a fresh snapshot. It never tries to patch the gap. A renderer that is sometimes wrong about the data is worse than one that is briefly empty.

The cost is that there are no optimistic updates. A button sends a named command and waits for the change to come back. Every click has a small delay, so main has to answer fast and batches have to stay small.

What I get for it: two windows can't disagree, a command that fails changes nothing on screen, and the renderer has no code that could do something it shouldn't.

It doesn't apply to everything. View state, like which tab is open or a half-typed message, lives in a separate store in the renderer, because nobody else needs to know it and waiting on main for it would be silly.

If you're starting an Electron app, I'd draw the line between "data" and "view" on day one. It's much harder to add later.

title: Run multiple isolated agents in a single Sandbox
description:
The @vercel/sandbox SDK now supports multiple Linux users and groups, so you can run agents side by side in a single Sandbox.

Each agent runs as its own user with a private home directory. A group opens a shared workspace when they need to collaborate. This makes multi-agent systems easier to build.

Call createUser for each agent; its commands and file operations run as that user, and users can't read, write, or list each other's files. To set up a shared directory, call createGroup and add users to it.

Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.
