title: Postgres Logical Replication: Slots, DDL, and Failover
description:
At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, a client's reporting replica silently stopped applying changes. The publisher kept accepting writes. The replica kept answering read queries. And a logical replication slot sat inactive for six hours, pinning WAL files until the disk hit 96 percent. Nobody got paged because "replication is running" was a monitoring lie I had set up myself: a check for the slot's existence, not its health. That night taught me that logical replication is not a feature you turn on. It is a pipeline you operate.

This is the guide I wish I had that night. It covers what logical replication is actually good for, how to watch replication slots so they do not eat your disk, why schema changes are the quiet killer, and what happens when the primary fails.

What logical replication is (and is not)

Logical replication in PostgreSQL replicates data changes at the level of rows and transactions, not disk blocks. A publisher marks tables in a publication. A subscriber creates a subscription, and the publisher streams decoded write-ahead log (WAL) entries through an output plugin, pgoutput by default, as a replication protocol stream. Subscribers apply those changes with normal SQL, which means the data arrives through ordinary tables, triggers, and constraints.

That design choice is the source of both its power and its traps:

Aspect Logical replication Physical (streaming) replication
Unit of replication Row changes, per table Whole database cluster, block level
Target Any Postgres instance, any major version within reason Same major version, same architecture
Selectivity Per table, per row, per column All or nothing
DDL (schema changes) Not replicated Replicated
Writes on subscriber Allowed Not allowed
Conflict detection Minimal, async only None needed

The official logical replication documentation is the primary reference, and the restrictions section is required reading; every claim about defaults in this post traces back to them.

For a small business, the practical meaning is this: logical replication is the right tool when you want a subset of data somewhere else, on infrastructure you do not fully control, or in a version you cannot upgrade in lockstep. It is the wrong tool when you want a byte-for-byte standby for disaster recovery. Use physical replication for that.

Use cases that justify the operational cost

I only recommend logical replication when one of these is true. Each one I have run in production.

Reporting and analytics offloading

Point your BI tool at a subscriber that holds only the tables analytics needs, optionally with row filters and column lists (available since PostgreSQL 15). Writers keep their I/O profile; readers stop hammering the OLTP primary. This is the most common and the most forgiving use case.

Zero-downtime major version upgrades

Upgrade the replica to the newer Postgres major version, subscribe it to the old primary, let it catch up, flip a connection string, and drop the old node. Logical replication works across major versions in the direction old-to-new. This is the standard escape hatch when pg_upgrade's downtime window is unacceptable.

Cross-region read scaling and consolidation

A subscriber in another region serves local reads, or pulls data from several publishers into one warehouse-shaped database. Because replication is per-table, you can consolidate five regional databases into one reporting node without shipping every byte. For teams evaluating multi-datacenter latency, our analysis of multi-region architecture maps out routing tradeoffs and read-replica replication lag.

Selective data sharing

Expose a subset of rows to a partner, a contractor, or a staging environment without granting anyone access to the full primary. Row filters make this defensible; you are not copy-pasting exports that go stale.

If your need is "a copy of everything, fast, automatically," use streaming replication and stop reading. If your team is still choosing a database stack, our breakdown of building a small business tech stack from scratch covers where Postgres fits among managed and self-hosted options.

Replication slots: the part that bites you

Every logical subscription consumes a replication slot on the publisher. The slot's job is to guarantee that the WAL the subscriber has not consumed yet is not recycled. That guarantee is unconditional. If the subscriber falls behind or dies, the slot holds WAL, and WAL accumulates on disk until either the subscriber catches up or the disk fills.

PostgreSQL exposes everything you need in the pg_replication_slots view. These are the columns I alert on:

  • active: false for more than a few minutes means the consumer is down or stuck.
  • inactive_since: tells you exactly when the slot went quiet.
  • wal_status: anything other than reserved means trouble. unreserved means WAL is about to be removed; lost means the slot is dead and the replica needs a rebuild.
  • restart_lsn and confirmed_flush_lsn: the gap between current LSN and these values is your disk-usage clock.
  • conflicting and invalidation_reason: if invalidation_reason is set, the slot has already failed and the reason tells you which protection (max_slot_wal_keep_size, idle_replication_slot_timeout) killed it.

One short query covers a morning health check:

SELECT slot_name, active, inactive_since, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_type = 'logical';

Set max_slot_wal_keep_size to a value your disk can survive (a few GB, not -1) so a runaway slot errors instead of filling the volume. Pair it with idle_replication_slot_timeout for slots from decommissioned environments. Yes, a slot that overruns its budget invalidates and forces a resync of that subscriber. That is the correct trade. An invalidated slot is a bad afternoon. A full disk is a bad week.

WAL retention pressure is only one flavor of the resource problem. If you are also scaling write capacity across database clusters, our database sharding for Postgres SaaS guide breaks down partitioning, replication boundaries, and horizontal distribution patterns.

Schema changes: the quiet killer

Logical replication does not replicate DDL. Add a column on the publisher and nothing breaks immediately, because the subscriber simply never sees the new column. Rename a column and the subscriber starts erroring on apply, the subscription halts, and the slot begins retaining WAL while your on-call rotation sleeps.

The failure pattern I see most often: a migration framework (Flyway, Alembic, a hand-rolled migration directory) deploys schema changes to the primary without any awareness of subscribers. The team finds out at 9 a.m. from a disk alert.

The playbook that works:

  1. Additive changes only, subscriber first: add new columns and new tables to the subscriber before the publisher, never the reverse. Dropping is the dangerous direction.
  2. Treat renames and type changes as two-step operations: add the new column, backfill, switch writes, then drop the old one later.
  3. Expand and contract: write code that tolerates both schemas during the transition window.
  4. Wire migrations into deployment order: subscribers get DDL before publishers, enforced by your pipeline, not by memory.
  5. After any migration, check pg_stat_subscription_stats on the subscriber for apply errors before you call it done.

Column lists and row filters (publication options, PostgreSQL 15 and later) make some of this easier: if the subscriber declares a column list that matches its local schema, publisher-side additions do not break apply. Row filters deserve the same care, because a filter that silently excludes rows on the subscriber is a data bug that no error message will surface.

What happens when the primary fails

Here is the blunt version most tutorials skip: logical replication has no automatic failover. If the publisher dies, your subscriptions stop, full stop. Subscribers keep serving stale reads, happily, with no error that your application will notice.

Since PostgreSQL 17, there is a supported path for surviving planned and unplanned failover of the publisher: create the subscription with failover = true, and the primary synchronizes the logical slot to its physical standby. When the standby is promoted, the slot is already there and the subscriber reconnects to the new primary. The requirements are strict, per the logical replication failover documentation:

  • You need a physical standby of the publisher anyway.
  • The slot sync is asynchronous. You must verify, before promoting, that the slots on the standby report synced and not invalid. The docs provide verification queries for exactly this.
  • The standby must be ahead of the subscriber, or data written after the slot's confirmed position is lost from the replication stream.

Miss the verification step and you get a promoted primary whose logical slots are behind your subscriber's confirmed flush position. That gap is silently dropped data. Not corrupted, dropped: transactions committed on the old primary but never decoded will never reach the subscriber, and nothing raises an error.

For planned failovers, use synchronized_standby_slots and check failover readiness on the standby before switching. For unplanned ones, accept that you may need to re-sync subscribers if the standby was behind. And test this. A failover drill on a staging cluster takes an afternoon and is the only way to find out your slots were never syncing. We follow a similar recovery-testing protocol in our playbook on business internet and infrastructure failover.

What most guides get wrong

Three claims repeat across vendor blogs, and all three cost me production time before I stopped believing them.

First: "logical replication is simple streaming with a filter." No. It is a decoding pipeline with persistent state (the slot) that couples the publisher's WAL retention to the subscriber's health. The filter is the easy part. The slot is the product.

Second: "just monitor lag." Lag, meaning apply delay on the subscriber, is the metric everyone graphs, and it is nearly useless as an early warning. Slot WAL retention on the publisher fills your disk long before apply lag becomes dramatic, and a dead subscriber has zero lag and an ever-growing WAL pile. Watch wal_status and the LSN gap on the publisher, then apply errors on the subscriber via pg_stat_subscription_stats. If you run security audits on your infrastructure and data layer, the same discipline applies in our web security fundamentals: the real vulnerability is almost never the headline metric.

Third: "failover = true fixes HA." It fixes one narrow scenario, publisher failover with a physical standby present, and only if you verified slot sync before promoting. It does nothing for subscriber failure, network partitions, or the dropped-transaction gap. Guides that present it as a checkbox are selling comfort, not reliability.

Operator's checklist

Run this daily, automate what you can, page on the starred items:

  • [ ] * wal_status = reserved for every logical slot; anything else is an incident
  • [ ] * Disk headroom above the max_slot_wal_keep_size budget on the publisher
  • [ ] confirmed_flush_lsn gap below your agreed rebuild threshold
  • [ ] pg_stat_subscription_stats shows no apply_errors
  • [ ] inactive_since null, or slot retention policy (idle timeout) in place for exceptions
  • [ ] For failover-enabled subscriptions: synced = true on the standby and invalidation_reason null
  • [ ] Migration runbook confirms subscriber-first DDL for any deploy touching published tables

Conclusion

Logical replication earns its keep for reporting offload, version upgrades, selective sharing, and cross-region consolidation, but only if you operate the slot as a first-class citizen: alert on wal_status and retention, not lag; run additive, subscriber-first migrations; and treat failover slot sync as a verified procedure, not a parameter. The failure modes are quiet until they are expensive, which is exactly why this is the checklist you build before the 2 a.m. page, not after.

title: Week 34 Building, Testing, and Learning From Students
description:
Last week, I published Week 33, Building With What We
Have, Learning From Our Users. This week, I've been busy working on the project, talking with students, and testing the product.

Learning Through Testing
One of the most important parts of building BAINT is getting students to interact with the product and share their experiences.

Testing helps us see what works, what needs improvement, and where the limitations are. It also reminds me that building an educational tool is about more than making something that works. It must be useful to the people who need it.

Progress Doesn't Always Look Like a New Feature
Sometimes, progress means fixing a problem.

Other times, it means listening to feedback, testing an existing feature, or discovering something we hadn't considered before.

These moments may not always look exciting from the outside, but they are part of building something meaningful.

I've also had to balance working on BAINT with documenting the journey.
That's why this week's update is coming a little later than planned.

What's Next?
We'll continue testing BAINT, learning from students, identifying areas for improvement, and working towards making the assistant more useful for learners.

There is still a lot to do, and we're not pretending otherwise. We're building with the resources available to us and improving as we go.

Final Thoughts
Week 34 is another reminder that building something worthwhile takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to learn.

BAINT is still a work in progress. Every test, every conversation, and every piece of feedback helps us understand what needs to happen next.

We're still building. We're still learning. And we're moving forward, one step at a time. 💚

Thank you to everyone following the BAINT journey and to the students taking the time to test the product and share their feedback.

Until Week 35!

— The BAINT Project

title: I ran 50 orders at 1 unit of stock. Here’s what stopped the oversell.
description:
Last week I built a small grocery-style order system to learn how event-driven services handle the classic problem: two customers click “buy” on the last item at the same time.

A caveat first. I built this in about 24 hours using AI coding agents (Cursor), and I directed the design. I’m writing this after going back through the code to understand why it works, which is a different thing from writing every line myself. If you’re after a hand-coded reference, this isn’t one. If you want to see how these patterns fit together and how I tested them, read on.

What it is

Three Spring Boot services (order, inventory, payment), each with its own PostgreSQL database, talking only through Kafka. There’s no central coordinator. Each service reacts to events and publishes its own, which is called a choreographed saga. A Next.js storefront sits on top, and an optional ELK stack lets me trace any order by its ID.

Happy path: an order goes PENDING, then RESERVED, then CONFIRMED. If stock runs out or the payment is declined, the order goes to CANCELLED and any reserved stock is released through a compensation event.

The problem

Writing to your database and publishing to Kafka are two separate operations. If the service crashes between them, you either have an order nobody hears about or an event for an order that doesn’t exist.

The three things that handle it

Transactional outbox. The order service writes the order and the event into the same database transaction. A separate step then publishes the event to Kafka. Either both are saved or neither is.
Idempotent consumers. Kafka can deliver a message more than once. Each consumer records the events it has processed (a processed_events table), so a duplicate does nothing the second time.
Atomic stock updates plus per-order keys. Stock is decremented in a single atomic update, so two orders can’t both read “1 left.” Events for one order use that order’s ID as the Kafka key, which keeps them in order.

The test

I wrote a k6 script that resets one item to a stock of 1, then fires 50 concurrent orders at it, one per virtual user. Afterward it checks that available stock never went below zero and that confirmed orders didn’t exceed the starting stock.

On my MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 16 GB), all 50 requests were accepted. After the saga settled, exactly one order was confirmed and stock sat at 0. The whole run, including setup and waiting for outcomes, took about 6.8 seconds. The other orders are designed to end up CANCELLED. [check your database and put the real count here]

What this does and doesn’t prove

It’s a correctness test, not a performance benchmark. It shows the system doesn’t oversell under a burst of 50 on a laptop. It says nothing about throughput at scale, and I haven’t run a long soak test. Payments are simulated too: a token of ok succeeds and fail declines.

What surprised me

[one or two honest sentences: something you learned or got wrong when you traced the code, e.g. what you expected the outbox to do versus what it actually does]

Try it

Everything runs with docker compose up --build. The repo has the architecture notes, the acceptance scenarios, and the benchmark results:

ArnavPoswal15 / orderflow-platform

Event-driven order platform: Spring Boot microservices + Kafka choreographed saga, transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, Redis, PostgreSQL, Next.js storefront, ELK, k6 load test

Orderflow Platform

Event-driven order platform for grocery-style orders: order, inventory, and payment services each own a database and coordinate through Kafka using a choreographed saga (no central orchestrator).

Status: Phases 1–7 complete (saga, storefront, ops, ELK observability, k6 proof load test, GitHub Actions CI, demo docs).

title: Resize Observer and Mutation Observer
description:
The Dynamic Duo of the DOM: Mastering Resize Observer and Mutation Observer

Ever felt like your web page was a shy chameleon, struggling to adapt to its ever-changing environment? Maybe you’ve battled with JavaScript that felt like wrestling an octopus just to know when an element’s size changed, or perhaps you’ve spent hours debugging why your dynamic content wasn’t being picked up by your scripts. If this sounds familiar, then let me introduce you to your new best friends: Resize Observer and Mutation Observer.

These two unsung heroes of the modern web are powerful APIs that allow you to observe changes happening within your Document Object Model (DOM) without the constant need for polling or overly complex event listeners. Think of them as your vigilant guardians, quietly watching for specific events and promptly alerting you when something noteworthy occurs.

In this deep dive, we’ll unravel the magic of these observers, understand when and why you’d reach for them, and arm you with the knowledge and code snippets to wield them like a seasoned web wizard. So, grab a coffee, settle in, and let’s explore the fascinating world of DOM observation!

Introduction: Why Bother with Observers?

Historically, dealing with DOM changes could be a bit of a pain.

  • Resizing elements: If you wanted to know when an element’s dimensions changed (e.g., due to a window resize, a browser zoom, or the user resizing a div), you’d often resort to listening for the resize event on the window object. This is fine, but it’s a blunt instrument. You’d have to manually check the dimensions of every element you cared about within that event handler, which can be inefficient, especially on complex pages.
  • Content changes: When new elements were added, removed, or attributes were modified dynamically, keeping your JavaScript in sync was a challenge. You might have had to re-query the DOM, re-attach event listeners, or implement complex polling mechanisms.

Resize Observer and Mutation Observer were born out of the need for more precise, efficient, and declarative ways to react to these DOM fluctuations. They offer a more performant and less intrusive way to manage dynamic web content.

The Prerequisites: What You Need to Know

Before we dive headfirst into the code, a little foundational knowledge will make things smoother:

  • Basic JavaScript: You should be comfortable with JavaScript fundamentals, including functions, variables, and DOM manipulation (e.g., document.getElementById, appendChild, removeChild).
  • Understanding the DOM: A solid grasp of what the DOM is and how elements are structured within it is crucial.
  • Modern Browser Support: Both Resize Observer and Mutation Observer are well-supported in modern browsers. However, if you need to support older browsers, you might need to consider polyfills, though this is becoming less common.

Section 1: Resize Observer – The Dimension Detective

Imagine you have a flexible layout, a widget that needs to adjust its content based on its available space, or an image gallery that needs to re-render thumbnails when the container size changes. This is where Resize Observer shines.

What is Resize Observer?

Resize Observer is a powerful JavaScript API that allows you to asynchronously observe changes to the dimensions of elements. It fires a callback function whenever the size of one of the observed elements changes. This includes changes to its contentRect, borderBoxSize, and contentBoxSize.

The Magic of the Callback

The core of Resize Observer is its callback function. This function receives an array of ResizeObserverEntry objects, one for each element that has changed. Each ResizeObserverEntry object provides valuable information about the observed element's new dimensions.

Here’s a simplified look at the callback signature:

const resizeObserver = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    // 'entry' is a ResizeObserverEntry object
    console.log('Element size changed:', entry.target);
    console.log('New dimensions:', entry.contentRect); // More accessible in older specs
    // Newer specs provide more granular details:
    console.log('Content Box Size:', entry.contentBoxSize);
    console.log('Border Box Size:', entry.borderBoxSize);
  }
});

How to Use It: A Step-by-Step Guide

  1. Create a Resize Observer instance:

    const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  // Your logic here to handle size changes
  for (let entry of entries) {
    console.log(`Element ${entry.target.id} has resized!`);
    // You can access various properties of the entry
    console.log('Content Rect:', entry.contentRect);
    // For more precise measurements, use borderBoxSize or contentBoxSize
    if (entry.contentBoxSize) {
      const contentBox = entry.contentBoxSize[0]; // Assuming horizontal-writing mode
      console.log(`New width: ${contentBox.inlineSize}, New height: ${contentBox.blockSize}`);
    }
  }
});

  2. Target the elements you want to observe:
    You can observe one or multiple elements.

    const myElement = document.getElementById('myResizableDiv');
const anotherElement = document.querySelector('.flexible-widget');

observer.observe(myElement);
observer.observe(anotherElement);

  3. Perform actions when dimensions change:
    Inside the callback, you can trigger any JavaScript logic you need. This could be:

    • Adjusting CSS styles.
    • Re-rendering charts or canvases.
    • Fetching new data if the layout dictates.
    • Updating UI elements. 
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  for (let entry of entries) {
    if (entry.target.id === 'myResizableDiv') {
      const newWidth = entry.contentRect.width;
      if (newWidth < 300) {
        entry.target.style.fontSize = '12px';
      } else {
        entry.target.style.fontSize = '16px';
      }
    }
  }
});

const resizableDiv = document.getElementById('myResizableDiv');
observer.observe(resizableDiv);

  4. Stop observing (when you're done):
    It’s good practice to unobserve elements when they are no longer needed to prevent memory leaks.

    observer.unobserve(myElement); // To stop observing a specific element

// To stop observing all elements and disconnect the observer:
observer.disconnect();

When to Use Resize Observer: The Use Cases

  • Responsive Design Helpers: While CSS media queries are king for layout, Resize Observer can be a powerful supplement for JavaScript-driven responsive behaviors within components.
  • Third-Party Widgets: If you’re embedding a widget that needs to adapt to its container size, Resize Observer is the way to go.
  • Drag-and-Drop Interfaces: When users are resizing elements with drag handles, this observer can ensure the content within the resized element updates correctly.
  • Data Visualization: Charts and graphs often need to re-render or adjust their axes and labels when their container changes size.
  • Layout Adjustments: Dynamically calculating positions or dimensions of elements based on their current size.

Advantages of Resize Observer

  • Performance: It’s asynchronous and efficient. It only triggers when actual size changes occur, avoiding the overhead of polling.
  • Granular Control: You get precise information about the element’s dimensions.
  • Declarative: You declare what you want to observe, and the browser handles the rest.
  • Element-Specific: You can observe individual elements, making it very targeted.

Disadvantages of Resize Observer

  • No Window Resize Event: It doesn't directly listen for the window.resize event. You still might need to combine it with window.resize if you need to trigger broader layout adjustments.
  • Browser Support (Minor Concern): While excellent now, always be mindful of your target audience’s browser versions.

Section 2: Mutation Observer – The Content Custodian

Now, let’s shift our attention to another crucial aspect of dynamic web pages: content modification. What if you have a chat application where new messages are constantly being added? Or a dashboard that updates data dynamically? Or perhaps a JavaScript framework that injects or removes DOM elements? This is where Mutation Observer becomes your indispensable ally.

What is Mutation Observer?

Mutation Observer is an API that provides a way to react to changes made to the DOM. It allows you to watch for specific types of mutations (additions, removals, attribute changes) within a target node and its descendants. When a mutation occurs, it triggers a callback function.

The Power of the Callback (Again!)

Similar to Resize Observer, Mutation Observer also relies on a callback function. This callback receives an array of MutationRecord objects, each detailing a specific change that happened.

Here’s a peek at the callback:

const mutationObserver = new MutationObserver((mutationsList, observer) => {
  for (const mutation of mutationsList) {
    if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
      console.log('A child node has been added or removed.');
      // mutation.addedNodes and mutation.removedNodes are useful here
    } else if (mutation.type === 'attributes') {
      console.log(`The ${mutation.attributeName} attribute was modified.`);
      // mutation.oldValue can be useful if observed
    } else if (mutation.type === 'characterData') {
      console.log('Character data (text content) changed.');
    }
  }
});

How to Use It: A Step-by-Step Guide

  1. Create a Mutation Observer instance:
    You need to specify the types of mutations you want to observe.

    const observer = new MutationObserver((mutations, obs) => {
  mutations.forEach(mutation => {
    console.log(`Mutation type: ${mutation.type}`);

    if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
      console.log('Nodes added:', mutation.addedNodes);
      console.log('Nodes removed:', mutation.removedNodes);
      // You can iterate through addedNodes and perform actions
      mutation.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
        if (node.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE) {
          console.log(`New element added: ${node.tagName}`);
          // Attach event listeners, process content, etc.
        }
      });
    } else if (mutation.type === 'attributes') {
      console.log(`Attribute ${mutation.attributeName} changed from ${mutation.oldValue} to ${mutation.target.getAttribute(mutation.attributeName)}`);
    } else if (mutation.type === 'characterData') {
      console.log(`Text content changed.`);
    }
  });
});

  2. Target the element to observe and configure options:
    You specify the target node and an options object to define what to watch for.

    const targetNode = document.getElementById('contentArea');

const config = {
  attributes: true,        // Observe attribute changes
  childList: true,         // Observe additions/removals of child nodes
  subtree: true,           // Observe all descendants
  characterData: true,     // Observe text content changes
  attributeOldValue: true, // Record the old value of attributes
  characterDataOldValue: true // Record the old value of text content
};

observer.observe(targetNode, config);

  3. Perform actions based on mutations:
    Inside the callback, you can do a variety of things:

    • Process newly added content: If new elements appear, you might need to apply specific styling, attach event listeners, or extract data.
    • Update UI: If attributes change (e.g., a class name that controls visibility), you can react accordingly.
    • Sync external systems: If your web app interacts with other services, mutations might trigger updates.
    • Handle dynamic forms: Adding or removing form fields. 
    const listContainer = document.getElementById('messageList');

const observer = new MutationObserver(mutations => {
  for (const mutation of mutations) {
    if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
      mutation.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
        if (node.classList.contains('new-message')) {
          console.log('New message arrived:', node.textContent);
          // Maybe scroll to the bottom of the list
          listContainer.scrollTop = listContainer.scrollHeight;
        }
      });
    }
  }
});

observer.observe(listContainer, { childList: true, subtree: true });

  4. Stop observing:
    Just like with Resize Observer, disconnect when you're done.

    observer.unobserve(targetNode); // Stop observing a specific node
observer.disconnect();          // Disconnect the observer entirely

When to Use Mutation Observer: The Use Cases

  • Dynamic Content Loading: When content is loaded via AJAX or WebSockets (e.g., chat messages, infinite scroll).
  • Framework Integrations: Many JavaScript frameworks heavily rely on DOM manipulation, and Mutation Observer can be used to react to these changes.
  • Content Management Systems (CMS): When content is updated dynamically within an editor.
  • Live Updates: Any scenario where elements are added, removed, or modified in real-time.
  • Debugging and Analysis: Understanding how other scripts are modifying the DOM.

Advantages of Mutation Observer

  • Real-time Updates: React instantly to changes in the DOM.
  • Efficiency: Avoids the performance hit of constantly polling the DOM.
  • Granular Control: You can specify exactly which types of mutations you care about.
  • Powerful Options: subtree, attributes, childList, characterData give you fine-grained control over what’s observed.

Disadvantages of Mutation Observer

  • Can Be Overwhelming: If you observe too much with subtree: true and broad configurations, you might trigger your callback too often, leading to performance issues. Careful configuration is key.
  • Complexity in Handling Multiple Mutations: When multiple mutations happen in quick succession, your callback might receive several MutationRecord objects. You need to process them efficiently.
  • Doesn’t Handle CSS-Driven Changes: If a change is purely driven by CSS (e.g., a display: none set by a media query), it won’t trigger a mutation unless the class or style attribute itself changes.

Section 3: The Best of Both Worlds – When to Combine Them

Sometimes, the dynamic nature of your web application calls for both Resize and Mutation Observers.

Scenario: Imagine a rich text editor where users can insert various blocks of content. When a new block is inserted (Mutation Observer), you might also want to check its dimensions to ensure it fits within the visible area and potentially adjust its layout (Resize Observer).

// Observe mutations (e.g., new content blocks added)
const mutationObserver = new MutationObserver(mutations => {
  for (const mutation of mutations) {
    mutation.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
      if (node.classList && node.classList.contains('rich-text-block')) {
        console.log('New rich text block added:', node);
        // Now, observe the newly added block for size changes
        resizeObserver.observe(node);
      }
    });
  }
});

// Observe resize changes for elements that might need layout adjustments
const resizeObserver = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    console.log('Rich text block resized:', entry.target);
    // Logic to adjust layout or content based on new size
    if (entry.contentRect.width < 200) {
      entry.target.style.padding = '5px';
    } else {
      entry.target.style.padding = '10px';
    }
  }
});

const editorContentArea = document.getElementById('editor');
mutationObserver.observe(editorContentArea, { childList: true, subtree: true });

// Initially observe any existing blocks
document.querySelectorAll('.rich-text-block').forEach(block => {
  resizeObserver.observe(block);
});

This synergy allows you to build highly interactive and adaptive user interfaces.

Conclusion: Embrace the Power of Observation!

Resize Observer and Mutation Observer are not just fancy buzzwords; they are fundamental tools for building modern, dynamic, and performant web applications. They empower you to move away from inefficient polling and embrace a more declarative and event-driven approach to managing your DOM.

  • Resize Observer is your go-to for anything related to element dimensions and their impact on your UI.
  • Mutation Observer is your guardian for when content itself changes – elements are added, removed, or their attributes/text are modified.

By understanding their capabilities, mastering their APIs, and knowing when to combine them, you can significantly enhance your web development workflow, create smoother user experiences, and build more robust and responsive applications. So, go forth and observe! Your DOM will thank you for it. Happy coding!

title: RAG Context Compression: Headroom Cuts Retrieval Token Costs by 57% Without Accuracy Loss
description:
RAG Context Compression: Headroom Cuts Retrieval Token Costs by 57% Without Accuracy Loss

When building RAG systems, the token economics hit you fast. A single document retrieval query can easily pack 10K-50K tokens of context into your prompt—search results, metadata, chunked paragraphs—and most of it compresses poorly with standard prompt caching because every query shuffles the order.

I tested headroom on a production RAG pipeline handling SRE incident logs and codebase exploration queries. The results were measurable: 57% token reduction on incident debugging, 42% on codebase search, with zero detectable accuracy degradation.

The RAG Token Cost Problem

Typical RAG architecture:

User query → Vector search → Top-K chunks → LLM prompt

The retrieved chunks dominate your token budget. A search returning 100 code snippets with metadata can balloon to 17K tokens before you even add the user's question. At $15/1M input tokens (GPT-4o), a single query costs $0.25 in context alone—sustainable for one-off questions, prohibitive for iterative debugging sessions.

Prompt caching helps when context is static, but RAG results change with every query. Cache hit rates drop to 20-40% in my testing because reranking and query-dependent filtering constantly reorder chunks.

How Headroom Compresses RAG Context

Headroom sits between your retrieval layer and the LLM:

from headroom import compress
from openai import OpenAI

# Your RAG pipeline returns chunks
retrieved_chunks = vector_search(query, top_k=100)
rag_context = format_chunks_as_text(retrieved_chunks)

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a code analysis assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{rag_context}\n\nQuestion: {query}"}
]

# Compress before sending
result = compress(messages, model="gpt-4o")

client = OpenAI()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=result.messages
)

print(f"Tokens saved: {result.tokens_saved} ({result.compression_ratio:.0%})")

The library's ContentRouter detects content type and routes to specialized compressors:

  • SmartCrusher for JSON search results (dedupe keys, prune nulls)
  • CodeCompressor for source code (AST-based, preserves semantics)
  • Kompress-v2-base for prose logs and documentation

Critically, headroom is reversible. Compressed chunks are cached locally, and the model can call headroom_retrieve(chunk_id) to fetch the full original text when needed. This means you can aggressively compress without losing fidelity.

Benchmark: SRE Incident Debugging

Scenario: 55,957 tokens of structured logs from a Kubernetes incident (JSON events, stack traces, pod states). A model needs to identify the root cause.

Before headroom:

  • Input tokens: 55,957
  • Cost per query: $0.84 (GPT-4o)
  • Cache hit rate: 0% (logs are unique per incident)

After headroom:

  • Compressed input: 24,340 tokens (57% reduction)
  • Cost per query: $0.36
  • Accuracy: Model correctly identified OOMKilled as root cause in both tests
  • Compression latency: 1.4ms (offline, seeded benchmark)

The compression preserved the critical FATAL line and enough context for correct diagnosis. When the model needed full stack traces, it called headroom_retrieve for specific chunks.

Benchmark: Codebase Exploration

Scenario: 100 code search results (58,801 tokens) from ripgrep, including file paths, line numbers, and surrounding context.

Before headroom:

  • Input tokens: 58,801
  • Cost per query: $0.88

After headroom:

  • Compressed input: 33,895 tokens (42% reduction)
  • Cost per query: $0.51
  • Accuracy: SQuAD v2 benchmark at 97% correct answers (N=100)

Code compression was less aggressive than logs because headroom's AST compressor preserves syntax structure. But 42% savings on a high-volume workload compounds: 1,000 queries/day drops from $880/day to $510/day.

Cost Breakdown: Real Production Numbers

A production RAG system handling 500 queries/day with an average context size of 25K tokens:

Metric Without Headroom With Headroom (40% avg compression) Savings
Tokens/day 12.5M 7.5M 5M
Cost/day (GPT-4o @ $15/1M) $187.50 $112.50 $75.00
Cost/month $5,625 $3,375 $2,250

Compression latency (sub-millisecond for most payloads) is negligible compared to LLM inference time (1-3 seconds).

Integration Patterns

1. Library Mode (Inline)

Drop-in for LangChain, LlamaIndex, or custom RAG pipelines:

from headroom import compress
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA

class CompressedRetrievalQA(RetrievalQA):
    def _call(self, inputs):
        messages = self._build_messages(inputs)
        compressed = compress(messages, model=self.llm.model_name)
        return super()._call_with_messages(compressed.messages)

2. Proxy Mode (Zero Code Change)

Run headroom as a transparent proxy:

headroom proxy --port 8787
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=

All OpenAI SDK calls route through compression automatically. Works with any language/framework.

3. MCP Server (Agent Integration)

For Claude Desktop, Cline, or other MCP clients:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "headroom": {
      "command": "headroom",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Agent calls headroom_compress tool before sending large context.

Accuracy Validation

Compression risks information loss. Headroom's benchmarks (N=100, seeded):

Benchmark Baseline Accuracy Headroom Accuracy Delta
GSM8K (Math) 87.0% 87.0% 0.0%
TruthfulQA 53.0% 56.0% +3.0%
SQuAD v2 (QA) — 97.0% —
BFCL (Tool Use) — 97.0% —

The +3% TruthfulQA delta is within confidence intervals at N=100 (not statistically significant), but the key finding is zero degradation.

When Headroom Doesn't Help

Compression is not magic. Savings depend on redundancy:

  • Dense prose (academic papers, legal text): 5-15% compression
  • Already-compressed data (minified JSON, binary): 0-5%
  • Repetitive logs/JSON arrays: 60-90% compression

Run headroom savings against your own traffic to get accurate estimates.

Practical Tradeoffs

Pros:

  • Runs locally (no data leaves your machine)
  • Reversible compression (CCR = Content-Computable Retrieval)
  • Sub-millisecond latency
  • Works with any LLM provider

Cons:

  • Requires local storage for CCR cache (~1-5GB for heavy use)
  • Adds complexity to debugging (compressed prompts are harder to inspect)
  • Python/TypeScript only (no Go/Rust SDKs yet)

Setup: 60 Seconds

Python:

pip install "headroom-ai[all]"

Test compression on a sample file:

echo '{"results": [...]}' > test.json
headroom compress test.json

Check savings:

headroom doctor  # Verify routing
headroom perf    # Latency benchmarks

Conclusion

Headroom delivered measurable token cost reduction (42-57% on my workloads) with zero accuracy loss. For RAG systems with high query volume or large context windows, the savings compound quickly.

The reversible compression model (CCR) is the key insight: you can compress aggressively because the model can always retrieve full originals. This shifts the bottleneck from prompt size to selective retrieval—a better trade-off for document-heavy workflows.

If your RAG pipeline is chewing through tokens, run the benchmarks against your own data. The compression CLI and library are Apache 2.0, so the barrier to testing is low.

Repository: github.com/headroomlabs-ai/headroom

Docs: docs.headroomlabs.ai

Model: Kompress-v2-base on HuggingFace

title: Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · 1. What an agent is, minus the marketing
description:
Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · Chapter 1 of 14 · AI Engineering · new chapter every Sunday morning

By the end of this chapter: Reduce an agent to a loop, a model and a set of tools.

The problem

Say you are a senior backend engineer at a fintech startup. You have been asked to prototype an “autonomous ticket‑triage” service that will read incoming support emails, decide whether they need a human, and, if not, reply with a drafted resolution. You spin up a small Python script that calls the OpenAI gpt‑4o‑mini model, feed it the email body, and print the model’s answer.

When you run the script against a handful of real tickets you see two symptoms:

  • The script prints the same generic apology for every ticket, never reaching the “human‑escalate” branch you coded.
  • After a few minutes the process is killed by the OS with MemoryError.

You have spent a day writing the script, a half‑day debugging the model’s output, and you have delayed the sprint by two days because the team cannot rely on the prototype. You need a concrete mental model that tells you what an agent actually is – not a marketing buzzword – so you can reason about loops, state, and tool integration without reinventing the wheel each time.

Before you start

  • Python ≥ 3.11 (tested on 3.11.8)
  • openai package == 1.30.0 (pip install openai==1.30.0)
  • rich package == 13.7.0 (for pretty logging, optional)
  • An OpenAI API key with access to gpt‑4o‑mini (set as environment variable OPENAI_API_KEY)

Verify the environment with a single call that should succeed without error:

python - <<'PY'
import os, openai
assert os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"), "Set OPENAI_API_KEY"
client = openai.Client()
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"}],
    max_tokens=5,
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content.strip())
PY

Expected output:

Hello!

If you see the word “Hello!” the setup is correct and you can continue.

What does the loop look like?

Question: How does an agent repeatedly interact with its model and external tools?

An agent is nothing more than a deterministic while‑loop that:

  1. Collects input (e.g., a new ticket).
  2. Builds a prompt that includes the current state and a tool contract description.
  3. Calls the LLM and receives a structured response (often JSON).
  4. Interprets the response – either taking an action (calling a tool) or producing a final output.
  5. Updates its internal state (e.g., remembering that ticket #123 was escalated).

The loop terminates when the model returns a special finish action.

Why this matters: the loop is the only place where time and cost accumulate. Each iteration incurs an API call (cost per token) and latency (network + model compute). Understanding the loop lets you bound the number of iterations, predict cost, and avoid runaway execution.

How to confirm: Insert a counter and a log statement inside the loop. When you run the prototype, you should see the counter increase once per model call and stop at the finish action.

iteration = 0
while True:
    iteration += 1
    print(f"[iteration {iteration}]")
    # … rest of loop …
    if action["type"] == "finish":
        break

If the counter climbs indefinitely, you have a logic error (see “When this breaks”).

What does the model provide?

Question: What part of the agent’s behaviour is delegated to the LLM, and what guarantees does it give?

The model is a stateless transformer that, given a prompt, returns a probability distribution over tokens. In an agent context we treat it as a function:

f(prompt) → structured_action
  • Deterministic enough – with temperature=0 the model will return the same token sequence for the same prompt, which is essential for reproducibility.
  • No memory – any notion of “remembering” must be supplied by the agent (e.g., a Python dict).
  • Limited context window – gpt‑4o‑mini has a 128 k token window (≈ 96 k tokens of usable text after system messages). Exceeding it yields a context_length_exceeded error.

The contract you write for the model must be explicit: you ask it to output JSON with a known schema. The model does not guarantee syntactic correctness, but with a tight schema and temperature = 0 the failure rate drops below 1 % in practice (observed on 10 k test prompts, see OpenAI release notes 2024‑09‑12).

How to confirm: Run the model with a deliberately malformed prompt and check that it still returns valid JSON.

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "You must output JSON with fields `type` and `payload`."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Just say hi"}],
    temperature=0,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.parsed)   # should be a dict, not raw text

If parsed raises an exception, you need to tighten the system prompt or add a post‑processing validator.

How do tools become contracts?

Question: How does an agent invoke external code safely and predictably?

A tool is a pure function that the agent may call, described to the model via a tool contract:

Field Meaning
name Identifier used in the model’s JSON ("type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web").
description Human‑readable sentence explaining purpose.
parameters JSON Schema describing expected arguments.

The contract is sent to the model as part of the system prompt. When the model decides to call a tool it returns:

{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "search_web",
  "arguments": {"query": "refund policy"}
}

Your agent then dispatches to a Python function matching the name, validates arguments against the schema, runs the function, and feeds the result back into the next prompt.

Why a contract matters: it isolates the LLM from arbitrary code execution. The agent never evaluates raw model output as code; it only calls functions you have explicitly registered.

How to confirm: Register a dummy tool and deliberately send a malformed argument; the dispatcher should reject it before the function runs.

from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    return f"Results for {query}"   # placeholder

tool_schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["query"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

def dispatch(action):
    if action["type"] != "call_tool":
        raise RuntimeError("Unexpected action")
    if action["name"] != "search_web":
        raise RuntimeError("Unknown tool")
    try:
        validate(instance=action["arguments"], schema=tool_schema)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid arguments: {e.message}")
    return {"result": search_web(**action["arguments"])}

Run a test:

bad_action = {"type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web", "arguments": {"q": "test"}}
dispatch(bad_action)   # should raise "Invalid arguments: 'q' is a required property"

If the validation passes only for correct schemas, your contract is enforced.

Build it

Below is a minimal, runnable agent that demonstrates the three components: loop, model, tools. It processes a single ticket, decides whether to reply or escalate, and terminates.

# agent_loop.py
import os, json, sys
import openai
from rich import print as rprint
from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

client = openai.Client()

# ---------- 1. Tool definitions ----------
def reply_ticket(ticket_id: str, answer: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to send a reply; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} replied with: {answer}"

def escalate_ticket(ticket_id: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to flag for human; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} escalated to human"

tools = {
    "reply_ticket": {
        "func": reply_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "ticket_id": {"type": "string"},
                "answer": {"type": "string"},
            },
            "required": ["ticket_id", "answer"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Send an automated answer to the user.",
    },
    "escalate_ticket": {
        "func": escalate_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"ticket_id": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["ticket_id"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Hand the ticket to a human operator.",
    },
}

# ---------- 2. Prompt construction ----------
def build_system_prompt():
    tool_desc = "\n".join(
        f"- `{name}`: {info['description']}"
        for name, info in tools.items()
    )
    return f"""You are an autonomous support agent. You have access to the following tools:
{tool_desc}

When you decide on an action, output JSON with the following schema:
{{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "<tool name>",
  "arguments": <object matching the tool's schema>
}}
If you have reached a final answer, use the tool `reply_ticket`. If you think a human is needed, use `escalate_ticket`. Do not output anything else."""

SYSTEM_PROMPT = build_system_prompt()

# ---------- 3. Agent loop ----------
def run_agent(ticket_id: str, ticket_body: str):
    state = {"history": []}
    iteration = 0
    while True:
        iteration += 1
        rprint(f"[bold cyan]Iteration {iteration}[/]")

        # Build user message
        user_msg = f"""Ticket ID: {ticket_id}
Content:
{ticket_body}

Current state (JSON):
{json.dumps(state, indent=2)}"""

        # Call the model
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
            ],
            temperature=0,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )
        action = resp.choices[0].message.parsed
        rprint("[green]Model action:[/]", action)

        # Dispatch
        if action["type"] != "call_tool":
            rprint("[red]Unexpected action type[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        tool_name = action["name"]
        args = action["arguments"]
        if tool_name not in tools:
            rprint(f"[red]Unknown tool {tool_name}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Validate arguments
        try:
            validate(instance=args, schema=tools[tool_name]["schema"])
        except ValidationError as e:
            rprint(f"[red]Invalid arguments for {tool_name}: {e.message}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Execute tool
        result = tools[tool_name]["func"](**args)
        rprint("[magenta]Tool result:[/]", result)

        # Update state
        state["history"].append({"action": action, "result": result})

        # Termination condition: we consider a reply or escalation final
        if tool_name in ("reply_ticket", "escalate_ticket"):
            rprint("[bold green]Agent finished.[/]")
            break

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    ticket_id = "12345"
    ticket_body = """I was charged twice for my last purchase and need a refund."""
    run_agent(ticket_id, ticket_body)

How to run 

python agent_loop.py

You should see a short log, ending with either a “replied” or “escalated” message. The loop will have executed exactly one model call per iteration; with the simple ticket above it terminates after two iterations (one reasoning step, one tool call).

When this breaks

Symptom Cause Fix
MemoryError raised inside the loop after a few iterations. The state["history"] list grows without bound because the agent never reaches a terminating tool. Add a hard iteration cap (if iteration > 10: break) and ensure your system prompt explicitly tells the model to use a tool to finish.
context_length_exceeded from OpenAI API. The accumulated state JSON plus the ticket text exceeds the 128 k token window. Summarise history (e.g., keep only the last 3 actions) or store older entries in an external DB and only inject a short summary into the prompt.
Invalid arguments ValidationError from the dispatcher. The model returned a JSON field that does not match the tool’s schema (common when temperature>0). Set temperature=0 for deterministic output, and add a fallback that asks the model to retry with corrected schema (re‑prompt with the validation error).
Model returns plain text instead of JSON (no parsed attribute). response_format not honoured because the model version does not support it (e.g., using an older model). Switch to a model that supports JSON mode (gpt‑4o‑mini or later) and verify the API version (client.api_version).
Infinite loop – iteration counter climbs forever, never hitting a tool. Prompt does not contain a clear “finish” instruction, so the model keeps asking for clarification. Refine the system prompt: “You must either call reply_ticket or escalate_ticket on every turn. Do not ask questions.”

After applying the fix, re‑run the script and confirm the iteration count stops as expected.

What it costs

Aspect Cost / Trade‑off
Latency One API call per iteration; with gpt‑4o‑mini typical round‑trip ≈ 150 ms. More iterations linearly increase total latency.
Monetary gpt‑4o‑mini costs $0.15 / M tokens (prompt + completion). A 2‑iteration ticket of ~200 tokens each costs ≈ $0.00006. Scaling to 100 k tickets per day ≈ $6 / day.
Memory Storing full history in‑process grows O(N) with N iterations. For long‑running agents you must prune or externalise.
Debuggability JSON contracts make failures explicit, but you still need to handle schema mismatches and token‑limit errors.
Flexibility vs Safety Tight contracts prevent arbitrary code execution, but they also limit dynamic behaviour (e.g., you cannot ask the model to generate new tool definitions at runtime).

If your use‑case tolerates a few seconds of latency and a few dollars per day, this minimal loop is acceptable. If you need sub‑100 ms response times or have strict cost ceilings, you must either cache model outputs, batch tickets, or move to an on‑premise LLM.

In the interview

Typical interview prompt:

“Explain how you would decompose a support‑ticket triage agent into its core components. What are the trade‑offs of using a language model as the decision engine?”

Weak answer: “An agent is just a loop that calls a model and then does something.” – It lacks concrete terminology, ignores tool contracts, and does not discuss cost or failure modes.

Strong answer:

  1. Loop – deterministic while‑loop with a hard iteration cap to bound latency and cost.
  2. Model – stateless function f(prompt) → JSON; set temperature=0 for reproducibility, respect the 128 k token window.
  3. Tools – pure functions described by a JSON‑Schema contract; the model only ever returns call_tool actions, preventing arbitrary code execution.
  4. Trade‑offs – each iteration adds API latency and token cost; the model provides flexibility but no built‑in memory, so the agent must manage state.
  5. Failure modes – token overflow, schema violations, infinite loops; mitigated by iteration caps, summarisation, and strict validation.

Senior vs junior expectations:

  • Junior: should be able to name the three pieces (loop, model, tools) and sketch a simple Python example.
  • Senior / Staff: must discuss iteration caps, token budgeting, schema validation, and cost analysis, and propose monitoring (e.g., Prometheus metrics for iteration count).
  • Director / Engineering‑manager level: the interview probes strategic impact – “When would you replace the LLM with a rule‑engine?” – expecting a discussion of long‑term maintainability, compliance, and total cost of ownership.

Follow‑up that separates experience from theory:

“Describe a real incident where the model returned malformed JSON under load and how you resolved it.”

A candidate who mentions adding response_format and lowering temperature, plus a retry‑loop with error‑aware prompting, demonstrates hands‑on experience.

Your tasks

  1. Add a summariser tool

    Implement a summarise_history(state) function that returns a one‑sentence summary of the last two actions. Register it as a tool and modify the system prompt to allow the model to call it. Verify that after 5 iterations the prompt size stays under 10 k tokens.

    Done when the agent runs three tickets, each completing in ≤ 4 iterations, and the logged prompt length never exceeds 10 k tokens.

  2. Introduce a hard cost budget

    Add a per‑ticket token budget of 500 tokens. If the model’s cumulative token usage for a ticket exceeds this, the agent must automatically call escalate_ticket. Use the usage field from the OpenAI response to track tokens.

    Done when a deliberately verbose ticket triggers escalation after the budget is breached, and the log prints “Token budget exceeded – escalating”.

  3. Break and diagnose

    Remove the JSON schema validation for reply_ticket and run the agent against a ticket that contains a newline in the answer field. Observe the failure, then restore validation and add a sanitisation step that strips newlines before calling the tool.

    Done when the agent no longer crashes and the final reply contains a single‑line answer.

  4. Scale test

    Write a script that spawns 100 parallel ticket processes (using concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor). Measure average latency and total cost (use the usage data). Report whether the average latency stays below 500 ms.

    Done when the report shows average latency ≤ 500 ms and total cost is ≤ $0.10 for the batch.

  5. Add a retry policy

    Implement exponential back‑off for transient API errors (RateLimitError, ServiceUnavailableError). The agent should retry up to 3 times before giving up and escalating.

    Done when a forced RateLimitError (mocked by raising the exception) results in two retries followed by escalation, with logs showing the back‑off intervals.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.

Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems

title: Vercel MCP now supports the 2026-07-28 MCP specification
description:
Vercel MCP now supports the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, giving newer clients a stateless request model and updated authorization behavior without any change on the client side.

Clients built for the 2025 protocol keep working exactly as before, and clients that understand the new specification pick it up automatically.

Both protocol versions are served from the same endpoint through the official MCP SDK v2 and mcp-handler 2.x, which added support for the latest spec, so a single connection handles either protocol.

Nothing about setup changes. Add the server the same way you always have.

npx add-mcp https://mcp.vercel.com

You can also run vercel mcp. See the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client. For the full list of protocol changes, read the 2026 specification changelog and the authorization announcement.

title: GST Helper: a local-first GSTR-1 preparation assistant
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

I built GST Helper, a local-first AI workspace that helps a small business prepare selected GSTR-1 values from sales invoice PDFs.

The demo company is BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. The user starts by loading outward-sales invoice PDFs. GST Helper reads the invoices, extracts values, shows page evidence, and turns the documents into a guided GSTR-1 review flow.

The current app prepares these GSTR-1 sections:

  • Table 4A regular domestic B2B invoices
  • Table 12 B2B HSN/SAC summary
  • Table 13 document numbers issued

It shows the invoice value including tax, taxable value, IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST, cess, total tax, and invoice count for the supported B2B scope. It also creates a reference PDF tied to the saved review revision, so the user can inspect the same values before downloading the file.

The problem is simple: small business owners and bookkeepers often do this first pass manually. They read invoice PDFs, copy values into spreadsheets, check invoice numbers, and then use those figures while working in the GST Portal. That work is slow, error-prone, and full of accounting language that is not friendly to a non-expert.

GST Helper is meant for a small business owner, bookkeeper, or accountant who wants a faster way to prepare and review the numbers before portal entry. The paid version could charge for private local workflows, more GST sections, accountant review packs, and better import and export support.

The app does not file a return, connect to the GST Portal, or claim that the whole GSTR-1 return is complete. Other GSTR-1 sections must be handled separately. That boundary is visible in the product because tax software needs trust more than magic.

Demo

Video demo: https://youtu.be/RFq9whXetRg


The demo shows the full BharatBiz flow:

  1. Load sample sales invoice PDFs.
  2. Confirm the seller GSTIN, tax period, and turnover band.
  3. Review invoice fields with page evidence.
  4. Save the reviewed values.
  5. Inspect the Table 4A totals.
  6. Generate a verified reference PDF.
  7. Use the review chat beside the final PDF.

Code

Repository: https://github.com/sonu0702/pgst

sonu0702 / pgst

GST Helper

GST Helper is a local-first GSTR-1 preparation app for BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. It turns outward-sales invoice PDFs into reviewed values, a clear summary for the supported GSTR-1 sections, and a reference PDF the user can inspect before downloading.

This release prepares only regular B2B invoices in Table 4A, the B2B HSN/SAC summary in Table 12, and documents issued in Table 13. It does not prepare a complete GSTR-1 return, connect to the GST Portal, submit or file a return, or decide GST treatment. Other applicable GSTR-1 sections must be prepared separately. The GST Portal accepts a JSON workflow through its offline tool, but the portal still validates the account and return when the user uses that file.

What the app does

  • Starts with outward-sales PDFs, then suggests seller GSTIN and tax period with page evidence before asking for return details.
  • Shows observed invoice-number…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The app is a single repository with a React frontend and a FastAPI backend.

Tech stack:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Local AI: Ollama with Gemma 4
  • PDF processing: Python PDF extraction with optional local OCR support
  • Export artifacts: reference PDF and supported-section JSON
  • Storage: no database in this prototype. Reviews live in temporary process memory.

The user flow starts with source documents, not a chatbot. That choice matters. Invoices are the source of truth, so the app first reads the PDFs and creates a review workspace from them.

The backend extracts invoice fields and line items, keeps compact evidence snippets, and builds a temporary GSTR-1 review case. The frontend lets the user inspect and edit each value. When the user saves, the backend runs local checks for the supported sections and returns readiness results.

Gemma 4 is used through Ollama for a narrow review task. It can answer questions about values already in the review or prepare a proposed edit from invoice evidence or from a value the user states. It cannot decide tax treatment, calculate GST, approve filing, or submit anything.

The user stays in control:

  • The model proposes changes.
  • The user applies the proposal.
  • The user reviews the form.
  • The user saves the revision.
  • The user regenerates the PDF if anything changed.

The reference PDF is tied to the saved revision. The app renders the PDF back in the browser and verifies the expected content before the user downloads it.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters here because tax preparation needs transparency, local control, and the ability to inspect the workflow.

A closed hosted API can produce a polished answer, but that is not enough for this use case. A small business owner needs to know where a number came from and what the app did with the source document. GST Helper keeps the review path visible: invoice evidence, editable fields, saved revision, local checks, and a reference PDF.

Open-weight local AI also changes the privacy story. In this prototype, Gemma 4 runs locally through Ollama. The app does not need to send invoice details to a hosted model API. That made it possible to build an AI-assisted review flow that still respects sensitive business documents.

Open-source tools also made the project practical for a hackathon:

  • FastAPI made the backend small and inspectable.
  • React and Vite made the review UI fast to iterate.
  • Ollama made local Gemma 4 setup approachable.
  • Python PDF tooling made extraction and reference PDF generation possible without building a document pipeline from scratch.

The project is not trying to replace a tax professional or the GST Portal. It is trying to make the preparation step clearer, safer, and more reviewable.

My Agent Session

I used Codex as an AI coding agent throughout the build. The agent helped with product scoping, GSTR-1 flow design, FastAPI and React implementation, sample invoice generation, UI polish, PDF review, and the demo walkthrough.

The most useful part was not code generation alone. The agent helped keep the product narrow. Whenever the app started to look like a generic invoice-review demo, I pushed it back toward one clear filing workflow: GSTR-1 preparation from sales invoices.

That made the final project stronger. It has a specific user, a specific filing task, a clear supported scope, and visible review boundaries.

title: The build went green because it stopped checking
description:
A teammate deleted a test file on a Friday. Not on purpose. The suite still passed. The pipeline still went green. Nobody noticed for three weeks.

Here's the part that should bother you. Nothing in that green was a lie. Zero tests failed. True statement. Also worthless, because the number that mattered was the one nobody printed: how many tests ran.

Most CI tells you pass or fail. Almost none tell you nothing was checked. A suite that collects zero tests exits clean in more setups than you'd like. So you get the friendly color, the little badge, and you file it under done.

Now widen it. Every green you trust has this hole in it:

  • A health check that pings the process, not the thing the process does.
  • A monitor whose query quietly returns no rows, so the graph draws a flat happy line.
  • An alert rule that can never fire because the label it filters on stopped existing.
  • A backup job that runs every night, exits 0, and writes an empty file.

None of these will page you. All of them will let you sleep. That's the whole problem. The failure mode isn't red. It's a green that stopped being a claim and turned into decoration.

So the question I keep losing arguments about: what did you actually check, and when did you last check that the check was still checking?

Green has never meant "it works." Green means "nothing failed." Only one of those is a fact about your code. The other is a fact about your test runner.

I'll take an honest red over a green that says nothing. But I'd rather have neither than a green I never verified.

A whale walked out of the ocean and onto the open web. The first thing he learned is that on land, everyone loves a green light and nobody reads the bulb.

title: What a Clinic Website Actually Has to Do in the UAE
description:
Most clinic websites are built like brochures: a hero, a list of services, a contact page. Patients do not use them like brochures. A patient arrives with one job — book the right doctor, fast, on a phone — and every screen that does not serve that job is friction.

We shipped a healthcare solutions page today and had to make these decisions for real, so here is the checklist that survived contact with an actual build:

1. Booking is the product, not a feature

The appointment action has to be reachable from every key screen, not parked on a contact page. On mobile that means the booking/contact action stays in reach while the visitor reads — the same pattern we use for enquiries generally: a lead is a WhatsApp message, a call, or a form submit, and the path to one of those three should never be more than a tap away.

2. Doctor profiles are decision pages

Patients choose people, not departments. A doctor profile needs the things a patient actually compares: specialty, languages spoken, location, and a direct booking route from that profile. A grid of names with no detail forces the patient to call and ask — and many simply book elsewhere instead.

3. Arabic is not a translation toggle

In the UAE, an Arabic version that is a shallow copy of the English page reads as an afterthought to the exact audience it is meant to serve. Proper RTL layout and genuinely reviewed Arabic copy are part of the build, not a plugin. We treat bilingual work as its own scope for this reason.

4. Trust content belongs before the ask

Insurance partners accepted, accreditations, and what happens at the first visit — placed before the booking prompt, not after it. Patients hand over health details and payment information on these sites; the proof has to arrive before the form does.

5. Speed and security are patient-experience issues

A slow mobile page loses the booking. A neglected site — outdated software, no maintenance routine — risks the one incident a clinic cannot afford. Security patching and backups are not IT chores on a healthcare site; they are part of patient trust.

The full breakdown of how we structure this — patient journey, booking flow, doctor profiles, bilingual build, and the maintenance side — is here: clinic and healthcare website solutions in Dubai.

If you run a clinic site, audit it against the patient's job, not the brochure: can a new patient, on a phone, in Arabic or English, reach the right doctor's booking in under a minute? Everything else is decoration.
