title: A post-quantum migration plan should print its arithmetic
description:
A cryptographic inventory lists what you have. A migration plan claims what to do first, and that claim is an opinion wearing a number. If you cannot recompute the score sitting next to a line, you have two moves available: accept the ordering, or ignore the tool. In my experience you ignore the tool.

I hit this building cbomscope (https://github.com/polycratia/cbomscope), which reads Go source and a live TLS handshake and writes a CycloneDX cryptography bill of materials. The inventory part was uncontroversial. A posture says what a quantum computer would do to an algorithm, which is a property of the algorithm, and nobody argues with a list. The plan command was different: it ranks the same assets by the work they imply, and the first version printed a sorted list with a score column and nothing else. It fell over the first time someone disagreed with it. They could not tell me which part they disagreed with, only that an RSA call in a test helper should not be sitting above the signature algorithm on a public endpoint. That is not feedback about the result. It is feedback about a weight, and the output gave them no way to say so.

The constraint

A migration plan gets read by people who have the authority to reorder it and information the tool does not have. This service is being decommissioned next quarter. That endpoint carries data with a ten-year confidentiality requirement. This dependency is pinned because the upgrade breaks an API nobody here controls. None of that is visible to a program that parses syntax trees and completes handshakes.

So the goal is not to be right about the order. It is to be legible enough that you can overrule one factor without throwing away the whole ordering. A hidden score forces an all-or-nothing judgement on the tool's credibility. A printed one shrinks the argument into something much smaller and much more productive: you think exposure should outweigh lifetime here, and now the conversation is about a number instead of about trust.

Small scales, declared

The weights are not literals buried in a scoring function. Each one is a named Factor (a label, a weight, and a reason), and the scoring functions do nothing but choose a row.

// postureFactor reports the weight of a posture, and false where the posture
// implies no migration at all. Anything it does not recognise — including an
// asset that never reached the classifier — is ranked as unjudged rather than
// settled: silence is not a clean bill of health.
func postureFactor(p asset.Posture) (Factor, bool) {
    switch p {
    case asset.QuantumSafe, asset.Hybrid, asset.NotApplicable:
        return Factor{}, false
    case asset.Broken:
        return brokenNow, true
    case asset.QuantumVulnerable:
        return shorFalls, true
    case asset.QuantumReduced:
        return resizable, true
    }
    return unjudged, true
}

func exposureFactor(a asset.Asset) Factor {
    switch {
    case a.Location.Host != "":
        return atEndpoint
    case a.Module != "":
        return inDependency
    default:
        return firstParty
    }
}

func lifetimeFactor(a asset.Asset) Factor {
    switch a.Primitive {
    case asset.KEM, asset.KeyAgree, asset.PKE:
        return keyExchange
    case asset.Signature:
        return signature
    }
    return storedData
}

Three questions, three scales, and the scales are small on purpose. Key exchange weighs 3 and a signature weighs 1, because the two run on different clocks: what is recorded off the wire today can be decrypted years from now, while a signature is forged at the moment it is verified. That is a deadline rather than a leak, and a deadline you can still move. A one-to-three range is a thing you can hold an opinion about. A zero-to-a-hundred range is not. It only looks more precise, and the extra digits are where fabricated confidence hides.

Why posture multiplies and the rest adds

exposure, lifetime := exposureFactor(a), lifetimeFactor(a)
report.Items = append(report.Items, Item{
    Asset:    a,
    Score:    posture.Weight * (exposure.Weight + lifetime.Weight),
    Posture:  posture,
    Exposure: exposure,
    Lifetime: lifetime,
})

The shape of the expression is itself a claim, and it should be one you can defend out loud. Exposure and lifetime add because they are independent reasons to move sooner: being reachable from the internet and protecting long-lived secrets are separate problems, and an asset with one of them is still work. Posture multiplies because it scales both. A classically broken primitive makes every other property worse, and a sound one makes them moot. Addition there would let a pile of mild factors out-rank something already broken, which is the failure mode people notice and do not forgive.

The expression goes next to the line

This is the whole argument in one method:

// Arithmetic is the score written out, so the number in a column can be checked
// against the line that carries it.
func (i Item) Arithmetic() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s (%d) × [%s (%d) + %s (%d)]",
        i.Posture.Name, i.Posture.Weight,
        i.Exposure.Name, i.Exposure.Weight,
        i.Lifetime.Name, i.Lifetime.Weight)
}

Every ranked line carries the expression that produced its number, in named terms rather than bare integers. You do not have to find the source, and you do not have to take my word for the ordering: you can see that this line scored where it did because it was found at an endpoint and because it is a key agreement, and you can decide that in your deployment the second term is wrong. The factors also survive the JSON output, along with the formula itself on the report, so a plan that travels into a ticket arrives with its reasoning attached instead of a column of integers somebody has to reverse-engineer later.

The same instinct runs one layer down. The classification table prints on its own, with the published source each verdict was read from, because a reviewer who wants to check a posture should not have to read the source to find out where the verdict came from. And a family missing from that listing is the honest shape of a gap.

Settled, not dropped

The first version filtered out the assets with nothing to do. That is the natural implementation and it is a quiet lie:

// Settled are the assets with no migration work: post-quantum, hybrid, or
// carrying no posture of their own. They are counted rather than dropped,
// because a report that omits what it checked reads exactly like one that
// never looked.
Settled []asset.Asset `json:"settled"`

A plan listing four items and a plan listing four items out of sixty are different documents, and the difference matters most to you when you are deciding whether to believe the first number. Post-quantum algorithms, hybrid key exchange, and protocol versions with no posture of their own all go into Settled with their locations intact. The hybrid line earns its place in particular: on a deployment that has already moved its key exchange, the fact that something was checked and found to need nothing is the single most useful sentence in the report.

The weight I expect to defend

Anything the classifier did not recognise, including an explicit unknown posture, ranks at 2, above the Grover-reduced assets at 1. People read that as a bug. It is the one weight I most want printed, because it is the one most worth arguing with: an asset nobody has judged is not a settled asset, and a ranking that sorts unknowns to the bottom turns a gap in the table into a clean bill of health. The same refusal shows up elsewhere in the tool. A key size of zero means not determined rather than small, the classical security level returns zero rather than invent a number, modulus sizes between the published pairs are left out rather than interpolated, and a citation stays empty on an unknown so that a printed source does not make a gap look checked.

If you decide unjudged should sit below resizable for your codebase, you are now making an informed local decision. That is a better outcome than agreement, I think, and it is only reachable because the number is shown in parts.

What I would do differently

The facts the tool cannot see still have nowhere to go. Today someone who knows a service is being decommissioned has to apply that knowledge in their head, after the sort. I would rather it entered as an exposure override on the input side, so the adjustment shows up inside the printed expression like every other factor. A plan corrected by a human should still be a plan whose arithmetic you can read, not one with a silent post-processing step bolted to the end.

I would also hold the line hard on scale size. Every request to make the ranking smarter arrives as a request for one more factor, and three factors with reasons beat seven with none. The moment the expression stops fitting beside the line it describes, it stops being checkable, and an unchecked score is back to being an opinion.

The product is the expression. The number is just what it evaluates to.

title: I Built a Remote to Answer Claude Code From My Phone
description:
Hello there!

If you run Claude Code or Codex for real work, you know the moment. You start a task, it runs for a while, and you go make a coffee. When you come back, the agent has been waiting ten minutes for you to answer one question.

"The fix is in. What should I do with it?"

That question is why I built Farol Remote. It lets you answer your coding agents from your phone, wherever you are, while the work keeps running on your Mac or on your own server.

A bit of context

Farol is a macOS terminal I made for coding agents. Its sidebar shows every session with a small dot: hollow when idle, breathing while the agent works, rippling when it waits for you, filled when it's done.

It tells you when an agent needs you. But only if you're at your Mac.

So the idea was simple. Put that sidebar in my pocket. See the sessions, read the conversation, and answer with a tap.

What the phone does

The iPhone app lists your sessions with their status and opens each one as its agent's conversation, not as a wall of terminal text.

When the agent asks for an approval or a question, the answers show up as buttons. One tap and it carries on. You can also reply with a slash command, send a screenshot for the agent to look at, review what changed file by file, and start a new session in a project.

It notifies you when an agent waits or finishes. And a Live Activity on the lock screen keeps count of the agents that work or wait, even with the app closed.

One phone can know several Macs and servers at once. Your work Mac and a server you run agents on show up in the same list, each session labeled with its host.

The hard part: the middle

A phone and a Mac don't talk to each other directly over the internet. Your Mac sits behind a home router, your phone is on 4G, and neither can reach the other.

So there's a relay in between. Both sides connect out to it, and it passes messages along.

That raises the obvious question. If everything goes through a server, what can that server see? These messages are your code, your prompts, and a phone that can type into your terminal. I didn't want the answer to be "trust me".

The goal became this: the relay passes messages it cannot read, and keeps none of them.

Pairing, once

It all starts with a QR code. On the Mac you turn on Remote in Settings and press Show code. On the phone you scan it.

The code carries three things: the relay's address, the Mac's public key, and a secret made just for that code. It's a link, and everything rides after the #.

func (o offer) link() string {
    text, _ := json.Marshal(o)
    return "https://farol.sh/pair#" + base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(text)
}

The part after the # is never sent to a server. So the secret never reaches the relay, which means the relay can't pair a device of its own.

The phone answers with one sealed message that proves two things at once: it holds the key it claims, and it saw the secret. A code works once and lasts two minutes. After that, the Mac knows the phone's key and the phone knows the Mac's.

Every connection

Each time they connect, both sides say hello in the clear with their public key and a random number made for this connection.

Then each direction becomes its own HPKE stream, sealed to the other side's key and signed with ours. I used CryptoKit's Curve25519_SHA256_ChachaPoly suite. Here's the sending side on the Mac and the phone:

public mutating func connect(to peer: ChannelHello, trusting trusted: [Data]) throws -> Data {
    guard trusted.contains(peer.key) else { throw RemoteError.unknownDevice }
    let sender = try HPKE.Sender(
        recipientKey: Curve25519.KeyAgreement.PublicKey(rawRepresentation: peer.key), ciphersuite: Pairing.suite,
        info: info(from: side, with: peer), authenticatedBy: me.secret)
    self.peer = peer
    self.sender = sender
    return sender.encapsulatedKey
}

The info includes both hello numbers. So a recording of an older connection doesn't open on a new one, and messages only open in the order they were sealed. If one fails to open, the connection ends.

What the relay actually sees

Mostly bytes.

It sees a public key, and a room name that's the hash of the host's key. That's how a Mac and its phones find each other without the relay learning who they are.

func room(public []byte) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(public)
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

Then it sees encrypted messages and how big they are. It stores none of it, and its log holds totals only.

Notifications without reading anything

This one was fun. I wanted a notification when an agent waits, even with the app closed. That means Apple has to push it, and something has to ask Apple.

The Mac asks the relay to forward a push. The relay sees the phone's notification token and one word: waiting or done. Which session it's about travels sealed, for the phone alone.

The Live Activity works the same way. The host keeps it current through the relay, so the counts on your lock screen move while the app sleeps.

Running Claude Code on a server with tmux

Some people run their agents on a machine that stays on, so they can close the laptop. For them there's farol-host, a small Go CLI.

curl -fsSL https://farol.sh/host.sh | sh
farol-host setup

Setup connects the hooks for Claude Code and Codex, keeps farol-host running with systemd, and shows a QR code to scan. Then every tmux window on that machine is a session on your phone, like a tab in Farol on the Mac.

tmux new -s api -c ~/code/api
claude

One protocol, two languages

The Mac and the iPhone share a Swift package. The server speaks the same protocol, written again in Go.

Two implementations of the same crypto and messages is a great way to have bugs that only show up on a real phone. So they check each other.

The Swift tests write sample messages and a sealed conversation to JSON files. The Go tests open those files and must read them exactly. When a message changes, I regenerate them:

FAROL_WRITE_WIRE=1 swift test

If Go and Swift disagree on a single field, a test fails before any phone sees it.

What's not covered yet

I'd rather say this upfront.

If a host's key were stolen later, traffic recorded from a phone to that host could be read. A host also doesn't prove itself to the relay yet, so someone who learned a room's name could knock the real host off. They couldn't read or send anything, but it's still on my list.

And the pairing and the encryption haven't had an outside review. If that's your thing, I'd love a second pair of eyes. It's all in one small repo, on purpose.

Try it

Farol is free and open source. The iPhone app is free too, in beta on TestFlight. In Farol, open Settings, choose Remote, turn it on, press Show code, and scan it from the app.

The security parts live in farol-remote: the Swift package, the relay, and farol-host. The security page goes deeper than this post.

Hope you find it useful! Feel free to open an issue or contribute. And next time your agent asks you a question while you're out, you can just answer it. ☕

title: Seedance 2.5 now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Seedance 2.5 from ByteDance is now available on AI Gateway. It can generate up to 30-second clips with synchronized audio, and takes up to 50 reference inputs in one request, spanning images, video, audio, and style.

A single clip holds camera movement and continuity without stitching shots together in post, and short clips can be extended, carrying over character, scene, and camera movement. Prompts work in more than ten languages.

Seedance 2.5 can also edit a finished video in place, swapping backgrounds, products, or characters while the frame, camera, and pacing stay fixed, so one shoot yields several variants.

Generating a video

Set model to bytedance/seedance-2.5 and call generateVideo from the AI SDK:

Adding image references

Pass image URLs in inputReferences and point at them in the prompt with [Image 1], [Image 2]. Tag each entry with its media type. Seedance treats an untagged URL as an image.

Combining reference types

Mix videos and images in the same request to pull different qualities from each: motion and camera work from a clip, a subject's appearance from a still.

Videos go in the same inputReferences array as images, tagged with a video media type. Numbering runs per type so the first video is [Video 1] and the first image is [Image 1], and both can appear in one prompt.

Editing a video

Referencing and editing use the same setup, so the prompt decides which you get. Ask the model to follow a clip's camera movement and it builds a new video from scratch. Ask it to change something in the clip and it edits the video you gave it.

You can reference and edit in one prompt, though results get less predictable, so it helps to be explicit about what each asset is for.

For the playground and API reference, see the model page, or browse every video model on AI Gateway.

title: A team name is an identity, a recovery code and a display label, and the only thing we validate is the length
description:
Nobody signs in to play a quiz at PubTrivia. Players scan the code on their table, a web page opens, they type a name, and they are in. No account, no app, no email. A hundred strangers in a pub, zero credentials between them.

Which means the name they type is doing three unrelated jobs at once, and I did not notice that until the third one bit.

Job one: validation, and there is almost none 

export function validatePlayerName(
    name: string,
): { valid: true } | { valid: false; error: 'invalid_name' } {
    const trimmed = name.trim()
    if (trimmed.length >= 1 && trimmed.length <= 30) {
        return { valid: true }
    }
    return { valid: false, error: GameError.INVALID_NAME }
}

That is the entire rule. Trim, then between 1 and 30 characters. No character class, no word list, no profanity filter.

The 30 is a layout number, not a safety number. Team names get read out loud and they go on a leaderboard that has to be legible from the other side of a room, and a name that does not fit the row is a worse problem than a name that is too short. There is no minimum beyond "not empty" because a table that wants to be called "7" has earned that.

What is deliberately absent is a filter. A pub quiz team will call itself something rude, that is most of the fun, and the host already has the only enforcement mechanism that works in a room: knowing whose table it is. Shipping a block list would mean maintaining a block list, in every language a tourist might bring in, forever, to solve a problem the person holding the microphone solves in four words.

Just above the validator in the join action there is a second length constant that is doing a genuinely defensive job, and the contrast is the point:

/** Longest answer text accepted. Options are short; this only bounds abuse. */
const MAX_ANSWER_LENGTH = 500

One number is about a leaderboard row. The other is about somebody with curl.

Job two: identity, enforced in application code

Names are unique per quiz, case insensitively, so the leaderboard never shows two of the same thing and nobody can pass themselves off as somebody else. The normalisation happens once, in the action:

const name = playerName.trim().replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
const sameName = (other: string) => other.toLowerCase() === name.toLowerCase()

Leading and trailing whitespace goes, and runs of internal whitespace collapse to one space, so "The Quiz Team" and "The Quiz Team" are the same entry rather than two rows that look identical on screen. That second rule is the one people forget, and a leaderboard is exactly where it shows.

The uniqueness itself is not a database constraint. There is no unique index on (session_id, lower(player_name)). It is one select, inside a transaction, behind an advisory lock:

await tx.execute(sql`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(${`join:${sessionId}`}, 0))`)

const clashes = await tx
    .select({ ... })
    .from(tableParticipantsTable)
    .where(
        and(
            eq(tableParticipantsTable.session_id, sessionId),
            or(
                eq(tableParticipantsTable.table_id, tableId),
                sql`lower(${tableParticipantsTable.player_name}) = lower(${name})`,
            ),
        ),
    )

One query fetches everybody this join could possibly collide with: the same table, or the same name, in either mode. The lock is there because the check is read-then-write, and two phones at the same table pressing Join in the same second both used to pass it.

It is worth being clear about what this does and does not catch, because "unique, case insensitive" sounds stronger than it is. There is no Unicode normalisation, so a name typed in NFC and the same name in NFD are two rows. There is no confusable folding, so Cyrillic "а" is not Latin "a". Zero-width characters are not stripped, and a name that is one zero-width space is 1 character and therefore valid. None of that matters for the leaderboard, and all of it matters for the next job.

Job three: the recovery code

Phones die. A phone that was holding a team's place in team mode is a real problem, because team mode gives one shared score to the whole table and the table has already joined. So re-typing the team name at the table's own code gives the place back:

if (config.team_mode) {
    const team = clashes.find((p) => p.table_id === tableId)
    if (team) {
        if (sameName(team.player_name)) {
            return { participantId: team.id, playerName: team.player_name, reclaimed: true }
        }
        return GameError.TABLE_ALREADY_JOINED
    }
}

The error message that goes with the second branch spells the rule out, because a player staring at a borrowed phone needs to be told exactly what to type:

This table has already joined. To rejoin on a new phone, enter your team name exactly as before.

So the name is a bearer credential. Knowing it, plus being able to scan the code on that table, hands you that table's participant row and its score.

Written down like that it sounds alarming, and then you remember where the system is. The attacker has to be in the room, at that table, with the card in front of them, typing the name of the team sitting there, while that team watches. The threat model of a pub quiz is not a threat model. The thing that made this design correct is the same thing that makes a paper answer sheet correct: the room is the authentication.

The usual case does not go near any of it. The device remembers:

const storageKey = (tableId: string) => `pub-trivia:player:${tableId}`

A refresh, a crashed tab, or iOS evicting the page while the phone was locked restores { sessionId, participantId, playerName } from localStorage and resumes, keyed per table so one phone can legitimately hold a place at two tables. Every read and write of it is wrapped in try, because private mode throws on access and a player in private mode should get a working game that merely cannot resume. The name-based reclaim only runs when the storage is gone with the phone.

Four refusals, four sentences

The join action can say no in four ways, and each error code maps to one sentence a stranger can act on:

case 'invalid_name':
    return `Please enter a ${teamMode ? 'team name' : 'name'} between 1 and 30 characters.`
case 'name_taken':
    return `That ${teamMode ? 'team name' : 'name'} is already taken in this quiz. Try another.`
case 'late_join_disabled':
    return 'The quiz has started and late joining is disabled. Wait for the next round.'
case 'table_already_joined':
    return 'This table has already joined. To rejoin on a new phone, enter your team name exactly as before.'

The mode-dependent wording is not decoration. In team mode the thing being rejected belongs to four people who chose it together, and "that name is taken" versus "that team name is taken" is the difference between a player retyping and a player assuming the app is broken.

The part I would generalise

The useful question is not "how do I validate a name". It is: how many jobs is this field doing?

Ours does three, and they want opposite things. As a label it wants to be short, loud and rude. As an identity it wants to be unique and normalised. As a recovery code it wants to be unguessable, which is the one property a name chosen to be shouted across a pub can never have.

We resolved that by letting the room carry the security and keeping the field cheerful. That is a correct answer for a quiz night and an obviously wrong one for anything with money in it. The mistake is not picking either, it is not noticing the field had been quietly promoted from label to credential and still being validated like a label.

description: "A practical engineering guide to Java 21 Scoped Values: Replacing ThreadLocal with Safer, Immutable Contexts. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [java, concurrency, backend, performance]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Java 21 Scoped Values: Replacing ThreadLocal with Safer, Immutable Contexts is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Java 21 Scoped Values: Replacing ThreadLocal with Safer, Immutable Contexts matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of java architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • The Memory Leaks And Inheritance Flaws Of Threadlocal In High-Concurrency Environments: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Scopedvalue: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Where(: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • ) Usage: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Java 21 Scoped Values: Replacing ThreadLocal with Safer, Immutable Contexts functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Java Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

// Production Implementation: Java 21 Scoped Values: Replacing ThreadLocal with Safer, Immutable Contexts
// Focus: The memory leaks and inheritance flaws of ThreadLocal in high-concurrency environments, ScopedValue.where(...) usage, and integration with Structured Concurrency.

package com.production.architecture;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public record TaskPayload(String id, String payload, Instant timestamp) {
    public TaskPayload {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id, "Task id cannot be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(payload, "Payload cannot be null");
    }
}

public class WorkloadEngine {
    private static final int VIRTUAL_POOL_CONCURRENCY = 100;
    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public WorkloadEngine() {
        this.executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    }

    public CompletableFuture<String> submitWorkload(TaskPayload task) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            try {
                return processInternal(task);
            } catch (Exception e) {
                throw new CompletionException("Pipeline execution failed for task: " + task.id(), e);
            }
        }, executor).orTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }

    private String processInternal(TaskPayload task) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(20));
        return "SUCCESS:" + task.id();
    }
}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: The $2M "Database Sharding" Migration I Cancelled with One Terminal Command
description:
Earlier last year, an urgent call arrived from the Group CTO of a high-growth Fintech SaaS processing billions in monthly volume. Their production database was pinning at 98% CPU utilization every afternoon. Customer checkout requests were timing out, and the board was in panic.

The internal engineering leadership had spent four months preparing an ambitious eighteen-month, $2,000,000 architectural migration: decomposing the monolithic database into thirty horizontal shards.

I asked for SSH read access to the telemetry cluster.

Within twenty minutes of inspecting pg_stat_activity and slow query logs, the real culprit emerged. It wasn't table volume. It was an unindexed multi-tenant tenant_id filter joined against an audit ledger table containing 400 million rows, executed on every customer balance check.

We issued a single zero-downtime index creation command and rebalanced the connection pooler timeouts.

CPU utilization dropped from 98% to 14% instantly. Database p99 latency plummeted from 3,400ms to 8ms. The $2M sharding rewrite was cancelled permanently, and the engineering department redirected its cognitive bandwidth to product features.

Before embarking on multi-million-dollar architectural overhauls, always verify whether your problem is true architectural saturation or simple operational neglect.

Key Takeaways & Architectural FAQs

Q: How do you tell the difference between true database scaling limits and a fixable query problem?

Inspect live telemetry (query execution plans and connection pool behavior) before any architecture decision. Most apparent scaling walls trace back to one unindexed query or an unbalanced connection pool, not a genuine capacity ceiling.

Q: Is a multi-year sharding migration ever actually necessary?

Sometimes, but only after the system has been proven to be hitting a true architectural ceiling under real load, not assumed to be the cause because CPU utilization looks high during a traffic spike.

title: AWS Transform Now Automates Azure-to-AWS Cloud-Native Code Conversion
description:
Originally published on PkLavc.

Confirmed facts

On October 16, 2026, AWS announced the general availability of Azure-to-AWS SDK code conversion in AWS Transform, a feature designed to automate migration of Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS.

The service identifies Azure service code within submitted .NET source code and converts it to equivalent AWS SDK calls, validating that changes are incorporated into the transformed output.

AWS Transform is available in eight AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London).

Conversion support includes Azure Functions to AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS. Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB conversion is available in preview status.

Technical analysis

The feature operates through an assessment phase where AWS Transform discovers Azure SDK usage in the submitted codebase, presenting conversion options in both an assessment report and modernization plan. Developers can accept these options or modify them before execution.

This approach addresses a significant engineering challenge in cross-cloud application modernization by automating what was previously manual code refactoring. The service's ability to translate service calls between cloud providers reduces migration complexity for .NET applications leveraging serverless and storage services.

The regional availability across eight AWS Regions suggests the service is designed for global enterprise use, though the announcement does not disclose processing requirements, data residency handling, or transformation accuracy metrics. The preview status of Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion indicates ongoing refinement of that specific mapping.

  • Supported conversions: Azure Functions → AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage → Amazon S3, Azure Queue Storage → Amazon SQS

  • Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion is in preview

title: crecheck v6.0 has been released
description:
Antananrivo, Madagascar - October 14, 2026

PostgreSQL credcheck extension

The credcheck PostgreSQL extension provides few general credential checks, which will be evaluated during the user creation, during the password change and user renaming. By using this extension, we can define a set of rules:

  • allow a specific set of credentials
  • reject a certain type of credentials
  • deny password that can be easily cracked
  • enforce use of an expiration date with a minimum of day for a password
  • define a password reuse policy
  • define the number of authentication failure allowed before a user is banned
  • define a delay on authentication failures
  • force users to change their password after first login
  • throw a warning N days before when the password user is about to expire
  • prohibit password changes
  • last login and boot/shutdown information
  • use of authentication failure with PgBouncer

Release 6.0 has been published,

This major release adds some new features and fix issues reported by users since last release.

  • Allow integration of the max_auth_failure feature with pgbouncer. See documentation.
  • Allow use of password_change_first_login with pgBouncer.
  • Add credcheck.password_valid_min setting to force a short VALID UNTIL window on newly created roles. Useful to force new users to change their password quickly when the client (DBeaver, pgAdmin, ...) does not support the error reported when credcheck.password_change_first_login is enabled.
  • Add an optional last-login history modelled on the Unix last(1)/wtmp. Records user sessions (name, login time, duration, backend pid, source IP and port, and optionally the last SQL query) plus PostgreSQL boot/shutdown/crash markers.
  • Change the behavior of the credcheck.no_password_logging to not hide the error statement anymore but instead to replace every PASSWORD '<literal>' clause with dots inplace of the literal to not expose the password in the log.
  • Add function pg_check_password( IN username name, IN password text ) to check a candidate password (and the associated username) against the credcheck username/password policy without creating or altering a role.
  • Fix privilege escalation via self ALTER ROLE when password_valid_until is set.
  • Fix memory leaks and a heap overflow.

Upgrade require a PostgreSQL restart to reload the credcheck library.

Complete list of changes and acknowledgements are available here

Links & Credits

credcheck is an open project under the PostgreSQL license maintained by HexaCluster. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/issues

About credcheck

The credcheck extension is developed and maintained by Gilles Darold at https://hexacluster.ai. If you need more information please https://hexacluster.ai/contact-us/.

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck#readme

title: How to Cut AI Image Costs by Reading the Pricing Page
description:
I billed more in one weekend of AI image generation than I earned from my first three months of stock sales. That was the moment I sat down and actually read the pricing page instead of skimming it. The fix cost me nothing but an hour of reading, and it cut my per-product image spend to a fraction of what it was across the 39 products I eventually shipped.

Here is what I learned, in the order I learned it.

The pricing page is a spec sheet, not marketing

I used to treat the pricing page like a checkout form I had to pass through. Wrong frame. It is a technical spec for your pipeline, and it answers questions your code needs to know:

  • Is billing per image, per credit, or per batch?
  • Does a higher resolution cost more, or is it free?
  • Do failed generations get refunded, or do you pay for the reject?
  • Is there a free tier, and what are its real limits?

Every one of those answers changes how you write your generation loop. I had a loop that fired one prompt, checked the result, and regenerated on failure. On a platform that charges for failed generations, that loop is a money shredder. On a platform that refunds failures, the same loop is fine. I was running the shredder version for weeks without noticing.

Resolution tiers are where the money hides

This one hurt the most. I was generating everything at the maximum resolution because I assumed stock sites wanted it. Then I read the review requirements properly instead of guessing.

Adobe Stock wants a minimum of 4 MP for vectors and images, but there is no prize for 20 MP when the reviewer checks the same things: title, keywords, no artifacts, no trademarked content. Vecteezy and Dreamstime have their own checks, and none of them reward padding pixels. What does reward padding pixels is the pricing page, which charges you for them.

The fix was boring: generate at the smallest tier that clears the platform's minimum, then upscale only if a specific product needs it. My preview-and-inspect step went from rendering at 300 dpi to inspecting at 60 dpi, which also mattered because my whole pipeline ran on 1 vCPU and 2 GB RAM. Lower resolution meant less memory per image, which meant I could keep the one-process-at-a-time habit without the box falling over.

Batch pricing changes your loop shape

Some engines give you a better effective rate when you request variations in a batch instead of one at a time. If that is true on your platform, the correct loop is: write one strong prompt, request the batch, pick the best, discard the rest. My old loop did the opposite, iterating the prompt one image at a time, paying the single-shot rate every time.

I rewrote the generation step around batch requests and my acceptance rate went up, because picking the best of four beats hoping the next single roll is better. Fewer total generations for the same number of keepers. That is the entire cost trick in one sentence.

Rejected uploads are a hidden per-image cost

Here is the part nobody prices in. Every image that gets generated, passes your own check, and then gets rejected by the platform's review is a sunk cost. Adobe rejects a wrong CSV header instantly. All three channels I upload to, Adobe with its 5-column header, Vecteezy with its 4-column header, Dreamstime with 15 columns, will bounce a file on metadata before a human ever looks at the art.

So a rejection that costs you zero generation money still costs you the generation you already paid for, plus the review wait, plus the risk of looking like a spam account if it happens often. The cheapest cost reduction is not a cheaper model. It is never wasting a generation you already paid for. That meant building the metadata CSVs to the exact column counts each platform demands, and keeping a ledger of what had already been uploaded so a re-run could never double-post or double-charge me.

Track cost per accepted asset, not cost per image

Once I fixed the above, I stopped looking at the invoice total and started tracking one number: what a finished, accepted, sellable asset costs me end to end. That number includes failed generations, rejected uploads, and the electricity on my tiny server. It went down for three reasons, in order of impact: batch requests instead of single shots, minimum viable resolution, and zero wasted generations from metadata rejections.

None of these required a cheaper provider. All of them required reading the pricing page as documentation.

The honest part

Everything above came out of one project: 39 packaged products, 856 MB of output, roughly 19,000 lines of pipeline code, 300+ pages of research behind the rules, all validated on a 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM box with no GPU. The four scripts that carry the lessons, the metadata builder for the Adobe, Vecteezy and Dreamstime formats, the upload tracker that prevents double-posting, the Markdown to PDF converter, and the product packager, are the same ones I use now. I put them together as a small kit because I kept rewriting them for friends. If you want the working versions instead of the descriptions, that is what it is.

title: How We Engineered a Zero-Boilerplate Composite Build Architecture for Enterprise Gradle Plugins
description:
The Monolithic Plugin Trap

When building enterprise Gradle plugins that handle deep bytecode tasks (like our JPA linter suite, JPersist), developers often fall into the classpath contamination trap. They bundle the core Java logic, framework dependencies (like Hibernate 5/6, EclipseLink, ANTLR4), and the Gradle API into a single monolithic project.

This creates massive friction for teams trying to scale:

  1. IDE Slowdowns: The integrated development environment struggles to separate compiler scopes, leading to indexing fatigue.
  2. Testing Nightmares: Gradle TestKit functional tests can leak runner classloaders and cause file-locking anomalies.
  3. Barriers to Entry: Outside contributors get intimidated by a complex, tightly-coupled dependency tree.

To solve this permanently, we recently underwent a massive structural migration for our v1.6.0 release track, transforming JPersist into a fully decoupled Symmetric Composite Build.

The Blueprint: Dual Isolated includeBuild Structures

Instead of using standard nested subprojects that leak compilation classpaths, we split the repository into two entirely independent execution containers right at the root directory level:

jpersist/persistence
├── settings.gradle        <-- The Conductor (Combines everything)
├── libraries/             <-- Isolated Build (Pure Java SPI Engines)
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── lint-persistence-api/
└── plugins/               <-- Isolated Build (Gradle Plugin Wrappers)
    ├── build.gradle
    └── jakarta-persistence-gradle-plugin/

In the root settings.gradle, we treat them as standalone environments using Gradle's includeBuild directive. This connects them as a unified ecosystem without letting their classpaths collide:

rootProject.name = 'jpersist'

// Include the decoupled core Java logic libraries
includeBuild('libraries')

// Include the isolated Gradle plugin definitions 
includeBuild('plugins')

Why This Composite Setup is a Developer Superpower

1. Absolute Compile-Time Classpath Separation

Our Java libraries inside libraries/ compile against native Hibernate 6 strings natively without knowing anything about Gradle or plugin lifecycles. Conversely, the plugin wrappers inside plugins/ pull those libraries down via standard coordinate notation strings:

dependencies {
    implementation 'io.github.jpersist.lint:lint-persistence-api:2.0.0'
}

During local testing, Gradle's composite build engine automatically intercepts these string coordinates and substitutes them with local project references seamlessly, eliminating manual local maven publishing steps completely.

2. Flawless Gradle TestKit Sandbox Testing

When running functional integration tests via TestKit, Gradle forks a separate JVM daemon. In standard layouts, this daemon can lock file paths or leak dependencies. With the composite build layout, plugins/ runs tests in an isolated sandbox, pulling pristine library binaries on-the-fly without colliding with the root build caching variables.

🌟 We're Open for Contributors! (Come Hack with Us)

With this pristine infrastructure locked down, we are officially opening JPersist to public contributions as we kick off the v1.7.0 - Performance & Multi-Tenancy tracks!

Thanks to the composite build separation, onboarding is incredibly easy. You just need JDK 17, and you can compile and verify the whole project immediately:

./gradlew -p plugins functionalTest

We have just logged our very first good first issue tickets on our public roadmap project board:

  • Ticket #68: [FEAT] Global modelgenProcessor Configuration.
  • Ticket #69: [FEAT] Isolated weavingClasspath Pipeline.

If you love advanced build systems engineering, bytecode scanning via ASM, or messing with ANTLR4 parsers, we would love to review your Pull Requests!

⭐ Explore the Roadmap & Grab an Issue: https://github.com/orgs/jpersist/projects

title: Building a Cloud-Native School ERP: Architecture, Real-Time Fleet Tracking, and Data Integrity
description:
Educational institutions frequently juggle an unmanageable software stack: a legacy desktop tool for accounting, spreadsheets for grades, fragmented messaging apps for parent communication, and disconnected standalone hardware for attendance.

When administrative tools operate in silos, data bottlenecks arise. Report cards require days of manual exports, fee reconciliation involves cross-referencing physical receipts, and parents are left waiting for fragmented updates.

At AcadHex, we approached this problem as a systems integration and distributed architecture challenge. Below is a look into how we architected a unified, multi-tenant Cloud School ERP designed to automate campus workflows in real time.

1. Core Architectural Pillars

A production-grade School Management System handles wide variations in traffic: minimal load during instructional hours, sudden spikes during morning gate check-ins, and heavy concurrent sessions during report-card releases or fee deadlines.

To balance these patterns, our platform relies on three key design principles:

  • Strict Multi-Tenancy & Data Isolation: Each school network or academy operates with strict logical data isolation. Tenant resolution occurs at the gateway layer via subdomain routing, with database connection pooling ensuring isolated tenant contexts while sharing compute resources efficiently.
  • Event-Driven Communication: Critical campus actions—such as biometric check-ins or fee receipts—emit domain events rather than triggering synchronous write chains.
  • Hardware-Agnostic Ingestion: Campuses deploy diverse hardware setups. Our API abstracts physical hardware (biometric terminals, GPS units) behind standardized webhook and telemetry ingestion pipelines. 
                +---------------------------------------+
                |          API Gateway & Routing        |
                |    (Tenant Resolution via Subdomain)   |
                +-------------------+-------------------+
                                    |
          +-------------------------+-------------------------+
          |                                                   |
+---------v---------+                               +---------v---------+
|  Real-Time Fleet  |                               |   Core Business   |
| Telemetry Service |                               |   Domain APIs     |
+---------+---------+                               +---------+---------+
          | (MQTT/UDP)                                        | (REST/RPC)
+---------v---------+                               +---------v---------+
| Hardware/Vehicles |                               | PostgreSQL / Read |
|   (GPS Devices)   |                               |      Replicas     |
+-------------------+                               +-------------------+

2. Ingesting Live GPS Fleet Telemetry at Scale

Managing student transportation demands reliable, low-latency telemetry. Traditional HTTP polling introduces unnecessary overhead for vehicle tracking updates transmitted every 3 to 5 seconds.

Telemetry Pipeline

  1. Device Packets: Onboard vehicle GPS trackers broadcast lightweight UDP/MQTT packets containing coordinates, speed, ignition status, and vehicle telemetry.
  2. Ingestion Layer: A Node.js worker layer decodes incoming binary/NMEA data payloads and validates device signatures.
  3. Geofencing & Event Triggers: Ingested coordinates pass through an in-memory spatial index. When a vehicle crosses a defined perimeter (e.g., Approaching Stop: Sector 4), the system triggers parent notification events.
  4. Broadcast via WebSockets: Real-time updates are published via Redis Pub/Sub directly to authenticated client dashboard sockets. 
interface VehicleTelemetryPacket {
  deviceId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  latitude: number;
  longitude: number;
  speedKmh: number;
  timestamp: number;
}

// Ingestion validation handler
export async function processTelemetry(packet: VehicleTelemetryPacket): Promise<void> {
  const { deviceId, tenantId, latitude, longitude } = packet;

  // 1. Update latest vehicle state in cache
  await cache.geoadd(`fleet:${tenantId}`, longitude, latitude, deviceId);

  // 2. Publish to authenticated active web/mobile listeners
  await pubsub.publish(`fleet:updates:${tenantId}`, JSON.stringify(packet));

  // 3. Evaluate active route geofences asynchronously
  queue.add('evaluate-geofence', { tenantId, deviceId, latitude, longitude });
}

3. Financial Consistency in Fee Automation

Automated fee collection requires strict consistency. Distributed transactions can fail midway if parent payments, fee concessions, ledger writes, and receipt generation are not handled within transactional boundaries.

We implement atomic transactions with idempotency keys across all collection endpoints:

-- Atomic ledger write pattern for fee processing
BEGIN;

-- 1. Lock invoice record to prevent concurrent double-collection
SELECT id, balance_due 
FROM student_invoices 
WHERE id = 'inv_98234' AND status = 'PENDING'
FOR UPDATE;

-- 2. Register successful transaction entry
INSERT INTO payment_transactions (
    id, invoice_id, amount_paid, gateway_ref, status, created_at
) VALUES (
    'txn_44102', 'inv_98234', 15000.00, 'pay_tok_live_891', 'SUCCESS', NOW()
);

-- 3. Reconcile balance and update invoice status
UPDATE student_invoices 
SET balance_due = balance_due - 15000.00,
    status = CASE WHEN (balance_due - 15000.00) <= 0 THEN 'SETTLED' ELSE 'PARTIAL' END,
    updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = 'inv_98234';

COMMIT;

Idempotency tokens on payment callbacks prevent duplicate receipts or balance miscalculations if a payment gateway retries a webhook during network fluctuations.

4. Hardware Integration: Biometric Attendance Pipelines

Connecting campus biometric hardware to cloud infrastructure presents practical challenges: school-level devices frequently experience intermittent offline states.

To prevent missing punch records, biometric terminals send batches using local storage replay:

  • Every punch is assigned a monotonically increasing sequence ID per device.
  • Devices buffer attendance records locally during network outages and flush payloads sequentially upon reconnection.
  • The API ingestion service deduplicates punches against a composite key (device_id, student_rfid, timestamp_minute) to guarantee zero duplicate markings while maintaining reliable attendance records.

5. System Design Takeaways

Building software for physical campus environments requires designing for edge-case resilience:

  1. Expect Intermittent Connectivity: Hardware bridges (turnstiles, vehicle tracking) must have built-in queuing and retry guarantees.
  2. Decouple Event Feeds from Query APIs: Separating live tracking feeds and heavy analytics queries prevents dashboard latency during peak morning check-ins.
  3. Prioritize Auditability: Administrative actions—grading adjustments, fee waivers, schedule updates—require immutable audit trails to maintain institutional trust.

By moving schools away from disconnected spreadsheets and legacy systems toward event-driven cloud platforms, administrators gain real-time oversight while parents stay informed.

title: Is "没事" really fine? A private texting copilot that runs on your own laptop
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

Team: @lydiazhang135, @shiyi_jiang_92dc7754aa4d9 and me.

Your partner sends two characters: 没事, "it's nothing." You have typed and deleted three replies. Is it really nothing? Do they want an apology, an explanation, or some space? And whatever you send next, do you want a cloud service to read the whole conversation first?

TL;DR

  • Paste your partner's message. A 322M model, Laya, reads the subtext in under half a second, and Gemma 4 E2B writes two replies; on a laptop CPU the first is done in about 3.6 s. You edit one and send it yourself.
  • Both models run on your own machine: by default nothing you paste leaves it, and with no per-message cost the app can sell for a one-time US$14.99 (¥68 in China), where the main cloud apps like it charge US$29.99–79.99 a year.
  • Fine-tuning the judge for about US$3 lifted its macro-F1 from 0.33 to 0.57 and its safety recall from 0% to 62% (the bar I set before training is 90%). The fine-tuned Gemma won 133 and lost 67 of 297 blind comparisons with stock Gemma (the rest tied). The app has used both since 18 October; a final, held-back exam comes next.
  • Try it in your browser (stand-in models, sample data), and recompute the evaluation numbers below with one command: npm run reproduce.

What I Built

Laya-Heart is a copilot for couples' chats. It runs as a web page on your own computer.

  1. Copy what your partner said, switch to the page and press Ctrl+V.
  2. Within a second, a small Laya card appears under their message: one to three short questions about it, with probabilities (Does "没事" really mean it's fine? What do they need now?), or a danger level from 1 to 10.
  3. Gemma 4 E2B starts writing two replies straight away. On a laptop CPU, the first is complete in about 3.6 s.
  4. Pick one, edit it, press Enter to copy it, and paste it into your chat app yourself.

Laya-Heart connects to no chat app and never sends a message for you. With the default settings, nothing you paste leaves your machine.

Each person you talk to gets a profile: their chat, saved on your PC, and a short "book" you write about them (nicknames, sore points, the day you met). When a new message touches on something in the book, Gemma gets the matching sentences. The app also saves facts from the chat on its own, in the chat's own words, with undo, and pins down relative dates: 下周六（10-24）是我生日, "next Saturday (Oct 24) is my birthday."

Safety rules are written in code, not left to a model. After every card, Laya answers one more, hidden question about safety, and the code also checks the chat for keywords. Signs of self-harm, or of abuse and control, bring up a notice; for self-harm, the reply options also include one written by a person, not by Gemma. If the chat looks like it involves a minor, nothing is drafted until you confirm that you are both adults. On the 300-chat practice exam described below, the notice came up on 13 of the 21 risky chats (the keyword rules alone caught 4) and on 1.8% of ordinary chats.

Who would pay for it? People who freeze over a text from someone they care about: new couples, long-distance couples, anxious texters. What I'd sell them is what a chatbot tab doesn't give: privacy (the chat stays on the PC), speed (one paste, replies in seconds, with the history and profile already there), and no subscription.

How many, and for how much? From public census and survey data, about 39–51 million Americans aged 20–34 have a partner and a smartphone, and 17–27 million of them can use a Windows PC. For China, the same estimate gives 138–162 million and 41–94 million. The main apps in this space (RIZZ, WingAI, YourMove and others) sell subscriptions: US$29.99–79.99 a year on the US App Store. I'd charge once: US$14.99, or ¥68 in China, for the ready-to-run app and its updates, while the code stays MIT. The market-size note has the sources and the arithmetic.

Demo

▶ Watch the 62-second demo (MP4, 4 MB, narrated with ElevenLabs, plays in the browser). Both models run on my laptop's CPU, the couple is made up, and nothing is sped up or cut. It was recorded on 16 October, before fine-tuning (zero-shot Laya, stock Gemma), by the script that drives the page. Afterwards I redrew the caption strip and the closing card in the same style, so the captions match the narration word for word; the app on screen is the recording itself.

▶ Try the online demo (中文), labeled sample data: the app's real page in your browser tab, with stand-ins for the two models, so its cards and replies are placeholders. Paste a line, pick a reply, edit it, add a profile; nothing leaves the tab. It is hosted on Render, with a mirror on Hugging Face.

Code

sykyyds3739 / laya-heart

Local-first couple-chat copilot: Laya reads the room, Gemma drafts, you press send. Built on Jev Chat Assistant.

Laya-Heart

A copilot for couple chats that runs as a web page on your own PC. Copy what your partner said, switch to the page and press Ctrl+V: a Laya card (a 322M-parameter decision model) hangs under their message within about half a second — one to three short questions about what they just said, with probabilities — and Gemma 4 E2B starts writing two replies straight away, a few seconds later they are on the right. Use this puts one into the I said box, where you can edit it; Enter copies it and adds it to the chat, and you paste it into your chat app yourself It connects to no chat app, sends nothing for you, and with default settings the chat never leaves your machine. Each person you chat with has a profile: their chat is kept on your PC, and you can write a short…

View on GitHub

The app is MIT-licensed and built on Jev Chat Assistant (MIT). Laya-Heart is not made or endorsed by the authors of Jev Chat Assistant; CREDITS.md lists exactly what I borrowed. The fine-tuning kit is on the train-kit branch (tag train-kit-rc1), with a Chinese manual for each model. The models are on Hugging Face: Laya, zero-shot and fine-tuned v3, as ONNX, and the fine-tuned Gemma v4 as GGUF.

One command reproduces the evaluation. npm run reproduce recomputes the fine-tuning report's 62 evaluation numbers from the raw data in eval/, offline, in about two seconds. npm run reproduce -- --models also downloads both Laya models at a pinned revision and re-runs them on your CPU: 68 checks, every probability within 0.001 of the recorded run.

How I Built It

Open piece Job License
Laya-multilingual by Convai Innovations (322M, built on mmBERT), fine-tuned here reads their message: probabilities for each card question Apache-2.0 (mmBERT: MIT)
Gemma 4 E2B by Google, fine-tuned here (Q4_K_M GGUF) writes the replies; picks facts worth keeping Apache-2.0
llama.cpp llama-server runs Gemma on the CPU MIT
onnxruntime-node and Laya's laya-ts runtime run Laya in a worker process MIT; Apache-2.0
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (through its API); Qwen3-14B/32B-AWQ (vLLM on Kaggle) training only: teachers that write and label practice chats MIT; Apache-2.0

The server is plain Node.js with one dependency (onnxruntime-node), and it listens on 127.0.0.1 only.

I built Laya-Heart with an AI coding agent (Claude Code): under my direction it wrote much of the code, ran the training and recorded the demo, and it helped draft this post.

Making a 2B model feel instant on a laptop CPU

On a laptop CPU, Gemma 4 E2B reads a prompt at about 55 tokens/s and writes about 12 tokens/s, so reading was most of the wait. At first I ran Gemma through Ollama's chat API, which reuses Gemma 4's sliding-window cache only when the prompt is exactly the same. So every new message meant re-reading the whole 400–475-token prompt: 6.4–9.4 s. Three changes removed most of that wait:

  • I start llama.cpp's llama-server myself with --swa-full, so it keeps everything it has already read.
  • The prompt is laid out for the cache: fixed rules first, then the chat, which only grows at the end, then a short tail that turns Laya's answers into instructions. A new message now costs 62–105 new tokens instead of 400+.
  • Replies start the moment the card is done, stream as they are written, and stop after two.

On my laptop (Intel i5-13420H, 16 GB of RAM, no discrete GPU), two five-turn runs with the fine-tuned models, traced in Sentry, gave median times of 0.44 s to the whole card, 3.6 s to the first complete reply and 5.8 s to both replies. That was on a busy machine with about 3 GB free; earlier runs with the stock models on an idle machine took 0.39 s, 3.5 s and 5.0 s, using about 2.3 GB of RAM for both models.

Getting started is meant to be boring: download the ZIP and double-click start.bat (macOS: start.command; Linux: ./start.sh). On the first start, one button downloads about 4.8 GB, resuming if it stops and checking each file against a pinned SHA-256. I have tested it on Windows 11.

Fine-tuning the judge (Laya)

Out of the box, Laya is a general-purpose judge that hasn't been tuned for couples' chats. So I built a training kit and ran it end to end:

  • Teacher A (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) writes 3,000 practice chats to fit chosen answers, then reads each one five times per question without seeing the intended answers; any intended answer the readings don't match is thrown out.
  • Teacher B (Qwen3, a different model family) writes and labels a separate 300-chat practice exam, so the model is never graded by the teacher that taught it.
  • Training runs on Kaggle's free T4 GPUs: three seeds in about an hour, keeping the best on the practice exam. The gates were set before training, among them: macro-F1 up by at least 0.20, no question worse by more than 0.02, and safety recall of at least 90% at the app's 0.8 alarm line.
On the 300-chat practice exam (teacher B: Qwen3-32B) Zero-shot Laya Fine-tuned (v3)
Judgment, macro-F1 over 11 questions 0.33 0.57
Calibration error (ECE) 0.15 0.07
Danger level, mean absolute error (1–10) 2.78 1.56
Safety recall at the 0.8 alarm line 0 of 21 13 of 21 (62%)
False alarms on ordinary chats 2.9% 1.4%

The 95% confidence interval for the F1 gain is 0.18 to 0.31. These are practice-exam numbers; a final, held-back exam comes next. Every question, gate and caveat is in the fine-tuning report.

Two of the gates are still ahead. Safety recall is 62%, against a bar of 90%: five of the eight risky chats it missed were abuse or control read as no risk, such as "You won't see your sister again unless it's through me." And F1 on "is the crisis over?" dipped by 0.08, against a limit of 0.02, on chats where even the teacher split its votes. Still, v3 raises the app's safety notice on 13 of the 21 risky chats instead of 4, so the app has run v3 since 18 October, and the held-back exam decides whether it stays.

The whole run cost about ¥23 (roughly US$3) in DeepSeek API calls and about 9 of Kaggle's 30 free weekly GPU hours. Running the kit end to end also turned up 41 issues in the code and the manuals, including a cache bug that had silently made 20% of the practice chats near-duplicates, fixed before the final training runs.

I trained three versions, v1 to v3, each with a different mix of practice data. What I learned:

  • Compare averages, not the best seed. Seeds of the same version differed by 0.02–0.05 in F1; averaged over their three seeds (leaving out the safety question), v1, v2 and v3 scored 0.57, 0.56 and 0.56.
  • Extra risky chats leak into other answers. Raising their share from 10% to 25% (v2) lifted recall on a separate safety check from 53% to 68%, but the model began calling more chats emergencies and missing a partner who is simply angry. In v3 they train only the safety question: recall on the check (47 fresh risky chats, 19 ordinary) reached 79% with no false alarms, and the side effects mostly went away.
  • You can't measure what your exam teacher can't write. Asked for 25 risky exam chats, Qwen3-14B put a clear signal in only 5; a stricter prompt and the bigger Qwen3-32B got the exam to 21.

Fine-tuning the writer (Gemma)

I also fine-tuned Gemma with the kit's Gemma manual. The app now downloads the fourth of four runs, chosen by a rule written before the results:

  • Data: 1,496 examples. In Chinese, teacher A wrote candidate reply sets to the app's exact prompt, the app's rules dropped bad sets, and the best-scored set became the training reply; the 108 English replies are stock Gemma's own drafts, filtered and scored the same way, so they stay within the app's 60 characters.
  • Training: a 47-minute Kaggle job on a T4 trained a LoRA (rank 16, two epochs) with Unsloth and exported a 3.4 GB Q4_K_M GGUF for the same llama-server.
  • Result: on all 297 practice-exam chats, teacher B (Qwen3-32B) compared it with stock Gemma blind, in both orders: 133 wins, 67 losses, 97 ties (61% with ties counting half; 65% on Chinese chats). It made things up or overpromised once; stock Gemma did 16 times.
  • Still open: on the kit's 50-chat self-check, every gate passes but one: the win rate came in at 0.54 against a bar of 0.55 (a second judging of the same 50 chats gave 0.57).

Dry-running the tester kit with an AI agent

For friends to try the app, I wrote a 15-minute tester kit: six made-up chats, closing questions about price, and a record sheet. An AI agent went through it on my laptop with the real build (fine-tuned Laya, stock Gemma): a dry run, not a user study, with no people and no payments. The flow held up, from an edited reply landing on the clipboard to 我下周六生日哦 ("my birthday is next Saturday") being saved as October 24. It also caught slips: two replies seemed to lose track of who was busy or of the latest topic, and one promised 我下个月肯定能回来 ("I'll definitely be back next month") with nothing in the chat to back it. That kind of overpromise is what the fine-tuned Gemma made once in 297 practice chats, against 16 times for stock Gemma.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Where open beat closed, here. Jev Chat Assistant, the app I built on, asks a closed, hosted judge by default and sends it the last ten lines of the chat. I can't tune that model, and its terms don't allow training a model on its answers. Laya's weights are open, so I fine-tuned it for couples' chats against my own bar: macro-F1 0.33 → 0.57, safety recall 0% → 62%. And it runs on the user's own PC, with 0 bytes sent.
  • Privacy you can check. A couple's chat is about as private as data gets, and the other person never agreed to send it anywhere. Open weights are what make this possible: both models run on your machine, the server listens only on 127.0.0.1, and a badge in the header counts the bytes each turn sends off the machine (zero by default). People are wary: 71% of US adults think AI will make their personal information less secure.
  • Costs that allow a one-time price. There is no per-message bill, and the whole fine-tuning run cost about US$3 plus free GPU hours, so the app can be a one-time purchase instead of a subscription.
  • A niche I can tune for. Reading the subtext in Chinese couples' chats (你最好是, "you'd better be"; 没事; 随便, "whatever") is a narrow task. I can train a small judge for it on my own data against my own gates, and when a result surprised me, I could open it up and see why: seed noise, the data mix, the exam teacher.
  • No lock-in. Point the settings at another GGUF file or Ollama model, or at a laya-serve endpoint, and the app uses it.

My Agent Session

## Privacy

- It connects to no chat app: no screen reading, no accessibility hooks, no clipboard watching.
  It sees only what you paste into the page or type.
- The server listens on `127.0.0.1` only, refuses requests whose Host is not its own (no DNS
  rebinding) and POSTs from other origins, sends no CORS headers, and serves the page under a
  strict Content-Security-Policy.
- With the defaults (Laya in a local worker, Gemma in a local llama-server), every turn sends
  0 bytes off the machine; the header badge shows the count.
- llama-server would answer any web page open in your browser (it allows every origin), so the
  app starts it with a random key each time: other pages get 401 and can't use the model or
  read its state. Only the health check stays open.
- The only time it goes online is the first start, when you press *Download*: it fetches the
  files listed under [Run it](#run-it) from GitHub and Hugging Face (or hf-mirror.com), sending
  nothing but the requests for those files.
- Each person's chat, the book you write about them and what was kept from the chat by itself
  (`auto.json`) are saved on this PC, in `~/.laya-heart/people/` (see
  [Profiles and memory](docs/how-it-works.md#profiles-and-memory)); deleting a person moves them to
  `~/.laya-heart/trash/` for 30 days. What to keep is picked by the local Gemma only: with a
  remote or Ollama drafter nothing is picked, and a look's line in `metrics.jsonl` holds only
  counts and times. Laya's cards are cached in memory by chat
  text until *Clear the chat* (in the profile) or exit. Also on disk: `settings.json` and `metrics.jsonl` (numbers only:
  stage times, token counts, bytes out, how many memory chunks a turn used) in `~/.laya-heart`,
  plus llama-server's log.
- A remote judge or drafter, if you set one, gets none of the memory: not the book, not the
  core card, not the chunks.
- Optional comparison backends — an HTTP judge (`laya-serve` or Jev) and an
  OpenAI-compatible drafter — are off by default; when they point at a remote host the badge
  turns amber. Their keys are never stored: settings name an environment variable instead.
- Never sends a message for you.

Development laptop: Intel i5-13420H (8 cores / 12 threads), 16 GB RAM, no discrete GPU,
Windows 11, plugged in. `npm run bench` plays made-up chats line by line through the HTTP API and
times every event from the moment the request is sent (2026-10-14, about 4 GB of RAM free). These
runs used zero-shot Laya, Ollama's llama-server and `gemma4:e2b`, before the switch to the official
build and to the fine-tuned models:

| Time from paste | Chat going on (turns 2–6) | New chat (5 chats) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laya's first answer | p50 0.32 s · p95 0.45 s | p50 0.22 s · p95 0.27 s |
| Whole card | p50 0.39 s · p95 0.96 s | p50 0.54 s · p95 0.70 s |
| First reply text on screen | p50 2.6 s · p95 3.4 s | p50 3.0 s · p95 3.2 s |
| First reply complete | p50 3.5 s · p95 5.1 s | p50 3.9 s · p95 4.7 s |
| Both replies, ranked | p50 5.0 s · p95 6.5 s | p50 4.9 s · p95 6.0 s |
| Tokens Gemma had to read (from cache) | 62–82 (257–348) | 81–105 (246–249) |

- Ready after `npm start`: 8–10 s in four runs (Laya 3–6 s and llama-server 5–6 s in parallel,
  then reading the fixed rules 2.6–3.7 s).
- The fine-tuned models against the previous default (2026-10-18, `node scripts/bench_latency.mjs --settings`,
  alternating, 2–3 runs each): Laya v3 with Gemma v4, and zero-shot Laya with Google's QAT file,
  both on the official llama-server. First reply p50 4.9 vs 5.5 s in a chat going on and 5.7 vs
  5.3 s in a new chat: no slower overall, and Gemma v4 held 0.14 GB less private memory. Both pairs
  measured slower that evening than the table (cards about 2 s, first replies about 5 s), so
  compare them with each other rather than with the table.
- These numbers move with whatever else the PC is doing. Runs while other programs kept the CPU busy gave
  cards of 1–3 s and first replies of 4–9 s; with 0.6 GB of RAM free (an office suite and a
  browser open) a turn took 8.1 s to the first reply and 14.7 s in all.
- Memory while running (end of a bench run): llama-server ≈ 1.6 GB, 0.83 GB of it private (the
  rest is the model file, mapped); Laya's worker ≈ 0.7 GB. Loading reads every Gemma weight once
