This is the part of a Claude Code session where the agent added Sentry tracing. It made tracing opt-in and numbers-only, so the app's promise still holds: with the defaults, nothing you paste leaves your PC. Then it didn't stop at its own unit tests. It pointed a made-up DSN at a receiver on localhost, ran a turn through the real Sentry SDK and read every byte that would have gone out. That check caught what the tests couldn't: Sentry 11 streams spans one at a time, so the hook it had written for whole transactions never ran. Nothing had leaked, but only because no text is ever put on a span. It moved the guard and proved it both ways: a span stuffed with chat text arrives with just its token count, and with the guard taken out, the same check fails and prints the leaked words. (The upload leaves out local paths, the agent's internal reasoning and screenshots.)

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 E2B writes the reply drafts, locally in llama.cpp (with --swa-full and a cache-friendly prompt), and picks which facts from the chat are worth keeping; the code checks that each appears in the chat word for word. The fine-tuned Gemma described above scored 61% against stock Gemma in 297 blind comparisons (ties counting half) and made things up or overpromised once instead of 16 times. Evidence: the model on Hugging Face, both models' drafts and teacher B's verdicts in eval/data/gemma, and npm run reproduce.

Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing. Every turn is one trace in the shape Sentry's AI Agents views expect: invoke_agent laya-heart for the turn; a gen_ai.decide span for each Laya answer (gen_ai.rerank when it puts the replies in order); gen_ai.chat for Gemma, with tokens in, tokens read from llama-server's cache, tokens out and time to first token; and gen_ai.memory.client for what the turn kept. Tracing is opt-in and numbers-only: no prompt, reply or memory is ever put on a span, a send hook drops any attribute outside an allowlist, and scripts/trace_check.mjs runs a turn through the real SDK into a receiver on localhost and searches every byte for the chat's words. Sentry agrees: Gemma's span reads No input for this span.

What 40 traced turns with the fine-tuned models showed:

  • In the turn above, on a busy CPU, three Laya calls (two card questions and the hidden safety question) take 1.25 s before Gemma starts. Gemma's prompt is 465 tokens, 378 of them already in llama-server's cache, so it reads 87 new ones (2.0 s) and writes 43 (3.9 s).
  • The AI Agents dashboard counted 288 Laya calls and 40 Gemma calls, 51,602 tokens in all, and its estimated cost stayed at $0: both models run on the laptop.

Building it turned up two bugs in the tracing itself. The first, Sentry 11 streaming spans one at a time so the scrubbing hook never ran, is in the agent session above. The second: the first real run arrived as one 194-span trace, because with the default integrations off nothing started a trace per request. Starting each turn with Sentry.startNewTrace fixed it; the old trace is still at the bottom of the list.

Best Use of Render. Render hosts the copilot's front end: the online demo is the app's real page, with its server's API running in the browser tab and stand-in models, so anyone can try every flow before downloading anything. It is a static site deployed from a public repository with no build step. That split is the point: Render serves the part that is fine to share, and the models, with the chats they read, stay on the user's PC.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. The demo video is narrated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech (eleven_multilingual_v2, the voice Sarah). I wrote 13 short lines, one for each caption or title card, and the captions show the same words. A script trims each clip and places it while its caption is on screen, ffmpeg mixes the speech under the recording, and a pass through ElevenLabs speech-to-text confirmed that every line is heard while its caption is showing. ElevenLabs voices the demo, not the app: the app itself never sends what you paste anywhere.

Best Use of GitHub Copilot. Not Copilot itself: this entry is for the category's GitHub Actions part. A test workflow runs on every push to main and every pull request, on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS: the unit tests, including the check that recomputes the report's 62 evaluation numbers, then the page in headless Chrome with the stand-in models, keeping the screenshots. It caught a bug the local runs hadn't shown: on macOS, the browser test hung at its last step until the job's 20-minute limit. Reproducing it locally pointed to the server's close(), which waited on a connection the page's poll kept busy. It now ends connections first, and the browser step fails within 8 minutes instead of 20.

Laya-Heart drafts chat replies; it is not counseling or crisis support. In a crisis, contact local emergency services or a helpline (China 12356, US 988). The other person may not have agreed to their messages being analyzed, so use it with care.

title: How to Bypass Aggressive JavaScript Anti-Copy Scripts Using Capture-Phase DOM Events
description:
Have you ever tried to copy a snippet of code, an error stack, or reference material from a web page, only to find that right-click is disabled, text selection is blocked, or your clipboard is silently swallowed?

Modern web applications implement anti-copy logic for various reasons (paywalls, content protection, cheating prevention in test portals). However, aggressive implementations frequently break accessibility and degrade basic developer ergonomics.

In this deep dive, let's explore how modern anti-copy scripts work under the hood, why traditional solutions like preventDefault overrides often fail, and how to reliably unblock them at the browser engine level.

1. How Anti-Copy Mechanisms Work Under the Hood

Hostile sites typically attack user interaction across two distinct browser layers:

Layer A: The DOM Event Pipeline

When you highlight text and press Ctrl+C (or right-click to open the context menu), the browser fires a sequence of DOM events:

  • Selection: selectstart, mousedown, mousemove, mouseup
  • Context Menu: contextmenu
  • Clipboard: copy, cut

A typical blocking script hooks into these events:

['copy', 'cut', 'contextmenu', 'selectstart'].forEach(eventType => {
  document.addEventListener(eventType, (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    e.stopPropagation();
    return false;
  });
});

By calling e.preventDefault(), the browser cancels its native default action. By calling e.stopPropagation(), bubbling is halted, preventing parent nodes or plugins from handling the interaction.

Layer B: CSS Selection Suppression

Even if event handlers are neutered, sites will commonly inject aggressive CSS rules to prevent the browser engine from creating text selection ranges:

* {
  -webkit-user-select: auto !important;
  user-select: auto !important;
}

When user-select: none is enforced on the <body> or root nodes, the mouse cursor cannot highlight characters, rendering keyboard shortcuts useless.

2. Why Naive Fixes Break Dynamic Applications

Many quick scripts attempt to solve this by monkey-patching document.oncopy = null or brute-forcing document.querySelectorAll('*').

The fatal flaw: Modern single-page applications (React, Vue, Monaco Editor, Google Docs, etc.) legitimately rely on synthetic event dispatching and custom text measurement. If you blindly strip all event listeners or nuke the DOM prototypes globally without fine-grained scoping, dynamic inputs will glitch, custom dropdowns will fail to close, and form validation will break.

3. The Robust Architectural Solution

To safely restore user control without breaking web application logic, we must intercept the event lifecycle at the Capture Phase:

Step 1: Intercepting at Capture Phase (useCapture: true)

The DOM event dispatch lifecycle has two main phases:

  1. Capture Phase (window -> document -> target)
  2. Bubble Phase (target -> document -> window)

Most blocking scripts listen in the bubbling phase. By registering our handler in the capture phase with high priority, we can intercept the event before the hostile page script even receives it:

const criticalEvents = ['copy', 'cut', 'contextmenu', 'selectstart'];

criticalEvents.forEach(type => {
  window.addEventListener(type, (event) => {
    // Stop other handlers on the current target from being called
    event.stopImmediatePropagation();
  }, { capture: true, passive: false });
});

Step 2: Forcing CSS Selection Overrides

To neutralize CSS suppression, we inject a non-destructive override stylesheet into document.head or document.documentElement:

const style = document.createElement('style');
style.id = '__unblock_selection_override';
style.textContent = `
  *, *::before, *::after {
    -webkit-user-select: auto !important;
    user-select: auto !important;
  }
`;
(document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(style);

4. Packaging into a Lightweight Offline Extension

If you only encounter blocked pages occasionally, running the snippets above inside your browser's DevTools Console is sufficient.

However, if you deal with documentation portals, learning systems, or technical knowledge bases every day, automating this workflow via a clean, 100% offline browser extension is much more convenient.

I packaged this exact capture-phase bypass, automatic CSS unblocking, and smart whitelist engine into EasyCopy PRO:

  • 100% Offline Execution: Runs locally inside your browser sandbox with zero external network requests or analytics telemetry.
  • Dynamic Site Protection: Isolates unblock rules so dynamic editors (like Google Docs or CodePen) continue functioning normally.
  • Store & Release Access: Currently in review on the official Microsoft Edge Add-ons store, with offline packages and licenses available directly via Gumroad.

Conclusion

The web was fundamentally built as an open, accessible medium for sharing information. While anti-scraping measures have legitimate security use cases, taking away basic user ergonomics like right-click and copy-paste harms normal users far more than automated bots.

Using the capture-phase pattern and CSS normalization above, you can restore full control over your browsing experience safely and reliably.

title: Introducing @zervonex/baileys - A Tailored Fork of the Baileys WhatsApp Web API
description:
As developers working heavily with automation, we often rely on the incredible WhiskeySockets/Baileys library to interact directly with the WhatsApp Web API.

However, maintaining long-term stability, implementing niche patches, and ensuring rapid upstream syncs for specific organizational workloads can sometimes require custom overrides.

To solve this for our production pipelines, we have officially published and open-sourced our custom-tailored ecosystem variant: @zervonex/baileys.

🚀 Why Use @zervonex/baileys

The @zervonex/baileys package is a dedicated, scoped fork built to ensure predictability, seamless integration, and stable session management in Node.js environments. By utilizing a scoped npm package under @zervonex, we ensure that updates are controlled, thoroughly tested, and safe from unexpected upstream breaking changes.

Key Highlights:

  • Fully Scoped & Managed: Eliminates package naming collisions and guarantees clean dependency trees.
  • Production Ready: Built out of a necessity for reliable, automated multi-device connectivity.
  • Seamless Transition: Maintains structural compatibility with the core Baileys API so you don't have to rewrite your codebase.

🛠️ Quick Start & Installation

You can integrate our fork into your Node.js or TypeScript application instantly using your preferred package manager.

# Using npm
npm install @zervonex/baileys

# Using yarn
yarn add @zervonex/baileys

# Using pnpm
pnpm add @zervonex/baileys

Basic Initialization Example 

async function connectToWhatsApp() {
    // Dynamically importing the modules using await import
    const { default: makeWASocket, useMultiFileAuthState } = await import("@zervonex/baileys");

    const { state, saveCreds } = await useMultiFileAuthState('auth_info_zervonex');

    const sock = makeWASocket({
        auth: state,
        printQRInTerminal: true
    });

    sock.ev.on('creds.update', saveCreds);

    sock.ev.on('connection.update', (update) => {
        const { connection, lastDisconnect } = update;
        if(connection === 'close') {
            console.log('Connection closed, reconnecting...');
            connectToWhatsApp();
        } else if(connection === 'open') {
            console.log('Opened connection successfully via @zervonex/baileys!');
        }
    });
}

connectToWhatsApp();

📦 View on Registry

Take a look at the live release, version history, and dependencies directly over on the npm registry:
👉 View @zervonex/baileys on npm

We are actively looking forward to refining this fork. Feel free to leave a comment below if you have any feature suggestions or compatibility questions!

title: Go Realtime Channel Semantics for Logistics State You Actually Store
description:
A realtime channel should carry a current logistics device event to authorized dashboard clients; it should not be treated as the system that remembers that event. The operational rule is blunt: commit durable device state to a database or log, publish a small notification that identifies the new state, and make every reconnect read from the durable source before resuming the live stream. Scope each connection token to the tenant, facility, and permitted topic, because a browser holding a token is an untrusted client even when the person using it is trusted.

TL;DR: the channel is a delivery path with connection state, not a database. It may retain bytes briefly in network buffers, and an implementation may offer replay, but neither property proves durable storage, complete history, or recovery after a retention boundary. Set separate SLOs for durable ingestion and dashboard freshness, then test the gap between them.

What does a realtime channel remember?

Usually, much less than the application needs.

A channel is a logical route over a transport: subscribers express interest, publishers send messages, and an intermediary or peer connection moves those messages while the relevant session exists. WebSocket standardizes a two-way connection over a single TCP connection. Server-Sent Events provides a one-way browser event stream over HTTP. WebRTC defines peer connections and data channels, with signaling left to the application. Those mechanisms differ, but none turns a shipment-status message into a durable business record by itself.

It helps to separate four kinds of state that are often collapsed into the word "realtime." Transport state includes sockets, sequence numbers, retransmission buffers, and heartbeats. Membership state answers which clients are presently attached. Delivery state may include a cursor, acknowledgement, or bounded replay window. Business state answers where device unit-4821 last reported, when it reported, and whether that observation supersedes an earlier one. Only the last category belongs in the authoritative store. Put another way, what a channel actually retains is an implementation detail with a boundary; what the logistics operation must remember is an application requirement.

This distinction matters for a fleet dashboard. Suppose a tracker reports in_transit at sequence 8142, the dashboard disconnects in an elevator, and sequences 8143 through 8151 arrive while it is away. A green socket indicator after reconnect says nothing about those nine observations. Unless the client supplies a cursor and the server can replay from durable history, the screen may look live while showing stale state.

Still stale.

No outage is required. A tab can sleep. A mobile network can change. A proxy can close an idle connection. Capacity can be exhausted while the database remains healthy. Designing on the assumption that every connected client observes every event confuses a favorable moment with a contract.

Store first, signal second

The safe write path gives persistence authority to one component and notification duty to another. Validate the device observation, enforce tenant ownership, write it with an idempotency key or monotonic device sequence, then publish an event containing the durable record identifier and enough routing metadata for subscribers to decide whether to refresh. If publication fails after commit, an outbox worker can retry. If publication happens before commit, a fast subscriber can request a record that does not exist yet.

That ordering is not decorative architecture. It defines recovery.

The following Go sketch keeps the contract small. The interfaces are generic on purpose; the database and broker can change without changing what a channel means.

package status

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    DeviceID string
    Sequence uint64
    State    string
    SeenAt   time.Time
}

type Event struct {
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    DeviceID string
    Sequence uint64
}

type Store interface {
    CommitWithOutbox(context.Context, Observation, Event) error
    Snapshot(context.Context, string, string, uint64) ([]Observation, error)
}

func Ingest(ctx context.Context, store Store, o Observation) error {
    if o.TenantID == "" || o.SiteID == "" || o.DeviceID == "" {
        return errors.New("missing routing identity")
    }
    if o.Sequence == 0 || o.SeenAt.IsZero() {
        return errors.New("missing ordering data")
    }

    e := Event{
        TenantID: o.TenantID,
        SiteID:   o.SiteID,
        DeviceID: o.DeviceID,
        Sequence: o.Sequence,
    }
    return store.CommitWithOutbox(ctx, o, e)
}

CommitWithOutbox represents one atomic database transaction, not a promise that two unrelated systems can be committed atomically. A relay reads committed outbox rows and publishes them; consumers tolerate duplicates by comparing the per-device sequence. The event is a prompt to fetch or apply a known version. The stored observation remains the recovery source.

The capacity plan must price both paths. For 40,000 connected devices reporting once every 30 seconds, the average ingest rate is about 1,333 observations per second before retries or bursts. If 2,000 dashboard sessions each watch 100 devices, indiscriminate broadcast creates a very different fan-out load from site-scoped delivery. Average rate is inadequate for sizing; test reconnect bursts, shift changes, and buffered device uploads, then define overload behavior before production traffic defines it for you.

Treat every dashboard as an untrusted subscriber

Authentication answers who received a token. Authorization must still constrain what that token can do. A useful channel grant binds at least the tenant, site or fleet partition, allowed operation, intended service, and a short expiry. The server derives subscription permissions from verified claims; it does not accept a tenant ID from the browser and assume the browser chose honestly.

JWT is a token format, not an authorization policy. RFC 8725 calls for validating the algorithm, issuer, and audience and for using explicit typing where confusion between kinds of JWT could occur. OAuth security guidance also warns against bearer-token exposure. A copied bearer token can be used by whoever possesses it until it expires or another control rejects it, so avoid putting it in a URL, log line, analytics payload, or reconnect diagnostic.

Here is a deliberately narrow verifier shape. The cryptographic verifier is injected because key selection, algorithm restrictions, issuer validation, and audience validation belong in a reviewed library-backed boundary, not in handwritten parsing code.

package authz

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Claims struct {
    Subject  string
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    Audience string
    CanRead  bool
    Expires  time.Time
}

type Verifier interface {
    Verify(context.Context, string) (Claims, error)
}

func AuthorizeSubscription(ctx context.Context, v Verifier, raw, tenant, site string, now time.Time) error {
    claims, err := v.Verify(ctx, raw)
    if err != nil {
        return errors.New("invalid channel token")
    }
    if claims.Audience != "status-stream" || !claims.CanRead || !now.Before(claims.Expires) {
        return errors.New("token cannot read status stream")
    }
    if claims.TenantID != tenant || claims.SiteID != site {
        return errors.New("subscription is outside token scope")
    }
    return nil
}

Do not send the durable history in the token. Do not let a wildcard subscription become the convenient default either. Wildcards multiply both the confidentiality impact of a mistake and the fan-out cost of a connection. For an operations screen spanning several sites, mint an explicit grant for that view or authorize a server-side group whose membership is controlled outside the client.

Reconnect from facts, not hope

The reconnect sequence is where the architecture admits what the channel does not store. First, the client requests a snapshot or changes after its last durable cursor. Next, it subscribes to the scoped live route. Finally, it reconciles any overlap by record ID and sequence. A server can reverse the first two steps internally, or establish the subscription before serving the snapshot, to close the race; the invariant is that the client has a cursor-backed bridge between history and live delivery.

A timestamp alone is a weak cursor when device clocks drift or multiple observations share the same timestamp. Prefer a server-assigned monotonic position for the log, while retaining the device sequence for per-device ordering and duplicate detection. Late observations still need a declared rule: event time may describe when the device measured something, but commit position describes when the platform accepted it.

Measure two SLOs separately. The ingest SLO covers accepted observations becoming durable. The freshness SLO covers an authorized dashboard reflecting the latest durable state within a target delay. A transport uptime metric cannot substitute for either one; a connection may be open while the consumer is stalled, unauthorized for the intended partition, or caught up to an incomplete source.

Useful alerts follow those boundaries: outbox age, publish retry rate, subscriber lag by partition, authorization denials, active connection count, and snapshot latency. Avoid tenant IDs and tokens as metric labels. High-cardinality identifiers can overwhelm a telemetry backend, while secrets in labels and logs create a separate incident.

Limitations and trade-offs across the layers

The decision is not "managed realtime or self-hosted realtime" as a single unit. Split it into transport, durable log, authorization, and state storage, because their failure domains and lock-in costs differ. The main limitation of a transient channel is intentional: it is not suitable as the sole record for audit, recovery, or delayed consumers. A durable log can cover those needs, but its trade-off is storage, retention governance, and more complex cursor management. Polling is sometimes the better choice for a small dashboard with loose freshness requirements because it removes persistent-connection operations, although it spends request capacity and detects changes later. These boundaries are how the term is best explained; no transport choice erases them.

Layer Managed service favors Self-hosted favors Exit question
Connection fan-out Lower routine on-call work and faster global rollout Protocol control and placement control Can clients move without changing event semantics?
Durable history Operational support for retention and replication Custom retention, locality, and tuning Can records and cursors be exported with ordering intact?
Token issuance Integration with an existing identity control plane Custom policy and isolated environments Are scopes standard claims or provider-specific rules?
State projection Rapid setup for common query patterns Exact schema, indexing, and reconciliation logic Can the authoritative record be rebuilt independently?

I would reject any design review that answers only with connection count. The capacity envelope needs publish rate, peak fan-out, message size, reconnect rate, replay depth, authorization checks per second, and the maximum tolerable lag. On-call load belongs in the same review: a self-hosted broker that saves a line item but requires expertise the team cannot staff is not cheaper in the engineering sense, while a managed layer whose proprietary cursor infects every client raises the eventual migration cost.

The practical middle ground is common: keep the domain record and cursor contract under application control, then choose operational ownership per layer. This preserves an honest recovery path without pretending infrastructure is interchangeable.

Verify failure and keep rollback boring

Test the contract by breaking the channel while leaving ingestion active. Record the last visible cursor, deliver at least three newer device observations, reconnect, and verify that the dashboard converges to the durable state without missing or double-applying an update. Repeat with duplicated messages, reversed device timestamps, an expired token, a valid token for the wrong site, and a reconnect wave large enough to exercise admission control.

The release gate should include a measurable recovery objective: after a channel interruption, a client with a valid scoped token reaches the latest committed cursor within the dashboard freshness SLO. Verify that an unauthorized site never appears in frames, snapshots, logs, or error details. Security correctness is a data-path property, not a successful login screenshot.

Roll back the live delivery component without rolling back the durable schema or accepting writes into an older incompatible format. During rollback, dashboards can poll the authoritative snapshot endpoint at a controlled interval, with jitter and request limits, while ingestion and outbox accumulation continue. Once live delivery returns, clients perform the same cursor reconciliation used for any reconnect. This is why the fallback is designed before the incident: it shares the source of truth instead of inventing a second one under pressure.

The final decision rule remains small. Persist the observation, authorize the route, and treat the channel as an accelerator. If losing a connection can erase the only copy of device state, the system has assigned storage responsibility to the wrong layer.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700

title: The Lock Type Didn't Make My Locks Faster
description:
A reviewer left one comment on my PR: "swap these lock(_gate) to the new Lock type, it's faster." I'd been meaning to try System.Threading.Lock anyway, and "faster" is the kind of word that gets me to actually do a thing. So I expected to come back with a nice before/after number, paste it in the thread, and feel clever. That's not what the stopwatch said.

Quick refresher on what the type even is. Since .NET 9 there's a real System.Threading.Lock class, and in C# 13 the lock statement knows about it. When you write lock(x) and x is a Lock, the compiler stops emitting Monitor.Enter/Monitor.Exit and lowers it to x.EnterScope() instead, which returns a disposable scope. Same keyword you've typed a thousand times, different machinery underneath. The pitch is a leaner lock that doesn't lean on the object header the way monitors do.

What I measured

I wanted the simplest honest question first: single thread, no contention, how long does it take to just grab and release the lock 50 million times while bumping a counter. Uncontended acquire/release is the path that runs on every lock you've ever written, contended or not, so if there's a cheap win hiding anywhere it should show up here.

object _objectGate = new();
Lock _lockGate = new();

// A: the classic, Monitor under the hood
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    lock (_objectGate) { c++; }

// B: same keyword, Lock type -> compiler calls EnterScope()
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    lock (_lockGate) { c++; }

// C: the explicit form B lowers to
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    using (_lockGate.EnterScope()) { c++; }

Conditions, so you can weigh the numbers: .NET 10, Release build, 50M acquisitions per round, best-of-9 after a warmup, running in a small 2-core Linux container. That's not a lab bench and I'm not pretending it is. I care about the ratio between A, B and C on the same box in the same breath, not the absolute nanoseconds.

The numbers that didn't cooperate

First run:

[A: lock(object)     ] best= 822.6 ms   16.45 ns/op
[B: lock(Lock)       ] best= 882.4 ms   17.65 ns/op
[C: Lock.EnterScope()] best= 801.9 ms   16.04 ns/op
B vs A speedup: 0.93x

So the new type came out slower than the plain object. I ran it again figuring I'd caught a bad round:

[A: lock(object)     ] best= 927.8 ms   18.56 ns/op
[B: lock(Lock)       ] best= 802.9 ms   16.06 ns/op
B vs A speedup: 1.16x

Now Lock is ahead by 16%. Run it a third time and it's 1.12x. The honest read isn't "Lock is 0.93x" or "Lock is 1.16x" — it's that on this box, in the uncontended path, the two are a coin flip. Everything lands in the 16–18 ns/op band and the ordering swaps depending on which run I squint at. There is no free 2x here. There's barely a difference I'd stake a sentence on.

That's the part I want to be straight about, because it would've been easy to run until I got the 1.16x round and paste only that. The win I went looking for isn't in this benchmark.

So why switch, then?

Here's the turn, and it's why I still took the reviewer's advice. The reason to reach for Lock was never the raw speed of an uncontended acquire — it's that the type closes a door you didn't know was open. With lock(someObject) you can lock on anything: a string, a boxed value, a public field some other class can also see and lock on. Every one of those is a bug waiting for a bad day. With a Lock field, the type says exactly what it's for, and if you try to lock something that isn't a Lock the compiler's fine but you've clearly signaled intent. The bigger one for me: the analyzer now flags await inside a lock(Lock) scope, because you can't hold an EnterScope() across an await. The old pattern let that compile and then deadlock in production at 2am.

So the value is the stuff that doesn't show up on a stopwatch at all. Clearer ownership, a type that can't be misused as a public gate, a compiler that catches the await-inside-lock footgun. The performance is, at worst, a wash, and the design is better. That's a fine trade — I just can't sell it with the number I thought I'd have.

My honest opinion: migrate your locks to Lock as you touch the code, not in a big mechanical sweep. A dedicated Lock field is the better default for new code and I'd push back in review on a fresh lock(new object()). But if you're eyeing a repo-wide find-and-replace because someone told you it's faster, don't. You'll burn a day and a risky diff chasing a speedup that, uncontended, isn't there. And note what I did not test honestly: heavy multi-threaded contention is where Lock's design is actually supposed to pay off, and two cores in a container is the worst possible place to measure that. I'm not going to hand you a contention number I don't trust.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself — a net10.0 console app, dotnet run -c Release. Nudge Iterations and Rounds to fit your box:

using System.Diagnostics;

const int Iterations = 50_000_000;
const int Rounds = 9;

object _objectGate = new();
Lock _lockGate = new();
long counter = 0;

// warm up both paths before timing
RunObjectLock(1_000_000, ref counter);
RunTypedLock(1_000_000, ref counter);
RunTypedLockExplicit(1_000_000, ref counter);
counter = 0;

Console.WriteLine($"iterations per round: {Iterations:N0}, rounds: {Rounds}");
Console.WriteLine($"processor count: {Environment.ProcessorCount}\n");

var objectMs   = BestOf(Rounds, () => RunObjectLock(Iterations, ref counter));
var typedMs    = BestOf(Rounds, () => RunTypedLock(Iterations, ref counter));
var explicitMs = BestOf(Rounds, () => RunTypedLockExplicit(Iterations, ref counter));

Report("A: lock(object)     ", objectMs, Iterations);
Report("B: lock(Lock)       ", typedMs, Iterations);
Report("C: Lock.EnterScope()", explicitMs, Iterations);
Console.WriteLine($"\nB vs A speedup: {objectMs / typedMs:F2}x");

double RunObjectLock(int n, ref long c)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (_objectGate) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    return sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
}

double RunTypedLock(int n, ref long c)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (_lockGate) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    return sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
}

double RunTypedLockExplicit(int n, ref long c)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) using (_lockGate.EnterScope()) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    return sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
}

static double BestOf(int rounds, Func<double> run)
{
    double best = double.MaxValue;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++) best = Math.Min(best, run());
    return best;
}

static void Report(string label, double ms, int iterations) =>
    Console.WriteLine($"[{label}] best={ms,7:F1} ms   {ms * 1_000_000.0 / iterations,5:F2} ns/op");

Have you swapped your locks over yet, and did you see anything on the clock, or was it a wash for you too? Curious whether a beefier box with real contention tells a different story.

Munchable's marketing site is a Next.js app with 426 URLs and one stylesheet. Not one stylesheet per component: one file, app/globals.css, 3,133 lines, imported once in the root layout.

$ find apps/web -name '*.module.css' | wc -l
0
$ grep -iE 'tailwind|styled|emotion|vanilla-extract' apps/web/package.json
$ ls apps/web | grep -iE 'postcss|tailwind'

Three empty results. The runtime dependencies are Next, React, Supabase, Stripe, Drizzle, Resend, OpenAI and the two workspace packages. There is no CSS tooling in the project at all, because globals.css is plain CSS that the browser could parse as typed: no nesting, no preprocessor, two !important in the whole file.

I did not set out to defend that. I set out to find out whether it had quietly become a problem, which meant counting. The counting is the interesting part.

Where the lines went

The file is divided by section comments, and they make it easy to measure:

Section Lines
Hero demo: the app scanning a real looking product 676
Feature-row phones 540
Support page 190
App store buttons 173
Legal + status pages 146
Editorial pages: conditions, ingredients, answers 148
Pricing 135
Everything else ~1,125

The top two entries are the same thing twice. They draw phones. The landing page shows the app running, five times, and none of those are screenshots: they are divs, spans and inline SVG, animated in CSS. I wrote about the decision to have zero images on that page separately; what I had never done is measure the bill.

1,216 lines, 38.8% of the stylesheet, for decoration on one page. The two prefixes those sections use, .sd- and .pm-, account for 78 of the 221 distinct class names in the file. A third of the stylesheet, and a third of its vocabulary, is scenery.

Now the other direction. 420 of the site's 426 URLs are the condition guides, the answer pages and the recipes. Every one of them renders into the same shell:

$ grep -rl 'legal-inner' apps/web/app --include='*.tsx'
privacy  licenses  answers  [question]  terms  about  recipes  recipes/[slug]  conditions  conditions/[slug]

.legal is a single readable column with type rules on it, 146 lines, and the editorial section that extends it for the guides is another 148. 294 lines carry 420 pages. Four lines of CSS per decorative phone-pixel, and seven-tenths of a line per page of actual content.

I want to be clear that this is not a complaint. Those 1,216 lines are the thing a visitor looks at for the first four seconds, and the 294 are a column of text that is supposed to get out of the way. The ratio is upside down relative to page count and right side up relative to attention. But I did not know the number before I counted it, and "where is my CSS" turned out to be a much better question than "how much CSS do I have".

What makes one global file survivable

The failure mode of a single global stylesheet is not length. It is two people writing .card for different cards. Four things keep that from happening here, and only one of them is a technique.

Prefix per section. .sd- is the scan demo, .pm- is the phone mock, .cond- is the condition guides, .nf- is the 404. The prefix is the module boundary, hand-maintained, visible in the markup. It is what CSS modules would give you automatically, bought with discipline instead of a build step.

Flat selectors. The deepest selector in the file is six parts, and the overwhelming majority are one or two. Nothing is written to out-specify anything else, which is why there are two !important rather than a hundred.

The section comments are the table of contents, and they say why rather than what:

/* ── Editorial pages: conditions, ingredients, food ──────────────────────────
   These share the .legal shell (a single readable column) and add the few
   extras the guides need. */

A token block at the top, 28 custom properties. Colours, three radii, two shadows, the max width, three font stacks. Every rule below pulls from them, so a brand change is a change to the top of one file.

That last one is a deliberate duplicate. The app's palette lives in @munchable/design-tokens, a workspace package the app, the web app and the video renderer all import. This file keeps its own copy, and why the copy is the right call is a decision I stand behind: a CSS custom property and a TypeScript constant are different artefacts, and generating one from the other buys consistency the design does not actually want. The marketing site is allowed to have a warmer section background than any app screen.

The markup side of the ledger 

className attributes across app/ and components/ : 558
.tsx files in those directories                  : 60
inline style objects                             : 2

Nine class attributes per file, and essentially no inline styles. That second number is the one I would watch. Inline styles are where a global stylesheet goes to die: the moment it becomes easier to write style={{ marginTop: 12 }} than to find out whether a utility exists, the file stops being the source of truth and starts being a historical record. Two is a number you can keep at two by looking at it occasionally.

When I would stop doing this

Honestly: when a second person joins, or when the site stops being mostly one page plus three templates.

The entire reason this works is that the site has a small number of page shapes. One landing page with a lot of bespoke art, one editorial shell used by 420 URLs, one form page, one admin area with its own file. A global stylesheet scales with the number of distinct page shapes, not with the number of pages, and those are wildly different numbers here.

What I would not do is adopt a framework to solve a problem I measured and did not find. The counting took ten minutes and answered the question better than any amount of opinion about utility classes would have.

See it working

  • munchable.app is the 1,216 lines. The phones are live DOM: zoom in, select the text on one of them, watch the scan animation run its four phases.
  • munchable.app/conditions/low-fodmap-ibs is the 294 lines, and so is is onion low FODMAP, and so are the other 418.
  • munchable.app/recipes/gentle-rice-congee is the same shell again with a recipe in it.

Reader's exercise, since the numbers above came out of the repository: open DevTools on the landing page and on any answer page and compare what is actually in the cascade for each. The gap is the post.

title: Amazon Braket now in scope for FedRAMP Class C
description:
Amazon Braket is now in scope for FedRAMP Class C in AWS US Regions where Braket is available. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is a US government-wide program that delivers a standard approach to the security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products and services.

With FedRAMP Class C authorization, government customers and the organizations that serve them can use Amazon Braket to explore quantum computing within an authorized boundary. The AWS-operated components of Braket, including the API and SDK, job orchestration and management, compilation, and result storage in Amazon S3, are within the FedRAMP-certified boundary, while quantum workloads execute on third-party Quantum Hardware Providers (QHPs) outside that boundary. All data sent to QHPs meets AWS' privacy and security requirements including removal of all personally identifiable information, data encryption in transit and at rest, and adherence to AWS' standard data retention and deletion policies.

To learn more about FedRAMP, visit AWS FedRAMP services and the FedRAMP Marketplace. To learn more about Amazon Braket, visit the Braket product page and Getting Started on Braket resources.

Regional Availability: US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon)

title: Why we built a blockchain with one vote per person
description:
Most blockchains say they are decentralized, but voting power usually follows money: more hardware or more coins means a bigger voice. We wanted to try the opposite, so we built MADAR Network: an independent layer-1 chain where every approved operator has exactly one vote.

The idea

  • One vote per person. An operator's weight does not grow with balance or hardware.
  • No master key. There is no sudo; every change to the rules needs two of three committee approvals.
  • It survives without us. Nodes find each other on their own; our website and servers are outside consensus.
  • Safety before liveness. If a safe decision cannot be made, the network pauses rather than accept a wrong history.

Why not invent new consensus?

We deliberately used proven parts: Polkadot SDK, BABE for block production and GRANDPA for finality, with no changes to the consensus algorithms. Our own work sits in a separate admission layer.

The hard part: one person, one vote

The real challenge is stopping one person from posing as many. Our answer at this stage is honest and slow:

  • The committee approves each new operator after talking to them directly, at most one new operator per day.
  • We never ask for ID documents or photos.
  • The approved account solves a memory-hard puzzle (pass or fail, so a faster machine gains nothing), and a fair draw picks who joins each round.

It is not perfect, and the whitepaper says where it is weak. But it keeps growth deliberate while the network learns.

Running a node should be simple

Operators install a desktop app, register, and after approval one button turns on voting. The app creates the voting keys on the operator's own computer and renews membership on time.

Where we are

MADAR is a public testnet today. The currency, MDR, only starts with the mainnet. We are now looking for the first ten independent operators in different places.

  • Whitepaper (English / Arabic): https://madar-network.com/whitepaper/
  • Source code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/MADAR-NETWORK/MADAR
  • Become an operator: https://madar-network.com/operators/

Questions and criticism are welcome in the comments.

This article was written with the help of an AI assistant and reviewed by the MADAR team.

title: The trust account invariant: one bank balance, many owners, and the check that catches commingling
description:
A property manager's trust account obeys one invariant: bank balance = every owner's balance + every security deposit held, at every moment. A second rule catches quieter commingling: no single owner's balance may go below zero, because if it does, another owner's money paid that owner's bill. Check both after every posting, not only at month end.

I work on ZeraBooks, and this is the cleanest data model I know for trust money. Below is a Python sketch. All figures are fictional and match the worked month on our property management page.

How do you model a trust account in code? 

from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal as D

class Trust:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bank = D("0")
        self.owner = defaultdict(lambda: D("0"))     # owed to each owner
        self.deposits = defaultdict(lambda: D("0"))  # held for each owner's tenants

    def post(self, owner: str, amount: D, kind: str):
        """amount is signed from the bank's view: + in, - out."""
        self.bank += amount
        if kind == "deposit":
            self.deposits[owner] += amount
        else:
            self.owner[owner] += amount
        self.check(owner)

    def check(self, owner: str):
        held = sum(self.owner.values()) + sum(self.deposits.values())
        assert self.bank == held, f"bank {self.bank} vs held {held}: does not reconcile"
        assert self.owner[owner] >= 0, f"{owner} is negative: another owner's money was used"

The first assertion is the reconciliation. The second is the one most spreadsheets don't have.

What does a clean month in the trust account look like?

Twelve units, three owners, an 8% fee on rent collected. The trust opens May with $9,600 of deposits.

t = Trust()
for owner, amt in [("Maple", "4800"), ("Elm", "3200"), ("Cedar", "1600")]:
    t.post(owner, D(amt), "deposit")                 # opening deposits, 9,600

t.post("Maple", D("8700.00"), "rent")
t.post("Elm",   D("6400.00"), "rent")
t.post("Elm",   D("75.00"),   "late fee")            # owner's under this agreement
t.post("Cedar", D("4200.00"), "rent")
t.post("Cedar", D("2100.00"), "deposit")             # new tenant

for owner, fee in [("Maple", "696.00"), ("Elm", "512.00"), ("Cedar", "336.00")]:
    t.post(owner, -D(fee), "fee to operating")

t.post("Maple", D("-640.00"), "repair")
t.post("Elm",   D("-380.00"), "repair")

for owner, paid in [("Maple", "7364.00"), ("Elm", "5583.00"), ("Cedar", "3864.00")]:
    t.post(owner, -D(paid), "owner payout")

print(t.bank, dict(t.owner), sum(t.deposits.values()))
# 11700.00, every owner balance 0.00, deposits 11700.00
Trust account, May Maple Court Elm Street Cedar Lane Total
Rent collected 8,700.00 6,400.00 4,200.00 19,300.00
Late fee 0.00 75.00 0.00 75.00
Management fee at 8% (696.00) (512.00) (336.00) (1,544.00)
Repairs paid (640.00) (380.00) 0.00 (1,020.00)
Paid out to owner (7,364.00) (5,583.00) (3,864.00) (16,811.00)
Owner balance, May 31 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00

Every post passes both assertions. On May 31 the bank shows $11,700.00, exactly the deposits held.


The bank side of the same idea in ZeraBooks: deposits, withdrawals and net must agree with the statement before a month is signed off.

How does commingling show up in the data?

Run the same month in a different order. Pay the Elm Street plumber on May 2, before Elm's rent has come in:

t = Trust()
# ...opening deposits as above...
t.post("Elm", D("-380.00"), "repair")
# AssertionError: Elm is negative: another owner's money was used

The bank balance is still positive, and the first assertion still holds, because the bank doesn't know whose money is whose. The $380 came out of money that belongs to Maple's owner or Cedar's tenants. In many states, that is what trust account rules prohibit, even if Elm's rent arrives the next day.

A month-end reconciliation can pass even when an owner went negative for two weeks in the middle. Check after every posting.

No code fixes this after the fact. The practice does: pay a repair from trust only when that owner's balance covers it, or have the owner fund a reserve first.

Which design choices keep the model honest?

  1. Keep deposits separate from owner balances. Both are liabilities, but deposits belong to tenants. An owner payout should never reach into the deposit total.
  2. Move fees out of trust as a transfer. The 8% fee is the manager's income only once it has moved to the operating account. In the trust model it is money leaving that owner's balance.
  3. Check after every post. Month-end checks miss mid-month negatives.
  4. Use Decimal for money. The invariant is an equality to the cent, and float sums drift.

Key takeaways

  • Invariant: trust bank balance = owner balances + deposits held, always.
  • Second rule: no owner below zero, or another owner's money paid their bill.
  • In the worked May, $1,544.00 of fees moved to operating and the trust closed at $11,700.00, all deposits.
  • Assert after every posting; month-end reconciliation alone can hide commingling.

FAQ

Why can the bank balance be fine while trust rules are broken?

Because the bank balance is a total. It can't tell whose money paid a bill. Only per-owner balances show that.

Is a security deposit an owner's money?

No. It is a liability to the tenant until the lease ends, so it is tracked apart from what is owed to the owner.

Does ZeraBooks keep tenant ledgers?

No. ZeraBooks is a general ledger, not property management software. It has no tenant ledgers, rent collection or portals; managers send reports from their property software.

The full month, with the owner statement mapped to Schedule E lines, is in the guide to bookkeeping for property management. Disclosure: I'm on the ZeraBooks team. ZeraBooks bookkeeping services reconcile trust and operating accounts monthly from uploaded statements, from $150 a month in U.S. dollars.

title: OAuth Test Tokens Need a Trust Boundary
description:
OAuth tests often stop at “the token was returned.” That proves the protocol completed, but it does not prove that the right client, tenant, user, or scope received access. A test token can be cryptographically valid and still represent a broken security boundary.

This matters most when a suite creates many short-lived accounts, uses disposable temporary email, or runs several OAuth flows in parallel. Test data is convenient, but it can hide a mix-up between identities. A useful test should explain not only that authentication succeeded, but why this token was allowed to exist.

What a test token should prove

A well-scoped OAuth test should answer five questions:

  • Which client initiated the authorization request?
  • Which test user and tenant approved it?
  • Which scopes were requested and which were granted?
  • Which redirect or device context was used?
  • Was this token issued once for this exact flow?

The access token itself may not carry enough information to answer all of them. Keep a server-side test record with a flow ID, client ID, subject ID, tenant ID, requested scopes, granted scopes, creation time, expiry, and consumption state. The record is the explanation behind the token.

Its easy to confuse “the API accepted my bearer token” with “the authorization policy worked.” Add assertions for audience, issuer, scopes, tenant ownership, and expiry. If the suite checks only a 200 response, a token for the wrong account can pass unnoticed.

Threat model the fixture boundary

The main threat is cross-test confusion. Imagine two workers requesting tokens at nearly the same time. One worker polls for a code, reads a message from a shared inbox, and completes the other worker's flow. Both tests may pass, while the system has just demonstrated that identity separation is weak.

There are quieter failures too. A token can leak through CI logs, a copied environment variable, a failed snapshot, or a support artifact. A test tenant may be deleted while its token remains usable. A mock authorization server can also become too permissive, teaching the suite that any client or scope combination is acceptable.

Model these as boundaries, not as random test flakiness:

  1. Client boundary: the authorization request and token exchange must use the same registered client.
  2. User boundary: the approved subject must match the account that the test created.
  3. Tenant boundary: resources must reject a token issued for a different tenant.
  4. Scope boundary: the granted set must be no broader than the approved set.
  5. Time boundary: the code and token must expire on a predictable schedule.

When a failure occurs, store identifiers and timestamps, not full tokens or message bodies. Reproducible email checks with Git diffs offers a related debugging lesson: small, reviewable evidence is more useful than an enormous capture of everything.

Keep scope and tenant state immutable

Once authorization starts, treat the client, tenant, redirect URI, and requested scope set as immutable. If a test needs different permissions, create a new flow. Updating one shared fixture in place feels efficient, but it makes replay and race conditions hard to reason about.

The token endpoint should validate the stored record before issuing anything:

if flow.expired or flow.consumed:
    reject()
if request.client_id != flow.client_id:
    reject()
if not requested_scopes <= flow.approved_scopes:
    reject()
if request.code != flow.device_code:
    reject()
consume_once(flow)
issue_token(flow.subject, flow.tenant, flow.approved_scopes)

The pseudocode is intentionally boring. Security tests benefit from boring state transitions. consume_once must be atomic under concurrency, and a retry after success should return a terminal result rather than minting another token.

The same rule applies to email verification around the flow. A message should be tied to one flow ID, one recipient, and one expected action. Keeping auth email state aligned is a useful companion pattern for ensuring that the UI, API, and message state do not silently disagree.

Use disposable email without making identity claims

Disposable email can be practical for isolated OAuth fixtures because it reduces the chance of touching a real inbox. It is a test transport, not proof of a person's identity, trustworthiness, or authorization intent. Do not let an address pattern decide whether a token is valid.

Give each worker a unique mailbox or message correlation value. Match on recipient, flow ID, and a bounded time window. A fixture should expire quick after the test finishes, and cleanup should revoke issued tokens where the provider supports it. Test strings such as “temp org mail” may appear in generated addresses, but they are not a security signal by themselves.

Avoid putting the address, authorization code, or token in a URL that can reach analytics or referrer logs. Redact them from failed assertions too. A short error such as “expected flow 812 to be consumed” is safer and usually more actionable than printing the entire message.

A safer review checklist

Before relying on an OAuth test suite, check the following:

  • Does every token assertion include client, subject, tenant, audience, scope, and expiry?
  • Can parallel workers ever read from the same mailbox without a correlation key?
  • Are authorization records single-use and consumed atomically?
  • Does the test server reject a changed client, redirect, tenant, or scope set?
  • Are test tokens short-lived, revocable, and absent from logs and snapshots?
  • Does a failed email wait identify the flow without exposing message contents?
  • Are the scopes is checked against the approved set rather than just the requested set?
  • Is cleanup safe if the test runner stops halfway through?

The goal is not to make test authentication look exactly like production. The goal is to preserve the important trust boundaries while keeping the fixtures small and disposable. A valid token is only one signal. When the suite records who requested it, what was approved, where it belongs, and when it must stop working, OAuth failures become security findings instead of mysterious green builds.

title: AI Gateway adds unified fast mode support
description:
AI Gateway has a unified fast mode abstraction, now in beta.

You can now request fast mode the same way for every model on AI Gateway. Set speed to fast, and the gateway serves the fast tier when it's available and falls back to standard speed when it isn't.

Fast mode trades a higher per-token cost for lower latency or higher throughput. You get it wherever it is available, without pinning a provider or wiring anything up yourself.

Requesting fast mode

Set speed to fast under providerOptions.gateway to upgrade the model to its fast serving path when one is routable:

You can also address a fast variant directly with its fast slug, such as anthropic/claude-opus-5-fast, which is the same as setting speed: 'fast' on the base model.

Use the speed option when you want to stay on the base model ID and fall back to standard speed. Use a fast slug when you want to name the fast variant directly, for example in a gateway.models fallback list. The speed option works across every AI Gateway API format.

Fast mode is available for a growing set of models. Find them in the models list with a lightning bolt next to the slug. Requesting fast mode on a model with no fast tier has no effect, and the request runs at standard speed. Fast variants of models are usually more expensive than the base model: check pricing for more details.

Using fast mode in coding agents

In Claude Code, toggle fast mode with /fast for Anthropic Opus models after setup. For other agents, select a fast slug in your model configuration, such as anthropic/claude-opus-5-fast.

For more information about fast mode, read the documentation.

title: Ten steps at 99% is 90%: retrying multi-step jobs
description:
Part 4 of 10: Reliable background jobs in Node.js, from zero.

By Sandro Dezerio, senior full-stack engineer.

The signup scenario is made up. It is the same one used in Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3. The failure rates come from a simulation with stated assumptions, not from real services.

A job with ten steps, where each step works 99% of the time, finishes about 90% of the time.

Nobody looks at a step that works 99% of the time and calls it unreliable. That is why the problem hides. Each step looks fine on its own, and the job as a whole fails about once in every ten runs.

In Part 3, every job was a single call: send one welcome email. Real jobs are rarely that small. This post looks at a job with several steps, shows what goes wrong when you retry it as one piece, and fixes it with the withRetry wrapper from Part 3, unchanged.

The job grows

Picture the signup job some time later. Sending the welcome email is no longer enough. The job now does ten things, in order:

  1. Save the user
  2. Create the billing customer
  3. Create the workspace
  4. Upload the default avatar
  5. Add the user to the CRM
  6. Subscribe the user to the newsletter
  7. Send the welcome email
  8. Notify the sales channel
  9. Record the analytics event
  10. Schedule the day-3 email

Each step calls something that can fail: a database, a payment provider, an email provider, an internal API. Assume each call fails 1% of the time, independently of the others. For a single call, 99% is a respectable number.

The arithmetic

Reliability multiplies. For the job to succeed, all ten steps must succeed, so the chance is 0.99 multiplied by itself ten times:

0.9910 = 0.904

About 96 jobs in every 1,000 fail somewhere along the way. With twenty steps, it would be about 18 in every 100.

To check this, and to see what each fix does, I wrote a simulation that runs 1,000,000 signup jobs through the queue from Part 2. Without retries, 90.398% of the jobs succeeded. The formula gives 90.438%, so the simulation and the math agree within sampling noise.

The failure rate is only half of the problem. Of the 96,024 jobs that failed, 85,902 failed after at least one step had already done its work. The user exists but has no workspace. The billing customer exists, but nobody got the welcome email. A failed job is often a half-finished job.

The obvious fix: retry the whole job

Part 3 already has a retry wrapper. The quickest fix is to wrap the whole job in withRetry, the same way Part 3 wrapped the email handler. With up to 3 attempts, the success rate jumps from 90.398% to 99.913%. That looks like a win, but the job now has a different problem.

When step 8 fails, the retry starts again from step 1. It saves the user again, creates the billing customer again, and sends the welcome email again. In the simulation, retrying the whole job did 462,891 steps a second time, and 29,564 users received the welcome email more than once. Nobody asked for either.

Some repeats are harmless, such as recording an analytics event twice. Others are not, such as a second billing customer for the same user.

The better fix: retry each step

The fix is to retry the step that failed, not the job. If step 8 fails, try step 8 again. Steps 1 to 7 already worked, so leave them alone.

The code adds one small file, workflow.ts. A job becomes a list of named steps, and the queue from Part 2 and the retry wrapper from Part 3 do not change:

import type { Handler } from "./queue.ts";
import { withRetry, type RetryOptions } from "./retry.ts";

/** One step of a job: a name and the work it does. */
export type Step<T> = { name: string; run: Handler<T> };

/** Run the steps in order. If one throws, the job stops there and the queue records the error. */
export function workflow<T>(steps: Step<T>[]): Handler<T> {
  return async (job) => {
    for (const step of steps) {
      await step.run(job);
    }
  };
}

/** Give each step its own retries, so a failing step never repeats the steps before it. */
export function retryEachStep<T>(steps: Step<T>[], options: RetryOptions): Step<T>[] {
  return steps.map((step) => ({ name: step.name, run: withRetry(step.run, options) }));
}

workflow turns a list of steps into a normal handler, so the queue does not need to know that the job has steps. retryEachStep wraps each step with withRetry from Part 3. The two strategies differ only in where the wrapper goes:

  • Whole job: withRetry(workflow(steps), options)
  • Each step: workflow(retryEachStep(steps, options))

Here is how a job with two steps looks:

import { SimpleQueue, type Job } from "./queue.ts";
import { retryEachStep, workflow, type Step } from "./workflow.ts";

const steps: Step<string>[] = [
  { name: "save the user", run: async (job: Job<string>) => console.log(`saving ${job.data}`) },
  { name: "send the welcome email", run: async (job: Job<string>) => console.log(`emailing ${job.data}`) },
];

const queue = new SimpleQueue<string>(
  workflow(retryEachStep(steps, { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 100, maxDelayMs: 2000, jitter: true })),
);
queue.add("ana@example.com");

The three strategies side by side

These are the results for 1,000,000 simulated signups, with up to 3 attempts in both retry strategies:

Strategy Succeeded Failed jobs Failed after some steps were done Calls per job Steps done again Users with 2+ welcome emails
No retries 90.398% 96,024 85,902 9.56 0 0
Retry the whole job 99.913% 867 865 10.57 462,891 29,564
Retry each step 99.999% 9 8 10.1 0 0

Retrying each step beats retrying the whole job in every column. Only 9 jobs failed out of 1,000,000. No step ran twice. And it made fewer calls than retrying the whole job (10.1 per job compared with 10.57), because a retry repeats one call instead of several.

The success rates also match the formulas. Retrying the whole job needs one attempt in which all ten steps pass, so a job fails only when all three attempts fail: 1 - (1 - 0.9910)3 = 99.913%. Retrying each step needs each step to fail three times in a row, which happens once in a million calls: (1 - 0.013)10 = 99.999%.

Inngest, a tool for running multi-step workflows, uses the same idea: "Each step.run() has its own retry counter, so one failing step does not restart earlier completed steps."

What retrying each step does not fix

A step that worked but did not say so. Sometimes the email provider sends the email, and the reply gets lost on the way back. The step sees a timeout and fails. A retry of that step sends the email again. I ran the simulation again with a lost reply on the email step 0.5% of the time:

Strategy Succeeded Steps done again Users with 2+ welcome emails
Retry each step, reply lost 0.5% of the time 99.999% 4,971 4,939

Retrying each step cannot tell the difference between "it did not happen" and "it happened, but I did not hear back." That is the job of an idempotency key, which Part 5 (coming soon) covers.

The jobs that still fail. Of the 9 failed jobs, 8 stopped halfway through, with some steps done. Per-step retries make this rare, but not impossible, and queue.failed does not say which step failed or which steps already ran. Later parts cover where these jobs go (Part 7) and how to see what happened to each one (Part 8).

Failures that come together. The simulation assumes every call fails independently. Real failures are often correlated: if the email provider is down for five minutes, all three attempts fail. Treat these numbers as a way to build intuition, not as a prediction.

A restart. The queue still lives in memory. If the process dies after step 4, nothing remembers that steps 1 to 4 were done. Part 6 moves the queue to Redis.

Takeaways

  1. Reliability multiplies: ten steps at 99% give a job that succeeds about 90% of the time.
  2. Retry the step that failed, not the whole job, so the steps that worked do not run again.
  3. Per-step retries still repeat a step whose reply was lost, so side effects need idempotency keys.

Try it

This is a teaching version of multi-step jobs. A more complete implementation comes later in the series. Keep queue.ts from Part 2 and retry.ts from Part 3, and save the workflow.ts file from above next to them. Then save this as simulate.ts:

import { SimpleQueue, type Handler } from "./queue.ts";
import { withRetry, type RetryOptions } from "./retry.ts";
import { retryEachStep, workflow, type Step } from "./workflow.ts";

// Illustrative assumptions (not a real system):
const JOBS = 1_000_000; // signups to simulate
const P_FAIL = 0.01;    // every call to a step fails 1% of the time, independently
const LOST_REPLY = 0.005; // table 2 only: the email goes out, but the reply is lost 0.5% of the time
const STEPS = [
  "save the user", "create the billing customer", "create the workspace", "upload the default avatar",
  "add to the CRM", "subscribe to the newsletter", "send the welcome email", "notify the sales channel",
  "record the analytics event", "schedule the day-3 email",
];
const EMAIL = "send the welcome email";
// Up to 3 attempts. The simulation counts outcomes, not time, so it skips the waits.
const retry: RetryOptions = { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 100, maxDelayMs: 2000, jitter: true, sleep: async () => {} };

// A small seeded random generator (mulberry32), so every run prints the same numbers.
function seededRandom(seed: number) {
  let a = seed;
  return () => {
    a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}

// What each signup job carries: how many times each step really did its work.
type Signup = { done: Record<string, number> };

async function simulate(build: (steps: Step<Signup>[]) => Handler<Signup>, lostReply: number) {
  const random = seededRandom(1);
  let calls = 0;
  const steps: Step<Signup>[] = STEPS.map((name) => ({
    name,
    run: async (job) => {
      calls++;
      if (random() < P_FAIL) throw new Error(`${name}: 503 service unavailable`);
      job.data.done[name] = (job.data.done[name] ?? 0) + 1; // the side effect happened
      if (name === EMAIL && random() < lostReply) throw new Error(`${name}: timeout, reply lost`);
    },
  }));
  const queue = new SimpleQueue<Signup>(build(steps));
  let repeatedSteps = 0;
  let twoEmails = 0;
  for (let start = 0; start < JOBS; start += 10_000) {
    const batch: Signup[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
      const signup: Signup = { done: {} };
      batch.push(signup);
      queue.add(signup);
    }
    await queue.onIdle();
    for (const signup of batch) {
      for (const times of Object.values(signup.done)) repeatedSteps += times - 1;
      if ((signup.done[EMAIL] ?? 0) > 1) twoEmails++;
    }
  }
  const failed = queue.failed.length;
  return {
    succeeded: `${((100 * (JOBS - failed)) / JOBS).toFixed(3)}%`,
    failed,
    halfDone: queue.failed.filter(({ job }) => Object.keys(job.data.done).length > 0).length,
    callsPerJob: Math.round((calls / JOBS) * 100) / 100,
    repeatedSteps,
    twoEmails,
  };
}

const pct = (p: number) => `${(100 * p).toFixed(3)}%`;
const oneTry = (1 - P_FAIL) ** STEPS.length;

async function main() {
  console.log(`1. ${JOBS.toLocaleString("en-US")} signups, ${STEPS.length} steps, each call fails ${P_FAIL * 100}% of the time`);
  console.table([
    { strategy: "no retries", formula: pct(oneTry), ...(await simulate((s) => workflow(s), 0)) },
    { strategy: "retry the whole job", formula: pct(1 - (1 - oneTry) ** 3), ...(await simulate((s) => withRetry(workflow(s), retry), 0)) },
    { strategy: "retry each step", formula: pct((1 - P_FAIL ** 3) ** STEPS.length), ...(await simulate((s) => workflow(retryEachStep(s, retry)), 0)) },
  ]);
  console.log(`2. Same, but the email provider loses the reply ${LOST_REPLY * 100}% of the time`);
  console.table([
    { strategy: "retry each step", ...(await simulate((s) => workflow(retryEachStep(s, retry)), LOST_REPLY)) },
  ]);
}
main();

Run it with Node.js 22, the version I tested:

pnpm dlx tsx simulate.ts

It runs 4,000,000 jobs, so it takes 15 to 20 seconds. The random generator is seeded, so you should see exactly these numbers:

1. 1,000,000 signups, 10 steps, each call fails 1% of the time
┌─────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────┬───────────┬────────┬──────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬───────────┐
│ (index) │ strategy              │ formula   │ succeeded │ failed │ halfDone │ callsPerJob │ repeatedSteps │ twoEmails │
├─────────┼───────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼───────────┤
│ 0       │ 'no retries'          │ '90.438%' │ '90.398%' │ 96024  │ 85902    │ 9.56        │ 0             │ 0         │
│ 1       │ 'retry the whole job' │ '99.913%' │ '99.913%' │ 867    │ 865      │ 10.57       │ 462891        │ 29564     │
│ 2       │ 'retry each step'     │ '99.999%' │ '99.999%' │ 9      │ 8        │ 10.1        │ 0             │ 0         │
└─────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────┴────────┴──────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴───────────┘
2. Same, but the email provider loses the reply 0.5% of the time
┌─────────┬───────────────────┬───────────┬────────┬──────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬───────────┐
│ (index) │ strategy          │ succeeded │ failed │ halfDone │ callsPerJob │ repeatedSteps │ twoEmails │
├─────────┼───────────────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼───────────┤
│ 0       │ 'retry each step' │ '99.999%' │ 11     │ 10       │ 10.11       │ 4971          │ 4939      │
└─────────┴───────────────────┴───────────┴────────┴──────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴───────────┘

Change P_FAIL or add steps to STEPS and see how quickly the "no retries" row drops.

Previous: How to retry failed jobs in Node.js without making it worse (Part 3).

Next: Part 5 (coming soon) looks at jobs that run twice and how idempotency keys stop the duplicates.

title: Study Copilot: Building an AI Agent That Acts on Connected Learning Data
description:
Study Copilot: Building an AI Agent That Acts on Connected Learning Data

Why we built it

Students are surrounded by courses, articles, quizzes, and notes, but the difficult question is often simple: what should I do next? A flat resource list cannot reliably account for prerequisites, weak areas, progress, and available time. Study Copilot turns those connections into an explainable next action.

The problem

A recommendation is only useful when it is relevant and actionable. Study Copilot retrieves a learner's graph context before deciding. It can recommend a topic, create a study plan, update progress, record a quiz attempt, mark a resource complete, and generate practice questions. State-changing actions require explicit confirmation.

FalkorDB as the learning graph

The graph contains User, Topic, Progress, SkillGap, Resource, Quiz, StudyPlan, and StudyPlanItem nodes. Relationships include HAS_PROGRESS, FOR_TOPIC, PREREQUISITE_OF, HAS_RESOURCE, HAS_QUIZ, and CONTAINS.

MATCH (u:User {id:$user_id})-[:HAS_PROGRESS]->(p:Progress)-[:FOR_TOPIC]->(t:Topic)
MATCH (candidate:Topic)
WHERE candidate.estimated_minutes <= $minutes
  AND NOT EXISTS {
    MATCH (pre:Topic)-[:PREREQUISITE_OF]->(candidate)
    WHERE NOT EXISTS {
      MATCH (u)-[:HAS_PROGRESS]->(mp:Progress)-[:FOR_TOPIC]->(pre)
      WHERE mp.mastery >= 0.7
    }
  }
RETURN candidate
ORDER BY candidate.difficulty

This query finds topics the learner is ready to study by checking that every prerequisite has at least 0.7 mastery. It then ranks eligible topics by difficulty, making the recommendation explainable and grounded in the learner’s graph context.

Agent architecture

The browser calls FastAPI. The agent asks StudyRepository for user context and next topics, then creates a structured decision. ActionService stages mutations and executes them only after approval. The repository sends parameterized Cypher to FalkorDB. This keeps retrieval, decision logic, safety, and persistence separated without requiring an external LLM key for the demo.

Feature walkthrough

  1. Ask, What should I study next? to see a graph-grounded recommendation.
  2. Ask, Create a study plan, then approve the pending action.
  3. Ask, Update my progress, Mark this resource complete, or Record a quiz attempt, and approve the mutation.
  4. Ask, Generate practice questions to retrieve the connected quiz for the recommended topic.

The UI exposes the retrieved context and action result so the user can see why the agent chose its recommendation.

What we learned

Connected data changes the agent's role from answer generation to evidence-based decision making. FalkorDB makes prerequisite traversal and relationship inspection natural, while confirmation gates provide a practical safety boundary for actions that change learner records.

Limitations and next steps

The demo uses deterministic intent routing and an in-memory pending-action store. Future work would add authenticated users, persistent audit events, richer question content, and an optional production LLM provider.

title: DeepsecBench: evaluating model performance in finding cybersecurity vulnerabilities
description:
Last week, OpenAI evaluated two models on an exploit benchmark within an isolated sandbox. Guardrails were reduced for testing, and the models found a vulnerability in their environment, accessed the internet, and reached Hugging Face's production database.

No human directed the action, but the breach is a clear example of how much more capable malicious attackers are when equipped with powerful AI models. But defenders have the same tools, and a clear advantage: knowledge of their own codebase. Hacks are initiated from the outside, so the single best defense is finding vulnerabilities from the inside before attackers do.

Today we're releasing DeepsecBench, a benchmark that evaluates how well different models find cybersecurity vulnerabilities in application code. For each model the report includes recall, precision, cost, and total time, and combines recall and precision into a single benchmark score. Here is a sample of model performance from the leaderboard:
