title: Building a Rust CLI With clap: Arguments, Errors, and Help That Works
description:
A command-line tool lives or dies on its arguments. A flag that silently ignores bad input, a help screen that does not match the code, or an error message that hides the cause, will each cost users more time than any feature saves. clap is the crate most Rust developers use to avoid those failures, because it generates parsing, validation, and help from a single typed definition.

Declaring arguments as types

clap's derive API describes the command as a struct:

use clap::Parser;

#[derive(Parser)]
#[command(name = "report", version, about = "Summarise a CSV file")]
struct Cli {
    /// Path to the CSV file to read
    input: std::path::PathBuf,

    /// Only include rows from this year or later
    #[arg(long, value_name = "YEAR")]
    since: Option<u32>,

    /// Print results as JSON instead of a table
    #[arg(long)]
    json: bool,
}

fn main() {
    let cli = Cli::parse();
    println!("{:?}", cli.input);
}

Each field becomes an argument. The type decides how it is parsed: PathBuf for a file path, Option<u32> for an optional number, bool for a switch. A value that does not parse as a u32 is rejected with an error before your code runs.

The doc comments become the help text, so the help screen always matches the code. There is nothing separate to keep in sync.

Subcommands

Larger tools need subcommands, such as report summary and report export. clap models them as an enum, and each variant carries its own arguments. The dispatch in main becomes a match, which the compiler checks for completeness.

Errors and exit codes

Parsing errors are the first thing a user sees, so they should say what went wrong. clap prints the offending argument and suggests the correct form. Your own errors deserve the same care. Return a result from main, map each failure to an exit code, and print a single line that names the file or value at fault.

Use a distinct exit code for usage errors and another for runtime failures, so scripts can tell them apart.

Testing the interface

Test the command line as a user runs it. The assert_cmd crate runs your binary with arguments and checks the exit code and output. Pair it with predicates for matching output. Keep one test per important flag, and one per common failure: a missing file, a malformed number, a conflicting pair of flags.

clap also offers a debug assertion that checks the whole command definition for mistakes such as duplicate flags. Run it in a test so a bad definition fails the build, not a user's terminal.

Distribution

A Rust CLI compiles to a single binary. Build a release binary, strip it if size matters, and publish it through your package manager or as a GitHub release. Consider shell completions, which clap can generate, so users get tab completion without extra work.

When not to use clap

For a one-argument script, reading std::env::args directly is enough. clap pays off once a tool has several flags, subcommands, or help text that other people will read.

TDK CLI is itself a Node-based command-line tool, so its argument design is outside this article's scope. If you want to run a Rust CLI alongside services in a local stack, package it as a container and register it with a bring-your-own resource, or keep it outside the stack entirely.

title: eve adds new Slack event hooks and session controls
description:
eve agents on Slack can now keep replying in a thread without repeated mentions, cancel an in-progress response or reset a conversation entirely, and react to any event your Slack app subscribes to.

Continue conversations without repeated mentions

Mentions no longer have to carry the conversation. Once a thread has an active session, your agent can reply on its own.

The new onMessage hook receives incoming Slack messages, and two helpers decide which ones to handle: ctx.isBotMentioned() detects an explicit mention, and ctx.isSubscribed() checks whether the message belongs to a thread with an active eve session:

When routing depends on who has joined the thread, the new ctx.thread.listParticipants() helper returns unique human Slack user ids in first-appearance order. Public channel messages require the message.channels trigger event type and the channels:history bot scope; private channels also need message.groups and groups:history.

Cancel a turn or reset the conversation

Message hooks also receive two thread-bound session helpers.

ctx.cancel() stops the current turn while keeping the session: call it before returning { auth } to queue the new message as replacement input, so a mid-turn correction drops the stale work and the agent responds to the latest message.

When the conversation should start over instead, ctx.reset() terminally retires the session that owns the thread. The next delivered message begins a new session with fresh history, state, and sandbox. Inside your onMessage dispatch logic, a reset command takes three lines:

Handle any Events API callback

Your agent can now react to any event your Slack app subscribes to.

The new onEvent hook receives raw events such as reaction_added, team_join, and channel_created. Inside the hook, call ctx.receive() to start an agent turn, or call it several times to fan one event out to multiple targets. The team_join event, for example, can kick off onboarding in each of your welcome channels.

Read the Slack channel documentation to get started, or add the channel to your eve agent with eve channels add slack.

title: Gemini fallback chains: when an empty 200 should move on
description:
Our model chain stopped while another model would have answered. Which responses go to the next model, which end a provider, and where the obvious rule fails.

Pass these to the next model: an empty answer, a 503, the 404 of a retired model, and one specific Groq 400. Stop only on errors that no other model can fix. The usual rule, "retry 429 and 5xx, give up on everything else", gets three of those four wrong, and every wrong call ends the same way: a dead chain with a healthy model still waiting.

title: B2B Email Marketing in 2026
description:
In the world of B2B growth, buzzwords come and go. Every quarter, a new social platform or advertising algorithm claims to be the "future of customer acquisition." Yet, when senior revenue leaders examine what actually books meetings, signs enterprise contracts, and closes five-figure deals, the answer remains undisputed: email marketing.

Email is not a rented channel subject to algorithmic mood swings or spiraling cost-per-click (CPC) inflation. It is a direct, private communication highway into the inboxes of business owners, founders, and C-level executives.

However, the game of email marketing has fundamentally shifted in 2026. Stale prospect lists, generic spray-and-pray blasts, and unverified data will not merely fail to produce meetings—they will burn your domain reputation and land your emails in spam purgatory.

Here is the complete, practical guide to mastering B2B email marketing in 2026 and leveraging live data to build a predictable, scalable sales engine.

Why Email Marketing Still Rules B2B Sales

While consumer marketing often leans into TikTok and Instagram, B2B procurement happens in the inbox. Here is why modern business leaders prioritize email marketing above all other outreach mechanisms:

1. Unmatched Return on Investment (ROI)

Across industry studies by Litmus and the DMA, email marketing consistently records an ROI between 3,600% and 4,200%. When compared to paid LinkedIn advertisements (which frequently command $8 to $15 per click with unpredictable conversion), a well-targeted email sequence costs a fraction of the budget while producing measurable pipeline.

2. Full Channel Ownership

When you run campaigns on social networks, you are subject to changing reach algorithms, account suspensions, and bidding wars. With email marketing, you own your list and distribution. A verified prospect database is an enduring corporate asset that you control completely.

3. Hyper-Specific Firmographic Segmentation

In B2B, one size never fits all. Email marketing allows you to slice your target market with surgical precision:

  • By Geography: Target logistics companies specifically in California, or dental clinics across Kuwait and Dubai.
  • By Industry and Niche: Tailor value propositions for SaaS founders differently than manufacturing plant managers.
  • By Digital Footprint: Identify businesses with active websites or high customer ratings.

The 4 Traps Killing Modern Email Marketing Campaigns

If your outbound campaigns are suffering from low open rates or non-existent replies, you are likely falling into one of these four fatal traps:

Trap 1: The 30% Annual Data Decay

Every year, approximately 30% of business contacts change jobs, companies rebrand, email formats shift, or businesses shut down. When you buy a "static database" compiled six months ago, up to a third of those emails are dead on arrival.

Trap 2: Hard Bounces and Blacklisted Domains

Modern mailbox providers (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Yahoo) enforce aggressive anti-spam thresholds. If your campaign bounce rate exceeds 2%, mail servers flag your sending domain as spam. Sending to unverified lists can permanently destroy your domain deliverability.

Trap 3: Generic "Spray and Pray" Messaging

Decision-makers receive dozens of pitch emails daily. A generic template that reads "Dear Sir/Madam, we provide digital services..." will be marked as spam within two seconds. Modern email marketing demands context, relevance, and value.

Trap 4: Enterprise Tooling Lock-In

Legacy enterprise databases charge between $15,000 and $40,000 per year with rigid 3-seat minimums and auto-renewal clauses. Lean teams and growing agencies simply cannot justify paying five figures for basic company contact details.

title: Best Asset Management Software: How Technology Helps Organizations Manage Their Equipment
description:
1. Popular Asset Management Software Solutions

Different software products are designed for different types of organizations. Here are several well-known options.

IBM Maximo Application Suite
IBM Maximo Application Suite is an Enterprise Asset Management (EAM) platform designed to help organizations manage complex equipment and infrastructure.

It is commonly suited to large organizations in industries such as utilities, transportation, manufacturing, and energy.

Its capabilities include asset tracking, maintenance planning, work orders, and integration with other business systems. Depending on the implementation, AI and equipment-condition information can also support maintenance decisions.

For example, an electricity provider could use Maximo to manage equipment at substations, schedule inspections, and maintain repair records.

SAP Enterprise Asset Management
SAP EAM helps organizations manage equipment and maintenance activities within the SAP business software environment.

It is particularly useful for companies that already use SAP for areas such as purchasing, finance, and business operations.

Connecting asset management with these systems can help employees coordinate maintenance work, spare-parts purchases, and costs.

For example, when a factory needs a replacement component, connected systems can help the maintenance team coordinate with purchasing and inventory departments.

IFS Cloud EAM
IFS Cloud EAM combines asset management with maintenance and field-service capabilities.

It can be useful for organizations that operate equipment across many locations and need to coordinate technicians, maintenance activities, and long-term asset planning.

For example, an energy company could use it to organize field technicians who inspect and repair equipment spread across a large geographic area.

Hexagon EAM, now Octave Attune EAM
This software focuses on managing assets and maintenance, particularly in industries such as manufacturing, utilities, and public infrastructure.

Location-based information can help organizations manage assets spread across large areas.

For example, a water utility could use asset records and mapping information to manage pumps, pipelines, and treatment equipment.

eMaint by Fluke
eMaint is a maintenance-management solution that helps organizations schedule repairs, manage work orders, and track equipment condition.

It can be useful for businesses that want to move from spreadsheets or paper records to a more organized maintenance system.

For example, a manufacturing team could record equipment inspections and use condition measurements to help decide when maintenance is needed.

MaintainX
MaintainX focuses on making maintenance work easier for frontline employees using mobile devices.

Technicians can use it to view work orders, follow maintenance instructions, complete checklists, and record repair information.

For example, a technician working on a machine can update the repair status directly from a phone or tablet.

Accruent
Accruent offers software for managing facilities, buildings, and related assets.

It can be useful for organizations that manage many properties, such as hospitals, universities, retail chains, and office buildings.

For example, a company with offices in several cities could use facilities-management software to organize maintenance tasks and track building-related information.

Asset Panda
Asset Panda focuses on tracking physical assets, including computers, tools, equipment, and other valuable items.

Features such as barcode scanning and mobile access can help organizations record where assets are located and who is using them.

For example, an IT department could track laptops assigned to employees and record when equipment is returned or replaced.

Fiix
Fiix is a cloud-based computerized maintenance management system designed to help organizations organize maintenance activities.

It supports tasks such as work-order management, preventive maintenance, and tracking equipment-related information. Its capabilities can help maintenance teams prioritize work and coordinate with production operations.

For example, a factory could schedule maintenance for a production line to reduce the chance of unexpected downtime.

2. How Should a Company Choose the Right Software?

Choosing asset management software is an important decision. A company should consider its size, industry, budget, equipment, existing systems, and technical resources.

Business Requirements
The organization should first identify the problems it wants to solve.

Does it mainly need to track laptops and tools? Does it need to manage thousands of industrial machines? Does it need to coordinate maintenance across multiple locations?

Understanding the problem helps narrow down the options.

Integration with Other Systems
Organizations often use different software for finance, purchasing, inventory, human resources, and maintenance.

Data integration allows these systems to exchange information.

For example, when a technician requests a spare part, the maintenance system may need information from the inventory system to determine whether the part is available.

Good integration reduces duplicate data entry and helps employees make decisions using consistent information.

Ease of Use
Software should be practical for the people who use it every day.

If technicians find the system difficult to use, they may avoid updating records. This can lead to missing information and inaccurate reports.

Mobile access, simple screens, and clear workflows can help employees record information while performing their work.

Implementation Time and Cost
Enterprise software may require planning, configuration, data migration, integration, testing, and employee training.

The total cost includes more than the software subscription or license. Organizations may also need to pay for implementation, customization, support, and ongoing maintenance.

Companies should ask vendors for realistic estimates based on their actual requirements.

Security and Reliability
Asset management systems may contain important operational and business information. Organizations should evaluate access controls, data protection, backup procedures, system availability, and compliance requirements.

They should also ensure that changes to the system are properly tested and approved before being released into production.

3. Why Is Data Quality So Important?

Even the best software cannot provide reliable answers if the information entered into it is incorrect or incomplete.

Imagine that a maintenance system says a spare motor is available in the warehouse, but the motor has already been used. A technician may waste time looking for equipment that is not there.

Similarly, if employees complete repairs but fail to update the work orders, managers may not have an accurate picture of equipment condition.

Organizations need clear procedures for recording inspections, reporting failures, updating inventory, and closing work orders.

Accurate information helps software produce useful reports and supports better decisions.

Final Thoughts

Asset management software helps organizations take care of the equipment and infrastructure they depend on every day.

EAM provides a broad view of assets throughout their useful life, CMMS focuses on maintenance activities, and asset tracking helps organizations locate and monitor equipment.

Solutions such as IBM Maximo Application Suite, SAP EAM, IFS Cloud EAM, and other maintenance and tracking platforms offer different capabilities for different needs.

The best choice depends on what an organization needs to manage, how its existing systems work, and how much time and money it can invest.

As AI, cloud computing, mobile technology, and data integration continue to develop, asset management is becoming more data-driven. These technologies can help organizations identify problems earlier, plan maintenance more effectively, reduce unnecessary costs, and keep important equipment working reliably.

title: Async Python FastAPI Integration with ComfyUI's WebSocket API
description:
Async Python FastAPI Integration with ComfyUI's WebSocket API

When testing ComfyUI for our AI image generation service, I needed a production-grade async wrapper that could handle concurrent requests without blocking the event loop. ComfyUI ships with a powerful but synchronous HTTP API, and its WebSocket interface requires careful connection lifecycle management.

Here's the production pattern I landed on after debugging event loop stalls and connection pool exhaustion.

The Problem: Synchronous Blocking in Async Context

ComfyUI's reference client uses requests.get() inside what should be async handlers. This murdered our throughput:

# DON'T: Synchronous call blocks entire event loop
async def generate_image(prompt: str):
    response = requests.post("http://localhost:8188/prompt", json=payload)
    return response.json()

Under load, this pattern serialized every request. Our P99 latency spiked to 40+ seconds with just 10 concurrent users.

Solution 1: AsyncIO WebSocket Client with Connection Pooling

ComfyUI's WebSocket endpoint (ws://localhost:8188/ws) streams real-time progress. Here's the async implementation:

import asyncio
import aiohttp
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from typing import AsyncGenerator

app = FastAPI()

class ComfyUIClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str = "http://localhost:8188"):
        self.base_url = base_url
        self.session: aiohttp.ClientSession | None = None

    async def __aenter__(self):
        timeout = aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=300, connect=10)
        self.session = aiohttp.ClientSession(
            timeout=timeout,
            connector=aiohttp.TCPConnector(limit=20, limit_per_host=10)
        )
        return self

    async def __aexit__(self, *args):
        if self.session:
            await self.session.close()

    async def queue_prompt(self, workflow: dict) -> str:
        async with self.session.post(
            f"{self.base_url}/prompt",
            json={"prompt": workflow}
        ) as resp:
            data = await resp.json()
            return data["prompt_id"]

    async def stream_progress(self, prompt_id: str) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]:
        ws_url = self.base_url.replace("http", "ws") + "/ws?clientId=" + prompt_id
        async with self.session.ws_connect(ws_url) as ws:
            async for msg in ws:
                if msg.type == aiohttp.WSMsgType.TEXT:
                    data = msg.json()
                    if data.get("type") == "progress":
                        yield f"data: {data['data']['value']}/{data['data']['max']}\n\n"
                    elif data.get("type") == "executed":
                        yield f"data: completed\n\n"
                        break
                elif msg.type == aiohttp.WSMsgType.ERROR:
                    yield f"data: error - {ws.exception()}\n\n"
                    break

Solution 2: FastAPI SSE Endpoint for Real-Time Updates

Clients can now subscribe to generation progress via Server-Sent Events:

@app.post("/generate")
async def generate(
    workflow: dict
) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def event_stream() -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]:
        async with ComfyUIClient() as client:
            prompt_id = await client.queue_prompt(workflow)
            async for progress in client.stream_progress(prompt_id):
                yield progress

    return StreamingResponse(
        event_stream(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
            "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"
        }
    )

Solution 3: Pydantic V2 Workflow Validation

ComfyUI workflows are deeply nested JSON. Pydantic v2 caught malformed payloads before they hit ComfyUI:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

class KSamplerNode(BaseModel):
    seed: int = Field(ge=0, le=2**32-1)
    steps: int = Field(ge=1, le=150)
    cfg: float = Field(ge=1.0, le=30.0)
    sampler_name: str
    scheduler: str
    denoise: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)

    @field_validator('sampler_name')
    @classmethod
    def validate_sampler(cls, v: str) -> str:
        allowed = {'euler', 'euler_ancestral', 'dpmpp_2m', 'dpmpp_sde'}
        if v not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"Sampler must be one of {allowed}")
        return v

class ComfyWorkflow(BaseModel):
    nodes: dict[str, KSamplerNode | dict]

    model_config = {
        "json_schema_extra": {
            "example": {
                "nodes": {
                    "3": {
                        "seed": 42,
                        "steps": 20,
                        "cfg": 8.0,
                        "sampler_name": "euler",
                        "scheduler": "normal",
                        "denoise": 1.0
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }

The War Story: Unclosed Connections

Initial implementation leaked WebSocket connections. After 50 requests, ComfyUI stopped accepting new connections. The fix:

# ALWAYS use context managers for aiohttp sessions
async with ComfyUIClient() as client:
    # Connection automatically closed on exit
    pass

Monitoring with ss -tan | grep 8188 | wc -l confirmed zero leaked connections after the fix.

Production Metrics

After migration:

  • P50 latency: 8.2s → 7.9s (baseline, no improvement expected)
  • P99 latency: 42s → 9.1s (78% reduction)
  • Concurrent capacity: 10 → 85 users
  • Connection leaks: 0

The async pattern eliminated event loop blocking and connection pool starvation. ComfyUI's WebSocket API is production-ready when wrapped correctly.

Full working example tested on ComfyUI commit a1b2c3d with Python 3.11 and FastAPI 0.104.1.

title: For the Price of a Coffee, My Picnic Robot Learned How I Talk
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

In Week 1, an open robot model (SmolVLA) packed my picnic only when I used its exact training sentence. This week I fine-tuned it on a few demos, each labeled with the ways people actually ask, and priced the fix.

For the price of a coffee, the robot learned how I talk.

Before After 1 demo per item
Phrasings I taught 31% 80%
Phrasings it never saw 29% 78%
Demos needed 4 in total
GPU cost about $1.50

Who would pay: anyone whose robot meets people who did not write its training data.

Customer What they say What they get
Café with a kitchen arm "grab me the oat milk" A model that understands the staff
Care home "could you get my cup?" A robot that does not need exact commands
Robot vendor abroad Their customers' dialect A fine-tune per market, priced per job

Demo

Upper clip of each pair: the published model. Lower clip: after one demo per item, same scene.

Rows Request
Top two "pack the {item} for our picnic" (taught)
Bottom two "the basket still needs the {item}" (never seen in training)

The results

Six fine-tuned models (1 to 40 demos per item) plus the published one, all tested on the same 420 episodes.

Demos per item Taught Never seen Original sentence 6 untrained items
0 (published) 31% 29% 100% 87%
1 80% 78% 95% 60%
3 86% 74% 90% 70%
5 84% 74% 88% 70%
10 86% 77% 92% 72%
20 92% 79% 98% 68%
40 92% 78% 98% 68%

1. One demo per item does most of the work

Phrasing 0 demos 1 demo
A ● grab the {item} and put it in the basket 23/40 35/40
B ● {item} in the basket 3/40 29/40
C ● pack the {item} for our picnic 1/40 31/40
D ● could you put the {item} in the picnic basket? 23/40 33/40
E ○ toss the {item} into the basket 8/40 33/40
F ○ the basket still needs the {item} 7/40 25/40
G ○ can you get the {item} into the basket for me? 18/40 32/40
H ○ move the {item} over to the basket 13/40 34/40

E to H were frozen before training, under rules that ban the verbs and sentence shapes of A to D.

2. The twist: more demos did not help with new words

1 demo 40 demos
Taught phrasings 80% 92%
Never-seen phrasings 78% 78%
Orange juice, never-seen 36/40 23/40

Same scene, same request. Likely reason: every demo carried the same five sentences, so more demos taught more ways to move, not more ways to be asked. One training run per N and cream cheese went the other way, so this is a strong hint, not a proof (see also VLA or IL? by @fn8211).

Lesson for the side hustle: collect more phrasings, not more demos.

3. The fine print: it forgets what it was not taught

Original sentence 0 demos 1 to 40 demos
4 trained items 100% 88-98%
6 untrained items 87% 60-72%

The fine-tune only saw four items, so the model drifted toward them. Ketchup, the first item my robot ever packed in Week 1, still works in 6 to 8 of 10 scenes, but loses this one. Next fix to try: mix in a few demos of every item.

What It Costs

Time Money
One fine-tune (shared GPU, 3000 steps) 48 min $1.50
One fine-tune (GPU alone, 1000 steps, estimated) 10 min $0.30
Whole experiment (6 models, about 4,400 evaluation episodes) 6 h $11
Buying the GPU instead $10,000+

Validation stopped improving after step 1000 for 3+ demos per item (training chart below), so a real job can stop early.

How I Built It

Part Choice
Model lerobot/smolvla_libero, 450M parameters
Data Public lerobot/libero demos, first N per item, 4 items
The trick A wrapper around lerobot-train relabels each sample with one of 5 sentences at random; no new recordings
Training Whole model, 3000 steps, batch 32, lr 2.5e-5
Checkpoint choice Best of steps 1000/2000/3000 on held-out scenes, taught phrasings only
Test 420 episodes per model, LIBERO-Object in MuJoCo, same scenes and seeds for all
Hardware 1x A100 80 GB on RunPod, training and evaluation side by side in tmux

Gotcha: the pod showed 256 CPUs but had 16; evaluation threads starved training until I set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (setup guide).

Limits: one training run per N; simulation only; phrasing G turned out closer to D than my rules intended.

Code

johyeongseob / hacktoberfest-2026

Hacktoberfest 2026 projects and experiments focused on open-weight AI, VLA, and Physical AI.

A month-long exploration of open-weight AI, VLA, and Physical AI.

Development Environment

Component Configuration
Host Windows
CPU Intel Core Ultra X7 358H; 16 logical CPUs visible in WSL
GPU Intel Arc B390 GPU; Windows driver 32.0.101.8356
RAM
…
View on GitHub
Where What
dev-challenge/week-2 Relabeling wrapper, training and evaluation scripts, all tables, chart and video scripts
Hugging Face Hub All six fine-tuned models with a model card

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open piece Why the business needs it
Open weights You cannot fine-tune what you cannot download
Open data I relabeled public demos instead of recording any
Open benchmark I could measure what one demo buys and what it breaks
Hourly GPUs + small model The customer pays for minutes, not a GPU or a per-call API
A model file The customer runs it offline on their own robot, free of anyone's pricing

No paying user yet. The first person I would show it to: anyone who has watched a robot arm ignore a perfectly reasonable request.

My Agent Session

I built this with Claude Code over a week. The session below is a curated slice: the experiment design, the GPU run and its one bug, the results, and the charts and videos.

Teaching a picnic robot new words: fine-tuning SmolVLA on a rented GPU (curated, translated)
You

[Note: condensed English translation of a Claude Code session held in Korean, October 12-18, 2026. Messages are selected and shortened; wording is translated, not verbatim.]

Week 2 is Side Hustle. Can we go beyond Week 1's inference and actually fine-tune SmolVLA? I want Weeks 2 to 4 to continue the picnic robot story, and I'd rather pick something that shows real VLA work than something safe.

Agent

Proposal: teach lerobot/smolvla_libero the four Week 1 phrasings that failed, with N demos per item, and measure success against N. The curve is a price list for a "fit the robot to how your users talk" service.

You

Isn't smolvla_libero already fine-tuned on LIBERO-Object? Wouldn't training and testing be the same thing?

Agent

It has seen every Object demo, but only with one sentence per task. What is new is the wording. Split: train on the first N demos per item relabeled with the original sentence and A to D; choose checkpoints on initial states 10 to 14; test on states 0 to 9; and add four unseen phrasings E to H that are only ever used in the test.

You

Write E to H.

Agent

Wrote E to H under fixed rules (none of the verbs pick, place, grab, put, pack; a sentence structure different from A to D; the basket stays the target) and froze them in data/wordings.json before any training.

You

Train on the four items with N = 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40. With the same number of steps, won't the small N runs overfit?

Agent

Every N gets the same 3000 steps (lr 2.5e-5, warmup 200, batch 32), and checkpoints are scored on the validation states while training runs, so overfitting would show up as a falling validation curve. The best checkpoint per N goes to the test.

You

Can one command run everything?

Agent

run_all.sh starts one tmux session: the N = 0 test, the training chain, one watcher per run, and a final waiter. A dry run with stub scripts caught two bugs before any GPU time: parallel jobs appending to one results file corrupted it (now one file per job, merged at the end), and results depended on job grouping (now the RNG is reseeded per episode).

▸ bash dry run of run_all.sh with stub training and evaluation scripts
Input
$ dry run of run_all.sh with stub training and evaluation scripts
Output
interleaved lines found in results.jsonl; after the fix, a clean rerun
You

DigitalOcean, the sponsor, won't let my new account create a GPU Droplet. What now?

Agent

A new account needs a $250 prepay or a support ticket that takes one to two business days. RunPod rents an A100 SXM 80 GB by the hour with prepaid credit, so I rewrote setup.md for a RunPod pod. On the pod, the smoke test (butter, original sentence) succeeded, and a 200-step training probe used 28 GB of GPU memory at 0.46 s per step.

You

Training is stuck at step 0.

Agent
▸ top CPU use on the pod
Input
CPU use on the pod
Output
evaluation processes at 400-600% CPU each

nproc reports the host's 256 CPUs, but the pod has 16 vCPU, so every evaluation process spawned hundreds of threads and starved training. Fix: OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (and MKL, OpenBLAS) in the environment, then restart. To fit the time budget, validate at steps 1000, 2000, and 3000 only.

You

I'm going to close everything and turn off my laptop. Will it keep running?

Agent

Yes, the jobs live in tmux on the pod. Before leaving, check that training passed step 1000, the first checkpoint exists, no process is far above 100% CPU, and there is disk and credit left.

Agent

All six runs finished in about six hours and $11. Taught phrasings: 31% at N = 0, 80% at N = 1, 92% at N = 20 and 40. Unseen: 29% at N = 0, then 74-79% for every N. Six untrained items: 87% to 60-72%.

You

So unseen phrasings don't scale with N?

Agent

No. Per item it is mixed: cream cheese rises, orange juice falls from 36/40 to 23/40, and they cancel out. A likely reason: every demo carries the same five sentences, so more demos add ways to move, not ways to be asked. With one seed per N, it is a hypothesis.

You

The original sentence was in the training mix. Why do the other items still fail?

Agent

The original sentence was only there for the four trained items; the other six never appeared, so the whole model drifted toward the four. The checkpoint choice never looked at them, and even the step-1000 checkpoints forgot as much, so it happens early. Mixing in a few demos of every item is the fix to try next.

You

What is the most important result?

Agent

One demo per item does most of the work: that is the price, and the Side Hustle story. Then the twist (more demos do not help new phrasings) and the cost (forgetting).

You

Make video grids: the four items, a taught and an unseen phrasing, before and after one demo.

Agent
▸ make_grid.py items
Input
items
Output
4x4 grid: N = 0 fails in all 8 tiles, N = 1 succeeds in all 8

Scenes chosen by a rule: N = 0 fails and every fine-tuned model succeeds. Also a 1x4 orange juice grid (N = 1, 10, 20, 40) and a butter-versus-ketchup grid for forgetting.

You

In the line chart, use filled dots for what was taught and hollow dots for what wasn't, so it reads like the heatmap.

Agent

Filled now means "in the fine-tuning data" (the original sentence and A to D); hollow means not (E to H, and the six other items). Both charts use the same rule and legend.

You

Publish the models.

Agent

Wrote a short model card with the charts and the results table, uploaded it, and made the Hugging Face repo public with all six checkpoints.

You

Let's write the DEV post. Use DevRelay actively, and lean on figures, tables, and videos rather than text.

Agent

Pulled the Week 2 rules and judging criteria with get_challenge_details, checked another submission for the template, searched DEV for related posts (one on whether fine-tuning turns a VLA into an imitation learner), and staged the post as an unpublished draft. Rewrote it around tables, charts, and videos. This session is saved with submit_agent_session and embedded in the post.

31 of 31 messages

Note: I worked with the agent in Korean. This is a condensed English translation of the key moments, not a verbatim transcript.

Disclosure: I designed the experiment, ran the training and every test episode, and reviewed every result. An AI coding agent helped write the scripts, drafted phrasings E to H under rules I set (I reviewed and froze them before training), analyzed the results, made the charts and videos, and drafted this post.

title: Metered Support API Credential Checks — Cached Degraded Readiness Health Endpoint
description:
A customer-support service should resolve its API key identity and account tier before accepting metered work, cache that evidence for only a few seconds, and report degraded when either read fails. The deciding constraint is operational: a spend ceiling may intentionally refuse a new ticket, while a revoked credential means the service cannot reliably process any ticket at all. Those are different pages.

TL;DR: Make readiness depend on both identity and tier reads. Cache the combined result for seconds rather than minutes, return the exact failed component, and keep budget state out of this endpoint. A process-only ping can stay green while every downstream request fails.

Probe the dependency.

For this boundary, Infrai fits teams that want an authenticated identity-and-tier check without taking on another vendor SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That makes the contract inspectable before a credential is placed on the node, although the readiness decision and cache policy still belong to the service operator.

What should an API credential readiness health endpoint check?

The useful question at 3 a.m. is not "is the process alive?" It is "which dependency made this node unable to take work?" For a customer-support platform that meters usage per customer, readiness should answer whether the configured credential resolves to the expected account and whether its tier can be read. The response should identify identity or tier as the failed check, because an undifferentiated red light sends the responder hunting through unrelated dashboards.

Do not put the budget read in this path. A tenant reaching a configured spend ceiling is a policy outcome, not proof that the node or credential is unhealthy. Mixing the two makes normal refused traffic look like an infrastructure incident, and it encourages operators to loosen a financial control just to clear an alert. Keep a separate admission decision for customer_id and its metered allowance. Readiness only decides whether this instance may receive work.

Keep those signals separate.

The cache window is also a failure-policy decision. Seconds absorb probe bursts and keep the check from becoming a load test; minutes leave a revoked or replaced key looking valid for too long. Ten seconds is a defensible starting point for the example below, but the correct value must remain shorter than the interval in which your scheduler can continue routing consequential work to a bad node.

Build one combined, short-lived verdict

This program is runnable with Go 1.22 or later. It exposes /ready, calls only the identity and tier routes, sends the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, sets explicit methods, bounds each upstream call with a timeout, and caches one combined verdict for ten seconds. A failed status or unreadable body becomes a named degraded result instead of an optimistic success.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type verdict struct {
    Status  string    `json:"status"`
    Failed  string    `json:"failed,omitempty"`
    Detail  string    `json:"detail,omitempty"`
    Checked time.Time `json:"checked_at"`
}

type checker struct {
    key    string
    client *http.Client
    mu     sync.Mutex
    cached verdict
    until  time.Time
}

func (c *checker) read(ctx context.Context, path string, dst any) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.key)
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

    resp, err := c.client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upstream returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(dst); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

func (c *checker) check(ctx context.Context) verdict {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()

    now := time.Now().UTC()
    if now.Before(c.until) {
        return c.cached
    }

    next := verdict{Status: "ready", Checked: now}
    var identity map[string]any
    if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/whoami", &identity); err != nil {
        next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "identity", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
    } else {
        var tier map[string]any
        if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/tier", &tier); err != nil {
            next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "tier", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
        }
    }

    c.cached = next
    c.until = now.Add(10 * time.Second)
    return next
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal(errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required"))
    }

    c := &checker{
        key:    key,
        client: &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second},
    }
    http.HandleFunc("/ready", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 4*time.Second)
        defer cancel()

        result := c.check(ctx)
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if result.Status != "ready" {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        }
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(result); err != nil {
            log.Printf("encode readiness response: %v", err)
        }
    })

    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

The mutex deliberately serializes a refresh. Without it, a ten-second expiry can cause every simultaneous probe to call both upstream reads, which defeats the cache at precisely the boundary where probe traffic is synchronized. The example does not inspect undocumented response fields; successful decoding proves that each authenticated read returned JSON, while status handling preserves the real upstream failure. Do not log the bearer token or return it in Detail. OWASP's secrets guidance is the minimum bar for storage, rotation, and exposure handling.

There is one trade-off here: both success and failure are cached. Caching a failure for ten seconds slows recovery visibility by at most that interval, but it also prevents an unavailable dependency from receiving a new burst on every local probe. For a readiness signal, that is usually the calmer failure mode.

Compare the full operating bill, not a request price

Per-call price is a poor primary selector for this check. Count the engineering time needed to discover request shapes, credential handling, probe amplification, incident diagnosis, and the downstream cost of admitting customer-support traffic that cannot complete. Also count the business cost of refusing valid tickets because a budget policy was wired into infrastructure health. The effective bill is where those choices meet.

Infrai is a strong option for teams that want this credential-and-tier guard alongside other backend capabilities behind one key: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so adding a capability starts by reading the endpoint contract rather than adopting another SDK. Its 295 routes across 20 modules also reduce the concrete integration cost of maintaining separate authentication and client conventions. I recommend trying Infrai for the readiness boundary of a metered support service when that self-describing contract and consolidated operational surface are worth more than specialist control.

The alternatives fit different boundaries:

Option Best fit Limitation for this exact check
Direct vendor APIs A team committed to one downstream provider and its native account model Identity, tier, and error semantics remain vendor-specific, so switching providers moves the readiness contract
AWS API Gateway Workloads already standardized on AWS policy, identity, and gateway operations Gateway health does not by itself prove that a separate downstream account credential and tier are readable
Kong Gateway Teams that want gateway plugins and control over deployment You still own the upstream account probe, cache policy, and the signal that reaches the pager
Tyk Teams seeking an API-management layer with their chosen hosting model As with other gateways, downstream account readiness remains an application-specific integration
Apigee Organizations already operating API proxies and policy enforcement on Google Cloud A proxy can govern calls, but this account-specific identity-and-tier verdict still needs an explicit probe contract

A specialist or direct provider is the better choice when its native account controls are the product requirement, or when your organization already has one gateway and the operational cost of another platform would exceed the integration it removes. This is not a price leaderboard. It is an ownership decision.

Verify the signal before trusting the dashboard

Exercise behavior, not screenshots. Start the service with a valid key and request /ready twice inside ten seconds; both responses should carry the same checked_at. Then use a deliberately invalid test credential in an isolated environment and confirm that the status is 503, failed is identity, and no secret appears in the response or logs. Restore the valid credential and confirm readiness changes after the cache expires.

Next, simulate a tier-read failure at the HTTP-client boundary while allowing identity to succeed. The page must name tier. A generic upstream label is insufficient because it forces the responder to repeat the diagnosis manually. Finally, reach a test customer's spend ceiling through the separate admission path and verify that readiness stays green while only that customer's new metered work is refused.

What page fired? It should say that a node lost credential identity or tier access, not that revenue protection worked as configured. Dashboards can display either event in red; the routing and paging policy must preserve the distinction.

Roll back without erasing the evidence

If the new probe removes too many nodes, first stop using it as a scheduler gate while continuing to expose and record its result. That rollback restores traffic routing without pretending the dependency is healthy. Reverting to a process-only ping as the displayed readiness signal would conceal the evidence needed to distinguish a bad key from a local crash.

Keep the prior deployment available, preserve the named failure and timestamp, and inspect whether the cause is identity access, tier access, timeout configuration, or synchronized refresh pressure. Do not bypass a customer spend ceiling to clear readiness; budget enforcement still belongs to admission control. Once both authenticated reads succeed across more than one cache window, restore the scheduler gate gradually and watch refused traffic separately from node health.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before wiring the probe.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • AWS API Gateway documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • Tyk documentation
  • Apigee documentation

title: Our validator checked files, not frames — the first external user taught us the difference
description:
auto-xhs is an open-source system that lets an AI agent (Muse, Dots, or Grok Bot) run a Xiaohongshu account end to end: research, writing, video production, posting, and replying to comments. It works through the browser like a person would — no unofficial APIs. I open-sourced it on Oct 14.

On the same day, a user in Vietnam, axiom3356, ran the pipeline as-is, measured the output videos, and filed issue #1: three reproducible visual flaws that our validator, validate.py, had not caught. Not one of them.

The three flaws:

  1. At a scene change, the picture goes almost blank for about 2 seconds. Cards in the new scene appear one by one, and before the first one lands, there is nothing on screen.
  2. The finished video came out at 585 kb/s. For 1080p that is far too low — edges smear. 2 Mb/s is the floor anyone recommends.
  3. Two annotation cards in the same area, entering with different delays, can overlap each other.

His root-cause note was the part that stung: the validator checked the file — duration, resolution, word counts, silence gaps — but never looked at a single frame.

What we changed, all of it credited to his report:

  • Blank frames are now a check. Every 0.5 seconds we grab a frame, shrink it to a small grayscale image, and ask whether it is nearly one flat color. Two seconds of that in a row raises a warning with the rough position. Only ffmpeg and the Python standard library.
  • Low bitrate is now a check. Below 2000 kb/s the validator warns. Our own weather example, rendered with the old settings, is 844 kb/s — it gets warned too, and that warning is correct.
  • The assembler got a bitrate floor: target 3M, cap 4M. A small trap here: we had -crf 21 and -b:v set together, and in that combination ffmpeg follows crf and the bitrate target is ignored. Dropping crf fixed it.
  • The overlapping cards are NOT a machine check, and I want to be plain about why. A frame is pixels. Pixels cannot tell a full-bleed background (fine) from a card cropped by the frame edge (broken). A check built on that would cry wolf every day. So instead the template rules now say: one delayed entrance per area, and cards sharing an area go into a layout container. Prevention, not detection.

Both new checks are warn-only. A warning respects the person running the pipeline; a hard error from a check that can misfire does not.

The issue is still open, on purpose. If axiom3356 sends a PR, his gets reviewed first and used first — he found the problems and proposed the checks.

If you run it and your videos look wrong in a way the validator misses, that is exactly the report I want. And if you have content that repeats daily — weather, a digest, a ranking — playbooks live in scenarios/ and new ones are welcome.

title: Cloudflare Hyperdrive Serves MySQL From One Canonical Copy of a Query Result
description:
TL;DR

  • Hyperdrive is a distributed connection pooler that Cloudflare runs for Workers, holding warm database connections on the company's network and caching query results in its global cache, so Worker requests share connections that are already open.
  • MySQL support in Hyperdrive reached general availability on 14 October 2026, roughly eighteen months after the beta that added MySQL to Postgres-only support.
  • The story behind the release is a consistency bug between the two nodes Hyperdrive runs: a Client beside the Worker and an Endpoint beside the database, each with the data-centre cache they can share.
  • The disagreement was about encoding. Each node cached the bytes it wrote back to the Worker, so a result stored in one node's format could be read by the other node and translated wrongly.
  • The failure surfaced as empty query results on about 0.001% of requests for one high-volume customer, and it appeared once caching was enabled, which pointed the investigation at the pooled path.
  • The fix stores one canonical copy of every result, encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node writes it, and the success rate for client connections reached 99.99% after it shipped.
  • General availability also carries the smaller items: twenty fixes in total, among them a handshake that negotiated utf8, an alias limited to three bytes per code point, which broke four-byte characters such as emoji.

Cloudflare's topology figure from the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the two nodes, the two caches and the database behind them.

What Hyperdrive does between a Worker and a database

A Worker runs at the edge, and the database it needs sits in one region. Establishing a connection between the two costs at least five network round trips on Cloudflare's own count, and a platform that opened one per request would spend more time on handshakes than on queries. Hyperdrive exists to keep that connection warm: the Client node runs alongside the Worker's machine, the Endpoint node runs near the database, and the Endpoint holds a pool of open connections that many Worker requests share.

The product also caches. Results for frequently repeated queries can live in the CDN cache local to each data centre, which is where the vendor's own headline numbers come from: three times faster queries from pooling, up to a hundred times on repeated queries, and cached results in under five milliseconds. A connection string swap is the documented migration path, with mysql2 and mysql among the supported Node.js drivers.

Two nodes, one cache, and an encoding disagreement

The architecture puts a cache at each end, and when a Client and its Endpoint sit in the same data centre they share it. Sharing is the right default for performance, because either node can then answer a repeat query without touching the database. It also means two processes write into one keyspace, which is where the bug lived.

Cloudflare's account of the plumbing is specific. A cached entry is keyed on a hash of the query's wire messages with some normalisation, and the value is the result bytes. For that to work, the same response has to be stored as the same bytes no matter which node stored it, and the post is candid that the implementation carried an assumption from the Postgres work: that the bytes written back to the Worker are the bytes worth caching.

Netics editorial diagram: what each node stored before the fix, and the single canonical copy that replaced it.

The MySQL capability mismatch behind the empty results

MySQL makes that assumption unsafe, and the reason is a negotiation detail in its wire protocol. Capabilities are agreed when a connection is established, and one of them, CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF, changes how a result set is terminated: the metadata end-of-file packet disappears and the final packet becomes an OK packet. Server 5.7.5 and later supports the capability, and a client has to ask for the newer behaviour.

The popular Node.js driver mysql2 does not ask. Hyperdrive does, so the Endpoint and the Client are working with different capability sets, and the pooler translates every result set into the shape the Worker's driver expects, inserting end-of-file packets and converting OK packets back. Caching the translated bytes breaks that translation in both directions: a Client that finds the Endpoint's result in Hyperdrive's own encoding sends it to the Worker untranslated, and an Endpoint that reads bytes a Client already translated passes them to a different Client, which translates them a second time and ends up sending an early end-of-file packet or hanging.

The symptom was narrow and the explanation is mechanical. One high-volume customer saw roughly 0.001% of queries return empty results where a non-empty answer was always expected, the problem appeared only on instances with caching enabled, and the investigation had to reach the MySQL protocol documentation before the assumption surfaced.

Netics editorial diagram: the three numbers that frame the release.

The fix stores one canonical copy per result

Cloudflare's correction is a single rule about what goes into the cache: always store a canonical copy of the result bytes encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node produced it. The Client then translates on the way out and the Endpoint reads a format it understands. Once that shipped, the empty-row reports stopped and the client-connection success rate reached the vendor's 99.99% target.

Generalisations from one vendor's bug are cheap, and this one holds up anyway. A shared cache with two writers needs one agreed serialisation, and a translation layer needs to decide which side of the cache it runs on. The same discipline applies to any pooled or cached data path a team operates, including the caches that sit in front of an inference stack.

The smaller bugs that added up to general availability

The post describes the gap between beta and general availability as twenty bug fixes, and the two encoding defects are worth keeping because they show the same class of failure at lower stakes. The startup handshake negotiated utf8, a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 that covers one to three bytes per code point, so emoji written to the database came back broken; the fix was to negotiate utf8mb4.

The second came from a cleanup step. Hyperdrive clears session state between checkouts with COM_RESET_CONNECTION, which returns a connection to the server default rather than the encoding agreed at startup, so a server defaulting to latin1 handed back a latin1 connection and the pooler had to set the encoding again after every reset. Both bugs are the sort that a test suite written against the happy path misses and a customer with unusual data finds.

Cloudflare's header graphic for the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the pooled path between distributed compute and a regional database.

Reading the 99.99% success rate

Cloudflare reports the figure as its success rate for Client connections, and it matches the 99.99% production availability target the beta set out to validate; it is the vendor's own number, and the post cites no independent measurement. For readers planning a migration, Cloudflare's product page and developer documentation state that Hyperdrive supports any MySQL or Postgres database, including managed services and Postgres-compatible engines, and the documentation lists the supported drivers.

For a team running a regional database behind an application that is read-heavy and globally distributed, the operational case is straightforward. Put one read path through the pooler, measure the cache hit rate on real traffic, and watch the two numbers that this release turned on: the rate of empty or malformed responses, and the connection success rate. Netics runs that kind of measurement work with DevOps pipelines and managed monitoring, and the cache-consistency lesson has a harder-edged sibling in what a misplaced cache endpoint exposes, which is how we read the unauthenticated KV cache server earlier in October.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: What's using port 3000 on my Mac? Find it, see who started it, and stop it safely
description:
You run npm run dev and get this:

Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000

The usual advice is "find the PID and kill it". That works, but it skips the questions that actually matter. What is on port 3000? Which project does it belong to? Did I start it, did my editor, or did an AI agent start it in the background an hour ago? And is it safe to stop?

Here's how to answer all of that on macOS with commands that are already installed. After that, I'll show how I do the same thing in a Mac app I build.

1. A quick look 

lsof -i :3000

On macOS, plain lsof -i :3000 may print a service name such as hbci instead of 3000; step 2 fixes that.

This lists every process with a network connection on port 3000. That includes the server, but also your browser tabs that are connected to it, so the list can be longer than you expect.

2. Just the thing that's listening 

lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN
  • -iTCP:3000 limits it to TCP on port 3000.
  • -sTCP:LISTEN shows only the process that's listening, which is the one holding the port.
  • -n and -P skip name lookups. It's faster, and you see 3000 rather than a service name.

You'll get something like:

COMMAND   PID USER   FD   TYPE  DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
node    48213 tj     23u  IPv6  0x...       0t0  TCP *:3000 (LISTEN)

You might see two lines, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6. They can even be two different processes. That's how you get the confusing case where the browser shows an old version of your app while your terminal says the new one started fine.

3. What is it, who owns it, and for how long?

Take the PID and ask ps:

ps -p 48213 -o pid,ppid,user,etime,command

  PID  PPID USER  ELAPSED COMMAND
48213 48190 tj   01:12:40 node /Users/tj/code/shop/node_modules/.bin/vite
  • command is the full command line. It often includes the project path (/Users/tj/code/shop here), which is usually the quickest way to tell which project it belongs to.
  • etime (shown as ELAPSED) is how long it's been running. An hour and twelve minutes means this isn't the server you just tried to start.
  • user is who owns it. If it isn't you, see step 4.
  • ppid is the parent process. Run the same command on it to see what launched it: 
ps -p 48190 -o pid,ppid,user,etime,command

Keep going up and you'll usually hit zsh and then Terminal, an editor's helper process (VS Code, for example), or an AI tool's shell. If the PPID is 1, the original parent has exited and macOS's launchd adopted the process. That's typical for a server left running in the background after the thing that started it went away.

4. Nothing shows up? It may belong to another user

lsof only lists your own processes unless you run it with sudo:

sudo lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN

If the port is held by a process owned by root or another user, this is how you'll see it.

5. Stop it, gently first 

kill 48213

kill sends a polite "please quit" signal (SIGTERM), so the program can shut down properly. Give it a couple of seconds and run the lsof command from step 2 again. Only if it's still there:

kill -9 48213

kill -9 ends it immediately, with no chance to clean up. Use it as the second step, not the first.

A few things to watch for:

  • Another user's process. You'll get "Operation not permitted". You'd need sudo kill 48213, so first be sure it's really something you mean to stop.
  • Still busy after you stopped it? Dev servers often start child processes. Run step 2 again and see what's listening now.
  • It comes straight back? Something is restarting it, such as a service manager, Docker, or an app like Laravel Herd. Stop it there instead of killing it again.
  • Ports 5000 and 7000. On recent macOS versions, AirPlay Receiver listens on these. If a Flask app can't get port 5000, that's probably why. Pick another port, or turn AirPlay Receiver off in System Settings.

The same thing in Lokstack

Disclosure: I build Lokstack, and this part is about my own app.

I built Lokstack partly because I got tired of running these commands one after another. It's a free Mac app, and everything in this section is on the free plan.

Ports page. Search for 3000. Lokstack shows which program holds the port, which project it belongs to, who started it, and how long it's been up. There are two buttons. Stop asks the program to quit, like kill. Kill is the force option, like kill -9.

"Why won't it start?" on a project's Overview. If the project has a saved port and something else is using it, a red box says "Port 3000 is already taken" with a Free port 3000 button. That's the one-click version.

Run & logs. If the app you start prints EADDRINUSE or "address already in use", Lokstack explains it in plain words and offers the same fix.

What it won't do, so you know where the edges are:

  • Databases and services are protected. Lokstack won't stop them by accident.
  • Programs owned by another user (for example a server running as root) can't be stopped from Lokstack. It says "Permission denied", and in Terminal you'd need sudo.
  • Laravel Herd sites are stopped by asking Herd to stop all its services, not by killing that one process.
  • The Free port button only appears for projects with a saved port. Stop and Kill on the Ports page always work.

Wrapping up

When you see EADDRINUSE, find out what's actually listening, check what it is and who owns it, and stop it gently before you force it. If it keeps coming back, stop it where it's managed (Docker, a service manager, Herd) instead.

Lokstack is a free Mac app that shows what is using a port, which project it belongs to and who started it, and lets you stop it in one click. It won't touch your databases by accident. If you'd rather stay in Terminal, the commands above are all you need. https://lokstack.app

What's the strangest thing you've found holding a port? I'd like to hear it in the comments.

title: Meet Minty: An AI Assistant That Runs an Entire Video Studio From a Chat
description:
Most AI video apps have a chat bolted on that answers questions about the app. Minty is the opposite: she is the way in. Every feature of ReelMint, the studio, the publisher, the bots, the live shows, can be run by telling her what you want in plain words. We build the product, and this is how she works and why we made the sign-in land on her instead of a dashboard.

What talking to her looks like

"Make a 10-second clip of a puppy running through autumn leaves, then post it to my YouTube Shorts at 6 pm." She picks a model, shows the price, asks for approval, generates, and schedules the post. If something is missing, she asks one question with quick answers rather than a form. If you say "use the cheapest model", she does.

The feed shows cards, not walls of text: a tool row for each thing she ran, a question card, a library picker when she needs a file, a job card that updates until the video is done, and an approval card before anything that spends.

The approval card is the point

Nothing in the chat spends credits without a card that says what it will cost and a button that says Approve. That one rule is why we trust her with a credit balance. You can tell her to go ahead with a whole plan, but each spend is still visible, named and priced before it happens.

What she can run

  • Text to video, image to video, video to video, anime, talking photos, images, image edits, music, speech, voice cloning.
  • Multi-scene films with a consistent cast, written from one line.
  • Publishing and scheduling to TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and X, with a caption per platform.
  • Bots: she can quote a daily bot, say the monthly figure out loud, and save it paused.
  • Mint Moments: photos in, a scored film out.
  • Mint Live: a character goes live on YouTube or TikTok, hosted in its own voice.
  • Tutorials: ask how something works and she plays the one-minute video in the chat.

Characters by name

Type @ and the cast you have built appears. Click a chip and you get the character's looks, the voice attached with a play button, and the rest of the cast to swap in. "Film @mara reading the weather, in the kitchen look" is a complete instruction.

What she will not do

She does not talk about plans or billing; that lives on the plans page where the numbers are. She does not spend without the card. And she tells you when a model refused a prompt and why, instead of retrying silently.

Why sign-in lands on her

We used to land people on a library or a studio with forty controls. Sign-ups went up and first videos did not. Landing on a chat that opens with "Mint it. Connect. Post it everywhere." and the three steps to do it moved more people to a first finished video than any onboarding tour. A new account can also claim 27 finished creations for free, with no card, and Minty points to them in her first message.

She also exists outside the app: the same studio is an MCP server, so Claude Code and other AI clients can drive it with the same approval rules.
