title: Learned Indexes in Rust v0.2: Answering Reddit, Adding Range Queries, and Beating slice::binary_search
description:
A few days ago, I published an architectural deep dive exploring a provocative question: What if we could replace comparison-based database trees (like B-Trees) with pure mathematical functions in Rust?

The response from the community across Dev.to and Reddit (r/rust, r/compsci, r/database) was incredible. It sparked great discussions, valid skepticism, and direct questions that deserved real engineering answers rather than theoretical debates.

Today, I released learned_index_lab v0.2.0. Before diving into the technical answers, here is a quick refresher on what this project is and what it proves.

1. What is Learned Index Lab, and What Does It Prove?

For more than 50 years, database storage engines (B-Trees, B+Trees, LSM-Trees) have relied on comparison-based pointer hierarchies. While reliable, traversing tree nodes introduces severe hardware penalties on modern CPU architectures:

  • Pointer Chasing: Every jump down a tree incurs memory dereferences across distant heap locations, triggering recurring L1/L2/L3 cache misses.
  • High Memory Overhead: A standard BTreeMap consumes ~45 MB of node pointers, balancing factors, and metadata for every 1,000,000 keys.
  • Branch Mispredictions: Repetitive binary branch decisions at each node stall deep CPU execution pipelines.

Originated by Kraska et al. (MIT / Google) and formalized by Ferragina & Vinciguerra (PVLDB 2020), Learned Indexes reframe indexing as a mathematical regression problem.

Given a sorted dataset, the index builder runs a single-pass streaming Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) that partitions the data into a tiny set of linear segments (y = ax + b). During lookup, the CPU executes an in-register arithmetic calculation predicting the exact position within a strict, provable error corridor [approx - ε, approx + ε], followed by a tightly bounded local search.

What the benchmarks prove:

  • Zero data loss & 100% exact lookups (0 false positives, 0 false negatives).
  • 99.97% memory reduction: Index metadata drops from 45.78 MB down to ~12 KB for 1,000,000 keys.
  • 3x to 4.5x faster lookups compared to standard BTreeMap.

2. Why v0.2.0? Answering the Community's Questions

The discussions on Reddit and Dev.to raised two critical questions that shaped this release:

Question 1: "Why only compare against BTreeMap? What about a flat sorted slice using slice::binary_search?"

This was the most frequent critique, and it is 100% valid.

A contiguous, pre-sorted Vec<u64> indexed via slice::binary_search has 0 KB of extra memory overhead. It eliminates heap pointer indirection entirely. How does a PGM learned index hold up against standard library binary search on a flat slice?

To answer this conclusively, I integrated slice::binary_search as an explicit baseline across all 10-run, 1,000,000-key statistical benchmarks in src/main.rs.

The Results (Average across 10 randomized runs, 1M keys, 100k queries):

Workload Distribution Flat slice::binary_search PGM-Index (v0.2.0) Speedup vs. Slice
Dense Sequential Time-Series (ε = 32) 152.7 ns/op 63.5 ns/op 2.41x faster
Uniform Sparse Random (ε = 16) 150.9 ns/op 70.5 ns/op 2.14x faster
Clustered Heavy-Tailed Lognormal (ε = 16) 141.0 ns/op 48.6 ns/op 2.90x faster

Why is PGM over 2x faster than a contiguous binary search?
A binary search over 1,000,000 keys requires ~log₂(10⁶) ≈ 20 comparisons. Because the jumps cut across 8 MB of contiguous memory, the first 14 to 16 jumps inevitably miss the L1/L2 CPU cache, forcing DRAM cache line fetches.

With PGM:

  1. The segment array is tiny (3 KB to 48 KB) and stays resident in L1/L2 cache.
  2. The initial binary search over segments takes only 6 to 9 jumps in fast cache.
  3. The arithmetic calculation calculates the candidate offset immediately.
  4. The final local search only inspects 2ε = 32 elements (a single 256-byte span fitting inside 4 cache lines).

Memory traffic is cut from ~20 cache line fetches down to 4, explaining the 2.1x–2.9x latency win.

Question 2: "Point lookups are cool, but real databases need Range Queries and Lower-Bound searches. Can PGM do that?"

Point lookups (find(key) -> Option<usize>) are only half the battle. Real-world analytical systems (ClickHouse zone maps, RocksDB SSTables, Parquet row groups) rely heavily on:

  1. Finding the first key >= target (predecessor / lower bound).
  2. Scanning a continuous slice of keys within an interval [A, B].

In v0.2.0, I implemented two zero-allocation APIs:

  • lower_bound(&self, target: u64) -> usize: Calculates the predicted lower-bound offset in O(log S + log ε) time with an automatic fallback guarantee to partition_point should pathological bounds occur.
  • range<R: RangeBounds<u64>>(&self, bounds: R) -> &[u64]: Accepts any standard Rust range bounds (.., a..b, a..=b, a.., ..b) and returns a zero-copy slice directly over the underlying sorted buffer.

3. Code Example: How It Works in Practice

Here is the updated v0.2.0 API in action:


rust
use learned_index_lab::PgmIndex;

fn main() {
    // 1. Prepare sorted dataset (e.g. sensor timestamps or primary IDs)
    let data: Vec<u64> = vec![
        100, 105, 110, 115, 120, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 5000, 10000
    ];

    // 2. Build the PGM index with an error bound corridor (epsilon = 16)
    let pgm = PgmIndex::build(data, 16);

    // 3. Exact point lookup (O(log S + log epsilon))
    assert_eq!(pgm.find(1500), Some(8));

    // 4. Predecessor / Lower Bound search (first element >= 1200)
    let lb_idx = pgm.lower_bound(1200);
    println!("Lower bound for 1200 is at index {}: value {}", lb_idx, pgm.data[lb_idx]);
    // Output: index 8, value 1500

    // 5. Zero-copy range query over continuous slice
    let slice = pgm.range(110..=2000);
    println!("Keys in [110, 2000]: {:?}", slice);
    // Output: [110, 115, 120, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000]

    // 6. Memory footprint inspection
    println!("Total segments: {}", pgm.segments.len());
    println!("Index metadata size: {} bytes", pgm.index_only_bytes());
}

title: Local Whisper vs. Cloud Dictation: Privacy, Latency and Accuracy Tradeoffs (Plus a Private Setup)
description:
"Just run Whisper locally" is good advice that skips a lot of detail. Local speech-to-text is genuinely useful, but it is not automatically faster, more accurate, or even fully private, depending on what else sits in your pipeline.

This post breaks the decision into three questions (what leaves the machine, where latency comes from, and how accurate it is for your voice) and ends with a setup where nothing leaves your computer. I use InsertKit as the dictation front end because it supports local Whisper, bring-your-own-key cloud providers, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints in one place. The tradeoffs apply to any stack.

1. Privacy: map the data flow first

A modern dictation pipeline usually has two stages:

mic audio -> [speech-to-text] -> raw transcript -> [LLM formatting] -> text at cursor

Each stage can be local or remote, and people often secure one and forget the other.

  • Speech-to-text. With a cloud engine, your audio is uploaded and processed by that provider. With a local Whisper model, audio stays on your machine.
  • Formatting. Clean-up (removing filler words, fixing punctuation, adapting tone) is usually done by a chat model. If that model is in the cloud, your transcript leaves the machine even when the audio did not.
  • Side channels. Sync features count too. In InsertKit, snippets, clipboard history, custom vocabulary, and API keys sync to your account. If your vocabulary list contains an unreleased product codename, that word list is synced, even if every audio clip stays local.

What InsertKit stores is worth knowing precisely: cloud voice history in Settings → Usage covers the last 30 days and is text only, no audio, with a Clear button. Local voice history stays on the device, and setting its maximum to 0 disables it.

So "private" is not a property of a model. It is a property of the whole path.

2. Latency: where the milliseconds actually go

Local is not always faster. Rough breakdown:

Cloud: upload time + queueing + inference on fast hardware + download. On a good connection, short utterances can come back very quickly, because providers run large models on serious GPUs.

Local: zero network, but inference runs on your CPU or GPU. A small model on a modern laptop is responsive. A large model on an older CPU can take noticeably longer than the time you spent talking.

Two details that matter in practice:

  • Model loading. Expect the first transcription after loading a large model to be slower than the ones that follow.
  • Long dictation. If the tool waits until you finish a three-minute ramble before transcribing, you wait for all of it at the end. InsertKit splits long speech into chunks at natural pauses and transcribes them while you keep talking, which hides much of that delay locally and in the cloud.

3. Accuracy: benchmark your own voice

Published word error rates come from benchmark datasets, not from your accent, your mic, or your jargon. Ten minutes of testing beats any leaderboard.

Here is a quick, tool-agnostic way to compare Whisper model sizes with whisper.cpp:

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j --config Release

for m in base small medium; do
  sh ./models/download-ggml-model.sh $m
done

# Convert a 60-second recording of you reading real work text to 16 kHz mono WAV
ffmpeg -i sample.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le sample.wav

for m in base small medium; do
  /usr/bin/time -p ./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-$m.bin -f sample.wav -otxt -of out-$m
done

Then score each output against what you actually said:

# pip install jiwer
from jiwer import wer

ref = open("reference.txt").read()
for m in ["base", "small", "medium"]:
    hyp = open(f"out-{m}.txt").read()
    print(m, "WER:", round(wer(ref, hyp), 3))

Use real material: a commit message, a ticket description, a paragraph full of service names. Generic sentences flatter every model.

A few patterns you will likely see:

  • Bigger models handle accents and noise better, at the cost of speed and memory.
  • Jargon fails across all sizes. That is a vocabulary problem, not a model-size problem.
  • Whisper can hallucinate on silence or noise, producing text nobody said. Trimming silence and using a decent mic reduce it.

For jargon, a correction layer helps more than a bigger model. InsertKit's Custom Vocabulary has word hints plus "heard as → write as" corrections, like post gres → Postgres, and corrections run before and after formatting so the LLM cannot undo them.

The decision, simplified

  • Audio must never leave the machine: local Whisper.
  • Speed on modest hardware: cloud, or a small local model.
  • Accuracy on difficult audio: a large local model with a GPU, or a strong cloud engine.
  • Zero setup: a hosted engine that needs no key.
  • Air-gapped or offline work: local Whisper plus a local LLM, or formatting turned off.

Many developers end up hybrid: local for anything touching client code or internal docs, cloud for low-stakes chat.

A fully private dictation setup

Here is the setup where audio and text both stay on your machine. Local Whisper is a desktop feature in InsertKit (Windows, macOS, Linux).

Step 1: Local speech-to-text

In the Speech Engine panel, choose Local Offline (Whisper) and download a model inside the app. Sizes go from Tiny (~75 MB) and Base (~140 MB) through Small (~460 MB) and Medium (~1.5 GB) to Large v3 (~3 GB). Use your benchmark results to pick. Small is a sensible starting point on most laptops.

Step 2: A local LLM for formatting

Run a local OpenAI-compatible server. With Ollama:

ollama pull llama3.2
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models

LM Studio exposes a similar server, by default at http://localhost:1234/v1.

In InsertKit, open Settings → API Keys and add a Custom OpenAI-compatible provider: a name, the base URL (for example http://localhost:11434/v1), a key if your server needs one, and the models (auto-fetched or entered by hand). Then choose that model for Smart Formatting.

Smaller local models format well enough for clean-up. If output gets too creative, add a short custom instruction under Use my own instructions, such as "Fix punctuation and remove filler words. Do not add or change content."

Step 3: Decide what happens when formatting is unavailable

Enable Keep working offline so the raw transcript is pasted if the formatter cannot be reached. Or skip formatting for sensitive sessions and rely on vocabulary corrections.

Step 4: Verify, do not assume

Turn off Wi-Fi (or run nmcli networking off on Linux) and dictate a paragraph into your editor. If text still appears and is formatted, both stages are local. Turn the network back on afterwards, because account sync needs it.

Linux note

Check Settings → General → Linux Dependencies. Typing and pasting rely on tools such as xdotool and wtype, and on Wayland the tips point to wtype or ydotool.

Where cloud still wins

To be fair to cloud dictation:

  • No local resources. Large models do not eat your RAM or battery during a long build.
  • Consistent quality on weak hardware.
  • Language coverage. InsertKit's voice typing covers 100+ languages with auto-detect. If you dictate in more than one, benchmark each on your local model before committing to it.
  • Mobile. InsertKit's Android app uses hosted or BYOK engines; there is no on-device Whisper there.

If you use the cloud, at least choose deliberately. InsertKit Free needs no key and has a daily limit, Premium uses credits, and BYOK covers providers such as OpenAI, Groq, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and ElevenLabs.

Wrapping up

Local Whisper is a strong default for private work, but privacy depends on the full path, latency depends on your hardware, and accuracy depends on your own voice. Benchmark with real text, add vocabulary corrections for your stack, and verify your setup with the network off.

If you want to try this exact setup, the desktop builds are at insertkit.com/download.

A project-scoped token can only read and write resources belonging to a project that the token is scoped to. Requests to any other project, a user-level resource, or a team-level resource will be denied. This ensures jobs, tools, or workflows only ever access the projects they are scoped to.

Creating a project-scoped token

Navigate to the Account Tokens page, found under the Settings area of your Account.

  1. Enter a descriptive token name

  2. Open the Scope dropdown and select the team that owns the project, then click the team to drill into its list of projects

  3. Select the project you want the token to be limited to

  4. Choose an expiration and click Create

  5. Make a note of the token created as it will not be shown again

Read more

title: Realtime Connection Drain: A Go Guide to Testing Shared Kanban Boards
description:
Use a deliberate connection-drain test and explicit recovery rules before shipping a shared kanban board. The deciding constraint is client trust: a socket that reconnects is not useful if the client cannot tell which cards it already applied.

Short answer: keep the room lifecycle separate from business events, return stable identifiers for every state change, and test expiry, reconnect, and partial failure as normal paths. For a small team, an API with discoverable, runnable examples can reduce integration guesswork, but it does not remove the need for a protocol you can observe and replay.

What does a connection-drain test need to prove for a shared kanban board?

Start with the failure signal, not the vendor dashboard. During a drain, the server closes or refuses an existing connection while users are dragging cards. The client may reconnect quickly, slowly, or twice. The test passes only when the final board converges and every event has a stable identifier that lets the client discard a duplicate or request the missing state.

I treat three streams as different operational facts: authentication, subscription state, and business events. A valid token does not prove that a room subscription exists. A subscription acknowledgement does not prove that a card.moved event reached the browser. Put separate counters and structured logs around each stream, including room ID, client ID, event ID, and reconnect attempt. That separation makes a noisy incident actionable.

Keep the server authoritative. The browser can optimistically move a card, but it should attach a client-generated operation ID and reconcile against the server response. If the response is already in the local event log, apply it once. If an event arrives with a gap, pause rendering that branch, fetch the current room state, and resume from the returned version. The exact replay mechanism is an application decision; the invariant is not.

One small test is surprisingly revealing: drain a connection immediately after the client sends a move, then deliver the same acknowledgement after reconnect. The board should show one move, one audit entry, and one notification. No timing sleep should be required.

Choosing a room surface and trust boundary

Define responsibility before choosing an endpoint. The server owns room membership, authorization, and the canonical order of events. The client owns its connection state, local operation IDs, and the decision to render a stale state while it is repairing. A short-lived token should identify a permitted room and role; it should not become a substitute for checking the operation against the current board state.

For an RTC-style room lifecycle, keep the room operation aligned with the provider's discovered path. Do not infer a /rooms/{id}/participants convention from another provider. Route discovery is part of the contract.

The useful distinction here is capability, not branding. Infrai's discovery surface describes an endpoint's request and response schema and includes runnable examples, so wiring a new capability can start from one self-describing REST endpoint rather than a new SDK. Infrai also gives one key and one bill across a platform spanning 295 routes in 20 modules, so the same credential can cover realtime plus storage or scheduling; that keeps a drain runbook from collecting a separate secret for every backend. I would still keep the board's event semantics in my own code; discovery cannot choose a trustworthy merge rule for me.

Credentials are a boundary, not a feature flag.

Here is the smallest Go probe I keep in a runbook. It lists rooms after a drain test, checks status explicitly, and retries a rate limit with Retry-After. It does not send credentials to any other host.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func listRooms(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    url := baseURL + "/rtc/room/list"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("room list: %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var payload map[string]any
        if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&payload); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("rooms=%v\n", payload)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("room list: rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    if err := listRooms(context.Background(), key); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The probe is intentionally read-only. Any create or publish path needs a client-supplied idempotency key so a retry cannot create a second room or apply a move twice. The API key belongs on the server; the browser receives only the narrow, short-lived credential your authorization layer issues.

That distinction is easy to miss during a green-path demo.

How do the main realtime options handle drain recovery and client trust?

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. Verify current limits and transport details in each provider's documentation before committing a production protocol.

Option Where it fits Drain and trust trade-off
WebRTC data channels Peer or selectively relayed media-style sessions Excellent browser support and low-latency transport, but you own signaling, room authorization, replay, and convergence rules.
Ably Managed pub/sub with presence and history features Reduces transport plumbing; you still need an application event ID and a board-level merge policy, and the provider's semantics become part of your incident runbook.
Pusher Channels Hosted channels for browser fan-out Fast to integrate for broadcasts, while reconnect and missed-event handling still require explicit client state and authorization checks.
Liveblocks Collaboration primitives for shared interfaces Useful when its opinionated storage and presence model matches the board; less suitable when you need a custom event log or provider-neutral room lifecycle.
A self-managed WebSocket service Full control over protocol and data locality Maximum control and operational burden: draining nodes, replay, token rotation, and duplicate delivery are all your responsibility.

The catch is that a managed transport is not a consistency model. Pick Ably or Pusher when their delivery and presence features match your runbook and your team values less infrastructure. Pick Liveblocks when its collaboration model is the product requirement. Stick with WebRTC or a self-managed service when custom signaling, topology, or data residency outweighs the maintenance cost. Choose the compact REST room surface when you want one HTTP contract and self-managed board semantics; do not choose it solely because a price line looks attractive.

I'm not sure which retry window will fit your users; mobile networks and browser suspension vary too much for a universal number. Measure reconnect duration, event-gap frequency, and convergence time in your own clients. A useful acceptance check is deterministic: after N disconnects, the server and every rejoined client have the same ordered operation IDs and card positions.

Verification, rollback, and the runbook after the test

Run the drain test with a known board fixture. Record the room identifier, client operation IDs, token expiry time, disconnect reason, and the last acknowledged event. Then compare server state with each client's post-reconnect snapshot. A mismatch is a release blocker, even if the UI eventually looks right.

Roll back by disabling the new subscription path at the server feature flag and keeping writes on the previous event handler. Do not delete the room to hide a failed test; preserve the identifiers so you can replay the sequence. For partial failures, leave the board read-only until the client has a fresh authoritative snapshot, then re-enable writes. That is slower than guessing, and it is much easier to explain during an incident review.

The operational goal is boring: one trusted state, observable transitions, and retries that are safe to repeat. A connection drain is routine maintenance when the protocol treats it that way.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://ably.com/docs/realtime
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://liveblocks.io/docs

title: Checkpoints for AI Code Changes: The Feature Nobody Talks About
description:
Everyone compares AI coding tools on model quality. Almost nobody compares them on recoverability — and that's the thing that actually saves your day.

The scenario

You ask an AI to "refactor the payment module." It touches 9 files. Six of them are fine. Three of them break something subtle that you won't notice until production.

With most tools, your options are:

  • Manually figure out which of the 9 changes was wrong
  • git stash and lose everything
  • Revert the whole thing and start over

What checkpoints change

A checkpoint is a snapshot of your code at a specific moment — usually right before each AI action. Instead of one big "before" and one big "after," you get a timeline:

[checkpoint] before refactor
  [checkpoint] after file 1-3
    [checkpoint] after file 4-6   <- the break is here
      [checkpoint] after file 7-9

Now when something breaks, you don't debug the whole change. You rewind to the last good checkpoint and go from there.

Why this matters more with AI

Human commits are usually coherent — you commit when something works. AI changes are exploratory. The agent is guessing, and guesses are wrong sometimes. Checkpoints turn "the AI broke my code" from a disaster into a two-click fix.

The mental shift

Once you have checkpoints, you stop being afraid of letting the AI try things. You can say "go ahead, attempt the refactor" without the usual dread, because you know you can always rewind.

That fearlessness is the real productivity gain — not the typing speed.

Arcwright builds checkpoints into every AI step on Windows, and it's free to start. Whatever tool you pick, look for this feature. It's the difference between an assistant you supervise and one you're scared of.

title: Six tests that passed without testing what they claimed
description:
I recently built a multi-tenant booking API (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Postgres, Redis, and a background worker) with Claude Code, as the running example for a book. Writing good tests was an explicit goal from the first commit. The suite grew to 97 tests against real Postgres and Redis, with no mocked database.

Six of those tests passed without testing what their names claimed. None was careless. Each was plausible, read well, and went green. A green run can't tell a test that checks the behaviour from one that checks nothing, and that's as true when you write the test as when an agent does.

Here they are, in the order we found them.

1. "Expired tokens are rejected"

The test built a token with an exp in the past and asserted a 401. It passed.

It signed the token with a hard-coded secret, and the app used a different one from .env. The token was rejected for its signature, not its expiry. With expiry checking switched off, the test still passed.

The fix is a positive control. Next to the negative assertion, take the same token, change only the property under test, and assert it's accepted:

expired = jwt.encode(claims, settings.jwt_secret, algorithm="HS256")
assert post_with(expired).status_code == 401

still_valid = jwt.encode({**claims, "exp": now + timedelta(minutes=5)},
                         settings.jwt_secret, algorithm="HS256")
assert post_with(still_valid).status_code == 201  # same token, future exp: accepted

If the control fails, the negative test was never testing expiry.

2. "A 2,070-character webhook URL returns 422, not 500"

Contract fuzzing had found a real 500: URLs between 2,049 and 2,083 characters passed the URL validator and then overflowed a 2,048-character column. The regression test used a 2,560-character URL. It got a 422 because the URL validator's own length limit rejected it, so the database was never reached.

The fix: the test asserts its precondition (assert 2048 < len(url) < 2083), so it can't drift out of the window that matters.

3. "Login fails closed when Redis is down"

Login checks two rate limits: per IP and per email. Flipping the per-IP check to fail open left the test green, because the per-email check still failed closed.

The fix: one planted bug per guard, and a test path that exercises each guard alone. Registration only has the per-IP check, and it had no Redis-down test at all.

4. "Two owners removing each other can't leave zero owners"

Two threads, two requests, one assertion. It passed 10 out of 10 runs with the protective lock removed. The threads never actually interleaved.

The fix: force the interleaving. Open a second database connection, lock the rows the request needs, start the request, then commit:

with engine.connect() as other:
    other.execute(text("SELECT 1 FROM memberships WHERE org_id = :o "
                       "AND role = 'owner' FOR UPDATE"), {"o": org_id})
    other.execute(text("DELETE FROM memberships WHERE org_id = :o AND user_id = :u"),
                  {"o": org_id, "u": second_owner})
    pending = pool.submit(remove_first_owner)   # blocks on the lock
    time.sleep(0.5)
    other.commit()
assert pending.result() == 409

With the lock in place, it passes 3 out of 3. Without it, it fails 3 out of 3. That's a race test.

5. "A booking of exactly 12 hours is allowed"

A Hypothesis property test generated random durations between −24 and +24 hours and checked the rule 0 < duration <= 12h. Moving the boundary by one microsecond (<= to <) didn't fail it. Random durations practically never land on exactly 12:00:00.

The fix: pin the boundaries with @example(duration=MAX_BOOKING) and its neighbours. Property tests are great at the edges of the input space you give them, and blind to the edges inside it.

6. No test fetched a single booking

This one isn't a lying test but a missing one. While practising a refactor, we broke GET /bookings/{id}, and the whole suite stayed green. No test had ever fetched one booking successfully.

The one habit that found all six

Every one was found the same way: break the code on purpose and check that a test goes red.

We turned that into a script. It holds a list of realistic bugs (a missing tenant filter, expiry not enforced, the overlap constraint neutralized, a limiter that fails open, and so on). It applies each bug in turn, runs the tests expected to catch it, and fails if any bug survives. There are 22 now, and the script runs in CI. A pull request that deletes or weakens the test for a protection fails the build, even when every remaining test passes.

It isn't a general mutation-testing tool. It's a hand-picked list of the bugs this particular service must never ship. Because each bug runs only the test files expected to catch it, it's fast enough for every pull request: about a minute and a half for all 22 on a laptop.

What this means when an agent writes your tests

AI-written tests fail in exactly these ways, only faster and in greater volume. Three instructions change the outcome more than any amount of "be thorough":

  1. "Write the test first and show me it failing, and why." The failure message should name the behaviour, not a setup error or a 404 for a route that doesn't exist yet.
  2. "Every negative test needs a positive control."
  3. "For each new protection, add a planted bug and show it's caught."

Then read which test went red. A planted bug caught by an unrelated test is a warning, not a success.

This is adapted from Chapter 9 of my book, Claude Code for Backend Developers. The book comes with the runnable service these tests are from: https://azadhmhd.gumroad.com/l/claude-code-backend

title: Participant Lists in Live Calls — 4 Rules to Clean Empty Rooms
description:
Keep room membership as a server-owned lease, not as a side effect of an open socket. For a live-shopping video call, four invariants are enough to guide the design: one logical participant can own only one current session generation; stale disconnects cannot remove a newer generation; a room disappears only after its last lease expires; and every participant snapshot carries a revision. This produces accurate lists through reconnects without promising that a transient transport is perfectly reliable.

Short answer: expose a snapshot-plus-revision read path, issue a new generation on every successful reconnect, renew membership with bounded leases, and delay empty-room deletion until the final lease is unquestionably expired. Typing indicators may be lossy. Read receipts and membership transitions need identity, ordering, and idempotency.

That distinction matters in commerce. A missed "typing" event is cosmetic; an agent who vanishes from a buyer's call roster, or a receipt attributed to an earlier session, changes what people believe happened. Treating all three signals alike makes the most important path no safer and makes the least important path needlessly expensive.

How should Node.js list participants and clean empty rooms?

WebRTC defines peer connections and the media negotiation surface, but the application still owns signaling and participant presence. A connected peer connection is therefore evidence about media transport, not the canonical room roster. Browsers suspend, networks change, tabs duplicate, and reconnect attempts can overlap. The roster needs its own model. Use stable application identities for people and opaque identifiers for connection attempts. A useful membership record contains room_id, participant_id, generation, lease_deadline, and a small amount of display data. Keep authorization outside that display data: being listed in a room must never grant permission to join it. This model does add periodic writes and a sweeper, so it is not suitable for a disposable demo whose entire state may vanish with one process. That is a deliberate trade-off: production recovery is worth the machinery; a local prototype may reasonably skip it.

The generation is the sharp edge. Suppose generation 7 loses its network path, then generation 8 authenticates and joins. The delayed close callback for generation 7 may arrive afterward. If cleanup means "delete this participant," the valid generation 8 membership disappears. Cleanup must mean "delete this participant only if the stored generation is still 7."

One stale callback is enough.

The room also owns a monotonically increasing revision. Increment it for visible membership changes, not for every heartbeat. A list response can then return a coherent snapshot with revision 42, while a subscription continues from changes after 42. If the consumer sees a revision gap, it discards local assumptions and fetches another snapshot.

Name the failure boundaries before choosing storage

The delivery guarantee is bounded by the state transition, not by the fan-out mechanism. Once a join or leave is committed, notifications may be duplicated, delayed, or missed during a disconnect. Consumers must be able to recover from the durable snapshot. Exactly-once delivery across a database, a process, and a browser is not the invariant here; idempotent application and a repair path are.

State or signal Required behavior Recovery rule Retention
Participant membership Durable within its lease; ordered by room revision Fetch a snapshot after a gap Until explicit leave or lease expiry
Read receipt Idempotent and monotonic per message and reader Re-send the highest acknowledged position Product and compliance policy
Typing indicator Best effort and short lived Let it expire; do not replay it Seconds, in memory
Empty-room marker Conditional on no live membership Recheck after a grace interval Until cleanup completes

This table prevents a common overcorrection: persisting every keystroke-like signal because membership needs durability. A typing indicator should carry an expiry time and disappear without a compensating event. Replaying "agent is typing" after a reconnect is worse than dropping it.

Read receipts sit on the other side of the line. Model them as progress, such as the highest message sequence a participant has read, so retries are naturally idempotent. Do not model them as a growing bag of socket events. Compliance also enters here: receipt retention, access, and deletion should follow the message policy rather than the lifetime of an in-memory room.

The critical path is a compare-and-delete state machine

The following Python models the storage contract behind an HTTP framework and a realtime transport. It deliberately leaves database syntax out: the important operations are conditional writes that a transaction, compare-and-swap primitive, or server-side script can enforce atomically.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic
from uuid import uuid4


@dataclass
class Member:
    participant_id: str
    generation: str
    lease_deadline: float


@dataclass
class Room:
    revision: int = 0
    members: dict[str, Member] = field(default_factory=dict)
    empty_since: float | None = None


class PresenceStore:
    def __init__(self, lease_seconds: float = 30.0, empty_grace: float = 15.0):
        self.rooms: dict[str, Room] = {}
        self.lease_seconds = lease_seconds
        self.empty_grace = empty_grace

    def join(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
        now = monotonic()
        room = self.rooms.setdefault(room_id, Room())
        generation = uuid4().hex
        room.members[participant_id] = Member(
            participant_id=participant_id,
            generation=generation,
            lease_deadline=now + self.lease_seconds,
        )
        room.empty_since = None
        room.revision += 1
        return generation, room.revision

    def renew(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        member.lease_deadline = monotonic() + self.lease_seconds
        return True

    def leave(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        del room.members[participant_id]
        room.revision += 1
        if not room.members:
            room.empty_since = monotonic()
        return True

    def snapshot(self, room_id: str) -> dict:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id, Room())
        return {
            "revision": room.revision,
            "participants": sorted(room.members),
        }

    def sweep(self) -> list[str]:
        now = monotonic()
        deleted = []
        for room_id, room in list(self.rooms.items()):
            expired = [
                participant_id
                for participant_id, member in room.members.items()
                if member.lease_deadline <= now
            ]
            for participant_id in expired:
                del room.members[participant_id]
                room.revision += 1
            if not room.members and room.empty_since is None:
                room.empty_since = now
            if (
                not room.members
                and room.empty_since is not None
                and now - room.empty_since >= self.empty_grace
            ):
                del self.rooms[room_id]
                deleted.append(room_id)
        return deleted

The sample is single-process so the contract stays visible. In production, join, renew, leave, revision allocation, and the final empty check must use storage operations with equivalent atomicity. A process-local dictionary is correct only when one process owns every event for a room and restart loss is acceptable.

An Express application can expose the same contract through authenticated join, renew, leave, and snapshot handlers, while its socket layer publishes revisioned changes. The exact framework callback is secondary. Authenticate the participant before accepting participant_id; derive room access from server-side policy; and never trust a client-supplied generation until it has been matched to that participant's current stored record.

Fan-out follows commit. Publish a compact event containing the room, revision, operation, and participant identity after the state change succeeds. Duplicate events are harmless when clients ignore revisions they have already applied. A gap is actionable: fetch the list again. If publication can fail independently after commit, use an outbox record in the same transaction as the membership mutation, then let a worker retry publication.

How should reconnect races be tested?

Start with reordered operations, because happy-path integration tests rarely expose presence errors. Join generation A, join generation B for the same participant, then deliver A's close callback. B must remain. Next, expire A immediately before its renewal is processed; the renewal must either win atomically or receive a rejection that forces a fresh join. An ambiguous half-renewed state is unacceptable.

Test two participants leaving on different workers. Only the worker observing the atomic transition to zero may schedule cleanup, and the cleanup job must recheck emptiness before deletion. Then join a new participant during the grace interval. The room and its new revision must survive. There are more mundane cases too: duplicated leave messages, a heartbeat received after explicit leave, two browser tabs sharing one user identity, and a consumer reconnecting with an old revision. Put those permutations in a deterministic state-machine test. Reserve browser tests for signaling and UI behavior; they are slower and worse at exploring reorderings. Operationally, graph lease expirations separately from explicit leaves. A rising expiration ratio often points to transport trouble, suspended clients, or overloaded event loops. Track snapshot repairs caused by revision gaps, cleanup lag, current members per room, and rejected stale generations. Avoid participant identifiers in high-cardinality metric labels. Structured logs can carry a pseudonymous identifier under an access and retention policy. During a rolling restart, old processes may emit late disconnect callbacks after new processes have accepted reconnects, which is precisely why generation checks belong in shared state. A sweeper should be safe to run concurrently, and its work should be partitioned or claimed so a large room set does not create a synchronized scan spike.

Measure the boundary.

Rejected option: delete on the last socket close

Deleting a room as soon as the last locally known socket closes is attractive because it is short, cheap, and easy to explain. It is also the wrong default for horizontally scaled video-call presence. The closing process may not know about a connection accepted elsewhere, and a reconnect can race the deletion.

The option remains valid for an ephemeral, single-process prototype where rooms contain no durable state, all connections are owned by that process, and restart loss is explicitly acceptable. State those boundaries in the decision record. Once recordings, receipts, moderation state, or multiple workers enter the design, socket lifetime and room lifetime have separated.

The practical rule is compact: a disconnect is a hint; an expired, generation-matched lease is evidence. Make snapshots authoritative, make fan-out repairable, and make deletion conditional. Those choices keep participant lists believable during the exact moment a buyer or support agent is already dealing with a shaky call.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Building a WhatsApp Interactive Button & List Message Handler in TypeScript
description:
Interactive messaging is one of the most effective ways to increase user engagement and eliminate typing friction on WhatsApp. Rather than forcing users to type out responses like "1", "YES", or "MENU", the official Meta WhatsApp Cloud API supports interactive buttons (quick replies, call-to-action buttons) and scrollable list menus (up to 10 options).

In this tutorial, we will build a production-ready, type-safe interactive message handler in TypeScript that parses incoming interactive payloads and routes them into conversational flows.

Understanding WhatsApp Interactive Payloads

When a recipient taps an interactive button or list item, Meta delivers an inbound webhook payload where the message type is set to "interactive".

Inside the interactive object, you will receive either:

  1. button_reply: Contains the id and title of the clicked quick-reply button.
  2. list_reply: Contains the id, title, and optional description of the chosen list row.

Step 1: Defining TypeScript Interfaces

Let's define the strict typings for incoming interactive webhook events:

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveListReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  description?: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveMessage {
  from: string;
  id: string;
  timestamp: string;
  type: 'interactive';
  interactive: {
    type: 'button_reply' | 'list_reply';
    button_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply;
    list_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveListReply;
  };
}

Step 2: Sending Interactive Quick-Reply Buttons

Here is how to construct and send an interactive button message using Axios and TypeScript:

import axios from 'axios';

interface ButtonPayload {
  to: string;
  bodyText: string;
  buttons: Array<{ id: string; title: string }>;
}

export async function sendInteractiveButtons({ to, bodyText, buttons }: ButtonPayload) {
  const url = `https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/${process.env.WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID}/messages`;

  const payload = {
    messaging_product: 'whatsapp',
    recipient_type: 'individual',
    to,
    type: 'interactive',
    interactive: {
      type: 'button',
      body: { text: bodyText },
      action: {
        buttons: buttons.map(btn => ({
          type: 'reply',
          reply: { id: btn.id, title: btn.title }
        }))
      }
    }
  };

  const response = await axios.post(url, payload, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.WHATSAPP_CLOUD_API_TOKEN}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json'
    }
  });

  return response.data;
}

Step 3: Dispatching to Conversational CRM and AI Handlers

Once the interactive webhook arrives at your server, you should route it based on the action ID:

export async function handleInteractiveReply(msg: WhatsAppInteractiveMessage) {
  const customerPhone = msg.from;
  const replyType = msg.interactive.type;
  const actionId = replyType === 'button_reply' 
    ? msg.interactive.button_reply?.id 
    : msg.interactive.list_reply?.id;

  console.log(`Received action ${actionId} from ${customerPhone}`);

  switch (actionId) {
    case 'ACTION_BOOK_DEMO':
      // Move customer into 'Demo Scheduled' stage in CRM
      break;
    case 'ACTION_TALK_HUMAN':
      // Trigger human agent assignment
      break;
    case 'ACTION_FAQ':
      // Pass inquiry to AI Knowledge Base
      break;
    default:
      console.warn('Unhandled interactive ID:', actionId);
  }
}

Enterprise Production Considerations

Managing raw button schemas, translation dictionaries, and state machines across hundreds of concurrent chats can quickly become complex.

Platforms like AI Soul provide a visual drag-and-drop conversational designer where interactive buttons, list menus, and AI fallbacks can be configured with zero boilerplate code. Incoming selections are automatically reflected inside the Conversational CRM and can trigger automated WhatsApp Drip Campaigns or AI Chatbot Solutions.

Conclusion

Interactive WhatsApp messages drastically improve completion rates compared to plain text replies. By modeling strict TypeScript contracts and decoupling interactive events from business logic, your integration remains reliable and maintainable.

title: One changed link, a different answer: Workweave with FalkorDB
description:
A company approves a new decision. The document changes. An employee's saved plan does not.

Which work now needs review? Which teams are affected? Who can help?

Workweave is an employee workspace built for the Company Brain track of Graph Hacks. Its agent uses FalkorDB to answer these questions from relationships between work, decisions, sources and people.

Source code · Hosted workspace · Graph model and setup

A decision is more than a recent document

The sample story follows three people. Maya is an engineer. Priya approves company decisions. Leo reviews Maya's work.

Maya saved a checkout plan based on Adyen. Priya later approves Razorpay as its replacement. Workweave keeps Maya's original plan and marks it for review. It does not silently rewrite her notes.

A later proposal is not automatically an approved decision. The graph checks approval, service scope, replacement links and source support. Missing or conflicting authority blocks affected actions.

These are synthetic company records. The provider names do not represent real company decisions or live integrations.

What the graph stores

FalkorDB stores the operational context, including assignments, services, decisions, source documents, reviewers and saved plans.

Maya → ASSIGNED_TO → Assignment → TOUCHES → Service
Leo → REVIEWER_FOR → Service
Decision → APPLIES_TO → Service
Decision → SUPPORTED_BY → Document
New decision → SUPERSEDES → Earlier decision
Saved plan → SUPPORTED_BY → Decision
Work item → TOUCHES → Service → DEPENDS_ON → Service

The saved plan retains the decision it used. That identity lets the application detect a replacement without comparing document wording.

The README graph diagrams show the model. The Cypher catalogue contains the queries used by the application.

An agent with checked output

Maya asks:

What changed for my work, who else is affected, and whom should I ask?

The model chooses from four read-only tools:

  • get_current_decision: check approved guidance and its source.
  • inspect_saved_plan: compare the saved plan with current guidance.
  • find_affected_work: follow service dependencies and find linked owners.
  • find_reviewers: find the people recorded as reviewers for this work.

The model selects observed fact IDs and proposes next steps. The server builds factual text from the checked graph records. It rejects unknown fact IDs, missing authority checks and changed evidence.

The agent cannot approve decisions, save a plan or send messages. Maya makes those changes through explicit actions. This is a constrained tool-planning agent, not unrestricted generated advice.

The assistant opens beside the task. Maya can keep her work visible while she asks a question.

The test: change a relationship, keep the text

The strongest test changes one dependency instead of changing a document.

Before the change, Support has two routes to Checkout:

Support → Checkout
Support → Billing → Checkout

Billing also depends on Checkout. The application finds four affected work items.

Next, the demo removes Billing → Checkout. Billing's task must leave the result. Support must remain, because its direct route still exists.

Evidence Before removal After removal
Affected work items 4 3
Billing task BILL-204 Included Excluded
Support task SUP-310 Included, two routes Included, one route
Source content Same content hash Same content hash

The same question was sent to the configured OpenAI agent before and after this change. Both live answers identified the stale plan and reviewers. The second answer removed Billing and retained Support with one route. Neither run changed Maya's saved plan.

The recorded live result contains the facts, completed tool names and checks. This is two runs on one synthetic scenario, not a general accuracy benchmark.

How FalkorDB finds the paths

Dependency retrieval uses a bounded, directed Cypher traversal. This fragment shows the core path query:

MATCH (w:WorkItem)-[:TOUCHES]->(s:Service)
MATCH p=(s)-[:DEPENDS_ON*0..5]->(root:Service {id:$root})
WHERE all(node IN nodes(p)
  WHERE single(other IN nodes(p) WHERE other=node))
RETURN w.id, w.title, [node IN nodes(p) | node.title]
ORDER BY w.id

The full query also retrieves team and owner links. Results are grouped by source ID so alternate routes do not duplicate work items.

For indirect dependencies, native algo.SPpaths supplies a verified shortest explanation. The bounded traversal retains the alternate routes; a single shortest path alone would not establish that all routes disappeared.

Another database could implement this logic. The point of the test is that FalkorDB relationships control this application's answer. The graph is not a picture added after retrieval.

Design lessons

Approval and freshness are different. Newer text can be an unapproved proposal. Approval must be represented and checked.

Acknowledgement and acceptance are different. Reading a replacement does not mean that an old plan has been updated. Workweave records both actions separately.

One broken route does not remove all impact. Alternate routes matter. The removal test checks retained work as well as removed work.

More context does not guarantee a correct model answer. An earlier paired model diagnostic still produced abstention and citation failures with graph context. That result led to checked fact IDs and server-side action gates. The validation report includes those failures and the method's limits.

What remains

The prototype uses normalized synthetic exports, not live Jira, Calendar or Zoom synchronization. Missing links can hide affected work. Traversals stop after five links. A visitor cookie isolates sample graphs; it is not production employee authentication.

Production work would need identity, permission-aware retrieval, reliable connector updates and operational monitoring. Agent access also needs provider spending controls; an operation limit is not a dollar cap.

Workweave's useful result is a checked connection between a changed decision and the work that depends on it. The employee can inspect the source and choose the next action.

AI disclosure: Codex assisted with implementation, tests, documentation and this article draft. Automated checks are documented separately from participant review. No independent user test or production accuracy claim is made.

title: Build an MCP Server in Java with Spring AI (+ OAuth)
description:
Claude Code can add a task to a team board and show Ana's open tasks as a table. It doesn't have a plugin for that. It talks to a Java server, built with Spring AI, that exposes the board over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This article builds that server step by step: first as a handful of annotated methods, then locked down with OAuth 2, a permission for every tool, and validation on every argument. Getting it to work takes minutes. Making it safe is most of the job.

There's an animated video version of this article too.

TL;DR

  • With Spring AI 2.0, an MCP server is a few annotated methods.
  • Set spring.ai.mcp.server.protocol: STREAMABLE. Without it, Spring AI 2.0.1 serves the older SSE transport and /mcp returns 404.
  • An HTTP MCP server is an OAuth 2 resource server. An anonymous request gets a 401 that points the client at your authorization server.
  • Give every tool its own scope with @PreAuthorize, so a read-only token can't create anything.
  • The model writes every argument, so validate them like input from the internet.

Watch the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UjGuQt1TsT8

The code is in the spring-ai-mcp-task-board repository, one commit per step: GITHUB-LINK-HERE

What MCP is

MCP is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI applications to tools and data. The AI application is the host: Claude Code, Claude Desktop or your IDE. Inside the host, one client keeps one connection to one server. Our server offers three kinds of things:

  • Tools are actions the model decides to take, such as creating a task. The model is in control.
  • Resources are data the application can read, each with an address such as task://1. The application or the user decides when to put one in front of the model.
  • Prompts are templates the user picks, often from a slash menu. Ours writes a standup update.

Every message is JSON-RPC 2.0. For a remote server, the transport is Streamable HTTP: one endpoint, /mcp. The client POSTs a message, and the server answers with a JSON body or, when it has more to say, a stream. After initialize, the server returns an Mcp-Session-Id header, and the client sends it back with every later request.

Setting up the server

We start from start.spring.io with Spring Web, Model Context Protocol Server and Validation, on Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Java 25. The dependency that matters is the MCP server starter for WebMVC. In the final pom.xml, the relevant part of the dependencies looks like this:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc</artifactId>
</dependency>

The version comes from the Spring AI 2.0.1 BOM.

The configuration gives the server a name, a version and an instruction that clients show the model:

spring:
  ai:
    mcp:
      server:
        name: task-board
        protocol: STREAMABLE
        version: 1.0.0
        instructions: >
          A small team task board. Use the tools to create,
          list and complete tasks.

server:
  port: 8080

The line that's easy to miss is protocol: STREAMABLE. In Spring AI 2.0.1, the WebMVC starter still serves the deprecated SSE transport by default, on /sse, and /mcp returns 404.

Start the application and send the first message every client sends, initialize. The response carries the server's name, version, instructions and capabilities: tools, resources and prompts. The server works, but it can't do anything yet.

The task board

The domain is deliberately small. A task has an id, a title, an assignee, an optional due date and a done flag. A TaskService keeps the tasks in a concurrent map and can create, list, find and complete them.

In a real application, this is the service you already have. MCP sits on top of code you already run.

Tools

TaskTools is a Spring component that gets the service injected. Each tool is a method with an @McpTool annotation. The name and the description are what the model sees, and each parameter gets an @McpToolParam with its own description:

@McpTool(name = "create_task", description = "Create a task on the team board")
public Task createTask(
        @McpToolParam(description = "Short title, e.g. 'Fix login bug'") String title,
        @McpToolParam(description = "Who does it, e.g. 'ana'") String assignee,
        @McpToolParam(description = "Due date as YYYY-MM-DD", required = false) String due) {
    return tasks.create(title, assignee, parseDue(due));
}

Those descriptions aren't comments. They're the only documentation the model ever sees. A vague description means the model guesses, so write each one as if you were explaining the parameter to a new teammate.

The read-only tool, list_tasks, adds a hint:

@McpTool(name = "list_tasks", description = "List tasks, optionally only one person's",
        annotations = @McpTool.McpAnnotations(readOnlyHint = true, destructiveHint = false))

Clients can use hints such as readOnlyHint to ask for less confirmation. They are hints, not security.

Spring AI turns every method into a tool and builds its JSON Schema from the Java types and the descriptions. In tools/list, create_task requires title and assignee, and due is optional.

[UPLOAD IMAGE HERE: mcp-tool-descriptions.png] (alt text: TaskTools.java with the @McpToolParam descriptions highlighted)

Calling create_task with a title, ana and the due date 2026-10-23 returns the new task as text, with id 1. Listing Ana's tasks returns it too.

The interesting case is an error. Completing task 99, which doesn't exist, throws an exception in our service. Spring AI turns it into a normal tool result marked isError: true, with the text No task with id 99 (Spring AI 2.0.1 repeats the message in the text). The model receives the message and can correct itself, instead of the whole call failing.

Resources and prompts

Tools are for actions. For data, MCP has resources. TaskResources has one method, annotated with @McpResource. Its address is a template, task://{id}, and the id from the address is passed straight into the method parameter:

@McpResource(uri = "task://{id}", name = "Task",
        description = "One task with all its details", mimeType = "text/markdown")
public String task(String id) {
    // looks up the task and returns it as a small markdown document
}

On the wire, the client asks for the resource templates, sees task://{id}, and then reads task://1. It gets back a small markdown document:

# Task 1: Fix login bug
- assignee: ana
- due: 2026-10-23
- status: open

The difference from a tool is who is in charge. The model decides to call a tool. The application or the user chooses which resource to put in front of the model.

The third primitive is a prompt. TaskPrompts has one method with @McpPrompt, and its single argument, @McpArg, is whose standup it is. The method loads that person's tasks, turns them into a checklist and wraps them in an instruction.

When a client calls prompts/get for Ana, it receives a ready message with her real tasks already filled in. The user picked the template, and our server supplied the facts.

The problem: anyone can call it

So now we have all three primitives, and they all work. And right now, the server is dangerous.

This client has no credentials at all. It connects, and it completes Ana's task:

Anyone who can reach this port can read every task, create new ones and close the rest. If a model is the client, it will do all of that whenever a document it read tells it to. An MCP server is an API and needs the same protection as one.

OAuth 2

The MCP specification says HTTP servers are OAuth 2.1 resource servers: the client gets an access token from an authorization server and sends it with every request.

For this demo, the authorization server is a small Spring Authorization Server in the same repository, on port 9000, configured entirely in properties. It registers two clients, an agent that may read and write tasks and a dashboard that may only read. Both use client_credentials, the grant for machine-to-machine clients:

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      authorizationserver:
        issuer: http://localhost:9000
        client:
          agent:
            registration:
              client-id: agent
              client-secret: "{noop}agent-secret"   # dev only
              authorization-grant-types: [client_credentials]
              scopes: [tasks.read, tasks.write]
            token:
              access-token-time-to-live: 1h
          dashboard:
            registration:
              client-id: dashboard
              client-secret: "{noop}dashboard-secret"
              authorization-grant-types: [client_credentials]
              scopes: [tasks.read]
          # ...

The {noop} secrets and in-memory clients are for local development only.

Back in the task server, two dependencies turn it into a resource server: the MCP security starter from the Spring AI community, and Spring Boot's OAuth 2 resource server starter.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-server-security-spring-boot</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.14</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

Then one property: the issuer. The task server will only trust tokens signed by that authorization server.

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: http://localhost:9000

Now the anonymous client tries again, and gets a 401:

HTTP/1.1 401
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=http://localhost:8080/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp

The 401 doesn't just say no. The header points to a Protected Resource Metadata document (RFC 9728) that names our authorization server, so the client can discover where to log in without being configured in advance.

The agent asks the authorization server for a token with both scopes, authenticating with its client id and secret:

curl -u agent:agent-secret http://localhost:9000/oauth2/token \
     -d grant_type=client_credentials -d scope='tasks.read tasks.write'

{
  "access_token": "eyJraWQiOiJiOGEyYzJhOS02YjY1…",
  "scope": "tasks.write tasks.read",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3599
}

The access token is a signed JWT. Decoded, its issuer is our authorization server, its subject is the agent, and its scope claim lists both permissions. It expires an hour after it was issued. The task server verifies the signature with keys it downloads from the issuer address.

With that token, initialize works again and returns 200, with a session id of its own.

One scope per tool

A valid token shouldn't mean you can do everything. The dashboard should be able to look, not touch.

We turn on method security with @EnableMethodSecurity in a small SecurityConfig, and then give every tool the scope it needs. Spring Security maps the JWT scope claim to SCOPE_ authorities, so the annotation is a one-liner:

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_tasks.write')")
@McpTool(name = "create_task", description = "Create a task on the team board")
public Task createTask(/* ... */) { /* ... */ }

Creating and completing tasks need tasks.write. Listing tasks, and reading the task resource, need tasks.read. The @PreAuthorize annotations work on @McpTool methods, because the MCP security starter supports them.

Now the dashboard's token can still list tasks. When it tries to create one, the call comes back as an error:

{
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Access Denied\r\nAccess Denied" }],
  "isError": true
}

The model sees why the call failed, and the board doesn't change. That's least privilege: an agent that only reads gets a token that can only read.

Validate every argument the model sends

The one people forget is validation. Every tool argument was written by a model that may have just read text from a stranger, so treat it like internet input.

The service checks each argument before it touches the board. The title must be between one and 120 characters. The assignee must look like a username: a short, lowercase name without spaces or quotes. The board also caps at 1,000 tasks:

if (title == null || title.isBlank() || title.length() > 120) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("title must be 1 to 120 characters");
}
if (assignee == null || !NAME.matcher(assignee).matches()) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("assignee must be a lowercase username like 'ana'");
}
// ...

The due date gets its own check in the tool. A bad date produces a message that tells the model the exact format to use, instead of a stack trace.

We tried three bad calls. An empty title and an assignee that looks like an SQL injection string are both rejected with a message stating the rule. And next friday as a due date gets this result:

{
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "due must look like 2026-10-23\r\ndue must look like 2026-10-23" }],
  "isError": true
}

The model reads the rule and fixes its own call.

Before production

The demo skips four things that matter in production. First, the audience. Our token's aud is agent, the client, not our server. In production, a token should name the server it's meant for, and that server should reject any token that names someone else. Otherwise a token issued for one service can be replayed against another. The MCP specification requires this check, and the security starter can perform it.

Second, never pass a client's token through to another API. Third, keep tokens short-lived: an hour is fine for a demo, and for agents, minutes are better. Fourth, when a person is behind the client, use the OAuth login with PKCE (RFC 7636), the flow MCP clients use when you sign in from the app. Client credentials are for machines.

The boring parts save you too: rate limits, a log of every tool call, HTTPS, and a real database instead of a map in memory.

Connecting Claude Code

Now let's connect a real agent. We register the server in Claude Code as an HTTP MCP server, with our URL and the agent's token sent as an Authorization header.

Then we ask Claude Code, in plain English, to add a task for Ana to review the MCP security pull request, due Friday, and to show Ana's open tasks. It finds the create-task tool. Because changing the board is a real action, Claude Code asks first and shows the exact arguments, with Friday as a real date. After approval, it lists Ana's tasks and answers with a table, straight from our Java server.

Recap

Spring AI turns annotated methods into tools, resources and prompts and handles the protocol. The real work is making the server safe: OAuth 2 on the endpoint, a scope for every tool, and validation on every argument. The full code is linked above, one commit per step. Build it, break it, then connect your own services.

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol specification, revision 2025-06-18
  • RFC 9728: OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata
  • MCP authorization (2025-06-18)
  • Spring AI MCP server docs
  • Spring AI community: MCP security
  • RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)

More animated system design and security explainers on the jean code van debug YouTube channel. Java developer? Join the Java devs squad on daily.dev.

title: Vercel Passport is now generally available
description:
Vercel Passport is now generally available.

Passport allows you to protect your Vercel deployments with your own identity provider. Visitors authenticate through Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or any OIDC provider before viewing a protected deployment, and Vercel forwards a signed identity token to the deployment so application code can build on who the visitor is.

Read visitor identity in application code

The getIdentity() helper in @vercel/passport reads the Vercel request context and returns the authenticated visitor. Vercel strips client-supplied values for the x-vercel-oidc-passport-token header and injects the verified token after Passport validates the session, so the identity your code receives is already verified.

The subject field is a stable identifier for the visitor, scoped to your team and the Vercel Connect application that links Passport to your identity provider, and externalSubject is the visitor's ID in the provider itself. The helper returns null only when a request arrives without a Passport session, because unauthenticated browser visitors are redirected to the identity provider before they ever reach your code.

In local development, getIdentity() returns a configurable development identity, so the same code path works without a real identity provider.

Authorize with groups from your identity provider

The signed Passport token can now carry additional identity claims from your provider, such as group membership. Request the groups scope and allowlist the claim in the Vercel Connect application that Passport uses, then read it from the identity payload:

The additional identity scopes documentation covers provider configuration, including a full Okta walkthrough.

Verify identity in downstream services

Forward the Passport token from your application to another backend as a bearer token and verify it there with verifyIdentity(), available in @vercel/passport 1.0.0 and later. The helper checks the token signature, the Passport claims, and that the token came from the expected project and environment:

Services outside JavaScript can verify the token as a standard JWT with the published JWKS. Learn more in the verify identity documentation.

Monitor Passport access

Every successful Passport authentication records a passport-access-granted event in both the Activity Log and Audit Logs, identifying the visitor and recording the protected hostname and project. The Activity Log view is already filtered to Passport access.

Bypass Passport for automated traffic

Protection Bypass for Automation now applies to Passport. Webhooks, cron jobs, and CI runs that already send a bypass secret in the x-vercel-protection-bypass header or query parameter keep working when you turn Passport on. Because Passport runs in Vercel's network before your deployment's routes and proxy functions, the secret has to be part of the original request rather than added by your own middleware. A bypassed request has no signed-in visitor, so getIdentity() returns null.

Bypass Passport with Trusted Sources

Trusted Sources offers the same bypass without a shared secret. Protected deployments accept short-lived OIDC tokens from the Vercel projects and external services you authorize, which is how the workflow that triggers eve from Slack reaches a Passport-protected deployment.

Protect custom environments

Passport now supports custom environments, so deployments in an environment like staging or qa get the same identity provider sign-in as your preview and production deployments.

Get started

Vercel Passport is available on the Enterprise plan. New guides cover identity provider setup, token claims, local development, forwarding identity between backends, and bypassing Passport for automation.

Set up Passport with your identity provider in the Passport documentation, or configure it programmatically through the Vercel API.

Read more

title: optimizing rust async executors for sub‑millisecond latency
description:
in a high‑frequency trading gateway we hit a hard 1 ms SLA for order‑book updates. the naive tokio default (multi‑threaded, work‑stealing) added ~300 µs of jitter because each task hopped between cores and suffered cache line ping‑pong.

The bottleneck

the OS scheduler tick (typically 1 ms on Linux) and the executor’s global queue are the two dominant sources of latency. when a task is woken it lands in a lock‑protected queue; the next worker thread may not see it until the next tick, inflating tail latency. this is a hardware‑level constraint: each core’s L1 cache must be refreshed, and a lock incurs a memory fence that serializes execution.

A leaner executor

building a single‑threaded, poll‑driven executor removes the lock and keeps the whole pipeline on one core, preserving cache locality. the trade‑off is reduced parallelism, so it only makes sense when the workload is I/O‑bound and can be multiplexed on a single core.

use std::future::Future;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};
use std::pin::Pin;

struct SpinExecutor {
    tasks: Vec<Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>>>,
}

impl SpinExecutor {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { tasks: Vec::new() } }
    fn spawn<F>(&mut self, f: F) where F: Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static {
        self.tasks.push(Box::pin(f));
    }
    fn run(&mut self) {
        while !self.tasks.is_empty() {
            let mut i = 0;
            while i < self.tasks.len() {
                let waker = futures::task::noop_waker_ref();
                let mut cx = Context::from_waker(waker);
                match self.tasks[i].as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
                    Poll::Ready(_) => { self.tasks.swap_remove(i); },
                    Poll::Pending => i += 1,
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut exec = SpinExecutor::new();
    exec.spawn(async { /* low‑latency I/O */ });
    exec.run();
}

The snippet shows a lock‑free, busy‑wait loop. in production you’d add a timerfd or epoll wait to avoid 100 % CPU, but the core idea stays: keep the task queue in thread‑local memory.

Trade‑offs and failure modes

  • CPU utilization – a pure spin loop can saturate a core; you need a back‑off strategy or integrate with epoll to sleep when idle.
  • Scalability – moving to N cores re‑introduces contention; hybrid models (per‑core queues + work‑stealing only for overflow) often hit the sweet spot.
  • Back‑pressure – without a bounded queue a burst of network packets can OOM the process; enforce a limit and drop or throttle early.
  • Debugging – standard tools (tokio console) assume the Tokio runtime; with a custom executor you lose that visibility and must instrument manually (e.g., perf record).

Real‑world results

on a 12‑core Xeon we measured a 40 % reduction in 99th‑percentile latency (from 1.2 ms to 720 µs) after switching to a per‑core spin executor and pinning the thread to a single CPU. the trade‑off was a modest 5 % drop in overall throughput, which the business accepted because tail latency directly impacted revenue.

anyone tackled sub‑millisecond latency with a custom async runtime on multi‑core hardware? how did you balance the CPU cost of spinning with the need for deterministic response times

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.
