title: Working with S3 Object Tags in Buckets: SET, MERGE and CLEAR
description:
A practical walkthrough for keeping Amazon S3 objects organized without changing what is inside the files.

Object tags are easy to overlook when you are busy uploading and moving files around S3. But once a bucket starts filling up, a few consistent labels can make objects easier to organize and manage. The part that matters is how you update them: replacing a tag set is not the same as adding a tag to what is already there.

I used Buckets by Serverless Creed to explore three useful actions—SET, MERGE and CLEAR—and checked the results in the AWS S3 console. I also compared the downloaded files with their original SHA-256 hashes to make sure the contents stayed exactly the same.

A quick look at object tags

An S3 object tag is a key-value pair attached to an object. For example, env=test, team=intern or phase=review can describe where a file belongs or how it is used. These are separate from the file itself and from ordinary user-defined object metadata. S3 allows up to ten tags per object.

Tags can be useful for organizing data and for AWS features that are configured to use them, including lifecycle rules and some access-control policies. That is why updating tags deserves a little more care than simply changing a filename.

Start with a small sample folder

I worked with a handful of harmless text files in a private S3 bucket:

  docs/readme.txt
  b.txt
  c.txt
  control.txt

The files were small enough to inspect easily. The bulk operations shown below target only b.txt and c.txt. I left control.txt with a separate control=keep tag so there was always an object to compare against the ones being updated.

The sample files as they appear in the Buckets object browser.

SET: replace the existing tags

SET is the option to choose when an object needs a completely new tag set. In Buckets, select the files, open the bulk tagging action and choose Set (replace). For this example, I entered team=intern.

The important word is replace: tags that were on the object before, but are not included in the new set, will be removed. Before applying the change, the dialog shows the exact object keys being updated. It is worth reading that list rather than assuming every visible folder or file is included.

SET preview in Buckets, with the new team tag and the exact object list.

The operation completes and Buckets displays the update result.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for SET.

I then opened the object details in AWS. The tag panel showed one tag, team=intern, which is the state I expected after a replacement.

AWS S3 shows the new tag set after SET.

MERGE: add a tag without losing the others

MERGE is more useful when the existing labels should stay. I kept team=intern, switched to Merge, and entered a new tag: phase=review. I left the remove-keys field empty.

That should leave both tags on the objects. If a tag key already exists, MERGE updates that key; keys not mentioned are preserved. This is usually a safer option for incremental changes than rebuilding the full tag list by hand.

MERGE adds phase=review while preserving the other tag keys.

The MERGE action completes successfully.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for MERGE.

The AWS object details now displayed both team=intern and phase=review. Checking the entire tag list is useful here: seeing only the new key would not prove that the earlier one survived.

Both team and phase are visible in the AWS object-tag panel.

CLEAR: remove tags, not the object

CLEAR does exactly what the name suggests: it removes the object’s tag set. In Buckets, choose Clear all after selecting the intended files. The confirmation makes the scope explicit and warns that tag-dependent lifecycle rules or policies may no longer match.

This is the step where I would be most careful in a real bucket. Clearing tags does not delete a file, but tags may be used by other AWS configurations. Always check the objects listed in the confirmation before proceeding.

CLEAR warns about removing all tags and shows the affected object keys.

Buckets confirms that the tag-removal operation completed.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for CLEAR.

Afterward, the AWS object details showed Tags (0). The AWS object details still identified b.txt; the wider Buckets capture also shows readme.txt remaining in the browser after tag removal. That distinction is important: removing tags is not the same thing as deleting objects.

The S3 tag section is empty after CLEAR.

A wider view of the Buckets object browser after tag removal.

The AWS object details page still shows the file and its empty tag set.

Independent verification and SHA-256 integrity checking

I kept control.txt out of the tagging changes. Its control=keep tag was still there at the end, which was a quick check that the untouched object had retained its original tag.

The control object keeps its original tag.

For file contents, I recorded SHA-256 hashes of the original text files before uploading them. After the tagging sequence, I downloaded the S3 objects into a separate folder and compared them with that original hash list. Run the check from the download folder, with the original hash list one directory above it:

shasum -a 256 -c ../original-hashes.txt

All four downloaded files match their original SHA-256 hashes.

The output was:

docs/readme.txt: OK
b.txt: OK
c.txt: OK
control.txt: OK

The AWS Console screenshot lists CRC64NVME as its stored checksum function. The SHA-256 verification here is a separate local comparison of the downloaded bytes against the original files.

All four checks returned OK. That gives two independent views of the outcome: the AWS Console shows how the tags changed, and the hash check shows that the downloaded file bytes matched the originals.

A few habits worth keeping

Three things made this workflow straightforward. First, use SET only when replacing the full tag set is intentional; use MERGE when existing labels should remain. Second, review the exact object list before any bulk operation, especially when folders and nested files are involved. Third, check the resulting tags in S3 rather than relying on a success message alone.

For a small example like this, the difference between SET, MERGE and CLEAR is easy to see. On a busy bucket, choosing the right operation—and verifying the final state—can save a lot of confusion later.

title: An agent that refuses to guess: building RepoGraph AI on FalkorDB
description:
When a new bug report lands in a large open-source project, the first question is rarely "How do I fix this?"

It is "Where do I even start?"

I contribute to Oppia, an open-source learning platform with thousands of files. For Graph Hacks (WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB), I built RepoGraph AI: give it an Oppia issue, and it ranks the files worth investigating, suggests tests to run, and shows the graph evidence behind its recommendations.

The important part is what happens when the evidence runs out: RepoGraph AI is designed to say so rather than inventing a confident answer.

  • Live demo: https://repograph-ai-cinoibbc8myjvoe8si5tk9.streamlit.app/
  • Source code: https://github.com/alok844937-design/repograph-ai
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/FjhqzvyKOs0

Why a graph?

Keyword search over source code is a strong baseline. But some useful clues about a bug aren't obvious from the words in its description. They may be hidden in the project's history: a related issue fixed a similar problem, a previous commit changed the relevant file, or a code relationship points to another place worth investigating.

RepoGraph AI uses FalkorDB to connect issues, commits, files, functions, tests, and other code relationships. Instead of returning only a ranked list, it also exposes the path behind a recommendation, so a developer can inspect why a file appeared.

This doesn't mean a graph is always better than keyword search. In my evaluation, both methods found a relevant file in the top five for 14 of 21 held-out issues. On a second set of 29 issues selected by a precommitted rule, keyword search hit 18, while graph-enhanced search hit 20.

Those results are promising, but modest. The graph alone performed worse than keyword search, and some issues still have insufficient evidence. The goal is not to claim that graphs solve issue localization; it's to test whether connected historical and structural evidence can make the investigation more useful and explainable.

How I built the graph

The graph has about 25,700 nodes and 39,000 edges, built from three sources:

  • Git history since 2022: commits whose message says Fix #N become (Commit)-[:FIXES]->(Issue), and the files each commit changed become (Commit)-[:TOUCHES]->(File).
  • GitHub issues: titles, bodies and parent/sub-issue links (CHILD_OF) from the GitHub API. Comments are never loaded, because they often name the fix.
  • Python AST over Oppia's backend: imports, functions, module constants, URL routes from main.py, and links between code and its tests. Oppia also loads storage models through a registry (Registry.import_*()), which plain import parsing cannot see, so those edges come from a mapping read out of Oppia's own code.

Every edge stores a provenance property: git_commit, github_parent, todo_comment, python_ast, registry_mapping, route_table. These sources are not equally reliable. A TODO(#issue) written by a developer is strong evidence; two files that often change in the same commits are only a correlation. So the app labels each piece of evidence as direct, related, structural or weak. An edge records a link; it is not proof that two files are related in meaning.

One of the core queries finds files changed by the fix of an issue's parent:

MATCH (:Issue {number: $n})-[:CHILD_OF]->(p:Issue)
      <-[:FIXES]-(c:Commit)-[:TOUCHES]->(f:File)
WHERE c.date < $cutoff
RETURN p.number, c.sha, c.date, f.path

The WHERE c.date < $cutoff line matters. For an issue that is already fixed, the graph only sees history from before its fix. Otherwise the fix commit itself would point straight at the answer, and every result would be inflated.

One issue, end to end: #25307

Issue #25307 asks for email retries to stop on 4xx errors. It names no file.

The graph walks:

#25307 → CHILD_OF → #18276 ← FIXES ← commit 2405253 → TOUCHES → core/controllers/tasks.py

A TODO(#25307) comment in the same file gives a second, independent path. Using only history from before the fix, core/controllers/tasks.py is ranked first, and the real fix did change it. The app also suggests the test to run first: core.controllers.tasks_test.

When the graph gets it wrong

Not every path leads somewhere useful. For #18371, keyword search ranked the fixed file 3rd. Adding graph evidence pushed it down to 22nd: the graph found strong-looking links into a different part of the code, and they outweighed the keyword signal. For #24470, every method missed.

These failures shaped one design decision: a gated mode that adds graph evidence only when the graph has direct support (the issue names a file, a TODO comment, or a related issue's fix). On the 29-issue set, the gated mode turned one miss into a hit and never turned a hit into a miss.

How the agent avoids guessing

On top of the graph sits a Gemini agent with three tools: related issues, file context, and keyword search. Three mechanisms keep it honest:

  1. Grounding. Any file or test the agent names that no tool returned is removed and counted. Across 23 plans, this removed 24 unsupported suggestions. The high-confidence plans had none.
  2. Abstention. I ran a triage agent on the 20 newest open Oppia issues. For the 14 outside its scope (frontend, CI and acceptance tests), it returned low-confidence plans with no files instead of inventing them.
  3. Fallback. If Gemini is unavailable, the app returns a graph-only plan rather than failing.

The triage agent writes each plan back into FalkorDB as (:Investigation)-[:SUGGESTS]->(:File). The investigation code never reads these nodes, so the agent's output can never become evidence for itself. Re-running the evaluation after the agent wrote its plans gave identical results.

For one open issue, #27595, the agent pointed to a specific function in email_services.py. I checked the code myself: the email regex really does run on the unstripped address. The pointer was right.

Evaluation and limitations

Keyword search Keyword + graph
21 held-out issues, hit@5 14/21 14/21
29 issues chosen by a precommitted rule, hit@5 18/29 (62%) 20/29 (69%)

hit@5 means at least one file changed by the real fix is in the top five. Keyword search runs on the code as it was just before each fix, and the selection rule for the 29-issue set was committed to git before the script was first run. The biggest single win was #24156: keyword search ranked the fixed file 28th; with the graph it was 5th, thanks to a sibling issue's fix.

The limitations are real:

  • Backend Python only. Most of Oppia's recent fixes are in the TypeScript frontend; of the first 150 issues my rule considered, 121 had no backend change at all.
  • Small evaluation. 50 issues in total. A difference of one or two issues should not be over-read.
  • History depends on commit messages. A fix that doesn't say Fix #N is invisible to the graph.
  • Abstention is not yet measured. I don't yet know how often "I don't know" hides a file that would have helped.

The evaluation dataset, with frozen issue texts, fix commits and file labels, is in the repository so anyone can check these numbers.

What comes next

  • A TypeScript graph for Oppia's frontend, where most of the work actually happens.
  • CI and test relationships, linking failing tests to the workflows and files behind them.
  • Incremental updates, so the graph follows new commits instead of being rebuilt.

The lesson I'm taking away: the most useful thing an investigation tool can say is not just where to look, but why, and when it honestly doesn't know.

Built with FalkorDB for Graph Hacks. I used Claude as a coding and writing assistant; Gemini powers the agent inside the product.

title: I Built Kiver: A Discovery Marketplace for Telegram Bots and Mini Apps
description:
Building a Telegram bot is one thing. Getting people to discover it is another.

That problem is what led me to build Kiver.

"https://www.getkiver.com" (https://www.getkiver.com)

The problem I wanted to solve

Telegram has an ecosystem of bots and Mini Apps for almost everything: AI assistants, productivity tools, finance, education, gaming, automation and more.

Developers spend time building these products, improving their features and trying to attract users. But once a bot is ready, discovery becomes a challenge of its own.

A Telegram link is useful, but it doesn't always give a product the broader visibility it needs. Potential users may not know the bot exists, and developers need more ways to put their work in front of relevant audiences.

I wanted to build something that could help bridge that gap.

What is Kiver?

Kiver is a discovery marketplace for Telegram bots and Mini Apps.

The idea is straightforward: help users find useful Telegram tools and give makers a public place to showcase what they've built.

On Kiver, users can:

  • Browse Telegram tools across different categories.
  • Search for bots by name, username or use case.
  • Explore individual product pages.
  • Upvote tools they find useful.
  • Open listed bots directly in Telegram.

For developers and makers, Kiver provides a way to turn a Telegram link into a dedicated, shareable product listing.

Giving Telegram tools a public home

One part of Kiver I'm particularly interested in is discoverability beyond Telegram itself.

A maker can submit a public Telegram link, review the listing details, select a category and publish a product page.

That page gives the tool a dedicated URL that can be shared in communities, included in documentation or discovered through search engines.

The goal is to create another discovery channel for Telegram products instead of relying entirely on someone already knowing a bot's username or receiving its link from another person.

Of course, a public page doesn't guarantee search rankings or new users. The challenge is building a useful directory that people actually want to visit.

I'm still growing it

Kiver is an early-stage project, and I'm starting to see traffic coming to the website.

It's not massive traffic, and I'm not going to pretend it is. But seeing people visit a product you're building is useful feedback. It gives me a reason to keep improving the experience, expanding the directory and thinking more carefully about how users discover and evaluate tools.

The next challenge is turning visits into something more meaningful: people finding useful products, makers getting discovered, and visitors returning because the directory helps them.

That's the kind of growth I want to build toward.

What I'd like to improve

There are several areas I'm interested in developing further:

  • Better discovery: Helping users find relevant tools without having to know their names beforehand.
  • More useful listings: Making it easier to understand what a bot does before opening it.
  • More makers: Bringing more developers into the directory so users have a wider selection of tools.
  • A stronger community: Making product feedback and voting more useful for both users and builders.

The important part is making the directory valuable to both sides. More listings are useful, but only if people can find tools that genuinely solve their problems.

Try Kiver

If you've built a Telegram bot or Mini App, you can explore the directory and submit your own project.

Website: https://www.getkiver.com

Browse the directory, see how listings work, or launch your own Telegram tool on the platform.

I'm building Kiver in public and would appreciate feedback from developers, indie hackers and anyone working in the Telegram ecosystem.

If you build Telegram tools, what is the biggest challenge you've faced when trying to get your first users?

I'd be interested to hear what has worked for you.

title: SQuAD's answer normalizer can mark a wrong answer correct: three verified hazards
description:
The exact-match and F1 scores in most question-answering and many open-ended LLM evals run every answer through one tiny, famous function first: SQuAD's normalize_answer. It lowercases, strips punctuation, drops the articles a/an/the, and collapses whitespace. It's pure standard library, so you can reproduce and check it exactly.

I built squad-normalize-hazards: a dependency-free, labeled, execution-verified corpus of three places where that normalization makes the score disagree with the obviously-intended outcome. Everything is pinned to HuggingFace evaluate commit 86baf12 and recomputed by stdlib tests.

1. Empty-collapse false positives (the squad metric)

A gold answer that is a bare article (a, an, the) or punctuation-only (...) normalizes to the empty string. The v1.1 scorer builds its gold list without filtering and compares by equality, so any prediction that also normalizes to empty — an article, punctuation, whitespace, even an empty refusal — scores exact-match 1.0.

Gold "the", prediction "a" → EM 1.0.

This is the same root cause that mosaicml/llm-foundry#1897 reported for a startswith-based matcher. The new part: it also bites the canonical, equality-based HF squad metric, not just prefix matchers. (I credited #1897 and did not open a PR — the reporter offered to.)

2. squad vs squad_v2 disagree on the same data

squad_v2 does filter golds that normalize to empty. So with a real co-alias — gold ["the", "red car"], prediction "a" — squad scores 1.0 (the wrong answer matches "the") while squad_v2 scores 0. Re-scoring a dataset from one to the other silently drops these spurious hits.

3. Punctuation glues articles in place

remove_punc runs before remove_articles and deletes punctuation without inserting a space. So a missing space keeps the article attached:

input normalized
end. the end
end.the endthe
the car car
the-car thecar

A model that writes end.the or the-car scores 0 against a gold the normalizer would otherwise have made equal — a false negative that depends only on spacing.

Reproduce 

python -m unittest -v test_squad_normalize_hazards.py

Standard library only. Code Apache-2.0, corpus CC BY 4.0.

Repo: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/squad-normalize-hazards

These are edge cases of a deliberate design choice, not a claim that the metric is broken in general — but they're exactly the inputs LLM graders produce, so they're worth knowing.

This research and write-up were made with AI, by MV2 of Munim, Inc.

title: How to Convert PDF to JPG Directly in the Browser Using JavaScript and PDF.js
description:
When developing modern web applications or document utility platforms, handling file conversions efficiently on the client side is a game-changer. Processing files directly in the browser reduces server costs, speeds up performance, and ensures complete user privacy.

In this guide, we will explore how to build a robust, pure client-side PDF-to-JPG converter using vanilla JavaScript and the powerful PDF.js library.

Why Choose Client-Side PDF Conversion?

Traditional file conversion relies heavily on backend infrastructure (like Python, Ghostscript, or cloud APIs) to unpack PDF pages and render them as images.

Shifting this process to the browser offers major benefits:

Zero Server Overhead: The client's browser handles all the heavy computation.

Instant Processing: Users do not need to wait for multi-step file uploads and downloads.

Data Security: Sensitive documents never leave the user's local machine.

Step-by-Step Implementation

  1. Include PDF.js via CDN To parse and render PDF files in the browser, Mozilla's PDF.js library is the industry standard. Include the worker and main library scripts in your HTML: 
<script 
src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/pdf.js/3.11.174/pdf.min.js"></script>
<script>
    pdfjsLib.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = 'https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/pdf.js/3.11.174/pdf.worker.min.js';
</script>

2. Core Conversion JavaScript Logic
Here is an asynchronous function that loads a selected PDF file, extracts the first page, renders it onto an HTML5 Canvas, and converts it into a downloadable JPG image format.

async function convertPdfFirstPageToJpg(pdfFile) {
    if (!pdfFile || pdfFile.type !== "application/pdf") {
        throw new Error("Please upload a valid PDF file.");
    }

    try {
        // 1. Read the PDF file into an ArrayBuffer
        const arrayBuffer = await pdfFile.arrayBuffer();

        // 2. Load the PDF document using PDF.js
        const loadingTask = pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: arrayBuffer });
        const pdfDocument = await loadingTask.promise;

        // 3. Fetch the first page of the PDF
        const page = await pdfDocument.getPage(1);

        // 4. Set up scale and viewport for rendering
        const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1.5 });
        const canvas = document.createElement("canvas");
        const context = canvas.getContext("2d");

        canvas.height = viewport.height;
        canvas.width = viewport.width;

        // 5. Render the PDF page content into the canvas context
        const renderContext = {
            canvasContext: context,
            viewport: viewport
        };
        await page.render(renderContext).promise;

        // 6. Convert canvas content into a JPG Data URL and trigger download
        const jpgDataUrl = canvas.toDataURL("image/jpeg", 0.9);

        const downloadLink = document.createElement("a");
        downloadLink.href = jpgDataUrl;
        downloadLink.download = "converted-page.jpg";
        downloadLink.click();

        console.log("PDF page successfully converted to JPG!");

    } catch (error) {
        console.error("Error during PDF to JPG conversion:", error);
    }
}

Handling Multi-Page PDFs

If your platform needs to handle large multi-page documents and convert every page into an individual JPG image, you can loop through all pages dynamically:

async function convertAllPdfPagesToJpg(pdfFile) {
    const arrayBuffer = await pdfFile.arrayBuffer();
    const pdfDocument = await pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: arrayBuffer }).promise;

    for (let pageNum = 1; pageNum <= pdfDocument.numPages; pageNum++) {
        const page = await pdfDocument.getPage(pageNum);
        const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1.5 });

        const canvas = document.createElement("canvas");
        const context = canvas.getContext("2d");
        canvas.height = viewport.height;
        canvas.width = viewport.width;

        await page.render({ canvasContext: context, viewport: viewport }).promise;

        const jpgDataUrl = canvas.toDataURL("image/jpeg", 0.85);

        // Save each page iteratively
        const link = document.createElement("a");
        link.href = jpgDataUrl;
        link.download = `page-${pageNum}.jpg`;
        link.click();
    }
}

Best Practices & Error Handling

Memory Management: Rendering high-resolution PDF pages can consume significant browser memory. Adjust the scale parameter (e.g., 1.0 or 1.5) to balance image clarity and performance.

File Validation: Always check the MIME type (application/pdf) and file extensions to prevent unexpected runtime parsing exceptions.

Conclusion
Building a client-side PDF-to-JPG converter gives developers a lightweight, scalable tool without relying on complex backend servers. With PDF.js and HTML5 Canvas, you can render high-quality document previews directly in the browser.

(Note: If you are looking for an instant, ready-to-use production web tool built on these concepts for everyday document management, you can check out pdftojpg.world)

title: Bun vs Node.js in 2026: Bun 1.4 vs Node 24 and 26, Benchmarked
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself on one machine, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Bun vs Node in 2026 comes down to this: Bun is a JavaScript runtime, package manager, bundler and test runner in one binary, built on JavaScriptCore and now written in Rust. Node.js is the V8-based runtime almost every server, library and hosting platform targets. Bun 1.4 reports Node.js 26 compatibility, so for many apps switching is now a runtime swap rather than a rewrite.

I benchmarked Bun 1.4.3 against Node.js 24.22 (the current LTS) and Node.js 26.12 (LTS from October 28) on one machine. I measured HTTP throughput with Hono, Express and plain node:http, a real Postgres-backed API, a large in-memory heap, startup, TypeScript execution, npm install vs bun install, next build, and native addons like sharp and bcrypt. Every number below comes from those runs.

TL;DR: should I switch from Node to Bun?

Use Bun as your package manager and script runner today: bun install was 13 to 29 times faster than npm in my tests and changes nothing at runtime. Consider Bun as your production runtime for new or dependency-light APIs, CLIs and serverless functions, where it was 1.4 to 1.8 times faster and used 25-70% less memory under load. Stay on Node.js for large existing services that depend on Node-specific APM, long-running stability or exotic native addons, and move to Node 26, which was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on most of my HTTP tests.

Node.js 24.22 Node.js 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Engine V8 V8 JavaScriptCore
Status (Oct 2026) LTS, maintenance from Oct 20 Current, LTS from Oct 28 Stable, 1.x
Hono JSON API, req/s 53,408 60,431 98,145
Express 5 JSON, req/s 35,764 38,530 55,382
Hono + Postgres, req/s 21,749 21,008 32,254 (pg), 33,694 (Bun.sql)
RSS under load, Hono JSON 105 MB 105 MB 36 MB
Startup (-e 0) 28.5 ms 26.3 ms 3.3 ms
Run a .ts file 62.6 ms 59.1 ms 3.8 ms
Install a Next.js app (cold) 15.4 s (npm) 1.15 s (bun)
Native addons tested All work All work All work (sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2)

What is Bun, and how is it different from Node.js?

Bun is an all-in-one toolkit: a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, an npm-compatible package manager, a bundler and a Jest-style test runner in one executable. Node.js is just the runtime and leans on npm, tsc or a loader, a bundler and a test framework from the ecosystem. Bun runs on Apple's JavaScriptCore engine; Node runs on Google's V8.

Bun aims to be a drop-in replacement. It implements Node's built-in modules (node:http, node:fs, node:crypto and the rest), reads package.json and node_modules the same way, and runs N-API native addons. It also adds its own faster APIs such as Bun.serve, Bun.sql and bun:sqlite.

What's new in Bun 1.4?

Bun 1.4 shipped on August 20, 2026, and it is the first Bun written in Rust instead of Zig. Per the Bun 1.4 release post, it adds "+1,517 tests from the Node.js test suite", fixes "over 2,900 issues", cuts idle CPU by 5x and memory by up to 35%, and "starts 50% faster on Linux." Bun now reports itself as Node.js 26 (process.versions.modules is 147).

It also absorbs common dependencies into the runtime: Bun.Image (image processing), Bun.WebView (headless browser), Bun.markdown, Bun.cron(), Bun.Terminal, plus bun run --parallel and bun test --parallel. Upgrading from 1.3 isn't free: the breaking changes list includes stricter TLS verification, YAML 1.2 parsing and no .env auto-loading when Bun is invoked as node. Vercel made 1.4 an explicit opt-in on its platform for the same reason.

How I benchmarked Bun vs Node.js

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3, all official Linux x64 builds.
  3. Apps. The same files ran on every runtime: a node:http hello server, a Bun.serve hello server (Bun only), a Hono 4.13 app, an Express 5.3 app, and a Hono route that reads one row from PostgreSQL 18 through pg 8.23 (or Bun.sql on Bun) with a 10-connection pool, across 10,000 users at random IDs.
  4. Method. For every configuration: start the server, warm up for 4 seconds, measure for 10 seconds, read RSS from /proc. Each configuration ran 3 times and I report the median. Every request returned 200.
  5. CLI timings used hyperfine 2.0.0 (40 runs for startup, 3 to 5 for installs and builds).

Postgres ran on the same machine without pinning, so the database test also measures a shared CPU. That's closer to a small VPS than to a tuned cluster.

Is Bun faster than Node.js?

For HTTP servers, yes, clearly. On the Hono JSON route Bun served 98,145 requests per second against 53,408 on Node 24 and 60,431 on Node 26: 1.84 times Node 24 and 1.62 times Node 26. Bun's advantage held on Express (1.55x Node 24) and on the plain node:http module (1.42x), and Bun.serve reached 128,461 requests per second.

Server (median of 3 x 10 s, 64 connections) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3 Bun vs Node 24
node:http hello 74,200 req/s 83,301 req/s 105,434 req/s 1.42x
Bun.serve hello 128,461 req/s 1.73x
Hono, 10-item JSON 53,408 req/s 60,431 req/s 98,145 req/s 1.84x
Express 5, same JSON 35,764 req/s 38,530 req/s 55,382 req/s 1.55x
Hono + Postgres (pg) 21,749 req/s 21,008 req/s 32,254 req/s 1.48x
Hono + Postgres (Bun.sql) 33,694 req/s 1.55x
600k-entry in-memory cache 53,314 req/s 61,908 req/s 68,134 req/s 1.28x

Latency followed throughput. On the Hono JSON route p99 was 2.10 ms on Node 24, 1.95 ms on Node 26 and 1.17 ms on Bun. On the Postgres route p99 was 4.75 ms, 6.95 ms and 3.98 ms, and 3.50 ms with Bun.sql.

Two results surprised me. First, Bun stayed about 1.5 times faster even with a real database query in every request, which is where many "it's all the database anyway" arguments end. My database was local and fast, though. Over a real network, round trips will shrink that gap. Second, Node 26 alone was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of the five HTTP tests (the Postgres route was a tie), so upgrading Node is the cheapest speedup available.

Does Bun use less memory than Node.js?

Yes. Idle, a node:http server used 58 MB RSS on Node 24 and 23 MB on Bun, while Bun.serve used 16 MB. Under load the Hono app held 105 MB on both Node versions and 36 MB on Bun. On the Postgres route Node 24 grew to 206 MB against 61 MB for Bun with pg and 56 MB with Bun.sql.

RSS (MB): idle / after 10 s load / peak Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
node:http hello 58 / 95 / 95 60 / 97 / 97 23 / 55 / 74
Hono JSON 70 / 105 / 105 66 / 105 / 105 28 / 36 / 45
Express JSON 65 / 97 / 97 66 / 96 / 96 40 / 72 / 81
Hono + Postgres 70 / 206 / 206 66 / 151 / 151 28 / 61 / 69
600k-entry cache 411 / 455 / 455 370 / 410 / 410 261 / 300 / 491

The cache test is the exception worth reading. Bun started with less memory but briefly peaked higher (491 MB) than Node (455 MB). Bun's garbage collector is a known weak spot under large, long-lived heaps. A Bun pull request from this year described a GC "storm" that made allocation-heavy handlers run "at roughly half of Node.js" with a 150 MB live set. That PR #35431 was closed without merging. In my 1.4.3 run with a bigger heap Bun was still 28% faster than Node 24, but test your own workload, not a hello world.

How fast does Bun start compared to Node.js?

Bun starts about 8 times faster. An empty script took a median 3.3 ms on Bun against 28.5 ms on Node 24 and 26.3 ms on Node 26. Running a TypeScript file took 3.8 ms on Bun against 62.6 ms on Node 24. Node's built-in type stripping uses a WebAssembly-based parser, and here it added about 34 ms over an empty script. bun run launched a package.json script in 3.1 ms against 95.1 ms for npm run.

Command (hyperfine median) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Empty script (-e 0) 28.5 ms 26.3 ms 3.3 ms
hello.ts (type annotations) 62.6 ms 59.1 ms 3.8 ms
import('express') 94.1 ms 65.3 ms
Run a no-op package.json script 95.1 ms (npm run) 3.1 ms (bun run)

Startup matters for CLIs, cron jobs, serverless cold starts and test watchers. It barely matters for a long-running API server. Both runtimes run TypeScript directly now: Node's type stripping has been stable since v24.12.0 but only removes erasable syntax and ignores tsconfig.json, while Bun transpiles full TypeScript, including enums.

Is bun install faster than npm?

Much faster. On a Next.js 16.4.2 app with Tailwind, ESLint and TypeScript (458 packages), a cold install with empty caches and no lockfile took 15.4 seconds with npm and 1.15 seconds with Bun, 13 times faster. A CI-style install from a lockfile with a warm cache took 4.6 seconds with npm ci and 0.16 seconds with bun install --frozen-lockfile, 29 times faster.

Install, Next.js 16.4.2 app (458 packages) npm 11.19 bun 1.4.3 Speedup
Cold: no cache, no lockfile (median of 3) 15.4 s 1.15 s 13x
Warm cache + lockfile (median of 5) 4.6 s 0.16 s 29x
Peak memory, warm install 758 MB 13.5 MB

This is the safest win in the whole comparison. bun install writes a normal node_modules, so you can keep running the app on Node. The cold number includes downloads over my server's network, so yours will vary.

# use Bun only as the package manager and script runner
bun install            # writes bun.lock and a normal node_modules
bun run build          # runs your package.json script with Node, as before
node server.js         # production stays on Node.js

Does Next.js work with Bun?

Yes. A Next.js 16.4.2 production build ran fine with bun --bun next build, in a median 3.03 seconds against 3.22 seconds on Node 24, about 6% faster. Turbopack does the heavy lifting in Rust either way, so the runtime matters less for builds than for serving requests. Without --bun, bun run build launches the Next.js CLI with Node because of its shebang.

bun install
bun --bun next build   # build with the Bun runtime
bun --bun next start   # serve with the Bun runtime

If you deploy with Docker, the base image changes from node:24-slim to oven/bun, and the rest of a production Next.js Dockerfile stays the same.

Do native modules work in Bun?

The common ones do. On Bun 1.4.3, sharp (image resize), better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2 and pg all installed from npm and passed the same smoke test as on Node 24. Bun runs N-API addons, which covers most popular native packages. Packages that pick a prebuilt binary by NODE_MODULE_VERSION need a build for 147, the ABI Bun 1.4 reports.

What still bites people is less about compatibility tables and more about operations: APM agents that patch Node internals, rare Node APIs, and memory behavior under months of traffic. The Bun Node.js compatibility page lists module-by-module status.

Is Bun faster at raw JavaScript?

Sometimes. CPU-bound micro-benchmarks were mixed, so don't expect a blanket speedup. Bun was about 3 times faster at parsing small JSON and 1.4 times faster than Node 26 on a 67 KB document, but JSON.stringify tied Node 26. Node 26 made a big jump over Node 24 on JSON, 1.8 times faster on stringify.

Single core, ops/s (mean of 2 runs) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
JSON.parse, 110 B 1,711,027 1,881,418 5,226,338
JSON.parse, 67 KB 3,854 5,224 7,118
JSON.stringify, 67 KB 6,539 11,634 11,644
SHA-256 of 1 KB (node:crypto) 751,142 751,912 853,054
Sort 100,000 numbers 55 60 90
Map set + get, 100,000 keys 102 134 168

I dropped one test: a regex replace on a constant string ran at 196 million operations per second on Bun, which means JavaScriptCore optimized the work away. That's the trouble with micro-benchmarks. Trust the HTTP and real-app numbers more than these.

Should I use Bun in production in 2026?

For new services, it's a reasonable default now. Bun 1.4 is fast, frugal and broadly compatible, and platforms such as Vercel Functions run it. For existing Node services, migrate only when you can measure the benefit and you have tested memory over days, not minutes. Trigger.dev reported a 5x throughput gain moving a service to Bun and also hit a Bun-only memory leak on the way.

Situation My pick
New API, CLI or worker with mainstream dependencies Bun (runtime + package manager)
Serverless or cron jobs where cold start dominates Bun
Existing large Node service with APM and on-call Node 26 + bun install in CI
Heavy use of exotic native addons or Node internals Node.js
NestJS or Next.js app Node in production for now, Bun for installs and scripts; test Bun in staging

How do I migrate a Node.js app to Bun?

Move in three steps and keep a way back at each one. First swap the package manager, then run your tests on Bun, then switch the production runtime behind a canary.

# 1. package manager only (zero runtime risk)
bun install                 # creates bun.lock next to package-lock.json

# 2. run tests and scripts on Bun
bun run test                # your existing test script
bun --bun run test          # force the Bun runtime even for "node" shebangs

# 3. run the server on Bun, keep the code portable
bun src/server.ts

// portable entry point: Bun.serve on Bun, @hono/node-server on Node
import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', (c) => c.json({ ok: true }))

if (typeof Bun !== 'undefined') {
  Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch: app.fetch })
} else {
  const { serve } = await import('@hono/node-server')
  serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 })
}

Frameworks built on Web standards, like Hono, make this painless because the same fetch handler runs on both. For database access, pg worked unchanged on Bun in my test, and Bun.sql is the built-in Postgres client that was 4% faster than pg on Bun in my test. If you're choosing an ORM, see Drizzle vs Prisma. If you self-host, Coolify runs a Bun Dockerfile like any other.

Common mistakes when comparing Bun and Node.js

  • Benchmarking hello world only. Bun.serve vs node:http showed a 1.73x gap; Express showed 1.55x and a large-heap handler 1.28x.
  • Comparing against an old Node. Node 26 was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of five HTTP tests. Compare against the Node you would actually run.
  • Ignoring memory over time. A 10-second run says nothing about a slow leak. Watch RSS for days in staging.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores. Pin the server and the load generator to separate CPUs, or the numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Forgetting --bun. bun run executes scripts whose CLI has a #!/usr/bin/env node shebang with Node unless you pass --bun.
  • Switching runtime and dependencies at once. Swap the package manager first; it gives most of the day-to-day win with none of the runtime risk.

Related: I also ran a NestJS 12 app on Bun 1.4.3: it served 1.49 times Node 24's requests per second on a hello route and started in 264 ms vs 361 ms. See the NestJS 12 migration guide.

Related: framework choice matters on Bun too. In Hono vs Express vs Fastify, Hono served 118,432 JSON requests per second on Bun 1.4.3, 1.62× its Node 24 result, while Express and Fastify gained less.

Key takeaways

  • Bun 1.4.3 served 1.84 times Node 24's requests per second on a Hono JSON API, and 1.48 times with a Postgres query in every request.
  • Bun used 25-70% less memory under load, for example 36 MB vs 105 MB RSS for the Hono app.
  • Bun started in 3.3 ms versus 26-29 ms for Node and ran a TypeScript file in 3.8 ms versus about 60 ms.
  • bun install was 13 times faster than npm cold and 29 times faster with a warm cache and lockfile.
  • Node 26 alone was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of five HTTP tests, a free upgrade when it becomes LTS on October 28.
  • sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2, pg and a Next.js 16.4 build all worked on Bun 1.4.3.
  • Adopt Bun as package manager first, then as runtime for new services; keep large existing Node services on Node 26 until you've tested memory over days.

FAQ

Is Bun faster than Node.js?

For HTTP servers, yes. In my tests Bun 1.4.3 served 98,145 requests per second on a Hono JSON API against 53,408 on Node.js 24 and 60,431 on Node.js 26. With a Postgres query in every request Bun was 1.48 times faster than Node 24. CPU-bound micro-benchmarks were mixed, so the gap depends on the workload.

Does Bun use less memory than Node.js?

Usually. Under load my Hono app used 36 MB RSS on Bun versus 105 MB on Node 24 and 26, and the Postgres route used 61 MB versus 206 MB on Node 24. With a large in-memory cache Bun idled lower but briefly peaked higher, at 491 MB against 455 MB, so test memory with your own data.

Is Bun production ready in 2026?

For many services, yes. Bun 1.4 passes 1,517 more Node.js test-suite tests than 1.3, runs common native addons, and is offered on platforms such as Vercel Functions. Teams still report Bun-specific memory issues under long-running load, so canary it and watch memory for days before moving a large existing service.

Is bun install faster than npm?

Yes. On a Next.js 16.4.2 app with 458 packages, a cold install took 15.4 seconds with npm and 1.15 seconds with Bun. A lockfile install with a warm cache took 4.6 seconds with npm ci and 0.16 seconds with bun install --frozen-lockfile. It writes a normal node_modules, so the app can still run on Node.

Does Next.js work with Bun?

Yes. A Next.js 16.4.2 production build succeeded with bun --bun next build in 3.03 seconds against 3.22 seconds on Node 24. Use the --bun flag, because bun run otherwise launches the Next.js CLI with Node due to its node shebang. Turbopack compiles in Rust either way, so builds gain little.

Do native modules like sharp and bcrypt work in Bun?

The popular ones do. On Bun 1.4.3, sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2 and pg installed from npm and passed the same smoke test as on Node 24. Bun runs N-API addons and reports NODE_MODULE_VERSION 147, so packages that select a prebuilt binary by ABI need a build for 147.

Should I upgrade to Node 26 or switch to Bun?

If you have a large existing service, upgrade to Node 26 first: it was 8 to 16 percent faster than Node 24 on most of my HTTP tests and becomes LTS on October 28, 2026. Switch the runtime to Bun when you start a new service or can measure a clear gain in staging.

What changed in Bun 1.4?

Bun 1.4, released August 20, 2026, is the first Bun written in Rust instead of Zig. It reports Node.js 26 compatibility, adds 1,517 Node.js test-suite tests, fixes over 2,900 issues, starts 50 percent faster on Linux, and adds built-ins such as Bun.Image, Bun.WebView, Bun.markdown and Bun.cron. It also has breaking changes worth reviewing.
