title: SMS OTP Login API — Resend Cooldowns and Rate Limits for Media Signup
description:
Put the abuse budget in the application, then keep SMS behind a replaceable transport contract. TL;DR: a media signup service should let the provider send and verify codes, while its own server owns resend cooldowns, failed-attempt limits, expiry, and session completion. Delivery reliability is the vendor test. State control is not.

That split matters because swapping the vendor behind the capability should not change signup code. It also gives the team one place to answer a less glamorous question: exactly how much abuse can one phone number, account, IP range, or destination country create before the application says no?

How should a Node.js SMS OTP login API control resends?

Start with a timeline, not an SDK. A reader requests a code, the service admits or rejects that request, a transport sends it, and the reader submits a code. Only then may the signup session advance. Each transition needs one owner.

The browser cannot own the cooldown. Two tabs defeat a countdown, and a script ignores it. The SMS provider cannot own the login session either. A successful code check proves control of the challenged number for that interaction; the application still decides which pending signup it unlocks.

The awkward middle is delivery. An accepted API call is not a received message. For this capability, delivery status and events are pulled rather than pushed, so real-time fallback orchestration is limited. If the product needs delivery insight, poll outside the user's request path with capped backoff. Do not keep an HTTP signup request open while waiting for a carrier state.

Short version: there are three clocks. The resend cooldown controls sends, the challenge expiry controls verification, and the polling budget controls how long delivery observation remains useful. Mixing them into one expiresAt field makes later failures needlessly hard to explain.

Three clocks. Three jobs.

Make the budget executable

I benchmark the admission invariant before comparing dashboards: 10 simultaneous resend attempts for one signup must yield one admitted operation. That number is a test workload, not a universal rate-limit recommendation. The policy thresholds still need evidence from the actual audience and destination mix.

The smallest useful model has explicit terminal states and atomic updates. It also keeps transport details out of the policy. This TypeScript is runnable as an in-process demonstration; replace MemoryStore with a shared store that provides atomic compare-and-update before running more than one application instance.

type Challenge = {
  status: "pending" | "verified" | "locked" | "expired";
  nextSendAt: number;
  expiresAt: number;
  failedAttempts: number;
};

type Decision =
  | { admitted: true; state: Challenge }
  | { admitted: false; reason: string; state?: Challenge };

class MemoryStore {
  private readonly values = new Map<string, Challenge>();

  update(key: string, change: (current?: Challenge) => Decision): Decision {
    const decision = change(this.values.get(key));
    if (decision.admitted) this.values.set(key, decision.state);
    return decision;
  }
}

const cooldownMs = 30_000;
const challengeLifetimeMs = 5 * 60_000;
const maxFailures = 5;

function admitSend(store: MemoryStore, signupId: string, now: number): Decision {
  return store.update(`signup:${signupId}`, (current) => {
    if (current?.status === "verified" || current?.status === "locked") {
      return { admitted: false, reason: `challenge is ${current.status}`, state: current };
    }
    if (current && current.nextSendAt > now) {
      return { admitted: false, reason: "resend cooldown active", state: current };
    }

    return {
      admitted: true,
      state: {
        status: "pending",
        nextSendAt: now + cooldownMs,
        expiresAt: now + challengeLifetimeMs,
        failedAttempts: current?.failedAttempts ?? 0,
      },
    };
  });
}

const store = new MemoryStore();
const now = Date.now();
const decisions = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => admitSend(store, "reader-42", now));
const admitted = decisions.filter((decision) => decision.admitted).length;

if (admitted !== 1) throw new Error(`expected one admission, received ${admitted}`);
console.log({ admitted, rejected: decisions.length - admitted, maxFailures });

The 30-second cooldown, five-minute lifetime, and five-failure ceiling make the example testable. They are not security guidance. Put them in policy configuration only after deciding who can change them and how that change is reviewed. Config bloat starts when every transport gets its own slightly different copy.

A production store must make admission atomic across processes. It should retain a challenge identifier, terminal status, failed-verification count, next-send time, and expiry server-side. Apply additional budgets by account, normalized phone number, IP range, and destination country. Geographic fencing and country-level spend cutoffs are application responsibilities here.

After admission, call the send operation with an idempotency key tied to that admitted transition. The adapter below is deliberately narrow. INFRAI_OTP_BODY contains JSON already validated against the current public discovery schema; keeping it external avoids inventing request fields that are not part of this article's verified contract. The call uses Bearer authentication, an explicit POST, response-status checks, and bounded exponential retry for HTTP 429 that honors Retry-After. It is runnable on a Node.js release with global fetch.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE_URL;
const rawBody = process.env.INFRAI_OTP_BODY;

if (!apiKey || !apiBaseUrl || !rawBody) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_API_BASE_URL, and INFRAI_OTP_BODY are required");
}

const body: unknown = JSON.parse(rawBody);
const idempotencyKey = `media-signup:${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function sendOtp(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/sms/otp`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const delayMs = retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)
        ? Number(retryAfter) * 1_000
        : Math.min(500 * 2 ** attempt, 8_000);
      await sleep(delayMs);
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`OTP send failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error("OTP send exhausted its retry budget");
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(await sendOtp()));

Verification gets its own explicit POST and must consume a failed-attempt budget atomically. Do not retry a verification blindly: a response can affect the application's attempt counter even when the network result is ambiguous. Generate or validate current request and response fields from discovery rather than copying a payload from an old tutorial. That is a boring boundary. Good. It keeps transport churn from leaking into the signup state machine.

Compare control planes before carrier claims

Vendor selection starts after the state machine passes. The useful comparison is which verification and delivery controls the service manages, because none of these products removes the application's responsibility for its authenticated session.

Option Service boundary Engineering consequence
Twilio Verify Verification-focused send and check workflow Application still owns signup authorization and its broader abuse policy
Vonage Verify Managed verification requests and checks Destination testing and session binding remain application work
AWS End User Messaging SMS SMS delivery within AWS IAM, regional configuration, and quota operations Team builds the complete challenge workflow and verification state
Infrai Stable REST capability contract with public schemas and one credential across backend modules Team owns cooldowns, attempts, geo controls, spend cutoffs, and polling orchestration

Test all four with the same cases: concurrent resend, wrong code, expired challenge, delayed delivery, and rate limiting. Then test physical handsets in the countries the media product serves. There is no honest substitute for that last step, and no supplied runtime measurement supports an uptime or latency winner.

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve the first look when a managed verification product is the desired boundary. AWS is coherent when IAM, regions, quotas, and operational ownership already sit there. Infrai fits a US/EU application flow when a plain REST contract, low credential sprawl, and a self-describing API matter: its public discovery describes full request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. The broader surface is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which can reduce adapter churn beyond this signup flow.

The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not suitable for a design that requires voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or webhook-driven fallback. Choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when their managed verification workflow and required channels match the design; choose AWS when AWS-native IAM and regional operations are the stronger constraint. The trade-off is less adapter and credential sprawl versus owning more orchestration in the application. NIST also classifies PSTN out-of-band authentication as restricted. SMS OTP is not phishing-resistant, so do not present it as the final word in account security.

No vendor fixes that.

What changes when signup volume grows

First, move challenge admission and failure consumption into a shared atomic store. Give records explicit retention and deletion rules. A phone identifier used to verify a media account should not quietly become a permanent audience profile.

Second, separate delivery observation from authentication. Poll status or events asynchronously only when the result changes a product decision. Cap attempts, back off, and stop after the observation window. Polling forever is config masquerading as reliability.

Third, make fallback a new state transition. Email fallback is not a managed email OTP feature here; the application must generate, store, expire, and verify that challenge itself. Scheduled email has no cancellation operation. If immediate cross-channel recovery is a hard requirement, pick a provider and architecture with the required push events and managed channels instead of burying this difference in a worker.

This is also where a single global rate limit breaks down. It can reject a legitimate signup spike while distributed abuse stays under each source threshold. Use layered budgets and record which one rejected a request. The exact thresholds belong to production evidence, not tutorial folklore.

The shipping rule

Ship only after one atomic application decision produces at most one idempotent send, and only a current, unexpired, under-budget challenge can complete its bound signup session. Keep that invariant independent of the SMS vendor.

Then choose the provider on delivery results in the real destination mix and on the control plane the team is willing to operate. The contract can stay put while the service behind it moves. The abuse budget stays yours either way.

References

  • NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management
  • Twilio Verify API documentation
  • Vonage Verify API overview
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance

title: Graph on one server: a 4-hop query 19 to 388 times faster than the incumbents
description:
Originally published on the Semurg blog: https://one.semurg.io/blog/graph-on-one-server. Every figure below is a row on https://one.semurg.io/benchmark#graph with the release it was measured on.

Graph databases are judged on traversals: start from one node, follow relationships out several hops, and return what you reach. We
ran that question on a public social graph against six graph databases, on one bare-metal server, with every engine's answer checked
against two independent reference implementations before anything was timed. This post has the results, the one place where it is
close, a mistake in our own benchmark kit, and the one command that reruns the whole thing on your own machine.

What we ran

  • The data: SNAP's com-Orkut social graph: 3.07 million people and 117.2 million relationships, loaded as published.
  • The machine: one Vultr bare-metal server, AMD EPYC 4345P (8 cores, 16 threads), 64 GB of memory, two NVMe disks, no GPU.
  • The engines: Semurg, Neo4j, ArangoDB, FalkorDB, FalkorDBLite, ArcadeDB and SurrealDB, each in Docker on that server, one after another, each with every thread, both data disks and no memory cap, its own recommended settings, and its fastest query form.
  • Two shapes of use: inside your application (Semurg linked into the client; the other engine's embedded mode where it has one, otherwise its fastest connection) and as a server (each engine through its own fastest connection).
  • Three cycles: cold, warm, warm again; the figure is the median of the warm cycles.

One query, 4 hops

Starting from one person, every distinct person within 4 hops (455,604 of them). As a server, Semurg answered in 3.83 ms; ArcadeDB
took 73.14 ms, FalkorDBLite 164.14 ms, FalkorDB 205.89 ms, Neo4j 281.40 ms and SurrealDB 1,484.92 ms. Across those
five server rows that is between 19 and 388 times faster. Inside the application the picture is the same: 3.84 ms for
Semurg against 93.08 ms for ArcadeDB's embedded mode and 1,360.65 ms for SurrealDB's.

Many queries at once

The same 4-hop question from 16 clients at once, each side driven by the same number of clients. As a server, Semurg answered 240.2
queries per second, ArcadeDB 28.0, FalkorDB 8.5 and Neo4j 2.6.

Walks to 131,072 hops

The ladder walks from the same person to every depth from 2 to 131,072 hops, checking each step against the reference. On this graph
everything reachable is reached within a few dozen hops, so past that point every engine is timing one full walk of the reachable
graph. As a server, Semurg's full walk took 95.22 ms; ArcadeDB's took 113.71 ms, FalkorDB's 412.67 ms and Neo4j's
14,033.83 ms. Inside the application Semurg's took 96.88 ms and ArcadeDB's embedded mode 459.74 ms.

The server comparison with ArcadeDB is the close one, and we care about it most. ArcadeDB answers its traversals from what it calls a
Graph Analytical View: an index of the whole graph it builds in memory when the database opens (the build is counted in its load
time). Semurg needs no such build when it opens. The next release carries two speed-ups to the graph walk; in our own test build they took the full walk from 96.4 ms to 81.1 ms on 8 threads (a test build, not a published release), and the published number follows the release.

What did not run, and why

A result we could not judge is shown as held, never dropped. In this run:

  • ArangoDB answered the 4-hop question correctly, but it was stopped by the out-of-memory killer during the many-at-once test, and the walk that followed found it already stopped. Our benchmark kit read that as a failure of the walk itself and set aside all of ArangoDB's results, its correct ones included. That was our kit's mistake, not ArangoDB's: the kit now checks that an engine is running before a walk starts, and ArangoDB is re-run on the next release. Until then its cells on the benchmark page read results pending.
  • FalkorDBLite's many-at-once run had failed requests and SurrealDB's had a zero median, so neither has a throughput figure; load times are held for every engine until each load has its run-to-run band.

Bigger than memory

Every domain we publish runs four classes: in the application and as a server, each on a dataset that fits in memory and one that
does not. This graph fits. The bigger-than-memory run uses SNAP's com-Friendster, a far larger social graph, with each engine held to a
fixed memory budget; its reference answers are still being computed, and the results go on the benchmark page when they finish.

Run it yourself

The kit that produced every number above is published. On a Linux machine with Docker, one command runs the graph benchmark for every
engine: curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/bench | sudo bash -s -- --graph. On a machine like ours it needs about 22 GB of free disk,
about 48 GB of memory for the largest engine, and about eight and a half hours (test tree, not a published release). Every figure,
every held row and the reason for each is on the benchmark page.

title: Catch Silent Outbound Failures When Dispatching Telegram Messages via PHP cURL
description:
When an order is placed on your web application or a user requests a notification through a Telegram bot, your backend needs to send an outbound message using the Telegram Bot API. Developers often reach for quick implementations like file_get_contents or a basic curl_exec script. On the surface, if the token is correct and the target chat ID is valid, the message delivers instantly. However, in production environments, this naïve implementation creates silent failures that leave customer orders unconfirmed and alert channels silent without raising backend exceptions.

An outbound HTTP request to Telegram can fail at four distinct layers: network socket timeouts, HTTP-level non-200 responses, malformed JSON bodies, and Telegram API-level rejection flags (ok: false). If your PHP script only verifies that curl_exec returned a non-false value, you will completely miss cases where Telegram rejects your payload due to broken HTML formatting, where a user has blocked the bot, or where API rate limits have been triggered.

The Failing Path: Why Basic cURL Calls Drop Messages

Consider a standard e-commerce webhook script processing a new purchase. It formats an HTML order summary with the buyer's input and fires off a POST request to sendMessage.

<?php
// Bad Example: Do not use in production
$token = getenv('BOT_TOKEN');
$chatId = $_POST['user_id'];
$userName = $_POST['user_name']; // e.g., "AT&T / Customer <John>"

$message = "<b>New Order!</b>\nCustomer: " . $userName;

$ch = curl_init("https://api.telegram.org/bot{$token}/sendMessage");
curl_setopt_array($ch, [
    CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER => true,
    CURLOPT_POST => true,
    CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS => [
        'chat_id' => $chatId,
        'text' => $message,
        'parse_mode' => 'HTML'
    ]
]);

$result = curl_exec($ch);
curl_close($ch);

// Flawed check: $result is a JSON string, which evaluates to boolean true
if ($result) {
    echo "Message sent successfully!";
}

When this script runs under normal conditions with clean customer names, it appears to work. But as soon as a customer inputs special characters like AT&T or enters an unescaped name like Customer <John>, the entire request breaks. Because parse_mode is set to HTML, Telegram expects valid XML-style tags. When it encounters raw ampersands or unclosed angle brackets, Telegram returns an HTTP 400 status with {"ok":false,"error_code":400,"description":"Bad Request: can't parse entities"}.

Because the naïve script only checks if ($result), it interprets Telegram's HTTP 400 response string as a successful execution. The variable $result contains the JSON string returned by Telegram, which evaluates to true when cast to a boolean condition in PHP. As a result, your order processing logic assumes the notification was sent, logs no errors, and moves forward, leaving the user with no confirmation message.

Furthermore, if Telegram's API endpoints experience transient latency or packet loss, cURL without explicit socket timeouts will hang indefinitely. If your PHP-FPM pool has 20 workers, 20 hanging cURL requests will quickly exhaust your server's process pool, crashing your backend application for all users.

Sanitizing Dynamic Input for Telegram HTML Mode

Telegram supports a limited subset of HTML tags: <b>, <i>, <a>, <code>, <pre>, and <u>. Any symbol outside these supported tags—specifically <, >, and &—must be converted to their corresponding HTML entities. Using strip_tags() is dangerous because it strips out legitimate text that resembles HTML tags, such as customer notes containing mathematically styled text or custom codes.

To safely inject user-generated content into an HTML-formatted message, you must run every dynamic variable through htmlspecialchars() before interpolating it into your message template. Do not pass the entire completed message string to htmlspecialchars(), as this will escape your intended structural tags like <b> into <b> text.

<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function formatOrderNotification(string $userName, string $productName, float $amount): string
{
    // Escape dynamic parameters individually before embedding
    $safeName = htmlspecialchars($userName, ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE | ENT_HTML5, 'UTF-8');
    $safeProduct = htmlspecialchars($productName, ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE | ENT_HTML5, 'UTF-8');
    $formattedAmount = number_format($amount, 2);

    return "<b>New Order Received</b>\n\n" .
           "<b>Customer:</b> {$safeName}\n" .
           "<b>Item:</b> {$safeProduct}\n" .
           "<b>Total:</b> \${$formattedAmount}";
}

Notice the flags passed to htmlspecialchars: ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE | ENT_HTML5. ENT_QUOTES ensures both single and double quotes are escaped, ENT_SUBSTITUTE replaces invalid code unit sequences with a Unicode replacement character instead of returning an empty string, and ENT_HTML5 ensures entity conversion conforms to modern standards.

Building a Four-Stage Verification cURL Dispatcher

To guarantee that an outbound Telegram message was received and accepted by Telegram's infrastructure, your PHP wrapper must execute four sequential validation steps:

  1. cURL Transport Level: Check curl_errno($ch) to ensure the HTTP request reached Telegram's servers without network timeouts, DNS lookup failures, or SSL handshake drops.
  2. HTTP Status Code Level: Verify curl_getinfo($ch, CURLINFO_HTTP_CODE). Telegram returns HTTP 200 on success, HTTP 400 for bad payloads, HTTP 403 when the bot was blocked by the user, and HTTP 429 when hit by rate limits.
  3. JSON Parsing Level: Execute json_decode($response, true) and immediately verify json_last_error() === JSON_ERROR_NONE. Malformed responses or upstream proxy error pages returning raw HTML will break subsequent array checks if unvalidated.
  4. Telegram API Level: Check $data['ok'] === true. If ok is false, extract $data['description'] and $data['error_code'] to trigger domain-specific fallback logic. 
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

class TelegramResponse
{
    public function __construct(
        public readonly bool $success,
        public readonly int $httpCode,
        public readonly ?array $data = null,
        public readonly ?string $errorMessage = null
    ) {}
}

function sendTelegramMessage(string $botToken, int|string $chatId, string $htmlText): TelegramResponse
{
    $url = "https://api.telegram.org/bot{$botToken}/sendMessage";

    $payload = json_encode([
        'chat_id' => $chatId,
        'text' => $htmlText,
        'parse_mode' => 'HTML',
        'disable_web_page_preview' => true
    ]);

    $ch = curl_init($url);
    curl_setopt_array($ch, [
        CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER => true,
        CURLOPT_POST => true,
        CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS => $payload,
        CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER => ['Content-Type: application/json'],
        CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT => 5, // Timeout for connection setup
        CURLOPT_TIMEOUT => 10,        // Timeout for total execution
    ]);

    $rawResponse = curl_exec($ch);
    $curlErrno = curl_errno($ch);
    $curlError = curl_error($ch);
    $httpCode = (int) curl_getinfo($ch, CURLINFO_HTTP_CODE);
    curl_close($ch);

    // Step 1: Check cURL Transport Error
    if ($curlErrno !== 0) {
        return new TelegramResponse(false, 0, null, "cURL Network Error ({$curlErrno}): {$curlError}");
    }

    // Step 2: Decode JSON
    /** @var array|null $decoded */
    $decoded = json_decode((string) $rawResponse, true);
    if (json_last_error() !== JSON_ERROR_NONE) {
        return new TelegramResponse(
            false, 
            $httpCode, 
            null, 
            "JSON Parse Error: " . json_last_error_msg() . " | Raw: " . substr((string)$rawResponse, 0, 100)
        );
    }

    // Step 3 & 4: Check HTTP Code and Telegram API Flag
    if ($httpCode !== 200 || !isset($decoded['ok']) || $decoded['ok'] !== true) {
        $apiDescription = $decoded['description'] ?? 'Unknown API error';
        $errorCode = $decoded['error_code'] ?? $httpCode;
        return new TelegramResponse(
            false, 
            $httpCode, 
            $decoded, 
            "Telegram API Error [{$errorCode}]: {$apiDescription}"
        );
    }

    return new TelegramResponse(true, $httpCode, $decoded);
}

Sending JSON formatted bodies via CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS with explicit Content-Type: application/json headers is preferred over sending raw POST arrays. Arrays trigger multipart/form-data encoding inside cURL, which increases payload size and introduces potential array-to-string conversion bugs when passing boolean or nested array flags.

Production Handling: Retries, Blocked Users, and Sanitized Logs

In production systems, network calls inevitably fail due to transient issues or rate limits. Your dispatching architecture must handle specific Telegram status codes gracefully without crashing your queue workers or leaking environment credentials.

Rate Limiting (HTTP 429)

Telegram enforces limits on API calls (typically 30 messages per second globally across all chats, or 1 message per second in a specific chat). When you exceed these limits, Telegram returns HTTP 429 along with a parameters object containing retry_after.

Bot Blocked or User Deactivated (HTTP 403)

When a user blocks your bot or deletes their Telegram account, Telegram returns HTTP 403 with the description Forbidden: bot was blocked by the user. Do not continue attempting to message this user on every scheduled background job. Intercept this status code and update your database to mark the user's notification status as disabled.

Sanitizing Log Files

Bot API tokens embedded directly inside target URLs (such as https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/sendMessage) present a security risk if logged raw to system files or external monitoring platforms. When logging failed cURL calls or transport errors, always redact the bot token before saving to disk.

<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function processOutboundMessage(string $token, int $userId, string $messageHtml, PDO $db): void
{
    $response = sendTelegramMessage($token, $userId, $messageHtml);

    if ($response->success) {
        // Message delivered successfully
        return;
    }

    $logContext = [
        'user_id' => $userId,
        'http_code' => $response->httpCode,
        'error' => $response->errorMessage,
    ];

    // Specific Error Handling
    if ($response->httpCode === 403) {
        // User blocked the bot: disable future notifications in DB
        $stmt = $db->prepare("UPDATE users SET telegram_notifications_enabled = 0 WHERE telegram_id = :id");
        $stmt->execute([':id' => $userId]);
        error_log("Telegram notification disabled for user {$userId}: User blocked bot.");
        return;
    }

    if ($response->httpCode === 429) {
        // Rate limited: extract retry_after parameter
        $retryAfter = $response->data['parameters']['retry_after'] ?? 5;
        error_log("Telegram Rate Limit Hit. Retry allowed after {$retryAfter} seconds.");
        // Here, re-queue the job with a delay matching $retryAfter
        return;
    }

    // Fallback: log error while sanitizing sensitive tokens
    $safeMessage = str_replace($token, '[REDACTED_TOKEN]', $response->errorMessage ?? '');
    error_log("Failed to send Telegram message to {$userId}: " . $safeMessage);
}

Handling outbound Telegram communication reliably in PHP requires treating every layer of the HTTP lifecycle with explicit checks rather than assuming successful transmission. Inspecting cURL transport errors, verifying HTTP response codes, parsing JSON safely, and escaping user input ensures your background workers run cleanly without dropping critical updates.

When building complex automation workflows or enterprise integrations, engineering teams rely on BotCreator — a studio that ships Telegram bots and Mini Apps with high-availability architectures and bulletproof backend integrations.

title: The Domain Was Just the Beginning: Building GraphGuard AI with FalkorDB
description:
The Domain Was Just the Beginning: Building GraphGuard AI with FalkorDB

One suspicious domain. A web of relationships. A different way to investigate.

By Team SynapGraph | Graph Hacks 2026 | Track 1 — Agents That Act on Connected Data

Every Threat Leaves a Trail. Can You Connect It?

Imagine an analyst investigating a suspicious domain.

At first, there is only a name on a screen.

But that name might point to an IP address. It might be associated with a digital certificate. It might appear in a threat-intelligence report. Each connection offers another clue, and every clue raises a new question.

Is this connection meaningful? Where did the information come from? What should the analyst investigate next?

The challenge is not simply collecting more security data. It is discovering how the pieces connect without confusing a clue with proof.

That question became the starting point for GraphGuard AI.

We are Team SynapGraph, and for Graph Hacks 2026, we set out to explore how graph databases and AI-assisted investigation workflows could make cybersecurity evidence easier to follow, understand, and investigate.

Our chosen track was Track 1: Agents That Act on Connected Data.

Our central idea was simple:

Don't just show the indicator. Show the relationships that give it context.

Meet GraphGuard AI: An Investigation That Follows the Connections

GraphGuard AI is a graph-powered cybersecurity investigation prototype designed to explore relationships between domains, IP addresses, certificates, and reports.

Instead of treating every indicator as an isolated record, the application uses a connected graph to retrieve related information and present it through an investigation workflow.

The technology stack brings together three key components:

  • FalkorDB — the relationship engine. Stores and queries the connected cybersecurity entities that underpin the investigation.
  • FastAPI — the investigation interface. Connects the backend workflow to API endpoints.
  • Streamlit — the analyst's workspace. Provides a dashboard for submitting indicators and reviewing results.

Docker supports the local development and demonstration environment.

Together, these components form a practical experiment in making connected security evidence easier to explore.

Why We Chose a Graph Instead of Another List

Traditional lists are useful when you need to know what you have.

Graphs become especially useful when you need to understand how things are connected.

Consider a simplified investigation:




Suspicious Domain
demo.example



RESOLVES_TO



IP Address
192.0.2.10 · documentation-only example IP



MENTIONED_IN



Intelligence Report
REPORT-001 · synthetic demonstration data

Illustrative graph path based on the project's synthetic demonstration data, not a real threat finding.

In FalkorDB, these connections can be represented as relationships between nodes and retrieved using graph queries.

GraphGuard AI's model includes paths such as:

  • Domain → RESOLVES_TO → IPAddress
  • Domain → PRESENTED_CERTIFICATE → Certificate
  • IPAddress → MENTIONED_IN → Report

This structure lets an investigation move beyond a single indicator and inspect the related entities that the graph contains.

The difference is important: the graph does not automatically establish guilt. It gives the analyst more context to evaluate.

Under the Hood: Turning Connections into Context

The investigation begins when a user submits a domain through the dashboard.

The backend receives the request and queries FalkorDB for matching graph entities and their relationships. The returned information can include associated IP addresses, certificate records, and intelligence-report references when those records exist in the graph.

The application then presents the available findings to the user.

The process follows a clear path:

Indicator → Graph Query → Connected Evidence → Analyst Review

FalkorDB is central to this workflow because the investigation depends on retrieving connected entities, not merely storing unrelated records.

The project also explores the wider possibility of passive intelligence enrichment, including DNS, registration information, certificate transparency, and public threat-intelligence sources. Any live enrichment must be distinguished from existing graph records so that users can tell where each observation originated.

The Most Important Feature Is What We Don't Claim

In cybersecurity, an incorrect conclusion can be more dangerous than an incomplete result.

Two domains sharing an IP address does not automatically make them malicious. A certificate connection does not prove an attack. A mention in a report must be interpreted in context.

That is why GraphGuard AI is designed around an evidence-first principle:

A connection is a lead. Evidence supports a hypothesis. Verification builds confidence.

The prototype's synthetic dataset demonstrates the investigation workflow; it is not proof of real-world detection accuracy. Likewise, any confidence value shown by the application should not be mistaken for a statistically validated probability of maliciousness.

Our aim is to help users follow the evidence, understand the relationships, and decide what deserves further investigation—not to replace human judgment with an unexplained verdict.

Building Under Hackathon Pressure

Graph Hacks 2026 gave us an opportunity to turn a concept into a working prototype within a short development window.

As Team SynapGraph, we focused on connecting the database, backend API, and dashboard into one locally runnable application.

The process involved more than writing code. We needed to think about the graph data model, how relationships should be queried, how findings should be presented, and how someone else could run the project.

We used AI-assisted development tools to accelerate parts of the workflow while keeping the project's actual implementation and limitations in view.

One lesson stood out: a project becomes much easier to explain when the architecture follows a clear idea. For GraphGuard AI, that idea is the relationship between an indicator and the evidence surrounding it.

What Comes Next: From Connected Data to Better Investigations

GraphGuard AI is a starting point, not a finished security platform.

Future work could explore:

  • More passive intelligence providers and clearly attributed observations.
  • Stronger provenance, freshness, and source-quality indicators.
  • Additional graph traversal and relationship analysis.
  • More comprehensive tests using carefully labelled datasets.
  • Better ways to explain why a particular connection is relevant.
  • Evaluation against known examples to measure where the approach succeeds and fails.

The long-term goal is not simply to produce a larger graph. It is to make the graph more useful to the person investigating it.

See the Project in Action

Explore the source code:

https://github.com/sudhir734/GraphGuard-Ai

Watch the demo:

https://youtu.be/gMyqtCTPSv8

GraphGuard AI is a hackathon prototype intended for demonstration and experimentation. Its findings should be independently verified before use in operational security decisions.

One Final Thought

A suspicious domain is a starting point, not a conclusion.

The real investigation begins when we ask what connects to it, what those connections actually mean, and which pieces of evidence deserve our attention.

With GraphGuard AI, we are exploring a simple but powerful idea: cybersecurity is not only about finding signals. It is about understanding the relationships between them.

Follow the connections. Question the evidence. Investigate with context.

Team SynapGraph | Graph Hacks 2026

title: Cold Starts, Lost Files, and Green Dots: Five Myths About Using a Free Server as Staging
description:
My demo broke at 9:58 PM. The same URL answered at 9:40. My code did not change in between.

That gap is the whole lesson. A free server is a shared, sleeping, replaceable machine. It is not a staging environment.

Below are five myths I kept repeating out loud. Then comes a 90-second probe that turns each one into a measurement.

Myth 1: "It returned 200, so it's up"

A 200 tells you one request finished. It says nothing about the next request.

Cold containers queue, boot, then answer. The status code hides all of that work.

So what did you actually measure? The status, or the latency budget?

Correct mental model: split the question into three.

  1. Liveness — the process exists.
  2. Readiness — it can serve a real request.
  3. Warmth — it can do that without a boot penalty.

Record connect time, time to first byte, and full body time separately. One number is not a diagnosis.

Myth 2: "My files will be there tomorrow"

Free tiers often rebuild the container between requests. Sometimes hourly. Sometimes weekly. You rarely get told which.

So don't assume persistence. Test it.

A canary is the cheapest test you have. Write a value, wait, read it back.

stamp=$(date +%s)
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/canary" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"v\":\"$stamp\"}"
sleep 120
curl -s "$BASE/canary?v=$stamp"

If the read-back is empty, your "temporary" upload directory is a story you tell your demo.

Correction: treat the filesystem as a cache. Keep state in an external store, or ship a seed script that rebuilds it on every boot.

Myth 3: "Free means I can retry CI forever"

Retries are cheap for you. They are not cheap for the host.

Many free tiers count requests, not successes. Worse, retry storms hit a cold service and trigger more boots.

Your pipeline gets slower. Your logs get noisier. Nothing gets fixed.

Correction: exponential backoff with jitter, a hard attempt cap, and one pre-warm request before the real one.

for i in 1 2 3; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 20 "$BASE/healthz")
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
  sleep $(( (2 ** i) + RANDOM % 3 ))
done

Myth 4: "Green locally means green remotely"

At least six things differ between your laptop and a free container:

  • Timezone — logs land on the wrong day.
  • Clock — token expiry and signed URLs drift.
  • Env vars — one missing key kills a code path you never exercised.
  • Filesystem — sometimes read-only, sometimes wiped.
  • Memory ceiling — your build is fine until it isn't.
  • Outbound network — allowlists and DNS behave differently.

None of these appear in a unit test. All of them appear in a demo.

Myth 5: "The health check proves demo readiness"

Most health endpoints are shallow. They return 200 while the connection pool is still warming.

A green dot means the route exists. It does not mean the first real user succeeds.

Correction: add one endpoint that touches a real dependency. Hit it twice before you present.

The probe: one script, one receipt

Here is the template I use now. It needs only bash, curl, and the Python standard library.

You supply two routes: /healthz and /canary. The second one stores and returns a small value.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# probe.py <base_url> [sleep_seconds] — stdlib only, writes receipt.json
import datetime, json, sys, time, urllib.request

BASE = sys.argv[1].rstrip("/")
WAIT = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 0.0

def timed(path, payload=None, timeout=25):
    req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, method="POST" if payload else "GET")
    if payload:
        req.add_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, data=payload, timeout=timeout) as r:
            body = r.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
            return {"path": path, "status": r.status,
                    "ms": round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1),
                    "body": body[:200]}
    except Exception as e:
        return {"path": path, "status": None,
                "ms": round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1),
                "error": str(e)[:200]}

stamp = str(int(time.time()))
checks = [
    timed("/healthz"),                                   # possibly cold
    timed("/healthz"),                                   # hopefully warm
    timed("/canary", payload=json.dumps({"v": stamp}).encode()),
]
time.sleep(WAIT)
checks.append(timed("/canary?v=" + stamp))               # canary read-back

receipt = {
    "base": BASE,
    "at": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    "wait_seconds": WAIT,
    "checks": checks,
}
json.dump(receipt, open("receipt.json", "w"), indent=2)
print(json.dumps(receipt, indent=2))

Run it twice. Once cold, once after a short pause.

python3 probe.py https://your-app.example 0 > cold.json
python3 probe.py https://your-app.example 120 > warm.json

Reading the receipt

Do not eyeball the whole file. Check four fields.

Field Healthy sign What a bad value means
healthz[0].ms vs healthz[1].ms Second call much faster Cold-start tax is real; pre-warm before demos
canary status 200 with the stored value Your endpoint is broken, not the host
read-back body Contains your stamp State did not survive; treat FS as cache
any error Empty Timeout or TLS issue; fix before blaming the app

Two runs prove very little about a month. Two runs prove a lot about tonight's demo.

Where a free model fits (and where it does not)

I use a model to summarize the receipt into three sentences for a shared channel. That is it.

A summary is not a gate. Never let a generated paragraph decide whether you ship.

For that write-up step I have used MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option, so the probe and the summary live in one place. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Run the probe yourself regardless of host. The numbers are yours, not mine.

Decision table: is a free server enough?

Situation Free server OK? What to do instead
Internal demo, one audience, you can redeploy Yes Pre-warm, keep a seed script ready
Overnight CI on every commit Risky Cache artifacts, cap retries at 3
Data you cannot rebuild No External database with backups
Latency-sensitive user tests No Paid tier or local container
Load or soak testing No Isolated environment you control
Teaching a workflow, first pass Yes Keep the probe in the repo

Limitations and who should not use this

The probe measures only what you instrument. It cannot see the host's scheduler, quotas, or eviction policy.

It also cannot promise anything about next month. Free tiers change shape without notice.

Skip this approach entirely if you need an SLA, handle regulated data, or run stateful services. Skip it if a mid-demo redeploy would cost you the deal.

Also skip it if you cannot write the canary endpoint. Without it, you are guessing.

What I changed

I stopped calling the free box "staging". I call it a demo target with a timer.

The receipt file now lives in the repo. Every demo starts with two runs and one glance at the table.

What would your 9:58 PM failure look like, if you measured it at 9:40?

title: Stop Letting Coding Agents Guess Call Chains: Tracing Blast Radius and Temporal Memory in FalkorDB
description:
When you change a helper function in a backend service, ask an LLM coding assistant, it will likely do one of two things: retrieve the function name from a vector database, or extract a few top-k chunks from a vector database and guess.

This is okay if the function is called directly from the test. It fails when your call chain is two or three hops long, or when an agent fails to find a solution to a problem today, saves the fact that it failed and moves on to tomorrow, when a commit alters the logic in the same module.

I created GraphTriage (github.com/Nimit15/GraphTriage): an Incident resolution and session memory system supported by FalkorDB Cloud for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 (Track 1: Agents That Act on Connected Data, Track 2: Agent Memory and Coordination).

GraphTriage is not a visualization supplement to the graph database, but rather it poses four specific questions using FalkorDB before an agent acts:

  1. Does the function or the test you are asking for exist in the graph? (If not, say NO right away rather than guess!)
  2. What is the exact call chain between the failed test and the broken function?
  3. What downstream functions and tests are contained within a blast radius of a change?
  4. Have we seen this fault signature before—and is that prior finding still ACTIVE, or has a newer commit marked it SUPERSEDED?

1. The Graph Schema mapping in FalkorDB

FalkorDB contains both repository (Track 1) and three-tier temporal memory (Track 2) data. Each workspace is separated at the database level using db.select_graph(f"graphtriage_ws_{workspace_id}"), to prevent memory leakage across tenants.

graph LR
    M[":Module"] <-- DEFINED_IN --- F1[":Function (Caller)"]
    F1 -- CALLS --> F2[":Function (Callee)"]
    T[":Test"] -- COVERS --> F1
    I[":EpisodicIncident"] -- IMPLICATES --> F2
    SF_NEW[":SemanticFact (ACTIVE)] -- APPLIES_TO --> F2
    SF_OLD[":SemanticFact (SUPERSEDED)]]
    PB[":ProceduralPlaybook"] -- REMEDIATES --> SF_NEW

Nodes and Relationships

Code Structure Nodes:

  • (:Module) — pulled the source files from the repository.

  • (:Function) — functions with module paths and line metadata, connected by [:DEFINED_IN] and directed [:CALLS] edges.

  • (:Test) — test cases exercising the functions they cover via [:COVERS] edges.

Three-Tier Memory Nodes:

  • (:EpisodicIncident) – raw incident data (stack trace, failing test name, session id, timestamp).

  • (:SemanticFact) — verified root-cause statements with temporal lifecycle properties (valid_from, valid_to, status: ‘ACTIVE’ | ‘SUPERSEDED’)

  • (:ProceduralPlaybook) - reusable remediation steps attached to recurrent fault signatures (e.g. KeyError: 'income'), keeping track of usage_countover sessions.

Figure 1. GraphTriage's local FalkorDB graph showing the code entities and relationships used for incident analysis.

2. Track 1: Explaining How the Graph Carries Out the Work (A Cypher That Contains No Text Written by a Large Language Model)

A design rule that I adhered to right from the beginning was that the agent should never generate raw Cypher queries at runtime. Allowing an LLM to produce ad-hoc Cypher queries would lead to syntax errors and the invention of hallucinated edge labels. In order to avoid this, the agent interacts with FalkorDB only via the parameterized methods in src/core/incident_resolver.py and the fixed tools that are available through the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) SDK (src/mcp/mcp_server.py):

  • trace_blast_radius

  • find_failure_path

  • run_targeted_tests

Step 1: Refusing to Speculate on Unknown Entities
Should you inquire of a typical RAG agent regarding a function that has been renamed or deleted, it will readily retrieve chunks of code that look similar and then fabricate an impact analysis.

In the function IncidentResolver._validate_entity_existence(), each analysis begins with a parameterized check for existence in FalkorDB:

def _validate_entity_existence(self, entity_name: str) -> bool:
    query = """
    MATCH (n)
    WHERE (n:Function OR n:Test OR n:Module)
      AND n.name = $entity_name
    RETURN count(n) AS count
    """
    result = self.graph.query(query, {"entity_name": entity_name})
    return result.result_set[0][0] > 0 if result.result_set else False

If FalkorDB returns 0, analyze_impact() halts immediately and returns status: "UNVERIFIED_ENTITY" with hops: 0 and an explicit refusal reason:

{
  "status": "UNVERIFIED_ENTITY",
  "hops": 0,
  "function_name": "non_existent_helper",
  "reason": "Function 'non_existent_helper' not found in graph; refusing to speculate without graph evidence",
  "affected_functions": [],
  "impact_path": []
}

Every decision the agent makes is traceable back to graph state: if the node isn't in FalkorDB, the agent refuses to guess.

Step 2: Tracing Real Bugs in sandbox_service
To test GraphTriage end-to-end without mocks, sandbox_service/app.py models a multi-function service (7 functions and 12 tests) containing three intentional regressions:

  1. process_user_data: raises KeyError: 'income' when optional dictionary keys are missing. 2. calculate_growth_rate: uses bitwise XOR (^) instead of exponentiation (**). 3. calculate_compound_interest: drops the exponent term in the compound formula.

When test_incident_process_user_data_missing_income fails, GraphTriage queries the call chain ([:COVERS]$\rightarrow$ [:CALLS]) in FalkorDB to trace the path from the failing test to the underlying function, then computes the blast radius (calculate_blast_radius) using PageRank (CALL algo.pageRank('Function', 'CALLS') with a < 2 node guard that falls back cleanly to direct relationship degree scoring).

Instead of re-running all 12 tests in the sandbox on every edit, the agent queries FalkorDB for only the :Test nodes connected to the affected subgraph and executes pytest on that targeted subset.

3. Track 2: Multi-Agent Handoffs & Replacing Old Information

When we store debugging history in a vector index that only adds new entries, old conclusions can stick around forever without anyone noticing.

In the files src/core/multi_agent_pipeline.py and src/core/temporal_memory.py, the GraphTriage system manages three specific agents. These agents pass information between each other using a structured process called AgentHandoff, with FalkorDB storing the data:

  1. The TriageAgent looks at the stack trace, pulls out a standard signature for the error (like KeyError: 'income'), records it as an EpisodicIncident, and then checks FalkorDB to see if there are any active SemanticFacts. 2. The BlastRadiusAgent takes the information from the TriageAgent, uses FalkorDB to find out how the failure spread and which functions were affected, and adds that graph evidence. 3. The MemoryCuratorAgent saves confirmed findings about the root cause as SemanticFact nodes and either finds or creates a ProceduralPlaybook.

Marking Old Facts as Replaced with [:SUPERSEDED]

Imagine a new code change affects how process_user_data handles default values. Instead of deleting the old SemanticFact (which would lose the debugging history) or just adding a new, conflicting fact, we use a function called supersede_fact(). This function sets an expiration date for the old fact, marks it as SUPERSEDED, and connects the new fact to the old one:

# Initial architectural finding saved in Session 1
memory.create_semantic_fact({
    "statement": "process_user_data should use user.get('income', 0)",
    "valid_from": "2026-10-17T10:00:00Z",
    "status": "ACTIVE"
})

# Superseded after schema update in Session 2
memory.supersede_fact(old_fact_id, {
    "statement": "process_user_data validates schema via default dict mapping",
    "valid_from": "2026-10-18T14:00:00Z",
    "status": "ACTIVE"
})

In Cypher, closing the old fact while preserving the lineage looks like this:

MATCH (old:SemanticFact {fact_id: $old_fact_id})
SET old.valid_to = $timestamp,
    old.status = 'SUPERSEDED'
CREATE (new:SemanticFact {
    fact_id: $new_fact_id,
    statement: $statement,
    valid_from: $timestamp,
    valid_to: null,
    status: 'ACTIVE'
})-[:SUPERSEDED]->(old)

When a future session queries memory, the fast retrieval path filters strictly on status = 'ACTIVE' AND valid_to IS NULL. The agent gets only current truth in its context window, while the [:SUPERSEDED]chain preserves the full audit trail.

Figure 2. GraphTriage's incident-resolver and temporal-memory tests running against a local FalkorDB instance (19 passed).

4. Engineering Lessons From Setting Up FalkorDB Cloud

When I built and tested this on Windows with a live FalkorDB Cloud, I learned some practical things:

1.
Centralizing Cloud Connection and Default Parameter Issues (src/core/db_connection.py):
At first, having default host="localhost" in our class constructors would quietly ignore the .env variables when setting up test data. We fixed this by putting all connection code into one place (db_connection.py). This setup loads .env variables and allows overriding them, splits the host and port, and has a fallback for SSL. Now, switching between our local Docker setup (localhost:6379) and FalkorDB Cloud is easy.

2.
MCP Server Startup and Module Name Conflicts:
We named our local folder src/mcp/, but this conflicted with the official mcp package we installed through pip. This happened when we set PYTHONPATH=/app/src in Docker. By changing to import from the project root (using PYTHONPATH=/app and running commands like python -m src.mcp.mcp_server) and giving InitializationOptions() to mcp_server.run(), we fixed the startup problems.

2.
Comparing Step-by-Step Path Finding vs. Wildcard Shortest Path:
In OpenCypher, how patterns with unbounded or undirected paths work can be different on various graph databases compared to Neo4j. We used specific directed relationships (like [:COVERS] and [:CALLS]) along with checking the call chain step-by-step and using a fallback based on how connected a node is. This made our path tracing completely predictable in all 8 integration tests. All tests passed, with one warning, and it took 10.49 seconds against the live FalkorDB Cloud.

5. Current Limitations & Next Steps

  • Language Parser Scope: The system currently takes in Python modules and follows pytest conventions; the next logical step is to expand the AST loader to support TypeScript and Go using Tree-sitter.

  • Containerized Test Runner: The current test execution runs in a subprocess with a time limit; putting test runs inside containers would make it more reliable for use in multi-user CI pipelines.

Repository & Disclosure

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Nimit15/GraphTriage

  • Hackathon Tracks: Track 1 (Agents That Act on Connected Data) and Track 2 (Agent Memory and Coordination)

  • Development & AI Disclosure: This project was built for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026. The graph schema design, FalkorDB Cloud connection layer, entity-existence refusal guard, call-chain and blast-radius logic, 3-stage agent handoff flow and temporal SUPERSEDED memory lifecycle (~75% of the engineering work) were. Checked by me. I used Claude Code (~25%) as an IDE coding assistant, for FastAPI/MCP scaffolding, synthetic sandbox bugs and initial test fixtures.

title: How We Built an Ultra-Lightweight Desktop AI Assistant (<35MB RAM) with Zero-DB RAG and Zero Bloat
description:
If you’ve tried running desktop AI assistants recently (LM Studio, Jan, AnythingLLM, Open-WebUI), you’ve probably noticed an infuriating trend:

Most desktop AI tools consume 800MB to 1.4GB of RAM before you even load a single neural weight into memory.

Why? Because almost every modern AI assistant is packaged as a bloated Electron container. When you finally load a 7B LLM (3GB VRAM), a vision model (2GB), and Whisper (1GB) for voice interaction, standard laptops and base 8GB Apple Silicon Macs instantly freeze or crash with brutal Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors.

We asked a fundamental question:

Can we build an autonomous, feature-packed desktop AI companion that idles at <35MB RAM, runs 100% offline, and never crashes an 8GB machine?

That was the birth of GhostOS (GitHub: GhostOS-ai/GhostOS). Here is the engineering story of how we pulled it off.

1. Ditching Electron: The ~35MB RAM Native Architecture

Electron bundles an entire Chromium browser and Node.js runtime for every single window.

Instead of Electron, GhostOS uses OS-native web rendering engines:

  • macOS: Apple WebKit
  • Windows: Microsoft Edge WebView2
  • Linux: WebKitGTK

The entire floating Casper mascot and Spotlight command bar (HUD) are rendered as transparent, frameless native webviews bridged directly to Python.

Baseline Idle RAM Comparison:
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ App                     │ Idle RAM (No LLM)│
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
│ Jan / AnythingLLM       │ ~850 MB – 1.2 GB │
│ LM Studio               │ ~700 MB – 950 MB │
│ GhostOS (Native Engine) │ ~35 MB           │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

The difference is a 25x reduction in RAM footprint. Your CPU fans stay silent.

2. Dynamic VRAM Juggler: Solving the Multi-Model OOM Trap

In an ideal workflow, you want:

  1. An LLM for reasoning and coding.
  2. A vision model for screen understanding.
  3. A speech model for voice input.

If you keep all three resident in GPU VRAM, you need at least 6GB–8GB of pure VRAM, leaving nothing for macOS or Windows OS compositor.

We implemented a Dynamic VRAM Juggler:

  • The engine maintains a hot-swap memory scheduler.
  • Models are unloaded to system cache and swapped into active GPU memory on-demand in <150ms.
  • Peak VRAM is strictly capped at ≤3.5GB, making it rock-solid on budget PCs and 8GB MacBooks.

3. Zero-DB RAG: Document Chat Without Docker or Chroma

Almost every RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) tutorial tells you to spin up Docker, install heavy vector databases (Chroma, Qdrant, Milvus), and download hundreds of megabytes of Python dependencies.

For a desktop tool, that’s crazy overkill.

We replaced the entire heavy vector stack with pure SQLite FTS5 (Full-Text Search 5) + BM25 ranking:

  • Zero external database daemon.
  • Zero network ports opened.
  • Drag-and-drop any PDF, code file, or markdown note directly onto Casper.
  • Document indexing happens in milliseconds with sub-millisecond retrieval latency.

4. 5 Killer Features That Elevate Productivity

  1. Ghostwriter (Global Clipboard AI): Select text anywhere — Slack, VS Code, Notes, Browser — hit your shortcut, and GhostOS rewrites, fixes grammar, or translates inline.
  2. Memory Vault: Cross-session persistent context graph stored in SQLite with zero VRAM overhead. GhostOS remembers your preferences and projects without wasting context tokens.
  3. Terminal Sandbox Lens: A proactive safety layer that intercepts dangerous commands (rm -rf, DROP DATABASE, raw dd, format C:) and explains the risks in plain English.
  4. Daily Standup & Commit Crafter: Analyzes your git diffs and terminal sessions to craft clean conventional commits and ready-to-share daily standup summaries.
  5. Auto-Minutes: Transcribes audio meetings and outputs an executive summary with actionable checklists.

5. 100% Paranoid Privacy Pledge

No telemetry. No tracking. No phone-home pings. GhostOS operates completely air-gapped with Wi-Fi switched off.

🚀 Quickstart: Try It in 30 Seconds

GhostOS is 100% open-source under the MIT license and published on PyPI.

# Install globally via pip
pip install ghostos-ai

# Launch your floating Casper desktop companion
ghost pet

Or clone the repo:

git clone https://github.com/GhostOS-ai/GhostOS.git
cd GhostOS
pip install -e .
ghost pet

  • PyPI Package: https://pypi.org/project/ghostos-ai
  • Author: KIB.best (Contact: GhostOS@kib.best)

title: A link that takes two seconds needs its own pending state, and next/link finally reports one
description:
A plain <Link> in the App Router gives the user nothing to look at between the click and the next screen. On a fast route nobody notices. On a route whose layout has to authenticate you and load your account first, the click looks dead for a second or two, and the honest user response to a dead click is to click again.

The usual answer is loading.tsx, and it does not cover this gap. A loading file only renders once the routing boundary it belongs to has been reached, which means after the target segment's layout has resolved. Leaving a practice session for the dashboard means waiting on the dashboard layout's session and user lookup before any loading UI of the destination exists. The window with no feedback is exactly the window loading.tsx cannot reach into.

useLinkStatus reports that window, and it reports it on the element the user is already looking at: the link they clicked.

Three pieces, all of them tiny

The hook only works inside a <Link> descendant, which makes it awkward to use directly and easy to wrap. We have three wrappers.

A spinner that exists only while its link is navigating:

export function LinkSpinner({ size = 16, className }: { size?: number; className?: string }) {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();
  if (!pending) return null;
  return <HugeiconsIcon icon={Loading03Icon} size={size} className={cn('animate-spin', className)} aria-hidden />;
}

A swap, for cases where the label itself should change:

export function LinkPending({ children, pending }: { children: React.ReactNode; pending: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { pending: isPending } = useLinkStatus();
  return <>{isPending ? pending : children}</>;
}

And the one that gets used: a button that navigates and reports its own progress, as a drop-in for <Button asChild><Link/></Button>.

<NavButton
  href="/dashboard/games"
  variant="ghost"
  size="sm"
  aria-label="Back to Games"
  icon={<HugeiconsIcon icon={ArrowLeft01Icon} size={16} />}
  pendingLabel="Exiting…"
>
  <span className="hidden sm:inline">Back to Games</span>
</NavButton>

Inside, the pending branch does three things at once: the leading icon becomes a spinner, the label becomes pendingLabel if one was given, and the trailing icon is dropped so the row does not grow while it is busy.

const { pending } = useLinkStatus();

return (
  <>
    {pending ? <HugeiconsIcon icon={Loading03Icon} size={16} className="animate-spin" aria-hidden /> : icon}
    <span aria-live="polite" className="inline-flex items-center gap-2">
      {pending && pendingLabel != null ? pendingLabel : children}
    </span>
    {!pending && trailingIcon}
  </>
);

Two details that were not obvious

The live region. A spinner is a visual-only signal. Swapping "Back to Games" for "Exiting…" inside an aria-live="polite" region means the change is announced rather than merely seen, so a screen reader user gets the same "yes, that worked" the sighted user gets from the spin. The spinner itself is aria-hidden, because announcing a spinner tells you nothing the label change has not already said.

That wrapper is a flex row for a reason. The first version used a plain <span> and any icon passed as a child, rather than through icon or trailingIcon, broke onto its own line. Tailwind's preflight sets svg { display: block }, so an inline SVG inside an inline wrapper stops behaving like text. inline-flex items-center gap-2 puts it back on the baseline. It is a two-class fix for a bug that looks like a React problem and is a CSS reset.

Where it is worth using

These three wrappers are imported by exactly five files, and every one of them sits behind sign-in: the shell around a practice session, the screen a finished session lands on, the shell around an assessment centre exercise, the dashboard, and the empty-state hero a brand new account sees. Eight call sites, three distinct pending labels: five say "Loading…", one says "Loading games…", and the two shells wrapped around work in progress say "Exiting…", because leaving mid-session is the one navigation where the user may be worried about what happens to what they are abandoning.

That is the whole heuristic: pending feedback on an instant link is noise. The prefetched links across our public pages, the provider catalogue or a test format page, resolve fast enough that a spinner on them would only ever flash, and none of them use these components. The buttons that need one are the buttons crossing into a layout that authenticates you first, which is why all five files are inside the signed-in app rather than on the pages describing the mock interview or the assessment centre exercises.

The general version of the rule: find the links that cross a layout doing input or output before it renders, and give exactly those their own pending state. For everything else, loading.tsx was already enough.

title: A small usability test for personal search tools
description:
A demo search often starts with a query the builder already knows will work. A more useful test starts with a person who remembers the purpose of a resource but not its title.

Here is a small test plan I would use before adding complexity to a personal search tool.

Prepare a realistic collection

Ask a participant to save five to ten resources they genuinely care about. Include a mixture of formats if the product supports them: an article, a screenshot, a link, or a note. Let them add context in their normal words.

Return later rather than testing immediately after saving. The delay is part of the task: the interface should help after the title has faded from memory.

Ask for an outcome, not a query

Instead of “search for onboarding,” ask: “Find the example you wanted to use for your project's welcome screen.” Let the participant choose their own search terms.

Record the first query, any reformulations, which results they inspect, and whether they identify the right resource. Ask them what makes a result look relevant. A result can be retrieved correctly and still be hard to recognize.

Diagnose the failure layer

If the resource never appears, investigate which searchable fields were available. If it appears but is overlooked, examine the title, preview, and saved context. If the user finds it but cannot reuse it, the destination or source may be the problem.

Those are different failures and need different changes. Improving ranking will not repair an unreadable result card.

Repeat after one focused change

Try a change such as exposing the user's note beneath the result title. Use another retrieval task and compare observations. With a small exploratory test, treat the outcome as a design clue rather than a population-wide performance claim.

Némos's “can you find it again?” prompt is useful because it shifts attention from how much we save to what saving lets us do later.

title: Our relative timestamps round instead of floor, so 91 seconds ago reads as 2m ago
description:
Notifio is a desktop app that checks rental search pages on a loop and emails you when a new listing shows up. Almost every number in its UI is a time: when a search was last checked, how long the check took, when a blocked host gets retried, when a listing turned up.

All of that goes through one 25-line file. I read it properly for the first time last week and found that it rounds, everywhere, and that rounding means two different things depending on which direction the clock is pointing.

The file 

/** Small shared formatters for the status strip and the finds list. */

/** "12s ago", "4m ago", "2h ago". Empty string for a null timestamp. */
export function relativeTime(at: number | null): string {
  if (!at) return "";
  const seconds = Math.max(0, Math.round((Date.now() - at) / 1000));
  if (seconds < 10) return "just now";
  if (seconds < 60) return `${seconds}s ago`;
  const minutes = Math.round(seconds / 60);
  if (minutes < 60) return `${minutes}m ago`;
  const hours = Math.round(minutes / 60);
  if (hours < 24) return `${hours}h ago`;
  return `${Math.round(hours / 24)}d ago`;
}

/** "in 45s", "in 3m". Used for the retry countdown on a blocked search. */
export function countdown(until: number): string {
  const ms = until - Date.now();
  if (ms <= 0) return "any moment";
  if (ms < 60_000) return `in ${Math.max(1, Math.round(ms / 1000))}s`;
  return `in ${Math.round(ms / 60_000)}m`;
}

/** "1.4s". Shown on a row so a slow site is visible rather than guessed at. */
export function seconds(ms: number | null): string {
  if (ms === null) return "";
  return `${(ms / 1000).toFixed(1)}s`;
}

Four Math.round calls in relativeTime, one in countdown. The conventional choice for elapsed time is Math.floor, and I want to argue that the conventional choice is wrong in one of these functions and right in the other.

Rounding an elapsed time can only overstate

relativeTime(Date.now() - 91_000) gives "2m ago". Ninety-one seconds is one minute and thirty-one seconds. Math.floor would say 1m ago, which is true and under-informative. Math.round says 2m ago, which is false and over-informative.

Work out the sign of the error and it stops being a toss-up. A rounded elapsed time is wrong in one direction only: it can claim something is older than it is by up to half a unit, and it can never claim something is newer than it is. Floor does the opposite. It can claim a check that happened 119 seconds ago was "1m ago", which is the direction that matters here, because every one of these timestamps is answering the same underlying question:

Is this thing still working?

A monitor that says last check 1m ago when it was really two minutes is a monitor reassuring you with a number it made up. A monitor that says 2m ago when it was really 91 seconds has rounded against itself. If the app is going to be wrong by up to thirty seconds, I want it wrong in the direction that makes me look at it.

That is not an accident of the implementation, but I cannot claim it was planned either. The comment above the function says "12s ago", "4m ago", "2h ago" and nothing about rounding. I am adopting it after the fact, which is a thing you are allowed to do as long as you write the reason down somewhere, which is partly what this post is.

Rounding a countdown breaks a promise

countdown is a different proposition, because it is not reporting, it is promising. It renders on the retry chip of a search whose host has told us to wait:

{waiting && (
  <button
    onClick={onRetry}
    title="Stop waiting and check this search again now"
    className={`${CHIP} group min-w-[104px] ...`}
  >
    <span className="group-hover:hidden">Retry {countdown(waiting)}</span>
    <span className="hidden group-hover:inline">Retry now</span>
  </button>
)}

With 89 seconds left, Math.round(89_000 / 60_000) is 1, so the chip says Retry in 1m. A minute later nothing has happened, because there are still 29 seconds to go. The chip has by then updated itself to in 29s, so it self-corrects rather than lying permanently, but there is a moment where the app said one minute and meant one and a half.

For a countdown, Math.ceil is the honest function. The error should fall on the same side as it does for elapsed time: never promise sooner than you can deliver. One character.

I have not changed it yet, and the reason is the thing hovering over that chip. Every countdown in this app is skippable. Hover the chip and the text swaps to Retry now, click it and the wait is over. We decided a while back that if the app shows you a countdown it has to let you out of it, and that decision takes most of the weight off the exact number. A countdown you can cancel is a hint. A countdown you cannot cancel is a contract, and a contract should round up.

Note also the Math.max(1, ...) on the seconds branch. Without it, 400ms remaining renders as in 0s, which is the single worst string a countdown can produce: it is both wrong and finished-looking. The floor of 1 means the chip counts in 2s, in 1s, any moment, and any moment is the right register for a number we do not actually control.

The clock that drives all of it

None of these functions are reactive. They read Date.now() when they run, and React does not re-render because time passed. So there is a hook whose entire job is to make a component re-render on a schedule:

export function useNow(intervalMs = 1000, active = true): number {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(() => Date.now());

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!active) return;
    const timer = setInterval(() => setNow(Date.now()), intervalMs);
    return () => clearInterval(timer);
  }, [intervalMs, active]);

  return now;
}

Three components call it, with three different intervals and three different conditions:

// SitesList: one second, but only while something is counting down.
useNow(1000, hasCountdown || app.status === "polling");

// MonitorCard: five seconds, only while the monitor is in an active state.
useNow(5000, isActive);

// RecentFinds: thirty seconds, only if there is anything in the list.
useNow(30_000, app.finds.length > 0);

The intervals are chosen against the formatter, not against the component. SitesList is the only one that renders a countdown, whose output changes every second below a minute, so it ticks every second. RecentFinds renders relativeTime on listings that are minutes to days old, where the string changes at most once a minute, so thirty seconds is already generous and a one-second tick would be 29 wasted renders out of 30.

The active flags matter more than the intervals. This app's whole job is to sit in the background for hours, and a React tree re-rendering once a second while nobody is looking at it is a laptop fan. hasCountdown is computed per render from whether any search has a nextRetryAt:

// Only tick while something is actually counting down.
const hasCountdown = sites.some((s) => {
  const nextRetryAt = app.runtimeFor(s)?.nextRetryAt;
  return nextRetryAt !== null && nextRetryAt !== undefined;
});

So the second-by-second timer exists only while a host is in backoff or a poll is in flight, and the rest of the time the tree is still. The dependency array is [intervalMs, active], so flipping active tears the interval down rather than leaving it running against a stale condition.

There is still a seam in SitesList: above one minute, countdown returns the same string for sixty consecutive ticks. The fix is to compute the next interesting moment and set a timeout for exactly that, and it is not worth it for one chip on an app with at most fifteen searches running.

What I would take from this

Pick the rounding mode from the sign of the error you can live with, not from what reads nicest. "Round to nearest" is the default because it minimises average error, and average error is almost never the thing that matters in a status line. What matters is which way the UI lies when it lies, and whether that direction makes the user check or relax.

Elapsed time: round up, make them look. Countdown: round up, make them wait. Both of those are the same rule, which is a good sign that it is the rule.

The app this came out of is at notifio.app, and there is a page per site it watches under alerts if you want to see what it is timing.
