title: Everything hackable will get hacked
description:
Over the past year, AI models have become much more capable of performing cybersecurity work. These changes are reshaping both the threats facing the web and the tools available to defend it. Right now, defenders have an advantage because they can use stronger models for defensive work than the open-weight models broadly available for offensive research. But this advantage will not always last. The gap will soon close.

I have both good news and bad news, neither of which is yet widely understood in the community.

  • Bad news: Near-frontier open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today. Kimi K3 is an Opus 4.X-class model with no relevant cybersecurity safeguards.

  • Good news: You do not need to wait for “Mythos access” or OpenAI’s cyber program to begin defensive cybersecurity work. Frontier models, with the notable exception of Fable 5, will perform defensive cybersecurity tasks today.

The uncertainty around Mythos 5's release seems to have created a kind of paralysis among defenders, many of whom are underutilizing the powerful tools available to them today. This post aims to give readers insight into how we're thinking about AI-enabled defensive cybersecurity at Vercel and why we think teams should be moving with more urgency.

The OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident

This YouTube video from OpenAI researchers on the widely reported security incident involving Hugging Face is an absolute must-watch for anyone concerned with cybersecurity. It clarifies that there were two separate security incidents exploiting vulnerabilities that will be found in most computer systems.

The gist is that models working on an OpenAI training run found 0-day vulnerabilities that allowed them to bypass egress internet restrictions, enabling communication between models and access to the broader internet. Once internet access was established, broader exploitation occurred.

Open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today

Open-weight model capabilities have been top of mind in the AI community lately, but it is less widely understood that Kimi K3, a popular open-weight model, has no effective safeguards against offensive cybersecurity work.

On DeepSec Bench, which measures application-code vulnerability discovery, it ranks highest among the open-weight models we evaluated, roughly matching Sonnet 5 and outperforming Opus 4.8.

I tasked Kimi K3 with trying to break out of Vercel Sandbox, and while it did not successfully escape, it mapped the guest-kernel attack surface, followed possible privilege escalation paths, built a VM environment to reproduce its ideas, and implemented and ran a fuzzer.

These are some excerpts from that research, beginning with an analysis of the guest-kernel attack surface.

The model followed that lead into candidate privilege escalation paths and considered what guest-kernel control could mean for a microVM escape.

When paths still needed testing, Kimi built a VM environment for reproductions and wrote a stateful fuzzer for the device path it was investigating.

While none of this produced an escape from Vercel Sandbox, it did show Kimi conducting an investigation on its own, and given the right vulnerable surface, this would lead to a successful exploit.

Frontier models can help defenders today

Much of the community assumed that meaningful security review would require access to Mythos-class models and therefore held off on using the models already available to them.

But that assumption has never been true. All the frontier models that we evaluated, with the notable exception of Fable 5, can perform defensive cybersecurity work today and have been able to do so throughout the year so far.

The rough heuristic I have observed is that models with safeguards will still make hypotheses about security vulnerabilities when they have access to source code, apparently because access to proprietary source code typically suggests a defensive use case. Attackers can also obtain source code, but I think source-code access is a reasonable working signal of defensive intent.

I personally discovered this in March, when I first heard about cyber variants and was also seeing AI code reviews find security issues in my own code. That made me wonder, “If code review can find issues in a diff, can I also run it across an entire codebase?” It turns out the answer was yes. From that experiment, I created deepsec, an open-source security harness for performing security analysis at scale across large codebases.

The temporary defensive advantage

Right now, OpenAI’s Sol 5.6 on XHigh is the best model for cybersecurity defense. It is much smarter than Kimi K3, the best available open-weight model without safeguards against offensive work. As defender, you have the better tool at your disposal, but you have to use it.

A full deepsec review will help you improve the security posture of your codebase by surfacing vulnerability hypotheses for you to investigate. In my experience, it is especially good at finding IDORs, XSS, and SSRF. The Hugging Face incident shows what this kind of application-level research looks like from the other side, since the models kept searching after an SSRF attempt was blocked and eventually found successful routes through file disclosure and template injection.

deepsec is open source and can run entirely in your own infrastructure with inference providers controlled by you. Vercel has no financial gain from you using it. It is really worth trying on your own source code.

Once the run finishes, review every finding yourself and compare the results with what your current security process already catches.

Continuous defense

AI model capabilities will continue to improve, and I expect open-weight models to catch up with Sol’s current performance on application-code vulnerability discovery even as frontier models advance again. We need to prepare for that cycle by continuously improving how we find and fix vulnerabilities as the models progress.

At Vercel, we run full deepsec reviews across mission-critical repositories every quarter and whenever a stronger model becomes available, in addition to automated security reviews on every pull request.

Those full reviews cost tens of thousands of dollars, which we consider a relatively small expense compared with what we spend on our HackerOne program or the opportunity cost of a security incident.

We have connected deepsec output to Vercel software factories for automated vulnerability processing and will share more about this work soon. As these reviews produce more findings, automatically managing them becomes the next frontier.

What Vercel is doing

As an immediate measure, we made the full egress firewall in Vercel Sandbox available on the Hobby plan, giving everyone access to the same network controls.

We are also working to launch a dedicated HackerOne program focused on finding zero-day vulnerabilities in Vercel Sandbox and the egress firewall. We want to redirect offensive model capabilities toward defensive work, so the program will cover AI costs for researchers who use AI Gateway and submit a vulnerability report that is accepted.

We also plan to extend deepsec to use the offensive capabilities of open-weight models and cyber variants of frontier models when triaging the vulnerability hypotheses it identifies.

Defenders can already use stronger models than those broadly available for offensive work. Teams should use that advantage now and continue reviewing their systems as the gap closes.

Takeaways

  • The cybersecurity threat from AI models is real.

  • Everybody can improve their defensive posture with tools like deepsec today.

  • Doing this is urgent, and the practice should continue as models improve.

Read more

title: Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components
description:
title: "Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-14T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [nextjs, react, webdev, frontend]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Static Site Generation (Ssg) With Generatestaticparams: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Parsing Mdx Files: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Syntax Highlighting With Rehype/Remark: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Optimizing Core Web Vitals: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Static site generation (SSG) with generateStaticParams, parsing MDX files, syntax highlighting with Rehype/Remark, and optimizing Core Web Vitals."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: 2026 Go Failure Alerts: Logs and Cron Notifications for Small SaaS
description:
Use exception groups as the primary deployment tripwire, add metrics only for rate, latency, and cost thresholds, and run a small poller that owns Slack or email delivery. For an e-commerce AI agent, that split gives rollback logic a narrow input surface and keeps notification code out of checkout.

TL;DR: start with errors, then add a few metrics that can change a release decision. Logs are evidence for investigation, not the easiest alert source. A separate healthcheck must watch the poller and scheduled agent runs, because a system that only reports failures cannot report a job that never started.

Rollback safety is the deciding constraint. Every alert should carry a release identifier, region, and workflow name. Keep the old version deployable until the observation window closes.

What should a small SaaS failure alert stack measure?

A checkout assistant can fail loudly, degrade gradually, or disappear. Those are different signals. A captured exception is the cleanest evidence of a crash. A metric is better for a rising failure ratio, a latency boundary, or an AI cost guardrail. A log line carries richer request context, but turning free-form text into a dependable threshold creates parsing and query maintenance at exactly the moment the team needs a boring rollback decision.

Use logs after the alert to reconstruct the request. Correlate them with trace_id and span_id where those fields exist, but do not mistake correlation fields for a distributed trace query or span tree. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, and session replay are separate capabilities. Choose a product that supplies them when the investigation requires them.

The silent case matters most. If the hourly catalog agent never runs, there may be no exception, log, or metric to query. Send a completion ping to an external dead-man switch such as Healthchecks.io. The alert poller itself needs the same treatment.

Use three operational contracts:

  1. A new exception group tied to the candidate release can stop rollout.
  2. Error ratio, latency, or cost crossing a predeclared limit can trigger rollback after enough samples exist.
  3. A missing heartbeat can page the owner, but should not automatically blame the latest release without corroboration.

The last distinction prevents a scheduler problem from causing a blind application rollback.

Put the rollback policy in code

The poller should query on a fixed cadence, convert provider responses into a small internal snapshot, evaluate one deterministic policy, and send a deduplicated notification. It records the last processed window so a retry does not deliver the same Slack alert twice. If delivery fails, retry with backoff and do not advance the checkpoint.

This runnable policy consumes an application-owned normalized snapshot; it makes no claim about a vendor response schema. It refuses incomplete data instead of quietly treating it as healthy.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    Release string `json:"release"`
    Region string `json:"region"`
    Requests int `json:"requests"`
    Errors int `json:"errors"`
    P95LatencyMS int `json:"p95_latency_ms"`
    CostUSD float64 `json:"cost_usd"`
    NewErrorGroups int `json:"new_error_groups"`
}

type Policy struct {
    MinRequests int
    MaxErrorRate float64
    MaxP95LatencyMS int
    MaxCostUSD float64
}

type Decision struct {
    Rollback bool `json:"rollback"`
    Reasons []string `json:"reasons"`
}

func evaluate(s Snapshot, p Policy) (Decision, error) {
    if s.Release == "" || s.Region == "" {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("release and region are required")
    }
    if s.Requests < 0 || s.Errors < 0 || s.Errors > s.Requests {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("invalid request counters")
    }
    d := Decision{}
    if s.NewErrorGroups > 0 {
        d.Rollback = true
        d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "new exception group")
    }
    if s.Requests >= p.MinRequests {
        rate := float64(s.Errors) / float64(s.Requests)
        if rate > p.MaxErrorRate {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "error-rate limit exceeded")
        }
        if s.P95LatencyMS > p.MaxP95LatencyMS {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "latency limit exceeded")
        }
        if s.CostUSD > p.MaxCostUSD {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "cost limit exceeded")
        }
    }
    return d, nil
}

func fetchErrorGroups() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("error groups: status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("error groups: rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    groups, err := fetchErrorGroups()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "fetched error groups for normalization")
    _ = groups

    var s Snapshot
    if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&s); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    p := Policy{100, 0.02, 2500, 12}
    d, err := evaluate(s, p)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(d); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Those numbers are illustrative policy values, not measurements or universal limits. Derive production limits from the checkout error budget and business guardrails. Keep the minimum sample condition: one failure in two requests says little, while a new crash signature may justify an immediate stop even at low volume.

Do not let the first poller iteration perform rollback directly. Write an immutable decision record and call a narrow deployment-control interface with a client-generated idempotency key covering release, region, window, and policy version. Replaying a window then repeats the same operation rather than creating a second rollback or page.

Choose the stack by the missing capability

Product names hide different operating models. Compare the path from signal to page and from page to rollback.

Option Best fit Operational trade-off
Sentry Exception-first triage where grouped errors drive response Add metrics and heartbeat monitoring when rollback also depends on latency, spend, or missing runs
Datadog Managed logs, metrics, traces, monitors, and notification integrations Control monitor scope, cardinality, and release tags or broad coverage produces ambiguous pages
Grafana Cloud Teams centered on Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana investigation Error grouping and application context require deliberate instrumentation or another error product
Amazon CloudWatch AWS-centered logs, metrics, alarms, and regional operations Log ingestion and query choices affect cost, so review pricing before logs become the alert substrate
Infrai One REST API and one key cover the integration; the API is self-describing, public discovery needs no key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples No native notifier, routing, escalation, synthetic check, or heartbeat monitor; the poller and dead-man switch are mandatory

Healthchecks.io complements these options by answering whether scheduled work checked in. PagerDuty can own routing and escalation when one Slack channel is no longer enough, but it does not improve the rollback signal.

For a small service, start with Sentry plus one metric backend if exception diagnostics are the daily need. Choose Datadog for managed cross-signal correlation, Grafana Cloud when Prometheus-compatible metrics are central, and CloudWatch when AWS-native operation matters more than a vendor-neutral query layer. The compact REST option fits when minimizing integration surface matters, provided owning the poller is an explicit on-call responsibility.

No winner covers every failure class. Pick the missing capability you cannot safely build.

Verify before allowing automatic rollback

Test with a canary release. Emit a known test exception tagged to the canary, feed a synthetic normalized snapshot to the policy, and verify that exactly one decision record and notification appear. Replay the window. Nothing new should be delivered.

Then provide a healthy snapshot above the minimum request count and confirm rollout continues. Provide too few requests and confirm the thresholds remain inconclusive rather than green. Stop the poller in a test environment and wait for the external heartbeat monitor to report the missing check-in. This verifies the detector's detector.

US and EU paths need separate region labels and checkpoints. Evaluate them independently so a healthy high-volume region cannot dilute a failing low-volume region. Send identifiers and decision reasons to Slack, not customer prompts, order details, or full log bodies.

A practical sequence is manual notification, manual rollback from a recorded decision, then automatic rollback for a small canary. Expand only after duplicate-delivery and stale-window tests pass.

Rollback runbook

When the gate fires, freeze promotion and preserve the candidate release identifier. Identify a new exception group, a threshold breach with enough samples, or a missing heartbeat. Confirm region and window freshness.

Rollback to the last known deployable version through the idempotent deployment-control operation. Keep collecting candidate and baseline signals during recovery; failure to restore the signal points toward a dependency, scheduler, or policy problem. Record the policy version, triggering window, reasons, and deployment result for the postmortem.

If notification fails, retry with exponential backoff and leave the checkpoint unchanged. If the query fails, report detector failure through its heartbeat path and make no health claim.

Unknown is not healthy.

References

  • Sentry Alerts: https://docs.sentry.io/product/alerts/
  • Datadog Monitors: https://docs.datadoghq.com/monitors/
  • Grafana Cloud Alerting: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/alerting-and-irm/alerting/
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/pricing/
  • Amazon CloudWatch alarms: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html
  • Healthchecks.io documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • PagerDuty incidents: https://support.pagerduty.com/main/docs/incidents

title: Distributed Cron Jobs
description:
Regular cron runs on one server. What happens when you have 10 servers? Each runs the job 10 times. That's a problem.

The Problem 

Single server cron: ✅ Job runs once at 2am
10-server fleet:    ❌ Job runs 10 times at 2am — duplicate emails, double charges!

Solutions

1. Dedicated Scheduler Node

  • One designated machine runs all cron jobs
  • ✅ Simple
  • ❌ Single point of failure — if this node dies, no cron jobs run

2. Leader Election + Cron

  • Cluster elects a leader (using etcd/ZooKeeper)
  • Only the leader runs cron jobs
  • If leader dies → new leader elected → cron resumes
  • ✅ No SPOF | ❌ Leader election complexity

3. Distributed Lock Before Job Execution 

def run_job():
    lock = redis.set("cron:daily-email", "locked", nx=True, ex=300)  # 5min TTL
    if not lock:
        return  # another node is running it
    try:
        send_daily_emails()
    finally:
        redis.delete("cron:daily-email")
  • ✅ Simple, works with existing Redis
  • ❌ Lock expiry must be > job duration, or use heartbeat extension

4. Dedicated Scheduling Services

  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler — cron without servers
  • Temporal.io — workflow orchestration with scheduling
  • Airflow — DAG-based job scheduling
  • Sidekiq-Cron (Ruby), Bull (Node.js)

Exactly-Once Execution

For critical jobs (billing, emails):

  1. Use idempotency keys in the job itself
  2. Record execution in DB before running: INSERT INTO job_runs (job_id, run_date) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING → if 0 rows inserted, skip
  3. Use a distributed lock with heartbeat

Observability for Cron

  • Alert if a job DIDN'T run (missed heartbeat)
  • Track job duration — sudden increase = something is wrong
  • Log job result (success/failure, records processed)
  • Tool: Healthchecks.io — cron monitoring via ping

title: Claude Code 2.1.302 Flips Two claude -p Defaults: Permission Mode and Fork Subagents
description:
• Book: AI Agents Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your nightly job calls claude -p with no --permission-mode. It ran fine on Thursday. After an upgrade, the same command can come back with its edits denied while the run itself carries on.

On October 16, Anthropic tagged Claude Code 2.1.302. Most of its 60-odd lines are fixes. Two of them change what a headless run does when your script doesn't say what it wants: the permission mode a claude -p or Agent SDK session starts in, and whether Claude can fork the conversation into subagents. If you run Claude Code in CI, on Amazon Bedrock or with telemetry off, read this before you bump the version.

The two lines that matter for scripts

Here they are, verbatim from the release notes:

Changed claude -p and Agent SDK sessions with no permission mode to start in default mode on third-party providers, with telemetry off or on a fresh install; --permission-mode auto keeps auto

Changed fork subagents (subagent_type: "fork") to be on by default in claude -p, the Agent SDK, the desktop app and VS Code, as they already are in the terminal; CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 turns them off, and claude mcp serve never offers them

The changelog tracker gradually.ai lists the same release on October 16 with the same two changes. Neither is flagged as breaking. But an unpinned script inherits whatever the default is, so both change what your job does.

Which mode your headless run starts in now

The permission modes page, as of October 18, still says a -p or Agent SDK session that doesn't fetch feature flags, "such as on a third-party provider or with telemetry off," starts in auto on v2.1.285 or later. In auto mode a classifier model reviews actions instead of you. Release 2.1.302 moves those sessions back to default, which the CLI calls Manual mode.

The third trigger in the note is a fresh install, and that one can reach CI on the Anthropic API too. The same permission-modes section notes that the first session after an install or upgrade can pick its starting mode before its feature flags arrive. A runner that installs Claude Code at the start of every job, with no saved config, can look like a fresh install every time.

Manual mode lets reads run without asking and prompts for most edits and shell commands. A -p run has nobody to answer that prompt. The headless docs are plain about it: "In a -p run with no host, these requests are denied either way."

So a job that leaned on the built-in default to edit files can come back with denials where it used to have a diff, whether it runs on a cloud provider (Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry), with telemetry off, or on a fresh runner. A job that lists every tool it needs with --allowedTools, or sets permissions.defaultMode in ~/.claude/settings.json or managed settings, keeps doing what it did. I haven't run 2.1.302 against Bedrock myself. This reading comes from the release note and the docs.

The fix is to stop relying on the default. Pick the mode in the command. For hands-off work with a classifier reviewing actions:

claude -p "Run the test suite and fix failures" \
  --permission-mode auto \
  --permission-prompts none

--permission-prompts none needs v2.1.259 or later, and it tells Claude not to retry a request nobody can approve. On Bedrock and the other cloud providers, auto mode only works with Sonnet 5 or later, Opus 4.7 or later, Haiku 5.5 and the Fable models. On any other model, the session starts in Manual anyway.

For locked-down CI, dontAsk denies anything that would prompt. Reads and read-only commands still run, plus whatever your --allowedTools entries allow:

claude -p "Apply the lint fixes" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm run lint *)"

To catch silent denials, read them from the stream. With stream-json, the final result message lists them in permission_denials. This pipes it through jq:

claude -p "Apply the lint fixes" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  | jq -c 'select(.type == "result")
           | .permission_denials'

Fork subagents are on in claude -p and the SDK

A fork, in the subagents docs, "is a subagent that inherits the entire conversation so far instead of starting fresh." It has the same system prompt, tools and model as the main session, and only its final result comes back. Because the prefix is identical, its first request reuses the parent's prompt cache, so the docs say a fork "costs less than a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context."

Until 2.1.302, that was an interactive-terminal default. As of October 18, the subagents page still says fork mode is off by default in -p and the Agent SDK. The release note is the newer word.

Fork mode changes more than forks. When it is on, the docs say Claude Code runs the subagents Claude spawns in the background, "forks and non-fork subagents alike," and removes the Agent tool's run_in_background parameter. Background subagents get a smaller built-in tool set than foreground ones, forks excepted. And a -p run stays open until background subagents finish, because their result is part of the final output. The same release also makes a subagent's own Agent calls run in the foreground by default in -p, the SDK, the desktop app and VS Code.

If a pipeline depends on custom subagents behaving as they did, turn fork mode off for that job:

export CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0
claude -p "Summarize the open TODOs" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk

To keep fork mode but stop Claude from spawning forks, the docs suggest denying the fork type with an Agent(fork) rule:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Agent(fork)"]
  }
}

The smaller lines worth knowing

The rest of the 2.1.302 notes are mostly fixes, but a few touch behaviour:

  • Prompt and agent hooks now run at most 12 of one event at a time; the rest wait their turn.
  • CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL picks the model for the client-side auto mode classifier. It doesn't change the server-side classifier.
  • The Read tool now refuses image sources over 128 MB, instead of loading any size into memory.
  • /config has an Idle compaction row to turn idle compaction off.
  • /design-sync and /design-login warn that standalone Claude Design closes. Anthropic's migration article puts it at December 14, 2026: design systems can be migrated, chats and comments are deleted after closure, and "public links to projects in the standalone version will no longer work."

Seeing the mode before an agent starts

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs Claude Code in a real terminal by default, as an interactive session, so the two -p defaults above don't apply there. The optional Agent view for Claude runs the Claude Agent SDK instead, so for those sessions the SDK defaults are the ones to check. In the ⌘N New task sheet (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux), shown below, the permission mode sits in a chip next to the agent and project, and a "Hermes will run" line shows the claude command before it starts.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: chips for Claude Code, the project, a new worktree, Accept edits, model and effort, and the "Hermes will run" preview of the claude command.

Hermes never answers a permission prompt for you. When an agent is blocked on one, the attention inbox counts it and ⌘I jumps to the agent that has waited longest. It's free, source-available under BSL 1.1, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. Download it here. Hermes is not affiliated with Anthropic.

Pin it, then upgrade

Before 2.1.302 reaches your runners, find the headless calls that never name a mode:

grep -rn "claude -p" .github/ scripts/ \
  | grep -v -- "--permission-mode"

That only catches one-line invocations. A command split across lines with \ needs a look by eye. Then add --permission-mode to each one, decide whether you want forks in that job, and set CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT to match.

Have you pinned the permission mode in your CI jobs, or were you riding the default? Tell me in the comments.

If this was useful

If you run coding agents unattended, I build Hermes IDE for the interactive side of the same work: one terminal per agent, one worktree per task.

Permission modes and forked subagents are two answers to the same old questions: how much autonomy an agent gets, and how one agent hands work to another. The AI Agents Pocket Guide covers those patterns, from tool-calling loops to multi-agent orchestration and guardrails, without tying them to one vendor's flags.

title: AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity
description:
AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity

The failure class, not just the identifier

CVE-2026-107282 is one entry in a batch of fixes published for AsyncHttpClient (AHC), the Java library that a large share of JVM services use to make outbound HTTP calls. The batch matters more than any single item because every entry in it has the same shape: the client decides who it is, or who it is talking to, from state that was computed for a different request. The result is a library that is diligent about authentication and still sends credentials to the wrong place.
The headline issue, affecting versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1, concerns cross-host request replay. When AHC re-issues a request against a different host, it updates the current request object but leaves the target request and the associated proxy context pointing at the original host. Path, Host header, Authorization credentials, or a cleartext body computed for host A can therefore be transmitted to host B.

Why that is a credential disclosure rather than a cosmetic bug

Consider a service that talks to an internal API and, after a redirect or a retry against a different endpoint, replays a request. The Authorization header was minted for the first host. The second host may be a third-party service, a different tenant's endpoint, or an attacker-controlled redirect target. Because the client decided the request was a replay, from its point of view nothing unusual happened; from the receiving end, a valid bearer token for an unrelated system just arrived in plaintext or in a header the receiver can read.
The same reasoning applies to the body. A replayed POST whose payload was assembled for the original destination can carry internal identifiers, query fragments or credentials to a host that was never meant to see them. In a microservice mesh where dozens of internal services trust bearer tokens issued by a shared issuer, a single misplaced header is enough to move laterally.
The practical lesson is about the object model, not about HTTP. Replay is inherently a copy operation, and every field of the copy has to be re-derived for the new destination. When one field is treated as immutable context, the copy is incomplete, and the incompleteness is invisible to any test that only checks whether the retry succeeded.

The rest of the batch

CVE-2026-107281 is arguably the more interesting sibling. The HTTP/1.1 connection pool key excludes the authenticated principal when connection-oriented NTLM or Negotiate authentication is in use, in versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1. A pooled connection that was established under one identity can therefore be handed to a different identity. Connection reuse is the entire point of a pool, and NTLM authenticates the connection rather than each request, so the substitution is not visible at the request layer. Any multi-tenant service that authenticates to a downstream system with NTLM through a shared client instance is exposed, and the failure is silent on both ends.
CVE-2026-107283, rated Low, is a cryptographic hygiene defect: Realm.Builder generates the HTTP Digest client nonce with ThreadLocalRandom rather than a cryptographically secure source, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. A predictable nonce weakens the replay protection that Digest was designed to provide, which makes an unrelated credential-exposure bug worse rather than better.
CVE-2026-107284, also Low, concerns WebSocketHandler.upgrade: a handshake whose Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or invalid is aborted, but the handler continues into pipeline installation. Failing to stop on a failed validation is exactly the pattern that turns a validation routine into a formality.
CVE-2026-107285, Medium at 5.9, involves proxy authentication on WebSocket requests tunnelled through CONNECT, where NettyRequestFactory.newNettyRequest and requestUri decide whether to attach proxy credentials, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. The details differ from the cross-host replay case, the reasoning does not: a decision about credentials is made from context that does not describe the request actually being sent.
A related defect in a different Java client shows how common the shape is. CVE-2026-107314 describes pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, in versions 42.7.11 through 42.7.13: when the requireAuth connection property excludes every authentication method the driver knows, for example by listing them all with negation, the driver enforces nothing and accepts any method the server offers. A configuration intended to restrict authentication produces no restriction at all. The score is 5.9 and the consequence is a downgrade to whatever the server proposes.

What to do

Upgrade. The AHC fixes are in 3.0.13 and 2.16.1 for the replay and pool-key issues, and in 3.0.12 and 2.16.1 for the proxy and WebSocket items, so the practical target is the newest build in the line you maintain. Because the library is a transitive dependency in most projects, the version that matters is the one resolved into the final artifact, not the one you typed.
Inventories should be resolved dependency trees, not dependency files. Ask the build for the effective version of org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client in every deployable, and rerun the query after a framework upgrade, because spring and cloud libraries routinely pin the version for you.
If NTLM or Negotiate authentication to a downstream system is in play, treat CVE-2026-107281 as the priority. It is the item that can cross an identity boundary inside your own infrastructure without any external redirect, and it will not appear in a request log that only records that a 200 was returned.
Review your own use of copies. Where your code builds a request for one destination and then reuses it for another, verify that the URI, Host header, credentials and body are all recomputed. The library fix closes the library's path; application-level copies have the same failure mode.
Rotate where exposure was possible. Any deployment that ran an affected version between the release of the fix and the upgrade may have delivered a credential to a host that should never have received it, and rotating is cheaper than reasoning about whether it did.

description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

LocalList is a lightweight, locally hosted web application that generates SEO-optimized product listings for platforms like Etsy and eBay.

It is designed for a very specific side hustle: small business owners, crafters, and vintage resellers who need polished, engaging product descriptions to drive sales, but cannot justify paying a monthly subscription for closed AI tools. LocalList solves the problem of recurring overhead by providing professional-grade AI copywriting entirely for free, running right on the seller's laptop.

Demo

UI Demo Link: LocalList on Streamlit Community Cloud

Code

badshahaditya57-sketch / Local-AI-Listing-Generator-for-Etsy-eBay

🛍️ LocalList: AI Listing Generator for Etsy & eBay

A lightweight, locally hosted web application that generates SEO-optimized, highly engaging product listings for e-commerce platforms like Etsy and eBay.

Built as a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 2: Side Hustle), this project demonstrates the power of open-weight models by providing small business owners with professional AI copywriting at zero recurring cost and with absolute data privacy.

✨ Features

  • Zero Subscription Costs: Runs entirely locally using open-weight models, eliminating the need for expensive API tokens.
  • 100% Data Privacy: Your unreleased product ideas, proprietary designs, and business data never leave your machine.
  • SEO-Optimized Output: Tailors descriptions specifically for Etsy or eBay search algorithms.
  • Clean UI: Powered by Streamlit for a fast, intuitive, and distraction-free workflow.

🛠️ Tech Stack

  • Frontend: Python, Streamlit
  • Local Inference: Ollama
  • LLM: Llama 3 (8B)
  • API Integration: Python requests module

🚀 Installation & Setup

Prerequisites

…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

I wanted the technical execution to be clean, fast, and accessible.

  • Frontend: I used Python and Streamlit to build a simple, intuitive web interface where sellers can input their product name, key features, and target platform.
  • Open-Source AI Core: The heavy lifting is done using Ollama running the open-weight Llama 3 model directly on my local machine.
  • Integration: The Streamlit app connects to the local Ollama API endpoint via HTTP requests. It takes the seller's inputs, wraps them in a highly optimized system prompt for e-commerce SEO, and streams the generated listing back to the UI.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For side hustlers, profit margins are razor-thin. Open innovation matters for this build because it fundamentally changes the unit economics of the tool.

If I built this on a closed, general-purpose API, I would have to pass those per-token costs onto the user, likely trapping them in a monthly subscription lock-in. By using an open-weight model running locally, the operational cost is literally zero.

Additionally, open innovation guarantees absolute data privacy. Crafters and designers often have unreleased products or proprietary crafting techniques. Because inference happens locally, their product ideas and drafts never leave their laptop, ensuring their data isn't secretly being used to train someone else's closed model.

My First User

I put this in front of a friend who sells upcycled vintage clothing on Etsy to get real-world validation.

  • What they said: They loved how fast and straightforward the interface was compared to prompting a generic chatbot.
  • Would they pay? They explicitly stated they despise monthly subscriptions for seller tools, but would gladly pay a one-time $15 fee to download a packaged desktop application version.
  • What they asked for next: Their immediate feature request was batch processing—the ability to upload a CSV of 20 unlisted items and have the local AI generate drafts for all of them while they step away to pack orders.

title: I Built a Company Brain on FalkorDB: Cited Answers, Real Expertise and Decisions That Stay Current
description:
TL;DR — For the WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB hackathon (Track 03: Company Brain) I built Hivemind, an agent that stores a company's documents, tickets, chats, meeting notes and GitHub activity as a FalkorDB knowledge graph. It answers questions like "Who should I ask about Kafka?" or "Why did we choose Postgres — and is that still true?" by walking the graph, cites every source, finds knowledge risks with graph algorithms, and generates sprint plans and PRDs from the same data. It runs in the cloud or fully offline with one Docker command.

💻 Code: github.com/Utkarsh2730/hivemind
🎬 Demo video: 3:30 walkthrough
📦 Run it offline: hivemind-offline.tar.gz — no accounts or API keys needed

The problem: the facts exist, the connections don't
Every company I've seen has the same knowledge problem. The information is written down — in Confluence pages, Jira tickets, Slack threads, meeting notes, pull requests — but the relationships between those pieces live only in people's heads:

A new engineer hits Kafka consumer lag. The runbook exists, the fix was discussed in Slack, someone was thanked for solving it last time — but which of the 40 people in the channel actually knows Kafka?
The team debates moving off Postgres. Didn't we decide this in March? Who decided? Was it later reversed?
The checkout launch is "blocked". By what? Who owns the blocker?
Sprint planning starts from a blank page every two weeks, even though every ticket, dependency and decision is already in the system.
Search returns documents. What people need are answers that follow relationships: person → wrote → runbook → about → Kafka; decision → made in → meeting → replaced by → newer decision; ticket → blocks → launch → assigned to → person.

That's a graph problem. So I built the product around a graph database instead of bolting a graph onto a vector store.

Why a graph (and why FalkorDB)
Vector search is great at "find text similar to my question". It is bad at questions whose answer is a path:

Question What it really needs
Who should I ask about Kafka? People connected to Kafka through evidence: what they authored, were assigned, were thanked for
Is the Postgres decision still current? Decision → SUPERSEDES chain → the latest active decision
Why is checkout blocked, and who can unblock it? Project ← mentioned by ← ticket ← BLOCKS ← ticket → assigned to → person
What happens if Tomas goes on leave? How many knowledge paths run through Tomas (betweenness centrality)
FalkorDB gave me everything I needed in one engine: openCypher for multi-hop traversals, full-text indexes for finding entry points, built-in graph algorithms (betweenness, PageRank, connected components), multiple isolated graphs per database (perfect for multi-tenancy), and a read-only query mode I could hand to an AI agent safely. It also runs anywhere — FalkorDB Cloud, Docker, or embedded on a laptop.

The rule I set myself, which is also the hackathon's rule: if the product still works without FalkorDB, the graph isn't doing real work. In Hivemind, every answer, ranking, decision trail, risk report and plan is a graph traversal.

What Hivemind does
The demo company is Lumen Pay, a fictional fintech: 12 people, 4 teams, 6 projects, 11 systems, and 27 documents, tickets, chat messages and meeting notes containing 7 decisions.

Ask with sources. "Who should I ask about Kafka consumer lag?" → Tomas Silva, because he wrote the consumer runbook and library and owns the Kafka upgrade — cited DOC-3, PLAT-21, MSG-2, MSG-3. Priya Nair formally owns the Event Bus, and Hivemind shows that too: knowing and owning are different edges.
Decision history. "What changed about customer login?" → the original Auth0 decision (now outdated) and the move to Keycloak (current), with the reasons and the meeting, RFC and message that recorded it.
Knowledge risks. Graph algorithms surface key connectors, systems only one person understands, stalled tickets and knowledge nobody is linked to.
Sprint plans and PRDs. Pick a project; Hivemind follows its tickets, BLOCKS chains, decisions and experts, schedules blockers first, suggests owners, and cites every line.
Stays current. Post "We're moving the ledger from Postgres to CockroachDB" and the old Postgres decision is marked outdated; the next ledger sprint plan already includes the migration.
Any company, any data. Create a private workspace, paste or upload documents, import a GitHub repo, or connect Slack, Jira, Linear and GitHub webhooks.

The graph model
Everything hangs off a few node types and a handful of relationships:

(Person)-[:MEMBER_OF]->(Team)-[:OWNS]->(Project)<-[:LEADS]-(Person)
(Project)-[:USES]->(System)
(Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(Person|Project|System|Team)
(Source)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(Person)
(Source)-[:BLOCKS|REFERENCES]->(Source)
(Person)-[:MADE]->(Decision)-[:DECIDED_IN]->(Source)
(Decision)-[:AFFECTS]->(Project|System)
(Decision)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(Decision)
A Source is any piece of knowledge — a doc, a ticket, a chat message, meeting notes, a GitHub issue or PR. When something new arrives, Hivemind links it to the people, projects and systems it mentions (names, aliases, @handles, ~100 well-known technologies, and AI extraction when a Claude key is configured), detects whether it records a decision, and connects it.

Deep dive 1: expertise from evidence, not the org chart
The question "who knows X?" is where a graph shines. Instead of trusting a owner field, Hivemind collects evidence paths and weights them:

// wrote about it (weight 3)
MATCH (p:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(s:Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k RETURN p.key AS person, s.key AS ev

// was assigned work on it (weight 2)
MATCH (s:Source)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(p:Person) MATCH (s)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k RETURN p.key AS person, s.key AS ev

// was named or thanked by a colleague in that context (weight 2)
MATCH (a:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(s:Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(p:Person), (s)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k AND a <> p RETURN p.key AS person, s.key AS ev

// made decisions about it (weight 2)
MATCH (p:Person)-[:MADE]->(d:Decision)-[:AFFECTS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k RETURN p.key AS person, d.key AS ev


Each piece of evidence counts once, scores are summed, and the top people are returned with their evidence keys — so the answer can cite exactly why Tomas ranks first. Formal owners come from a separate LEADS query and are shown alongside, because the gap between the two is often the most useful insight.

Deep dive 2: decisions that stay current
Decisions are first-class nodes. Each one points to where it was made and what it affects:

MATCH (p:Person)-[:MADE]->(:Decision {key: $k}) RETURN p.name, p.role
MATCH (:Decision {key: $k})-[:DECIDED_IN]->(s) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[:AUTHORED]->(s)
RETURN s.key, s.title, a.name
MATCH (n)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(:Decision {key: $k}) RETURN n.key, n.title

When new content records a decision, Hivemind looks for active decisions touching the same systems (and the same project, when both name one) and marks them replaced:

MATCH (d:Decision {status: 'active'})-[:AFFECTS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $affects RETURN d.key, d.title, collect(e.key)

MATCH (n:Decision {key: $new}), (o:Decision {key: $old})
SET o.status = 'superseded' MERGE (n)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(o)
The hard part wasn't the query — it was false positives. My first decision detector treated "PR approved, thanks!" and "we'll look into it" as decisions. I narrowed it to phrases that actually record a choice ("we decided", "we're moving", "going with", "switching to"…), added tests for the phrases that must not trigger it, and made every change reversible: removing a decision (or the message that created it) restores whatever it had superseded. A knowledge base people can't correct is one they stop trusting.

Deep dive 3: retrieval, and the bug my eval caught
Graph traversal needs good entry points. FalkorDB's full-text indexes provide them:

CALL db.idx.fulltext.createNodeIndex('Source', 'text', 'title')
CALL db.idx.fulltext.queryNodes('Source', $term) YIELD node, score
I built a small accuracy check — 10 questions about the demo company, each requiring specific facts and specific citations. It scored 9/10. The failure was "What do we know about the Stripe retry storm incident?": the most relevant ticket, which matched every word of the question, wasn't in the top results.

Two causes. First, my result formatting re-sorted sources by date, throwing away relevance. Second, a single OR-style query (Stripe|retry|storm|incident) didn't reward documents matching more of the terms. The fix: query each term separately, then rank by how many terms a node matched, and by summed score as a tie-breaker. The eval went to 10/10 and has stayed there. Small evals are cheap, and they find real bugs.

Deep dive 4: knowledge risks with graph algorithms
This is the feature only a graph can do. FalkorDB ships algorithms as procedures:

// key connectors: people on the most paths between knowledge
CALL algo.betweenness({
nodeLabels: ['Person','Source','Project','System','Decision'],
relationshipTypes: ['AUTHORED','MENTIONS','LEADS','USES','MADE','AFFECTS','DECIDED_IN','ASSIGNED_TO']})
YIELD node, score WHERE node:Person
RETURN node.name, score ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5

// central topics: what most work depends on
CALL algo.pageRank(null, null) YIELD node, score
WHERE node:Project OR node:System RETURN node.name, score ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5

// unconnected knowledge: items outside the main component
CALL algo.WCC({nodeLabels: ['Person','Team','Project','System','Source','Decision']})
YIELD node, componentId RETURN componentId, collect(node.key), count(node)
Combined with the expertise query (a system where one person holds almost all the evidence) and a Cypher check for tickets that are blocked, long in progress, or blocking others, "Where are our biggest knowledge risks?" returns things like: Tomas, Maya and Lena are key connectors; only Noor has hands-on evidence on Auth0 and Keycloak; PAY-52 is blocking the checkout launch.

Deep dive 5: sprint plans from BLOCKS chains
Planning is a traversal too. For a project, Hivemind gathers the tickets that mention it, plus anything that blocks them even if it belongs to another team:

MATCH (b:Source)-[:BLOCKS]->(s:Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(:Project {key: $k})
OPTIONAL MATCH (b)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(a)
RETURN b.key, b.title, b.status, a.name, s.key AS blocks
Priorities fall out of the graph: work that blocks other work is P0 and goes first, blocked work is P0 right after it, in-progress work is P1, the rest P2. Owners come from assignees, or — if a ticket is unassigned — from the person with the most hands-on evidence for the systems it mentions. Recent technical decisions with no ticket yet become rollout items. That's why, after the CockroachDB message, the ledger's sprint plan includes "Plan and roll out: Move the ledger from Postgres to CockroachDB" without anyone writing a ticket.

The agent: tools over a graph, with or without an LLM
The agent gets a small, specific toolset instead of raw database access:

search_knowledge — full-text entry points
entity_profile — everything about a person, project or system
who_knows — the expertise ranking above
decision_trail — decisions, sources and supersession
company_insights — the graph algorithms
run_cypher — read-only escape hatch
Every agent query runs through FalkorDB's read-only mode (GRAPH.RO_QUERY) and write keywords are rejected, so a model can never modify the graph. With an Anthropic API key, Claude plans the tool calls and writes the answer; without one, a rule-based planner calls the same tools — that mode answers all 10 eval questions correctly, which is what makes the fully offline build useful. The UI streams each tool call as it happens and highlights the subgraph the answer used, so you can see how it got there.

Multi-tenant by design: one graph per company
Any company can register a private workspace. Each one is a separate FalkorDB graph (cb_), so data never mixes; a registry graph stores only SHA-256 hashes of access keys. From there, knowledge flows in from paste and upload, a GitHub import (issues, PRs and comments become tickets, docs and messages; contributors become people), a Slack app (signature-verified events, a /hivemind slash command, history import or an export zip), and Jira/Linear/GitHub webhooks. Decisions can be announced back to Slack, Teams, Discord or Google Chat, and an MCP server lets Claude Desktop or Cursor query the brain directly.

Shipping it offline (and proving it works)
I wanted judges — and companies that can't send data to the cloud — to run Hivemind with no internet and no accounts. That meant three things:

No runtime CDN calls. Fonts, the graph library and images are bundled; I verified both pages render with every external host blocked.
One-command self-hosting. docker compose up -d starts FalkorDB (with a persistent volume) and the app.
An air-gapped bundle. A script saves both Docker images and an installer into one 204 MB archive.

I didn't have Docker on my laptop, so I let GitHub Actions prove it instead. On every push and release, CI runs the unit tests and the accuracy check against a real FalkorDB server, starts the Docker stack, builds the offline bundle, deletes the images, reinstalls the bundle from scratch exactly as a judge would, and runs a smoke test: landing page, bundled assets, demo data, a cited answer, the graph-algorithm insights, a sprint plan and creating a workspace. Only then is the bundle attached to the release.

Testing
21 automated tests: workspace isolation, access keys, people de-duplication ("Arjun", "arjun", "Arjun R." and "Arjun Rao" are one person), decision detection and reversal, deletion, cited answers, sprint ordering, PRD structure, the graph algorithms, the full API including streamed answers, Slack signature verification and slash commands, Jira/Linear/GitHub/generic webhooks, and the notification host allowlist.
Accuracy check: 10/10 demo questions with the required facts and citations.
Scale: 400 items import in under a second; above 450 nodes the graph view shows an overview and loads only the subgraph behind each answer.
Real data: importing FalkorDB/falkordb-py produced 61 items from 18 contributors, an expertise ranking and a sprint plan from open issues.
What I learned
Model the evidence, not the conclusion. Storing "Tomas is the Kafka expert" would go stale. Storing what Tomas wrote, fixed and was thanked for lets the graph recompute the conclusion every time.
Make the graph correctable. Decision detection will sometimes be wrong. Undo, and restoring what was superseded, mattered more than a smarter regex.
Show the path. Highlighting the exact subgraph and citing every claim did more for trust than any wording in the answer.
Graph algorithms answer questions people don't know to ask. Nobody types "compute betweenness centrality", but everyone wants to know who the single point of failure is.
Write the eval early. Ten questions caught a ranking bug I would never have noticed by clicking around.
Let CI test what you can't. The offline Docker path was tested end to end on GitHub's runners before any judge touched it.
What's next
SSO and roles instead of private links, encrypted connection secrets, Confluence and Notion connectors, local embeddings for semantic linking without internet, and one-click "Add to Slack" distribution.

Try it
Watch: the 3:30 demo
Run offline: download hivemind-offline.tar.gz, then tar -xzf hivemind-offline.tar.gz && cd bundle && ./install.sh and open http://localhost:8000
From source: git clone https://github.com/Utkarsh2730/hivemind.git && cd hivemind && docker compose up -d
Read the code: github.com/Utkarsh2730/hivemind — the README lists every Cypher query the product depends on.
Built for the WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB hackathon, Track 03 — Company Brain. Lumen Pay and everyone in it are fictional. In line with the hackathon rules: I built Hivemind with an AI coding assistant, Anthropic's Claude (via Claude Code), which helped debug code, tests, UI and documentation; I chose the problem, directed the product and design decisions, and reviewed and tested the result.

Thanks to FalkorDB and WeMakeDevs for the hackathon. If you build something on a knowledge graph, I'd love to see it — find me on GitHub at @Utkarsh2730.

title: Sports Score Feeds: Realtime API Boundaries Under Serverless Connection Limits
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API surface that fits serverless connection limits, and make reconnect, expiry, authorization, and duplicate delivery explicit parts of the sports score feed rather than accidental behavior.

The feed is a small distributed system, even when the payload is only a score change. A browser or mobile client holds a connection for as long as it can; a serverless function, by contrast, is designed to start, do bounded work, and disappear. Treating those two lifetimes as interchangeable is how a match-winning goal turns into a stale screen.

What is the bill and the boundary in a live score feed?

The visible spend is rarely the whole cost. A useful workload model has four terms: connection lifetime, fan-out publishes, recovery traffic, and the engineering needed to reconcile state. Connection lifetime is the first boundary to measure because a serverless runtime may not be the right place to keep thousands of sockets open. The publish path should therefore be short-lived and stateless, while a dedicated realtime service owns connection management.

For a sports feed, the dominant business event is not “the client received bytes.” It is “the client can prove which score revision it has.” Attach a stable event identifier and a monotonic feed revision to each event in your domain model. On reconnect, the client sends the last revision it has acknowledged; the recovery path can then replay or refresh state without guessing whether a duplicate is new.

That choice changes downstream spend. You may retain fewer transient delivery records because the durable ledger is the score snapshot plus an audit trail of revisions, not an infinite socket transcript. The catch is that deleting delivery history removes a convenient forensic trail: when a broadcaster disputes a late update, you need the audit record and request identifier to explain what was published and when.

Infrai is one candidate for this short-lived boundary. Infrai has one key and one bill through a plain REST API, letting any runtime call the realtime publish operations without installing or versioning an SDK while leaving the connection fleet with a service designed to own it.

Keep these signals separate. Authentication answers who may connect, subscription state answers which channel they joined, and business events answer what happened in the game. Mixing them makes a token expiry look like a score correction and makes incident review unnecessarily expensive.

How should serverless connection limits shape API boundaries?

The boundary should be a command interface for short work: publish one event or publish a bounded batch, then return. In the verified realtime surface, those operations are POST /v1/realtime/publish and POST /v1/realtime/publish/batch. A serverless handler can validate the event, attach its stable identifier, call the publish operation, and exit; it does not need to poll or own a long-lived client socket.

This is where a plain REST API can be a practical fit. Infrai exposes backend capabilities through HTTP, so a Go service can use the standard library and keep its existing deployment model; there is no SDK lifecycle to coordinate with a short-lived function. The same request boundary also lets an operations team observe request IDs, latency, vendor metadata, and cost alongside the application trace, which is useful when a feed is busiest and the reconciliation queue is growing.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the stateless publish boundary when your team values one HTTP integration and wants authentication, delivery telemetry, and business-event accounting kept in the same operational vocabulary. It is not a reason to move connection ownership into a function, and it does not remove the need for a client-side recovery protocol.

Here is a deliberately schema-neutral Go caller. The payload is supplied by the application, so the example does not pretend to know fields that belong to your score domain.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := os.Getenv("INFRAI_PAYLOAD")
    if key == "" || payload == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_PAYLOAD are required")
    }
    // Equivalent probe shape for discovery tooling: curl -X POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish -d '{}'

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "score-feed-"+os.Getenv("FEED_EVENT_ID"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: %s", body)) }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("publish rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

Measure first.

Which realtime option fits a sports score feed?

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on who owns the socket, how much recovery state you retain, and whether your existing platform already supplies identity and fan-out.

Option Where it fits Trade-off to verify
Infrai realtime API Stateless HTTP publish from serverless handlers; one key and one REST surface can simplify a mixed backend You still design connection lifecycle, replay, and client trust; validate the exact limits for your regions
Ably A managed pub/sub product for teams that want connection and presence concerns in a specialist service Adds another platform boundary and its own channel, identity, and retention model
Pusher Channels A focused hosted channel service with familiar client integrations The application must map its authorization and recovery semantics onto the provider's channel model
AWS AppSync Useful when the feed already lives in an AWS GraphQL and identity stack GraphQL schema and resolver operations become part of the operational surface, which may be more machinery than a small publish command

Those descriptions are starting points, not benchmarks. Your mileage may vary with regional latency, burst size, and the number of subscribers per match; I am not sure which provider will produce the lowest effective bill without your event rate and retention policy. Compare the complete operating bill, including connection capacity, replay storage, observability, and the staff time spent maintaining adapters.

What does recovery look like when delivery is duplicated?

Assume reconnects, expiry, and partial failures are normal states. A client can receive an event, lose its acknowledgement, and receive the same event again. The consumer must treat the stable event identifier as an idempotency key, persist the highest verified revision, and make applying an older revision a no-op.

Authorization deserves the same precision. Issue a token scoped to the competition, match, or channel the client is allowed to read; do not infer trust from the fact that a socket was once authenticated. On expiry, refresh credentials and resubscribe deliberately. If authorization changes during a match, the client should stop rendering private updates before it attempts recovery.

Testing should exercise realistic latency, duplicate delivery, and rejected authorization, not only the happy path. A useful test records the sequence of revisions seen by the client, injects a reconnect between two publishes, and verifies that the final score and audit trail are identical whether the second event arrives once or twice. Test partial batch acceptance as a first-class result if your publish contract allows it; a caller that assumes an all-or-nothing outcome can silently drop one game in a multi-match update.

The short version is boring by design: stable identifiers, observable boundaries, and an explicit replay decision. Boring systems reconcile cleanly.

No polling.

Where should you choose a specialist instead?

Choose Ably or Pusher when the main problem is operating a large connection fleet and you prefer a specialist's client, presence, and channel tooling. Choose AppSync when GraphQL authorization, schema evolution, and AWS-native operations are already non-negotiable. Stick with a direct provider integration when your compliance team requires a narrowly scoped data path or when an existing contract gives you the recovery semantics you need.

Infrai is a poor fit when your organization cannot accept a general REST integration boundary, needs a provider-specific feature outside the published realtime surface, or requires connection behavior that your serverless platform cannot observe. Cost is one dimension of the decision, not the decision itself; model the retained score snapshots, recovery reads, and on-call effort before comparing invoices.

For any option, document the invariant that matters most: after a reconnect, a client can reconcile to the authoritative score without trusting delivery order. That invariant is more durable than a vendor label or a per-call price.

If this boundary fits your system, verify the request contract in the realtime publish documentation before wiring it into a serverless handler.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/realtime
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://ably.com/docs
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appsync/

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/realtime
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: DeepSeek V4 Pro now runs updated weights on AI Gateway
description:
DeepSeek V4 Pro now runs on updated weights on AI Gateway. They are used by default when you call deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, so existing requests pick them up with no change to the model ID or your code.

To use the updated DeepSeek V4 Pro, set model to deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-0813 in the AI SDK. AI Gateway will route to providers with the new weights:

To run V4 Pro in a coding agent, use vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup to connect your agents to AI Gateway, then select deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-0813 in the agent's model configuration. See the coding agents guide.

title: Integrating OpenAI Function Calling with Meta WhatsApp Cloud API
description:
Traditional chatbot flows rely on static decision trees (Press 1 for Sales, Press 2 for Support). While predictable, they create severe user friction when a prospect wants a personalized answer or needs to check order status, book an appointment, or check flight updates.

By integrating OpenAI's Function Calling (Tools API) directly into your WhatsApp Cloud API webhook, your AI agent can converse naturally while executing backend API calls deterministically.

In this architecture guide, we demonstrate how to connect an LLM tool loop with WhatsApp interactive messaging.

The Function Calling Execution Loop

When a user messages on WhatsApp:

  1. Ingest Inbound Message: Webhook receives the message payload from Meta.
  2. Query Model with Tool Declarations: Pass the user's message along with defined tool schemas (e.g., check_order_status, book_demo_slot).
  3. Model Tool Decision: If the user intends to perform an action, the LLM emits a tool_calls payload instead of raw text.
  4. Execute Internal Business Logic: Run the database lookup or CRM update with the LLM's structured arguments.
  5. Synthesize Final Natural Response: Pass the tool output back to the LLM to format a friendly WhatsApp response.
  6. Dispatch WhatsApp Message: Send the formatted text or interactive button back via WhatsApp Cloud API.

Step 1: Defining the Tool Schema

Declare your functions using JSON schema:

const tools = [
  {
    type: "function",
    function: {
      name: "check_order_status",
      description: "Lookup the real-time shipping status and tracking code for an order",
      parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          order_id: {
            type: "string",
            description: "The 6 to 8 character order tracking ID, e.g. ORD-1092"
          }
        },
        required: ["order_id"]
      }
    }
  }
];

Step 2: The Agentic Execution Function 

import OpenAI from "openai";
const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function handleWhatsAppAgentQuery(customerPhone, userMessage) {
  const messages = [
    { role: "system", content: "You are the helpful customer service assistant for our store on WhatsApp. Keep responses concise, warm, and mobile-friendly." },
    { role: "user", content: userMessage }
  ];

  const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
    model: "gpt-4o-mini",
    messages: messages,
    tools: tools,
    tool_choice: "auto"
  });

  const responseMessage = response.choices[0].message;

  // Check if model decided to call a function
  if (responseMessage.tool_calls) {
    for (const toolCall of responseMessage.tool_calls) {
      if (toolCall.function.name === "check_order_status") {
        const args = JSON.parse(toolCall.function.arguments);

        // Execute real DB query
        const orderData = await queryOrderDatabase(args.order_id);

        messages.push(responseMessage);
        messages.push({
          role: "tool",
          tool_call_id: toolCall.id,
          content: JSON.stringify(orderData)
        });

        // Get final answer from LLM
        const secondResponse = await openai.chat.completions.create({
          model: "gpt-4o-mini",
          messages: messages
        });

        return secondResponse.choices[0].message.content;
      }
    }
  }

  return responseMessage.content;
}

Step 3: Guardrails and Human Agent Handoff

Even the best LLMs can misunderstand complex edge cases. In production:

  • Set strict confidence thresholds: If the user expresses frustration or asks to "talk to human", trigger an immediate handoff flag.
  • Lock session context: Store the conversation history in Redis or PostgreSQL keyed by the user's phone number with a 24-hour expiration window.

Turnkey AI Agents with AI Soul

Rather than maintaining custom OpenAI token budgets, rate limit queues, vector embeddings, and WebSocket handoffs yourself, platforms like AI Soul offer an enterprise-ready solution.

With AI Soul's WhatsApp AI Chatbot, you can train autonomous LLM agents directly on your website URL, product catalogs, and PDFs with zero code. Furthermore, AI Soul's built-in Conversational CRM provides visual Kanban deal pipelines and multi-agent shared team inboxes so your human team can intervene whenever needed.

Summary

OpenAI Function Calling transforms WhatsApp bots from simple FAQ repeaters into autonomous digital employees capable of booking appointments, qualifying B2B prospects, and recovering lost sales.
